Country of Publication: India. Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
The Śrī Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra, together with the commentary composed by Rāmeśvara:
He whose lotus-hand holds a blazing axe, adorned with a mass of matted locks...
May the descendant of Bhṛgu, with a serene soul, grant long life.
First Section: The Ritual of Initiation (Dīkṣā-vidhi).
Regarding the "Vṛtti" section: here, by the word *vṛtti*, one should understand the commentary titled *Saubhāgyodaya* upon this root text.

For knowledge regarding the author of this commentary, its title, the time of its composition, and other such details, the subject matter may be seen in the first section of the second appendix [below].
Herein is the benediction.
I salute the elephant-faced Lord, whose chest is reddened by the cosmetic paste smeared from the breasts of Śrī Vallabhā, and whose splendor is like that of ten million rising suns.
I contemplate this supreme Mother, who is the radiance within the Supreme Śiva, closely united with the state of full I-consciousness,
yet who subsequently assumes the state of duality.

Those powers, who exist as the five *pretas* and are the guardians of the abode of Supreme Śiva— namely desire, intellect, action, and the rest— who are my own rays and have become the protectors of the world's manifestation and its destroyers;
she who, in the form of *paśyantī* and the others, manifests the entire web of words for all living beings.
May this goddess of speech, who destroys the impurity of the mind, sport within my mouth.

I bow to Nāthendra, who shines with the illustrious Yaśovantī on his left side, who is the thunderbolt for the mountain of ignorance, and whose abode is fashioned within the lotus of my heart by the Creator.
I bow to that lord of heroes, the sixth glorious incarnation of Viṣṇu, who, having been born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, destroyed the kṣatriyas twenty-one times over.
I bow to the Subrahmaṇya, my father, and to my guru and mother;
for the attainment of the fruit [of my work], they alone are my refuge.
Having deliberated upon various tantras and the extensive treatises on Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya,
and having thoroughly refined them using manuscripts brought from various regions;
In accordance with his understanding, he expands upon the hidden meaning of the *Kalpasūtra* composed by Jāmadagnya for the sake of attaining perfection in the worship of Śrīvidyā.
Rāmeśvara, born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, was impelled by the venerable Lalitā.
The Section on Initiation (Dīkṣā): Here, indeed, the venerable Lord Paraśurāma, out of compassion for those of dull intellect in this modern age,
[has summarized] the countless [teachings] composed by Śiva— [from which it is understood that this work contains the essence of all tantric scriptures].

"The Lord Śiva is the agent"— this [point] is to be seen in the third section of the second supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*). Having thoroughly examined and synthesized all the tantras, he makes this formal declaration, demonstrating the short path (*laghumārga*) which is the means for accomplishing the fourth human goal (*puruṣārtha*):
Now, therefore, the Blessed Śrī Jāmadagnya Rāma begins this section from here—

the method of meditating upon Him, the account of the previous birth of His father, the great seer Śrī Jamadagni, and so forth— [to be seen in the second supplement, section 2]. [From here onwards, up to the preceding verse 33, concerning initiation (*dīkṣā*)...]

Everything that needs to be known regarding the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) up to the end of the Sūtra-bhāṣya should be understood; however, it should be known that the commencement of the practical application (*prayoga*) of initiation begins from the thirty-fourth sūtra. We shall now explain [it]. || 1 ||
Now, the word *atha* indicates auspiciousness:
"In ancient times, these two—the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—emerged from Brahman after piercing his throat; therefore, both are auspicious."

This is because of such traditional authority (*smaraṇa*). Furthermore, the word *ataḥ* indicates immediate succession (*ānantarya*). When there is a requirement for a limit (*avadhi*) to that succession, either the performance of an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) or the purification of various systems (*nānātantrapariśodhana*), being proximate, is connected as the limit. Alternatively, the two words *atha* and *ataḥ* taken together indicate the commencement [of a work], as in the case of "Now, therefore, [the exposition of] the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*athāto darśapūrṇamāsau*).

"We shall explain"—in this commentary on the Āpastamba Sūtra, the words "atha" (now) and "ataḥ" (hence) are generally employed by the elders at the commencement of a section (*prakaraṇa*). In some instances, they are also used to indicate immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), as in: "These Bhṛgus have been explained; now, therefore, [the section] on the Aṅgirases," and so forth. Likewise, not...

Furthermore, here the meaning of "immediate" (*ānantarya*) is [so called] because no other preceding immediate factor is perceived; this is according to the text. The author of the Sūtras will analyze the category of *dīkṣā* later on. And the category of "exegesis" (*vyākhyā*) is the detailed explanation of a word whose intended meaning is hidden. In the present context, [this refers to] hidden meanings.
The definition is thus fulfilled: a *kalpasūtra* is that which provides a detailed exposition by synthesizing the various *tantras*.
"I am the one who employs words conducive to the knowledge concerning initiation" (p.
This is the established meaning.

We shall explain [it]—the use of the plural number is intended to include other teachers who promote the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*), just as in common worldly usage, when one says "we shall perform a heavy task," others are also included. By this...

It has been indicated that the explanation of the *dīkṣā* is extremely difficult. Alternatively, its meaning is this: when both two and one are intended to be expressed by the word *asmad*, the plural form of *asmad* shall be used;
and thus, since the word *asmad* denoting the agent ends in the plural, for the sake of establishing grammatical agreement (*sāmānavacanatva*) with it—
"We shall explain" is the plural form.
Refutation of the Doubt Regarding the Invalidity of the Tantras:

Now, it may be argued that the exposition of the *Kalpasūtras* by those who follow the Veda is improper, because they are included among the *Tantras*, and since the *Tantras* are rooted solely in greed, they lack authority. As it has been stated in the *Vārttika*:
The Bhaṭṭapādas state:
"And here, many other causes such as greed are perceived;
when these are present and observed, there is no inference of any other [underlying] cause."
And the Śākyas and others, while everywhere performing the teaching of the Dharma,
never perform it as being free from the net of causes.
Nor do they assert that [the Purāṇas] are rooted in the Veda like those of Gautama and others;
rather, reasons are stated which stand far removed from dharma.
And these are precisely those who do not offer even verbal worship;
for they are indeed heretics, though established in ritual action, and mere rationalists.
Thus, those other [systems] which have not been accepted by the knowers of the three Vedas (*trayīvid*),
which have fallen under the shadow of some mixed garb,
and which are intent upon the purposes of winning over the world, gain, honor, and fame— [are likewise to be rejected].

These are compositions based on views contrary to the three Vedas, disconnected from reason, and rooted in greed and other [faults] perceived through direct perception, inference, analogy, presumptive testimony, and logic; they are the foundations for dharma and adharma as accepted by the texts of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and Śākya [Buddhist] schools.
[These practices], which are capable of neutralizing poison, subjugating others, driving them away, or causing madness,

and which are based on the power of witnessing occasional supernatural successes, are merely scented by the faint fragrance of a few meanings consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti— such as non-violence, truthful speech, self-restraint, charity, and compassion.
Those teachings which primarily concern livelihoods and other such matters, and which are based on the practice of eating mixed with the customs of barbarians—
it is precisely these that are established here as being unworthy of reliance, by means of both scriptural contradiction and the observation of their underlying causes.
And so it is stated in the second chapter of the *Brahmagītā* within the *Śrīsūtasamhitā*:
"One who abandons this Vedic path and resorts to another path is like one who discards the milk-rice held in his own hand and licks his own elbow."
If liberation for living beings were possible through a path other than the Veda,
then they would perceive jars and such objects even in total darkness without the aid of light.
"Therefore, the matter proclaimed by the Veda is indeed true, truly declared by me;
for a matter known through any other means is not true from the perspective of ultimate reality. Thus [it is said].
"In each of those cases, they propound arguments according to their own strength;
it is my conviction that all such disputations are contrary to the Śruti and the Smṛti."
In the forty-first chapter of the Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa:
"What is the use of saying more here? Without that which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti, one who performs even the slightest act whatsoever shall become a sinner; of this there is no doubt."
Thus, the censure of non-Vedic paths is heard. Also, in the Agni Purāṇa, in the dialogue between the mass of the Vedas and the denizens of hell:
"Those who have received initiation into the Tantras with minds corrupted by greed..."
"Having abandoned the Vedic path, we are being consumed by him. Thus [it is said].
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Puṣkara-māhātmya*:
"And those in the world who are heretics, tantrikas, and atheists—
for them this sacred ford is difficult to attain..."
Thus, by this censure of the Tantric person, the untrustworthiness of the Tantra is made clear. Likewise, since such censures of Tantra are frequently encountered in many other Purāṇas as well,
it is quite evident that the scripture which prescribes the worship of the *pañcaka* (the five) has greed as its sole foundation.

It has been established that the scripture concerning the acquisition and retention of the residence of the Visarjanīya has greed as its sole root. What, then, is the contradiction in the fact that a servant of the group of five (pañcaka) has greed as its root? Therefore, if it is argued that this scripture should not be explained by those who accept the authority of the Vedas (āstikas)—do not say so; for [the meaning of the scripture is the acceptance of the authority of the Tantric scriptures].
Do the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda accept the Purāṇas, such as the Padma-purāṇa and others, as authoritative sources, or not?
If they are accepted as authoritative, then in them the authority of the Tantras is frequently heard regarding specific qualified practitioners (*adhikāri-viśeṣa*). For instance, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
In the second chapter of the *Brahmagītā*:
"Nevertheless, an object seen in a dream by one dwelling in heaven indeed becomes an indicator for the attainment of true objects in the waking state."
In the same way, even those who have strayed from the path will undoubtedly achieve the attainment of the goal proclaimed by the Veda.

Therefore, in due investigation, paths other than the Veda are certainly not to be abandoned. (By this much it is established that resorting to paths of dharma other than the Veda is not unscriptural, just as resorting to the Veda itself is not.)
In the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, within the *Śivamāhātmyakhaṇḍa*, the fifth chapter states:
"The worship of the Supreme Śakti is proclaimed to be of two kinds."
Through the division of external and internal, the external is considered to be of two kinds.
O best of the twice-born, there are two [paths], the Vedic and the Tantric;
however, that Tantric one belongs only to the Tantric practitioner and not to anyone else, while the Vedic belongs indeed to the Vedic practitioner.
"Thus, O Brahmins, the worship of all the gods is established. So it is said.
Thus, in the Muktikhaṇḍa of the Sūtasaṃhitā—
[by this it is shown that] the Pāñcarātra and other Tantras [have their root in the Veda, and from them the Vaidikas...]
Thus, it is established that both the statement regarding the acceptance of portions not contradicted by the Vedas and [the acceptance of] what was uttered by Paraśiva are [valid].
For those who hold the Vedas as their foundation are authoritative;
indeed, they are not independent, and therefore, when examined, they are not rooted in delusion.
"Nevertheless, that portion of the paths which is not contradicted by the Veda is said to be authoritative for certain qualified aspirants. Thus,
O Goddess, I am attainable by the Tantrikas through an intermediary."
"And: 'I am attainable without mediation by those who are solely devoted to the Vedas. Thus it is said.
Thus, in that very same Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa, in the nineteenth chapter:
"The Dharma taught in the Śaiva Āgamas was previously declared to be twofold:
one arising from the downward stream (adhaḥsrotas) and the other arising from the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas)."
O twice-born ones, arising from the dharma of downward-flowing currents, that which arises from upward-flowing currents is superior;
it is divided into many types according to the classifications of the Kāmika and other tantras.
"The dharma arising from the downward flow is thus divided in many ways;
the Smārta dharmas are greater than the dharma arising from the upward flow.
Thus it is stated in that same twenty-second chapter.
Therefore, O best of Veda-knowers, the authority of other paths exists only regarding liberation from this [world] and not here; their validity applies only through this sequential process.
Therefore, Mahādeva, abiding on the path of Vedānta, bestows liberation without delay; however, He who is situated elsewhere does so only gradually.
"It bestows supreme liberation—such is the eternal Vedic revelation. Thus [it is said].
In that very same [text] (p. 6):
"Therefore, a mortal established in the Veda should not resort to another path."
Therefore, there is no doubt that the paths are authoritative according to the distinction of those qualified [to follow them].
In that very same [chapter], when one [section] has been completed, the verses therein are as follows:
"Regarding the essential nature of the Lord, likewise regarding the cause of bondage,
regarding the cause of the world, and likewise regarding liberation, knowledge, and so forth."
Those wise ones who discern the portions of the various paths that are inconsistent with Vedānta [do so] for the sake of those of dull intellect whose minds are shrouded by great delusion.

They have proceeded not according to the actual facts, but merely in accordance with their own desires—just as a man, having pointed out a blade of grass, seized a cow that was running away. [Note: In this context, it should be observed how much the Tantric scriptures rely upon the established tenets of the Vedas.]
Having first displayed such trivial objects of desire, Maheśvara subsequently bestows supreme knowledge in accordance with their ripening.
"Therefore, since these paths and this [system of] valid cognition have been taught by Śiva according to the path he himself described,
how could Śiva be a speaker of falsehood?"
Likewise, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The scriptures declare that this knowledge must be guarded like one's own mother or brother."

Thus is the presentation of the scriptures as authoritative sources. Likewise, it should be understood that herein the instruction for performing rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) according to the Tantric method, as well as the attainment of their fruits through that method, have been described.
In the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*, within the section on the greatness of *pradoṣa*, the worship of *pradoṣa* is presented according to the Tantric method.

The instruction given to the Brahmin and the prince, and the attainment of the fruit by him—thus the historical account (itihāsa) is clearly understood. In the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, within the hymn of Gajendra, there is the phrase: "To the great ocean of the tradition of the Śarva-āgamas.
Śrīdhara Svāmin explains that "āgamas" refers to the *tantras* such as the *Pāñcarātra*. Likewise...
"In the hymn of praise to Brahmā, this form is likewise described as worthy of worship by those seeking the highest good, whether they follow the Vedic or Tantric traditions, O bull among men."
Likewise, in the eleventh skandha, in the instruction on the feeding of camels (*karabhojana*), in the procedure for the worship of the door, and in the worship of Kali,
there are these words: "O King, those who desire to know the Supreme worship by means of both the Vedas and the Tantras."
"Listen likewise to how it is even in the Age of Strife (kali-yuga) through the ritual procedures of various tantras. Thus [it is said].
"By means of the prescriptions of various tantras"—this indicates that in the Kali age, the path of the tantras (*tantramārga*) is predominant;
such is the explanation of Śrīdharasvāmī. Likewise, it is stated in the Eleventh Book (*ekādaśaskandha*), in the instruction to Uddhava (p.
"Vedic, Tantric, and mixed—thus my sacrifice is threefold. (Bhagavad Gītā 4.7).

Thus, worship has been taught by the Blessed Lord as being of two kinds, distinguished as Vedic and Tantric. By this much it is established that the Tantric worship of the Blessed Lord is also approved; this is perceived by all.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata*, within the *Arjunastuti*:
"Salutations to You, who are to be known through the Vedas and Agamas, and whose intellect is pure."
Thousands of such statements establishing the authority of the Tantras are found;
they are not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length. Likewise, there are statements in the venerable Mahābhārata that establish the authority of the path of Yoga.

These [principles] are heard repeatedly in the *Bhagavadgītā*, the *Mokṣadharma*, and other texts; likewise, they are found at every step in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, and all the Purāṇas. This being so, how could the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda declare the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Tantric systems to be invalid? Or rather, he would not.
It cannot be said that the Purāṇas lack authority,
for the Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras are indeed these fourteen branches of knowledge.

Thus, because of the comprehensive enumeration of the sciences (*vidyā*), and because even in the Veda— where it says "the *Atharvāṅgirasas*, the Brāhmaṇas, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas"— the Purāṇa is included among the authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*), [it follows that] by this [the authority of] the Tantric scriptures,
the Brāhmaṇas, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras is established as being rooted in the Veda.
[The authority is indeed perceived]. Thus, by these aforementioned collections of statements and other such [evidences],
once the authority of the Tantras is established, it cannot be rendered invalid even by Brahmā himself.
Refutation of the Doubt that All Tantras are Outside the Veda:

Now, it may be argued that while the authority of the Tantras may apply to specific qualified persons—such as men who have fallen away from the Vedas, women, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes—it does not apply to the Vedic community; nor does the Tantra apply to anyone outside the Vedic fold.

It cannot be said that there is an absence of authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) restricting the scope of eligibility (adhikāra), because it has been previously stated in the Sūta-saṃhitā that [the practice] "is for the Tantrika alone and not for anyone else; for the Vedic [practice] is for the Vaidika. Likewise, in the Muktikhaṇḍa of the very same Sūta-saṃhitā:
"But for those living beings who have completely fallen away from the Vedic path, the paths such as the Pāñcarātra are beneficial by virtue of time alone. Thus [it is said].
In that very *Sūtagītā*:
"For those humans who have strayed from the path of the Vedas,
Śambhu— the omniscient Lord of all and the Guru of gurus— has declared the Tantra."
For those devoted to the path of the Vedas, there is nothing at all beneficial there; everything spoken here is entirely true and complete.

Thus, because of the statement regarding other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it is argued that therefore even the *pramāṇas* are *tantras* only for one who has strayed from the Vedic path, and not for a follower of the Vedas—[we reply:

No; as for the statement from the *Sūtagītā*, "and that which has fallen from the path of the Vedas," the word *tantra* therein refers to a specific *tantra*. That *tantra* is well known in the South as the *Śaivāgama*, and it is practiced by those known colloquially as *jaṅgamas*. If it is asked how this very [statement] serves as a proof:

There is an indicative proof in the very vicinity of the previously mentioned statement: "The sign (liṅga), which destroys all suffering, is declared in all tantras to belong to those who have fallen from the path of the Vedas; it should be worn therein."
Therefore, those who are devoted to the path of the Vedas should never hold that [view]. Thus [it is said].

In this regard, it is established by the Śaiva Āgamas that wearing the *liṅga* is a means for attaining manifold fruits. Furthermore, the practice is observed among those who follow that tradition, wherein they wear the *liṅga* on the right arm or around the neck. And as in this statement, [it applies] to those who have fallen from the path of the Vedas regarding all the Tantras.

The word "iti" implies that the answer has been set forth. And thus, the fact that the wearing of the *liṅga* is taught in a particular Tantra is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the statement that "that Tantra [is intended] for those who have fallen away from the Veda. Just as the term "animal" (*paśu*) is restricted by the indicative power of the mantra "of the goat, of the omentum, of the fat," so it is here. Furthermore:
In the glorious *Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa*, the inquiry of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa:

"O King of kings, [tell me of] that easy means to liberation for women and Śūdras, which bestows liberation upon the castes such as Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and upon those in the various stages of life (*āśramas*)."
"Speak that which benefits the world to my brother, who is your devotee. Thus [he said].
Following that, beginning with "Śrī Rāma said," one should indeed perform the worship of the ten enclosures (daśāvaraṇa-pūjā) as prescribed in the Āgamas;
the expert in Tantra should diligently perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed rite.
"By means of the path taught in the Āgamas—and by the *kuṇḍa*—the one most skilled in the Āgamas [is established]," so it is said. [In some places, it reads "by the path spoken by Agastya."]

Thus, when the question is raised as to the means for liberation regarding the castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and the stages of life such as the student (brahmacarya), the answer— that worship as prescribed in the Āgamas must be performed— is a conclusion that has no other recourse; this, which establishes Tantric practice even within the Vedic fold, should be accepted by one who desires to know the truth and is free from envy.

It is impossible to abandon [this interpretation]. For when asked, "Is Caitra skilled?", no authoritative person would say, "Maitra is skilled. Therefore, the reference to Śrī Rāma follows the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others;
for in the world, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who is not a follower of the Vedas is not well-known, nor indeed is there such a thing as a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya [who is not so].
Or, one who has fallen due to a great sin such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and has strayed from the Vedic path—
since in that case both Brahminhood and the state of having slipped from the Vedic path exist, it must be said that he alone is qualified for what is taught in the Tantras;
this is stated in the section on the worship procedure which serves as the answer to the question regarding the auspicious [lineage] of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth.
Having attained the status of the twice-born according to the method prescribed by one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*,
a human being should first perform the morning bath for the purification of the body.
By means of the mantras proclaimed in the Vedic tantras, according to the procedure for smearing with clay.

Thus, by means of this *dvandva* compound, it is ordained that for a single person alone, both Vedic mantras and Tantric mantras constitute the means of performing the ritual bath. Accordingly, by accepting that this is an injunction for the general practice of Tantra directed toward those outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*), the authority of the words of Śrī Rāma is maintained.
This is indeed impossible even for the teachers of the gods (the Vedas). Thus, in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, in the Eleventh Canto, within the instructions to Uddhava, it is said:
"By both the Veda and the Tantra, [I am attained] for the sake of the perfection of both."
In the conclusion of that very [work], it is said:
"Thus, by means of the paths of ritual action belonging to both the Vedic and Tantric traditions,
a person worshipping me on both sides attains from me his desired perfection."

Therefore, the statement "those who have fallen from the path of the Śruti" refers to those who wear the *jaṅgama* and other [Śaiva] emblems. Likewise, in the previously mentioned statement from the *Muktikhaṇḍa*, "the paths such as the Pāñcarātra," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) does not include the Śaiva Āgamas accepted by the *jaṅgamas*.

Because it has been established that works such as the *Jñānārṇava*, the *Kalpasūtra*, and others concern those who have fallen away from the Vedas, they form a single coherent whole with that [text]. Furthermore, in the *Śivamāhātmyakhaṇḍa*, beginning with the words "But the worship of the Supreme Śakti...
and so forth...
O best of the twice-born, it is both Vedic and Tantric;
however, that which is Tantric belongs only to the Tantrika and not to anyone else, while the Vedic belongs only to the Vaidika.
The meaning of this statement is as follows: the Vedic initiate is one consecrated by the sacraments such as the *upanayana* prescribed in his own *gṛhya-sūtra*;

the Tantric initiate is one consecrated by initiation (*dīkṣā*) preceded by the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth, as set forth in the Tantras. One who is called "Tantric" is not someone who has fallen away from the path of the Vedas, for such a person has already been refuted previously. And thus, by this statement—

Occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as Vedic bathing and worship are prescribed on the occasion of the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*) and similar events. On the occasion of Tantric initiation (*tantra-dīkṣā*), occasional rites such as Tantric bathing and worship are ordained. Where there is only one occasion, there is only one [rite]:
purely Vedic for those such as Śūdras, and purely Tantric for others. Where both [occasions] apply, there is the performance of both.
Nothing whatsoever contradicts this; and by this much alone, the instruction for the three castes regarding both Vedic and Tantric rites is established (see *Dvi-pariśiṣṭa*, 2, Vi0, p.
2). The meaning of this very point has been clarified in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"By those of the three castes, after the conclusion of the Vedic rites, all Tantric rites are performed. Thus it is said.

Śrī Rāma also stated this very same point in brief: "By means of mantras proclaimed in the Vedas and Tantras. Therefore, the conclusion that the practice of all Tantras is ultimately outside the Veda is merely a manifestation of delusion resulting from not consulting other scriptural statements. As for the Pāñcarātra and similar systems...

The activity [of initiation] proceeds solely with reference to that which has entered the path of hearing; for it is performed by directly addressing him by name. The same applies to the Kāpālika as well—(p.
O lords of sages, there is no qualification for those who follow the Vedas in the Pāñcarātra, nor in the Kāpāla, nor even in the Kālamukha; it is simply not so, it is not so.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*, the intention of the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda is indeed established regarding this very point. For this reason alone, among the tantras, the name of the *Pāñcarātra* is mentioned separately; it is not that all tantras are included therein, especially those that are contrary to the Vedas.

Furthermore, because practices contrary to the Smṛtis are found there in abundance; for not even the slightest performance of rites contrary to the Vedas is observed in the Śākta and other Tantras, as is the case with the followers of Śākya and others.
As for those statements beginning with "having abandoned this path of the Veda," they refer to the Vaidika [who has strayed].

For it is heard [in scripture] that one who completely abandons the Vedic path and resorts solely to the Tantric path is censured by such words as "except for... (*vinā*). Alternatively, having previously disparaged the Vedic path, [it is said]: "Therefore, the matter taught in the Vedas is indeed true, truly true."

Regarding the doubt: there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in assuming a single injunction—that the path of the Veda must be followed—by combining all the specific arthavādas in the form of censure and praise. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a conjunction of the Tantric rite with the censure; therefore, by the praise "therefore [the path] declared in the Veda," there is an injunction for the Vedic rite.

If one were to assume [it applies to all], there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). The previously cited statement from the *Agni Purāṇa* and the *Padma Purāṇa* refer specifically to particular Tantras, according to the reasoning stated above. For this very reason, even the venerable Vidyāraṇya Svāmin has stated in that same work that statements in the Tantras such as "one initiated into the Tantras" and so forth—which appear to be condemnatory—are actually intended to praise the Vedic path.

This has been explained. In this very same manner, the wise should infer other subjects regarding Yoga, even though its authority has been refuted by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda; however, because it is not relevant to the present topic and for fear of excessive length, it is not written here.
Compared to the statements of Bhaṭṭapāda, the authority of the Purāṇas and the Tantras is superior.

Therefore, it is indeed proper that a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) should be restricted in accordance with a stronger one; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between these two—namely, the Smṛti stating, "A Brāhmaṇa should observe celibacy for forty-eight years," and the Śruti stating, "One who has fathered a son and whose hair is still black should establish the sacred fires. In this manner:

Indeed, it is not well known that a man who has fathered a son and possesses black hair is eligible for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) after forty-eight years. Therefore, when there is a conflict between these two, one must follow the more authoritative *śruti*; consequently, the term "Brāhmaṇa" found in the *smṛti* refers to those who are blind and so forth.

Otherwise, the very treatise composed by those same [authors], which establishes that there is no contradiction with the Śruti because such a person lacks eligibility for the primary Vedic rites (*śrautakarman*),
would be contradicted. Therefore, those who follow the Vedas have eligibility for the rituals propounded in the Tantras of the Śāktas, Gāṇeśas, and so forth.

It has been established by the preceding arguments that this is indeed the intention of the Bhaṭṭapādas. By this, those who stubbornly deny that Vaidikas have no authority regarding Tantric rites are cast far away. By this same reasoning, the refutation of the authority of the Tantras written by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita should also be understood as overturned by the wise.

The systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of even the statements of the *Purāṇas* has already been stated. As for what was said—that the scripture enjoining the acceptance of the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) has a solely perceptible purpose and was composed on the basis of greed—that is equally applicable to such Vedic passages as "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma" and "Wine-cups are taken. For indeed, [it is not the case that these lack a transcendental purpose].

Even Brahmā would be unable to establish the status of validity by casting aside the conviction that "this is a means of valid cognition. Therefore, for the followers of the Veda, the very specific conviction that "the Veda is a means of valid cognition because it arose through the force of prior impressions" (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) is the primary factor that establishes its validity. And from that, [it follows that...]

Only those [teachings] that are not in contradiction with it possess authority because they are rooted in it; however, that which contradicts it is simply non-authoritative, even if it is Vedic. Furthermore—as for the Śrīsundarī Tantras: p. 11) just as...

The six *sūtras* of Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, and others, which constitute the supplements to the Taittirīya branch, are authoritative; likewise, by this much [it is established that] the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*, the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, and so forth, as well as the *Sundarī-tāpinī*, the *Pañca-bhāvanā*, and the *Kaulopaniṣad*.
In the phrase "only the means of valid knowledge" (pramāṇānyeva), this is what is implied.

The *Sundarītāpinī*, the *Pañcakabhāvanā*, and the *Kaulopaniṣat* are the remaining [texts], which are of the nature of commentaries on that [work] and are not fabricated by one's own imagination. Therefore, because they are of the nature of commentaries on the Vedas, they may be accepted without hesitation by those who follow the Vedas (*vaidika*).
These are to be accepted. We shall explain later how the practice of the five makāras and so forth is not contrary to the Vedas.
The *Sundarī-vidyā* is the domain of those whose minds are pure;

even though it is acceptable to the Vedists, not all Vedists have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this. Just as, although the nature of Brahman is propounded in the Veda in the form of the Upaniṣadic portions, there is no [universal] qualification for the inquiry into it [for everyone].

While there is eligibility for all, eligibility here belongs only to those Vaidikas who are endowed with the fourfold qualifications; thus, only certain individuals have eligibility. For instance, for a Brāhmaṇa, the first stage begins from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and consists of the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*).
Thereafter, having heard the censure of one ignorant of the meaning— "This Sthāṇu was indeed a mere bearer of burdens"—
and the fruit of knowing the meaning— "He who knows the meaning enjoys all prosperity," he studied poetry,
grammar, etymology, and logic in order to achieve mastery over the knowledge of meaning.

Having studied the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* and understood the meaning of the Vedas, one should not consider one's purpose fulfilled through mere knowledge alone; for, having heard the censure in the Smṛtis against one who knows the meaning but does not perform the rites, he ascends to the stage of performance and undertakes the ritual action prescribed by all the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

When, having practiced through many births, one's mind is purified by those actions, and one becomes neither excessively attached nor excessively detached to *saṃsāra*, then one becomes fit for ascending to the stage of devotion (*bhakti*). As it is said in the *Bhāgavata*:
"Neither dispassionate nor attached—devotion-yoga (bhakti-yoga) grants him perfection. Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that when one is neither despondent nor attached, then the yoga of devotion bestows perfection.
Without ascending to such a stage of devotion, the attainment of the supreme human goal is never possible.
As it is said in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata:
"Devotion to the Blessed One that is signless is more powerful than spiritual accomplishment;
it quickly consumes the sheath, just as fire consumes what has been swallowed. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the nature of devotion (*bhakti*):

the Naiyāyikas maintain that devotion is a specific, non-artificial, and natural form of knowledge characterized by the mode of "being worthy of worship. Others hold that devotion is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) assuming the form of the Blessed Lord as its object.
The modification consists of transformation. Regarding this, the proof is as follows:
"May that joy which belongs to the undiscriminating toward sense objects—[the joy] of me who remembers you—not depart from my heart."
Thus, in response to Prahlāda’s request for love directed toward the Blessed One, the Śrī Bhagavān spoke these words:
"Devotion to me already exists within you; it shall become even greater than this."
(As stated on p. 12:

"May there be the attainment of devotion," [and] by means of the granting of a boon, [he prayed], "May I have memory [of this]. [From here, regarding the study of the meaningful Veda—both in terms of devotion and reverence—there exists a collection of authoritative proofs. Thus, it is simply a supplication for devotion.
It is understood that giving a cloth to one who asks for a jar is not appropriate.
Therefore, the ancient authorities maintain that devotion (*bhakti*) is the continuous remembrance of the Blessed One; it is also designated as "unconditioned love" (*nirupādhikī prīti*).

"And unswerving devotion to Me through the yoga of exclusive concentration"—this statement of the Blessed Lord as well refers to the uninterrupted remembrance of the Blessed Lord. And this is appropriate, because this very meaning has been stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam. For instance:
"That which is the natural functioning of the single-minded state within the *sattva* of those gods who possess the marks of virtue and whose actions are based on sacred revelation—
that indeed is devotion to the Blessed One (*bhāgavatī bhakti*). Thus it is said.

The meaning is this: those by which the *guṇas*—the objects—are characterized or known are the senses; the deities who preside over these senses possess a state of being (*vṛtti*) directed toward Hara alone, who is the embodiment of *sattva*.

That state which is without cause, free from desire, natural, and accomplished without effort is called devotion (*bhakti*). *Ānuśrava* refers to the Veda; the ritual action proclaimed therein is *ānuśravika* karma.
The word "yeṣām" (of whom) is an epithet for the gods. By this, it is indicated that the means for devotion is scriptural action (*ānuśravika-karma*).

Therefore, it is established that devotion (*bhakti*) is simply a mental state (*manovṛtti*) having the form of the Blessed Lord. Thus: "Now, therefore, the desire to know devotion; it is supreme attachment to the Lord"—this is the *Śāṇḍilya-sūtra*.
Regarding the fact that worship is a means to devotion:

one who desires to ascend to such a stage of devotion should perform the worship of the Lord, which serves as its means. Worship, it should be noted, is the selfless renunciation of all things for the sake of the Lord.
Listening to the discourse of the Blessed One, chanting the mantras of the Blessed One,
and proclaiming the hymns of praise to the names of the Blessed One— any one of these [is a cause of devotion]. Regarding its being a cause of devotion,
it is stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata:
Furthermore, I shall declare the supreme cause of devotion to Me:
constant faith in My nectar-like stories, perpetual chanting of My names,
steadfastness in worship, and the praising of Me with hymns of praise.
Devotion in service, saluting with all one's limbs,
the renunciation of wealth, enjoyments, and pleasures for my sake;
whatever sacrifice, gift, oblation, recitation, or vow has been performed for my sake— [all this is offered].
"O Uddhava, for those humans who thus offer themselves through these dharmas, devotion to me arises; what other goal remains for them? Thus [it is said].
Precisely because devotion (*bhakti*) is the means for *upāsanā*, Śrī Bhāskararāya states in the *Setubandha*: "Devotion is twofold:

secondary (*gauṇī*) and primary (*mukhyā*). Among these, the former consists of meditation, worship, recitation, chanting of names, and so forth, pertaining to the Saguna Brahman, and it admits of being combined [with other practices]. But supreme devotion (*parabhakti*)..."

13) It has been stated that these are of the nature of a specific attachment (*anurāga*) produced by this [devotion]. Such devotion is possible only toward the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahman*). This Brahman with attributes, in accordance with the attachment of its own worshiper, [acts accordingly].

He assumes various forms such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others; it is precisely the means for devotion to each of those specific forms that are expounded in the Tantras and Purāṇas. The Vedic texts that serve as their source, known as Upaniṣads, are also found in the form of the *Nṛsiṃhatāpinī*, the *Rāmatāpinī*, and so forth.
Regarding Sundarī, there are the Tripuropaniṣad, the Bhāvanopaniṣad, and others.
When a verbal certainty regarding the Supreme Brahman taught therein has arisen, at that time there is neither excessive attachment to saṃsāra nor excessive detachment from it. And he—

One who possesses such qualification is entitled to the practice of devotion (*bhakti-sādhana-upāsti*). Furthermore, the attainment of such qualification and the desire to ascend the stages of devotion (*bhakti-bhūmikā*) are not obtainable through meager merit, but are gained only through the virtuous deeds accumulated over many millions of births. Even among those, the devotion to Sundarī is far more remote than that.
As it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"For one who has not uttered the names of other deities for ten million births,
faith arises only in the utterance of the name of the Śrī Devī."
"In such a way that one may become a worshiper of Śrīvidyā in one's final birth. Thus [it is said].
In another place as well:
"Only by one who is in their final birth, or by Śaṅkara himself,
is this glorious fifteen-syllable Vidyā obtained."

"Śrīvidyā alone is the singular cause of liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. (In this regard, the Vedic scripture, "Through knowledge one attains immortality," should also be cited. Thus it is said.
The Śruti also says:

"Those who have not heard [the Vedas] and those who have heard them; those who perform sacrifices and those who do not—going to the heavenly world, they do not look back, for they know Indra and Agni. Like grains of sand, they come together, impelled by the rays."
From this world and from yonder world, the seers with their speckled [vessels] have bestowed [it].
Thus it is stated in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.

The qualification for the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*) is to be known solely by one's own internal organ (*svāntaḥkaraṇa*); likewise, the qualification for the stage of such devotion (*bhakti-bhūmikā*) is to be known solely by one's own internal organ, and not by others.
It is not perceptible, nor can it be inferred through a particular state or a particular age, because their deviation is observed;

for we see that even in childhood, Prahlāda, Dhruva, and others attained such a stage. In some cases, there is an inference based on a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); even that is a valid cognition (*pramā*).
It may perhaps be so; as for example, in the *Āgastya-saṃhitā*, in the words of a Brahmin addressed to Virūpākṣa when inquiring about his daughter:
"O daughter, O treasure-house of merit, by virtue of the accumulations of merit from previous lives..."
"O lady of excellent vows, though you have only been established for three years on this most difficult stage of devotion,
receive from me the seed-syllable of Gaurī, which is the seed of the universe."
(As stated on p. 14:
"Because the knowledge of the location of the maiden arises through inference alone. Furthermore, in the *Manthānabhairavatantra*, there is an injunction that inference must be performed:
"Having considered the suitability [of the disciple] for one, two, three, four, or five years,
as well as their devotion and qualities, according to the order of the castes and mixed castes,
one who is single-minded should subsequently impart the Vidyā according to the sequence already described. Thus it is said.

Nevertheless, since an inference may sometimes lead to a deceptive course of action, one who engages in the undertaking of initiation (*dīkṣā*) should proceed only after having properly investigated his own qualification (*adhikāra*). Otherwise,
if one who lacks qualification were to engage in it, then the result would be the same as that which occurs when a Śūdra undertakes the study of the Vedas.

That same consequence would apply to this case as well, since the fact of being performed by one lacking the requisite qualification (*anadhikārin*) is equal. Therefore, having reflected within one's own mind regarding the qualification (*adhikāra*), only he who is fit to ascend to the aforementioned stage is truly a *brāhmaṇa*. [In this regard: "Indeed, women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—even they attain the supreme goal; how much more so the meritorious *brāhmaṇas*?"

"Likewise, there are devoted royal sages"—thus the meaning of the Gītā also follows [from verses 9.31–32]. Whether a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, one of mixed birth, a woman, or whoever else it may be, anyone in this world who is not despondent, who is not attached, and whose senses are conquered—that person alone is qualified; it is established that one who has fallen outside the path of the Vedas is not qualified.

Therefore, the *Kalpasūtra* must be explained by those who follow the Veda; for this very reason, it was revealed to the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda by the Supreme Deity in a dream within a *tantra* text that follows the *Prapañca* [tradition].
It has been taught that he must certainly be examined by those versed in the Tantras;

furthermore, the composition of the treatise named *Sāra* is also highly appropriate. And just as the Śivas composed the Tantras out of compassion for those who had strayed from the path of the Vedas, so too did the venerable Bhagavatpāda [compose this work] out of compassion for them.

It cannot be said that this is a "creation" (nirmita), nor should it be stated that this is not a means of proof (sādhaka). The venerable teacher’s partiality lies solely toward the Vedic path, and not toward anything else; for were it otherwise, he might have composed treatises following the teachings of the Buddha and others as well. Furthermore, in his own work on mental worship (*mānasapūjā*):
Reciting those mantras from the three Vedas with joy and great reverence, I perform this ritual bath for you; O Mother, accept it out of love.

Thus, by the mention of the combination (*samuccaya*) of the Tantric and Vedic [traditions] in this verse, it is very clear that the intended meaning is that being Tantric and being Vedic are not contradictory. Therefore, this Kalpasūtra should be explained by the followers of the Vedas (*vaidika*).
Dispelling the Doubt Regarding the Prohibition of Tantric Practice in the Kali Age:

Now, it may be argued that while Brahmins may indeed have the qualification for Tantra, they do not have it in the Kali Age. This was stated in the *Brāhma Purāṇa* during the enumeration of things to be avoided in the Kali Age:
The initiation into mantras and so forth for all [classes], the carrying of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
the departure on the Great Journey (mahāprasthāna), and the immolation of cows in the Gosava sacrifice.

Since it is heard that these [practices] are to be avoided in the Kali Yuga, all the preceding statements are to be reconciled as referring to the Kṛta and other ages; for a prohibition does not function except by presupposing a prior possibility of occurrence.

It should not be argued that, since the two [prohibitions] would be of equal force once they are established by the preceding statements, there might simply be an option (vikalpa) based on the principle of the final quarter of the tenth book (*daśamika-caramapāda-nyāya*)—namely, "one does not perform those two for the animal sacrifice.
For an option would exist only if there were a prohibition; however, this is not a prohibition. Rather, it is the rule: "In the *yajati* offerings, one says 'ye yajāmahe'..."

If it is argued that, just as in the case of the statement "one does not [perform] at the *anuyāja* offerings," the injunction "the wise man should undergo initiation" (*dīkṣāṃ kurvīta matimān*) and the injunction "in the Kali age,

mantra-initiation (*mantradīkṣā*) should not be performed" form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), and thus— by means of a partial exclusion (*paryudāsa*)— it follows that initiation is to be performed in any era other than Kali, thereby leaving no room for an option (*vikalpa*), then this is not so.
In the Brāhma [Purāṇa], the statement "and the initiation into the mantra for all" is not found in the many manuscripts;
therefore, such a reading as found in the small manuscripts is indeed unauthoritative. Even if there were an insistence that it is authoritative, nevertheless—in the Laiṅga [Purāṇa]:

"The worship of Śambhu in the Kali age is performed by means of this very extent of ritual network; even for Brahmins and others, the tantric rites are taught and remembered for the Kali age as well, and solely through the Āgama, and not otherwise. Thus it is said.
The statement that in the Kali Yuga worship must be performed solely through the *tantra* method has already been cited previously:
"In the Kali Yuga, O Great Goddess, [the goddess] is well-worshipped by Brāhmaṇas and others [through the tantra]."

Thus, since it is found in the *Rahasyārṇava* and many other tantras such as the *Rudrayāmala* that [these practices] are to be performed in the Kali age, the statement in the *Brāhma Purāṇa*— in accordance with the use of the plural number— establishes that they must be performed in the Kali age by one who is exceedingly vigilant and has conquered the senses and so forth. Therefore:

At the conclusion of Brahmā’s speech, it was not stated that "these should not be performed in the Kali age"; rather, it was said that these were suspended at the beginning of the Kali age by great-souled beings for the sake of protecting the world. Thus, the fruit of their suspension is stated to be the benefit of the world. And the benefit is as follows: whoever has conquered his senses [should know] these duties...

If one were to engage in action by casting the burden onto the scripture, thinking "these must necessarily be performed," then another person, blinded by passion, might likewise engage in action placing passion at the forefront and surely fall; therefore, renunciation is for the sake of favoring such a person.
It is not intended as a prohibition, like the rule "one must not eat on the eleventh day. Śrī Śiva [expresses] this very point:
In the tantras, it has been revealed in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
"Equal to the vow of walking on the edge of a sword, it is the cause for the restraint of the mind;
for one of steady mind, it is easily attained, fruitful, and bestows swift accomplishment."
O Supreme Goddess, for anyone else, it would be fruitless and a cause of suffering. Thus [it is said].
In the Tripurārṇava it is also said: "On this side is wine, on that side meat, and likewise various kinds of foods;
there are young women, richly adorned with beautiful attire, their eyes reddened with intoxication."

"In that regard, O Goddess, the state of having a restrained mind is indeed exceedingly difficult to achieve in every respect; how could this be possible for one devoid of devotion and faith? Thus it is said.

Therefore, even in the Kali age, there is no obstacle whatsoever to initiation for those whose senses are restrained. [By this much, it is implied that only one of stable mind is qualified for the rites taught in the Tantras.]
16) Regarding initiation being the first step:
is it not improper [to say] "we shall explain initiation," when it is that very thing whose explanation was previously promised?

If it is argued that this would contradict the context because many other practices—such as the worship of Gaṇeśa and Śrīvidyā, which are distinct from initiation (*dīkṣā*)—are discussed here as subjects to be explained; we reply:

in this case, the meaning [of the term *dīkṣā*] is, by way of its non-abandoning of its own primary sense (*ajahatsvārthavṛtti*), merely the ritual action that serves as a means for devotion to Śrī Lalitā. Here...

The utterance of the word "dīkṣā" is for the purpose of making known that initiation is the beginning of everything. By this it is intended that worship must not be performed by one who is uninitiated. For this very reason, the *Paramānanda Tantra* states:
"Initiation shall be the first step of the mansion of liberation."

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra*— specifically regarding the statement "We shall explain the sacrifice" (*yajñaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*)— the author of the *Vaijayantī* accepted the term *yajña* as having a non-abandoning of its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā vṛtti*) precisely because of such an incongruity; [and likewise] the *Traipura-siddhānta* accepts that its author is Paramaśiva.

In that context, regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is the instruction that one should proclaim the *Traipurasiddhānta* as an ancillary part of it. In response to the inquiry, "What indeed is this *Traipurasiddhānta*, and from what source does its authority (*prāmāṇya*) derive?", the author first establishes the preliminary foundation (*bhūmikā*) to state that the authority of such a Siddhānta rests upon its being proclaimed by Śiva.

The Blessed Lord, the venerable Paramaśiva, having assumed various states through his divine play, [manifested] the eighteen branches of knowledge beginning with the Vedas and all philosophical systems (as briefly shown in the commentary below this sūtra regarding the summary view of the eighteen sciences, all philosophical schools, and the five traditions).

Having been questioned by the five faces of the Goddess Bhairavī—who consists of consciousness and is non-different from his own self—[as seen in the two supplements of the *Paramārthasāra* regarding the meaning: "From where have these traditions (āmnāyas) arisen, and what is their purpose? he expounded the five traditions (*pañcāmnāyas*), which are the very essence of the ultimate reality.
He prostrated to those who have become the very essence. || 2 ||
In order that even the slightest suspicion of invalidity may not touch the sciences expounded here,
[the author says] "the Blessed One" (bhagavān):
"Of complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, and prosperity..."
And because of knowledge and dispassion, as well as these six, he is remembered as "Bhagavat."

Thus, the Blessed One is endowed with such sixfold sovereign powers (ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya). Now, one might object: "Since Paramaśiva transcends all categories (tattvātīta) and is devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), his status as the author of knowledge (vidyākartṛtva) is not possible. To this, he says: "The Bhaṭṭāraka. This means "the King," according to the lexicon which states: "Rājā, Bhaṭṭāraka, Deva. He is the possessor of the attribute consisting of lordship over the universe (jagadīśvaratva).
The meaning of that is "having illusion as its limiting adjunct" (māyopādhika). Alternatively, the Lord (bhaṭṭāraka) is the one who delights in the drama of the form of the world;

for the word *bhaṭṭāraka* is used in the *Prasannarāghava* play as an address to one who delights in drama, namely "O Lord," and because the term "the King is the Lord" belongs to the category of dramatic terminology. As it is said of him:

Thus, both the status of being the creator of the world and the status of being the author of knowledge are indeed possible. Alternatively—since the Lord Paramaśiva is perfect, there is an absence of any object to be accomplished; how then [could he act]?

[The question is: "Is he the author of the sciences? To this, he says: "The Bhaṭṭāraka. This means "the King. Just as the activity of a king is seen for the benefit of others even when it is not required for himself, so it is here. Regarding the phrase "the eighteen sciences beginning with Śruti": this is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound, meaning those of which Śruti is the first. And thus, the Śrutis [are as follows]:...

The four auxiliary branches are grammar, ritual, prosody, and astronomy; and the six [other branches] are etymology, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra—these are the fourteen sciences (*vidyās*).
To these are added the four: Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Nītiśāstra.

Thus, there are eighteen sciences (*vidyās*). "All philosophical systems" (*sarvāṇi darśanāni*) refers to the Śākta system and so forth. "Philosophical system" (*darśana*) means that by which something is seen; it signifies a treatise (*śāstra*) that is a means for attaining knowledge—namely, the Śākta philosophical treatise—and the same applies to what follows. [These include] the Śaiva philosophical system, the Vaiṣṇava philosophical system, and the Brāhma philosophical system.

There are six systems of philosophy: the Saura-darśana and the Bauddha-darśana, and so forth. Having effortlessly and without exertion assumed those respective states—that is, having attained the state of Īśvara—and having taken on the forms of Pāṇini, Vyāsa, and others, He composed and created the grammatical treatises, Purāṇas, and other works.
Regarding the proof of the Veda’s being of human origin: [In this context, regarding the two views on whether the Lord’s Veda is non-human or human in origin—see Appendix 2, verse 5.
Now, since the Veda is eternal and thus not of human origin, how can it be said to have been created by God? Nor is it the case that...
If it is argued that its very eternality is unestablished because of the Vedic scripture stating, "By the speech that is multiform and eternal," we say: no;
for the Vedas were indeed composed by the Lord, according to the scripture, "From Him the meters were born. Furthermore:
"Of these eighteen branches of knowledge with their diverse paths..."
The original author is Śiva himself, the wielder of the trident, the Great Lord Maheśvara.

This is because of the traditional authority (*smṛti*) [of Manu]. Furthermore, the inference that "the Veda is of human origin because it is a collection of sentences, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works" is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, in the scriptural passage, "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings," the quality of being the "Lord" (*īśānatva*) consists precisely in the nature of being the author. Nor does its being of human origin entail the defects of a person...

It should not be argued that [the scripture] would be subject to doubt regarding its lack of authority because of the possibility of error, negligence, a desire to deceive, or incapacity; for in the case of the Lord (Īśvara), since ignorance and other such factors—which are the means of establishing defects—are absent, defects are impossible. By this, [it is established...]

The eternality of the Tantras has also been refuted. In the passage "by speech, eternal and multiform," the quality of eternality must be understood figuratively as consisting in not being composed by a fallible person, in accordance with the aforementioned collection of proofs. Nor should it be argued: "What is the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) against the opposite view?"
Because it is more reasonable to grant further favor [to the Vedas], therefore all the sciences (vidyās) are indeed composed by persons.
Regarding the specific purpose for the composition of this Tantra:
one might object that since the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) already exist, the further composition of this scripture (*āmnāya*) is redundant;
therefore, he says, "consisting of consciousness" (*saṃvinmayī*). This is the intended meaning: the goal of human life is happiness, and that [happiness] is innate.

And [the word] "artificial" (*kṛtrima*) refers to this. Natural [human ends] consist of liberation (*mokṣa*). The artificial one is that which is called desire (*kāma*), the third human end (*puruṣārtha*). Dharma is the means for both of these. Wealth (*artha*) is also a means for that [dharma]. Thus, there are four objects of human desire, whether directly or through a succession of means. Among them:
Only the means for attaining artificial human goals have been explicitly set forth through the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
That which is the non-artificial human goal—its means is the non-artificial [path].

It was not clearly set forth [in the Vedas]. Furthermore, since artificial instruction is of no benefit to people, he composed the *Āmnāyavidyā* (the Science of Tradition) with the desire to lift up the world itself, which was submerged in the mire of suffering. Or rather, it is the means of liberation for those who are ignorant of the meaning of the entire Veda and who lack the qualification for it.

He composed the *Āmnāyavidyā*, which is the essence of all the Vedas. In that work as well, [it is seen in Dvi-pariśiṣṭa-vivaraṇa 4], "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) means undivided sentience, that is to say, light;
[the phrase] "consisting of that" (*tanmayyā*) means non-different from that. By this, the meaning is established: she questions her own self through this aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
This has been stated by Appaya Dīkṣita in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*:
"The single Brahman-consciousness is eternal, free from even a trace of defect, and unsurpassed bliss;
yet, through the power of Māyā, it becomes differentiated into the two-fold distinction of 'attribute' (*dharma*) and 'substratum' (*dharmī*)."

"In that [state], dharma consists of experience pertaining to all objects and the power conducive to all effects; while qualities such as desire and the like exist, the substratum remains one alone. Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "Since even living beings such as ourselves possess the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayatva*), what is the distinction between them and the Śrī Bhairava? To this, the Lord provides the qualifying epithet "Bhagavat" (the Blessed One).
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *bhagavat* has already been explained previously. And thus:

The word "Bhagavat" indicates that she does not fail to ask because her knowledge is obscured by the *āṇava* and other impurities as is the case with ordinary living beings; rather, although she is omniscient, she asks with some hidden intention.
For instance, Śiva, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*), himself becomes reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and introduces the question. In this regard:

The purpose of this is as follows: to make it known that even a learned person, though capable and possessing knowledge acquired through the reading of books and other means, cannot achieve the goal of life merely by that; rather, one must proceed solely along the path taught by the Guru.
To demonstrate this, the question is posed by assuming another form. As it is said in the Svacchandatantra:
"Abiding himself in the roles of both teacher and disciple, Sadāśiva brought down the Tantra through dialogues consisting of questions and answers. Thus [it is said].

The word "only" (*eva*) in the Vedic passage, "To know that, one should approach a guru alone," also expresses this very same meaning. To illuminate this very point, the two qualifiers "by the Blessed One" and "non-different from her own Self" are used. As for the meaning of the term *Bhairavī*: [she is so called] because of the sustaining (*bharaṇa*) and delighting (*ramana*) of the world.

She is to be known as Bhairavī because, at the time of creation, she vomits forth that which was residing within the womb of Paramaśiva during the dissolution; [in this regard, there are many proofs such as the verse in the *Śrī Lalitāsahasranāma* (verse 126) stating "the witness of the great dissolution," as well as passages from other tantras and so forth]. By her—

"Questioned" means one to whom a question has been posed. This is an epithet of the aforementioned Lord Paramaśiva Bhaṭṭāraka. "By five faces"—namely, those known as Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna—he [reveals] the five Āmnāyas: the Pūrvāmnāya, Dakṣiṇāmnāya, and so forth.
Regarding those named the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), and the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya)—
[see Appendix 4 for the knowledge useful for understanding the meaning of these five traditions]—
although the word *āmnāya* is primarily used in the sense of the Veda, according to the lexicon which states: "The feminine *śruti*, the Veda, and *āmnāya* [are synonyms]."

Nevertheless, because they set forth the essence of the sacred tradition (āmnāya)—that is to say, by revealing the core secrets of Vedic subjects, it is established that the Tantras indeed set forth the sacred tradition and bestow liberation. Here too, the word "āmnāya" is used figuratively. By this—

19) The view that the tantras of certain [schools] are independent authorities like the Vedas has been refuted. The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the uncreated, fourth human goal (*turīya-puruṣārtha*); [the tantras] are honored as being the essence (*sāra*) within that.

By this, it is indicated that the person is uniquely desirable and exceedingly secret. Out of compassion for those unable to grasp the entire meaning of the Vedas, Śiva extracted their essential meaning and composed the five Āmnāyas. || 2 ||
Being supremely compassionate toward those who are even more dull-witted than those [already mentioned], the venerable Paraśurāma, desiring to set forth the established tenets of the Traipura system,
begins to speak by summarizing the essential points contained therein:
In this regard, the established conclusion is as follows: || 3 ||
In that regard, within the five traditional systems (pañcāmnāya), this "siddhānta" to be described hereafter refers to an object that is the subject of a conclusion produced by critical inquiry.

By this section of the text ending here, the suspicion regarding the lack of authority arising from the [alleged] fabrication of the meaning of the doctrine to be expounded by one's own imagination is dispelled.

The meaning is this: that time at which this universe exists in a subtle form within the belly of Paraśiva is indeed dissolution (*pralaya*). Such a dissolution is known solely through the scriptures. In the same way, so too is creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
In that context, dissolution refers to the Supreme Brahman abiding solely in its own essential nature, while the individual soul (*jīva*) [remains].

It is as if in deep sleep. At that time, the multitude of individual souls (*jīva-rāśi*), their unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and all the five elements remain in a subtle form within [the Supreme], just as a banyan tree exists in potential within a banyan seed. As it is stated in the *Śaktisūtrabhāṣya*: "Even while swallowing the universe, Paramaśiva does not do so in its entirety, but rather establishes it in part, in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)."

Thus, that very *saṃskāra* (latent impression) serves as the auxiliary cause for the creative will (*sisṛkṣā*) of Īśvara; otherwise, the occurrence of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) could not be avoided. This being the case, in the world, when there is union (*sāmarasya*) between husband and wife, a portion of the white drop (*bindu*) situated at the opening of the *vidhi* enters the womb and attains oneness with the red drop.

When that occurs, then Brahman alone, devoid of the manifestation of external and internal existence, shines forth. Its capacity to produce an embryo is observed; likewise, at the time prior to creation, the union of Śiva and Śakti also takes place by virtue of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings. || 3 ||
There are thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). [The meaning of each of these as *sphoṭa* shall be seen below, up until the end of this commentary on the sūtra.
To elaborate upon that very point, he begins to set forth the network of principles:
The universe consists of thirty-six principles.

Thus, when He who abides in His own absolute nature forms a union with those powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action— thinking "May I be many, may I procreate"— the objective creation and the verbal creation arise sequentially and simultaneously, like a sprout and its shadow.

(20) If it is objected that the powers of will, knowledge, and action would necessarily be impermanent because they are beginningless [in their manifestation], we reply: this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
For there exists a subtle form of that very [power] which is the cause of that triad and is named *Śāntā*.

Because the form of Paraśiva is eternal, it follows that Paramaśiva himself, when qualified by such an adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*), becomes the referent of the term "Kevalaśiva. He alone is the first among the principles (*tattva*s).
That aforementioned desire to emit, which consists of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is Śakti; she is the second principle.

As it has been stated in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*: "In that regard, the subject (*dharmī*) exercises agency over the fivefold creative acts of the worlds, while the attribute (*dharma*) assumes a primordial male form. [Note: Here, the first written character appears as if it were 'vi'.]
She maintains the state of being the material cause of the entire universe;
having assumed a female form, she becomes the divine queen of her own refuge, the primordial creator.
Furthermore, the two divisions of Dharma proclaimed by the knowers of the Vedas are said to be like Brahmā himself, reaching the pinnacle of the sacred law. Thus it is said.

The perception of the aforementioned world as "I" (ahantayā) is that which possesses such a clear cognitive state (*vṛtti*) called "I"; this is the third principle (*tattva*), denoted by the term Sadāśiva.
That which possesses the cognitive state directed solely toward difference, namely "this is the world," is denoted by the term Īśvara.
The fourth principle is the Tattva.
That mental state (vṛtti) belonging to Sadāśiva, which takes the form "I am the universe," is denoted by the term Vidyā; it is the fifth principle.
The mental modification (*vṛtti*) residing in Īśvara, which takes the form "this world," has difference as its object and is denoted by the term *māyā*;

it is the sixth principle (*tattva*). Possessing the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) of the previously mentioned *vidyā*, the cognition opposed to that is denoted by the term *avidyā*; it is the seventh [principle].

The principle (*tattva*): that very agency residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), which is contracted by some slight degree of agency, is what is designated by the term *kalā*; it is the eighth principle.

According to the manner previously stated, that very eternal contentment which resides in the *jīva* becomes the ninth principle, termed *rāga*, when it is contracted by a lack of contentment regarding certain objects.
When the eternity residing in the *jīva* is veiled, that same eternity [manifests as the notions] "it exists," "it is born," and "it grows."
Because it undergoes transformation, diminishes, and perishes—through its association with these six states—it is contracted and designated by the term "time"; this is the tenth principle (*tattva*).
Due to the non-difference between Paraśiva and the individual soul (*jīva*), just as there is absolute sovereignty (*sarvasvātantrya*) in Paraśiva, so too does it belong to the *jīva*.

The concealment of all sovereignty, which was previously effected by the aforementioned Vidyā, depends upon another cause; that which it depends upon is designated by the term "Niyati" (Restriction), and is the eleventh [principle]. (Note: *Vi-ātra-ādyā-ityādyanekapadāni* and *pāṭhāntare pṛthaksantyanyatra* appear as parenthetical notes indicating various alternative readings found elsewhere.)

The *tattva* [is as follows]: the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the substratum of such [principles] as necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), attachment (*rāga*), limited agency (*kalā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), is the twelfth *tattva*. Nature (*prakṛti*), which is the state of equilibrium of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and is synonymous with the mind (*citta*), is the thirteenth.
The principle [of mind]: when sattva and tamas are overcome and rajas predominates, that which is designated by the term "manas" and serves as the cause of volition is the fourteenth principle.
Having overcome rajas and tamas, the internal organ dominated by sattva— designated by the term "intellect" (buddhi)—
is the cause of determination; it is the fifteenth principle (tattva).

When the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), dominated by *tamas* and having overcome *rajas* and *sattva*, is designated by the term "I-maker" (*ahaṃkāra*), it is the sixteenth principle, the cause of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The sense-organ that perceives sound, the ear, is the seventeenth principle.
The sense organ that perceives touch is the skin, the eighteenth principle;
the sense organ that perceives form is the eye, the nineteenth principle;
the sense organ that perceives taste is the tongue, the twentieth principle.

The sense organ that perceives odor is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*); it is the twenty-first principle (*tattva*). The vocal organ (*vāgindriya*) conducive to the utterance of articulate speech is the twenty-second principle. The hand (*pāṇi*), the sense organ conducive to grasping and relinquishing, is the twenty-third principle.
The organ conducive to movement is the foot, the twenty-fourth principle (*tattva*).
The organ that produces the discharge of waste is the anus, the twenty-fifth principle.
The organ that produces sexual union is the generative organ (*upastha*), the twenty-sixth principle.
Sound, in the form of subtle ether, is the twenty-seventh principle;
touch, in the form of subtle air, is the twenty-eighth principle;
and form, in the form of subtle fire, is the twenty-ninth principle.
Taste in the form of subtle water is the thirtieth principle;
smell in the form of subtle earth is the thirty-first principle;
and gross space, whose nature is vacuity, is the thirty-second principle.
Air, characterized by the quality of constant motion, is the thirty-third principle;
fire, characterized by heat, is the thirty-fourth principle;
and water, characterized by fluidity, is the thirty-fifth principle.

Earth, possessing the quality of solidity, is the thirty-sixth and final principle (*tattva*). [In this text, both in the root verses and the commentary—36—the thirty-six principles along with their meanings are specified.
This collection of such principles is non-different from the conventional object of discourse known as the "universe" or "world. Regarding the stated meaning:
The authority for this is found in the Paramānanda Tantra: "That which is solidity is earth; fluidity is indeed called water;
heat is fire; movement is air; and space is the void."
The subtle form of these, however, is that in which the divisions have not yet emerged:
smell, touch, form, taste, and sound are indeed the *tanmātras*.
The five sense organs of these [beings]— namely the nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin,
and the ear— are indeed engaged in the function of perceiving [their respective objects].
The pentad consisting of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure is the nature of the Adhiṣṭhāna [cakra]; therefore, it is not treated separately.
That instrument consists of what are called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals;
it is said to be present throughout the entire body, though its manifestation is clearly evident [in specific locations].
O Śivā, the mind is the instrument of volition, while the intellect effects determination;
it is like a mirror, the ground for the reflections of conceptual constructions.
Egoism (ahaṃkāra) is described as having the nature of such conceit;
it consists of the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, known respectively as suffering, pleasure, and delusion.
That which is called the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) arises from the predominance of those [qualities];
however, the equilibrium of the causal qualities (guṇas) is termed primordial nature (prakṛti).
The Puruṣa is said to be distinct from that [Prakṛti]; he is complete, yet his powers are contracted.
These are consciousness (cit), bliss (ānanda), will (icchā), knowledge (jñāna), and likewise action (kriyā).
The powers, though complete, become limited as the kalās and so forth;
indeed, the power of action (kriyā-śakti), whose nature is universal agency, became the kalā.
Knowledge exists in the form of limited agency, while omniscience is likewise [of that nature];
the intellect is the cognizer of those very objects which are the reflections within it.
Due to contraction, that which is called *vidyā* (knowledge) is itself proclaimed as *avidyā* (ignorance);
and that same [power] which is characterized by contraction is called *icchā* (will), known as eternal satisfaction.
Passion (rāga) is in one case called non-contentment, and in another it takes the form of attachment;
the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is known as eternal existence (nityasattā), and time (kāla) arises from the conjunction with the six states of being.
The power of bliss is declared to be universal sovereignty;
however, due to contraction caused by dependence on another, it is known as necessity (niyati).
O Goddess Māyā, beloved of Bhairava, you are of independent nature, yet endowed with this very unbroken essence through your skill in creating differentiation.
By concealing her own nature through differentiation, she takes on the form of the categories (tattvas);
yet, having abandoned that differentiation of her own nature, she is intent upon the realization of unity.
That which consists of the manifestation of ultimate reality is designated as *śuddhavidyā*;
it makes manifest all entities, whose distinctness is clearly apparent, by means of its own non-differentiation.

O Goddess, Īśvara has been described; however, this [Īśvara] is said to be "unmanifest" (aspaṣṭa)— the word division here should be understood as *tān aspaṣṭān*— whereas Sadāśiva is declared to be of the nature of awakening.
One perceives only "I am," which consists of non-difference from one's own true nature.
