The power (śakti) which consists of the latent impressions of conceptual proliferation (prapañca-vāsanā) is so designated.
"Free from conceptual proliferation, consisting of the single essence of consciousness—this is declared to be the principle of Śiva. Thus [it is said].

A detailed exposition of the essential nature of these [principles], from Śiva down to the earth (kṣiti), exists at length in the Mṛgendrasaṃhitā; however, for fear of prolixity, it has not been written here, but only as much as is necessary has been recorded.
The Determination of the Number of Principles:

Now, if it is asked—"Since the Sāṅkhyas have established the doctrine that there are twenty-four principles, how can there be thirty-six principles?"—it is replied: There are twelve principles in addition to the twenty-four, beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Śiva. They are not...
Is your statement that [these] do not exist because there is a lack of authoritative evidence, or that they are included within the twenty-four principles?
It is not the first, because the very word of the venerable Lord Paraśurāma serves as authority;
for it is heard in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Salutations again and again to the Lord of the temple consisting of thirty-six principles."

Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Paramānanda Tantra*: "This wheel of principles (*tattvacakra*) is indeed proclaimed to be thirty-sixfold. Nor is the second [position] tenable, because it is impossible for [beings] beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Śiva—who possess mutually contradictory attributes as previously described—to be included [within those categories]. Nor...

It should not be argued that this contradicts the statement in the *Mahābhārata*, "The principles (*tattva*) are twenty-four, and the Puruṣa is beyond them," because [the text] concludes right there since the subsequent twelve principles are extremely difficult to comprehend, and it is intended for those of dull intellect to be told only those principles that are very easy to understand up to the point of *prakṛti*. And thus:

Since both statements are authoritative according to the distinction between their respective intended audiences (*adhikārī*), by this [argument] one who asserts that there are only five principles (*tattva*)—
relying on the *Vāsiṣṭha* statement that "in all cases there are five elements, and a sixth does not exist"— is refuted, for that [statement] is intended solely for those of extremely dull intellect.

If it is objected: "If possessing contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmavattva*) is the criterion for being a distinct principle (*tattva*), then a pot and a cloth—which possess the contradictory attributes of 'pot-ness' and 'cloth-ness'—would also have to be considered distinct principles," we reply:
No. Do you intend to establish that they are principles beyond the thirty-six? Or rather...

Is it being argued that the reality of cloth (*paṭatattva*) would be distinct from the reality of the jar (*ghaṭarūpatattva*)? Not the first [alternative], because since there is no contradiction between the properties of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) with respect to hardness (*kāṭhinya*), which is the unique property of earth, their distinctness is not established. As for the second [alternative], it is simply a case of proving what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is precisely the point.
It has been stated in the Sūtasaṃhitā, preceded by a description of the definition of reality (tattva):
"That which remains until the dissolution [of the world], bestowing experience upon all beings—that is declared to be reality (tattva); therefore, the body, a jar, and the like are not reality."
By this, this suspicion is utterly refuted.
(p. 24) Although in other tantras there are initially only three principles— namely, the principle of the self (ātmatattva), the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva),
and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva)— therein, the principle of the self is twenty-fourfold, beginning with earth and ending with primordial matter (prakṛti).

Its specific characteristic is absolute insentience (*kevalajaḍatva*). The principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) extends from the Puruṣa down to Māyā and is sevenfold. Its definition consists in possessing both insentience and the capacity for illumination.
For instance, just as in a mass of iron that has attained identity with fire, there is a capacity for illumination despite its being insentient.

In a mass of iron, its insentience (*jaḍatva*) is evident during the state when it has not attained identity with fire. Likewise, in fire, both its insentience and its luminosity (*prakāśakatva*) are evident during the state when it has attained identity with the mass of iron. Similarly, in the Person (*puruṣa*), who is of the nature of light, [these qualities are evident] in the insentient factors such as Necessity (*niyati*) and the rest when they have attained identity with Him.

Luminosity resides in the *puruṣa*, while insentience resides in *niyati* and the other [categories]. Insentience in *niyati* and the rest, and luminosity in the *puruṣa*, are evident. In this manner, the *vidyā-tattva* possesses a mixed nature.
From *śuddhavidyā* up to Śiva, the *śiva-tattva* is fivefold; its specific characteristic is as follows:
Thus, the intermediate classification as "the state of being the illuminator of the absolute" has been made; nevertheless, even there, at the time of the conclusion, it is said:
"O Maheśvarī, such indeed is the wheel of principles (tattvacakra), consisting of thirty-six kinds."
Thus, since the very same Dharma that was taught there has been taught here as well, there is no contradiction with it.
In fact, in the twenty-second chapter of the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, it is asked: "O Lord of the Universe, O Master, how many principles (tattvas) have been enumerated by the sages?
Some say there are twenty-six, while others say twenty-five."

Beginning with "Some say seven, some nine, and some six," and so forth, after establishing twenty-eight principles according to His own view in response to Uddhava’s question, the Blessed Lord provided the justification for the views of those who maintain contradictory numbers such as seven and others.
Thus, the various enumerations of the principles (tattvas) have been made by the sages;

all are logical because they possess sound reasoning—what in them is unseemly? [By this much, those who claim that the words of the sages are not authoritative, asserting that "there is no single sage whose word is authoritative," are merely creators of false meanings.]
"They have been sent far away"—this is a piercing remark; even today, some such people remain utterly deluded regarding the true meaning of the word *guhā*.
Thus he spoke. This alone should be seen as the solution in this matter. || 4 ||
Having thus explained the division of the principles (*tattva*), he begins to describe the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*):
Śiva, when enveloped by the bodily sheath (*kañcuka*), is the *jīva*; when free from the sheath, he is Śiva.
a. Paraśiva.
Thus, even for the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), there is again a twofold nature in their general form:

in some there is solely the state of being the object of vision (*dṛśyatva*), and in others solely the state of being the seer (*draṣṭṛtva*). The former applies to the insentient (*jaḍa*) principles, while the latter applies exclusively to the sentient.
(25) But surely, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is included within the categories of reality (*tattva*), whereas Paraśiva is not, a distinction between the two follows.
This being the case, how can the non-dual (*advaita*) doctrine of the Tantrikas be established? To this, he says: "The body... and so forth. This...

The state [of bondage] is as follows: Paraśiva, who is entirely independent, by means of his inscrutable *māyā*, conceals that perfect sovereignty (*svātantrya*) which resides within himself and consists in independence from anything else. That sovereignty which is thus concealed—limited sovereignty—is called the *āṇava-mala*. Indeed, it is the *āṇava-mala* itself.
It is also called ignorance (avidyā).
If it is objected that "one's own perfect sovereignty conceals its own discourse," it is replied:

just as the sun becomes obscured by clouds created by its own rays, so too there is no impediment to its self-veiling through its own ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the distinction is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).
It is real; thus, the sense is that there is no loss of non-duality.

If it is asked, "How can Paraśiva, whose essential nature is undivided consciousness, be obscured by the limited impurity (āṇavamala)?"—it is as follows: The power of Māyā is indefinable; therefore, there is no room for doubt regarding how this occurs, even in the case of accomplishing the impossible. For this very reason it has been said:
"What is impossible in Māyā, which brings about even the most difficult of things? Thus [it is said].
Also in the Subhagodaya:
"The intellect, divided by Māyā, constantly obstructs the unrestrained power of that [consciousness] within all beings who are its own parts, just as the shore obstructs the ocean."

Thus, covered by the impurity of *āṇava*, the individual soul (*aṇu*) itself, being limited by the body, perceives other infinite souls—likewise limited by bodies—as distinct from itself. That is the impurity consisting of *māyā*. Thus, defiled by this impurity of *māyā* which takes the form of the manifestation of duality, they perform auspicious and inauspicious actions.

They possess the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [experience]. This is the impurity of action (*kārma-mala*). These three kinds of impurities are designated by the term "body" (*śarīra*). Śiva himself, when enveloped by that which is of the nature of a sheath (*kañcuka*) or a covering (*ācchādana*), is the individual soul (*jīva*). As it is said in the *Paramārthasāra*:
"That which is the supreme sovereignty of Maheśa, the accomplishment of the impossible—that is the Goddess Māyā-śakti, the self-concealment of Śiva. Thus [it is said].
In the *Subhagodaya* it is also said:
"This person, his form limited by her and all his powers withdrawn,
is like the sun at twilight— reddened and with its rays retracted— incapable even of self-illumination."

Alternatively—the body is threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme. The first is that set forth in the verse on meditation; the second is of the nature of mantra; and the third consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The meaning is that Śiva, enveloped by these bodies, is himself the primordial principle (ādyatattva) and is indeed the individual soul (jīva). The implication is that since the state of being a soul exists in him alone, what need is there to mention others? By this, it is suggested that even the attainment of the nature of Śiva is not the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha).

Such living beings are of three kinds: pure (*śuddha*), impure (*aśuddha*), and mixed (*miśra*). The first are those beginning with Śiva and ending with Sadāśiva, because they lack ignorance (*ajñāna*). The impure are humans and others.
The mixed are Vasiṣṭha and others. He who is free from such coverings (*kañcuka*) is Paraśiva, who transcends the categories (*tattvātīta*).
This is the meaning. || 5 ||
Having thus described the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) as being the very essence of the human goal (puruṣārtha), he points out what that human goal is:
"Self-reflection is the human goal. (6)
The *vimarśa*—the recognition in the form "I am He"—of one's own nature as that of Paraśiva is as follows:

just as someone who has forgotten a gold ornament on their neck and runs from place to place in search of it, upon having their latent impressions awakened by someone else, perceives it on their own neck; so too [is the realization of Śiva].

The meaning is that the re-acquisition of the knowledge of one's own true nature—which had been forgotten—is the uncreated (akṛtrima) goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha). Furthermore, the attainment of such a goal of human endeavor will not occur without the grace of the Lord. This was stated by the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (Gītā 7.14).
Furthermore, devotion to the Blessed One arises only through the worship of the Blessed One; therefore, the worship of the Blessed One is, by traditional succession, the means to liberation.
Regarding the description of the qualities of mantra:
indeed, [the term] "yoga and so forth" [should be understood to include] Vedānta, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā, Vaiśeṣika, and others.

Many scriptures are found stating that such a human goal (puruṣārtha) is attained [the meaning is: there are many authoritative rites prescribed in various scriptures that establish the human goal in the form of liberation]. If it is asked, "Why is the necessity of spiritual practice (upāsanā) being described?"—
There is a necessity for spiritual practice (*upāsanā*). However, the liberation obtained through yoga and other such means is not free from rebirth.
As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"Even though he is liberated from bondage, the Lord binds him again."
"Bound, he transmigrates further as long as he does not find the Divine. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in another place it is said:

"At the beginning of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha creates again those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth; therefore, liberation such as this is not equal [to the ultimate state]."
p.

27) Therefore, since it is established that meditation alone is the primary means, and since recitation (*japa*) is also present within meditation, the mantra is the principal instrument therein. [From here, the Blessed Lord Rāma [explains] by means of the seventh, eighth, and ninth aphorisms.]
It should be noted that [this passage] introduces the gravity of the necessity for the various mantras of the deities to become the very heart of one's worship.
Thus, in order to generate faith in the practitioner (*upāsaka*), he describes their qualities and functions:
"Words consist of phonemes (*varṇa*) and are eternal (*nitya*). (7)
The meaning is that mantras— sounds consisting of phonemes or collections of phonemes— are eternal,
in the sense that they possess the same ontological status as root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). However, this does not mean they are uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time,
because once ignorance is removed, the deities distinct from one's own true nature and the mantras denoting them cease to exist.

Nor should it be argued that since the Vedas and other texts— distinguished by their specific sequential order— are described as eternal (*nityatva*) and as enduring for a single kalpa, this [work] too, being of such a nature, cannot possess an eternity consisting in a duration longer than that; for the mantras are of the nature of the subtle bodies of the deities, and the body of a deity...
Because it exists simultaneously with ignorance. || 7 ||
Alternatively,
according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*, "The seven crores of great mantras issued from the mouth of Śiva";
thus, because mantras also have a beginning, they cannot be coeval with ignorance (*avidyā*), since the latter is beginningless.
For this very reason, since praise as "manifold" on account of possessing qualities common to others would be possible, [the author], being dissatisfied with that,
states another unique quality of the mantras: "The inconceivable power of the mantras" (8).

The genitive case in "mantrāṇām" (of the mantras) is used in the sense of the locative; thus, it means "in the mantras. "Acintya-śaktayaḥ" means those mantras whose power (*śakti*) is inconceivable (*acintya*). The word "tattā" (that state) is to be supplied as the predicate: "they possess that state.

Furthermore, the inconceivability of this power consists in its being beyond the scope of logical reasoning (*tarka*). By this, it is shown that the previously mentioned *māyā* is likewise inconceivable and difficult to restrain.

Nevertheless, it has been established that within the mantras there exists, by way of their divine play (līlā), a power capable of removing even those [obstacles], a power even greater than that, which brings about the cessation of ignorance (avidyā) that veils knowledge. || 8 ||

Regarding the auxiliary causes for the accomplishment of mantras—namely, the auxiliary causes required when a desired effect is to be produced by means of a mantra—he says: "Through tradition and faith, all success [is attained]. (9)

"Tradition" (*saṃpradāya*) refers to following the conduct of the lineage of gurus. "Faith" (*viśvāsa*) is the certainty regarding mantras that they are the means for attaining results. The remainder [of the meaning] is that through a mantra accompanied by these two, all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) come to be. Although in the world, by means of a single staff and a single action, only a jar is produced and not...

A cloth [is produced]; thus, by means of a shuttle, a loom, and so forth, it is a cloth and not a jar. In this way, it is observed in the world that every cause produces only one specific effect. Nevertheless, mantras are not like that;
therefore, the word "all" (*sarva*) is used to indicate that a single mantra alone produces whatever is desired. By this—
Furthermore, for the sake of engaging the listener, the quality of being situated within the mantra is also established. || 9 ||
(28) Now, one might ask: how can this statement, whose meaning contradicts worldly consensus, be considered authoritative?
To this, he says:
Validity consists primarily in trustworthiness. || 10 ||

Validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being the producer of a cognition that possesses a particular qualifier (*tadvati tatprakāraka*) and which generates an activity that results in successful correspondence (*saṃvādi*).

"Established for all" (*sarvasiddhi*) refers to that which abounds in conviction (*viśvāsa*) as residing in the previously mentioned statement. Here, the meaning of the term "conviction" (*viśvāsa*) is the ascertainment of the trustworthiness (*āptatva*) of the speaker of the statement. From the word *bahu*, the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*) is understood.

The suffix *iṣṭhan* is used here. Regarding this, the Pāṇinian sūtra *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* means that these two suffixes, *tama* and *iṣṭhan*, occur in their own sense (*svārthe*) when [the base] expresses a meaning characterized by excellence. Thus, once *iṣṭhan* has been applied in its own sense, the rule *iṣṭhasya ca* applies, which states that there is elision (*lopa*) of the *iṣṭhan* following the word *bahu*. This is according to the rule *bahor lope bhū ca bahoḥ*.

The meaning of that is: there is the addition of the suffix *iṭ* and the substitution of *bhū*. Thus, when the substitution of *bhū* and the addition of *iṭ* have occurred, the word *bhūyiṣṭha* denotes a human goal characterized by extreme abundance.

Furthermore, the state of being abundant in trust toward the Person (*puruṣa*) is established through the relationship of being produced subsequently to oneself and having that [Person] as its object.

The state of being a locus where doubt characterized by a lack of trust does not arise [is predicated] of that person who is the substratum [of the cognition], because the syntactic connection (abhedānvaya) with identity is sublated. The word *bhūyiṣṭha* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "the object of knowledge which is the substratum of the greatest number [of cognitions]. Its connection with identity occurs within its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).
The meaning is that the authority of this scripture is to be known solely by those persons who possess absolute trust;
the implication is that the authority of the scripture is entirely inaccessible to those characterized by fallacious reasoning. As it has been said by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda:
"For those matters which are accessible through the scriptures alone, one should not refute them by means of logic. Thus [it is said].
Some, however, say that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is an abundance (*bhūyiṣṭha*) or plurality (*bāhulya*) of faith. This is to be considered;

for, according to Pāṇini’s grammatical rules, the word *bhūyiṣṭha* refers to a person (*puruṣa*), and thus its application to the attribute of plurality is untenable. And if one were to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) regarding the attribute, then—

The position that [prāmāṇya] has its locus in that which is dependent on me alone is indeed superior; not the other. For if it were otherwise, even though there is a plurality [of instances], since it is impossible for the dharma (prāmāṇya) to have an identity-connection with the locus of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a single instance due to its being equal in status to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one would have to assume a locus of indication in the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, namely, the prāmāṇya related to the plurality of the expressed meanings.

And the relation must be stated as nothing other than "being knowable by a cognition residing in its own locus"; and thus it is identical to my own view. Regarding this point, [the opponent's position] involves an excessive definition of *dharma* and the recourse to a cumbersome *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound. Therefore, this alone is the correct interpretation.
Better.
Śrī Skanda spoke very clearly regarding such abundance of faith:
"O Agastya, what is the use of much speaking? Listen to my definitive word; no doubt should be entertained here, for from that which is doubted, no fruit indeed arises."

"However many tantras and numerous nets of mantras exist in the mortal world"— here he states another auxiliary factor: [the purification] of the guru, the mantra, the deity, the self, the mind, and the vital breath.
From the thorough churning of oneness arises the realization of the inner self. || 11 ||

The Guru and the others are clear [in their meaning]. The winds are the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*). The "churning" of these [elements] through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the production of their unity; by that, there arises the realization (*vitti*) of the inner self, the *pratyagātman*.
The phrase "feeling arises" is the ellipsis; the identity of the self and the deity is clear upon the removal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The identity of the deity and the mantra exists through their relationship as the signified and the signifier. The same applies to the guru.
The identity of the mind and the vital breath (*pavana*) is shown in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Air is not significantly different from the mind; therefore, by its restraint, the mind attains stillness. Thus it is said.
Although such a certainty cannot actually exist at the time of meditation, nevertheless, this must be brought forth for even a moment as an auxiliary element of the meditation.
The fruit of worship in the form of *japa*—or rather, he states the fruit of worship performed with the mantra as the instrument, accompanied by faith in the tradition—is as follows:
"The guru-mantra. The "grinding out of unity" (*aikya-niṣphālana*) means the determination of unity; through that, there arises the knowledge of the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
The meaning is distinguished by the word "bhavati" (it exists).

Umānandanātha, however, maintains that regarding the phrase "gurumantra" (the guru and the mantra): in the *Ārambhollāsa*, there is the contemplation of the identity between the guru, the mantra, the deity, and one's own self; this is one means. Furthermore, another means is the knowledge that the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are to be restrained by a single effort; through these two, the accomplishment of the goal occurs.

They have explained it thus; but that is to be considered. From the phrase "due to the threshing" (*niṣphālanāt*), only a single meaning—either in the form of a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) or in the form of the cognition that [the rice] is to be stopped by a single effort—would be understood, not multiple meanings, according to the maxim that "a word uttered once conveys only one meaning at a time. Otherwise, from the word *hari*...
Because there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous cognition of all fourteen meanings. Furthermore,
if the word-meanings that constitute a *dvandva* compound were to connect with a distinct action,
then it would be merely a case of *anvācaya* (conjunction), as in the example "Go for alms and bring the cow," since *anvācaya* occurs when there is a difference in action.

Because of that definition: for the definition of a *dvandva* (copulative compound) is the simultaneous co-occurrence (*anvaya*) in a single action, and its fulfillment is impossible in every respect according to that [opponent’s] view. Nor should it be argued that such usage as "Cut the *dhava* and *khadira* trees; look at them" would not be possible; for such usage is simply unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*).
Because it has been established by all. || 11 ||

The procedure for worship in the form of adoration (*arcana*)—up to this point, through the praise of the mantra and the statement of its auxiliary causes—the ritual action performed by means of the mantra and its injunction must be inferred. And thus, it is precisely of the nature of *japa* (repetition). In this way...
Having described the form of worship consisting of recitation (*japa*), he now enjoins the form of worship consisting of ritual adoration (*pūjā*):
"Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is established within the body; its manifestors are the five *makāras*. Worship with them should be done in secret; from public display comes hell. (12)

Just as Brahman is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), so too it is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*). Just as one does not perceive the nature of consciousness when it is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*), so too one does not perceive the essential nature of bliss when it is veiled by suffering (*duḥkha*). This occurs whenever suffering in the form of a heavy burden or the like is removed.
Even now, one perceives the limited form of Brahman itself through the limitation of the body;
such bliss is limited and established within the body by means of the limitation of the body. Of that—

The "manifestors" (*abhivyañjakāḥ*) are those which produce direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding that [object], namely the five *makāras*. Up to this point, there has been a praise of the substances being enjoined for the sake of motivating the practitioner; the implied meaning is: "Since these five *makāras* are thus excellent, one should therefore perform worship with them in secret, without public display."
By this [verse], the ritual action consisting of worship characterized by secrecy, material offerings, and both [of these] is prescribed.

If it is argued that, in the injunction of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭa-karma-vidhi*), praise must pertain to the action alone—since there is a rule that only that which is enjoined can be praised—we say no. Because in an injunction of a qualified entity, the injunction of the qualifier is necessarily implied, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can serve as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that [injunction of the qualifier], just as in the case of the text: "One should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta*).

Even in the injunction regarding a ritual distinguished by a deity, there is praise of the deity through the statement, "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," and similarly, there is concealment regarding the ritual. This concealment consists in the absence of general knowledge concerning the object of the knowledge of the animal's behavior; because this [injunction] takes the form of a qualified injunction, the concealment serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). From the manifestation of that very [knowledge], hell results.

Praise in the form of censure: for example, "If one were to collect [the materials] with the skin of domestic animals, he would afflict domestic animals with pain"—being in the form of censure, this serves as a supplement to the praise, "He collects them with a black antelope skin. Likewise, if by chance [the skin] becomes manifest before that, there is no expiation (prāyaścitta) arising from the omission of a constituent part of the sacrifice.
There is another expiation for the purpose of avoiding hell.
"From manifestation," meaning from the opposite of concealment; the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*); "niraya" means "without a place" (*niraka*).

But the venerable Bhāsurānandanātha says: "For those who possess other forms of initiation, there is merely a deficiency in the ritual (*kratuviguṇya*) when they manifest their own [specific] duty; however, in this case, if there is such a deficiency, there is indeed hell. To that effect, the Lord Paraśurāma said: "From manifestation comes hell. According to his view, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

I, being of little intelligence, do not know the means for avoiding such defects as the abandonment of the subject at hand and the assumption that something is for the sake of a person not under discussion. || 12 ||
The Duties of a Lay Devotee (Upāsaka-dharma): Having thus described worship as firmness in cultivation, he speaks of the duties of a lay devotee:
"From firmness in cultivation comes the accomplishment of the Command. (13)

In such mental states as "I know this," the discernment that "this [object] is superior" because it appears as the "I" (ahantā) in relation to the objective category (padārtha)—this alone is the meaning of the term *bhāvanā* across all mental states.
Its firmness is its lack of laxity. Through this, the accomplishment of the Command (*ājñāsiddhi*) occurs, which is the capacity for both restraint and grace.

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By way of praising the firmness of cultivation (*bhāvanādārḍhya*), the injunction for such cultivation at all times is to be inferred;

[this refers to] the non-censure of all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśanānindana*). From this, the venerable one’s reverence for the Tantric teachings is even more worthy of reflection. [Censure (*nindā*)].
He states another rule for the lay follower:
"Not disparaging any philosophical system" (p. 31). || 14 ||

The meaning is that one must not engage in the censure of those philosophical systems (*darśana*) and scriptures that enjoin the worship of other deities. By censuring them, doubt arises among their respective adherents, leading to a lack of confidence in the very systems they themselves have adopted. Furthermore, because such a person lacks qualification for this [present] scripture, they fall away from both.
It would perish like a scattered cloud. Śrī Kṛṣṇa also spoke of this very same meaning:
"One should not create a division of intellect among the ignorant who are attached to action."
"One should not revile the worlds," so also says the Śruti.

Is it not established that the absence of the sin produced by the mental confusion of others is the fruit of this [meditation], and that this is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? If it is asked, "How can this be included among the duties of a meditator (*upāsaka*), which produce the excellence of a sacrifice (*kratu*)?", it is replied: This too is useful for the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*) which arises from meditation.

If one asks, "How so? it is as follows: if, like a severed cloud, one remains indifferent toward the destruction of others, yet at that very time engages in censure, then the vision of all beings as oneself—which requires indifference even toward the destruction of others—has not been attained; thus, the state of being the self of all (sarvātmatā) remains unestablished.
There is no failure in establishing the fruit arising from worship. In the case of the *prayāja* and other such rites, there is subservience to the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*).

This very quality is what constitutes being a means for accomplishing the *apūrva* (unseen potency) to be achieved by the sacrifice. Since, in the present context, subservience to the sacrifice is established by the aforementioned reasoning, there is no defect whatsoever. || 14 ||
He states the third dharma, which is non-counting of anything: "Non-counting of anything whatsoever. (15)

If even the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati) should speak in contradiction to one's own scripture, then he must not be counted as a guru. For this very reason, the Śruti also says: "One should not count anyone [as a guru]. || 15 ||
He states the fourth [topic], the disclosure of the secret to a worthy disciple:
"The disclosure of the secret to a worthy disciple. (16)

The word "should be done" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*). It is an exception to the prohibition "one should not speak of the secret of the Self," and not an exception to the rule "worship [the deity] in secrecy"; for if it were the latter, there would be no possibility of manifesting the worship before fellow-initiates (*sāmayika*) other than one's own disciple. Therefore, this secret of the Self—

One should not speak of the form of one's own established doctrine to those among the followers of the *sāmāyika* who are not [true] disciples; rather, the meaning is that one should speak it to a good disciple. The quality of being a disciple (*śiṣyatva*) has been set forth in the *Tantrarāja* (p.
Handsome, fair-faced, pure, endowed with faith, and of very steady disposition; free from greed, firm-limbed, acting after due consideration, and having his senses conquered.
"One who is faithful and possesses firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity—such a person should be a disciple; any other causes suffering for the guru. Thus it is said.
In the Ātmapurāṇa as well, it is said:
"The knowledge of Brahman, having become exceedingly distressed, went to a Brāhmaṇa most devoted to Brahman, saying:
'Always protect me, as you would a woman of noble birth.'"
Beginning with these words:
"Always avoid me from those [persons] in whom such faults as these exist;
for by acting thus constantly, I shall be like a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) to you."

The characteristics of unworthy disciples (asattvalakṣaṇa) are to be known in detail from the Kulārṇava [see Appendix 2, section 6, for the knowledge of the characteristics of unworthy disciples]. || 16 ||
He states the fifth duty as the constant pursuit of knowledge: "The constant application of knowledge. (17)
"Always" means at all times, except for the periods prescribed for the performance of daily obligatory rites such as worship; the meaning is "at every [other] time.

The ellipsis to be supplied is that one must perform the "recollection" (*anusaṃhati*) of the "knowledge" (*vidyā*), which is the mantra denoting one's own deity to be worshipped, and the reflection upon the meaning expounded therein.

Alternatively, the meaning is that one should always perform recitation (*japa*) with the mind in continuous succession. Nor should it be suspected that recitation is improper for one who is devoid of rules regarding posture and so forth, because there is no rule whatsoever pertaining to mental [recitation]. As it is said in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
In mental [recitation], the merit is multiplied infinitely; there is no restriction at all therein.
Whether walking, lying down, sitting, or eating, or wherever one may be—whether unwashed or impure—no fault is found therein.
Also in the Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra: "He who, whether restrained or unrestrained, while performing his daily rites, recites the Vidyā mentally alone at all times [attains success]."
Nevertheless, that pure one becomes instantly serene. Thus [it is said].
(33) If there were no restriction on the term "one who is always in distress," then it would follow that the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) could be neglected.
Therefore, as in the case of the statement "all desire wealth," a restriction is necessary. 17.
The sixth duty is stated as: "Constant immersion in Śiva-nature. (18)

The meaning of "constantly" (*satatam*) here is the same as that of the word "always" (*sadā*) found in the preceding sūtra. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the immersion into, or the manifestation of, Śiva-nature must be brought about. The intended sense is that one should contemplate "I am Śiva" at times other than those occupied with the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).

In reality, however, this alternative is proposed with respect to the preceding method; otherwise, it would be impossible to accomplish both meditations simultaneously. The sense is that at times other than those for worship and so forth, one or the other should be practiced [implying that, for the sake of worship, the Self residing within is to be worshipped].

The intended meaning is: after having conceived [the deity] even externally in the form of an image and so forth, and having worshipped it, may there arise in devotees the manifestation of a meditative realization (*bhāvanā*)—consistent with the established doctrine of Vedānta—that "I am that very same God" or "I am the Self."
Or rather: the former teaching is for those of dull faculties, while this is for those of primary (or superior) faculties. || 18 ||
He states the seventh [requirement], the avoidance of desire and so forth:
the avoidance of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, unrighteous violence, theft, and what is loathed by the world.
[Contrary to worldly norms, he is hated by women. || 19 ||

Desire (*kāma*) is indeed an object-oriented longing, taking the form "may this be mine. Anger (*krodha*) is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) produced by the predominance of *tamas*. Greed (*lobha*) is a particular kind of extreme attachment that obstructs the relinquishing of ownership over objects such as wealth. Delusion (*moha*)...

Intoxication (*mada*) is the failure to discriminate between what ought and ought not to be done; it is pride. Envy (*mātsarya*) is the attribution of faults to those possessing virtues, born of hatred. Unprescribed violence (*avihitahiṃsā*) is the slaughter of animals and the like for the sake of consumption out of passion. Theft (*steya*) is the taking of another's property without their consent. That which is loathed by the world (*lokavidviṣṭa*) is [sexual intercourse] even with one regarded as a mother, in private.
Conversation with the wives of others and so forth. The ellipsis implies that the avoidance and renunciation of these must be practiced. || 19 ||
The eighth dharma is service to a single guru; it is stated as "service to a single guru is without doubt" [extending until the conclusion of this sūtra and its commentary].
There is an instruction regarding the practice of honoring [the teacher] as the sole guru and so forth. || 20 ||
In the analysis of the compound *asaṃśayaḥ* as "that in which no doubt exists," it serves as an adjective qualifying the singular worship of the Guru;
the difference in gender is a Vedic archaism (*ārṣa*).
The meaning is as follows: if, while serving many gurus, one were to speak something contrary to what was previously stated by a guru, then doubt would certainly arise;
however, when serving a single guru, such doubt would not arise. Therefore, the intended meaning is that one should serve a single guru.

Since the service of the guru is already established by the preceding sūtra through the two factors of tradition and faith, this re-enactment is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) whose purpose is to exclude reliance on another guru, signifying that one should not resort to a different guru after having relied upon one.
An Investigation into the Meaning of the Method for Worshipping a Single Guru:

Now, it may be argued that resorting to *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is not appropriate, because it entails the three defects [of abandoning what is established, enjoining what is unestablished, and implying the prohibition of something else].
Regarding this *parisaṃkhyā* mentioned here, it is stated in the *Arthasaṃgraha* composed by Laugākṣibhāskara, on page 15.

In the analysis of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification), it is characterized by three defects: the abandonment of the literal meaning, the postulation of a meaning not heard [in the text], and the sublation of what has already been established. Thus, *parisaṅkhyā* possesses these three flaws. Here, the meaning of this verse is also easily understood; however—

Having referred to the teacher who is to be worshipped, only oneness is enjoined; the exclusion of others, however, follows from the fear of omitting an auxiliary (*aṅga*), because oneness is an auxiliary, and its omission would result if one were to worship another teacher. Nor can it be argued that even when resorting to two or more teachers, there is oneness in each individual teacher.

It must be asked: how can there be an omission of the suffix *aṅ*? For it is not "oneness" (*ekatva*) in the form of a numerical category that is prescribed, because as a property common to all entities whatsoever, it would lack the power of exclusion (*avyāvartakatvāt*). Rather, what is intended is the state of being devoid of a second member of the same class; however, if one were to resort to another [technical] term for "heavy" (*guru*), the omission of that suffix would be unavoidable. Therefore, one should not resort to another term for "heavy."

If it is argued that the injunction of oneness alone is superior—let the injunction of oneness be so; however, Śrī Śiva has revealed this very same meaning in the Tantras by way of a different formulation. In the Rudrayāmala:
"It should not be given to the disciples of others; it should be given only to one's own disciples. Thus [it is said].
In the Kulārṇava:
"Having properly obtained a Kula-guru, one should not resort to another guru."
Also in the Yoginītantra: "It should not be given to the disciples of others, nor to an atheist, O Mistress of the Kula."
Even in the *Upaniṣad* it is said: "The Guru is one. In some places, this same point is stated regarding the duty of the disciple;
in other places, it is expressed through a different formulation regarding the duty of the Guru, namely that he should not speak [the teaching] to another disciple.
In both cases, the conclusion is the same: the fruit consists in the worship of a single Guru. This is the intended meaning of these [texts].

The meaning of these words appears as follows: it should be supplied that [this occurs] "when the Guru, who cuts through one's own doubts, is present" within the previously mentioned *Rudrayāmala*, *Kulārṇava*, and *Yoginītantras*. Otherwise— (p.
"Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, goes from one teacher to another. Thus it is said.

In another tantra, the *Śaktirahasya*, it is stated: "The gurus in the Kaula tradition are infinite. Otherwise, such statements would be rendered devoid of meaning. By this [it is shown that] the previous guru was either not omniscient and thus incapable of severing one's own doubts, or else, though capable, failed to sever his own doubts.
A deceased disciple of such a kind should, according to the saying "one greedy for honey [should seek another tree]," resort to another guru.
Even if that other guru possesses only limited knowledge, as long as he is alive, one should accept what is taught by him with his permission. This too has been stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
And one should report to the Lord any mantras, āgamas, and so forth that have been heard elsewhere.
One should accept that by the command of the guru and avoid what is undesirable to him. Thus it is said.

If one is unable to determine for oneself the relative degree of seniority among gurus, one should not abandon the path of whichever guru one has accepted. However, if one is capable of making such a determination, one should privately explain the matter with supporting reasons to that guru and, with his permission, act according to the scriptures.

One should accept it. Even if the guru is alive but does not grant permission due to malice or other such motives, one may disregard him and follow the authoritative path prescribed by the scriptures. This has been clearly stated in the *Tripurārahasya*:
"The wise person, having reflected with his intellect upon what was spoken by the guru and purified by the scriptures..."
"One should perform the Upāsana correctly; otherwise, it is lost. Thus [it is said].

All these points have been made known by the statement "like one greedy for honey. The intended meaning of this sūtra, "service to a single guru," should be described according to the force of the aforementioned arguments.

And those who describe the intention behind the writing of Śrī Bhāskararāya in his *Kaulopaniṣadbhāṣya*—namely, that "whatever is illogical is logical" and that "the oral tradition of the Guru must be accepted even if it is incorrect"—do not understand the true nature of that intention. If one asks, "What is this intention? it is said in reply:
If, in the midst of the Kaulika practice, one's own guru or another Kaulika should act in contradiction to their own established doctrine,
and if [the disciple], overcome by compassion, should seek to enlighten them, he may do so after informing the guru, provided the guru is still living. Or,
if another person who is merely a talkative pedant should set out to defame the Kaula path, [he himself should respond].

Even if one is not proficient due to that deficiency, one should not abandon the conviction regarding its authority there. For this very reason, it is written: "One should not censure the Kaulika practice. Thus, while there is no doubt in oneself regarding the Guru's possession of some knowledge, his mastery of many tantras is certain through long association; yet he does not live.

If a statement found in some Tantra is contrary to that practice, then, because the practice is weaker, its lack of authority— consisting in non-performance— lasts until the source of authority upon which it is based is discovered; this applies to the performance of rites prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti.

According to the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, however, the distinction is that in the Kaula tradition, even that which contradicts the scriptures must be practiced during the aforementioned state of certainty; but this does not apply when there is a certainty regarding the teacher’s dull-wittedness. Likewise, such an intention exists in that very context—namely, in the case of the teacher—because [the teaching] is obtainable solely through the tradition of a true guru.

36) This is made known by the qualification "being a sentient being. The reality here is this: the reason consisting in "possessing conduct that contradicts many scriptures" is an inferential mark for the non-omniscience of the guru, whereas [the reason] in its entirety is an inferential mark for his omniscience.
It is the occasional occurrence of something contrary to that [scripture], while being permitted by scripture.

Now, since the *Kādimata* states the characteristics of a Guru as being "handsome, fair-faced, pure, well-marked, and a knower of many Tantras," how could a disciple appoint as a Guru one who frequently practices in contradiction to the Tantras? For it is not possible that a learned man, having resided for a year for the sake of service, would be ignorant.
It is possible. If one asks how such an example can be both possible and logically consistent:

it is because for one who was previously initiated during a state of ignorance solely through the intensity of faith and had accepted such a guru, but later acquired knowledge through study and other means, [the former state] occurs due to the aforementioned cause.

Because inference is possible, such a prior practice must indeed be abandoned. If one has, by chance, entered upon a wrong path, then even the tradition of a true guru must be abandoned after that point of entering the wrong path, because it is determined to be non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*). Enough of this prolixity.

Amṛtānandanātha, however, states in his commentary on the *Yoginītantra*: "It should not be given to the disciples of others" means that those who have mastered all secrets and the entire supreme reality through the lineage succession (*pāraṃparyakrama*) in other systems of knowledge (*vidyā*), and who have received the complete initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), are the "disciples of others"; [the teaching] should not be given to them.

And this statement from the Kulārṇava is supreme; for it says: "This should be given to those outside [this tradition], just as a bee, greedy for honey, [sips from many flowers]. Regarding such a rule, they say that the authority (māna) belongs only to the Guru who performs the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), and his sandals (pādukā) alone [are authoritative].

That is not so; this statement is merely an indicator of the status of being a *guru* for one who performs the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*. If that were the case, the phrase "the sandals of him alone" would be redundant. If the status of being a *guru* and his name are enjoined within the *gurupādukā* mantra, then the rule "he who performs initiation is the *guru*" implies that his name alone is [to be placed] in the *pādukā*.
"Should be joined"—this is another sentence. And thus, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "that" (*saḥ*) [is unnecessary], because when only the guru's name is being enjoined, its application to the mantra of the guru’s sandals is already established by the other statement, "should be joined";
therefore, the redundancy of the remainder of the text is unavoidable. Consequently, by the statement "greedy for honey" (*madhulubdhaḥ*),...

When various gurus have attained perfection, this [rule] serves as the regulator when all names are applicable to the *pādukā-mantra*. If it were otherwise, there would be no accomplishment of what is desired by others;
on the contrary, by this statement, only the attainment of various gurus is indicated. Therefore, the path we have described is indeed the superior one.
Moreover, the authority of practices contrary to the scriptures is observed even among experts of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, such as the marriage of a maternal cousin among the Āndhras,
as well as the absence of wearing bodices among Dravidian women.
Upon seeing a woman wearing a bodice who is not wearing a bodice,
or seeing a widow with her hair loose, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Thus, this contradicts the statement of Aṅgiras; therefore, there is no sublation whatsoever.

37) If one were to trust only in the guru, then even while standing, if he were to perform the voiding of urine or excrement, it would follow that one must do so as well. And if there is some statement regarding one who is learned in many tantras...

Upon seeing something contrary to that [scripture], one apprehends its lack of authority regarding that practice; does this apprehension of non-authority apply to that specific part, or to the whole? Not the first, because in the world, when there is a practice by someone like Caitra whose lack of authority has not been previously apprehended, if a lack of authority were ever apprehended in one instance, it would follow that it must be so in all instances.

It is observed in the world that people do not place their trust due to the suspicion of invalidity; likewise here as well, if there is a single instance of deviation, the consequence would be the non-performance of all [actions] due to such suspicion. And that suspicion does not depart anywhere without the observation of a fundamental basis (*mūla*). If one were to exert oneself for the sake of purifying the basis in every case, then—

The rule for following the tradition would be rendered meaningless. Nor should it be argued that where there is an alternative consisting of two options, the rule for practicing the tradition of one's own guru becomes meaningful; for if these two options were established as distinct according to the difference in qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), then in the Tantric scriptures—

The state of being an object of conceptual construction would not exist in any way whatsoever. Just as, for example, regarding the placement of the special arghya vessel, there were options such as a tripod, a quadruped, or no support at all, and the Guru practiced the tripod alone, and the disciple likewise practiced it; sometimes the tripod was lost and the quadruped was obtained by him.

The performance [of the rite] would not occur because it has not been performed by the Guru; thus, there would be no manifestation of an option (*vikalpa*). For an option exists only when two positions are combined within a single ritual action performed by one person through distinct applications (*prayoga*).

Furthermore, the rule of placing trust in the words of the guru would be rendered useless. For one who is intent on investigating the source of a teaching for the sake of removing doubt, how could there be such extreme trust in the guru’s words? Therefore, having inferred the guru’s competence—[in order to know what kind of guru is intended here and to understand that knowledge]—one should proceed.
And one should have faith in the words of the true guru.

Umānandanātha, having concluded the statement "serving a single guru," applied the phrase "there is no doubt anywhere" and explained it as meaning that there is no doubt regarding the words of the guru, at the beginning of the scriptures, and everywhere else. That is not so; for all success comes through faith in the tradition, and authority consists primarily in faith.
For, since this very meaning has already been established by these two [preceding statements], its repetition would result in tautology. || 20 ||
He states the ninth quality, non-possessiveness in all respects: "Non-possessiveness in all respects. (21)

In all instances, such as in the *Mañcapañcaka* and other texts, "niṣparigrahatā" means the state of being "niṣparigraha. One who is "niṣparigraha" is one from whom "parigraha"—meaning possession or desire—has departed. According to Amarasimha: "Wife, retinue, property, and the root of curses are 'parigrahas'. Here, the root of "parigraha," which is "taking" (*ādāna*), is indeed desire itself. Following such a lexicon:

The word *parigraha* denotes desire; the meaning is that one should not accept [possessions] out of the desire, "May my collection of things increase. This very point is clearly established in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (p.
38): [text follows].

Since the consumption of liquor was ordained for the Gandharvas and likewise the immolation of animals is not considered violence, they know this pure self-dharma: that sexual union is for the sake of progeny and not for pleasure.
But those men who, not knowing this, are arrogant, full of self-conceit,
and boldly mistreat animals— they devour them after death.

Thus, "eating by smelling" is declared in the scripture; "eating" refers to the act of slaying animals and the like for the sake of a deity with the intention of relinquishment, which is called "slaughtering."
Alternatively, in all cases regarding every mere object, one must cultivate non-possessiveness—that is, the relinquishing of the sense of "mine" through one's own intellect;
in other words, the feeling of "mineness" (mamatā) must be abandoned everywhere.

Furthermore, the statement in the *Nityotsava-nibandha* that wealth should not be acquired with the intention of personal enjoyment is contrary to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Jaimini, who— in the fourth chapter— refuted the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and concluded that the acquisition of wealth is solely for the sake of the person (*kevalapuruṣārtha*).
He states the tenth dharma, which consists of action preceded by the renunciation of its fruit:
"Performing action while having abandoned its fruit. (22)
The previously mentioned result is artificial, as is its means—namely, dharma, artha, and kāma.

The meaning of the word "result" (phala) is the desire directed toward that result. Having abandoned that, one performs the prescribed action; this is the implied sense. The meaning is that optional (kāmya) action should not be performed. Optional action...

Since it is stated that "one should act" while omitting the word "fruit" where one ought to have said "it should not be done," it is understood that even those actions performed for the sake of desire (kāmya-karmāṇi) must be undertaken with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord.
But is it not said in the Bhagavad Gītā:
"O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom"?

If it is argued that the worship with desire (*sakāmopāsanā*) has been taught by the Blessed One, and thus there is a contradiction—[we reply]: No; by the verse "Those four kinds of devotees who worship Me," the natural disposition of the world (*lokasvabhāva*) has been shown. [The Lord] declared that "desirable action (*kāmya-karma*) should not be performed. For this very reason...
And he who renounces the fruits of action is called a renouncer.
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is constantly disciplined, and who is devoted to the One alone, is preeminent.
Thus ends the praise of action free from desire. || 22 ||
(On page 39) He states the eleventh duty: the non-omission of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).
The omission of obligatory duties [is a transgression]. || 23 ||

That which is both constant and an action is "constant action" (*nityakarman*), such as bathing, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), worship, and so forth. The omission of that—its non-performance—is "the omission of constant action" (*nityakarmalopa*). That practitioner in whom the omission of constant action does not exist is one for whom there is no omission of constant action (*anityakarmalopa*). The word "should be" (*bhavet*) is to be supplied. The meaning is that constant action must necessarily be performed.

While it should have been stated simply that "the obligatory rite must be performed," the statement is made by way of negation (vyatireka) to indicate that in the case of its omission, there is not only a deficiency in the sacrifice, but also sin and rebirth in hell. || 23 ||

Now, in response to the doubt as to how the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) is to be performed when the five-fold time (*pañcakāla*)—which serves as its means—is not obtained, he says: "Even when the five-fold time is not obtained, there is the recollection of the obligatory sequence. (24)
In the absence of the five [ingredients], there is no lapse of the ritual (*karmalopa*) because the primary substance is not present;

rather, the sequence of the obligatory rite (*nityakrama*), the obligatory worship (*nityapūjā*), its retrospective recollection (*pratyavamṛṣṭi*), and its performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) must be carried out even by means of a substitute (*pratinidhi*). This is the remainder [of the argument].
Now, one might object: "In the sixth chapter, it was stated that in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, in the absence of rice (*vrīhi*), there is a lapse of the ritual."

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached as follows: since the visible result of the *puroḍāśa* cake can be achieved even with *nīvāra* grass, the requirement for *vrīhi* rice in the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) may be omitted; furthermore, because an obligatory rite can tolerate the omission of some of its subsidiary parts, both obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*) may be performed even by means of a substitute (*pratinidhi*).

If it is argued that, since such a principle is rooted in logic, the practice of using substitutes (*pratinidhi*) is observed even in Vedic and Smārta rituals, and therefore a scriptural injunction (*vacana*) is redundant here as well because the substitute is established by that very reasoning—[the answer is:
no. For while [the substitute] might apply to occasional rites (*naimittika*) by the same logic as it applies to obligatory rites (*nitya*), in that case, by means of the substitute...

Let there be no accomplishment through the sequence of occasional rites (*naimittika*), because this is for that specific purpose. Nor does it follow from this that, in the absence [of the primary], that which is distinct from the obligatory (*nitya*) need not be performed; for if that were the case, it would take the form of an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) based on Vedic scripture (as seen in the commentary on the Sūtra following this section, in the marginal note of the *Kārikā*).

It must be stated that there arises a triad of defects— namely, the abandonment of one's own purpose (*svārthatyāga*), the assumption of another’s purpose (*parārthakalpanā*), and the sublation of what has been obtained (*prāptabādha*)—

as argued by Pārthasārathi in the *Tantraratna* within the section on the *Abhyudayeṣṭi*, regarding the fear of the redundancy of the sentence "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts" (*tredhā taṇḍulān vibhajet*), which leads to the principle that a sentence is completed with each individual subject (*pratyuddeśyaṃ vākyaparisamāpti*).

A split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) has been accepted; how much more so, then, in accepting three defects out of such fear? For this very reason, our supreme gurus, the venerable and worshipful P. Bhāskararāya, stated in the *Setubandha* on the *Uttara-catuśśatī*: "[Having understood this much, these are the venerable feet of the illustrious Bhāṣyakṛt, our supreme preceptor...]"

In the second verse, two hundred [units] further, within the section on occasional rites (*naimittika-prakaraṇa*), it is stated: "One should especially perform the wheel-worship (*cakrapūjā*) for the yoginīs. Having first explained the word *viśeṣeṇa* (especially) found in the root text as meaning "by means of an abundance of foods such as edibles and non-edibles, etc., in comparison to the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) due to the preeminence of the yoginīs and heroes," [the author proceeds].

The meaning is: "by means of dissatisfaction with that" or "by means of a special substance. Therefore, even in the case of daily worship (*nityapūjā*), [the rite proceeds] despite the non-availability of a special substance.

Having explained that the mention of "accomplishment by means of a substitute" indicates permission only for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) and not elsewhere, this very statement is shown as the proof for this point. || 24 ||
He states the twelfth quality, fearlessness everywhere:
"Fearlessness everywhere [in all respects]. || 25 ||
In every respect and from all sides, when adopting the fivefold manifestation (*pañcakasvīkāra*) and following the Kaula path, one must achieve the state of being "fearless" (*nirbhaya*);
that is, he from whom fear has departed regarding all those scriptures which teach of hell and other such states. This is the sense to be understood. All of those [scriptures]...

The meaning is that although the scriptures may indeed frighten one who possesses passion, let them do so; however, I am not one possessed by passion, but rather am impelled by the scripture. Thus, through the firm determination that "I have no fear," one should achieve fearlessness. || 25 ||
The Dharma that constitutes the very essence of all is the oblation (*homa*) into the supreme *śiva* of one's own self.

He describes the Dharma which is the essence of all established doctrines (*siddhānta*): "All that is knowable is the sacrificial offering (*havya*); the senses are the ladles (*sruk*); and the powers (*śakti*) are the flames (*jvālā*)."

One's own self is Śiva, the purifier, and one is oneself the officiating priest. [The weight of the venerable *Brahmabhāvanā* and other tantric texts beginning with this sūtra is evident here. || 26 ||

The word "iti" (thus) implies that one should meditate in this manner; the phrase "by means of the modifications of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttibhiḥ*)—the meaning of the words *vedya* and so forth in this sūtra is very clear in the commentary below—should be supplied at the beginning of the term *vedyam*. Everything cognizable by the modifications of the internal organ is to be regarded as an oblation (*havis*).

One should contemplate as follows: just as an oblation cast into the fire assumes the form of that [fire], so too, when all the objects of consciousness (vedya) are offered into the fire of Śiva, they attain the nature of Śiva; therefore, it is appropriate to contemplate them as being the oblation itself.
Only the *juhū*—which serves as the receptacle for such an oblation and functions as the instrument of the *homa*—is understood by the term *sruk*.

Although the *dhruvā* and other vessels are also denoted by the word *sruk*, they are unsuitable within the context of the *homa-bhāvanā* because, despite being designated as *sruk*, they do not function as instruments of the *homa*. [From here onwards...]

By the passage of the Bhāṣya ending with "aprakṛtavicāreṇa," it is shown that there is very little scriptural significance in the singular and plural numbers residing in the single word that serves as a qualifier.
Nor should it be argued that the plural number is untenable because of the singularity of the *sruva* ladles, for [the plural is justified] by the multiplicity of the sense organs (*indriya*).

The plural number is used so that the qualifier may be in grammatical agreement (samānavacana) with its referent. Nor is there a rule requiring non-agreement in number in cases where something is superimposed upon another; for this very reason, it is said in the *Naiṣadha* (p.

By the use of the particle *eva* here, it is indicated that when one is unable to perform a ritual oneself due to another task, one may employ a son, a beloved wife, or others as a substitute agent (*kartṛ-pratinidhi*), and it is established by scripture that through such a substitute, the fruit born of that action accrues [to the original performer]. However, it is suggested that if this sacrifice is performed by a substitute, the fruit produced by the action does not belong to oneself.
The fruit of cultivation is the attainment of one's true self.
Thus, he states the fruit of cultivation performed in this manner:
"The fruit is the discernment of consciousness free from objects. (27)

The fruit is the discernment of consciousness (citi) which is objectless and non-conceptual in form; this refers to the aforementioned meditation [meaning the true meditation stated from the 13th sūtra on page 30 up to the end of the 27th sūtra]. This is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 27 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the use of attaining such a fruit? To this, he says:
"There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self. (28)

"Superior to the attainment of self"—that is, superior to the attainment of one's own nature—the phrase "the highest fruit" from the preceding sūtra is supplied here. The meaning is that nothing exists beyond it; it does not exist [beyond]. The Śruti confirms this point: "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal," and "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here."

He establishes this: no one disputes that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). Therefore, the sense is that through such contemplation, the attainment of the supreme human goal occurs. Previously—in the first section, on page 26, in the sixth aphorism—the investigation into the dog was the human goal.
By this, the nature of the goal of human endeavor has been established; since this constitutes a praise here, there is no tautology.

Up to this point, having examined the two works spoken by Śrī Paraśurāma— which consist of the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) of the five traditions (*pañcāmnāya*)— these have been celebrated for their names, meanings, and greatness. However, a certain Keśavaśarman, being incapable of understanding their intended meaning, seeks to refute them.

Thus, he uttered these senseless ravings out of sheer envy alone; for by the mere sight of that work, the wise will come to know its lack of logical foundation. However, for the sake of dispelling the doubts of those of dull intellect, I myself have demonstrated in my own *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* that those arguments are nothing but mere prattle.
It is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity; those who desire to know it should learn it from that very source. || 28 ||
The conclusion of the established doctrine:
beginning with "In this regard, this is the established doctrine," he concludes the matter under discussion—this is the style of the treatise. || 29 ||

This very style of the scripture mentioned previously is the "śāstra"—that which instructs (śāsti)—in the form of the five traditions (pañcāmnāya); it is its style (śailī), its manner (rīti). This is the completion of the sense. || 29 ||
42) This knowledge is extremely secret; [the author] praises such a scripture for the sake of inciting the listener to engage with it:
Like a courtesan, the sciences such as the Vedas are manifest;
this science, however, is hidden within all philosophical systems.
The sciences, beginning with the Vedas, are as easily accessible as courtesans. By the word "beginning" (ādi), the Smṛtis and other texts are included.

Just as the enjoyment of a courtesan is easily obtained through the expenditure of wealth and such, so too the acquisition of the knowledge of the Vedas and other sciences is easily obtained by the giving of wealth and other gifts. That study is rooted in greed is established by the scripture itself.
Among the six types of occupations, it has been established that three are means of livelihood;
however, this Brahmavidyā, which serves as the means for liberation, cannot be obtained even by the expenditure of millions of gold coins, but is obtainable solely through the grace of the Guru.

If it is asked, "Why would the Guru not show compassion even upon the expenditure of abundant wealth?"—the answer is that he simply would not. For one by whom the knowledge of Brahman has been attained, ten million pieces of gold are more insignificant than a blade of grass;
how, then, could there be greed for such things?

[Objection: Let it be that one engages [in worldly activity] out of greed; nevertheless, since there is no loss to oneself when engaging in the gift of knowledge at the request of another, let one engage in it. Moreover, this is more manifest than the former [point], because while the previous knowledge was obtainable only by one possessing wealth, this [knowledge] can be obtained even by one who is destitute. [Reply: No, for a learned man does not [act] merely at the request of another.
One who acts would act only after seeing the accomplishment of the desired effect regarding the object he has set forth, and not in vain.

In the present case, this knowledge of Brahman, when imparted to those with defiled internal organs, is not only fruitless, but it actually destroys the knowledge of the teacher as well. Regarding this matter, Yāska has cited the following Śruti:
"Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained; thus shall I be full of power.
The meaning of this is very clear."
The knowledge of Brahman, having been thoroughly refined, went to a Brāhmaṇa most devoted to Brahman, saying:
"Always protect me, as you would a woman born of noble family;
I am your inexhaustible treasure, both in this world and in the next."
Beginning with these words:
"Always avoid me from those [teachers] in whom such faults as these exist;
for by acting thus constantly, I shall be to you like a wish-fulfilling cow."
Otherwise, I shall become barren, like a creeper devoid of fruit.
By such statements as these, it is heard that for a guru himself, the destruction of his own knowledge occurs when imparting knowledge to an unworthy recipient.
How, then, could he teach knowledge to an unworthy person merely out of a desire to help others? A fit recipient for such instruction is difficult to find.

Therefore, [the locative case] "among all philosophical systems" (*sarvadarśaneṣu*) is used in the sense of selection; the meaning is that this aforementioned knowledge is hidden and difficult to obtain.

But contemporary teachers are sellers of the knowledge of Brahman like merchants; in that case, there is neither true teacherhood nor the removal of the disciple's distress. On the contrary, he too, being engaged in the passion for the pursuit of wealth, surely falls. Thus, both of them perform only the means for falling, not the means for liberation.
As it is said in the *Kulārṇava* [Prabodhacandrodaya, 1.1]:
"There are many gurus who plunder the wealth of their disciples;
but rare, O Goddess, is this guru who removes the suffering of his disciples."
Thus, enough with further elaboration. || 30 ||
The procedure for initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*):
having thus far restated the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—
meaning the established doctrine concerning the worship and mantras of the respective deities— the practitioner must first...
He states the action to be performed:
"In that regard, the wise man should by all means undergo initiation. (31)

The seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) has the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*); the meaning of the base (*prakṛty-artha*) is the worship of Śrīvidyā; the sense of the sixth case is a relation, specifically the state of occurring immediately prior to that [initiation]; this [relation] connects by way of being the locus (*āśrayatā*) within the referent of the term "initiation" (*dīkṣā*), and that [initiation] connects with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) by way of the relation of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*). And thus:

The specific understanding is that one should contemplate the desired object through initiation (dīkṣā) which immediately precedes the worship of Śrīvidyā; for this very reason, it is an originative injunction (utpattividhi). In every way, a wise person who has already ascended—or is desirous of ascending—the aforementioned stages [as indicated by the word "mārurukṣuḥ" in the commentary] must do so, precisely because of the inherent force of the meaning of these words.

This is also a rule concerning qualification (*adhikāravidhi*). It is established that qualification belongs only to one who desires to ascend to such a stage (*bhūmikā*), and indeed only to one who has already ascended, and not to anyone else.

If it is asked, "How can both the status of being an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) and the status of being an injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) reside in one and the same injunction?"—the answer is: no, because such is observed in cases like "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā" (*citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ*). Furthermore, it was established previously that in the case of meditation (*upāsanā*), there is qualification for one who has ascended to such a stage [and not for one merely desiring to ascend].

For initiation (*dīkṣā*) is not meditation (*upāsanā*); how then could there be a requirement for such qualification even here? And as for the statement that initiation is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of meditation, this is merely a restatement of a matter established by logic—namely, "he who is qualified for the principal (*pradhāna*) is [automatically] qualified for its subordinate parts"—which has been expressed by the word "intelligent" (*matimān*).

That interpretation is not satisfactory, because the reiteration would be rendered purposeless due to the absence of any result, and because initiation possesses its own independent fruit and is therefore not a subordinate member [of the ritual]. By this very [reasoning], p.
The eligibility for initiation (dīkṣā) is prescribed for one who has ascended to such a stage [i.e., the seeker of liberation (rurukṣu)—a.

It will be stated later that only one who has been initiated is eligible for spiritual practice (upāsanā). This being the case, the state of having ascended to the aforementioned stages is an implicit requirement for spiritual practice [i.e., the state of being a seeker of liberation (rurukṣutva)—a.].
The Definition of Initiation (*dīkṣā*) and its Result:

Now, what is the nature of initiation? It cannot first of all be defined as "an action that generates fitness for meditation," because there is no evidence for the existence of such a generative capacity. Nor can it be known through perception, since [initiation] is a transcendental (*alaukika*) matter.
It is not possible. Nor is there inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor is there a scriptural statement (*śruti*) such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," from which its status as a cause could be established.
And just as for the twice-born there is no eligibility for all ritual acts without initiation (*upanayana*), so too here there is none without it.

"O descendant of Bhṛgu, [one should perform] initiation"— thus, because the *Tripurārahasya* establishes that the causal relation is rooted in negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), just as "in the absence of a staff,

there is the absence of a jar," one might say that the causal relation is thereby proven. However, this must be stated [with qualification], for the passage "the initiated person should practice meditation" is merely a praise of the eligibility for meditation (*upāsanādhikāri*).

If it is asked, "What then is the fruit of initiation (dīkṣā)?"—it is said: it is the destruction of that impurity in the form of sin accumulated over infinite millions of births. This has been stated in the *Tantrāloka* [specifically in its commentary on the *Niśāṭana*, which is the commentary on the *Tantrāloka*]: [The text continues: "The fruit of initiation is the destruction of the impurity consisting of sins accumulated over infinite millions of births. Thus it is said in the *Tantrāloka*.
Even when the internal knowledge consisting of the individual self has dissolved through initiation,
conceptual construction may still arise, because that which resides in the intellect has not yet ceased.
Liberation occurs only at the end of the body through the destruction of personal ignorance;
however, upon the cessation of intellectual ignorance, it is certain through the uprooting of conceptual construction.
"At that very moment, liberation occurs," so it was said by the Creator in the venerable *Niśāṭana*. Thus [it is stated].

The meaning of this is as follows: knowledge is twofold, namely, the spiritual (*pauruṣa*) and the intellectual (*bauddha*).
