Among these, spiritual knowledge consists of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Intellectual knowledge is that which arises from the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), takes the form of the final mental modification (*caramavṛtti*), and is called the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This [intellectual knowledge] also serves as the veil for ignorance (*ajñāna*).

It is twofold. Among these, the *pauruṣa* [impurity] is the sin residing in the person (*puruṣa*). The *bauddha* [impurity] is the cognition of duality. Therein, although the *pauruṣa* knowledge is destroyed by initiation (*dīkṣā*), because the *bauddha* impurity is to be destroyed only by the knowledge of the scriptures (*śāstra-jñāna*), liberation occurs at that very moment upon the attainment of the knowledge of the *Āgama-siddhānta* immediately following initiation—if [this is done].
It is said that for such a person, no knowledge of the scriptures has been acquired and only initiation has occurred; yet, at the end of the body, liberation occurs.
Nor should it be doubted how liberation can happen at the end of the body if the impurities of the intellect (*bauddhamala*) are absent; for the *Tripurārahasya* states:
"But those who possess initiation, having reached the world higher than the highest at the end of the body..."
They have been fully awakened by Sadāśiva, who is the very form of Śiva.
Thus, since such a doubt has been refuted;

likewise, even in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the *agniṣṭoma* and other Vedic sacrifices, it is heard [in scripture]: "for the removal of evil" (*pāpmano 'pahatyai*).

Similarly, in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā as well, regarding the production of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) resulting from the sacrifice through initiation, [it is compared] to the production of crops and so forth.
In the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*, it is established that [the practice] is like the plowing of a field, serving as a means of purifying the self. (p. 45)

In the first chapter, there is also the sign that as soon as the five-syllable mantra entered the king's ear, infinite crows emerged from his body. Likewise, in the Paramānanda Tantra, in the etymological explanation of the term "initiation" (dīkṣā):
"Union with Śiva is bestowed (dīyate) and the bondage of the fetters is torn asunder (dīryate/kṣīyate); therefore it is called initiation (dīkṣā). And so forth.
Thus, in accordance with many such authorities, [this refers to] the statement establishing negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti).
Because it is of the nature of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), this definition would thus be impossible.
If it is argued that, following the primary sense of the statement—"By this [work], the introduction of the twelfth chapter occurs within the mass of bliss of good fortune;
now he asks for initiation, which establishes her fitness for worship along with its ancillaries"—a justification is impossible, we say: no.
Because the very definition of being faultless is the state of performing a function that serves to remove the human impurities which are obstacles to liberation.

Nor should it be said that this investigation of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛtalakṣaṇa*) and the subsequent investigation into its purpose—which depends upon the former—are useless for actual practice and are thus merely an examination of a crow’s teeth intended to display pure scholarship;
for there is indeed a distinction regarding practice: if [the investigation] generates the aforementioned fitness (*yogyatā*), then...

In the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for initiation, [it is stated] "for the sake of establishing fitness" according to one view, and "for the sake of the destruction of sin" according to the other view.

An investigation into the methods of the ritual resolve (*dīkṣā-saṃkalpa*). [From here follows the occasion for the disciple’s resolve to receive initiation (*dīkṣā*) and its investigation— furthermore, this is to be seen in Volume 2, Part 10, Section 5, for the sake of knowledge concerning the object of all resolves.]
Furthermore, that which appears in the *Nityotsavanibandha*—
namely, "Desiring my own welfare, I shall receive initiation from such-and-such a guru for the purpose of acquiring such-and-such a vidyā"—
was written through extreme inattention. For instance, let alone that phrase "desiring welfare" (*śreyaskāma*).

For the destruction of sin is, in some sense, itself a form of spiritual welfare (*śreyaḥ*). As for the claim that [initiation] is "for the purpose of acquiring such-and-such a knowledge," that is utterly impure, because it has been established that initiation has the singular function of destroying sin.
Or, let it be that its purpose is the acquisition of knowledge—like the son of a barren woman—even so, one who desires spiritual welfare...

If that [result] were obtained by this very [means], then this word would be entirely redundant. Nor should it be argued that the acquisition of the knowledge of the *śreyas* (the highest good) and the [acquisition of the sacrifice itself] are two distinct results, and therefore both are mentioned; for although the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are the means for all fruits—as in the rule "the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* for all [desires]"—their distinctness as results occurs only through a difference in performance (*prayoga*), not through a single performance.
The claim that there are two fruits is to be disregarded because it contradicts the logic established in the *Cāturthika* [section]. For this very reason, the *Tantraratna* states:
"In the world, it is observed that a single [cause] produces a single, fixed, and uniform fruit through a single type of operation.
In that case, let the property of producing a uniform [fruit] from all [causes] be set aside by the scriptural statement; but by what [authority] is the production of a single fruit [set aside]?"

"Let it be refuted," said Pārthasārathi. Furthermore, the meaning of the term *dīkṣā* consists of the entry of power (*śakti-praveśa*), the placement of steps (*caraṇa-vinyāsa*), and the instruction of mantras (*mantra-upadeśa*). Is it such an initiation that is the means to the fruit, or rather the grasping of it? In the first case, regarding the resolve (*saṃkalpa*):

In the first case, which means "I shall produce the action that serves as the means for the result," the phrase "I shall grasp the word denoting the action that serves as the means for the result" is redundant. In the second case, [the question arises whether] the grasping itself is the means.

[This view] is rootless and contradicts previous statements. Furthermore, is the fruit of pronouncing "of such-and-such a guru" perceived or unperceived, as in the case of pronouncing the lunar day (tithi) and so forth? It cannot be the first [alternative], for apart from the manifestation of one's own will—namely, "May this person be my guru"—it is difficult to describe any other perceived fruit; and that [will] arises precisely through the act of choosing him as written down.

What purpose could there be in pronouncing these? It cannot be the latter [that they produce an unseen merit (*apūrva*)], because of the statement, "having proclaimed the place and time," which establishes that those [names] generate an *apūrva*. Indeed, there is no such statement as "having pronounced the names of the teachers" by which an unseen merit might arise from them.

Furthermore, the desired fruit—consisting of the acquisition of the knowledge of the highest good—is inherent to oneself (*svaniṣṭha*). If that were the case, the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in "I shall grasp" (*grahīṣyāmi*) would contradict the grammatical rule of Pāṇini: "The *parasmaipada* is used when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*)" for roots marked with a svarita accent or the letter *ṇ*. Thus, because it is beset by many such defects, [the opponent's position is untenable].

The mere intention (*saṃkalpa*) is not to be disregarded; rather, for the sake of removing ignorance regarding human effort, the very resolution "I shall be initiated by means of the Śrīvidyā" is superior.

The enumeration of the eight limbs, which constitutes a component of the Tantric resolve (*saṃkalpa*), [this description of the eight limbs is not found in some authoritative sources]. There is no mention of the eight limbs in the resolve for the disciple, because, being devoid of initiation (*dīkṣā*), he lacks the qualification for the Tantric path. Hereafter...
In the teacher’s formal resolve (saṃkalpa), that mention is necessary; likewise, for the disciple as well, there must be a mention in the rites occurring subsequent to initiation.

If it is asked, "Since it is not mentioned in the *Aṣṭāṅga-sūtra*, why is it included here?"—this is true. Although there is no explicit mention [there], nevertheless, in all rites belonging to the Śruti and Smṛti, a preliminary resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is observed to be invariably present at the outset. In the present case as well, such a resolve is likewise necessary. The necessity of the resolve is stated in the root text:

An even greater worship of Gaṇeśa is now described. What is called *saṃkalpa* is a formal resolve (*pratijñā*) concerning the performance of a specific rite, preceded by the mention of the present time and place and accompanied by the mention of the intended fruit. As it is said in the *Rahasyārṇava*:
"Uttering the name of the country where the practitioner resides, having delineated that very place at that time, and having stated the vow for the ritual—
'I [shall perform this] with a view toward the fruit'— this is the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) following the gesture of the hand held like a vessel of water. Thus it is said.

In this context, because time— consisting of five components— is closely related [to the ritual] by way of the "maxim of accepting the horse" (*aśvapratigrahanyāya*) to that which consists of eight components, it is necessary for those who follow the Sūtras to mention the eight components. Therefore,
the eight components and the method of accomplishing them are now stated.

In that regard, the eight components are: 1) the yuga, 2) the revolution (parivṛtti), 3) the year, 4) the month, 5) the day, 6) the constant (nityā), 7) the weekday, and 8) the rising of the ghaṭikā. According to the Tantric scripture, there are 36 yugas; for one yuga there are 36 revolutions; for one revolution there are 36 years; for one year there are 16 months; and for one month there are 36 days.
Thirty *nityās*, nine *vāras*, and five *ghaṭikā*-arising; thus is the means for the accomplishment of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅgasiddhi*) described.

on whichever day one desires the *ahargaṇa*, one should add to the *ahargaṇa* the number of that [day's] transit (*saṃkrānti*) which occurred immediately prior to it— a number which will be explained— and then, starting from that transit...
One should add the number of days elapsed up to the desired day;

this becomes the *ahargaṇa* (day-count) for the desired day. In that regard, from Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces, [one calculates] the ghaṭīs starting from the beginning of the Yuga and so forth.

The names are stated as follows: the names of the thirty-six years of the *yugas* (cycles) are, in sequence, the names of the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*. Just as the first *yuga* consists of the letter *a*, so too the second is *aya*, *kaya*, and so on; this should be understood for the subsequent *parivṛtti*-years as well. [This applies to] the sixteen months.

The names are, in sequence, the sixteen vowels. On the thirty-six days, the thirty-six letters from *a* to *kṣ*, together with the *anusvāra*, combined with the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, constitute the names in order. For example:

Regarding the phrase "the day of the Śiva-tattva": there are thirty syllables, beginning with *a* and ending with the *anusvāra*, devoid of the final vowel (*aḥ*), arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order. There are fifteen Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā; these, combined in both direct and reverse order, total thirty. The names of the Nityās are as follows: *aṃ* Kāmeśvarī.

Regarding the phrase "in the eternal": for the nine days, there are nine syllables in sequence: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, and ṣa. [These correspond to] Prakāśānandanātha, Vimarśānandanātha, Ānandānandanātha, Jñānānandanātha, Satyānandanātha, Pūrṇānandanātha, Svabhāvānandanātha, [and so forth].

Pratibhānanda-nātha, Dattānanda-nātha, and Subhagānanda-nātha—these are the nine Nāthas. The nine vowels which are the excellent days (vāra) correspond respectively to the nine Nāthas as the nine days. For example: *aṃ* is the day of Prakāśānanda-nātha.

The names of the five *udaya-ghaṭikās* should be known as the five syllables *a*, *e*, *ca*, *ta*, and *ya* in their respective order. Thus, the mention of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) is necessary at the beginning of Tantric rites and the like. Since the specific location is not mentioned in the Tantra, the mention follows that of the Smṛti.

However, some tantrikas, following the *Paramānandatantra*, maintain that the eight-limbed [vow] (*aṣṭāṅga*) is not innate (*sahaja*), asserting instead a synthesis of the time well-known in the scriptures, stating: "Having mentioned both place and time, one should likewise abide in the eight limbs.
To this, we reply: regarding the phrase "place and time," what kind of time is intended here? This is what must be clarified.
The eight-limbed path mentioned in the *Tantra* is not intended as a rule for their simultaneous practice, due to the inherent force of the word "only" (*eva*).
Thus, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "I, belonging to such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), studying such-and-such branch (*śākhā*), and named such-and-such (Śarmā, etc.),

for the sake of attaining the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) and for the sake of obtaining the grace of my desired deity, choose you— belonging to such-and-such lineage, studying such-and-such branch, and named such-and-such (Śarmā)— to be my preceptor (*guru*)."
What is the use of following the Kalpasūtras?

Whether it be much or little, whatever has been proclaimed for a particular person in their own Gṛhya-sūtra— when that much of the scriptural purpose has been performed, everything is considered performed.

Following this statement (p. 49), regarding whether this ritual application is performed by synthesizing all tantras or according to one's own preference without synthesizing other tantras: it cannot be the former, because the selection [of a specific tantra] is not mentioned in the Sūtra.

In the second [case], according to another tantra, the abandonment of the image, the selection of Brahmā and others, the preparation of the sacrificial porridge (caru), and its consumption is improper. The third [case] is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination and is simply untrustworthy. Furthermore, in another tantra—
"O Maheśvarī, I choose you as the preceptor (ācārya) for the purpose of performing and causing the performance of the initiation rite (dīkṣākarma)," [saying this] near her feet.

Thus, even when the act of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) is about to be performed, he says that one should simply say, "I choose you as the preceptor" (*ācāryaṃ vṛṇe*). In all cases of choosing officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), whether in Śrauta or Smārta rites, the established practice is: "In this establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), I choose you as the Adhvaryu," or "In this rite called the Udyāpana, I choose you as my preceptor."

It is observed that here, however, having abandoned the term *karma* which denotes the fruit, it is written in the *varaṇavākya* for the sake of accomplishing the goal of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and for the sake of favor (*anugraha*). This is exceedingly strange. Therefore, those who follow the Sūtras should not perform the *varaṇa*. Nor, in the absence of *varaṇa*, by one who has not been chosen as a Guru...

It must be stated how the ritual action (karman) is to be performed; for that [action] is possible even through a worldly request such as "Please confer initiation upon me. Indeed, we do not reject the request in every respect; rather, we simply maintain that the request is a constituent part of the ritual action.

In the same way, the *puṇyāhavācana* and the *nāndīśrāddha* are not to be performed [here], because they have not been mentioned. Nor can it be argued that there should be no incorporation of other ritual manuals (*tantrāntara*); nevertheless, the *puṇyāhavācana* and the *nāndīśrāddha*, being established by *smṛti*, are unavoidable. Otherwise, even the act of sipping water (*ācamana*), which is required by the rule "one should sip water after sneezing," would likewise not take place.

It should be said that this would be so if the Puṇyāhavācana and Nāndīśrāddha were merely followed as they are already established by the Smṛti within the Tantric system; however, in another Tantra it is stated:
"Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should pronounce the Puṇyāha and worship the Nāndīmukhas."

Thus, the injunction would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, this very point serves as the indicator that the Smṛti-based dharmas, such as the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) rites, do not enter as auxiliary parts of the ritual (*karmāṅga*). Furthermore, that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), such as "one should sip water after sneezing" and "one should not eat *kalañja*," is already established and unavoidable.

Nor should it be said that there would likewise be no attainment of the qualities characterized as those of disciple and teacher; for there is indeed scope for their attainment. In that regard, one should fulfill the expectancy even by taking what is found in another tantra, provided that without it the expectancy is not satisfied. Expectancy is a factor in verbal cognition.

There are two kinds [of expectancy]: that which has already arisen (*utthita*) and that which is to be aroused (*utthāpyā*). For example, when the first [type] is expressed as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the questions "What does he cook?", "With what does he cook?", and "Who is cooking? arise spontaneously. In the second case, such as "He cooks little" (*stokaṃ pacati*), the expectancy "How does he cook? must be aroused due to the fear of the word *stoka* being redundant. In the former instance, [the expectancy] arises naturally.

Since verbal expectancy (*śābdākāṅkṣā*) is not resolved without a word, it is necessary to supply a word either through *adhyāhāra* (mental insertion) or by taking one from another location. In that case, rather than resorting to *adhyāhāra*, it is better to satisfy the expectancy with a word already present in another part of the system (*tantrāntara*). This being so, the wise person [who follows this]—[this connected...]*

[Sūtra 31 on leaf 43: When it is stated that "one should initiate," since mere intelligence (*matimattva*) alone does not serve as a differentiator, the inquiry necessarily arises: "What kind of intelligence [is required]?

The fulfillment of the expectation raised [by the question] "What is intelligence? is conceived as nothing other than possessing the characteristics of a disciple as described in other Tantras. In this way, because the subsequent Sūtra (Sūtra 34 on page 53) states, "Having thus set the disciple in motion toward the Krama by means of a true Guru," [the definition of intelligence] serves to fulfill that very expectation regarding what constitutes "being" (*sattva*).

And the characteristics of the *guru* should also be applied. For this very reason, the teachers of the Baudhāyana school say: "One should not mix them together. Regarding this, Bhavasvāmin states that one who belongs to a different recension (*śākhā*) than those mentioned in the Śālikī recension should not mix those options; that is, one should not effect a combination within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*). [This applies] to the Brāhmaṇas.

Because of the multiplicity of Vedic branches, their infinity, and because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to summarize their entire meaning, the teachers composed the Kalpasūtras with the thought that people might attain all the fruits of ritual action by understanding and performing only that much which is easily comprehended.

The refutation of this is found in that very same [work]: "Those stated without qualification and those stated with qualification are connected as supplements. On this point, Bhavasvāmin says: "Those stated with qualification—namely, the specific qualities of what was stated generally—are connected as supplements, that is, as auxiliary parts, even if they are mentioned in other sūtras; they are not [connected] mutually among themselves."

An example of the term *saṃsādayet* (he should set down together) is as follows: according to Baudhāyana, there is the taking of the *vasatīvarī* waters alone for the purpose of pressing the Soma; however, in another Sūtra, there is a combination of both the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *ekadhānā* grains. Accordingly, when the *ekadhānā* grains are obtained by the followers of Baudhāyana, they do not [set them down] separately from one another.

"One should set them aside"—thus, according to Baudhāyana, only the cutting of the branch is mentioned. In other sūtras, both the cutting and the bringing of the branch are accompanied by mantras; those too one should not set aside.
Other examples may be cited in this same manner. An example of an exception to this is as follows:

According to Baudhāyana, only a *palāśa* branch is prescribed for the *sānnāyya* offering; however, if such a branch cannot be obtained by those following his *sūtra*, a *śamī* branch mentioned in another *sūtra* should be taken. In this regard, the root [of the argument] is that since there arises an expectancy as to what kind of branch should be taken when the aforementioned one is unavailable, another *sūtra* serves to fulfill that requirement.

Regarding the prescription for the *śamī* branch: thus, in the *Baudhāyana-śrautasūtra*, it is prescribed without qualification that "one adds fuel to the fires. When there arises a specific requirement as to how the adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*) is to be performed, [the text states]: "having formed a lap to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire," and "sitting with knees raised, [he adds fuel] to the *āhavanīya* fire. Regarding the *anvāhāryapacana* fire—
[In this case, one might expect "the Adhvaryu" to be mentioned. Thus, the ritual details (dharma) mentioned in other sūtras are fit to be connected as supplementary elements (śeṣa).
However, there is no such expectancy for the previously mentioned single *dhānā* (fried grains). Therefore, there is no combination (*samuccaya*).
By this same reasoning, even those who follow this sūtra [should not adopt] the three vessels or four vessels mentioned in other systems (*tantra*).

The statement that "the placing of the vessels is improper" is clearly incorrect. For if there were a general rule stating simply that "one should place the vessels," then a specific inquiry would arise as to how many vessels there are and how one should place them; only then would there be occasion for the application of a scriptural exception (apavāda). But such is not the case here.
By means of which it may be so.

By this [it is meant that], in the manual (*nibandha*), for the sake of purifying the reality of oneself and those who have taken the conventional vows, one should place a worldly water-pot (*kalaśa*) behind the Goddess and pour some consecrated substance into it.

Even the written record is baseless, because it is stated that the specific remainder of the *arghya* water is to be disposed of by offering it as an oblation in the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*) along with the learned (*śiṣṭas*).
For this very reason, the teacher Baudhāyana, having stated that one should not cause a confusion of scriptures, also spoke of the transgression incurred by causing such confusion:
"He who, while abiding by his own scripture, acts according to another's scripture [incurs sin]."
"For one who disregards his own scripture, it is equal to the murder of an embryo. Thus [it is said].
Nor can it be argued that, although performance may not occur in the case of an indifferent act according to the manner previously stated, one must nevertheless perform that which, if left undone,
incurs much censure in another scriptural text— since,
in the section concerning curdling (*ātañcana*), after stating "that which is done with *kvala*-berries is demonic," there is a deprecation of the *kvala* berries.

In another recensional branch (*śākhā*), it is prescribed: "He curdles [the milk] with curds" (*dadhnā'tanakti*). In yet another recensional branch, the curdling with *kvala* fruits is prescribed, stating: "The herbs, the *pūtika* plants, and the *kvalas*. Thus, there is much censure regarding the performance of the *patnīsaṃyāja* and the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings in the ancestral rite (*pitryā*).

It is heard in some places that no censure was uttered by the followers of Baudhāyana. Merely on that basis, disregarding the censure of others, the learned followers of Baudhāyana perform the *samiṣṭayajus* offering. Therefore, censure found in another scripture is of no consequence.
And in the *Tripurārahasya* it is said:

"O Rāma, that action which is not mentioned in the Tantras, yet is indicated in others, and which is unconditioned and free from conceptual construction—that is the [true] rite. [Cf. Ḍāmarī-vyākhyā, A 1].
Therefore, it should be accepted from another source; this is the definitive conclusion of the treatise.

Thus, it must be stated that this constitutes an "absence of application" (*gativiraha*), because when there is censure in another scripture for its non-performance, yet an option (*vikalpa*) in one's own scripture, the censure therein applies only to that which is to be observed according to the other scripture, since by that much alone there is no abandonment of one's own scripture. For example, in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, there is a censure of the *agnicayana* (fire-piling) rite in the context of the *vājapeya*.
No censure has been leveled against Baudhāyana; rather, according to the general rule (codaka-śāstra), it is presented as an option alongside the *uttaravedi*.

In that case, since there is no deficiency even when following one's own school (*sva-śāstra*) in performing the *uttaravedi*, the prohibition must also be respected—meaning that either the *uttaravedi* alone should be performed, or the piling (*cayana*).

Likewise, here too, in such a case, this statement is for the purpose of ritual performance and not for the purpose of subverting the eternally revealed scripture. We shall explain another interpretation of this statement in detail in the section on Śrīvidyā.
Or let it be that there is an abundance of results in this [text], as connected with the phrase "in the commentary below"—
O Maheśvarī, one should avoid whatever is prohibited in another Tantra,
because that [other Tantra] is indeed a single scripture due to the unity of the mantra and the unity of the deity.
Therefore, one should avoid whatever is prohibited in one's own scripture;
however, being competent, one may incorporate other [practices] not mentioned in it that are otherwise independent.
As long as one performs other practices that are not in conflict with one's own independent system,
it is certain that his spiritual prosperity will increase;
furthermore, he may indeed take whatever he desires from another source.

Thus, according to the statements of other tantras, there is an abundance of merit in the performance of the *puṇyāhavācana* and other rites when they are combined; the secret is that there is no deficiency even if they are not performed. Furthermore, an excess of vessels—which contradicts one's own scripture—should indeed be avoided, as will be shown later regarding the words of the written tantras.
[In the section on the preparation of the vessels within the commentary on the thirty-first sūtra of the third chapter of the *Śrīkrama*, which is to follow hereafter:

because it is possible to understand [this rule] according to the method that will be explained in the section on the preparation of the vessels (*pātrāsādana-prakaraṇa*), there is not even a trace of inconsistency; for what has been indicated in a single ritual application is required for all ritual actions in general.
And the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that that which possesses an invariable relation must be apprehended from one thing and not from another;
we shall clarify this in detail later.
And thus, the person who, having synthesized all systems, has determined the full extent of the auxiliary members (*aṅga*)—

For one who is capable of accomplishing it by composing a single uniform ritual procedure (*prayogavidhi*) and performing it, there will surely be a greater excellence of merit (*śreyaḥ*) from such an act for that omniscient person. However, he who is incapable of this may take only the desired [elements] and so forth from another tantra.

One will indeed achieve one's purpose simply by following the practice of one's own scripture alone. It is not appropriate to apply the "half-old-woman" logic (*ardhajaratīyanyāya*)—that is, to adopt certain elements from other systems while rejecting others.
The author of the commentary, failing to perceive even a scent of this reasoning, arbitrarily adopts some [elements] and rejects others.
One who abandons [this] should be considered a "beloved of the gods"; enough with excessive deliberation.

By the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*)—[it should be understood that this refers to the word *sarvathā* found in the thirty-first sūtra of this very section]—it is indicated that without initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is no absolute liberation. The clear proof for this has already been written previously from the *Tripurārahasya*. || 31 ||

Having thus prescribed the threefold initiation (*dīkṣā*), [the author] first divides that initiation— which possesses internal subdivisions— in order to establish their connection with a single time, and demonstrates the property that serves as the basis for that division among them.
He prescribes a quality consisting of a simultaneous connection with all three [initiations]:
"There are three initiations—the Śāktī, the Śāmbhavī, and the Māntrī.
Among these, the Śāktī [is so called] because of the entry of power (śakti), and the Śāmbhavī because of the placement of the feet.
The mantra-practitioner should perform all [these rites] by means of the mantra as it has been taught. || 32 ||

Having made a division up to the word "these," there is the naming of them. Among those [categories], he explains the meaning of the term *śāktī* (pertaining to power) with the words "due to the entry of power. The word "born" (*jātā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Alternatively, in the phrase "due to the entry of power," the ablative case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
(53) The initiation (*dīkṣā*) beginning with "entry into power" (*śaktipraveśana*) means that it has "entry into power" as its cause. The same applies further on.
In the term *praveśanād*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in its own sense (as a noun). Regarding what is called "entry into power," [it is explained] further on [at this very point].

This refers to the meaning of the two sūtras [35–36] in the *Dīkṣāvidhi*. The ritual action described starting from "washed with that nectar" up to "having burned the bonds" is as follows: what is called "the placement of the feet" is the visualization, performed by the guru upon the head of the disciple, of the red and white feet of Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara.
The instruction of the mantra (mantropadeśa), however, is clear:
it consists of the utterance of sounds by the guru, intended solely for the hearing of the disciple.
All [the mantras] mentioned previously are included. By the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and the three," their connection to a single time is indicated. The word "and" (ca) [serves this purpose].

The term *sāhitya* denotes association; and *sāhitya* consists in being connected at one and the same time. Thus, the resulting meaning is that one should perform all the initiations (*dīkṣās*) together. || 32 ||
He states the opinion of others: "Some say one by one. (33)

By the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), it is indicated that there is a conjunction of the three [periods] and merely a difference in time. By the particle *vā*, it is suggested that in the interim, a long duration of time should be observed, and not merely three days. || 33 ||
From here on,

he describes the procedure performed by the Guru: "The true Guru, having initiated the sequence with all its constituent parts and offered oblations while filled with youthful exuberance, summons the disciple and binds his mouth with a cloth."
Having sprinkled him with drops from the vessels of Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā, Vārtālī, Parā, and Pātra, and having caused him to hear the Siddhānta; || 34 ||
Having set forth and performed the sequential worship (*krama*) together with its limbs (*aṅga*), that is, the worship of the principal deity;

here, the limbs are Gaṇapati, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī, while the principal deity is Lalitā. Here, by the word "limbs" (*aṅga*), the sequence of the limbs (*aṅgakrama*) is indicated; the meaning is: the sequence of the principal [deity] together with the sequence of the limbs.
If it is asked, "How is this known?", listen: at the very beginning of this second section— in the first sūtra of the second section, which begins with "Thus, 'existent' (sad)..."—
it is stated that one who has received initiation from a true guru [should worship Gāṇanāyakī] for the removal of obstacles to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā.

Regarding the instruction "one should contemplate the manual," that which is performed for the removal of obstacles is seen in the world to be the primary [auxiliary] (*aṅga*). For example, when one intent on an audience with a king is stopped midway by gatekeepers, that act of waiting is considered an auxiliary to the audience with the king. And this is not so for every living being.

It should not be argued that this statement is redundant because the worship of Gaṇapati is already established even for every ritual action in order to avoid obstacles— based on the ringing of the bell stating "Gaṇapati is the destroyer of obstacles" due to the presence of the suspicion of obstacles— for [this purpose can also be achieved] by the recitation of the Vināyaka-stava.

In some instances, because the destruction of obstacles is taught as part of the propitiation, there arises the possibility of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that the removal of obstacles to the worship of Śrīvidyā must be accomplished by this very [rite] alone, should it occur on the side of the propitiation. Likewise, at the beginning of the third section: "Having thus worshipped Gaṇapati, with all disturbances of obstacles dispelled..."

One should begin the ritual sequence of Śrī Lalitā, the sole sovereign of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), as indicated by the gerund suffix (-ktvā) in the phrase "having [performed this]," just as in the injunction: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī."

The status of the worship of Lalitā as a subsidiary (aṅga) is clear. Nor can it be argued that, just as in the sentence "having piled the fire" (*agniṃ citvā*), the preceding rite is primary and the subsequent rite is subsidiary, so too here the worship of Lalitā performed subsequently would necessarily become a subsidiary to the propitiation of Gaṇapati.

It cannot be said that the priority of the act of piling (*cayana*) is determined by the suffix *-ktvā* alone; rather, because it possesses a fruit—namely, "one desiring offspring should pile," "one desiring cattle should pile"—the piling is primary. In its proximity, the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, which lacks a fruit, [is subordinate], according to the principle that "that which lacks a fruit in the proximity of that which possesses a fruit [is subordinate]."

By the principle of "being a part of that" (*tadaṅga*), it constitutes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Likewise, since the worship of Lalitā is heard in scripture to have liberation as its fruit, it is established that the very fruit which belongs to the worship of Śrī Lalitā through the medium of the worship of Vighna (Gaṇeśa) is the fruit of this [worship of Vighna] itself;
thus its status as an auxiliary is determined. For this very reason, [the text says]: "Having performed the Vāravantīya Sāman upon the Revatī verses..."

In the injunction "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this," the *vāravantīya* chant does not have primacy. Nor should it be argued that this is merely a rule regarding simple temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*), as in the case of "having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma. For in that instance, by the phrase "one should sacrifice with Soma," the [independence] of the Soma sacrifice from the New and Full Moon sacrifices [is established].

Since [the rites] have already been produced by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings, those sentences merely enjoin the sequence; however, in the present case, because there is no other sentence for the production of the Lalitā sequence, it is the injunction of an action qualified by that sequence. Furthermore, this is not so [as in the previous case], because in that instance both possess independent fruits, whereas here such is not the case.
It is merely a prescription for the sequence, nor is there any loss of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal.
By this, the objection that "having worshipped the Saṅgītamātṛkā in this manner, one should duly propitiate Kolamukhī"—
that even here there is a mutual relationship of being the primary and the subordinate for both— is refuted.
Because it has the form of seeing the king as its fruit, it lacks an independent fruit of its own.

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, there would be the necessity of repeating [the rite] at every performance as in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice; for we do not say that it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the principal [rite], but rather that it is an auxiliary to the commencement of the *Lalitākrama*, like the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* [iṣṭi]. For this very reason, it is heard in that scriptural statement: "One should commence the *Lalitākrama*."

The very resolve, "I shall bring about a sequence [of moments] related to a moment that is not the locus for the destruction of the act of worship performed by myself," is the meaning of the term "commencement" (ārambha). This occurs only once; therefore, there is no possibility of it having to be repeated.

By this, the doubt that the meditation on Gaṇeśa in the heart-lotus as an ancillary to the worship of Gaṇapati, and the meditation on Lalitā during the Brāhma-muhūrta, would both result in being performed at the same time— and thus be contradictory— is also dispelled.
Thus, Śyāmā’s status as a limb [of the Goddess] is established in the *Śyāmopāstikhaṇḍa*;

her position as the chief minister is indicated by the term "Śyāmā"; and the status of Kolamukhī as the commander-in-chief and that of Parā as the sovereign queen are established in the section on their worship by the terms "mahārājñyāḥ" and "daṇḍanāyikāsthānīyā" respectively.
And by the phrase "the heart of the Lion-throne science," this is made perfectly clear.
Therefore, these are the limb-deities; the meaning resulting [from this] is that one should arrange the sequence of the principal deity together with their sequence.
55) Although these may be designated by the term "limbs" (*aṅga*) as subsidiary deities in the worship of the principal deity,
in the present worship all five— [here, by the word "five," Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā...]— are included.

The group of five beginning with Vārtālī is to be understood as equally primary. Elsewhere, having accepted their status as subsidiary members (*aṅga*) established by other means, and having indicated Gaṇapati and the others in that very form, the word "together" (*saha*) merely enjoins the performance of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for all of them simultaneously. When such a *tantra* exists, the order of the deities follows the very order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

The entire collection of subsidiaries (*aṅgakalāpa*) that will be described hereafter is obtained through extension (*atideśa*). Among those, for those subsidiaries for which a common performance (*tantra*) is possible, they are to be performed in that very manner;
however, for those whose properties are contradictory and for whom such a common performance is not possible, [the rule is] by sequential performance of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*). This...

The characteristics of *padārthānusamaya* (performance according to individual items) and *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performance according to sections) are to be seen in the eighth subject matter of the *Pariśiṣṭa*.
For those cases where *padārthānusamaya* is not possible, [the procedure is] by way of *kāṇḍānusamaya*.
A wise person should apply these as appropriate; however, they are not written here for fear of excessive length in this book.
The phrase "gradually" (*kramaṃ pravartya*) and so forth is found on folio 53, following the word located in Sūtra 34.

Since the performance of the *homa* is already established by the word "having set in motion" (*pravartya*) alone, the statement "having offered the oblation" (*hutvā*)— which is also to be seen below—
is intended to establish that the time following the *homa* constitutes an integral part of the ritual for summoning the disciple.

Although it might be possible to say "having offered" (*hutvā*) even here— in order to indicate its obligatory nature despite its being optional at the time of the sequence ahead where it is obtained as an alternative— nevertheless, because of the statement ahead that "one should sprinkle him with the drops from the vessels of Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā, Vārtālī, and Parā," [the offering is indeed required].

It is established that there is no completion of the sequence [of rites]. In that case, since there is an expectancy for time—namely, "When should the summoning of the disciple be performed?"—it is appropriate to prescribe that [time] alone, rather than prescribing both [the time and the act], because that would result in the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*). Even in the alternative where the *homa* is not performed, [the time is defined as] the period subsequent to that which is indicated by it.
This is like the expression "the new moon day occurs with the calves.

By this, the statement in the *Nibandha*— "having summoned the disciple at the end of the dismissal of the special vessels"— is refuted, because there is no remainder of that [offering] due to the removal of all the special *arghya* vessels.
Furthermore, it is because sprinkling him with drops of water from the general *arghya* vessel of the five vessels contradicts the context of one's own [textual] arrangement.

In reality, however, the natural meaning of "having offered" (*hutvā*) is "having offered the remainder of the oblation into one's own self. For this very reason, the natural meaning of what will be stated later—"possessing the fresh radiance generated by such an offering"—is that "fresh radiance" (*taruṇollāsa*) is a particular state. Its detailed explanation is found in the commentary on the *Caraṇakhaṇḍa*.
This is clear [from Sūtra 82 in Chapter 10 and Sūtra 18 in Chapter 18].

By the phrase "having summoned the disciple," it is indicated that until that point, the disciple has no entry into the interior. Having uttered the disciple's name in the vocative case, one should say, "Come! Just as the summoning of the cows in the *Pravargya* rite is an integral part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), so too is this [summoning] an integral part of the ritual. Therefore, regarding the matter of his arrival by means other than [this specific method],...
The meaning is that one should not reveal one's own intention.

By this, the statement in the *Nibandha*— that immediately after the selection (*varaṇa*), the teacher, together with his disciple, should at that very moment go to a secluded place for initiation— is refuted, because it is impossible to summon a disciple who is standing nearby; nor is it for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
It must be stated that it is an "invocation," because when a perceptible cause is possible, it is improper to postulate an imperceptible one.
The remainder is clear.

In this context, by the word "vessel" (*pātra*), the vessel for the special *arghya* offering is to be understood—[that is, the word "vessel" found here should be taken as the word "vessel" occurring in the phrase "by the drops from the vessel" in the fifty-third verse and the thirty-fourth sūtra]. If one asks how this is so, it is as follows: if it were merely the general *arghya* vessel, then its...
Since the accomplishment of the tantra is like that of the *praṇītā* water, and because that [water] is one and connected to everything,

it would have been briefly formulated as "with drops from the general *arghya*. Nor is there a possibility of a brief formulation such as "with drops from the vessels of special *arghya*" even in your own position.

It should not be said that the effort [involved] in [the compound] *gaṇapatilalita* and so forth is useless; for if that were the case, since the plurality denoting the number of the predicate would—by the principle of the *kapiñjala* section—resolve itself as three, there would be no attainment of five vessels at all. Nor even so...

It should not be argued that the *laghusūtra* could possibly read "pañcaviśeṣārghyapātraiḥ" (with five special arghya vessels); for we do not teach the addition or omission of syllables in a sūtra as a basis for interpretation. Rather, in the case of the general arghya, because it is singular, the phrase "up to the end of Parā" would be redundant; whereas in the case of the special arghya...
The phrase "for the sake of obtaining five bowls" is meaningful; furthermore, an excess of syllables cannot be restricted in the case of the independent intentions [of the author].

In reality, however, there is no *tantra* (shared procedure) like that of the *praṇītā* water-vessel, because in the case of Gaṇapati, Lalitā, and others, the consecration of the general *arghya* does not possess a single uniform form; for a shared procedure is impossible between two distinct ritual properties (*dharma*). Nor can it be asked how there could be a shared procedure for principal rites that possess distinct properties.
This is to be doubted. *Tantra* refers to the simultaneous performance of principal rites, not merely their single performance.

Here, however, a single performance has been stated, which is indeed improper; for simultaneous performance certainly does occur. Therefore, this is not an indicator for the taking of the special *arghya* by means of the word "vessel" (*pātra*), but rather [it applies] after having offered (*hutvā*).

Having stated "possessing youthful radiance," it is subsequently said "with the drops from the vessel" (*pātrabindubhiḥ*); therefore, by the word *pātra*, that substance which has become the means for the *homa* is indicated as being present in the mind, and not the general *arghya* substance which is not so intended. Furthermore, for the Tantrikas, the word *bindu* refers primarily to the principal substance.

She is established by convention as "satisfied by the libation of the *bindu*," according to the usage in the *Lalitāsahasranāma*. For this very reason, the word *bindu* itself is also indicative [of her]. And thus, in the taking of the special *arghya*, this alone is the proof.

Having sprinkled that disciple with water, [he performs the rite]; this is the teacher’s duty because it constitutes the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the disciple. The remainder is easy to understand.
By this [statement], the line in the *Nibandha* which says, "reciting the root-mantra of Gaṇapati and so forth,

having sprinkled him with drops of water from the general *arghya* of the five vessels," is entirely spurious and fabricated by one's own imagination, because it contradicts the [established] tradition.

Having caused [the disciple] to hear the *siddhānta*— that is, the collection of sentences that set forth the established doctrine, [whereby the term "previously mentioned" refers to the sentences concerning knowledge, training, and so forth, stated from the third *anugata*-sūtra up to the end of the thirty-first sūtra]— he causes him to recite this hearing, which is for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), just as in the case of the injunction: "He causes him to recite the *kḷpti* verses."
It is not for the sake of understanding the meaning, because it is impossible to comprehend such an exceedingly profound subject within that much time.

Therefore, the previously mentioned statements— [by the word "previously mentioned," the meaning is the statements concerning the training in knowledge and so forth, as taught from the third sutra up to the thirty-first sutra].
One should cause [the disciple] to hear that [the ritual] generates an unseen force (*apūrva*) which acts as a cooperative cause for the *apūrva* resulting from initiation (*dīkṣā*). || 34 ||
(p. 57) Śāmbhavī Initiation.
Now he describes the Śāmbhavī initiation:
having visualized his [the disciple's] head as having red and white feet, it is washed with that nectar.
One should adorn the entire body. || 35 ||

"Upon his head" means upon the head of the disciple. "Red and white feet"—red because Kāmeśvarī is of the nature of *rajas*. As it has been said: "One should meditate on the supreme Mother as having red feet.
This is also stated in the *Śyāmārahasya*:
"The red foot of the Goddess is proclaimed to be the nature of *rajas*, while the white foot that supports it is of the nature of *sattva*. Thus [it is said].
By this, the white-footed rite (*śuklacaraṇa*) is also explained. The singular form [of the compound] is used because it consists of parts of living beings.

Having meditated—that is, having contemplated—that nectar, which is the water associated with the feet, he should make the disciple such that all his sins have been washed away and destroyed by that nectar. This is the meaning.
Although the performance of the act by the student— the referent of the external term— is not possible, nevertheless,

according to the maxim that "when a prescription or prohibition involving a qualification is applicable, if there is an obstruction regarding the qualified object, it transfers to the qualification," the sense is that the performance of the destruction of sin— which is a qualification of the student— is indeed possible. All of that...
The Guru should adorn and decorate the body with perfumes, garments, ornaments, flowers, and so forth; this is the Śākta initiation— thus he speaks of the Śākta initiation.
Having meditated upon that surging wave of light, blazing like a flaming fire, extending from its base up to the cavity of Brahmā, one burns away his bonds of sin with its rays. || 36 ||
The "root" (*mūla*) of that disciple refers to the location of the four-petalled lotus situated between the anus and the genitals, which serves as the support;
"up to the root" (*āmūlam*) means up to that limit. Having thus stated the lower limit, he states the upper limit:
"up to the aperture of Brahma" (*ābrahmabilaṃ*), meaning up to the aperture of Brahma, which is the support for the thousand-petalled lotus.

Having meditated upon consciousness—of which the remainder of the sentence is "saṃvidam" (consciousness)—as being blazing, and therefore possessing waves of light, and thus resembling fire accompanied by flames;
because it resembles blazing fire, its capacity to burn the fetters of sin is logically established. [The burning of the fetter of sin...]
Thus there is no cultivation; for this very reason, it says "having burned."

Although it appears that, following the sequence of the text here, Śāmbhavī comes first and then Śāktī, nevertheless, because it was stated at the beginning, at the time of the division of initiations (*dīkṣā-vibhāga-velā*), that they are "Śāktī, Śāmbhavī, and Māntrī," the conclusion must be interpreted otherwise in accordance with the beginning.

By the principle of the section beginning with "The Veda" (*vedopakramādhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, immediately after the burning of those fetters, [there is the removal] of that impurity in the form of their ashes.
Because it is logical that the water emerging from the feet serves the purpose of washing those [feet], the sequence of purpose (*arthakrama*) is also established.
Thus, it is proven that one should first accomplish the *śākta* initiation and subsequently perform the *śāmbhavī*.

Some maintain that the entire collection of auxiliary rites (aṅgakalāpa), beginning with "The Guru, having initiated the sequence" and ending with "having caused [the disciple] to hear the Siddhānta," belongs to these two [initiations] alone, by virtue of both context (prakaraṇa) and proximity (sannidhi), just as the *śundhana* mantra belongs to the *sānnāyya* offering. That is not correct; for if that were the case, then in the third initiation—later on...

The injunction that "having caused [the sacrificer] to swallow the first sprinkled [portion] with the tip of the second fragment" is untenable; for since the rule prescribes a sequence of constituent parts (*aṅga*), and this [swallowing] is not such a constituent part, there is no application of sequence therein, and consequently, the categories of "first" and "second" do not exist. Furthermore, it is impossible to take what is unrefined and merely worldly (*laukika*).

Therefore, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), proximity (*sannidhi*) is set aside, and [the rite] is an ancillary (*aṅga*) for all three. And thus, when following the alternative that one [should initiate] each one individually, then at the third initiation the aforementioned ancillaries are to be performed.
By this, through the flowing of nectar (*amṛta-kṣaraṇa*), one should remove both external and internal impurity (*mala*). Now...

The second occurrence of the statement "one should burn his bonds with its rays"— meaning "with the rays of that wave of light"— beginning from "from the disciple's *mūlādhāra*," has been written down and refuted;
for since the external and internal impurities have already been removed by the previous initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is an absence of such impurity in this case.

Furthermore, because burning is impossible through the higher initiation (*uttaradīkṣā*). Nor should it be argued that the impurity (*mala*) removed by the prior initiation remains outside and is burned by the higher initiation; for fire manifested within the body can only destroy the impurity residing within the body, not that which has been cast outside. Therefore, our own tradition alone is correct.
"We perceive that 'it is well' is the appropriate response. (36)
The initiation through mantra (*māntrī-dīkṣā*) begins with the statement of the application of that initiation:
[1] the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), [2] the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), [3] the four aromatics (*caturjāta*), [4] *takkoḷa*, [5] *madayantī*, [6] *sahadevī*, and *dūrvā* grass.

[7] Ashes, [8] earth, [9] sandalwood, [10] saffron, [11] gorocanā, [12] camphor, and [13] scented water— having filled a new pitcher with these, wrapped it in a pair of cloths (with new garments), worshipped it with the six-limbed rite of Bālā, and placed the maṇḍalas of Śrī Śyāmā and Vārtālī therein;

Having worshipped with the three *āvaraṇa-mantras* and protected with the *astra-mantra*, one should display the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās— [the knowledge of the extraction of numerous mudrās, such as the *astra*, *dhenu*, and *yoni*, is to be seen in the independent *Dvi-pariśiṣṭa*, section 15]. || 37 ||

Trikatu consists of long pepper (pippalī), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and black pepper (marīca). Triphalā consists of chebulic myrobalan (harītakī), emblic myrobalan (dhātrī), and beleric myrobalan (vibhītaka).
As it is stated in the Vaidyasāra:
"Dry ginger, black pepper, and long pepper are declared to be known by the name trikaṭu."
"Triphalā is thus defined as the combination of pathyā, dhātrī, and vibhītaka. Thus it is said.
The "fourfold" consists of ushira, ela, lavanga, and nāgakesara. As it is stated in the *Madanamahārṇava* (p.
"Lavanga, elā, and uśīra are proclaimed as the 'three fragrances' (*trisugandha*)."
They declare that the "four-fold" (caturjāta) consists of [the three spices] combined with nāgakesara. Thus [it is said].

*Takkola*— well-known in the Gurjara country by the name *Cinīkabālā*, and here the term *kaṅkola* should generally be understood— is a specific substance resembling black pepper, to be consumed with betel leaf as a remedy for coldness.
*Madayantī* and *sahadevī* are well-known in medical science as wild plants; *dūrvā*, ashes, and clay are well-known.

As for the inclusion of "seven clods of earth" (*saptamṛttikā*) under the term *mṛttikā* in the Nibandha, that is without foundation. If the term *mṛttikā* everywhere implied seven clods of earth, then the explicit mention of "seven" in the passage from the *Mūlanakṣatrajananaśānti*—
namely, "joined with seven clods of earth and combined with five sprouts"— would be redundant.
In the same way, there would also be such a contingency in the case of the rule: "One should thus fetch clay for the purpose of bathing."

The phrase "yuktaṃ etaiḥ" (joined with these) is a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (compound with the middle term elided), meaning "together with water. Since it is impossible for [the word] "vāsitaṃ" (scented/perfumed) to be construed with *dūrvā* and the other items, [it must refer to the water]. *Candana* is well known. *Kuṅkuma* is from Kashmir. *Rocanā* is *gorocana*. *Karpūra* is well known. By that water which has been perfumed with these...

A new, unused water-pot, wrapped in a pair of cloths, [should be consecrated] with the six-limbed ritual of Bālā [for the sake of knowing the extraction of the mantras of the deities, the seers, the meters, and the subject matter of the six-limbed nyāsa of the Śrī Bālā Tryakṣarī mantra; see Appendix 9, Section vi]. Aiṃ.
"Namaḥ to the heart"—thus, by repeating the three seed-syllables twice in sequence; [Note:

Regarding the procedure for performing the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) without the specific mention of the mantra for each limb, that is to be understood from the nineteenth sūtra and its commentary in the *Śrīkrama* of the third section; however, the direct [textual evidence] is found in the *Dvīpaśikha*, 9.]

It exists in the [respective] locations. According to the method to be described, [they are placed] in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest corners, as well as in the directions starting from the east in the center, respectively. Here, by the name "six limbs" (ṣaḍaṅga), there is an extension of the aforementioned attributes. The meaning is that one should cast—that is, establish—the wheels of Śrī, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī.

When there is an expectancy as to "where," it must be in the water-jar itself because of its proximity. Even there, by the force of the natural sense of the words, it is not to be placed upon a full vessel or similar object, but rather in the water;
[here, it should be understood that "in the water" means specifically in the water contained within the jar].

Although it could be argued that, since the specific location for the extraction has not been stated and by virtue of contextual fitness (*yogyatā*), one might say "in the vicinity of the jar," nevertheless—

because worship on the ground is impossible without the installation of the *cakra*, and because such installation is thus obtained either through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) or by extension (*atideśa*)— it is already established and therefore [the specific location] is redundant.
Due to the fear that the word "having thrown" would otherwise be redundant, the act of casting [the substance] into water is necessary.

Nor should it be said that its placement is established by presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) or other means as being anywhere at all, rather than specifically in the location near the jar; for there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating the jar itself as the locus in relation to the location near the jar.

Furthermore, the worship of the wheel situated near the jar cannot be considered a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the jar, because it is not connected to it. In this context, the consecration of the jar occurs previously with the words "having worshipped with the six limbs" (*ṣaḍaṅgair abhyarcya*), and likewise with "having protected with the weapon-mantra" (*astreṇa saṃrakṣya*) and so forth. How can [the worship of the wheel] be sandwiched between these two?

That [offering], being distinct from its consecration, would be of a different class. Therefore, the casting of the wheels occurs in the water itself, and the worship is performed right there; indeed, the casting into the water takes place at the very moment the commencement of the worship begins. Consequently, there is no room for the doubt as to how the wheels can be moved after the invocation (*āvāhana*).

Alternatively, the statement "having cast [the deity] into the vase" must be understood as an exception to the rule that one should not move [the deity] until the final dismissal (*visarjana*). This interpretation alone is logical; otherwise, the entire sequence of ritual actions (*sāṅga-krama*) would be compromised.
Immediately after the word "nirvartya," one should say "nikṣipya kalaśe" (having cast it into the jar).

Regarding the three [deities], Lalitā and the others—[these three goddesses, Śrīlalitā, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī, as mentioned in the 53rd leaf of the *Anugata* and in the sūtra; thus they are to be known]. Of Lalitā and the others...

By the phrase "with the *āvaraṇa* mantras," there is an exclusion of the worship consisting solely of the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). "Having worshipped" means having performed the ritual adoration.
This unprecedented worship is prescribed by this [text]. Following the worship, the extraction (*uddharaṇa*) follows as a matter of course.

However, the worship is to be performed solely with *kula*-substances—that is, with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) contained in their respective special *arghya* vessels—since only the performance of the unprecedented worship is enjoined. Having performed only that much, the extraction of the *cakra* should be carried out.
Placing scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) upon wheels that have been lifted out of water is established as the correct procedure.
Having protected [the area] with the mantra "phaṭ" using the *astra* [for the purpose of this *astra-mudrā*, and for the purpose of the *dhenu-yoni-mudrā* standing before it—see Dvi. Pa. Śi.
15.7/14, 15.8/1–2, 15.8/2], making it unassailable by *rakṣas*, *bhūtas*, and *piśācas*; [the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās are well-known].
Having displayed it, one should place it upon that. || 37 ||
Regarding the Mātṛkā Yantra, he says [the procedure immediately following that]:
"The golden pericarp joined with Śiva, with eight filaments provided with pairs of vowels."

In the Mātṛkāyantra, which consists of eight petals joined with the eight groups of letters—ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, and la—situated in the eight directions, with the syllables *ṭhaṃ* and *vaṃ* in the square [the disciple...].
[This Mātṛkā-cakra would become well-known by looking at the commentary below. ...the disciple.
Having placed [the image] therein, one should bathe it with that water from the jar while reciting the three vidyās. || 38 ||

*Śiva* is the letter *ha*; joined with that is the golden letter *sau*. That [letter] is in the pericarp, which is the central region of the lotus—such is [the seat]. Here, a *visarga* should also be added above the previously mentioned letters, because the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda stated: "The pericarp consists of the letters of space (*vyoma*), moon (*indu*), water (*au*), and the tongue (*rasanā*) [i.e., *ha-so-a-u*]. (Thus...)

It should be understood that [the seed-syllables] are produced as *ca*, *ha*, *sa*, and *auḥ*. All of these are qualifiers of the lotus (*kamala*). The vowels (*svarāḥ*) are sixteen, beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga; their "pairing" (*dvandva*) refers to two by two.

That which is "endowed with" (*juṣṭa*) or joined by this [pairing] is the eight filaments (*kiñjalkāṣṭaka*), which are specific locations situated between the pairs of petals—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

*Kaśca*, *caśca*, *ṭaśca*, *taśca*, *paśca*, *yaśca*, *śaśca*, and *laśca* form a *dvandva* compound. According to the grammatical maxim that "a word heard at the end of a *dvandva* is connected with each member individually," the term *varga* (class) is connected with all [the preceding members]. Thus, beginning from the *ka*-class (*kavarga*)...

(61) There are five letters each up to the *pavarga*; the *yavarga* has four, and the *śavarga* is likewise; the *lavarga* is represented by *lakṣ*. Thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has eight petals joined with the eight groups [of consonants]."
The practical meaning is that one should write each group [of letters] on each individual petal.

When there is a requirement for a sequential order in the inscription of colors upon the filaments and petals, the sequence of the eastern direction (prācyadikrama) alone must be maintained. Although the true east cannot exist simultaneously for both the petals and the filaments, nevertheless, when inscribing according to the method of drawing a lotus pond, the east is determined by the pericarp (karṇikā), and [the sequence] follows that very orientation.
The sequence for writing the phonemes upon the petals should be investigated.

Regarding the eight directions beginning with the East and ending with the Northeast, in which the syllables *va* and *ṭha* are situated—such a square (note: in the subsequent text, the word *asra* should be understood as ending in the dental *s*)—in such a yantra known as the Mātṛkā, the disciple... [is placed]. (Note: The term *bahuvrīhi* refers to the compound "in which [the syllables are situated]. The word *asra*, meaning "corner" or "point," is here to be understood as ending in the dental *s*.)
Having settled, that is, having established.

Thus, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus like a lotus-pond, and having drawn a square devoid of doors outside of it— [here, in the subsequent text, the word *asra* should be understood as ending in the dental *s*]—
and having written "hsauḥ" in the pericarp, one should write "a, ā," etc., in sequence upon the filaments starting from the east.

Having written two vowels on each filament and one vowel within the petals— at the previously mentioned locations (which should be understood as being based on the central divisions of the petals situated in the directions starting from the East)— one should write the eight groups of consonants beginning with *ka*,
placing one group inside each [petal], and outside of that, a square.

[In this upcoming text, it should be understood that the word *asra* ends with a dental *s*. The collective meaning is that one should write "vaṃ" and "ṭhaṃ" in the eight directions beginning with the east. As it was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:
"The lotus whose pericarp consists of the letters of space (*vyoma*), moon (*indu*), earth (*aurasa*), and water (*nārṇa*), and whose filaments flash with pairs of vowels..."
Within the petals, the three groups beginning with the five groups, the *ya* group, and the five vowels are placed in sequence;

it is surrounded by the city of the earth (*kṣoṇīpura*), joined with the letter *la*, the letter *la*, and the *lāṅgali* [the letter *ṅa*], situated in the directions starting from the east. [Note: In this upcoming text, the word *asra* should be understood as ending in the dental *s*.]
"The lotus of the letter [Oṃ] situated on the head destroys poison and disease; it is the conqueror of death. Thus [it is said].
*Vyoma* is the letter *ha*; *indu* is the letter *sa*; *au* is its own form; *rasanārṇa* is the *visarga*; the end of *lā* is the letter *va*;
*lāṅgali* is the letter *ṭha*; the remainder is clear.
One should bathe [the deity] with the three vidyās of Śrī, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī—[here, by the word *vārtālī* one should understand *vārāhī*;

and by the word *vidyā*, one should understand the root mantras of those three]—in such a way that there is contact with water on all limbs. By the qualification "with that," it is meant that if other water is insufficient, one should proceed accordingly.
It is indicated that there is nothing to be grasped; this very state is called the "Full Empowerment" (pūrṇābhiṣeka). || 38 ||
He concludes the initiation through mantras (māntrī-dīkṣā):
Having seated the disciple— who is dressed in fine silk, anointed with unguents, adorned with ornaments, wearing a garland, and is well-composed— beside him,
and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā upon his limbs, he places three [mantras] into the hand of that disciple, whose face-cloth has been removed.

Having placed pieces of sandalwood that have been sprinkled first and then smeared with it, along with pieces of flowers, and having caused them to be consumed with the *tattva* mantras, one should instruct the girl in her right ear and subsequently recite the desired mantra.
The passage beginning with "sadukūlam" and ending with "pārśve niveśya" is clear in its meaning. Regarding the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa*:

[This *nyāsa* must be taken from numerous tantric texts such as the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*, and not from modern books. Just as it is performed on one's own body according to what is stated in other tantras, so too should it be performed on the body of the disciple.
Having placed it in the hand of one whose face-cloth was previously bound— meaning, he whose mouth-covering had been tied up.

This refers to the three initiations according to the Tantric system; however, according to some opinions, in the case of sequential initiation, the emission (visarga) occurs at the conclusion of each respective initiation.
Alternatively, since the author of the Sūtra intends only the initiation according to the Tantra system, the sealing of the mouth is performed specifically within the Tantric framework.
Just as in the case of the statement, "He first anoints the sacrificial post here with clarified butter [which was] first sprinkled," and likewise, "In this very manner,
they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the second tail-portion (*jāghanī*)."

In reality, however, because the sequence was prescribed previously and the consecrated remnant of that [sequence] still exists, one should not discard the vessels for that duration for the sake of the consecration of what is to be used later— just as in the case of the rule: "One prepares the *udayanīya* offering with the scrapings (*niṣkāsa*) of the *prāyaṇīya*."
Because it has been established, the gift consists only of the first and second portions that have been consecrated and sprinkled, but not of that which is unconsecrated.

Since the number three is already obtained through the plural number itself according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*, the further qualification "three" (*trīn*) indicates that the placing is not done for all three at once, but rather one by one, just as in the expression "he lays on two enclosing-sticks" (*dvau paridhī paridadhāti*).

With the three *tattva-mantras*: "I purify the *ātmatattva*, namaḥ svāhā; I purify the *vidyātattva*, namaḥ svāhā; I purify the *śivatattva*, namaḥ svāhā. Because of the hearing of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the word "having caused to swallow" (*grāsayitvā*), the consumption occurs immediately after the permission of the preceptor. "Bālā" refers to the three-syllabled [mantra].

Having thus taught the final limb, one should state—that is, teach—the desired mantra in the form of either the *pañcadaśī* or the *ṣoḍaśī*; this is the meaning. [From here until the end of the commentary on Sūtra 39, the scriptural doctrine regarding the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*) consists in the inclusion of both the *pañcadaśī* and the *ṣoḍaśī*.]

Now, one might object: "This is not the injunction for the sixteenth [syllable], because by the singular word 'manu' (the mantra), there is an injunction for the fifteenth alone. Nor should it be argued: "What is the determining factor against the opposite view? For, immediately following the instruction for the child, the fifteenth alone is what is expected, and thus it is that very one which is grasped by the singular number. [Not so.]

[The phrase] "lack of a determining factor" (*vinigamanāviraha*) is an addition [found in manuscript *ba* 2]. Furthermore, if the instruction regarding the *ṣoḍaśī* were intended in this tantra, then one would perform its extraction (*uddhāra*).
Since there is no such extraction here, if you argue that it is therefore not intended, we say: no. For it is not [the case that] by following a singular expression...

[The reading "tatsiddhiḥ" is an addition found in manuscript Ba 2. For there is a rule that everywhere, even when words expressing number function as qualifiers of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs only with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), since it is observed that they also connect with that which delimits it. And thus:

The singular number is justified as being accompanied by the genus (*jāti*). If that were the case, how could there be an exclusion of the *ṣoḍaśī* based on that [singular number]? Otherwise, in the rule "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," there would be no prohibition against killing two Brāhmaṇas. Or, let it be that the singular number is intended to be significant; even so, it does not [follow].
The cessation of the sixteenth [vowel] is the most excellent according to the scriptural statement;
63) it occurs after the subsequent instruction of that single sixteenth [vowel].

Since there is no contradiction in teaching the fifteenth [vowel] at the occasion of instructing the *Śyāmāraśmimālā* and other vidyās, the claim that it is not included because it was not extracted is also untenable; for if even the fifteenth were not extracted, its instruction would likewise not occur.

Nor should it be said that she is extracted by the phrase "the power Mādana" in the midst of the five rays to be meditated upon at the *mūlādhāra*; for that fifteenth [vowel] is not extracted as something common to all, but rather [this group of five garlands of rays exists from the ninth section, verse 28, of the *Sūtrānta*].

She consists of the five rays as her constituent parts; for this very reason, she is called "Mahāvidyā" (the Great Knowledge) therein. Otherwise, even for Brahmā, it would be difficult to justify the significance of the word "tasyāḥ" (of her).
Therefore, the Vidyā is one, accompanied by the previously described limbs (aṅga), sub-limbs (upāṅga), minor limbs (pratyaṅga), and the sandals (pādukā).
How could knowledge, being a constituent part of that [ignorance], become the primary entity?

Furthermore, when it is said, "What is not cited in an independent treatise (svatantra) is not to be accepted," is this the intention of the author of the Sūtra being extracted, or is it being extracted by another statement to the effect that "what is not cited in an independent treatise is not to be accepted"?
It cannot be the first, because there is no indicative mark (liṅga) within the Sūtra itself that extracts such an intention. Moreover—

The three-syllable mantra of Bālā has not been extracted anywhere, yet the author himself says, "teach Bālā. By this, the intention of the Sūtra-author is very clear: that even if it has not been extracted, it should be accepted. Nor is this the case in the *Raśmimālās* [meaning: in the 29th Sūtra of the section on the common procedure for all, at the beginning of the 10th Khaṇḍa].

It must be stated that when it is said, "having taught Bālā," because she is extracted as a limb (*aṅga*) of Śrī and as the nine-syllabled Bālā, she alone is to be understood. If the nine-syllabled vidyā is intended by the word "Bālā," then,
in the subsequent extraction of the mantras of the fifteen Nityās, [in Sūtra 9 of the Lalitā section] it is indeed Bālā who is [the Kulasundarī].

[It is] said to be "Kumārī-vā. [If one were to argue that] Kumārī is Kulasundarī because the color of Kumārī is prescribed in the *Kulasundarī-mantra*, then it would follow that that [mantra] also consists of nine syllables. We shall state the refutation of this undesirable consequence when we extract the *Kulasundarī-mantra*. Thus...

In the section on the *Śrīvidyā-nyāsa*, regarding the statement "having performed the six-limb assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating the *Bālā* mantra twice," the practice of performing the six-limb assignment by repeating the nine-syllable mantra is contrary to all traditions. Therefore, the *Bālā* used here is not the nine-syllable one, but rather the three-syllable one; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Raśmimālā*:
In the nine-syllable mantra, the limb of Śrī is stated as "bāle" and not "bālā.

We shall explain a collection of even more arguments regarding this in the extraction of the Raśmimālā mantra (starting from Sūtra 9 in the tenth section, beginning with "pañcemā—" and ending with Sūtra 28). Alternatively—

The connection should be understood as: "We shall explain by means of a text consisting of fifty sūtras. Therefore, there may be a three-syllable [mantra]. However, the *bālā* has not been extracted anywhere; rather, it is traditionally held that she was taught by taking what was established in another tantra.
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtra: "having caused [her] to swallow by means of the reality-mantras (*tattvamantra*)," yet those mantras have not been extracted.

Thus, in the Vārāhī-prakaraṇa, the three qualities-mantras and so forth have not been extracted; therefore, it is established as the final conclusion that this was not the intention of the author of the Sūtra.
Not the second, because such a scripture is not found anywhere.

Furthermore, at the conclusion of this initiation, three qualifications of the disciple are heard: "the disciple, having contemplated fullness," "one who has known what was to be known," and "one who possesses authority over all mantras. Among these, "fullness" (pūrṇatva) means being devoid of any remainder of that which is to be received from the Guru. If...

(64) If the fulfillment of all defects of initiation occurs through the fifteenth [day] alone, then, since the remaining performance of the *ṣoḍaśī* (sixteenth-day rite) still exists, how can there be an injunction for the cultivation of fullness? In this very way, the state of having known what is to be known (*viditaveditavyatva*) is untenable.
