Nor should it be argued that, according to the author of the Sūtras, the purpose is fulfilled and perfection is attained by the fifteenth alone, and thus liberation is established by that alone without any inconsistency; for even so, what would be the point of instructing the fifteenth in the context of one who is qualified for all the mantras?

Either the qualification (*adhikāra*) is accepted for the sixteenth [day] as well, or the term "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*) is restricted to that which is distinct from the sixteenth. It cannot be the first case, because it would follow that the sixteenth day produces less fruit than the fifteenth; for one who is qualified for a major task is necessarily qualified for a minor task.

Just as one who is authorized to cross the Ganges is not necessarily authorized to cross a small irrigation canal, and the reverse is not observed in the world; nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because there is no evidence for such a restriction.
Therefore, when investigated thus without partiality, we see no obstacle whatsoever to the inclusion of both the fifteenth and sixteenth [tithis] by the term "desired mantra."
Or, let it be granted for the sake of others' satisfaction that the Sūtrakāra intended only the initiation of the Pañcadaśī;

nevertheless, one who has received that initiation— or even a minor initiation— must not enter a maṇḍala of the Ṣoḍaśī belonging to a follower of another Tantra, just as a king does not enter the house of a servant.
Maheśvarānandanātha says: "That is not so. For instance, regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), what constitutes its 'smallness'?

Is it the small number of syllables in the mantra, or is it the mantra's being a means for achieving only small results? In the first case, there would follow the absurd conclusion that the initiation of Vārāhī is superior to the Śrīvidyā initiation, and that the initiation of Śyāmā is even more superior than that."

In the second [chapter], it is heard that the very same fruit which belongs to the initiation of the *ṣoḍaśī* in another tantra also belongs to this one; this is understood through such words as "one who has accomplished his purpose," "one who knows everything that is to be known," and "one who is liberated while living" [the meaning is: by the words found in the sūtras at the conclusion of those respective sections]. And thus, because they are equal, there is no [difference].
The state of having received an incomplete initiation.

If it is objected: "In that case, what is the status of the scriptural statement in another tantra that the initiation of the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī-dīkṣā*) is an inferior initiation?"—the answer is: No. For in a tantra where there is a conjunction of both the sixteenth day (*ṣoḍaśī*) and the fifteenth day initiations, the initiation of the fifteenth day yields an incomplete fruit, whereas the initiation of the sixteenth day is complete in that same way.

Regarding both those who follow the Tantras, one has been initiated into the fifteen-fold [system] and the other into the sixteen-fold [system]; since there remains further work to be done for the former, he is considered incomplete. Therefore, it is logical that one who has been initiated by a Guru should not enter his mandala. But here, since equal results are established by authoritative means, how can there be a state of being a Guru?
Lightness. One should investigate this without dogmatic insistence.

Nor should it be argued that there is indeed lightness or heaviness of the result based on the lightness or heaviness of the cause; for if that were so, consider two people seeking only fire: one of them produces fire by means of iron and stone.

It is produced by the friction of a single fire-drill. In that case, compared to the former, for the production of the subsequent fire, there is an increase in time, an increase in persons, and an increase in exertion; thus, due to the weight of many causes, that fire would possess the capacity to produce greater combustion. Likewise...
Because the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) of Āpastamba is twice as long as that of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* according to the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*, for those who follow the *Āpastamba-sūtra*... [p. 65]

There would be the attainment of twice the heavenly rebirth; there would be the attainment of a heavier burden for one following the Baudhāyana-sūtra compared to one following the Āpastamba-sūtra. Therefore, apart from the production of greater fruit, it is difficult to define any other "heaviness" (gurutva) regarding the initiation (dīkṣā).

Since that [qualification] is absent in the present case, how can there be the status of one who has undergone the "light initiation" (*laghudīkṣā*) for a follower of the Sūtra? Even though the practice involving the Guru yields an equal result, one engages in it because the scripture itself states that the fruit does not accrue to its qualified practitioner without the practice inherited through the lineage of one's own previous Gurus; it is not out of a desire for an increase in the fruit. As in the *Atirātra*...

In passages such as "He takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup" and "He does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*," the establishment of a gradation of results is appropriate because, in the absence of such a scriptural injunction [regarding a fixed result], a systematic arrangement can be made according to the difference in the qualifications (*adhikārin*) of the practitioners. Therefore, in this case, there is no deficiency or excess regarding the number of initiations (*dīkṣā*).
The remainder should be inferred by the wise.

This position was accepted and refuted merely for the sake of pleasing others; in reality, however, it was stated previously that there is no obstacle to including the *ṣoḍaśī* under the term "desired mantra."

Nor should it be said that in the passage, "and having mentally repeated ten times the root-vidyā, whether beginning with *ka* or beginning with *ha*, at the time of death," the terms "beginning with *ka*" or "beginning with *ha*" are qualifiers of the vidyā that serve as an indicator (*liṅga*) for the absence of the *Ṣoḍaśī* [Vidyā] here; for by those two qualifiers...
Granted that the *ṣoḍaśī* might be excluded by those two [mantras] recited in proximity to the performance at the time of dawn as being subordinate to it,
nevertheless, what power do they have to exclude the *ṣoḍaśī* from all instances?
It is like the king’s command, "Bring a horse," uttered at the time of going to a garden.

Even though there is no contradiction regarding the vehicle such as a palanquin used for going to the monastery, a statement involving horses and foot-soldiers is never capable of contradicting other means of transport.

Therefore, the instruction on the *ṣoḍaśī* is necessary even for those who follow the Sūtras. Beyond this, the wise should investigate further, setting aside all dogmatic insistence; for in the discernment of the true nature of Dharma, partiality toward one's own view leads only to hell—enough said. (39)

The instruction regarding the naming of the disciple: the master describes the remaining ritual actions as follows— then, having placed his own foot upon the disciple’s head, [he should recite] all the mantras either once or in succession.
Having instructed [the disciple] according to his qualification and having caused him to touch one of his own limbs,
he should assign him a name consisting of two, three, or four syllables— beginning with the letter of the *mātṛkā* corresponding to that limb and ending with the word "Ānandanātha. || 40 ||

By the word "tataḥ" (then), it is indicated that the dharmas to be described hereafter constitute subsequent subsidiaries (*uttarāṅga*). According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"In the absence of a specific instruction, one should understand the right foot [of one's own guru]"—one should place only the right foot. Regarding the phrase "all mantras," since the context restricts the scope to all words [within that specific section], it is as in the statement: "All desire to obtain the *hāriyojana* cup."
Just as in that [preceding] manner, [one should worship] the mantras that constitute the limbs (*aṅga*) of Śrīvidyā— namely, Gaṇapati, Śyāmā,
Vārtālī, Parā, Pañcadaśī, Nityā, Raśmimālā, and so forth— [from this point onward...]
The meaning is "those which are about to be described. Regarding the phrase "all at once" (*sakṛdvā*), the particle *vā* has the sense of *eva* (only/just);

thus, it means "at that very moment. Alternatively, it may mean "gradually" or "at the time of each respective meditation. By the expression "according to one's qualification," an option based on specific circumstances (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) is indicated: for one who possesses an abundance of devotion and faith, [the result occurs] at that very moment.

"Gradually for one who possesses slightly less [of that]" means as follows: in the phrase "upon his own limbs," the word *aṅga* refers to the parts of the body. He should give the command, "Perform the touch. Then, whichever limb the disciple touches, [the mantra] is that which has as its initial letter the syllable used in the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* for that [limb]. Such is the meaning.
This is a specific qualification of the name. For example, upon touching the head, the syllable *a* is the first letter of the Mātṛkā;
that [name] which begins with it is "Amṛtānandanātha. This same principle is to be applied everywhere. The phrase beginning with "or two syllables" is clear in meaning.
It is evident that the name ends with the word "Ānandanātha. One should assign such a name to that disciple.
One should establish [it]. || 40 ||
Regarding the bestowal of the mantra of the Guru’s sandals (gurupādukā), which was previously omitted, he speaks again:
before instructing the disciple, one should give him one's own sandals joined with the six *tāra* mantras. || 41 ||

Immediately after the second morsel has been consumed and before the instruction is given, one should impart to him the mantra consisting of his own name— given at the time of initiation— followed by the word *pādukā* and joined with the six *tārās*. Regarding these six *tārās*, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Dear One, Vāgbhava, Parā, Śrī, Kālībīja, Bhuvaneśī, and Manmatha—these six are proclaimed as the Tārās. Thus it is said.
"I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of Amukānandanātha."
By this, the objection that the mantra for the sandals placed in the commentary was fabricated because it is not found in the Sūtras is refuted.

Although, according to the order of the recitation (pāṭhakrama), the instruction would logically apply to this very point, nevertheless, as in the case of the rule "the Āśvina cup is taken tenth," its sublation by the order of the Śruti (śrautakrama) is appropriate. || 41 ||
Having instructed him in conduct, discipline, and so forth;

having contemplated the heart-consciousness; having wiped his limbs three times with the threefold Vidyā; having embraced him and smelled the crown of his head, one should make him one's own self-form. || 42 ||

Having instructed— that is, having taught— the conduct (*ācāra*) to be described in the tenth section [the meaning being that it refers to what will be taught from sūtra 57, "There is no conflict with all beings," up to sūtra 80],
he [instructed] him— the pupil— into the *hārda*, which is the consciousness (*caitanya*) connected with the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*). This is the ellipsis.
The meaning is: having touched and meditated upon the disciple as non-different from the consciousness residing in one's own heart.

By means of the three vidyās—that is, by the *Śrī-vidyā*, *Śyāmā-vidyā*, and *Vārtālī-vidyā*. Having recited the three vidyās simultaneously, the cleansing (*parimārjana*) is performed first; then twice [with each vidyā]; and then he sprinkles [the disciple] three times silently, but not in the manner described previously.
[The phrase] "with three [times]" means three times. If that were the case, one would have said simply "with the three vidyās" (p.
By using the instrumental case in the expression "by means of the triad of vidyās," singularity is understood as a qualifying attribute. Therefore, it is not so.

"Parimārjana" (cleansing) means touching the entire body of the disciple with one's own hand. Having embraced him, having smelled his head, one should make him one's own self-form; just as one's own self is free from the impurities of human nature that obstruct liberation, so should one make him. || 42 ||
The disciple’s entitlement to all mantras—

from the words "the true guru" up to this point [meaning from the beginning of Sūtra 34 on the western leaf until the end of the commentary on this sūtra]— constitutes the ritual action performed by the guru; hereafter, [the ritual action is that of the disciple].
The action performed by the disciple takes place as follows:

the disciple, having contemplated fullness and thus accomplished his purpose, honors that guru with wealth according to his capacity; having known what is to be known, he becomes authorized in all mantras. May there be auspiciousness! || 43 ||

Thus ends the "Rite of Initiation" (*Dīkṣāvidhi*) in the *Kalpasūtra* composed by the illustrious Paraśurāma— the destroyer of the wicked Kṣatriya clans born from the womb of Reṇukā, the preceptor of the Bhārgava lineage, the son of Jamadagni, the foremost disciple of the Great God (Mahādeva), and the venerable Mahākaulācārya.
The first section:

Fullness (*pūrṇatā*) has already been explained. Therefore, he is one by whom the goal has been accomplished, that is, the means to liberation (*mokṣasādhana*). Regarding the word *tam*, which denotes time: the meaning is "at this very time. If it is taken as an adjective qualifying the Guru, [the meaning is likewise].

Because it would otherwise be redundant; or rather, because of the statement that "when the Guru's own Guru is present, one should worship only the *praguru* (the great-grandteacher)," the word "him" (*tam*) is used to indicate that this [worship] should not occasionally be applied elsewhere than to the [intended] service.
This is according to the principle: "A lord of a hundred thousand should give a hundred thousand [coins], while a poor man should give a single cowrie, each according to his capacity."

"Having served" means having satisfied. "By whom that which is to be known"—that is, what is to be understood—is "known," meaning he is omniscient (*sarvajña*). This implies that one becomes authorized over all mantras, namely the seventy million mantras of the Saura, Vaiṣṇava, and other traditions. By this instruction, the instruction of all mantras is accomplished.

The meaning is that there is no prohibition against reading books and the like. As it is stated in another Tantra: "Only by one who is in their final birth, or by one for whom Śaṅkara himself is pleased, is this venerable sixteen-syllabled Vidyā (or fifteen-syllabled Vidyā) directly obtained through a true Guru."
"O Maheśānī, all the great mantras abide here within the seed like the body of a tree; therefore, it shall be most excellent. Thus [it is said].

The word "Śiva" serves as the indicator that the section commenced— the so-called *Dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*, which begins from the first sūtra on the final leaf, "Now, therefore, we shall explain initiation (*dīkṣā*)," and extends up to the end of the sixty-seventh leaf— is completed. || 43 ||

Thus ends the section on Initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*), comprising the first part, in the commentary on the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* titled *Saubhāgyodaya*, composed by Śrī Rāmeśvara. Furthermore, upon the repetition of the *sūtra*, that which requires correction should be indicated.
"And the remaining portion is complete by the grace of the Primordial Goddess. Thus ends the first section.

[Even more extensive and clear applications of initiation (dīkṣā) are found in the *Śrī Mahānirvāṇa* and other Tantras, as well as in the *Dīkṣollāsa*, *Dīkṣāprakāśa*, and the *Tāntrikasvatantrapaddhati*; however—]
And since this aforementioned application is also stated in the Sūtra issued from the mouth of the Blessed Lord, it is indeed most excellent.
68] The Second Auspicious Section: The Manual of Gaṇanāyaka.
The Procedure for the Worship of Śrī Gaṇanāyaka:

Having completed the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the first section, the author, desiring to expound the section on the worship of Śrī Lalitā, begins by setting forth the worship of Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, which serves as a preliminary limb (*pūrvāṅga*) to that worship.
Thus, having received initiation from a true guru, one should contemplate the ritual manual of Gaṇeśa in order to remove obstacles to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā. || 1 ||

In this manner, by the previously described method, he is one by whom initiation (*dīkṣā*) has been received from a true guru—one who possesses the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures. By this it is indicated that only one possessing such initiation is qualified for the worship of Śrīvidyā, and no other. Mahāvidyā refers to the Pañcadaśī.

Or it is the *ṣoḍaśī* [Vidyā]. Its propitiation is *japa*. Alternatively, because the Great Vidyā is Śrī Lalitā—due to the non-difference between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*)—her propitiation is worship until the attainment of the fruit; those obstacles which act as impediments to its arising [are removed by this].

"Vighnas"—according to Amarasimha, "vighna," "antarāya," and "pratyūha" are synonyms—[meaning] obstacles; for their "apohāya," that is, for their destruction, one should "āmṛśet" (contemplate) the "gāṇanāyakīṃ paddhatim"—the path or way related to Gaṇeśa.
According to Amarasimha, "saraṇiḥ," "paddhatiḥ," "padyā," "vartanī," and "ekapadī" are synonyms; thus, the meaning is the path of worship. One should contemplate this.

One should accept this. It was stated previously [in the commentary on Sūtra 53, page 34, section 1-khaṇḍa-53 of the *Nāma*] that this constitutes an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the worship of Śrī Lalitā; such is the meaning to be understood. || 1 ||

Having thus stated the necessity of the worship of Gaṇanāyaka— namely, that the morning duties beginning with meditation and ending with libations (*tarpaṇa*) must be performed for the reason that Gaṇapati is the limb-deity (*aṅgadevatā*) of Lalitā Devī and so forth— he now describes the method of that worship.
He elaborates:
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he is seated in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the *dvādaśānta*.

With his entire body bathed by the spreading flow of the nectar-essence trickling from the pair of the Guru’s feet, he— having restrained the movement of his breath and mind— meditates upon the Lord of Elephants (Gaṇeśa), who blazes within the center of the lotus of his heart,
as ruddy as ten million rising suns, the expiation for all faults; then,
his own body turned pale-red by the mass of that [Lord's] radiance, he goes outside.

Having voided his excrement and urine, and having performed the cleansing of his teeth, bathing, putting on his garments, and offering the *arghya* to the Sun, he should offer the *arghya* with the mantra:
"We know that Great Gaṇapati, who dwells in the rising sun;
we meditate upon him whose face is curved; may that Tusked One inspire us. Having thus offered the *arghya*, he should perform his daily duties (*nityakṛtya*).
Having performed this, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) in four rounds [this knowledge regarding the fourfold libation is very clear in the commentary on both sūtras of this section].
Longevity, health, sovereignty, strength, nourishment, great fame,
poetic talent, enjoyment, and liberation result from the fourfold repetition of the propitiation. (2)

Having risen from bed during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, that is, at dawn— the remainder of the sentence being "from the bed"— [the phrase] "at the *dvādaśānta*" (which does not appear in manuscript B from "itadādi" to "ityantaṃ") refers to the point above the forehead, ending at the top of the skull,
which is designated by the term *dvādaśānta*. This has been stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The dvādaśānta is above the forehead, ending at the upper limit of the forehead. Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, within the gross body at the *dvādaśānta*, there are thirty-two lotuses situated along the *suṣumnā* channel; among them, there are two thousand-petaled lotuses: one at the very bottom named *akula*, which faces upward, and one at the very top.

There is another [cakra] named Dvādaśānta, which is downward-facing. The authoritative evidence for this is to be found in detail in the *Setubandha*, our supreme teacher’s commentary on the *Yoginītantra-uttaracatuḥśatī*. It is not written here for fear of excessive length. By the word "this" [in the original], [it refers to] the Dvādaśānta—
Thus, this word located in the sūtra is to be understood as a qualifier of the lotus (*kamala*) by way of the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*).

Although the word *dvādaśānte*, ending in the locative case, cannot logically be construed with the lotus—which is a constituent member of the compound—due to the lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*) consisting in its dependence on another word that forms part of the compound; [nevertheless, it is so construed].

Because there is no semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) that would necessitate a compound, a compound is not justified; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such usage as "the king's wealthy elephants" (*ṛddhasya rājamātaṅgāḥ*). Nevertheless, even in the case of "at the end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānte*), it is a compound ending in a locative suffix, like "the king's wealthy elephants," and the absence of the elision of the locative case-ending is archaic (*chāndasa*).
The lotus known as the *dvādaśānta* has the pair of feet of the Guru situated in the center of its pericarp; from that couple flows nectar,
and by the expansion— that is, the spreading— of the essence of that nectar, all one's limbs are drenched and saturated.

The phrase "for whom [this] has thus become" is the ellipsis. The word "having become" (*bhūtvā*) refers to what was stated previously; "one whose movement of breath and mind is restrained" (*niyamitapavanamanogatiḥ*) is an adjective qualifying the agent of meditation, serving as a specifier of the agent and thus constituting an ancillary element (*aṅga*) of meditation, just as in the injunction "he offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāman juhoti*). By whom the movement of the breath and mind is restrained—that is, by whom the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) and the mind (*manaḥ*) are made immovable.
The meaning is "having performed. Without the restraint of the mind and breath (*manaḥ-pavana-nirodha*), one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*) is not possible;
and without one-pointedness, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is not possible. Therefore, the sense is that these two are essential.
Within the center of the heart-lotus is the *anāhata* [the *anāhata* is so named because it is located in the heart].
The word "blazing" (*jvalantam*) indicates that it acts as the burner of the sins residing within one's own body.

By the phrase "reddish like the tip of the rising sun" (*udyadaruṇakoṭipāṭalam*), through this hyperbolic simile (*abhūtopamāna*), it is indicated that there is nothing else comparable to this within the entire universe. [It is] the expiation for all defects; of all...

The expiation (*nirveṣa*) of one's own faults: those from whom *veṣa*—that is, *svarūpa* (intrinsic form)—has departed are *nirveṣāḥ*, meaning they are devoid of their own nature or destroyed; this is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is primary. Thus, by the etymology "that from which the state of being *nirveṣa* (the absence of form) arises," it means that which destroys all faults residing within one's own body.

The meaning of the result is as follows: "anekapa" means an elephant (*dvipa* or *gaja*). Having meditated upon one whose face is such [as that of an elephant], his body was rendered *pāṭala*—that is, made white-and-red—by the mass (*paṭala*) or collection of the radiance of that deity. The suffix *cvi* is used here in the sense of "becoming what it was not before. Thus, he is one by whom his own body has been brought to a state of being white-and-red; for *pāṭala* is indeed white-and-red.
Thus says Amara. By this, the meaning is that one should meditate for as long as the state of being pale-red remains possible within one's own body.
Up to this point—that is, up to the end of the action described in the subsequent root text as "his body turned pink by the mass of its radiance"—is the ritual for the place of rest;
for it has been stated that one subsequently goes outside. This going outside is obtained through recollection (*smṛti*).

And by this, the voiding of feces and urine is restated. Here, since there exists a general injunction stating "having performed the cleaning of the teeth," the reading "[satīti sādhīyān pāṭhaḥ]" (the reading "provided that" is more correct) is preferred. When the expectation arises as to how the performance is to be done, [it is resolved] by the fact that the Tantric rules take precedence over the Smārta ones.

By the principle of "accepting the horse" (*aśvapratigrahanyāya*), because of their proximity, only those ritual elements (*dharma*) mentioned in other *tantras* are to be adopted, and not those from the *Smṛti* tradition. Since the *Śrīkrama* is more closely related to other *tantras* than it is to the *Smṛti*, the requirement for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) should be fulfilled solely from those other *tantras*, beginning with the ritual bath (*snāna*) and ending with the offering of water to the Sun (*sūryārghya*).

The authors of the *Nibandha*, however, in their *Gaṇapatipaddhati*, having stated the application of the three seed-syllables—*Śrī*, *Māyā*, and *Kāma*—to be employed when joining the *Tritārī* within mantras, cited the *Śrīvidyārṇavatantra* as their authority for that. This is to be considered; for instance, in the *Śrīkrama*, it is stated everywhere:

At the beginning of the mantras, one should utter "tritārī" according to the Śyāmā-krama; at the beginning of the mantras, one should utter the "kumārī-yoga" according to the Vārāhī-krama; having uttered "vāc" and "glauṃ," all mantras are to be recited according to this manual (paddhati); according to the Parā-krama, "all the Parā-krama mantras should be preceded by 'sauvarṇa'," as stated in the Sūtra.

Since it is not recited in the *Gaṇapratikrama*, it is very clearly understood that for the author of the Sūtra—who would otherwise have recited it—there is no application of seed-syllables (*bīja-yoga*) in these mantras at all. This being the case, how can there be a following of the *Vidyārnava Tantra*?
Alternatively, since the conjunction of *vāk*, *māyā*, and *kamalā* will be mentioned in the *Śrīkrama* regarding the *Śyenayāga*.
Because it exists as a limb of all his [mantras], just like fresh butter, it would also be obtained as a limb of this Śrīvidyā;
therefore, to set that aside and follow another tantra is devoid of justification.
For one who abides by his own scripture yet acts according to another scripture [is at fault].
For him who disregards his own scripture, that act is equal to the murder of a learned Brahmin.
And because of this traditional teaching (smṛti).
Having offered [the water] with the words "To Mahāgaṇapati, who abides like the rising sun," this phrase functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

By the expression "to him who abides like the rising sun," one should perform meditation upon such a sun; [regarding the offering of *arghya*—note by Śrī—] subsequently, from the passage beginning with "Siddhalakṣmī" found in Sūtra 4 on page 72, [one should meditate upon] Vighneśvara.

"Having meditated" means according to the method stated at the end of the sūtra; it is indicated that [the rite] should be performed according to the method to be described in the section on worship (saparyā).

In the *Nibandha*, it is stated that there is an offering of three *arghya*s; however, the source for this must be sought. This is because the singular number is clearly evident from the predicate word *arghyam*, which ends in the singular. Nor can it be a case of repetition (*abhyāsa*), as there is no word indicating such repetition.
Nor is it an extension (*atideśa*) of what is prescribed in the *Śrīkrama*, since by the explicit statement, only that which concludes with the *sūryārghya* is extended.
Because there is no evidence for the extension of those subsequent dharmas.
Having performed the daily duties, such as the Agnihotra sacrifice and others—

by this it is indicated that the *tarpaṇa* (libation) to be described later in four rounds is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the meditation (*upāsti*) itself through the context (*prakaraṇa*), thereby dispelling the misconception that it is an auxiliary of the *arghya* offering due to its proximity (*sannidhāna*).

This is the originative injunction for the fourfold libation (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇa*). In this context, "fourfold libation" is the name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), and not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), because the fourfold repetition will be explained later—in the third sūtra and its commentary (as should be understood). And thus: "He performs the Agnihotra."
Thus, as in this case, by changing the case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*),

its status as the meaning of the third case is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as being the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of the verbal root.
The sequence is as follows: there are four repetitions or recitations (*āvṛttis*) regarding the constituent actions of whatever rite is performed;

this constitutes the "fourfold repetition libation" (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇa*). Although in the first libation there are twelve repetitions rather than four, nevertheless, according to the principle of creation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*) and following the logic of abundance (*bhūmātva*), even in a libation that does not consist of four repetitions, [the designation applies].

The conventional designation is "the fourfold libation" (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇam*). Here, since there is no connection with the verb *kam* (to desire), longevity, health, and so forth do not connect as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Rather, it is solely for the purpose of assisting the worship of Śrī Gaṇapati. Otherwise, [it would be like] the statement: "He offers the fuel-sticks; he becomes established in this world."

Because, according to the Vedic text, it would follow that even the *prayāja* offerings possess results such as "firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*); therefore, the passage beginning with "longevity and health" (*āyurārogya*) is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*).

Furthermore, rather than writing "for the attainment of long life, health, and so forth," the author of the manual (Nibandhakāra) has rightly written the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as "for the pleasure of Gaṇapati. However, one must seek the authoritative source for the passage beginning with "in a river or similar place" and ending with "having performed the five-fold offerings" (*pañcopacārān ācarya*).
The direction [of this argument] is that what is fabricated by one's own intellect is simply not to be believed. || 2 ||
He clarifies that very point: having first offered libations twelve times with the root mantra,
one should offer each of the twenty-eight syllables of the mantra, ending with *svāhā*, four times each, as well as the root mantra.

Having offered libations four times, one should again offer to Śrī and Śrīpati, Girijā and Girijāpati, Rati and Ratipati, Mahī and Mahīpati, Mahālakṣmī and Mahālakṣmīpati [the absence of sandhi here is an archaic Vedic usage].

Among the thirteen pairs [of deities], one deity from each pair— namely Ṛddhi, Āmodā, Samṛddhi, Pramodā, Kānti, Sumukhā, Madanāvatī, Durmukhā, Madadravā, Avighnadrāviṇī, Vighnakartṛ, Vasudhārā, Śaṅkhanidhi, Vasumatī, and Padmanidhi— is recited four times, as is the root mantra four times.
Thus one should perform the libations; in this way, there are four hundred and forty-four libations. || 3 ||

The libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with the mantra "Having uttered the root [mantra], I offer libation" (mūlam uccārya tarpayāmi). In this same manner, it should be joined to the root-mantra in every instance hereafter. Regarding the phrase "libation four times," it is not the repetition of the action that is prescribed, but rather the repetition of the mantra itself.
Although the word "twelve times" (dvādaśavāram) ends in the accusative case, it functions like the expression "he cooks a little" (stokam pacati), where the number refers to the mantra-repetition.
It might be argued that [the term] ought to be an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), and thus repetition of the action alone would be established;

nevertheless, since forty-four hundred offerings (*tarpaṇa*) occur hereafter, a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is established by the number mentioned in the Sūtra, and therefore it cannot be a mere repetition of the action. Hence—

Immediately after "twelve times," it should be supplemented with "having repeated. For this very reason, later on, the repetition of the mantra itself is clearly heard in the root text through the statement: "the root [mantra] four times, and each one four times.
If it were a repetition of the ritual action (*kriyā*), then the recitation of the mantra would necessarily occur only once. And that...

This is refuted by the requirement of the subsequent number. Alternatively, although there may be repetition of the action due to the distinctness of the substances, there will nevertheless be repetition of the mantra; moreover, since the repetition of the mantra is explicit later on, here too—being associated with that—there must be repetition of the mantra. After the words "four times," the word "having uttered" (*uccārya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. By the phrase "ending with *svāhā*,"...

It is indicated that the *svāhākāra* is an integral component of the mantra for each syllable. (p. 72) Since the whole—the specific mantra—has Gaṇapati as its deity, it is clear that its constituent parts likewise have him as their deity. Therefore:

At the end of "svāhā," the phrase "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy) should also be joined. Thus, for each syllable of the root mantra, there is the addition of a bindu according to the tradition of the learned; then follows the utterance of "svāhā," and then "tarpayāmi" as previously stated. In this manner, it is done four times; then again four times with the root mantra. This applies to all [syllables].
This is to be applied according to the [specific] castes (*varṇa*). First, by the phrase "having satiated twelve times," one group is indicated.

Following that, by the phrase "having satiated four times," the final satiation (*antatarpaṇa*) is indicated as another group. In this sūtra, moreover, by the word "again" (*punaḥ*), the satiation of the thirteen pairs (*mithuna*) is indicated as yet another group.

The result of indicating the three groups (*gaṇa*) is as follows: since each individual group generates its own unique transcendental merit (*apūrva*), if one forgets even a single [verse] within that group, the performance must begin again from the start of that specific group, and not from the very beginning of the entire collection.
This is just as when a portion of a mantra is omitted, one must repeat that mantra starting from its beginning.

"Śrī-Śrīpati" is one [name], and "Girijā-Girijāpati" is another; in this manner, it should be understood that there is one couple consisting of a feminine-ending term and a masculine-ending term. Based on the etymology "one for whom no obstacles (vighnāḥ) exist after the flow of passion (madadrava)," the word *avighna* is masculine. The rest is clear. Thus...
In the thirteen pairs [of deities], one should pronounce each deity in the accusative case and join it with the formula "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*).

Thus, according to the aforementioned method, the satiation of a single deity should be performed four times; thereafter, it should be done four times with the root mantra as before. In this manner, by the stated procedure, the satiations are to be performed in sequence according to the specified number.
Thus, there are 228 root libations (*mūlatarpaṇa*), 112 libations for the [deities of the] letters (*varṇatarpaṇa*), and 104 libations for the couples (*mithunatarpaṇa*);
in total, these amount to the previously stated number of 444 libations. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Having thus described the sequence of libations (tarpaṇa) beginning with entering the sacrificial hall and ending with the meditation on Vighneśvara, he begins to state the procedure for worship:
"Now, the ritual of sacrifice— having entered the house, having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), [at] the doorway..."
On both sides [to Bhadrakālī and Bhairava], above the door [to Lambodara] with "Obeisance" (namaḥ);
having thus entered within, stood upon the seat with the seat-mantra, performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), applied the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa),
and performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra, [he should contemplate] the Deity within himself.
His sides are embraced by Siddhalakṣmī; he has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, is reddish in color,

and possesses eleven hands adorned with a citron, a mace, a *puṇḍra* flower, a sugarcane bow, a trident, the *sudarśana* discus, a conch, a noose, a lotus, a cluster of grain, the tip of his own tusk, and a jeweled jar.
Having meditated upon Vighneśvara, whose temples are split open, who is filled with bliss, and who is the master of obstacles, the destroyer of all impediments; || 4 ||

Now, this is a statement concerning another topic. By this, the section on libation (*tarpaṇa*) is concluded. Thus, through this context, the relationship of subordinate and principal between libation and worship (*upāsanā*) is indicated. Consequently, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the libation to the sequence of the limbs of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The word "it is said" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By the phrase "having returned home,"...

It is indicated that the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed outside the house, such as at a river or similar location. "Having smeared the sacrificial ground" (sthaṇḍila)—that is, the place of sacrifice—with cow dung; this is the implied remainder [of the sentence].

The purification of the site (*sthalaśuddhi*) is restated here because it has already been established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By this, the sequence [of the ritual acts] is not intended to be significant. Furthermore, if one were to argue that the recitation here is for the purpose of establishing the sequence—out of fear of futility due to the lack of a specific result in a mere restatement—that would be the case.

When this is said, then the smearing (upalepa) should be performed immediately prior to the worship of the door (dvārapūjā). Regarding the phrase "on both sides," since no specific instruction is given, the right side is first and the left side afterwards.
The right and left to be taken here are those which are on the outside when exiting from the door; it is in that very place that it is done accordingly.

This is according to the ritual procedure (*vyavahāra*), but not at the moment of entry. The word "namas" is followed by the remainder of the sentence, "one should worship. The deity is understood from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantra. By the phrase "having entered within," it is established that the worship of the door must be performed while remaining outside. By the phrase "with the seat-mantra" (*āsanamantra*), this seat-mantra [is as follows:]—hereafter.

In the sixth section of the *Śyāmākramīya*, in the sixth sūtra, it should be understood that the mantra to be recited is "Obeisance to the Lotus-Throne of the Support-Power" (*ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*).
This is because the mantra recited in the *Śyāmāprakaraṇa* is to be understood here due to its proximity; for this very reason, one should not adopt a mantra found in another tantra.
Regarding the demonstration of baseless doctrines stated in the *Nibandha*: as for what is written in the *Nibandha*— namely, that one should light lamps all around, consume betel,
and sprinkle the seat with the third seed-syllable of the *Bāla* [the third seed-syllable being *sauḥ*]— that [is to be refuted].

This question arises: what is the authority in another tantra that establishes this, or is it stated in this very tantra— in the *Śrīkrama*, specifically in the third section (the 11th *sūtra* regarding "having offered the measure of lamps" [meaning in the *sūtra* concerning lamps])— that the sprinkling of the seat is performed with the third seed-syllable of *Bālā*?

It is stated in the *Parāpaddhati* [in the commentary on Sūtra 6 of Khaṇḍa 8 of the *Agraparakrama*]: "Is there for all of them an extended application (*atideśa*) scripture that brings them about? Not the first, because that has already been refuted. In the second case, the extended application is threefold: extended application by statement (*vacanātideśa*), extended application by name (*nāmātideśa*)," and so forth.

An extension based on inference arises from a desire [for analogy]. Among those, what kind of extension is this? It is not a direct statement, such as "the rest is the same as the Śyena," for there is no statement here saying "the remainder is the same as the Śrīkrama.
Therefore, the first [type of extension] is not applicable. Nor is it by name, as in "one should perform the Agnihotra for a month," where one would perform the Śrīkrama under that name.

For there is no such conventional usage; therefore, the second [alternative] is not tenable. As for the third, it is an extended application (*atideśa*), as follows: when it is stated, "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *saurya* oblation of cooked rice," because of the connection with the verb root "to desire" (*kam*), there arises an expectancy for an action—namely, "What should one do regarding spiritual luster?"—and this [statement] fulfills that expectancy. Subsequently, when the expectancy arises as to "By what means should one perform it?", the meaning of the verbal root [supplies the answer].

It connects as an instrument (*karaṇatvena*). Since the collection of subsidiary parts (*aṅgakalāpa*) has not been recited, [the question] "How should one perform it? remains; therefore, to satisfy that expectancy, a word is supplied—namely, "sauryaṃ carum" (a rice-offering for Sūrya)—on the basis of similarity, such as having *oṣadhi* as its substance and possessing a manifest indicative mark (*vyaktaliṅga*), just like the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
The injunction is "one should offer [the oblation] like the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Consequently, the ritual details (dharmas) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa are extended [to this sacrifice].
For there is no such expectancy here [for those details], since the primary rite together with its subsidiaries is recited here [in its entirety].

Furthermore, if the acquisition of ritual properties (dharma) occurred solely through extended application (atideśa), then, since the mantra for the seat has already been established by the statement in the *Śrīkrama*, "seated upon the seat with the seat-mantra" (*pīṭhamanunā āsane samupaviṣṭaḥ*), its re-enactment would be redundant once it is obtained through extended application; this being the case, it follows the logic of the *Gṛhamedhīya* butter-portion offerings (*ājyabhāga*).

74) He clarifies that only what has been stated is to be performed and nothing more than this. And in this way, how could there be the application of anything beyond this? Furthermore—the attainment of dharma from the *Śrīkrama* occurs through extended application (*atideśa*).

Does that [requirement] apply only to the limbs (*aṅga*) or to all dharmas? If you say it applies to the limbs, by what is the absence of consecration (*abhimantraṇābhāva*) with the ninety-four mantras established? For it is not as if one chooses [the Hotṛ] only when he is a seer (*ṛṣi*), nor is there such a rule in the Sūtra that the consecration must be performed with the ninety-four mantras.

There exists the notion that "it must be performed," by which [the objection] is refuted. Furthermore, in my view, since the relationship between original material (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*) does not exist, as long as it is said "it must be performed," there is no such statement here; therefore, it is logical that there should be no consecration (*anabhimantraṇa*) with the ninety-four mantras.
In your view, this would contradict the context—this is the additional reading in manuscript *ba*. 2.
The position that there is an extension of whatever dharma whatsoever would be pleasing only to those who are dear to the gods (the foolish), but not to the wise.
Therefore, we do not perceive even a mustard-seed’s worth of authoritative evidence that establishes the previously mentioned doctrine.

Thus, certain [elements] written here in the *Śrīkrama* are rootless; likewise, those stated in the *Śyāmākrama* are without authority and have been interpolated into the *Śrīkrama* and elsewhere. For a doctrine devoid of authority does not exist.

This must be so. Therefore, even the wise follow a work that has been rendered confused at will by one who is ignorant of the scent of Mīmāṃsā but possesses only knowledge of the Sanskrit language; herein, some do not even perform a critical examination. In this regard—

We consider it logical that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is indeed the power of the Kali Age and nothing else; therefore, those [rites] belonging to that [era] are not to be performed. Only that which is explicitly stated should be done. Where something is indicated as being to be taken from elsewhere—such as by means of the *āsana-mantra*—that should be adopted; however, nothing written down by anyone without due deliberation is authoritative.

Due to the absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), no *apūrva* (transcendental result) would arise from its performance. If it were to arise, then there would likewise be an extension of the ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices into the Agnihotra, and an extension of the properties of the Jyotiṣṭoma into the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Therefore, a confusion [of rituals] based on one's own whim is without authority.
The insistence [on this view] is not to be trusted; enough with this excessive elaboration.

Furthermore: In the treatise, a single modification (vikṛti) is never seen to have multiple original forms (prakṛti), nor has such a thing been heard of before. This author [mentions] certain properties located in other sections by means of the word "saurya," such as those consisting of the seat, the sprinkling, and so forth.

How could one who attempts to synthesize into a single place various practices found in different sections— such as the chewing of betel and so forth, which are situated in the *Śrīvidyā* section (with the addition of "in another tantra" according to the *Ba* manuscript)— be a knower of the true nature of dharma?

Furthermore, it is not as in the case where the properties (*dharma*) belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* are extended (*atideśa*) to the *Dvādaśāha*, and from there, by extension, those properties situated within that context are further extended to the *Dvirātra* and so forth; likewise, Śrīvidyā is the root archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*), and from her, by extension, [the practices] such as betel-chewing are obtained for Parā.

Let all those specific characteristics consisting of the preparation of the seat and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), which accompany that [rite], be extended by analogy to Gaṇapati, who occupies the position of the archetype (prakṛti) for the two-night sacrifice and others. This being the case, it should not be said that there is a multiplicity of archetypes; for if the supreme [goddess] has Śrī as her archetype, then the wearing of ornaments follows precisely through such extension.

Since that [attainment] is already established in its own context, the phrase "one whose body is adorned" would be redundant. Likewise, many other elements such as the striking with the left heel and so forth would be superfluous. It recurs in the case of the distinctness of substances.
As for the writing of "pūjayāmi" as the remainder of the mantra in the *Nibandha* during the *tarpaṇa* mantra, that is incorrect.

If there were no difference between *tarpaṇa* and *pūjana*, then later on [the text] would have simply said, "one should perform the *tarpaṇa* of the five enclosures," rather than saying, "one should perform the *pūjā*. This is because the verbal forms are used with distinct roots.

Therefore, a difference in meaning is also necessary. When there is a difference in meaning, it is clear that the mantra characterized by worship (pūjā-liṅgaka) is not an ancillary part of the libation (tarpaṇa). Thus, in the Nibandha, after the worship of the principal deity, the worship of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the three lineages (oghatraya) is also mentioned. If the source for this is another Tantra, its inclusion here [is justified].
It has already been stated that [it] does not exist; therefore, it should not be performed.

The two couples are the second enclosure; the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās) are the third enclosure; Brāhmī and the others are the fourth enclosure; and Indra and the others are the fifth enclosure—one should thus perform the worship of the five enclosures.
Regarding the worship of the five obstructions (*pañcāvaraṇī-pūjā*), it states the location for the satiation of the principal deity therein—(and elaborates upon that in detail):
the deity is in the triangle; within the interior of that hexagon are the four couples beginning with Śrī and Śrīpati, as well as the limbs (*aṅga*).
The six pairs beginning with Ṛddhi and Āmoda are on the hexagon; two pairs are on both sides of the hexagon, and the limbs (aṅgas) are at its joints.

On the eight petals, Brāhmī and the others are to be worshipped, and in the four corners and the eight directions, Indra and the others are to be worshipped. In all cases, the name of the deity is preceded by "Śrī."
Having uttered the word "pādukā," one should append the eight-syllable mantra "pūjayāmi. || 8 ||

The deity is to be propitiated within the triangle; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Since that triangle and the hexagon have no space mentioned between them, one should worship the four pairs beginning with Śrī and Śrīpati in the directions starting from the east, in accordance with the sequence of the recitation of the fourfold propitiation. This much constitutes the first enclosure (āvaraṇa).

Beginning with the couple Ṛddhi and Āmoda, there are six couples in the six-pointed corners. This pair of couples following them is on the two sides of the hexagon; this constitutes the second enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). In the hexagonal yantra, where one line meets another, that is a junction (*sandhi*). There are six such junctions.
In such junctions, since no specific order has been stated—

and because the previously mentioned order of the corners starting from Agni (SE), Īśa (NE), Asura (SW), and Vāyu (NW) is impossible here— one should disregard that order so that the lines terminate toward the east or toward the north.

One should worship the six limbs. Thus ends the third enclosure. Regarding the sequence for the eight petals, that which is stated in the *Śrīvidyārṇava* is as follows: for the first four [syllables], starting from the west and proceeding clockwise; for the subsequent ones...
The eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, are to be worshipped in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest (Vāyavyā) in clockwise order;
this is the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*). In the square, one should worship the respective lords of the directions in the eight directions starting from the east.
Since there is a requirement for mantras here, the mantras of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) as stated in the proximate *Śyāmākrama* [are to be used]. (Agra-6)
In the *Khaṇḍa* on the *Śyāmākrama*, fourteen lines from the root text contain the mantras of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), which are to be adopted.

Alternatively, one may use the name-mantra conjoined with the eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī*) that will be described hereafter. [In this context, the eight-syllabled mantra is "I worship the venerable sandals" (*śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*), and the name-mantra is "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Indra" (*oṃ śrī indrāya namaḥ*).]

This is the intended meaning of the foregoing. Thus ends the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*). He states a certain general rule (*paribhāṣā*) applicable to all [practices] that is useful for ritual performance, beginning with the words "In all cases" (*sarvatra*). "In all cases" refers to the general category of worship;
"in the names of the deities" means in the name-mantras (*nāmamantra*). The locative case ending signifies inclusion (*ghaṭakatva*). "Preceded by *śrī*" (*śrīpūrvaṃ*)...
First, having uttered the word "Śrī," then "Pādukā," and then "Pūjayāmi"; thus, it amounts to saying "I worship the Śrī-pādukā. || 8 ||

Furthermore, having performed the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth for Gaṇanātha, and having thus worshipped the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), one should again offer tenfold libations to the deity Gaṇanātha,
serve him with the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and [recite] *praṇava* and *māyā* at the end [of the mantra]: "To all obstructors, to all beings..."

Having recited "Hūṃ Svāhā" three times and offered the *bali* oblation, one should summon a single *baṭuka* with the thought that he is Gaṇapati, and a single *śakti* with the thought that she is Siddhalakṣmī;
having worshipped them with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having given the *ādimopādimamadhyama* offerings, [one prays: "May there be no obstacles for me..."
Having caused the favor to be granted with the words, "May there be success in the mantra," and having paid homage, one should recite it according to one's capacity. || 9 ||

Having worshipped—that is, having honored—the *pañcāvaraṇī*, which is the collective group (*samūha*) of the five deities of the obstructions (*āvaraṇadevatā*) in the manner thus described; [the term *pañcāvaraṇī* is derived from *pañca-āvaraṇa* with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to Pāṇini’s rule on *dvigoḥ*]; by the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is indicated that just as there was previously a worship of the five obstructions, so too here one worships the *pañcāvaraṇī*.

This too is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Thus, the misconception that it is an injunction for the mere performance (*kāma*) is dispelled. It is indicated that [the rite] falls within the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*). "Tenfold" means ten times.
Furthermore, the method of libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be understood from the end of the commentary on Sūtra 7 on pages 80–81 of this section.

This has already been explained previously. Furthermore, the sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) are enumerated in the *Paramānanda-tantra* as follows: water for the feet (*pādya*), water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*). [Regarding these modes of service, see Dīpikā-pañjikā-śiromaṇi-vivaraṇa.]

O Śivā, [one should offer] a bath, clothing, ornaments, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and also betel; as well as the waving of lights, the añjali gesture, circumambulation, and prostration.
"One should indeed count the offerings individually, O Goddess, sixteen for each. Thus it is said.
Or, at the outset, the sixteen services mentioned in the Sūtra may be performed.
In this regard, the fire sacrifice (homa) mentioned in the ritual manual as a constituent part of the worship is without foundation.
The *praṇava* is well known; *māyā* is *hrīṃ*. At the end and at the beginning of these two, one should recite the remainder ending with *svāhā*.
This is the mantra for the offering of the *bali*. Having recited this mantra three times, one should then perform the *balidāna*.

The desired materials for the *bali* offering should be taken as prescribed in the *Śrīkrama*. Regarding the location, that stated in the *Śrīkrama* is from one's own left side. The phrase "with the thought of Gaṇapati" is to be construed with the word "having worshipped.
This means having meditated upon the form of Gaṇapati. [This follows] the order of recitation.

Setting aside the sequence of the ritual acts, first comes the invocation (*āvāhana*), then the visualization (*bhāvana*), and then the worship (*arcana*); the same applies to what follows. Here, the invocation and other rites for both [deities] are performed according to the *padārthānusamaya* method (as seen in Dīpikā, Pañjikā, Śikṣā, and Vivaraṇa 8, for the distinction between *kāṇḍānusamaya* and *padārthānusamaya*).

It is not like collyrium and so forth, according to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (section-by-section) method; for here, there is no sublation, and because it is possible for all [the offerings] to have equal proximity to the primary [deities]. Having offered the first clearly, the second at the beginning, and the third in the middle—this is the consecration of the disposal (*pratipatti-saṃskāra*) for those in the middle.
This is because of the mention of the second [offering]. Its meaning is that one should consecrate the substance with the gift.

Thus, following the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), if there is a defect in the substance, this [consecration] alone serves as its removal. The sense is that, having caused grace to be bestowed, one should personally bring about their satisfaction so that grace may arise for both of them.
The passage beginning with "namas" and ending with "japet" is clear in its meaning.

Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Nibandha* regarding the worship of the *baṭuka* and the *suvāsinī* after the recitation has been clarified by this [work] as being contrary to the *sūtra*. || 9 ||
Regarding the dismissal of Gaṇapati:

if the fire-ritual (agnikārya) has been successfully completed, one should offer oblations into the fire that has been consecrated according to the rules prior to the offering to Bali, using the mantras beginning with Śrī and Śrīpati and ending with Vighnakartṛ, each concluded with "svāhā. Then, having returned, one should [worship] the Deity three times.

Having satisfied [the deities] with the appropriate offerings, having accepted the five elements (pañcaka), and having dissolved the Great Gaṇapati into oneself, one whose resolve is perfected should wander happily; may all be auspicious. || 10 ||

Thus ends the second section, the Gaṇapatiprakaraṇa, within the Kalpasūtra composed by the venerable Kulācārya, the great teacher Śrī Bhārgava Paraśurāma— the foremost disciple of Mahādeva, born from the womb of Reṇukā, and the destroyer of the race of wicked Kṣatriyas.

By the word "yadi" (if), the optional nature of the *homa*—whether it has been performed or not—is indicated. By the phrase "prior to Bali," the sequence and location [of the offering] are indicated. "According to rule" (*vidhivat*) means according to the method of the *homa* procedure explained previously in the ninth section, or according to the procedure that will be described hereafter.
The nature of the mantra is: "To Śrī and Śrīpati, Svāhā."

Regarding the division of the mantra written in the *Nibandha* as "svāhā to Śrī" and "svāhā to Śrīpati," this is the question: is the couple one deity, or are they two deities? In the first case, the division of the mantra into two is inappropriate; in the second case, [it would apply] to the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the *Nibandha*, the inclusion of the collective mantra (*samaṣṭimantra*) in the form "I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī-Śrīpati" is improper;

therefore, it should be disregarded as being contrary to the context. Nor should it be argued that, according to your own view, the same application of the collective mantra would follow even in the case of the fourfold libation (*tarpaṇa*), for in that instance, one worships each individual deity within the couples four times.
It proceeds with the words, "without having gratified the couples. In the section on worship, it simply states that one should worship the couples alone;
by this, the status of the couple as the deity is made clear. The same applies to the context of the fire-oblation (homa).

By the phrase "Śrī, Śrīpati, and so forth," it is made clear that the couple constitutes a single deity (*ekadevatā*). Otherwise, he would have simply said "beginning with Yā [Yama] and ending with Vighnakartṛ"; thus, the inclusion of Śrīpati would be redundant. Nor can it be argued that in the phrase "ending with Vighnakartṛ" there is an inclusion of a single deity; for if each were a separate deity, why [would such a qualification be necessary]?

It must be stated that [the term] would not be informative (*jñāpaka*). If this were informative regarding the essential nature of the mantra, then since Śrī, Śrīpati, and so forth would already be obtained by the phrase "by those ending with the makers of obstacles" (*vighnakartṛntaiḥ*), the inclusion of "Śrī, Śrīpati, and so forth" (*śrīśrīpatyādī*) would be redundant; therefore, it is meaningful as being informative of the mantra's essential nature. [The phrase is] "by those ending with the makers of obstacles."
Since it is meaningful as that which causes the cessation of the subsequent pair, everything is consistent. Therefore,

in the fourfold repetition of the libation (*tarpaṇa*), for the sake of completing the count of four hundred and forty-four libations according to the previously stated reasoning, [one should perform] each one—

Regarding deityhood: even in the context of deityhood, as well as in worship (*pūjā*) and *homa*, deityhood functions only as a distributed property (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), according to the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). Therefore, the nature of the mantra is exactly as we have stated.
By the phrase "up to those who cause obstacles," there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the fire and the couple.

Regarding the phrase "having offered" (*hutvā*), when there is an expectancy for a substance, *ājya* (clarified butter) alone is used according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "when no specific substance is prescribed, *ājya* is the material. However, in the case of a specific desire, a particular substance such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and so forth may be used. By the expression "returning again," it is indicated that the place of the oblation (*homapradeśa*) is distinct from the place of worship (*pūjāpradeśa*). The remainder is as before. [This is to be done] by those who are qualified.

Together with those who are conversant with the tradition, we shall clarify the inherent meaning of this qualification in detail later on, at the end of the commentary on Sūtra 30 in the third section of the *Śrīkrama*, beginning with the words: "Nowadays, those whose senses are unsubdued... Having accepted and adopted the five-fold group (*pañcaka*) in the *Śrīkrama*.
According to the procedure that will be described here, the word "saha" (together) does not necessarily imply that the item must be procured even in the absence of a suitable object;

rather, in its absence, it merely prescribes the expiation for the omission of an auxiliary element (*aṅga*). However, when it is present, there is a requirement of concomitance (*sāhitya*); and when it is absent, one simply takes the *prastara* (grass-bundle) by itself along with the branch.

It is like the expression "he strikes. Since the limits for the worship of Gaṇapati are not mentioned here, as is the case with [the worship of] Śyāmā and others, and since the number of recitations (japa) is also not mentioned, one must take refuge in another tantra. Regarding that, the statement from another tantra is found in the *Tantrasāra*:

"With a concentrated mind, one should meditate on the mantra and recite it four hundred thousand times, together with four thousand [additional recitations]. One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten thousand times using eight substances, such as sweetmeats (modaka) and others. Thus it is said.

Having performed the dismissal with the *udvāsana-mudrā*, one whose resolve is accomplished and whose task is finished should dwell happily—this phrase is to be understood as the final word in the last sūtra of this section. This demonstrates that for one who has performed the prescribed rite, there is not only the destruction of obstacles, but also this further fruit. By this...

The phrase "having made a firm resolve" (*kṛtasaṅkalpa*) indicates that whatever is desired is accomplished through the worship of Anaṅga-Svatantra-Gaṇanāyaka, even if it is not an auxiliary means for the worship of Śrīvidyā.
(For detailed knowledge regarding the specific procedure for this worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa, see the *Śrīprapañcasāra*).
The *Gaṇeśapurāṇa*, *Śāradātilaka*, *Mantramahodadhi*, and other Tantric texts should be consulted.
"May there be auspiciousness" (*śivam*) indicates the conclusion of the section, as before.
Thus ends the second section, titled "The Manual of Gaṇanāyaka," in the commentary on the Paraśurāma-sūtra named Saubhāgyodaya, composed by Śrī Rāmeśvara.

Upon the completion of the Sūtra, that which was to be purified must be indicated, and the remaining portion shall be fulfilled by the grace of the Primordial One. (Thus ends the second section. Śrīḥ.
Third Section – The Śrīkrama: The Chapter on Lalitā.
[I bow to Her] who is united with the three eternal currents (nityaughatraya), enveloped by the eight enclosures (aṣṭāvaraṇa) and the six limbs (aṅgaṣaṭka).
For those who contemplate it, words flow effortlessly from the mouth through its grace.
Thus, having described the worship of Gaṇapati as an ancillary to the worship of Śrī Lalitā by means of the first section,

he begins to state the ritual sequence (*krama*) of the Supreme Deity, Śrī Lalitā: "Having thus worshipped Gaṇapati, with all obstacles and disturbances dispelled, [one should proceed] toward the sole leader of the circle of powers (*śakticakra*)."
One should begin the ritual sequence of Śrī Lalitā. || 1 ||
By the passage ending with "evam" and "vighnavyatikaraḥ," it is indicated that one should first perform the worship of Gaṇapati for some time, and only thereafter begin the worship of Śrī Lalitā.

Thus, having worshipped—that is, having practiced—in the manner previously described, all [obstacles] have been shaken off, meaning they have been dispelled. All [desires] are complete, meaning they are entirely fulfilled.
By whom the occurrences and aggregations of obstacles [are overcome].

This primary status of the worship of Gaṇanāyaka is a qualification of the eligible practitioner (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). This is an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*); furthermore, due to the natural force of the preceding qualification, it is also an injunctive statement regarding eligibility (*adhikāravidhi*). Alternatively, this is not a qualification of the eligible practitioner; for if that were the case, [the following would apply].

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the worship of Gaṇapati would become a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the fire-worship (*agnimopāsana*). Nor is this an acceptable conclusion.

There are six means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for establishing subsidiarity, namely the three beginning with direct statement (*śruti*) and the three beginning with indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the third book [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*].

Among these, subsidiarity established by the third means of proof—syntactical connection (*vākya*)—is not sublated here, due to the absence of any indicative mark (*liṅga*) or direct statement (*śruti*) that could contradict it.
Since it is impossible to deny that the constituent parts are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
what is enjoined here is either the worship of Lalitā as qualified by the sequence consisting in its occurring subsequent to the worship of Gaṇapati;
or else, this undertaking is qualified by a specific sequence which itself is qualified by the qualities consisting in the preceding worship.

By this, worship performed with grace at that time is enjoined. The phrase "with all obstacles and disturbances dispelled" is a restatement of the previously mentioned result. Thus, what is called the "commencement" (ārambha) is a specific kind of resolve (*saṅkalpa*), such as "I shall begin the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. By the words "one should begin the Lalitā-rite," [the practice] is intended to continue for as long as one lives.
The resolve, "I shall perform [the worship]," is established. Its subsidiary part is the propitiation of Gaṇapati.

Furthermore, this resolve, characterized by these qualities, is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) to the worship of Śrī Lalitā—functioning like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—because it possesses the definition stated in Jaimini’s Sūtra: "That by which a substance is not intended to be processed. It is not [a proximate auxiliary].

Furthermore, it must be stated what the difference is in the performance [of the rite] whether [the qualification] is a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) or whether it takes the form of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) as just explained. If it were a qualification of the eligible person, then one who has not performed the worship of Gaṇapati due to negligence or the like, or one who lacks eligibility such as being blind, would be unable to begin the worship of Lalitā.

Just as in the case of one who has performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when there is a lack of fruit from the ritual action performed up to that point, one should then abandon the worship of Lalitā and, having attained the requisite qualification by performing the worship of Gaṇapati,
subsequently perform the worship of Śrīvidyā; this applies according to the view of the specific injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Since the commencement [of the rite] is an ancillary part of the worship of Gaṇapati, and that commencement is an ancillary part of the worship of Lalitā,
86) when the commencement occurs through forgetfulness, something is prescribed for the purpose of removing the defect produced by the omission of an ancillary element.

Expiation does not follow the subsidiary parts, but rather involves the repetition of the principal rite. Nor should it be argued that, rather than omitting the subsidiary entirely, it is better to perform it—since the principal rite does not depend upon the subsidiaries—and thus let there be no repetition, while the subsidiary alone is performed. This must not be said.

To the extent that the primary auxiliary acts possess the status of being cooperative factors for the production of the *apūrva* by the principal act, [this applies] in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*).

However, because there is an absence of cooperative factors for the production of the *apūrva* by the principal act, and because the principal act has perished immediately thereafter, even the performance of the auxiliaries alone would be futile. In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), however, they must be performed as long as one lives.

When it is stated that "it must be performed free from the omission of any auxiliary (aṅga)," a contraction of the phrase "all auxiliaries" (sakalāṅgam) is appropriate— meaning "as many auxiliaries as are possible" or "as many auxiliaries as are known"— out of fear that the scripture would otherwise incur invalidity due to being impossible to carry out. And so:

It was established in the sixth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that the production of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is postulated by means of the principal rite together with whatever subsidiaries are known according to one's capacity. Thus, since the worship of Lalitā is obligatory, even if some unknown subsidiary is omitted, the *apūrva* is generated by the principal rite accompanied by the other subsidiaries; therefore, the performance of that specific subsidiary would be rendered useless.
There is no re-performance of the ancillary rite consisting of the worship of Gaṇapati when it has been omitted.

If something must be performed for the sake of removing obstacles, then either the recitation of the Vināyaka-stava or the muttering of its specific mantra should be done. Such is the deliberation regarding these varieties of performance.
This has been done; let the wise investigate further than this.

The "circles of power" (*śakticakra*) of the sole sovereign of the circles of power refer to the five circles—beginning with the triangle—among the nine circles that constitute the components of the Śrīcakra. As it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"By means of the four circles of Śiva and the five circles of Śakti..."
The Śrīcakra, perfected with nine wheels, is the body of Śiva and Śivā.
"The triangle, the octagon, the two decagons, and the fourteen-spoked [wheel]—these are the five wheels of Śakti. Thus it is said.

Of them, she is the one principal heroine; or else, *śaktayaḥ* refers to married women, and their *cakra* is the assembly; among them, she is this one, the peerless heroine (*nāyikā*), the sovereign (*nāthā*), the most excellent (*śreṣṭhā*). Nor is it the case that [the compound is invalid], for the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) does not apply here because the particle *na* is used in the sense of exclusion (*nirdhāraṇe*).

How is this meaning to be stated? Even though the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is prohibited, there is no obstacle to it being a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*), just as in the case of *puruṣottama*. Alternatively, the powers (*śakti*) are those which accomplish the various effects residing in their respective objects; the one, non-dual leader (*nāyikā*) is the impeller of their collection. As it has been said:
In the Śrī Devībhāgavata: "O best of sages, know that all the powers, from Śiva down to the earthly king, who accomplish their respective tasks, are impelled by me alone."

Alternatively, the "powers" (śaktayaḥ) are Śyāmā, Vārtālī, and so forth; they themselves constitute the "circle" (cakra), meaning the retinue, according to the usage of the learned that "the circle is to be served, as a king is to be served. The term "sole mistress of those [powers]" (tāsām ekanāyikā) means she who is the unique controller.
By this, the preeminence of Śrīvidyā is indicated. Thus, she is the "sole mistress of the circle of powers."

The quality belongs to Lalitā. And thus, the deityhood of the qualified [entity] exists because, in the originative injunction (utpattivākya), the deity is that which is qualified by the qualities heard therein; as in "to Agni Pavamāna" and "to Agni... [etc.].
This is because of the rule that the deity heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) must be mentioned everywhere, as in the case of the mantra "To Pāvaka," and so forth.
Thus, wherever the mention of the deity's name is mandatory, it must be mentioned as qualified by its attributes,
such as in the case of the *sandhyā-japa* and the *sandhyā-pūjā*, where [the deity] is the sole sovereign of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*).

"I shall perform such-and-such a rite for the pleasure of Śrī Lalitā"—thus is the declaration made. Otherwise, in the Pavamāneṣṭi sacrifice, there would simply be "I offer what is pleasing to Agni. Therefore, in this context, the connection with the deity as qualified by the specific attribute must be performed within the mantras. [This applies to] the sequence, the worship, and the spiritual practice.
or one should undertake it.
The etymological explanation of the name Lalitā is given in the Padma Purāṇa:
"She shines (lalate) transcending the worlds; therefore she is called Lalitā."

Regarding this, our supreme preceptors have shown another etymological interpretation suggested by the word "ca" (and) in their *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "Lalita" refers to a specific kind of action born from the emotion of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic love); she who possesses that is Lalitā.
By this, it is implied that this form has the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) as its primary essence. || 1 ||

Next, he teaches the meditation and other practices to be performed during the *brāhmamuhūrta* by means of two sūtras— [the portion from "tataḥ" onwards, including "from now on, the daily rites to be performed by the worshipper of Lalitā," is found in the Ba manuscript]— beginning with the meditation upon the Guru.
During the *brāhma-muhūrta*, a Brahmin, having abandoned sleep, should contemplate his Guru as the form of Paramaśiva for the dissolution of his sins. || 2 ||
The Brāhma-muhūrta: having divided the day, which consists of sixty ghaṭikās, into thirty parts, the twenty-eighth muhūrta is the Brāhma. As it is said in the Devībhāgavata:
"That which is the twenty-eighth muhūrta is named after Brahmā."

Having risen at that time, the wise man should contemplate his own welfare. Furthermore, there is another definition of the *brāhmamuhūrta* well-known in the Purāṇas; therein, the prohibition against sleeping is also found in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, the *Ratnāvalī*, and other such texts, as follows:
The third muhūrta of the last watch of the night is to be known as the Brāhma; it is prescribed for waking.

Five times five [twenty-five] units constitute the time of dawn (uṣaḥkāla); seven times five [thirty-five] is the rising of the dawn-red (aruṇodaya); eight times five [forty] is considered morning (prātaḥ), after which sunrise (sūryodaya) is said to occur.
Regarding the fruit [of this], Dhanvantari says: "The acceptance [of gifts] from the virtuous for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and affection is supreme;
one who practices in this manner shall attain eternal residence in heaven."

And in the *Ratnāvalī*: "Sleep during the *brāhma-muhūrta* causes the destruction of merit; if a twice-born man sleeps then out of delusion, he is purified by a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance. Thus [it is said].

In that context, the Brāhmaṇa, having abandoned sleep, wakes up. Although the abandonment of sleep is generally obtained through traditional recollection (*smṛti*) at that time, it is enjoined by this [Vedic] injunction as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), because it was not otherwise established as such.
Its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice is like the rule "one should not speak untruth" found in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Regarding the excellence of that state of being free from sleep, it is stated in the *Tripurārahasya*:
"When two muhūrtas remain until the rising of the sun,
that time is declared as the dawn (uṣaḥkāla), which brings auspiciousness to practitioners."
O Rāma, at that time, whatever object a person contemplates with an unwavering mind, that very thing arises for him by the natural power of the moment and the occasion.
