But he who, in this time which resembles a wish-fulfilling tree, does not awaken;
or having awakened, being of exceedingly dull intellect, does not reflect upon his own welfare.
"Falling away from all his own goals, he sinks like a cow in the mud. Thus it is said.

Having arisen at such a time for the sake of destroying all sins— the dative case here is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*)— Śiva [here, as in the commentary on Sūtra 1 on the previous page 7,
where the author of the Vṛtti cites the verse beginning with *śrutipathagalitānām*, the venerable Sūta also calls the Lord Śiva the "Guru of Gurus"; likewise, in this place also, the Lord...]
Even the illustrious Rāma, son of Jamadagni, declared this Parameṣṭhin, the illustrious Śiva-Paramaśiva, to be his Guru.

This very quality of being preeminent in worshipfulness and the state of being my own deity belong to the Lord who is the Guru of Gurus—[as stated by] the author of the *Dvitiyavritti-diparishistaka* on the *Paushkara-kashmiri-sutra*:
"He alone is the Guru, none other than him."
Having thus touched [the object] and meditated upon it in the mind. || 2 ||

Having visualized the root-consciousness (*mūlasaṃvit*) blazing from its base up to the opening of the aperture (*vidhibila*), tawny like ten million flashes of lightning and glowing like the rising sun, and having thereby destroyed the web of impurities with its rays, one should mentally repeat the root-mantra, beginning with either *ka* or *ha*, ten times. || 3 ||

The root is the *ādhāra-cakra*; from that as the beginning, up to the aperture of the *vidhi*, it is connected with the phrase "blazing" (*jvalantīm*). Like millions of flashes of lightning (*taṭitkoṭayaḥ*), it is tawny (*kaḍārām*) or brownish-red;
like the young sun (*taruṇadivākaraḥ*), the sun situated in the middle of the sky, it is golden-yellow (*piñjarām*), and for that very reason, it is blazing.

Having meditated upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlasaṃvid*), which is the mind free from objects, and by means of its rays— the rays that are flames of the nature of consciousness— he is one by whom the nets, that is, the multitudes, of impurities have been struck down and removed; being such, he [should recite] with his mind the fifteen-syllable *vidyā*, either the *kādi* form worshipped by Kāma, or the *hādi* form worshipped by Lopāmudrā.
Having meditated upon the phonemes distinguished by their sequence.

In this commentary (*nibandha*), the recitation of one's own guru’s sandals (*pādukā*), the salutation with the five mudrās, and other verses composed according to one's own whim have been written down. These are not intended by the Sūtra and are to be disregarded. The same applies to the mantras for cleaning the teeth (*dantadhāvana*), as well as the rule regarding twenty mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*). All of these [are unauthorized].
Those that are immeasurable should be abandoned. || 3 ||
Next, regarding the ritual of bathing and the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*): concerning the act of bathing,
when the time for bathing has arrived, one should apply [the water] three times to the head with the root mantra.
Having drunk three handfuls of water consecrated with that [mantra] three times, having satiated the ancestors three times with water, having sprinkled oneself three times,
and having put on two garments [with the *mūla-mantra*—

this phrase is added in manuscript *ba2*], and having uttered "Hrāṃ Haṃsaḥ" [accompanied by the three long vowels upon returning home— this phrase is added in manuscript *ta*], and having uttered "Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Saḥ."
Having offered the arghya three times with the mantra "Svāhā to Mārtāṇḍabhairava, accompanied by the Śakti Prakāśa, to Savitṛ," [he proceeds]. || 4 ||

89) When the ritual of bathing has arrived, that is, at the occasion for bathing; by this, its occurrence subsequent to the Vedic bath is indicated. This very meaning is clearly stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"After the Vedic rites have been performed by members of the three castes, all Tantric rites are then carried out."

In this context, there is a repetition of the mantra for each individual *añjali*. Since the plural number in the word *añjalīn* establishes a plurality of substances, a repetition of the action also follows, because it has been established in the eleventh [book] that a repetition of the mantra occurs when there is a plurality of substances. When the expectation arises as to where the [substance] is to be given, the answer is "on one's own head," because that is appropriate due to its nature as part of the bathing ritual.

[The word] *pūraṇīyam* [is to be supplied]. "With the root" means while reciting the root mantra; that is its meaning. "Three times" refers to those [waters] consecrated by that [mantra], i.e., consecrated by the root mantra. The word "three times" connects with the word "consecrated," because of its proximity and not with the word "having drunk," because of its remoteness. Therefore, [one should drink] water that has been consecrated by the root mantra three times, only once [per application].

Regarding the consumption [of the offering]: having satiated [the deity] three times while reciting the root mantra, one performs the recitation of the mantra once—namely, "I satisfy Śrī Lalitā, the sole leader of the circle of powers (śakticakra)"—because this constitutes the repetition of the ritual action (*kriyā*). However, it was already established previously that in the case of a fourfold satiation, there is only a repetition of the mantra (*mantra-āvṛtti*) and not a repetition of the ritual action. For indeed...
There is a scriptural injunction that brings about a distinction in the substance; therefore, the mantra is used only once.

The same applies to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). The word "self" (*ātmānam*) refers to the body, because a refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by sprinkling cannot pertain to the primary meaning [of the self]. This is because no specific mantras are prescribed for the acts of satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and sprinkling.
One should apply [the term] "with the root [mantra]. As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"O Supreme Goddess, when no mantra is specified, one should employ the root mantra."

It is not the case that [the phrase] "having given with the root-mantra" (mūlena dattvā) is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* [from the preceding]; for if that were so, then even in the case of [the phrase] "those consecrated by that" (tadabhimantritāḥ), the word "that" (tat-) would be redundant due to the supply of the same *anuṣaṅga*. Therefore, there must indeed be an *adhyāhāra* (supplying a missing word). The act of putting on the garment—which is already established by traditional law (*smṛti*)—is merely restated here; its meaning is: "reciting the root-mantra while putting on the garment. [Note: The portion in brackets marked "ba 2" is an additional reading.]

The fruit of that is to be understood as the knowledge that the rite of bathing has been completed. Having said this—[according to the *ba* manuscript, there is an additional passage: "having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) 'I shall perform the Tantric twilight ritual (*tāntrikasandhyā*) after the Vedic twilight ritual']"—one should omit only this much; the mantra for offering the *arghya* water ends with *svāhā*. Even though [the purpose] is evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra itself...

If the deity has already been obtained [as the recipient], the mention of Savitṛ would be redundant. Nevertheless, regarding the phrase "having given the arghya," the meaning of the act of giving (*dāna*) consists in the renunciation of a substance intended for a deity, preceded by the destruction of one's own ownership. And that [renunciation] takes the form: "This belongs to such-and-such a deity, not to me. In that context, according to the indicative power of the mantra, it is: "This belongs to Mārtaṇḍabhairava, not to me."

It is established. Just as in the case of the rule "one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," the dative form "to Savitṛ" is used to set aside that [previous application]. Here too, since it is impossible to give again a substance already given once, it is established that there is a different substance in the subsequent offering. And thus, due to the distinctness of the substances, there is a repetition of the mantra, just as in the following example:
The mantra for threshing various kinds of seeds. || 5 ||
Then, the visualization of the Śrīcakra and the offering of *arghya* to the Goddess within the solar disc are prescribed:
having meditated upon the wheel of nine triangles (*navayonicakra*) in the center of that disc, [this is the explicit Śrī Tripurā Gāyatrī as follows]:
*Aiṃ tripurasundari vidmahe klīṃ pīṭhakāmini dhīmahi | tannaḥ klinnā*.

Having uttered "vācam uccārya," [one says] "tripurasundari vidmahe"; having uttered "kāmam uccārya," [one says] "pīṭhakāmini dhīmahi"; having uttered "śaktim uccārya," [one says] "tannaḥ klinnā pracodayāt. Having thus offered *arghya* three times to the Great Goddess, and having touched [the vessel] one hundred and eight times while reciting the mantra, one should observe silence. || 5 ||

In the center of that solar disc, which appears as a circular form, is the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*), a wheel in which there are nine *yoni*s: four facing outward and five facing toward oneself.
The meaning is "the Śrīcakra. As it is stated in the Kāmikāgama: "The nine-yoni is the Śrīcakra.
Also in the Sundarīhṛdaya: "The nine-yoni is declared to be the Śrīcakra, the cause of the origin of the universe.
The rest is clear. "Speech" refers to the first *kūṭa*.

"Whose lotus-face has the singular nature of the glorious *vāgbhava* syllable"—according to this authoritative source, one should recite the portion ending with *vidmahe* immediately after the first *kūṭa*. Then follows the desire, which is the middle *kūṭa*;
as it is stated in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:
Between the Śakti and Vāgbhava [syllables], the Kāmarāja is renowned;
it is a mixture of red and white luster... thus.

Having uttered that, one should recite: "O Pīṭhakāminī, meditate [on us]. Then, having uttered the third Śaktikūṭa, one should recite from the *Sahasranāma*: "She who bears the lower part of the waist which has attained oneness with the Śaktikūṭa. Thereafter, one should recite up to the end with "May [He] impel [us]. This...

It is also called the *Tripurā-gāyatrī*. The remainder is as before. Having contemplated and recited [the mantra], the rest is clear. Regarding this, what is stated by the authors of the *Nibandhas* is as follows: beginning with the drawing of a circle one cubit in size in the water during the bath, up to the consecration seven times with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should contemplate oneself three times during the *sandhyā*.

The section ending with "having sprinkled" (prokṣya) belongs to another tantra; it should not be touched by one who follows this tantra. If it were touched, then for what reason would the three daily junctions (sandhyā-traya) and the sequence of the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa-krama) have been abandoned? If that [other tantra] is authoritative, let him state its source. || 5 ||
Regarding the entry into the sacrificial hall and so forth, he says:

"Having gone to the sacrificial hall, whether having performed the ritual preparations (*kḷptākalpa*) or being free from such preparations (*saṅkalpākalpa*), [he should sit] on the seat with the *pīṭha-mantra*."
He sat down together. || 6 ||

Having gone to the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), that is, the place of worship; by this it is established that the twilight rites (*sandhyā*) are performed outside in water, such as in a river and so forth. "Adorned" (*kḷpta*) means one by whom ornaments (*ākalpa*) have been worn. This wearing of ornaments is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the performer of worship. Therefore, those things which are to be worn by the performer of worship in the world [should be understood here].

Those ornaments must certainly be worn, and this is possible for the wealthy. This being the case, it would follow that a poor person—who is incapable of possessing ornaments as part of his physical being—would have no entitlement, just like a blind person or others.

Therefore, he says: "or one whose attire is fashioned by resolve" (*saṅkalpākalpa*). One whose attire (*ākalpa*) is fashioned (*kalpita*) by resolve (*saṅkalpa*), that is, by a mental act—such a person [is entitled].

Or rather, it means one who wears ornaments created by the mind; thus, the sense is that even a poor person has the qualification [for this practice]. Furthermore, the inclusion of ornaments abounding in rubies (padmarāga) is intended, even though there are specific restrictions regarding particular ornaments found in other tantras.
As for the fact that the consumption of betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) is mentioned in the *Nibandha* during the worship of the door-gods (*dvārapūjā*),

that is not intended by the author of the Sūtra. Alternatively, since the performance of the ritual takes place in the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), going there is established as a matter of course.

Furthermore, by stating "having gone again to the sacrificial temple" (punaryāgamandiraṃ gatvā)—which would otherwise be redundant—the mention of this phrase, which signifies "having entered within the station of the Gaṇapati-krama," indicates an extension of the attributes belonging to that [Gaṇapati-krama] to the end.
For this very reason, this term does not appear in the Vārāhī-krama. Consequently, it applies to the Śrī-krama and the Śyāmā-krama.
Let there be the worship of the door; nevertheless, in the Śrīkrama, the consumption of betel is entirely without foundation.

"Pīṭhamanu" has been explained previously. Regarding the word "samupaviṣṭaḥ," the prefix *sam-* indicates that one should remain seated on a single seat until the completion [of the rite]. Therefore, by means of whichever posture—such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or another—one does not experience fatigue while remaining until the end, by that posture [one should sit].
The meaning is that one should remain [steadfast].

In the *Nibandha*, it is stated that there should be consecration by reciting the third seed-syllable twelve times and sprinkling with the root mantra; however, that should be understood as not approved by the *Sūtra*.
He states the *tritārī* (the triple-star mantra) which is useful for this worship:
"Having uttered the *tritārī*, one should cast a handful of flowers on the ground with the words: *namaḥ raktadvādaśaśaktiyuktāya dīpanāthāya*. (7)

Having uttered the three *tārās* as will be described [meaning: in this very sūtra and its commentary below], one should recite up to the end with "namaḥ". This is the mantra for the worship of Dīpanātha. With this, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the ground. A *puṣpāñjali* is a heap of flowers held in the hollowed palms.
Thus it is said in the Agastyasaṃhitā, in the section on the ritual for Monday: "A handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*) consists of a cluster of blossoms held between the two palms joined together. (7)
Regarding the rule for the conjunction of the *tritārī* with all mantras, he states a certain technical definition applicable to all mantras:
"The conjunction of the *tritārī* occurs at the beginning of all mantras. The *tritārī* consists of Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā. (8)

In this context, by restricting the scope of the word "all" (*sarva*) through the force of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*), the meaning is that [the *tritārī*] applies to those mantras recited subsequent to this which constitute the ancillaries (*aṅga*) of the worship of Śrīvidyā.
By this, it is established that there is no application of the *tritārī* in the mantras preceding this one. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Setubandha*:

It is established that since the *tritārī* is recited in conjunction [with the mantra] in the *Kalpasūtra* after entering the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), it should be understood that this conjunction does not exist within the mantras prior to that point. By the word "at the beginning" (*ādau*), the exclusion of the end is indicated. While one could simply say "conjunction" (*yoga*), the prefix *sam-* was employed so that the pronunciation of the *tritārī* would be made explicit. Therefore...

If, during the recitation of any part of the mantra, even a single syllable is omitted due to a defect such as lack of proficiency in pronunciation, then the mantra must be recited again; in that case as well, the application of the *tritārī* is indicated.
Alternatively, if after the recitation of the *tritārī*, the recitation of the mantra is interrupted by some obstacle—

In such a case, a momentary delay is indicated by the recitation of the *tritārī* without interruption, even though the application of the *tritārī* has already been achieved through this very [method] in the mantra for the worship of Dīpanātha. (p. 92) Even so, in that [instance],...

The statement "having uttered the *tritārī*" is redundant; nevertheless, by saying "having uttered the *tritārī* there," it indicates that the *tritārī* is a constituent part of that mantra. Furthermore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) prescribes the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of mantras through their conjunction with the *tritārī*, and thus it is not useless.
As for that which is stated in the *Nibandha*— namely, the salutation to Gaṇapati following the worship of Dīpanātha, the salutation to the Guru,

the pervasive [placement] from the thumb to the little finger, and the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath)— all of that belongs to other tantras or other contexts and should not be employed in the practice of Śrīvidyā.

Regarding the inquiry as to what constitutes the "three stars" (*tritārī*) here, he says: "The three stars. *Vāk* is the twelfth vowel accompanied by the nasal bindu. *Māyā* is the fourth vowel accompanied by the nasal bindu, following the second semivowel together with the fourth sibilant. *Kamalā* is the fourth vowel accompanied by the nasal bindu, above the second semivowel together with the first sibilant. These are the meanings denoted by the term "three stars."
The word "become" is to be understood as the ellipsis. [Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—this is the combined three-star mantra (tritārī-mantra).
We shall state the authoritative evidence for the aforementioned meanings of speech and the other faculties later on. || 8 ||
Regarding the nature of the Śrīcakra and the materials for its accomplishment, he describes the nature of the Śrīcakra and the materials for its accomplishment hereafter:
"In front [is] the form of the union of the five Śaktis and the four Śrīkaṇṭhas, consisting of three earth-seats, three folds, and the earth-lord..."

Having placed the great king of wheels— which consists of the lotus, the triangle, the square, the circle, the eight-petaled lotus, the world-mountain, the mountain of the gods, Brahmā, the sun, the moon, the quarters, the intermediate directions, the trident, the bindu, and the wheel— either inscribed with vermilion and saffron,
or engraved upon gold, silver, the five metals, jewels, crystal, and so forth. || 9 ||
The word *purataḥ* (in front) is syntactically connected with the word *niveśya* (having placed). The five powers (*pañcaśaktayaḥ*) are the wheels of power (*śakticakrāṇi*);
the four Śrīkaṇṭhas are the four wheels of Śiva (*śivacakrāṇi*). Their nature as a fusion is their non-differentiated essence.
By this qualification, it is indicated that knowledge of such an essential nature is necessary at the beginning of worship and other rites.
The method of this union and the necessity of such knowledge at the time of worship are stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In the triangle, the point (*bindu*) is joined; in the eight-spoked [wheel], the eight-petalled lotus."
Within the sixteen-spoked [cakra] of the two ten-spoked [cakras], there is the earth-abode in the world-petal.
He who knows the relationship of inseparable concomitance between the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the Cakras, is a knower of the Cakra.
Thus, he who worships the Śrīcakra even once without knowing its divisions does not obtain that fruit, nor is Lalitāmbā pleased with him. So it is said.

93) This very same meaning has been extensively established in the Tantras; however, for fear of excessive length, the relevant passages have not been written here. [The mandala consists of] three earth-seats surrounded by three square lines.
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the power of the square-shaped ground is stated in the words of another Tantra:
"Having drawn a circle outside of that, one should draw a square outside of that. This has also been written by our supreme guru in the *Setubandha* regarding the "ground-dwelling" (*bhūgṛha*).
It is called "the square."
Regarding the justification for drawing three doorless squares within the Śrīcakra:

if it is asked—"But since the statement in another Tantra uses the singular 'a square' (*caturasrakam*), it is understood that there is only one square; whereas here it is said 'three squares' (*caturasratrayam*). How can this be, given the contradiction between the two?"—the answer is as follows: no.

This is because various alternative arrangements are possible according to the differences among individuals who follow their respective tantras. Thus, for those following the Sūtra system, the *bhūpura* (earth-fortress) in the Śrīcakra is without gates, as it has not been mentioned [in that context].

Is it not the case that in the *Tripurārṇava* it is stated: "Then, from that [mandala], there is a triad of earth-purī (bhūpura) adorned with gates"? Likewise, in the *Nityātantra*: "Thus, the abode of the three earths is adorned with four gates," and in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*: "The surrounding circle and the earth-purī are beautified by four gates."

If it is argued that, following the precedent of such primary tantras, the presence of doors should also be postulated here [in this context], we say no; for in the *Yāmala* scripture it is stated: "This Śrīcakra of the Supreme Deity is said to consist of three enclosures (*vṛtta*) and three earth-forts (*dharaṇīsadana*)," and because other tantras likewise mention the *bhūpura* (earth-fort) without doors, the doubt [regarding their necessity] is difficult to dispel.

Nor should it be said that this is unreliable because no author has ever written of a *bhūpura* (enclosure) devoid of gates; for in the forty-third verse of the *Saundaryalaharī*, no mention of gates is made.
This is because the venerable Bhagavatpāda himself accepts precisely the position we have stated.

Likewise, in the *Prapañcasārasaṅgraha*, Śrī Vidyāraṇyasvāmin has also written in accordance with our own view, using the passage: "In some instances, a square is found within the Śrīcakra even though it lacks a gateway."

The same is the case in the *Aticirantana-Śiṅgabhūpāla-paddhati* as well. While engaged in searching for this, other statements from various other treatises will also be encountered; however, since this much suffices, no further special effort has been made.

Thus, because the author of the *Nityotsava*, who possesses a sense of special pride in thinking "I am a follower of the Sūtras," has written at the point of describing the method for drawing the *Śrīcakra* that one should "manifest the four-gated *bhūpura*," he has consequently failed to properly examine the Sūtra. This was done merely by following the crowd out of a desire to conform to the ways of others.
It is clearly written thus.
Furthermore, the author of the *Nibandhana* himself recorded in his own work that he was a disciple of Śrī Bhāskararāya.

In the *Setubandha* composed by Śrī Bhāskararāya, the third position is stated as follows: "It consists of three lines in each direction and lacks any general doorway. Regarding this position, the *Kalpasūtra* [is as follows]:...
It is written as "favorable."

Furthermore, since the *Kalpasūtra* prescribes that "the conjunction with the *tritārī* occurs at the beginning of all mantras" specifically after entering the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), it is established in the *Setubandha* that this conjunction does not apply to those mantras preceding that point; thus,
this [application] is deceptive regarding the *raśmimālā* mantras.

And in the *Sandhyāvandana*, he employed the *tritārī*; likewise, he employed the fourfold gate. This being so, what kind of person is he who, not knowing even the doctrine of the Guru, writes according to his own whim?
We do not know what kind of lay follower he was, nor the nature of his relationship as teacher and disciple.

Furthermore, if one first inscribes the absence of the general door (*dvārasāmānyābhāva*) in the *Setubandha*, and subsequently examines its true nature, then in that very context— in works such as the *Yāmalakalpasūtra*— the position regarding the absence of the general door exists only through either the negation (*pratiṣedha*) or the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the door.

Since it is written that what is being postulated merely by the non-mention of a door is nothing but rashness, how can it be said that [the author] is ignorant of the Guru’s doctrine? In that case, let us set aside for now the question of his knowledge of the Guru’s doctrine regarding the doors; however, there is ignorance of the Guru’s doctrine regarding the application of the *tritārī* in the *raśmimālā* mantras and the *sandhyā* mantras.

It has become as hard as adamant. By this, we clearly perceive it to be logical that even the tradition claiming "this work was edited by the independent master of all systems, Śrī Bhāskararāya" is baseless.

"Three folds" means three circles. Regarding this point, many [authorities] hold that there are two circles for the pericarps of the sixteen-petaled and eight-petaled lotuses, and one circle outside of those;
thus, there are three circles, not three circles surrounding two lotuses. As for the *Kalpasūtra* stating "three folds," [it refers to this].

Regarding the statement in the *Yāmala*, "the three circles and the three abodes of the earth," and the statement in the *Yoginītantra*, "the square form is Jyeṣṭhā and the triple circle is Vāmā," they say that all such passages refer exclusively to the three aforementioned circles.
Regarding the justification for drawing the five circles within the Śrīcakra,
our supreme preceptors state here in the *Setubandha*, on the occasion of describing the drawing of the Śrīcakra by means of another method that will be explained:
Outside, one should draw two lotuses with eight and sixteen petals respectively;
then one should draw a circle of qualities (guṇavṛtta), and outside of that, a square.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, by the natural force of the words (*padasvārasyena*), there are three circles outside the two lotuses; following that, the remainder is the enclosure of the earth (*bhūpūra*). Here, the singular number is not intended to be significant.
In this way, there are five circles. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 10, verses 72–73):
There are these two verses:
"O Maheśānī, outside of this, draw a circle resembling the full moon;
O Mīnākṣī, make it beautiful with eight petals."
"Likewise, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should draw a sixteen-petaled [lotus];
outside of that, O Queen of the Gods, there are three circles (trivṛtta) accompanied by the Mātṛkās.
Here, by the phrase "outside of that" (*tadbāhya*), it is very clearly stated that there are three circles in addition to the circle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Other commentators of that work, out of dogmatic adherence, have written the half-verse beginning with "tadbāhye" in their own manuscripts; for this mode of writing the syllables is not found in any tantra, and because the statement regarding its being accompanied by a *mātṛkā* [is] inexplicable in many instances.
Having restated the view of others— that [the passage] is an interpolation because it is not found in manuscripts—
he refutes that position by stating: "If it were an interpolation, then two verses would result, since there is no statement prescribing a third meter."
Since it is written that in the *Saṃhitā* and in other tantras there are clearly three external circles, [the authors of] the *Setubandha* established that there are five circles.
Regarding this, Maheśvarānandanātha states: "Having drawn a circle outside of that, one should draw a square outside of that."

In the *Paramānandatantra*, it is stated with the singular "circle" (*vṛttam*); in the *Tripurārṇava*, *Nityātantra*, *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, and *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, it is said: "Then the circle of the city-gates," "the circle consisting of three abodes of the earth," "the enclosure and the city-gate," and "well-rounded, O Supreme Goddess."

By the force of the singular number, having established that there are only three circles— namely, the two circles of the pericarp together with [the third]— he then restates the view of the Setubandha and refutes it,
noting that in many manuscripts, the citations from the Jñānārṇava of the Vāmakeśvaratantra are not found in the Setubandha itself.
Having cited the writing of Śrī Bhāskararāya as their authority, they refuted the Setubandha.

This particular method is unestablished; it was not mentioned by them at the occasion of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Setubandha* because it is not found in many manuscripts. Rather, it was introduced at the time of restating the opponent’s position (*vādimata*).
And that is merely the opponent’s own writing. For that reason, how could the view of Śrī Bhāskararāya be refuted?

On the contrary, Rāya himself, by writing in the midst of my book, has provided two refutations: first, that [the passage] is indeed authoritative, and second, that it results in the occurrence of two metrical feet (vṛtta). Furthermore, no one wrote anything controversial regarding the statement in the Vāmakeśvaratantra. This being so, such a groundless attribution of fault there is merely...

It is solely for the purpose of manifesting one's own scholarship. Therefore, without providing an interpretation for the statement from the Vāmakeśvaratantra which establishes three meters, as well as for the Jñānārṇava, the cessation of the five meters will not be achieved.
And if, solely on the strength of the etymological singular number, one were to accept that by the dual word *yāmalaka*— having separately stated "eight petals" and "sixteen petals"—

the word *traya* (three) heard subsequently in the phrase *vṛttatraye* is redundant in the sense of being a mere restatement of the aggregate, then [one would have to conclude] that such is the form of Vāmā.

In the phrase "the three circles" (*bhramitrayam*), effort is made to conceive of the very rotation that constitutes the parts of the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled [lotuses] as having the nature of Vāmā. If that is so, then the singular number is equally applicable in the phrase "and the square outside of that" (*tadbāhye caturasrakam*). There are scriptural statements that support this:

In the Vāmakeśvaratantra, it says "the halo and the city of the earth" (pariveṣaṃ bhūpuraṃ ca); in that same work, in the sixth chapter, it says "the form of Vāmā is four-cornered" (vāmārūpaṃ catuṣkoṇam); and in the Pūrvatanttra, it says "one should then make a circle of qualities and outside of that a square" (guṇavṛttaṃ tataḥ kuryāccaturasraṃ ca tadbahiḥ); and in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā, it says "then a perfect circle, O Supreme Goddess" (suvṛttaṃ parameśāni tato).

There are such scriptural statements as "one should draw the image of the earth" (*bhu-bimbaṃ mālikhet*). Such being the case, for one who relies solely on the singular number, there is here in this *Paramānanda-tantra-ṭippaṇī* the writing of Maheśvarānandanātha: "a square, three squares" (*caturasraṃ caturasratrayam*)—[the phrase "that triad of squares is by means of three finger-breadths" (*tribhiraṅgulaiḥ*) is an addition in manuscript Ba].2.
It is indeed contrary to the context.

If it is argued that the singular number found in such Tantric statements as "and if there is a triad of earth-purāṇas adorned with doors" is not intended to be significant, then what offense has been committed by the use of the singular in the word *vṛttam* (the circle)? In this way, the use of the singular for a plural is frequently encountered in both worldly and Vedic usage; for example, in common parlance, one says "the house."
Regarding the statement "there is grain, [namely] rice has been produced" (p.
96), where it says "the cause for its arising," the learned authorities maintain that in such instances the singular number is used to denote a genus (*jāti*). A Brāhmaṇa...

The expression *mama daivatam* is an ancient usage. In the Śruti, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice for one with many wives, there are numerous instances such as "having girded the wife, he sweeps the house," and so forth. Similarly, in the case of a paramour (*upapati*), there is by no means a total lack of justification for the singular number.

Furthermore, in the aforementioned instances, one cannot justify the singular number by assuming that it indicates plurality through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) due to the force of a subverting argument; for if one were to adopt that same position here as well,
then in the passage from the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, "guṇavṛttaṃ tataḥ," one would have to assume secondary indication for the word "tataḥ" itself.
The status of [the word] as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) must be stated; however, that is not possible.

Therefore, because the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, which contains the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), and the *Paramānandatantra*, which contains the singular form "in that" (*tatra*), possess equal force—since both are external to it—the [meaning] follows from the singular form. Thus...

Why, then, is not the singular number itself intended, by resorting either to the view that it is figurative (*lakṣaṇā*) or the view that it is unintended (*avivakṣā*)? For there is no determining factor to show that, when one of two [numbers] must be interpreted otherwise,
the singular is unintended on the basis of the natural sense of the word *tataḥ*, rather than the opposite.

This must be stated: when it becomes necessary to interpret one of two meanings—the meaning of the suffix and the meaning of the nominal stem—differently from the other, the nominal stem (prātipadika) is more powerful;
therefore, it is the meaning of the number and the suffix that must be interpreted otherwise in accordance with it. As it was said by the venerable Vidyāraṇyasvāmin:
The rule that a *ṛc* verse is to be recited three times is a property of its position, not a primary property;
for it is feminine in gender, and thus the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) possesses greater force.

Thus, there are many arguments establishing the predominance of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); however, for fear of excessive length, I have recorded only those formulated by the learned authorities. Therefore, following the principle that "from that which has become a nominal stem" (*tataḥ*), it should be understood as being in the singular number; otherwise, it would not be so. Thus, the wise should abandon their obstinacy.

When one who seeks only the truth investigates all the Tantras, setting aside the literal intent of mere words, it is established that five circles are intended in the Śrīyantra. Let us now return to the subject at hand.

Regarding the term *bhūpapatram*: "bhūpā" is a convention for the number sixteen; thus, it refers to that [lotus] which has sixteen petals. *Dikpatram*: "dik" is a designation for the number eight; thus, it refers to that [lotus] which has that many petals. *Bhuvanāram*: "bhuvanam" is a designation for the number fourteen.
"Tāvadara" means "so many spokes," and "tāvatkoṇa" means "so many corners. Regarding "druhiṇāra," the term "druhiṇa" is a designation for the number ten;

this is because in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* and other texts, ten Prajāpatis—Kardama and others—are well known as the causes of creation. Thus, "tāvadara" means "ten-spoked. By this, it is also [referred to as] "vidhikoṇa" (the corner of Brahmā).
This has been largely explained. The term *dik* (direction) has also been explained. The triangle (*trikoṇa*) and the point (*bindu*) are clear.

By the word *mayam*, the state of being a single unified totality (*samaṣṭi*) is indicated. Regarding "the Great King of Wheels" (*mahācakrarāja*), this is a name for the Śrīcakra; its greatness and worthiness of worship are established by the grammatical rule that the root *maha* means "worship."

And thus, the meaning is that it is worthy of worship by all, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others. "Sindūra" is well-known, and "kuṅkuma" is saffron from Kāśmīra; [the word] is written with either of these. Alternatively, since their association is understood through a dvandva compound, it is written with kuṅkuma together with sindūra.

The moderns (navyāḥ), however, state that when the array (prastāra) is written upon the ground, it should be filled with saffron powder if it is a Meru-array, and with vermilion powder if it is otherwise; the authority for this must be investigated.
Since the method of drawing [the yantra] has been explained in detail in the *Setubandha* composed by our supreme preceptor, it is not written here.
Thus far, the procedure for constructing the daily yantra at the time of worship has been stated.
Now, he describes the method of worship even for an accomplished (*siddha*) yantra, as well as the rules regarding the materials for constructing the yantra:

By the words beginning with "cāmīkara": *cāmīkara* is gold (*suvarṇa*), and *kaladhauta* is silver (*raupya*). Although the word *kaladhauta* can also denote gold—according to the lexicon which states, "Kaladhauta refers to silver and gold"—nevertheless, since gold has already been mentioned previously, it must here refer to silver. *Pañcaloha* (the five metals) [is as follows].
The characteristics of that [liṅga] are stated in the *Tantrasāra* and the *Bṛhatpāñcarātra*:
"Silver is said to possess the qualities of a king;
there should be ten parts of gold, twelve parts of copper, and five parts of iron."
"Six parts of brass are proclaimed to be fivefold metal (pañcaloha)."

*Ārakūṭa* is brass; the rest is clear. *Ratnāni* refers to emeralds and other gems, engraved upon them according to the previously mentioned scripture. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), copper, stone, and the like mentioned in the *Paramānanda-tantra* are to be understood. This too is an attribute of the aforementioned *cakrarāja*.
Having placed such a wheel-king in front.
In this context, worship is primary; however, in its absence, one should also accept a substitute as prescribed in other tantras. As it is said in the *Paramānandatantra*:
"The fruit is single-fold when [the deity is worshipped] in a mirror, and double-fold when in a book."
There may be four types in an image, and sixteen in Śāligrāma stones.
O Goddess, it is proclaimed that the merit from worshipping at Śivanābha yields a hundredfold fulfillment of human goals,
while at Narmadā, the fruit is a thousandfold.
"In the Kuṇḍalī, the vision of the deity becomes multiplied a hundred thousandfold;
moreover, the worship performed in the Cakrarāja bestows infinite fruit. Thus it is said.

However, according to the order of recitation, in the absence of each subsequent item, each preceding one should be accepted. It is precisely this intended meaning that is indicated by the scriptural mention of the gradation of results. *Kuṇḍalī* refers to the *śeṣa-kuṇḍalī*. *Pustaka* refers to the manuscript of the *Kula-śāstra*. *Pratimā* refers to the form [of the deity] residing in the verses of meditation (*dhyāna-śloka*).
The remainder is clear.

Since the consecration of a yantra (*yantrapratiṣṭhā*) is not mentioned in the Sūtras, it should not be performed by those who follow the Sūtras. Likewise, the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) should also not be performed by those who follow the Sūtras, because it is neither mentioned nor required [in them]. In reality, regarding the consecration of a yantra—
p.
98) Since it falls outside the application of the ritual worship (*pūjāprayoga*), when there is a desire for further prosperity,
that which is taught in another tantra should be performed [regarding the matter of whether or not to perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of this yantra— *ddi0*].
Appendix 11-vi. [The visible: For example, the recitation of the *Sahasranāma* and so forth. In performing these, there is prosperity (*abhyudaya*);

yet for those who follow the Sūtras, there is no loss even in their non-performance. Or, for instance, the sacrament (*saṃskāra*) of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), which is prescribed in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*; because it is not mentioned in other Sūtras, it is governed by the rule "whether much or little" (*bahvalpaṃ vā*).

The people of the Draviḍa and Āndhra regions do not perform the consecration of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), holding that there is no loss [of merit] from its non-performance. However, the people of the Mahārāṣṭra region, considering it to bring about prosperity (*abhyudaya*) when performed, do carry out the consecration.
Similarly, regarding the consecration of the *cakrarāja*, there is prosperity in performing it; for those who follow the Sūtras, there is no loss from its non-performance. || 9 ||
Next, he describes the sequence of worship for the temple and so forth, beginning with the temple-worship:
therein, in the Great Wheel (mahācakra), [one worships] the Ocean of Nectar (amṛtāmbhonidhi), the Jewel Island (ratnadvīpa), and the Great Garden of Various Trees (nānāvṛkṣamahodyāna).
To the grove of wish-fulfilling trees, to the grove of *santāna* creepers, to the grove of yellow sandalwood, to the grove of *mandārava* flowers, to the grove of *pārijāta* flowers,
to the grove of *kadamba* trees, to the wall of *puṣyarāga* jewels, and to the wall of *padmarāga* jewels.
To the one with a wall of *gomedaka* jewels, to the one with a wall of *vajra* jewels,

to the one with a wall of *vaiḍūrya* jewels, to the one with a wall of *indranīla* jewels, to the one with a wall of *muktā* jewels, to the one with a wall of *marakata* jewels, to the one with a wall of *vidruma* jewels, and to the one with a pavilion of *māṇikya* gems.

To the pavilion with a thousand pillars; to the pool of nectar, the pool of bliss, and the pool of discernment; to the exhalation of the morning sun, the exhalation of moonlight, and the great enclosure of erotic grace; to the forest of great lotuses; and to the sovereign palace of the wish-fulfilling gem.

To the eastern gate consisting of the Eastern Tradition; to the southern gate consisting of the Southern Tradition; to the western gate consisting of the Western Tradition; to the northern gate consisting of the Northern Tradition;
to the circle of jewel-lamps; to the great lion-throne made of jewels.
To the one whose single bedpost is composed of Brahmā, whose single bedpost is composed of Viṣṇu,
whose single bedpost is composed of Rudra, whose single bedpost is composed of Īśvara,
whose single bed-plank is composed of Sadāśiva, and whose mattress is made of swan-down;
For a great pillow of swan’s down, for a saffron-colored bedspread, for a great canopy, and for a great curtain—[in this manuscript, the earlier reading "yavanikāyai" appears to be a scribal error;
thus, the word "yamanikā" or "javanikā" is appropriate here. Cf. Amarakośa, Book 2].
In the section on human beings—for example: "A curtain (*pratisīrā*) is a screen (*javanikā*), and it is also called a *tiraskāriṇī*. (Verse 120). Herein: [Commentary:

*Pratisīrā*, *javanikā*, and *tiraskāriṇī*—the term *tiraskāriṇī* is sufficient. With the forty-four mantras beginning with "Obeisance" (*namaḥ*), all of that [is accomplished] by means of the forty-four mantras of the [forty-four] pavilions. (Variant reading: *ba 2*).
Having meditated upon and having worshipped [him]. || 10 ||

In this context, the phrase "situated in the sacrificial hall" (*yāgamandire sthite*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Furthermore, this is an adjective for the term "great wheel" (*mahācakra*). Alternatively, "therein" (*tatra*) means "in what has been written," which connects with the preceding sūtra's expression "having placed in front. [The term] "great wheel" (*mahācakra*)— [End of fragment]

"Having meditated upon" and "having worshipped" are connected with what follows. "Amṛtāmbhonidhiḥ" means the ocean of nectar. "Ratnamayo dvīpaḥ" is an island consisting of jewels; it refers to a place suitable for dwelling, that is to say, high ground. "Udyānaṃ" is a pleasure grove; as Amarasimha states: "A pleasure grove (ākrīḍa) for a man is called an udyāna. "Vṛkṣavāṭikā" is a small garden (upavana).
"Vṛkṣavāṭikā" means a grove of trees in a domestic garden, according to Amara. "Kalpa" and so forth are names for celestial trees (surataru).
These five are the divine trees: Mandāra, Pārijātaka, Santāna, Kalpavṛkṣa, and Haricandana (which may also be masculine), according to Amara.
The *kadamba* is well known. The "nine jewels" (*navaratna*) consist of varieties beginning with *puṣparāga* and ending with *vidruma*;

their "enclosure wall" (*prākāra*) is a rampart constructed all around the exterior of the house. *Māṇikya* is ruby (*padmarāga*), and its "pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*) is a structure made of it. A "pond" (*vāpī*) is a long tank. An "emission" (*udgāra*) is a red-colored, highly pleasing object.

As it is stated in the *Tryakṣarakośa*: "The word *udgāra* [denotes] the color red and an object of great delight. A circle of lamps made of jewels; *haṃsatūla* refers to the fine feathers located beneath the wings of a particular kind of bird, known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

*Parā* is well known. *Mahopadhāna* is well known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *loḍu*. *Kausumbhāstaraṇa* refers to a fine cloth of red color spread over the bed to prevent its soiling; in the Mahārāṣṭrī language, it is called *palaṅgapūsa*.

This is well known. A *vitāna* is a cloth fastened above that prevents the falling of earth and other substances from the upper space. A *yavanikā* [see the notes on the marks at pages 98, lines 4–5] is well known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *ṣaḍudā*. The rest is self-evident.

In this manner, the word "namaḥ" is to be joined with all [the names] ending in the dative case, as in the mantra "yā te agne 'yāśayā. Having first meditated upon the objects expressed by these forty-four mantras within the Śrīcakra, one should perform their worship:
first the meditation on one, then the worship, then the meditation on the next.

Therefore, the sequence "then [follows] their worship" (tatastāsyarcanam) is obtained from the natural force of the word *tattat* (each respective one). Otherwise, according to the logical principle of *padārthānusamaya* (performing each item for all objects in succession), meditation and worship would have been obtained; thus, it should be understood that this [sequence] sets aside that [principle] by means of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) in the word *tattat*. || 10 ||

He describes the offering of lamps, the worship of the wheel, and the placement of perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth: "One should place perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and the like on the right side, and lamps all around" (regarding the matter of the lamps).

In the supplement (13.29): "The visible [form] is seen. Having offered [the oblation] with the root mantra and having worshipped the wheel, one should worship the first triangle with the three sections of the root mantra. 11.

In the phrase "akṣatādīn" (unbroken rice, etc.), the word "ādi" (etcetera) includes the first, second, and so forth. This [phrase] connects with the word "etasya" (of this). In that context, "giving" (*dāna*) does not mean any mere renunciation (*tyāga*) intended for a deity; rather, it is the gathering together of the materials for worship in one place, as in the expression "he collects the sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni saṃbharati*). Of this...

The fruit [of these actions] is the swift attainment of each respective [result] at the time of its offering. The giving and placing of lamps on both sides all around is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). By means of the word "ca" (and) following the word "having given" (*dattvā*), [the two acts are connected].
The repetition [of the rule] has been indicated for the sake of completing the sentence with respect to each individual object of reference, because such repetition is necessary.

Therefore, the difference in meaning of the root *dā* does not constitute a fault. Nor should it be asked by what authority this is the meaning of the root *dā*; for we see such usage as "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*) and "he gives his feet to the masseur" (*saṃvāhakasya caraṇau dadāti*).

Just as in expressions such as "he gives fear to the enemy," a meaning is inferred based on fitness (*yogyatā*), so too here a fitting meaning is inferred. By the word *abhitaḥ* ("on both sides"), it is made known that however many lamps there are on one side, there are exactly that many on the other side. The result of this is the removal of darkness. By this [lamp-lighting], in the house of worship—
The meaning is that the absence of darkness in general is the effect. If an additional lamp is placed on one side, then behind it, the darkness in the form of its shadow will fall.
If they are lit equally on all sides, there will be no darkness anywhere; this is the meaning. This is the restriction regarding both sides.

The meaning is evident. Having worshipped with the root mantra (mūla) and the fifteen-syllable mantra (pañcadaśī) the wheel consisting of nine wheels—the collective wheel (samaṣṭicakra)—here, worship consists simply of the scattering of flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata). With the three sections—the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—this pertains to the first [wheel] at the time of the initial construction of the wheels.

Regarding the three spokes (*asra*) of the wheel, because they are doubled, they are treated as a singular unit. This is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for in that case, since the worship of a single part within a single wheel consisting of three triangles would not require three mantras, it would result in the fault of optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), as in the case of the mantra "May Bhaga divide you two. Nor is it like the rule "He takes up the spade with four [fingers]."

It might be argued that let there be a collective compound (*samuccaya*); nevertheless, even so, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, the fault lies in the assumption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the meaning of another word. In the case of a *dvigu* compound, however, three peaks are appropriate for the three corners. The word "having worshipped" (*abhyarcya*) is understood from the preceding [verse]. Since no specific order is mentioned, [the worship] proceeds clockwise starting from one's own front. || 11 ||
Regarding the causes for the purification of the self, such as drying and so forth,
he then states those causes for the purification of the self beginning with drying:
"Drying, burning, and bathing are performed by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) associated with the colors of air, fire, and water."
Having performed [the rite] || 12 ||

The letter *yaṃ* is the color of wind; *raṃ* is the color of fire; *vaṃ* is the color of water. The power of drying (*śoṣakatā*) is well-known in the world as belonging to wind; therefore, that [power] also exists in its [wind’s] color. Consequently, by means of it, there is drying, which is the destruction of the watery portion.
In the same way, by means of the color of fire, there is burning, which is the reduction to ashes; likewise, of those ashes...

Having performed the solidification and immersion by means of the water-form (*udakavarṇa*), the word "and" (*ca*) implies that one should also include the production of solidity by means of the earth-seed syllable *laṃ*— as taught in other tantras and situated in the section on Śyāmā— as well as the arising of the body of Śambhu. Alternatively:
Because it occurs in close proximity, only that which is situated within the section on Śyāmā should be taken [as seen in the root text, commentary, and [Agra-6 Khaṇḍa,

Śyāmākrama-9 Sūtra]]. When there is an expectancy for an object (*karman*) regarding actions such as drying (*śoṣaṇa*), the visible gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*) or the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is the object.

That which is well-known in other tantras should be accepted. By the statement "through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) joined with the syllables," while uttering the syllable *yaṃ*, one should restrain the vital breaths on all sides; thereafter, one should contemplate the drying up of the body.
Furthermore, regarding the wind [in the section on Śyāmā, in the root text and commentary on Sūtra 9 of the Śyāmākrama in the first section]:

And it is visible; for Piṅgalā performed the practice by means of drawing [the breath], since that meaning has been made known by the phrase "by means of prāṇāyāmas. It is exactly the same in what follows as well.

101) As for those mantras from the section on Vārāhī, such as "one should dry up the body of contraction," which have been written in the *Nibandha*, they are rootless and should be rejected because they are not based on the *sūtras*. However, that which is found in the section on Śyāmā...

The accomplishment of solidity and the arising of the body of Śambhu—established by the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) indicated by the word "ca"—is to be performed [by the author of the Sūtras, the venerable...]. 12.
Breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Next, he states the rule for breath control:
"Having performed breath control three times. (13)

Prāṇāyāma, however, should be understood according to the method that will be explained in the section on Śyāmā [meaning: according to the method stated in Sūtra 10 of Khaṇḍa 6 of the Śyāmākrama]. || 13 ||
Following that, the expulsion of obstructing spirits and the application of the vajra-armour (*vajrakavaca*) should be performed; thus he says:
"May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth—those beings who are creators of obstacles."

"May they perish by the command of Śiva! Having spoken thus, striking the ground with the heel of his left foot, clapping his hands, and turning his face upward, he should perform the triple *tāla* (clapping) while identifying himself with the Goddess, and then apply the network of the adamantine armor (*vajrakavaca*) upon his own body. || 14 ||

With the mantra "apasarpantu...", there is a striking of the ground with the *pārṣṇi*—the back part of the foot—and a clapping or rubbing of the two hands; the face is turned upward and then tilted sideways. The ellipsis implies that these actions are performed together [with the mantra]. Then, three *tāla* beats are made with the palms facing downward.

With the right thumb, middle finger, and index finger, one strikes the palm of the left hand three times with sound; having performed that and generated [the state], one should contemplate: "I am non-different from the goddess Upasaya. By the phrase "in one's own body," the body of the deity is excluded. [One should apply] the vajra-armor, which is a network of placements (nyāsa) in the form of an impenetrable armor.
One should perform—that is, carry out—the collection of nyāsas that is about to be described. || 14 ||
When there is the inquiry, "What is this network of nyāsas? and specifically, "What is the karaśuddhi-nyāsa?", he first describes the karaśuddhi-nyāsa:
"Having performed the purification of the hands with Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, and the third [letter] joined with the Bindu, from the middle fingers to the palms."

Śrīkaṇṭha is Śiva, represented by the letter *a*; this is because in the *Yoginītantra*, in the fifteenth chapter, there is a count of the letters beginning with "the group of ten starting with Śrīkaṇṭha. Ananta is the long vowel *ā*;
according to the *Tantrasāra*, regarding the mantra *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ*, Ananta is conjoined with the *bindu* (anusvāra) and possesses *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), *brahmā* (*oṃ*), *agni* (*ra*), and *tāra* (*oṃ*).

Thus, from the extraction [of the syllables]: *binduyujau* (joined with the *bindu*) refers to *śrīkaṇṭha* and *ananta*; this is the compound. The third [syllable] is the third of the *bāla* [mantra], namely *sauḥ*. And thus, by means of this mantra: *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*.
By whom the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) has been performed starting from the middle finger down to the palms;
that is to say, one should place [the mantras] upon the middle, ring, little, and thumb fingers, as well as on the palms and the backs of the hands.
This is the *karaśuddhi-nyāsa*. (15)
The ritual placement for self-protection (*ātmarakṣānyāsa*). Regarding the ritual placement for self-protection, he says:
having uttered "Kumārī" (here, by the word *kumārī* and the subsequent word *bālā*, [the mantra] *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ* [is intended]).

Thus, the three-syllabled mantra of Bālā should be taken up; then, placing the *añjali* at the heart while reciting "Mahātripurasundarī, protect, protect me—the immortal consciousness," [one should meditate on oneself]. || 16 ||

Having uttered "Kumārī" and "Bālā," and having omitted the two syllables "pada," one should place the palms joined at the heart while reciting up to the end with "rakṣa rakṣa. This is the ritual placement for self-protection (ātmarakṣānyāsa). || 16 ||
The Installation of the Four Seats:

Regarding the installation of the four seats, he says— having uttered *māyā*, *kāma*, and *śakti*, and having offered his own seat with the mantra "Salutation to the Seat of the Self of the Goddess"— || 17 ||
The *māyā* [bīja] is clearly established as *hrīṃ* in many places; the *kāma* [bīja] is *klīm*. As it is stated in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"The son of the sage called out to him from nearby with 'klīṃ'."
But Sudarśana, having heard that, clearly grasped the primordial syllable.
"And he spoke that seed-syllable, known as Kāmarāja, accompanied by the *anusvāra*, again and again; it was then grasped by the mind. Thus [it is said].

According to the *Kośa* (lexicon), "Śakti" refers to Sauriti, Śakti, and Parā as the third [syllable]. Although it might be possible to understand the term "Kāma-śakti" as referring to the second and third *kūṭas* of the Pañcadaśī-mantra— just as it does for the Tripurā-gāyatrī—
since evidence for that interpretation has also been shown, nevertheless:
The *mādana* (the letter *ka*) conjoined with *śakti* (the letter *ī*), joined with the fourth vowel (*ī*),
enriched above by the central moon-drop (*bindu*), is extracted as the *kāmarāja*.
It is conjoined with the end of *śānta* (the letter *ha*) and the beginning of *ka* (the letter *a*), and joined with the end of the letter *ai*.

Thus, in the Yoginītantra, this is the very meaning of the extraction of this mantra: *mādana* is the letter *ka*; *śakti* (or *śakra*) is the letter *la*; the fourth vowel is *ī*; the end of *śānta* is *sa*; *kādi* is the *visarga*; and the end of that which ends in *aikāra* is *au*. One should recite it while omitting [the final syllable].

The mantra ending in *namaḥ* is *manu*. Thus, having offered a seat for oneself with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to the seat of the Self of the Goddess," one should scatter flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon that seat. || 17 ||
Then, with two verses, he extracts the mantras for the Cakrāsana and others:

having uttered *Śiva-yug-bālā*, [one says] *śrīcakrāsanāya namaḥ*; having uttered *Śiva-bhṛgu-yug-bālā*, [one says] *sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ*; and having uttered *bhuvana-amadanau blem*, [one says] *sādhyasiddhāsanāya*.
Having performed the seat for the deity of the wheel-mantra within the wheel by means of the three mantras beginning with "namaḥ," [verse 18].

The letter *ha* is Śiva; for according to the lexicon, "Śiva is *ha*, *ha* is Śiva, the sky, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)"—thus it is *haṃsa*. Joined with that is *Bālā*. Here, by the word *bālā*, the phoneme of *Bālā* is intended; thus, the conjunction with the phoneme *ha* is prescribed with reference to the phoneme of *Bālā*.
Consequently, it is established that the letter *ha* is a limb (*aṅga*) of the phoneme of *Bālā*. And so it is.

According to the maxim that "the repetition of auxiliary elements occurs for each primary element," the conjunction with the letter *ha* applies to all three classes [of mantras]. Furthermore, since a consonant is not observed at the end of a vowel, it must be joined at the very beginning. Thus, *haiṃ hklīṃ hsauḥ śrīcakrāsanāya namaḥ* is one mantra. [In the term] *śivabhṛguyuk*, *śiva* refers to the letter *ha* and *bhṛgu*...

The letter *sa* is the seed of the universe (*jagadbīja*) within the section on the letter *sa*; it is named Śakti, as stated in the *Nandanakośa*: "I am that [seed], Vegavatī, Bhṛgu. The second mantra, joined with both of these, is: *hsraiṃ hsklīṃ hssauḥ sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ*. *Bhuvanā* and *Bhuvaneśvarī*—its mantra is of the nature of the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Thus it is extracted from the *Devībhāgavata*: "Śiva, Māyā, Agni, and Bindu. Here, Śiva is the letter *ha*;
Māyā is the letter *ī*; Agni is the letter *ra*; and Bindu is well known. Through the conjunction of these, *hrīṃ* is formed.
Furthermore, according to the lexicon (*kośa*), "Bhuvaneśī, Lajjā, Hṛllekhā, and Kuladevatā" [refer to this same syllable]. In the present context as well, that very same [syllable] is Madana.

This has been explained. And thus: *hrīṃ klīṃ bleṃ sādhyasiddhāsanāya namaḥ*—this is the third mantra. Having thus sequentially fashioned the seat of the deity of the mantra within the wheel (cakra) by means of these three mantras, this is called the "Installation of the Four Seats" (*caturāsananyāsa*). || 18 ||
The Six-Limbed Nyāsa of Bālā:

Next, he describes the six-limbed [nyāsa] of Bālā— having performed the six limbs by repeating the Bālā mantra twice, with the placement of fingers according to the sequence of three, two, one, ten, three, and two.

One who has performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) for the heart and so forth, by repeating the Bālā mantra with its six syllables in sequence using three or more fingers—this is the meaning. [This is to be seen in Dvi. Pa. Śi. Vi. 9 for the sake of knowing the six limbs of this Bālā mantra. Such is he. This is the very point.
It is clearly stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā (p.
"One should place [the mudrā] on the heart with the three fingers excluding the little finger and the thumb."
The knower of mantras should place [the syllables] on the head by means of the middle and navel fingers.
Having placed the *śikhā* with the thumb, one should place the armor (*kavaca*) with the ten [fingers];
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the placement of the eyes (*netra*) with the mantras prescribed for the heart.
"Then, O beloved, one should place the weapon [mudrā] with the index and middle fingers. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) of Bālā. || 19 ||
The Nyāsa of the Yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī.
Now, he describes the nyāsa of the yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī:
having uttered *sa-bindu na co blūm* [at the beginning of the names of the eight goddesses beginning with Śrī-Vaśinī who reside here].
For the sake of knowing the extraction of the seed-syllables beginning with *grāhyo* and *cārya b-lam*, [it is] to be seen in the *Dvi-pa-śi* (the second chapter of the *Śrīvidyārṇava*).

"Salutation to Vaśinī Vāgdevatā"—thus on the head. In all cases, there is the addition of the *bindu* (anusvāra) to the consonant groups (*vargas*). Having uttered the *ka*-group and *kala hrīṃ* [here it should be understood as *klhrīṃ*], "Salutation to Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatā"—thus [on the forehead].

Having uttered *cuṃ* on the forehead; saying *nvlīṃ*, "Salutation to Vāgdevatā Modinī," [place it] between the eyebrows. Having uttered *ṭuṃ*; saying *ylūṃ*, "Salutation to Vāgdevatā Vimalā," [place it] at the throat. Having pronounced *tuṃ*;
saying *jmrīṃ*, "Salutation to Vāgdevatā Aruṇā," [place it] at the heart. And having uttered *puṃ* and *hslvyūṃ*.

"Salutation to Jayinīvāgdevatā"—thus at the navel. Having uttered the four [vowels] beginning with *yā* and *jhryūṃ*, "Salutation to Sarveśvarīvāgdevatā"—thus at the *liṅga*. Having pronounced the six [consonants] beginning with *śā* and *kṣmrīṃ*, "Salutation to Kaulinīvāgdevatā"—thus at the base. || 20 ||

Having uttered those vowels from *a* to *visarga*, both with and without the nasal dot (*bindu*), ending with "namaḥ," this is the mantra of Vaśinī. Thus: *aṃ āṃ— aṃ aḥ blūṃ vaśinīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ*;
one should place this on the head. Now, since the application of the nasal dot has been mentioned for all [vowels] here, but not elsewhere, he says: "everywhere."

The meaning is clear. Regarding "the *ka*-group" (*kavarga*): the *ka*-group is well known, [but here] it is accompanied by the bindu (*m*). In the case of *kala hrīṃ*, there is the inclusion of the consonants alone. This is according to the maxim: "Letters existing within a composite whole are seen in its constituent parts. And this position was adopted by Śrī Bhāskararāya in the *Setubandha*.

In the course of explaining the phrase "the ethereal seed-syllable below," the line of commentary states that the ethereal element refers to the group of *haṃsa* syllables, and from among those, only the letter *ha* alone should be taken. The reason for taking it in this way here as well is found precisely in the *Setubandha*: "This mantra of Kāmeśvarī consists of twenty-three syllables."

When the letters *ka* and *la*, distinguished by the vowel *ra*, are included, as in the formulation "I worship the sandal (pādukā) joined with the two *tārīs*," the mantra "Hīṃ Śrīṃ Klhrīṃ, I worship the sandal of Kāmeśvarī-Vāgdevatā-Kāmeśvarī" consists of twenty-five syllables. Therefore:

There is the grasping of mere consonants alone. It has been explained in detail in the *Varivasyārahasya*, during the enumeration of the fifteen letters, that consonants do not possess the status of being [independent] phonemes (*varṇa*). And thus: *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ kalhrīṃ* to the Goddess of Speech, Kāmeśvarī.
One should place "namaḥ" on the forehead. [The syllable] "cuṃ" represents the *ca*-group (*cavarga*), because of the rule "cuṃ" being marked with an *u* (indicating it is an *udit*),
which triggers the application of the grammatical rule "aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ," whereby a vowel marked with *u* includes its homogeneous sounds.
The inclusion of the *ca*-group: having recited the mantra ending with "namas" for the *ca*-group, one should place it between the eyebrows.

For the *ṭa*-group, it is as before (*ṭuṃ*). The rest is clear. Regarding the letters *ha*, *sa*, *la*, and *va*, the inclusion of the consonants alone is as before. "That which is the beginning of the tetrad" means that which is the first of the group of four.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) compound where the qualities are included within the whole (*tadguṇasaṃvijñānabahuvrīhi*). And thus: *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*.
In the expression "the six beginning with śa" (*śādiṣaṭka*), the compound is likewise as previously explained. || 20 ||
The Deposition of the Root Mantra:
Having thus described the deposition of the Yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī, he now speaks of the deposition of the root mantra and so forth:
"One should place the fifteen syllables of the root vidyā on the head, the base, the heart, and the three eyes."
Having performed the sixfold placement upon the two ears, the mouth, the pair of arms, the back, the pair of knees, and the navel, one should perform the placement either in the wheel or elsewhere.
The three eyes should be understood as being together with the space between the eyebrows; the two ears refer to the pair of auditory organs;

the remaining locations are clear. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence upon the fifteen aforementioned locations using the fifteen root syllables, accompanied by the *bindu* and ending with *namaḥ*. This is the sixfold (*ṣoḍhā*), that is, the sixfold [ritual] for Gaṇeśa, the planets, and—

The placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa) according to the divisions of constellations, yoginīs, zodiac signs, and sacred seats (pīṭha) is taught in other tantras. By the phrase "having placed [them] again," it is indicated that this may be performed or omitted at will. || 21 ||

Having thus taught the ritual placements (nyāsa) for the sake of attaining the nature of the Goddess, he now instructs on the procedure for placing the vessels (pātra), which constitutes a limb of the worship, beginning with the setting out of the vessels and the preparation of the general arghya offering.
Having prepared a mandala consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square on the left side with pure water,
having worshipped it with flowers, and having established a conch vessel along with its stand, having filled it with pure water, and having offered the initial drop—
Having worshipped with the six-limbed rite and consecrated with the Vidyā, one should sprinkle oneself and the articles of worship with droplets of that water. || 22 ||

By the phrase "with pure water," it is indicated that [the deity] has been worshipped with perfumes, unbroken grains, and flowers, as stated in the *Gaṇapatipaddhati* (in the root text, Sūtra 5, page 77 of Section 2). "Pure" means with water filtered through a cloth. On one's own left side.

Having formed [the mandala] starting from the triangle and ending with the square—because it consists of the rules and procedures, and because it possesses expectancy—according to the method of exiting by means of the Matsyamudrā as taught in the Śyāmākrama [meaning: according to the manner stated in Sūtra 18 of Khaṇḍa 6], one should worship it with flowers. The phrase "sādhāram" (with its support) refers to "therein," and so forth.

Regarding the installation of the support-vessel (*ādhāra*) and the conch, and the filling of them with pure water, when there is a requirement for a mantra, one may choose either the mantra found in the section on Gaṇapati or that found in the section on Śyāmā, as there is no difference in their proximity [to the ritual context]. However, there is no worship of the *kalās* such as Pāvaka and others within the support-vessel and the other vessels.
Because it has not been stated, because it has not been indicated, and because it is not required here; but in reality,
in comparison with Śyāmā-Gaṇapati—

Since the mantras for the base of the special arghya vessel (viśeṣārghyapātra) and so forth found in the Śrīvidyāprakaraṇa are present here, those very ones should be adopted. Even therein, only as much as is required should be taken, and not that which is unnecessary, just as in the rule: "He mixes the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa with milk."

The conjunction with the initial *bindu* is the consecration of the conch-water. In the word *bindum*, the number inherent in the predicate (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant; therefore, no transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises from the offering of two *bindus*. Nor should it be argued that because the accusative case-ending is heard in *bindum*, that very [conjunction] must be the subject (*uddeśya*).
Since there is no mention of an application (*viniyoga*) for the *bindu* when its application is required, it is not a consecration of the *bindu*;

rather, it is a consecration of the water, because the application of the water is heard [in the text] immediately following. Furthermore, since there is a rule that only the object to be consecrated is the objective (*uddeśya*), the *bindu* is what is enjoined. Therefore, the number associated with it is indeed intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).

Having worshipped the deities of the six limbs in the corners of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu with the six-limbed mantras, [one should proceed]. Regarding the singular number used for "with the limb" (*aṅgena*), it is either an archaic usage (*ārṣa*) indicating plurality,
or it follows the logic of the *pāśādhikaraṇa* (the section on fetters), since a single-ness cannot logically apply to the six mantras.

In reality, however, since the number of recitations for the auxiliary mantras (*aṅgamantra*) is already indicated by the word "six" (*ṣaṭ*) itself, the purpose of the singular suffix is indeed not intended to be expressed. Thus, the use of the default singular number alone is appropriate. Nor should it be argued that this results in a loss of grammatical concord with the word "six," which expresses the qualifier; for [the meaning is conveyed] by the word "six."
Because there is no logical inconsistency in accepting it as a component of a compound, by this [word] too, it is merely a consecration of water.

Alternatively, one should satisfy the deities of the six limbs within that very water of the conch by repeating the three *kūṭas* twice in sequence, using the mantras beginning with "To the Heart, *namaḥ*; I satisfy the *śrīpādukā* of the Heart-power" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ hṛdayaśaktiśrīpādukāṃ tarpayāmi*), and so forth. And why would there be any need for [the word] "having worshipped" (*abhyarcya*) if its purpose were merely to indicate satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*)?

It should be stated as "māna" (the measure). For it is explained in the *Setubandha* that the term "yoginī" refers to the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) of Tripurasundarī, based on the passage from the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*: "one should gratify the yoginīs therein."

Having consecrated with the fifteenfold Vidyā— that is, having refined that water through the act of consecration— one should sprinkle oneself, one’s own body, and the materials for worship, such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), with its droplets— its drops. Herein:

By the principle of the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*, it would follow that the means of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) consists of only three drops, as indicated by the word "drops" (*vipruḍbhiḥ*); however, the prefix *sam-* is employed to set aside this logical conclusion. Thus, the meaning is that one should sprinkle so that the articles for worship are thoroughly drenched with water. || 22 ||
The Ritual for the Special Arghya (the Purification of the Arghya):

Having thus performed the production of the general arghya and having brought about satisfaction with it, he states the ritual for the special arghya and describes the satisfaction derived from the special arghya.

Having prepared a maṇḍala consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square with that water, one should worship the center with the Vidyā, the triangle with the sections of the Vidyā, and the hexagon with the repetition of the seed-syllables (or, according to Ga., the double repetition of the seed-syllables). Then, uttering the mantra "to the fire-maṇḍala whose self consists of ten kalās," one should worship.
Having established [the vessel] with "Obeisance to the support of the arghya-vessel," and having worshipped the support, [one worships] the purifying kalās. || 23 ||
"With that water" means with the water of the general *arghya* offering. "The rest is as before. "In the center" means in the middle of the triangle.

"With the Vidyā" means having worshipped with the collective Vidyā; this applies everywhere. "With the parts of the Vidyā" means with the three *kūṭas*; [this refers to] the triangle, meaning the three corners of the triangle. Its justification has been shown previously. "By the repetition of the seed-syllables."
[The meaning is: "in the manner stated in the two sūtras 19–22 on the preceding pages 103–105.

By the double repetition of the three *kūṭas*. The nature of a *kūṭa* as a seed-syllable (*bīja*) is established with proof as being the form of each individual seed-syllable for each individual *kūṭa*, in order to account for the sixteen-syllabled nature of the venerable *Ṣoḍaśākṣarī*.

This has been elaborated by our supreme preceptors in the *Varivasyārahasya*; it is not written here for fear of excessive length. Since the specific order is not mentioned, one may proceed either clockwise starting from the east or clockwise starting from one's own front, according to the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "The mantra ends with *namaḥ*, or it may end with *pādukā*."
"Vācam—Aiṃ. This is stated in the Devībhāgavata: "The Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Māyā-bīja as the third—if these reside in one's mind, no one is able to cause him any harm."
Having thus begun, and introducing a narrative to praise the first seed-syllable, Vāgbhava, [it says]:
"When one distressed by fear sees a tiger or similar beast in the forest and utters 'Ai Ai!',
even though [the syllable] is devoid of the nasal drop (bindu), it is said that it indeed grants the desired object."

By praising the status of the cause and fruit through the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic of that which is devoid of the *bindu*, it is established that the letter *ai* with the *bindu* is the *vāgbhava*. Furthermore, from the extraction of the *bālā* mantra in the *Nityārahasya*: "O Goddess, the first is *vāgbhava*, the second is *kāmarāja*," and [from the statement]: "The solar vowel (*ravisvara*) joined with the *bindu* is declared to be the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable."

And from the seed-sheath (*bījakośa*): since there is an expectation as to what kind of support (*ādhāra*) it is, one should take the "three steps" (*tripadādi*) and so forth mentioned in another tantra for the sake of knowing the nature of the support here. [The subject matter is to be consulted in the supplement (pariśiṣṭa), page 12. These are the names of the fiery lunar digits (*kalā*) of Fire, Sun, and Moon.
The fire-related *kalās* are found right here before us in the sixteenth root-sūtra of the sixth section of the *Śrīśyāmākrama*;

they should be taken from there. [Regarding this, for the sake of determining what vessel is to be used and of what form it should be, see Dvivedi-Pañcānana-Śivopādhyāya-viracita, verse 12. With [the mantras] ending in the fourth case and *namo*, [one should proceed].
[The deity is] visible. One should worship [the deities] in the form of the eastern and other directions with their respective names, in the form of the eastern and other directions;
for such is the statement in the *Paramānandatantra*. However, Bhāskararāya, in the *Setubandha*, stated that this is done by proceeding clockwise starting from the west. || 23 ||

Above Madana, having prepared the vessel with the mantra "Obeisance to the Arghya-vessel, which is the solar mandala consisting of twelve kalās," and touching the vessel, one should contemplate the solar kalās (the names of these kalās of Fire, Sun,
and Moon are explicitly given hereafter).
In the sixteenth root-sūtra of the sixth section of the *Śrīśyāmākramīya*, it is stated: "Then they are to be taken up.
