Having filled [the vessel] with the mantra: *sauḥ somamaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane arghyāmṛtāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the lunar orb, whose essence consists of sixteen digits, the nectar of the offering), and having offered the first [syllable] and worshipped the second and middle [syllables], [one asks]: of what substance is the vessel for the Moon?
And of what form is that which is to be grasped? For that purpose, [it is said]: "The sixteen digits (kalās) are visible. (Dṛśyaviveka, verse 12). 24.

Madana has been explained in detail in the *Caturāsananyāsa*. The rest is clear. Regarding the word "having touched" (*saṃspṛśya*), before this [word], there is the phrase beginning with "therein" (*tatra*); that is, having touched—that is, having worshipped—the solar digits (*saurīḥ kalāḥ*) such as Tapinī and the others, in that vessel (*pātre*).

Although the root *spṛś* does not have "worship" as its meaning, nevertheless, because it occurs within the sentence "having worshipped the lunar digits (*kalā*) of the Moon after having worshipped the fiery digits," the vessel [here]— for what substance and of what form should it be taken?— is to be seen from Dīpikā, Paddhati, Śirōmaṇi, and Vivaraṇa (12).

Furthermore, because of the statement in the *Yoginītantra*, "Having established [the deity] there, one should worship the digit of the Sun (*sūryakalā*)," the intended meaning must be understood as referring specifically to the act of worship. Having filled the first (*ādima*)—that is, the initial—and the "following the first" (*upādima*), which is the second, and the middle, which is the third; this is also an elliptical indication for the fourth and fifth. [As stated] in the *Siddhāntagrantha*:

In the first section, it was stated that there are five *makāras* and that worship is performed with them in secrecy. In that very context, having given and having established [the offering], [one worships] the sixteen digits (*kalās*) of the Moon, beginning with Amṛtā and ending with Pūrṇāmṛtā. || 24 ||

There, having drawn a triangle with lines beginning with the letter *ka*, radiant with a swan situated between the letters *ha* and *la*, its corners joined by the powers of Speech (*Vāk*), Desire (*Kāma*), and Energy (*Śakti*); having worshipped it with the *Haṃsa* mantra and drawn a circle outside it containing a hexagon;
and having worshipped the hexagon with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) starting from the front side, one should consecrate it seven times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Having offered perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having sprinkled the articles of worship with their droplets, one should make everything consist of the Vidyā; then, touching it, one should mutter the ninety-four mantras.
There, having worshipped the first substance according to the previously mentioned sequence,
one should draw a single line from the west to the northeast using the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga (*ḥ*).
Then, one should draw [another line] from the northeast to the southeast using the sixteen letters beginning with the *ka*-group and ending with *ta*.

One should produce another line. Then, one should produce the third line, extending from the southeast to the west, with the sixteen letters beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*. This being so, those [letters] consist of the syllables whose initial letters are *a*, *ka*, and *tha*—namely, the long forms of *ā*, *kha*, *pa*, and so forth.

That triangle in which the lines are non-different from those [letters] has lines consisting of *akatha* and so forth; this is an adjective qualifying the triangle. "Ha" and "the pair of lakṣas"—between them, in the middle, stands the group of syllables "haṃsa"; by that, it is radiant—having written "haṃ" on the right side of the substance.
To the north of that, one should write the two syllables *haṃ sa*; to the north of those, one should write *lakṣe*. Thus, it takes the form described above.

In this way, the three syllables of Bālā are the powers of Speech (Vāk), Will (Kāma), and Energy (Śakti). Alternatively, they are the three root-peak-syllables (*mūlakūṭatraya*). This is the authoritative source.

Both meanings have already been explained previously. Having drawn a triangle characterized by these three such qualifiers— that is, one in which the corners are joined— having worshipped it with the mantra "haṃsaḥ haṃsaḥ" using flowers and other offerings, and having drawn a circle and a hexagon outside the triangle;

Having worshipped the six corners of the hexagon— starting from the front portion and proceeding clockwise from the tip facing oneself— with the root-mantras of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [and] having repeated the root-mantra seven times,
those [substances] were placed and offered into that [hexagon].

"By means of perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, and lamps, one should become such a worshiper"—this is an implied injunction (*ārthika*) regarding the specific qualification that the offering of these [substances] must be performed within the specific ritual procedure (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). "Having made it identical with, that is, non-different from, *vidyā*—which is supreme consciousness—one should meditate upon it. That refers to the first [mantra] and so forth; [one should meditate upon] the ninety-four mantras.
Those which will be described hereafter. || 25 ||
(p. 109) He states those mantras:
the thirty-eight digits of the threefold fire, encapsulated by the *tritārī* and the *namaḥ*. [The *sṛṣṭi*-...

The ten powers of Brahmā are: supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), memory (*smṛti*), intelligence (*medhā*), beauty (*kānti*), fortune (*lakṣmī*), splendor (*dyuti*), stability (*sthirā*), steadfastness (*sthiti*), and perfection (*siddhi*). The ten powers of Viṣṇu are: old age (*jarā*), protection (*pālinī*), peace (*śānti*), sovereignty (*īśvarī*), pleasure (*ratikāmike*), the boon-giver (*varadā*), joy (*āhlādinī*), love (*prīti*), longevity (*dīrghā*), and [the power of] Viṣṇu (*viṣṇu*).

[The ten powers of Rudra are: the fierce one (*tīkṣṇā*), the terrible one (*raudrī*), fear (*bhayā*), sleep (*nidrā*), lassitude (*tandrī*), hunger (*kṣudhā*), anger (*krodhinī*), action (*kriyā*), belching (*udgārī*), and death (*mṛtyu*).
[In some places here, at the location of the upward-moving breath (udgārī), "the firebrand" (ulkā) is mentioned. There are ten Rudrakalās.
The four Īśvarakalās are yellow, white, reddish, and black.
[The remaining Kalās are: Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, Mocikā, and Parā.
The sixteen digits of Sadāśiva are Sūkṣmā, Asūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Jñānā, Ajñānā, Amṛtāpyāyinī, Vyāpinī, and Vyomarūpā.
The *haṃsa* (swan) dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house;

dwelling among men, dwelling in the best, dwelling in truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the cows, born of truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth (*ṛtam bṛhat*). For that valor Viṣṇu is praised, like a terrifying beast, roaming far, dwelling in the mountains, whose three wide strides...

In his strides he dwells upon all worlds. We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. May I be liberated from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not be separated from immortality. The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye fixed in the sky. Thus the sages...

The wise and watchful ones kindle [the fire] at that which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu. May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow an embryo. May the two Aśvins [bestow] an embryo upon you.
"May the two gods, the wearers of lotus-garlands, bestow [it] here"—thus should the reading *puṣkarasrajau* be understood.
These are the five mantras. Including the root-vidyā, there are ninety-four mantras in total. 26.

The *tritārī* has been previously mentioned [the extraction of the *tritārī* is found on folio 91, line 3 of the *Anugata*, in the eighth *sūtra* of the *Śrīkramīya-khaṇḍa*; it is also explicitly present here below in the commentary]. Between the two words "tritārī" and "namaḥ," one should recite ninety-four mantras. In this way, it becomes encapsulated by the two. As in the world:
Just as when something is placed inside a casket or a box, the object is brought into a state of existing within the middle of the lower part and the upper part of the container,
so too, first comes the *tritārī*, then one mantra from among the ninety-four mantras, and then *namaḥ*. Thus...
When there is a mantra, it becomes encapsulated by two [syllables]. The triad of splendors consists of fire, sun, and moon;
their *kalās* (p.

The thirty-eight [kalās], beginning with Dhūmrārcis and ending with Pūrṇāmṛtā, which will be described in the Śyāmākrama, [these three—the kalās of fire, sun, and moon—are present in their original form in the root text itself under the explicit names in the sixth section, the eighteenth sūtra of the Śrīśyāmākrama; therefore, they should be taken from there]. The nature of the mantra is as follows:

Tu Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Dhūmrārciṣe Namaḥ. [These three are the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon; they exist in their original form in the root text of the *Śrīśyāmākrama*, chapter 18, verse 6, where they appear by their direct names.
Therefore, they should be taken from there. The same should be understood for what follows. In the expression "sṛṣṭi-ṛddhi," there is no euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

This is an archaic (ārṣa) form; alternatively, there is no sandhi because of the optional rule *ṛtyakaḥ*. The rest is clear. The "fire digits" (*vahnikalāḥ*)—these three digits of fire, sun, and moon—are found in the original root text itself at the sixth section, in the *Śrīśyāmākrama*, in the eighteenth sūtra; they should be taken from there. The "sun digits" (*sūryakalāḥ*).

[These three digits of fire, sun, and moon exist in their very root form in the sixteenth sūtra of the Śrīśyāmākrama in the sixth section ahead; therefore, they should be taken from there. —12. The lunar digits:
[These three digits of fire, sun, and moon exist under their manifest names in the sixth section ahead...]

[They exist in the root itself within the *Śrīśyāmākrama*, sūtra 18; therefore, they should be taken from there. 16. The *kalās* of Brahmā—10; the *kalās* of Viṣṇu—10; the *kalās* of Rudra—10; the *kalās* of Īśvara—4; the *kalās* of Sadāśiva—16.
Thus, all the *kalās* together amount to 88. Even though [the mantra] is "haṃ saḥ śuciṣat" (haṃsaḥ śuciṣat).

Although there are seven verses beginning with "ityārabhya" and ending with "puṣkarasrajāv," nevertheless, by the statement "ityete pañca mantrāḥ" (these are five mantras), the fourth and fifth [verses] are combined into one mantra, and the sixth and seventh are combined into one mantra. Because they possess a single characteristic (*ekaliṅgatvāt*), their unification is appropriate only in those two cases, but not elsewhere. This is the root-vidyā (*mūlavidyā*).

The Fifteenth [Chapter]. The previously mentioned eight and eighty-eight mantras, together with the five root-vidyās, amounting to all of them combined, result in ninety-four mantras. The established meaning is that one should consecrate the substance by means of these [mantras]. || 26 ||
Now, some indeed prescribe the consecration with five [verses] beginning with "akhaṇḍādyaiḥ. || 27 ||

By the word "atha" (now/then), a specific sequence is indicated, namely that [the mantra] follows immediately after the ninety-fourth mantra. Here, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is not possible because there is no fixed textual tradition (*svamatābhāvāt*). Therefore, "atha" is necessary. "Ha" is used as a poetic embellishment (*śabdālaṅkāra*). By the word "eke" (some), its optional nature (*pākṣikatva*) is indicated. "Those whose first [mantra] is unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa-ādya*); that is to say...
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on the cognition of its qualities (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

[In this context, by the phrase "which are the Akhaṇḍa and others," it should be understood that the question refers to which mantras beginning with the word *akhaṇḍa* are those mentioned in the word "Akhaṇḍa and others" in the aforementioned Sūtra 27. In response to the inquiry, "Which are the Akhaṇḍa and others?", he says:
O Mistress of the Akula, place within this Self, which is the supreme nectar and the source of unbroken, singular-flavored bliss, the spontaneous radiance of your own will.
O Supreme One, who abides in the non-clan (akula), whose form is nectar, and who produces pure gnosis—
place the state of immortality within this substance which has a moist form.
Having achieved a state of uniformity with that very form within my own essential nature,
and having become the embodiment of supreme nectar, O Consciousness, manifest within me!
Thus, there are three *anuṣṭubh* verses concerning knowledge.

111) [In the Vedabhāṣya, the learned author of the Sūtrabhāṣya analyzes the meanings of the five mantras beginning with "akhaṇḍa," whose meanings were previously stated to be difficult to comprehend. Regarding the meaning of the Vedic mantras:

Because they are explicit, having set aside those Vedic mantras whose meanings are similarly explicit, I shall reveal the meaning of certain easily understood Tantric mantras. Regarding the words "Akhaṇḍa" and so forth: this triad of mantras beginning with "Akhaṇḍa" is a constituent part of the prayer to the Goddess Sudhā, as indicated by its characteristic mark (liṅga).

It ought to be so. Furthermore, by the stronger [the word "balavatā" here being a qualifier of "liṅgena"], on account of the second-case *śruti* following the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the consecration. In accordance with this, in the *Paramānanda-tantra*, regarding the passage "one should mutter these three, enriched by the three seed-syllables, there in four ways," [it means] while touching.
Thus, [the word "iti"] is to be supplied. And so, its status as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is established.

Furthermore, the statement in the *Paramānanda-ṭippaṇī* that "the passage beginning with 'akhaṇḍa' is a prayer to the goddess Sudhā" is erroneous. [This is because] by the second Śruti, the name [is established]; [this refers to] the word "āmananti" found in the twenty-seventh Sūtra above.

It should be understood here that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used because the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) functions as the object of the action; for no one accepts the sublation of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) by indicative mark (*liṅga*) in such a manner. Here, the meaning of the mantra is as follows:
"Akula" refers to the two thousand-petaled lotuses. One of these is the support of all lotuses and faces upward.
A lotus situated below the *mūlādhāra* is that one which is designated as *akula*.

This is stated during the commentary on the verse from the *Yoginītantra*: "In *akula* and in that which is known as *viṣu*," referring to the eight-petaled lotus above the thousand-petaled lotus located at the very bottom, and above that, the six-petaled [lotus].

Regarding the cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra*: according to the *Setubandha*, the six-petaled *kulapadma* is situated below the *mūlādhāra*, while the eight-petaled and thousand-petaled lotuses situated below that are called *akula*. Likewise, the thousand-petaled lotus with downward-facing petals situated at the *brahmarandhra* is also *akula*. Thus it has been said:
In the Tripurārṇava:
Above the Suṣumṇā is the station of the Guru, possessing a luster equal to the brilliance of ten million moons,
facing downwards, and adorned with a thousand petals.
One should know that to be Akula... [as stated].
In the Paramānanda Tantra it is also said: "The practitioner, having risen in the morning, [should visualize] his own Guru within the Brahma-aperture,
in the lotus at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] inside the previously mentioned Kula-lotus."

Thus, having established that both thousand-petaled lotuses are designated as *akula*, in the present context it is specifically the one located at the *brahmarandhra* that is intended, because it alone is the source of the flowing nectar (*amṛta*). In this context, *akula* refers to the lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra*; its presiding deity is the *nāyikā*. In addressing her, [the text says] "O *akulanāyikā*" (here, in the root text).

The term *akulanāyikā* and its meaning have been adopted; however, since in the root text and commentary on verse 38 of the sixth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*, only the word *kula* appears, I hope that the lack of contradiction between the words of both Śrī Śiva and Jamadagni may be properly reconciled.
[That which is] unfragmented (*akhaṇḍa*), uninterrupted (*avicchinna*), of a single flavor (*ekarasa*), and unmixed with suffering (*duḥkhāsaṃbhinna*)—which...

Ānanda is that which makes manifest or reveals; in such a state, there is the supreme, most excellent nectar (sudhā) located in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which bestows immortality. In that Self—that is, in its own essential nature—within this substance...
Establish—that is, place—the vibration, which is the power of manifestation (*prakāśa-śakti*), of that consciousness which is autonomous and independent.
O Supreme One, establish and bring about immortality in this object which possesses a moist form (*klinna-rūpin*), for it contains that [moisture] within it. *Akula* has been explained.

In that context, the nature of the deity presiding over the substance is such that its own form is like the form of the nectar (*amṛta*) existing therein; this is a qualifier of the word *parā*. Furthermore, "the producer of pure knowledge" (*śuddhajñānakarī*), meaning the bringer forth of the manifestation of the knowledge of one's true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), is also a qualifier of *parā*. As for that which...

Regarding the statement that "in the supreme mass of the bliss of good fortune" (*saubhāgyānandasandohe pare*) is a locative case ending used as an adjective qualifying the object (*vastu*), that is incorrect because it would result in a remote syntactic connection (*dūrānvaya*). Rather, it means: "in that which possesses the form of that Supreme Brahman"—that is to say, in the very nature of the Supreme Brahman—and "in me," who possess that form, who am the recipient of the special *arghya* offering, and who am identified with the body.

The meaning of the three mantras is: "Becoming that which is supreme, immortal, and bliss—that is, taking its form—having achieved a state of uniformity (*aikarasya*), which is the single-form nature of consciousness (*cit*), cause the radiance of consciousness to manifest the light of one's own true nature.
They are *anuṣṭubh*s, meaning they possess the *anuṣṭubh* meter; for the Śruti states, "The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables."

The *vidyās* are the mantras. This triad of *vidyās*—meaning this very triad of *vidyās* consisting of the three verses beginning with "akhaṇḍa" as stated in Sūtra 28—taken together, produces a single unseen potency (*apūrva*), just like the triad of *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifices. In the subsequent mantras, the word "atho" [is used].

Because they conclude with the word *prakrama* (the beginning), and because this triad is seen to have a collective application (*samaṣṭi-viniyoga*) even in another tantra due to its essential nature (*rasatva*), when one mantra is omitted, there is a recitation of the triad again; it is not merely that much [here, the commentary on the three verses beginning with "akhaṇḍa" comes to an end]. || 28 || 2

He states the fourth mantra, that of Amṛteśī: "Then, having uttered 'vācaṃ blūṃ jhaum' and 'jūṃ saḥ', [the mantra is] 'amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya svāhā'; this is the fourth mantra. (29)

One should utter "Vācyam-aiṃ" and then the word "iti," having set aside the rest of the mantra's form. Its meaning is: "O Amṛte (Nectar), cause nectar to flow into this substance. The remaining words are adjectives for "Amṛte";
their meaning is clear. || 29 ||
Then he extracts the fifth mantra: Vāgbhava, *vada vada*, then *vāgvādini*, *vāṅmadanaklinne*, *kledini*, *kledaya*,
the pair for great agitation (*mahākṣobhaṃ kuru*), *mādanaṃ*, *śaktiṃ*, *mokṣaṃ*, *kuru kuru*, and the sound *hasa*.

This fifth vidyā consists of the fourteen and fifteen piṇḍas, together with the fourteenth and sixteenth piṇḍas; having consecrated that arghya, which is composed of light, with these [mantras]— || 30 ||

The nature of the mantra: *aiṃ vada vada vāgvādini aiṃ klīṃ klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru kuru klīṃ sauḥ mokṣaṃ kuru kuru hasauṃ shauḥ*.

Thus, this is the fifth knowledge (*vidyā*). Having consecrated [the water] with these five [mantras], one should prepare that *arghya* consisting of light and free from defects. By this, it is indicated that the removal of curses and so forth mentioned in other tantras is accomplished by this very [rite].
If it is asked, "How is this intention established by the expression 'consisting of light' (jyotirmaya)?"—it is replied:

"Light" (jyotis) is a synonym for manifestation (prakāśa). The suffix *mayaṭ* here has the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). Where there is admixture with impurity within a manifestation, an abundance of that manifestation is not possible, as is the case, for example, with the sun when it is eclipsed.

When impurity is removed, an abundance of light is experienced right there, just as it is with a mirror that reveals the face. Likewise, in this case too, the nature of being composed of light cannot manifest in a substance afflicted by various stains such as dust and dirt; however, once all impurities have been dispelled through consecration with the aforementioned ninety-nine mantras, [it becomes manifest].
It becomes composed of light; for that very reason, it is said, "having made it composed of light.
By this, the claim of certain individuals—that there is also a conjunction with the removal of curses mentioned in other tantras—is indeed unworthy of belief.

[From here until the completion of the 30th leaf of the Sūtrabhāṣya, the author of the Vṛtti has adorned the placement of the two vessels. Thus, the establishment of the primacy [of this practice] is demonstrated;
and those such as Maheśvarānandanātha and others [have stated] in another Tantra regarding the daily worship:

Regarding the statement "as before, however, there are three bowls," they argued that since there is no prohibition stating it should not be made from thread (*sūtra*), even those who follow the *Sūtras* should make the three bowls from thread. To them, this question is posed: Is the state of having three bowls established because there is no prohibition stating it should not be made from thread, or because it is mentioned in another *Tantra*, or...?

Is it because there is no prohibition in its own sūtra despite the existence of such a rule in another tantra, or because of the hearing of a prohibition against two vessels in another tantra? It cannot be the first, for in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice," the absence of a prohibition such as "not with wheat" would imply that the apūrva (transcendental result) could be achieved even through the use of wheat. Nor can it be the second, for if that were the case...

Since the worship of Saṅgītamātṛkā, Vārāhī, and others as taught in the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* constitutes an ancillary (*aṅga*) of Śrīvidyā—as stated in the *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*—it would follow that for others as well, the abandonment of such ancillaries would be irrational.
By this, the third position is also refuted. Nor is the fourth [position] tenable; for instance, that which is from that...
"O Goddess, one should never, under any circumstances, use two vessels"—this is the prohibition. And as for the censure:
"O Śivā, by using two vessels out of laziness or otherwise, a man is deprived of the fruit of his worship and undergoes a state of transformation."

Thus, "three vessels" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) supplementary to the injunction. Otherwise, since the exclusion of two vessels would already follow from the injunction of three vessels itself, the prohibition would be rendered redundant due to the absence of any resulting fruit in the form of its own negation. And if it is argued that the injunction effects mere engagement while the prohibition effects the cessation of what is other than that, then [the case of] eleven...

In the case of the injunction "he performs the *prayāja*s," since there is no statement specifying "twelve" or "ten," the *apūrva* would result from ten or twelve *prayāja*s. Therefore, since the prohibition regarding the cessation of the two vessels would be purposeless by itself, it must be a mere explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to that injunction. This is the function of the explanatory supplement.

The intent lies solely in the praise; there is no character of negation in that [text]. How, then, can the proof for the existence of three vessels (*tripātratva*) in another system (*tantrāntara*) be established by means of a negation?

Furthermore, when the question arises as to how many vessels there are in this tantra, since no specific rule is heard in its own sūtra, the statement from another tantra— namely, "as before, there are three vessels"— is indeed [the authority].

The opposing view holds that the possession of three bowls fulfills one's desire and accomplishes the goal; for if that were the case, since there would be no possibility of possessing even two bowls, the prohibition [of having more than one] would be rendered utterly irrelevant.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that, according to your view, since there is no prior acquisition of two vessels (*dvipātra*), how can the authority of the sentence "one should not make two vessels" be considered;
for there is no rule that a prohibition contained within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must be preceded by a prior acquisition, as it [the prohibition] functions in its own right.

Because there is no intended meaning [in that literal sense]. Therefore, even the prohibition of something not otherwise established is logically consistent, as in: "Fire is not to be piled in the intermediate space nor in the sky; if one were to pile it in the intermediate space, he would afflict the intermediate space with pain. Such a statement does not have its primary purpose (tātparya) in its own literal meaning, but rather in mere praise (prāśastya). And that [praise] is uncontradicted.

Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence for a relationship of original form (prakṛti) and modification (vikṛti) between the two tantras, such that one could be prohibited because it has been obtained [elsewhere]. Indeed, the prohibition of what has not been obtained is unheard of even in a dream.

Furthermore, even in the case of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for the pleasure of others, let there be a negation of what has been superimposed; nevertheless, their desired goal is not established. For instance, the *Kalpasūtra* prescribes the use of two vessels, while the *Paramānandatantra* prohibits them; such being the case, the two tantras would possess equal authority.

It would result in a mere option (*vikalpa*), like the options regarding the taking or not taking [of food]. If one were to accept the superiority of the prohibitory scripture solely by personal preference, the position of taking it would be utterly sublated; thus, there would be no option at all. For Maheśvarānandanātha and others, who maintain that the practice of using two vessels is unscriptural, an option does not exist.
For this is not desired; moreover, it is difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, in the Paraśurāma-sūtra, it is not stated explicitly that "one should prepare two vessels";

rather, the injunction must be inferred based on the textual reading regarding the employment of two vessels. Therefore, the statement "O Goddess, one should certainly not make two vessels" is an explicit prohibition (*pratyakṣa-niṣedha*). And thus, by means of this explicit [prohibition], the inferential [injunction] is [sublated].

It is contradicted. In a case where both apprehension and non-apprehension occur, it is logical to entertain an alternative view that both are perceptual; however, in the present instance, this cannot be said, because of the disparity [between the two cases]. In the *adhrigu-praiṣa* of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is the mantra: "Sixty-four are his ribs. In that context, "ribs" (*vaḍkrayaḥ*) refers to the ribs located on the sides of this animal.

The meaning of that [text] is "twenty-six. This mantra is obtained by extension (*atideśa*) because it is a modification of the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice] in the *aśvamedha*. Such being the case, there exists another mantra in the *aśvamedha*: "Thirty-four ribs of the horse, the kinsman of the gods. By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of that mantra, it is understood that the horse has thirty-four ribs.

Success! When that [sacrifice] is established, there arises the mantra: "Its ribs are twenty-six. Due to the contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "twenty-six," a modification (*ūha*) is obtained by substituting "its ribs are thirty-four" in its place.
This being the case, it is further heard in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Aśvamedha sacrifice: "One should not say 'thirty-four'."
"One should say 'twenty-six' alone. Here, since the rule for modification (*ūha*) stating "thirty-four" is inferential (*ānumānika*), it is set aside;
thus, the prohibition "not thirty-four" operates as a constant rule.
Having stated this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the response follows: where there is an inferential injunction and a direct (*pratyakṣa*) prohibition...
In that case, it must be admitted that both possess equal strength; for indeed, the state of being strong or weak is never inherent in an entity.

Rather, [the preference for one over another] is caused by the rapidity or delay of its presentation when there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For example, in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the spreading of the altar (*vedyāstaraṇa*) is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*). In that case, when there is an expectancy as to "by what means should the spreading of the altar be performed," if there were no word expressing the instrument (*sādhana*), then—

Having recalled the means of spreading the grass-bed from the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), one should mentally superimpose the *kuśa* grasses; thereafter, the requirement must be fulfilled by postulating an inferential scriptural statement (*ānumānika-śabda-kalpanā*) that "the spreading with *kuśa* grasses should be performed as in the archetype. Even after that, [the rule] "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds" applies immediately.

When the requirement for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is satisfied by the arrows presented through a directly perceived statement (*pratyakṣavākya*), the instructional scripture (*bodhakaśāstra*) lacks expectancy regarding that portion and is therefore weak. In the present case, because the prohibition "one should not say 'thirty-four'" is dependent upon a prior application (*prāpti*), the injunction must first be postulated on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "thirty-four for the *vājins*. Only after that [postulation] does the following occur.

A prohibition, which arises subsequently to turn back a person already engaged in an action according to an injunction, is not capable of completely subverting that upon which it depends for its own existence; rather, it subverts it only partially. Therefore, in such a case—as in the example where the rule regarding *śara* grass arises after the rule regarding *kuśa* grass—the prohibition [subverts the injunction only in part].

Prior to the postulation of an injunction, [the action] is capable of being undertaken. Therefore, in such a case, because the inferred injunction and the perceptible prohibition possess equal force, an option (*vikalpa*) alone prevails; this was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the fourth quarter of the ninth chapter in Jaimini’s system. In the present instance as well, since they possess equal force, there is an option.
It is difficult to avoid.

Furthermore, if— by the statement in the *Sūtra* regarding the placement [of the vessels] along with the procedure for the two vessels— the injunction for two vessels were not inferred in the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), and if it were instead assumed that the mention of two vessels follows other tantras and is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaka*) of a third as well, then in all tantras there would be only the practice of three vessels.

Since the two vessels are accepted [by you] as being part of the Tantra, and since there is no one who initiates the practice of the two vessels, the injunction for the two vessels is equivalent to a hare's horn; likewise, its prohibition is also equivalent to that. Therefore, by what means can the point you desire be established? This is a rope with a noose at both ends. Consequently:
Those who follow the Kalpasūtras and the Yoginītantras should perform the practice of using two vessels without hesitation.

As for that which was stated in the nineteenth chapter of the *Paramānandatantra-ṭippaṇī*, titled *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*, on the occasion of commenting upon the fifteenth verse: "But surely, would not the two vessels prescribed in the *Paraśurāmasūtra*, the *Vāmakeśvara-tantra*, and other scriptures be contradicted?"

Listen: since the worship according to the secondary rule (*anukalpa-pūjā*) and its two vessels will be clearly explained in the next chapter (*ullāsa*), this *tantra*—the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* and so forth—is intended for that secondary rule of worship. For this very reason, it is easy to say that there is an absence of mantras for the removal of curses (*śāpamocana*) therein. Alternatively, it is intended for those practicing self-yoga (*ātmayoga*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava* that for those devoted to the yoga of the Self, "the omission of a limb does not cause failure" (*nāṅgalopena hīyate*). For this same reason, the venerable Bhāskararāya has established in his *Setubandha* that the abbreviated worship involving a single vessel and so forth is intended for those who are habituated to practice. Now...
Or else, one may take the side of the supreme adversary. As it is said in the Tantra:
"Having indeed prepared a pair of vessels for direct perception, one shall incur a curse."
In some places, it was taught by me myself as pertaining to the time of the ultimate attainment.
Thus did the venerable Maheśvarānandanātha state three positions; that [last one] is to be reflected upon.

The method described in the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* is not the primary one; rather, it is the position that accepts a substitute. Thus, in the first position, there are the five *makāras* which manifest that [state], and through them, worship is performed in secret.

Similarly, regarding the phrase "having first purified," this means having placed the initial bindu; "having filled," means having satisfied the initial [syllable] with the group of five (mapañcaka); and for the subsequent hundred-verse statements beginning with "having satisfied," which occupy the position of the sūtras, there should indeed be the insertion of the *kuṇḍala*. Furthermore, even in the absence of the group of five...

By the sūtra "the constant review of the sequence," it is made perfectly clear that the *maṇḍala* (pañcaka) holds primacy in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*). This being the case, the claim that the sūtra refers to a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) is a mere scribal error, rooted in a failure to reconcile the preceding and following sūtras, and must therefore be rejected.

Furthermore, the absence of the release from the curse has been put forward as a reason to prove this position; however, that is utterly groundless and irrelevant. For instance, what is called "release from the curse" is it seen as the production of whiteness through a subsequent action upon something that was previously black?

Or is the fruit that, through purification (*saṃmārjana*) and so forth, an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises which constitutes the body of the means for sacrifice, as in the case of the *sruk* ladle? It is not the first [alternative], because even by repeating a thousand times a mantra that releases one from a curse, no transformation of the prior form is observed. Nor is it the second.
In some tantras there is elaboration, and in some tantras there is brevity;
yet, by relying upon a single tantra, the ritual action is likewise performed correctly.
O Rāma, everything has been accomplished by him through the path of the venerable Guru.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Tripurārahasya*:

"Whether much or little has been prescribed for anyone in their own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, when that much of the scriptural meaning has been performed by him, everything [or 'all'— this is an alternative reading] becomes accomplished."
It would have been accomplished.

Thus, by the authority of the *Bodhāyana-smṛti*, since the essential nature that produces the sacrifice is obtained through the very purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) prescribed for the primary substance, the mantras for liberation from the curse have no application therein;
how, then, could this reason establish that the Sūtra refers to a substitute (*pratinidhi*)? Furthermore, in the absence of the primary [substance]...
When a substitute is accepted, as many primary properties as are applicable to that substitute proceed accordingly—
just as when there is an absence of *vrīhi* rice, the properties of *vrīhi* apply to *nīvāra* millet, or when there is an absence of *soma*, the properties of *soma* apply to *pūtīka* plants;
it has been established in the system of Jaimini (*Jaiminīya-tantra*) that even modification (*ūha*) does not occur in such cases— and people indeed practice this way.
The learned authorities are likewise [of this opinion]. This being the case, who can prevent the absence of mantras for the removal of curses in the case of a substitute?
Thus, by employing a reason that is absolutely unestablished—like the claim that fire is not hot—they have most clearly revealed their own ignorance.

Nor is the second position tenable. For instance, does the ritual action (*karman*) prescribed in all the *sūtras* of Paraśurāma, beginning from initiation (*dīkṣā*), refer primarily to the practice of yoga, or is it merely worship? It cannot be the first, because the state of being a practitioner of yoga prior to initiation is impossible. [Furthermore, one should not speak] in the presence of those who are uninitiated...
Because of the prohibition, "One should not recite the *Śivapaddhati*," there is an absence of hearing the Tantric Siddhānta;
and since yoga is impossible without such hearing, it is impossible to say that this initiation is for those practicing yoga.
Regarding the second case—whether one who practices in this manner and performs the worship prescribed by this Tantra possesses the initiation taught in this Tantra, or not?

Only one who has been initiated by means of another tantra, whose mind has been fully ripened through the independent practice over time, possesses the qualification for the worship described in this sūtra.
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because the meditation (dhyāna) favored by you is not accomplished in the moment immediately following initiation;

this is experienced by everyone. Thus, having performed initiation in accordance with the Sūtra, since one lacks the qualification for the worship prescribed in this Tantra due to being a non-yogin, one must resort to another Tantra for the purpose of worship.
This must be done. For it is said:
"He who, while abiding by his own scripture, practices the scripture of another, incurs the sin of killing an embryo and treats his own scripture with contempt."
Thus ends the transgression of the prohibition. Furthermore, by the aphorism, "After initiation,

one should follow the procedure of Gaṇanāyaka in order to remove obstacles to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā," it is stated that the worship of Gaṇapati is the means for destroying the impediments to the adoration of Lalitā.

For the ripening of the mind, which is to be accomplished through the worship of Lalitā, occurs immediately after that; from that, the aforementioned yoga follows. Subsequently, eligibility for the practice of the two vessels (dvipātra) must be stated. That [eligibility] is not possible in the worship of Gaṇapati, because since the worship of Gaṇapati occurs simultaneously with obstacles, the aforementioned yoga is absent at that time. Furthermore, regarding the worship of Gaṇapati:
Since two bowls are mentioned there, the application of two bowls must necessarily be accepted in that case.
And thus, what prevents the assumption of a qualification that has been observed to deviate in one instance from applying elsewhere as well?
This follows the maxim: "What need is there for a woman who has once proven unfaithful to veil herself with a garment elsewhere?"

Nor should it be said: "The non-yogi, having abandoned the worship of Gaṇapati, should perform only the worship of Lalitā alone—following another tantra—until the attainment of yoga-siddhi, but not the worship of Gaṇapati; or else, even in the worship of Gaṇapati, let another tantra be resorted to. For if that were the case, then...

Otherwise, one would have to declare the Sūtra itself to be invalid, [which states]: "Having worshipped Gaṇapati, with all obstacles dispelled, one should begin the Krama of Śrī Lalitā, the sole leader of the circle of Śaktis.
Furthermore, the mention of the worship of Gaṇapati in the Sūtra would be rendered purposeless; it does not mean that the worship of Lalitā is to be performed prior [to the worship of Gaṇapati].

Because, due to his lack of qualification (*ayogitva*), he lacks the authority for that [practice] at that time; and because it serves no purpose even after the attainment of the fruit through the practice of *lalita*, it is not to be performed. Thus, its futility is unavoidable.
Nor should it be argued that because the prohibition of using two vessels occurs in the section on the *Lalitā* [Kalpa], the lack of qualification for non-yogins applies only there;
for elsewhere, their qualification for the practice of using two vessels certainly exists, as there is no such prohibition.
This is because, at the time of performing the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*) of the venerable *Lalitā*, [the rule serves] to ensure the accomplishment of freedom from obstacles.

This is because the followers of Maheśvarānandanātha— who, following the *Paraśurāmasūtra*, perform the worship of all Gaṇapatis and, at the time of arranging the vessels (*pātrāsādana*), reject the practice of two vessels (*dvipātraprayoga*) in favor of the practice of three vessels (*tripātraprayoga*)— do not approve of this position; nor is it [established] by another tantra.

The second position is that one who has been initiated and whose mind has matured through independent practice possesses the qualification for the worship prescribed in the Sūtra; however, this is not the case, because if it were so, the mention of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Sūtra would be redundant. Thus, as a proof for this position, there is the statement from the *Tripurārṇava* regarding those intent on self-yoga (*ātmayoga*): [text follows].

He wrote that "one does not fall [from dharma] by the omission of a limb. That is extremely weak. Its meaning is that for practitioners of yoga (*yogābhyāsinaḥ*), the omission of a limb is not a fault. His established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the rule concerning the two vessels mentioned in the Sūtra is intended specifically for the particular qualified practitioner who is a yogi. And thus, in the practice of a yogi, there is no need for a third vessel.

Just as the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) in the *sāmidhenī* verses connected to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice performed by a Vaiśya is not a subordinate element (*anaṅga*), so too there is no omission of a subordinate element (*aṅgalopa*) at all; thus, since there is no fault in the omission of a subordinate element, this serves as a proof for his own position.

The statement regarding the cause is like grasping at the son of a barren woman as something that accomplishes its own effect; and as for the practice of abbreviated worship using a single vessel and so forth in this regard, it is intended for those who are habituated to such practice.

The agreement regarding the *Setubandha* commentary has been shown, yet that too is unproven; no such line exists anywhere in the *Setubandha*. On the contrary, it establishes the performance using only two actors (*dvipātraprayoga*). For instance, [the passage] belonging to the preceding *Catuḥśatī*:
One should quickly place the *arghya* water in a vessel made of gold or other materials that has a stand,
mixed with *rocanā*, camphor, saffron, and *laghu-kastūrī*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon the elements as fire, sun, and moon;
one should recite the mantra ten times and thereby satisfy the Yoginīs with that.

In the course of explaining these two verses, this statement from the *Pūrvatantra* refers to the general *arghya*, while the statement from the *Uttaratantra*— “One should establish the *arghya* in the center of both the Śrīcakra and oneself”— refers to the special *arghya*; at the end of that [section], the *arghya* is likewise established specifically.

"The best of practitioners should accomplish [this]"— having rejected the ancient commentary which holds that this refers to either the *guru-pātra* or the *ātma-pātra*, and having also rejected another opinion which holds that the statement found in the *Pūrvatantra* refers specifically to the *viśeṣārghya*, [it is established that] the procedure for the *sāmānyārghya* in the *Pūrvatantra* is [to be understood] by means of [the procedure] residing in the *Uttaratantra*.

By the statement "of the Śrīcakra and of the self," the rule regarding place and time applies to that [the Śrīcakra] alone; likewise, by the phrase "the arghya especially," one establishes the rule for the special arghya along with the extension of the previous dharmas. Then, at the time of the conclusion, it is stated: "Therefore, according to this tantra, for both alone..."

Śrī Bhāskararāya merely established the arrangement of two vessels, stating that "the installation is desired. (And this [arrangement] is suitable for us, but not suitable for others. He did not say that this practice belongs exclusively to yogins.
As for that which is stated in the *Setubandha* regarding another section:

because the detailed exposition of the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*)—as found in the *Yoginītantra-uttaracatuḥśatī*—is absent in other tantras, and because even the *Tantrarāja* is dependent upon this [work], this tantra is the most excellent; and its dependence on this is as follows.

Because it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "One should meditate by means of the clear method proclaimed in the *Nityāhṛdaya*," this *Nityāhṛdaya* is the name of the *Uttaratantra*. For although only a few external sacrificial components (*bāhyayāgāṅga*) are mentioned here, for those whose practice is characterized by firmness in internal worship (*antaraṅgopāsti*), fulfillment is possible through that much alone.

It is "to be conceptualized" because it has been written [in that manner]. Since the establishment of only the two [deities] is intended according to this very tantra as previously written—preceded by the refutation of the two [other] traditions—the word *etat* (this) in the sentence refers to the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*.
For, in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*, only those with purified internal organs (*śuddhāntaḥkaraṇa*) have the qualification; therefore, for them, there is indeed the practice [of those two].

"The established doctrine (siddhānta) intended [by us] is that there are two vessels; it is with this very intention that our commentary on the *Setubandha* also agrees. This too is not correct, because, in that case, there would be an absence of a rule for the production of the water for the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) in the *Uttaratantra*.

For those who practice according to the *Kevalottara-catuḥśatī-tantra* alone, the preparation of only the special *arghya* vessel would be required, not that of two vessels. Consequently, the statement in the concluding passage— that "the installation of the two [vessels] is desired according to this tantra"— would indeed be contradicted.

Therefore, by this word "tantra," the preceding and subsequent four-hundred-verse sections are unified; thus, the intended meaning is precisely that [the work is for] those who follow the complete tantra.

For this very reason, the application (*viniyoga*) of the general *arghya* produced in the previous *Catuḥśatī* will be stated in the eighth chapter; thus, the commentary on the *Setubandha* is consistent. By this, it is clear that what is taught in the earlier and later Tantras is one and the same. Such worship is accessible even to one whose mind is not yet matured; accordingly, there are two vessels.
It is difficult to ward off.

As for the statement in the *Setubandha* that even if only the few external limbs of sacrifice are described, there is fulfillment for those whose practice consists of the internal limbs by that much alone— that does not refer to one who follows this particular tantra; rather, it refers to one who,
following the *Tantrarāja*, performs worship previously and [attains fulfillment] over time.

Regarding the statement, "When the cultivation preceded by the purification of the mind has been perfected, one who acts in this manner constantly is liberated; there is no doubt in this," since the word "constantly" implies that even after the external sacrifice with its constituent parts is completed, the performance of the worship along with its auxiliary parts (sāṅgopāsti) should continue for as long as one lives, this [present rule] serves as an exception to that.

"One should meditate by means of the clear method taught in the *Nityāhṛdaya*. This means that one should perform that meditation which consists of the prior performance of external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*), by means of the clear method taught therein in the *Nityāhṛdaya*, which is the latter part of the *Catuḥśatī*. [This is because] in the *Tantrarāja*, due to the great number of components for external sacrifice, there is the practice of yoga.
For those desiring to practice yoga preceded by the performance of that [tantric discipline], when a doubt arises as to what should be abandoned and what should be adopted due to a lack of time,
one who wishes to practice yoga need not perform the entire collection of ancillaries (aṅgakalāpa) prescribed in the *Tantrarāja* for as long as one lives; rather—

The followers of the *Tantrarāja* maintain that one should perform the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*) using only the collection of minor limbs (*alpāṅgakalāpa*) taught in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*, and that by that alone its fulfillment is achieved; this [view] is intended to convey the doctrine of the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*. However, it does not follow from this that the entire *tantra* [is exhausted].

Even Brahmā is able to accomplish [the goal] for one intent on the practice of yoga. This being so, since the statement in the *Tantrarāja*—by the phrase "the Heart of Nityā"—specifies that it is only the *Uttara-catuḥśatī* (the latter four hundred verses) that concerns the practice of yoga, the recitation of the *Pūrva-catuḥśatī* (the former four hundred verses) would otherwise be redundant. Therefore, by the authority of the *Tantrarāja*, for those whose minds are fully matured...

For those skilled in the practice of yoga, there is the worship of a single vessel— specifically the special *arghya* vessel— as described in the latter *Catuḥśatikā*, using the collective mantra (*samaṣṭimantra*). For those whose minds are not yet matured but who follow the *Yoginītantras*, there is the practice of two vessels, combining both the former and the latter *Catuḥśatikās*.
This is the essential reality regarding the intention behind the *Setubandha*; likewise for those who follow the *Sūtras*, so enough with further elaboration.
Nor is it the third position— that it is the supreme view— because the statement supporting that third position is as follows:
"By making a pair of vessels in the direct perception [of the rite], one shall incur a curse."
In some instances, it was taught by me alone for the time of the ultimate downfall.

Regarding this written [text]: does the phrase "he who would violate that [vow], him one should punish with a hundred" indicate that violating the two vessels is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) in the form of a prohibition;
or is the second half a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to it; or rather, is the undesirability established by the first half alone?

By the second half [of the verse], two things are stated: the occurrence of an offense and its subsequent permission; or alternatively, the entire verse may be intended solely for the purpose of expressing that permission. It is not the first case, because the second half, being in the form of an *arthavāda*, has as its primary purport mere praise, rather than [prescribing] the time of the offense.

Because it is impossible for [the scripture] to be an authorizer [of what is already known], its own stated position cannot be established. Furthermore, one must state that by demonstrating that using two vessels is a means to an undesirable end, [the scripture] turns back a person who has already engaged in using two vessels. In that case, is the cause of engagement in the practice of using two vessels passion (*rāga*) or another system (*tantrāntara*)?
Not the first [alternative]: "One should use three bowls.
120) As long as the injunction exists, for one who is faithful and afraid of violating a subsidiary rule (*aṅga*), there can never be an attachment to using two bowls.

The first [alternative] is possible. As for the second alternative, it is difficult to avoid, since a response has already been given previously. By this, the second position is refuted. Therefore, by necessity, wherever this statement is recited in a tantra, there the rule of three vessels must indeed apply; the first half of that verse is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to it, while the second half—

For those who follow the *tantras* concerning the ritual of the three vessels (*tripātra*), it is permitted to adopt the practice of the two vessels (*dvipātra*) as taught in their own respective *tantras* when a supreme transgression has occurred.
A wise person should not speak untruth; untruth is the destroyer of Dharma.
When one has fallen into a situation where life is at risk, speaking untruth does not incur any fault.
Thus, the third position alone is correct. This very point was clarified by the teacher Bodhāyana:
"He who, while his own scripture exists, conducts himself according to another's scripture, thereby disregarding his own scripture, incurs a sin equal to that of killing an embryo."
"One should apply the injunctions of one's own Vedic school, together with the merits of other schools, for the sake of investigating ritual actions and in times of distress. Thus [it is said].

An illustration of this has been shown by Bhavasvāmin: for example, regarding the *saumya* ritual procedure (*tantra*) at the third pressing (*savana*), the *Śāliki-śākhā* states it is "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*), whereas another branch (*śākhā*) states "everything is like the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsavat*).

It should be performed by the followers of their respective branches exactly as stated [in their own texts]. However, in the event of an emergency (*āpatti*), even all [branches] must perform it silently. Thus...

Furthermore, how could one establish that the scriptural injunction permitting the use of three or more vessels during times of distress applies only when such distress has not yet occurred? Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
Those who follow the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* and the *Yoginī-tantra* may, without hesitation, employ only two vessels.
It must be performed.

Now, having established that the statements in other tantras which criticize the practice of using two vessels (*dvipātra*) are merely supplementary to the injunctions and intended for a specific purpose, those who follow the *Sūtra* have made the proposition: "The practice of using two vessels alone must be performed; contact with other tantras must not be made.
In doing so, they have criticized other [tantras] as being unsaid in their own *tantra* and as being indicated [only indirectly].
If one asks, "What is the scriptural example for the rule that [something] should be taken from another tantra?"—listen: immediately preceding this very statement, it says:
"In some tantras there is elaboration; in some tantras there is condensation."
O Rāma, by relying on a single Tantra and performing his duties correctly,
he has accomplished everything through the path of the venerable Guru.

By this, when the cessation of those ritual components of worship that are not essential to the worship— namely, all rites not mentioned as independent— is stated, it indicates what is not mentioned in the Tantra;
and by the phrase "and thus some ritual components are included," as well as by the phrase "likewise others are also refuted," [the meaning is established].

It is heard that there is great censure for the non-performance of certain acts that constitute essential limbs (*anaṅga*) of worship, such as the recitation of the *Sahasranāma*. Regarding its non-performance—(p.
How can one be a devotee without reciting this hymn? How could one please Maheśvarī without chanting the Thousand Names?
A person of deluded intellect who desires spiritual perfection while excluding the Thousand Secret Names would be like one who wishes to see forms without the aid of eyes.

"Surely one desires the cessation of hunger without food," and by such statements, censure is heard even regarding the non-study [of the text]. That which exists in another tantra must certainly be adopted.
This is precisely the intended meaning of the statement from the *Tripurārahasya*. However, whatever is not contradicted by one's own tantra [is also to be accepted].

The intention of the previously cited statement from another tantra, "one should practice," is also precisely this: that one should not resort to other tantras regarding the auxiliary components of a single ritual application. With the exception of what is indicated or required for the ritual auxiliaries, there is not even the slightest admission of anything situated in another tantra.
This is the ultimate conclusion. For this very reason, it is stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam:

"Indeed, for whom is that dharma—which, though created by men according to their own will, is distinct from the [four] stages of life (āśrama), yet ordained by one's own nature—not desired for the sake of tranquility?"

Thus he states this very point. Regarding this verse, [the Lord] says that even for the sake of increasing one's own merit (*dharmabhūyastva*), the duty of another (*paradharma*) should not be performed after the performance of one's own duty, because it is useless;
thus says Śrīdhara Svāmī: "By nature... This explains the verse. || 30 ||
He states the ritual duty to be performed with the drops contained in that vessel:

"Having worshipped the sandals of the Guru three times on the head with those drops" [the knowledge of the mantra of the *Śrīgurupādukātantra* mentioned here is found in verses 6–10 of the second supplement].
[These subjects are to be seen on 6/11, 6/14, 6/16/1, 6/16/5, and from 6/18 to 6/20. The moist [element] blazes; I am the light. The light blazes; I am Brahman. That which I am, I am Brahman.
I am; I am Brahman. I alone am I; I offer myself with the mantra *svāhā*.
One should offer that drop as an oblation into the kuṇḍalinī of one's own self. || 31 ||

With those drops— namely, the drops of the special *arghya*— one should sprinkle three times, that is, thrice, upon the head at the "twelfth place" (*dvādaśāntasthāna*) [which means the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); this meaning has been clarified on page 69 of the commentary on the Sūtras in the second section of the *Śrīgaṇapatikrama*].

Having worshipped the Guru’s sandals (gurupādukā) and having made an offering of substances intended for the Guru’s sandals, one should [offer] that drop—the meaning being the drop remaining from the sacrifice to the Guru’s sandals—by means of the mantra ending in *svāhā*, namely *ārdrāṃ jvalati iti svāhā*.
This is because pronouns refer to what is proximate, and it is precisely the remainder given to the sandals that is proximate; therefore, it belongs to them.

And because of the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "Taking the remainder, one should practice the yoga while reciting. [This refers to] within one's own *kuṇḍalinī*, which is the fire of consciousness (*cidvahnau*). The nature of *kuṇḍalinī* is described in another tantra (p.
Then, having meditated upon a white pericarp in the support, and then upon a red one;
within the cavity of the pericarp-cluster, it has the form of three and a half circles.
Having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī energy, which resembles a sleeping serpent and is thinner than a lotus fiber... [thus it is said].
By the word "juhuyāt" (one should offer), it is indicated that in this rite a firm notion of *homa* (fire-offering) must be maintained, and not a notion of drinking.

By the word "bindum" (a drop), the extreme smallness of the sacrificial substance is indicated. By the accusative case in "bindum," the *pratipatti-saṃskāra* (the ritual of disposal/consignment) is also indicated. [The remainder] given to the *gurupādukā* [is to be used] for the *homa*.
The meaning is that one should perform the consecration; therefore, in the absence of a remnant, there is no oblation.
Regarding the justification for the rule on taking family property:
indeed, it should be understood that from this point until the end of the commentary on sūtra 31, there is a refutation of the consumption of liquor;
however, it must also be noted that in certain instances, its defense has been set forth as well.

In all the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, the drinking of liquor is included among the five great sins (*pañcamahāpātaka*). As the venerable Yājñavalkya stated: "The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the four great sins; association with them is the fifth" (Prāyaścittādhyāya, Chapter 3, Verse 21).

Manu also says: "Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife, and association with those who commit these acts—these they call the great sins" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.7.21.8).
Since [the consumption of substances] is enumerated among the five great sins, how can the use of substances for pleasure as taught in the Tantras be justified?
This must be so. For in those very tantras where the consumption of substances is enjoined, prohibitions are frequently encountered within those same tantras. As it says in the Kulārṇava:
"Merely by the sight of liquor, one should look at the sun."
Merely by smelling that [substance], one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O Śivā, for touching liquor, the rule is that one should bathe if it reaches the knees, fast if it reaches the navel,
and observe a three-night fast if it goes above the navel.
If one has intentionally drunk liquor, one should cast that blazing [iron ball] into one's mouth;
having been completely burnt by it, one then attains purification.
Thus it is said that this is the expiation for the fault arising from the consumption of intoxicants.
Also in the Tripurārṇava:
"If a twice-born man should drink liquor even once out of desire or delusion,
he must be abandoned by those who know the Tantras without hesitation, even if he is learned."
Also in the Devīyāmala:
"The wise man should renounce both the smelling and the seeing of liquor. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is: "One should abandon even [the desire for] vision; how much more so the abandonment of drink? There are likewise many other scriptural statements from other systems; they are not written here for fear of excessive length. Therefore:

If it is argued that the scripture concerning the appropriation of family property is not to be trusted, we say no; for these statements merely serve to turn one away from the drinking of liquor which is prompted by passion. Otherwise, the engagement in acts for the sake of the sacrifice would be desired [even if forbidden], just as the injunction "one sacrifices a Brahmin for a Brahmin" [would be desired] despite the prohibition "one must not kill a Brahmin."
Otherwise, the authority of the Veda would be undermined. This very point has been clearly stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam:

"That the consumption of liquor was ordained for the sense of smell, and that the immolation of an animal is not violence, and likewise that sexual intercourse is for the sake of progeny and not for pleasure—those who know this are indeed aware of their own pure dharma."
But those men who, not knowing this, are arrogant, full of self-conceit,
and confidently harm animals— they devour them after death.

Thus, according to the text: therefore, because the injunction for accepting specific substances—which has no other scope—must be assumed to serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*), and because the prohibition serves solely the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), there is no identity of purpose between them.
For this very reason, it is precisely to indicate this intention that the *Tripurārṇava* and the *Kulārṇava* state "due to desire" (*kāmakṛta*) and "committed out of desire" (*kāmakṛte*).
The verse has been recited. Likewise, in another tantra:
"O lady of excellent hips, there is a fault elsewhere, but no fault is found in the sacrifice;
just as the killing of a horse occurs in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha."
Thus, by means of an illustration, he confirms the very point already stated.

In this *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*, having stated in the section on the purification of inner disposition (*bhāvaśodhana*) that even for a heroic Brāhmaṇa milk alone [is permitted], and for others not even that, Nṛsiṃhācārya has conducted an extensive discussion to reinforce the very same proposition stated earlier in another place. To illustrate:
Substances consecrated by inspection, sprinkling, meditation, mantras, and mudrās become fit for libation and bring delight to the deity.
In this context, *tarpaṇa* means drinking; however, this refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas, because for a Brāhmaṇa, the taking up of such [liquor] is prohibited.
Is it not so— that Brāhmaṇas may always drink it, Kṣatriyas when battle approaches, Vaiśyas when engaging in financial transactions, but Śūdras never at all?
Thus, in the *Kulārṇava*, regarding the Sautrāmaṇī rite within the Kula tradition, a Brāhmaṇa should drink the *surā* liquor.
Thus, according to the *Samayācāra-tantra*,
in the Kṛta age the Goddess was worshipped in due order by the four castes with offerings of milk, ghee, honey, and flour; in the Tretā age, she was worshipped with ghee by all classes.
In the Dvāpara age she was worshipped with honey by all castes;
in the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped by the gods with auspicious *āsava* liquors.

If it is asked, "Since this is stated in the *Yāmala*, how can there be no qualification for a Brāhmaṇa?"— it is replied: "Brāhmaṇas [are purified] by milk, Kṣatriyas by clarified butter, and others than those by honey and liquor"— thus, according to the sequence of the castes, there are indeed distinctions of substances, as stated in the *Laghu-stava* and in the *Jñānārṇava* regarding the substance.
"In that very same [text] it is stated: 'A Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with [liquor] of the *sāttvika* type alone. Likewise, after describing the various types of *āsava*, it says:
'In this manner a Kṣatriya may also give [it], but never the *paiṣṭī* [type]."
Coconut water in a vessel of bell-metal, and likewise cow's milk and honey in a vessel of copper.
A gift should never be given by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya to a Brāhmaṇa;

by such a mere act of giving, the Brāhmaṇa becomes diminished in lifespan (or, according to another reading, "the Brāhmaṇa becomes degraded"). [Note: In this case, due to the weight of the syllable *vrā-* in the alternative reading, there is a fear of violating the meter.]
The reading "hīnāyūḥ" and so forth would be quite correct [as it causes one to return].
Thus, in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"The Brāhmaṇas should be gratified with milk, those born of the royal lineage with ghee,
the Vaiśyas with honey, and those of the Śūdra caste with fermented liquors (āsava)."
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra,
it is specifically ordained that the offering and consumption of wine must be performed;
a Brāhmaṇa, however, should prepare honey-wine in a copper vessel.
Thus, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*,
it is said that by giving liquor— or by drinking it— a Brāhmaṇa falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa;
and by giving the blood of his own body, he incurs the sin of self-slaughter.
Thus, in the *Haṃsamāheśvaratantra*, within the section on the Dharma of the Kali Age (*kalidharmaprakaraṇa*) in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*,

since Harinātha Upādhyāya has stated that the prohibition against taking wine (*surāgrahaṇaniṣedha*) is intended for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the prohibition for a Brāhmaṇa is absolute; this is established by the elision of the vowel 'a' (*akārapraśleṣa*) in the phrase "brāhmaṇais tu sadāpeyā" (Brāhmaṇas [should] never drink).
Because for a Kṣatriya, battle is impossible when he is incapacitated at the time of combat; and for a Vaiśya, [it is impossible] otherwise at the time of lending wealth. (p. 125)

For if one were to give twenty when a gift of twenty was required by a person of impaired intellect, it would result in the obligation of giving a hundred or more. Therefore, the meaning is that she is never to be drunk [as wine] by Śūdras; rather, she is always to be drunk [as water]. And thus, in the verse "O Goddess, in the Kali age she is to be worshipped with pure liquors (āsava) alone," it must be understood that the term "all castes" (sarvavarṇa), which is supplied from the context, refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas.
Now, milk is produced from trees; clarified butter originates from bark;
honey arises from the juice of flowers; and spirituous liquor is produced from rice.

If it is argued that because specific terms such as *kṣīra* (milk) and others are defined in the *Bhairavītantra* as particular types of *āsava* (fermented liquor), the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for a Brāhmaṇa is thereby understood to exist therein—this appears to be the case here. Regarding the question of how milk and the other substances constitute the *bhairavakalpa*, this statement [is given]: "Therefore, the milk is that which originates from trees..."

The meaning is that *vārkṣa* refers to *maireya*. The same applies hereafter. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of using terms such as "milk-tree" (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) in the reverse order, according to the maxim: "One should not state the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) without first stating the restatement (*anuvāda*).
As for *odana*, it arises from rice grains; therefore, even for a Śūdra, liquor (*āsava*) alone [is used] in place of *odana*.

The meaning is that rice cooked separately (*pṛthagodana*) and fermented liquor (*āsava*) should not be given by Brāhmaṇas and others. This is because of the written statement and because of such Smṛti texts as: "Raw food [given] by the hand of a Śūdra is called 'cooked food' (if prepared by him), and cooked food is called 'leftover' (*ucchiṣṭa*). etc.

Nor should it be argued that because the curse of Śukra pertains specifically to Brāhmaṇas, the injunction for its removal from wine is untenable; for since it is established by scripture that even a Śūdra always possesses the qualification [for this rite], the liberation from Śukra’s curse serves a transcendental (adṛṣṭa) purpose.

Furthermore, by the following passage: "Moreover, in cases such as 'one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse,' just as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) prevails over indicative mark (*liṅga*), so too—by parity of reasoning—the directly stated prohibitive injunction, such as 'a Brāhmaṇa having given liquor,' prevails over the injunction for the gift of *maireya* liquor which is to be inferred from the [context of] the release from a curse. Thus ends the writing.
The Nṛsiṃha Paṇḍitas have strengthened their thesis that [the *jīvanmukti*] pertains only to those other than Brāhmaṇas;

however, that is extremely weak. For instance, they have cited the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*, "by means of *sāttvika* substances," as a proof for their own position. This is based on a complete lack of critical investigation. As for *sāttvika* substance...

A name such as "vrīhi" (rice) and so forth is not something established by worldly convention alone. Therefore, when there arises the inquiry, "What is that *sāttvika* substance?", the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *sāttvika* is to be understood solely through the scripture, just as the rules of grammar govern the relationship between base and suffix. That scripture is found in the *Tripurārṇava*:
Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī—these are declared to be the three kinds of intoxicating substances.
That which is produced from sugarcane juice or honey is Gauḍī; it is remembered as being of the nature of Sattva.
O Śivā, that which is produced from madhūka flowers, grapes, palm trees, and so forth, is celebrated by the knowers as *mādhvī*; it is of the nature of *rajas*.
"That which is made from ground rice flour is known as *tāmasī* and nourishing (*pauṣṭikī*);
that which is known for the Brāhmaṇa is *sāttvikī*, while that for the King (Kṣatriya) and the Vaiśya is *rājasī*. Thus it is said.

This being the case, we certainly conclude that the proposition in the scripture—that [the rule] pertains to those other than Brāhmaṇas—is rooted in ignorance. Likewise, one should know that which is found in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "One should not [drink] coconut water from a bronze vessel."
Having prescribed the rule regarding primary substances and their substitutes for rites performed by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas,

and having established an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the aforementioned substances for rites performed by Brāhmaṇas, it is stated as a supplementary part of that exclusion: "By offering [the substance] in this manner alone, a Brāhmaṇa would become short-lived."
He praises by means of censure in the form of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*): "How could this statement be effective for you?"

Nor should it be argued that the exclusion of Brahmins and others as agents occurs simply by virtue of [the injunction] having Kṣatriyas and others as its agents— just as the exclusion of wheat occurs through the restriction to rice— and consequently, how could such [an agent] be obtained in a performance by a Brahmin, or how could there be an exclusive specification (parisaṅkhyā) for the purpose of excluding him? For the example is dissimilar.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is untenable without a substance; thus, by way of this objection, when rice (vrīhi) is obtained as a possible option—just like other substances—the rule is established that "it must be rice alone. By that much, since the Darśapūrṇamāsa no longer has a requirement for another substance, the exclusion of others follows as a matter of course (*ārthika*). This applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Although there is no expectancy for a substance in a performance carried out by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya due to the restrictive rule regarding substitutes,

since such expectancy for a substance exists when the performer is a Brāhmaṇa, this [rule] is appropriately a preclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) because it applies even in that case; therefore, the fulfillment of the proposition is like the birth of a son from a eunuch.

Furthermore, the citation from the *Bhairavītantra* stating, "Brāhmaṇas are to be satisfied with milk," which was written as an authoritative proof, is merely a deception of the ignorant; for in the *Bhairavītantra* itself, immediately following this statement, the substances such as milk are determined by the phrase, "Milk is that which arises from trees. As for that [other] milk...

If one takes the phrase "produced from a tree" (*vṛkṣasamudbhūta*) to mean that its milk performs the function of being produced from a tree, and thus concludes that the function of being produced from a tree— namely, satiation— is enjoined with respect to milk which is already well-known, that is incorrect.
For does the meaning of the three words beginning with "produced from a tree" consist in a general substance (*dravyasāmānya*), or in a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*)?

In the first case, because the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—which consists of the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) in the form of "being produced from a tree"—is sublated with respect to that which is delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*), there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the general [meaning] for that which is capable of denoting the specific. This being so, there is an abandonment of the literal denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) as it is heard; for by the word "produced from a tree" itself, [the term applies] to clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like.
If [the injunction] were possible, there would be the redundancy of words such as "tat-phala" (that fruit) and so on, which have the same meaning.

In the second alternative—that the word "vṛkṣasamudbhava" (produced from a tree) refers to a specific substance—the effect of that specific substance is enjoined in the milk. Is that [effect] something perceived, or is it a means to an unperceived result?

A scriptural function is enjoined. In the first case, the injunction would be purposeless, since [the requirement] can be known from common worldly practice itself. In the second case, just as in the instance "the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," the function performed by the scriptural rule "one should tether the animal to the sacrificial post" is enjoined for the threshing-floor post; so too [is it here].

Is that which is already obtained through another scripture being enjoined, or is that which is not obtained through another scripture being enjoined? In the first case, since the effects of being produced from a tree—such as the satiation [of ancestors] with milk—are already secured by the statement "milk is produced from a tree," the scriptural injunction "Brāhmaṇas should be satiated with milk" would be redundant; for indeed...
