Having stated, "The threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," it is separately enjoined that "one should tether the animal to the threshing-floor post. This would be an injunction for something whose purpose is not otherwise established; likewise, it would follow that even things such as the son of a barren woman could be enjoined as performing the duties of a husband and wife. In my view, however, [the injunction] is: "Brāhmaṇas are to be satisfied with milk."

The rule regarding the substances for the *tarpaṇa* rite serves as an indicator of a specific intended meaning, overriding the conventional sense of the word "milk" (*kṣīra*) by stating that "milk is that which is produced from trees. Thus, there is no redundancy whatsoever, nor is there even a scent of inconsistency. Even though...

Since it lacks injunctive force (*vidhāyakatva*), its purposelessness (*vaiyyarthya*) must be assumed. Nevertheless, [in the passage] "He offers the eight-potherd cake to Agni; [he offers] that which belongs to Soma..."

Having prescribed eight oblations beginning with the *caru* in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice, the designation "Vaiśvadeva" was applied to the entire collection by the injunction, "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva. Consequently, in the rule "In spring, one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," when the Viśvedeva sacrifice alone would otherwise be understood as the rite to be performed in spring, that [previous understanding] is set aside by this new designation.

It is stated in the Jaimini-tantra that a statement is purposeful when it brings about the accomplishment of the eight types of sacrifice; thus, it ought to be purposeful. And it is not the case that one should employ the word *kṣīra* (milk), which is already extremely well-established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and then abandon that conventional power.
It should not be said that such an alternative explanation has never been seen anywhere; for it is stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"One whose death is imminent shall not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, nor likewise the constellation of the Seven Sages... [and so forth].

Having first stated this, Arundhatī herself explained it by saying "the tip of the nose," and so forth. There are hundreds of such instances; however, no more has been written here for lack of necessity.

In this statement, regarding the fourth quarter [of the verse], the phrase "āsava derived from rice" (*taṇḍulodbhavam*) is also indicative of that which is derived from flour (*piṣṭodbhava*). As stated in the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra*:
"O Maheśvarī, milk, clarified butter, honey, and likewise āsava..."
The wise should understand that [these] arise respectively from the powder of tree bark and flowers.

In this regard, since the convention of "āsava" has been established even for that which is made from flour (*paiṣṭa*), by this [argument] the entire passage stating that "in the view of the opponent,

the reason consisting of the insertion of a staff would result in the erroneous application of terms such as 'milk-tree' (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) in the opposite sense, because the subject to be restated (*anuvādya*) has not been stated as a proof for that" is refuted.

Because it is described as being that which apprehends the specific meaning and the intended purport (*tātparya*), there is not even a trace here of the relationship between the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheyabhāva*). For this very reason, in the section on Names (*nāmadheya-pāda*), it is held that in the case of "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the name itself lacks inherent authority regarding Dharma because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*); rather, [its authority is derivative].
It is established in the authoritative treatises that the Veda belongs to the officiating priests because it serves as a reminder of the rules for their performance.

Or, let it be granted for the sake of pleasing others that the designation "milk" is prescribed with reference to what is produced from a tree, even though it is not sanctioned by the scriptures; nevertheless, the punishment cast upon this view by the opponent is unbearable. For that imposition of punishment is based on the established pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever is first mentioned [is the primary]," yet that [pervasion] is unproven.

Because there are hundreds of instances of deviation [in the Veda], such as "He offers with curd," "Those who are sacrificers are the officiating priests," and "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu. If it is asked, "What then is the status of the authoritative statement that 'one should not state the subject (anuvādya) without [first stating] the predicate'?
[the answer is: in the absence of a subverting factor, that which is mentioned first generally becomes the subject (uddeśya).

His intention is as follows: in the present context, regarding milk, the injunction that it "originates from a tree" is itself a contradiction due to its utter futility. How was this not understood by the opponent? Similarly, when one asserts that the word "rice-originated" in the phrase "liquor originates from rice" has "cooked rice" as its meaning—

By writing that raw food belongs to a Śūdra because it is the means of accomplishing that [cooked food], he became an object of ridicule even for children. By this [it is shown] that... (Laghustavaratna, p.

The argument regarding the status of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*) has been set aside, because terms such as "milk" (*kṣīra*) and so forth are understood there in their conventional sense. As for the claim that the direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), "A Brāhmaṇa, having given wine," possesses greater authority than the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the release from Śukra’s curse—that too is trivial; for indeed, [the text does not say] "a Brāhmaṇa... [but rather "one who is a Brāhmaṇa"].

In the statement, "By giving liquor, one falls from the very status of a Brāhmaṇa," there is the hearing of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sense of prohibition; however, the injunction is to be inferred through the censure of the act of giving liquor. Thus, we do not know what answer one who asserts that this [injunction] is a direct scriptural revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) would give in the assembly of the learned. And so it is.

Without providing a solution for the literal scriptural statement found in the *kulācāra* (family tradition) regarding the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice— which includes the liberation from Śukra’s curse, stating that "a Brāhmaṇa should drink *surā*"— you merely assert with your own mouth that it refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas, [applying this to] all others.
One who generates delusion [regarding this] should be considered as excluded from the Tantras.

And thus, this systematic arrangement of the statements—namely, that in the passage "by means of a sattvic substance" (*dravyeṇa sāttvikena*), the arrangement of the statement from the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* found in the *Laghustava*, "the Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk" (*kṣīreṇa brāhmaṇais tarpyāḥ*)—has been shown. Likewise, as for the statement from the *Bhairavītantra*: "the Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk."

And as for that which is stated sequentially in the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra* by the Brāhmaṇas and others with milk, clarified butter, honey, and fermented liquor [or honey and flour-based substances],
and as for the statement in the *Laghustava*, because those are of a general nature, they are authoritative in light of the statement in the *Yāmala*.

The concluding summary here is: "Successively with the four substances consisting of milk, ghee, honey, and flour. And thus, since milk and the other substances are always obtained without distinction through the *Bhairavī* and other Tantras, the statement from the *Yāmala* serves to effect a restriction, specifying particular substances like milk for particular times and particular performers. As for that which...

"A Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with sattvic substances while she resides in the ocean of knowledge"— since this statement from the *Yāmala* does not permit restriction because the term "milk" (*kṣīra*) refers to sattvic substances such as sugarcane juice and honey, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the performance by a Brāhmaṇa practitioner throughout the four ages.

It is attained. Thus, by the statement "the *rājasī* belongs to the king and the merchant," it is proclaimed by the experts that when the ritual is performed by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the wine produced from the *madhūka* flower, grapes, the palmyra palm, and so forth, is called *mādhvī*. O Śivā, that is the *rājasī* [as stated in the fourth chapter].
It should be placed at the foot.
Thus, by this explanation, since the substances whose nature is as previously stated are always available,

the designation "milk" and so forth does not apply to a collection of these aforementioned items; rather, it applies when a substance whose nature is bark— suitable for a Kṣatriya— is available in the Kṛta Yuga, even if that substance is of the nature of grapes and the like.

There is an option regarding attainment. Since the two statements concerning the Śūdra are of a single form, there is no option once [the rite] has been performed. In the same way, one should infer for oneself the appropriate application for the Tretā and other ages. In the Kali age, for a Brāhmaṇa, [the consumption of] sugarcane juice and honey is established by the words of the Jñānārṇava and Tripurārṇava.
"In the Kali age, she is to be worshipped by all castes with *āsava* alone. This being so:
"In the Kṛta age, O Dear One, she is to be worshipped by Śūdras with manifest *āsava*;
in the Tretā, by Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and in the Dvāpara age, by kings and others."
In the Kali age, O Great Goddess, she is worshipped by Brahmins and others.

If the statement from the *Rahasyārṇava*—“p. 129)” —is applicable, then, by means of the words “other than [those for] the Kṛta [age],” a distinction regarding substances other than [the standard ones] is established for all castes; furthermore, by the statement of the *Rahasyārṇava*, there is also an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) for anyone other than a Śūdra.

That being the case, when the three castes have performed [the rite], there is an option regarding the perceptible substance. Alternatively, even in the *Rahasyārṇava*, in a performance by a Śūdra associated with the Kṛta Yuga, an *āsava* (fermented liquor) having rice as its primary material is prescribed. Thus, through another tantra, the attainment of *āsava* for the Śūdra is established.
The assumption that this is a *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) out of fear of redundancy (*vaiyyarthya*) is not to be trusted.

If that were the case, since a substance is required for a rite performed by a Brāhmaṇa or others, milk and so forth should be taken from another ritual manual (*tantra*); there would be no option (*vikalpa*). In the same way, there is the statement from the *Rahasyārṇava* regarding the *tretā* fire.

It prescribes *āsava* for both Śūdras and Vaiśyas. That being the case, by this [text], *āsava* is obtained for the Vaiśya; and by the statement of the *Yāmala*, clarified butter (*dhṛta*) is obtained. Here, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Thus, in the Dvāpara age, there is an option between *āsava* and honey (*madhu*) for both Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas according to the two cited statements. However, in the Kali age, it is for both [classes].

Since there is no contradiction due to their being of a single nature, this alone is indeed the case; it is logical that this is the correct position, not the position of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*). And thus, in the statement from the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, "where it is necessarily specified," the phrase "in the absence of the primary" (*mukhyālābhe*) must be supplied. [This applies] when the primary is unavailable.

The meaning of that [statement] is that a Brāhmaṇa should place honey in a copper vessel in its place. This being the case, it contradicts the statement from the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "In the case of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, it is thus; but never for a twice-born [Brāhmaṇa] in copper. Thus, because the two statements possess equal force, an option (*vikalpa*) cannot be avoided.
Even in the view of the opponent.

As for the statement from the *Haṃsamāheśvaratantra* [Haṃsapārameśvara-ba 1], "A Brāhmaṇa who gives liquor falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa," if that were situated in that tantra near the rules regarding family substances (*kuladravya*) for Kṣatriyas and others, then it would be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) supplementary to them— just as [the statement] "others are non-animals" [is supplementary to the rule concerning cows].

It is like the expression *aśvebhyaḥ* (from horses). If it were not in proximity to that [term], then it would refer to a Brāhmaṇa who has not conquered his senses, because the prohibition against giving wealth to such a person will be stated later. As for the statement from the *Kulārṇava*, "It should never be drunk by Brāhmaṇas," one must apply elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *a* [to read it as *na peyam*] regarding this [rule].

The opponent's intention is that a prohibition has been made for Brahmins because they are intent upon the supreme human goals (puruṣārtha). This is because of the writing of reasons for such prohibitions, such as the impossibility of a Kṣatriya engaging in battle when he is incapacitated at the time of combat;
and this [prohibition] is indeed acceptable to us.

We also maintain that a Brāhmaṇa has no right to accept wealth beyond what is required for the sacrificial rite (*kratvartha*). Furthermore, the prohibition against taking up liquor (*surāgraha*) during the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice in the Kali age, as stated by Harinātha, is also acceptable to us;
however, such a prohibition does not extend to the family tradition (*kulācāra*).
The status of being a *sautrāmaṇi* sacrifice associated with the Kali age is the delimiting factor for the object of the prohibition against liquor;

since the family custom (*kulācāra*) is not pervaded by that [delimiting factor], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in its inclusion under the *kaimutika-nyāya*. Therefore, as there is not even a trace of the objections raised by others regarding the case of Brāhmaṇas, [the practice is valid].

Since [the practice] has been demonstrated for a thousand practitioners, for one who accepts the authority of the Tantra, the primary preference for worship performed by Brāhmaṇas and others is established by scripture; and that [preference], even for a Brāhmaṇa, cannot be abandoned. And thus—
Without the perfuming of the substances, O Dear One, one should neither meditate nor recite;
O Great Goddess, for those who do so, there is suffering at every step.
There is no mantra without liquor, nor is there liquor without mantra.
Thus, in the Kulārṇava, it is said:
"Without wine and meat, worship shall be fruitless."
Thus, O Maheśvarī, in the conduct of the observance (samayācāra), having tasted [the substance] without a valid reason and being possessed by agitation,
one should perform neither worship nor recitation, neither meditation nor reflection.
Thus, in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
"He who performs my worship without wine (ali) and meat (piśita) shall become a bringer of suffering and a beast for the Yoginīs."
Thus, in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Whoever performs your worship devoid of the primary substances shall be consumed by your wrath and reduced to ashes; it cannot be otherwise."
Thus it is established in the *Samayāṅgamātṛkā*: such statements as these are supported.

Furthermore, when examined with an unartificial mind, it appears that the portion ending with "and [the text] other than the Brāhmaṇas is supreme" is impure. Let impartial scholars investigate further than this.
This very point is established in the commentary on the seventh mantra of the *Tripuropaniṣad*: "Having understood this, the wise rejoice."

As for that which was established by us in the *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*— having first asserted our own settled position— that the eligibility of Brāhmaṇas was proven on the grounds that since consecration with Vedic mantras is prescribed, there would be no scope for it if the rite were intended for the worship of Śūdras, and thus the injunction would result in being rendered purposeless; that [is now addressed].

However, that [interpretation] is extremely weak. In the case of the statement, "A chariot-maker (rathakāra) should perform the fire-consecration (ādhāna) during the rainy season," the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) sets aside the etymological derivation (*yoga*), thereby establishing the eligibility for the consecration for one born of a mixed caste (*saṅkara-jāti*).

Subsequently, it is inferred that he must also study the Veda required for that rite; thus, by the logic of the sixth book (*ṣāṣṭha-nyāya*), the eligibility of the Śūdra is established through reasoning regarding the recitation of Vedic mantras.
Because, as long as [the means] are employed, the authority is unavoidable; for this reason, what one desires is not established by this [authority].

Up to this point, the determination of eligibility (*adhikāra*) has been established for the Brāhmaṇa. Even though this eligibility has been so established, it does not apply to everyone; rather, does it apply only to one who has conquered the senses and is free from desire and the like? For this very reason, it is said in the *Paramānandatantra*:
But this, O Great Goddess, is the supreme Kaula path,
which is rightly equal to the vow of walking on the edge of a sword, for it has the restraint of the mind as its cause.

"O Supreme Goddess, for one whose mind is steady, [this practice] is easily attained, fruitful, and bestows swift success; for another, it would be fruitless and a cause of suffering. Thus [it is said].
In the Tripurārṇava as well:
"This is the supreme dharma spoken by Śiva, which bestows the attainment of happiness."
It is easily attained by one who has conquered the senses, but not by another even in infinite births.
It is sufficient to produce delusion in an instant, merely by being remembered, even for those of perpetual celibacy who have renounced everything and dwell in no fixed abode.
For this very reason, all of this has been declared here as the cause for attaining perfection:
from this [side] wine, from that meat, and likewise various kinds of food.
There, among young women richly adorned with beautiful attire, their eyes rolling from intoxication,
it is indeed exceedingly difficult to maintain self-restraint of the mind in every respect.
"O Goddess, how could this belong to one who is devoid of devotion and faith? Thus [it is said].
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Because the tantras are extremely profound, their true nature is also strictly concealed.
[The practitioner should be] a Brahmin who knows the essential truth of the meaning of the Vedic scriptures, who is intelligent and self-controlled."
"One who is capable of extracting the meaning of the hidden tantras through churning shall be an authority on the Kaula path; any other shall be a partaker of suffering. Thus it is said.
In the Kulārṇava: "That liquor which, when consumed during the day, might even delude the gods—
that auspicious maireya, having drunk it, the man who does not undergo transformation [is a true devotee]."
"Having become devoted to Śiva in Japan, he was liberated, as was that Kaulika. Thus [it is said].

Even by the Blessed Paraśurāma, in the Kaula tradition, as the primary duty, it was stated: "The avoidance of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, unenjoined violence, theft, that which is contrary to the world, and that which is loathed by the world. [This sūtra spoken by the Blessed One is found on page 33, section 19 of the latter part.]

This has been established. Therefore, just as only those with sight have the qualification for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices according to the requirements of the auxiliary rites such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), and not the blind,
so too only one who has conquered the senses has the qualification according to the requirements of the auxiliaries such as the avoidance of desire, anger, and so forth, and no other.
This is the intention of the author of the Sūtra. Similarly, many such statements are found in other tantras as well;
however, they have not been written here because they serve no further purpose and for fear of making the work too voluminous.

Nowadays, those who have not conquered their senses, whose tongues are fickle, who are devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, and who— blinded by passion for women— assume the status of Kaulas, are greedy for mere material wealth;
disregarding written words and without considering their own authority, they act only to fulfill their own desires.

Having disregarded such statements from the *Kulārṇava* as "having drunk, having drunk again, having drunk," [one should drink] the substance up to the throat, those who— whether ignorant of its true intent or knowing it—
are yet deceivers, practice according to their own whims.

They act [thus], yet they do not find happiness anywhere, either here or in the hereafter; on the contrary, by the command of the illustrious Dharmarāja, they surely undergo the torments produced by their great transgressions. There is no doubt in this matter.
There is doubt. Such fallen persons should not be remembered in tantric assemblies;
for this very reason, even a detailed mockery of such Kaulikas has been made in the *Prabodhacandrodaya*.
Therefore, at the commencement [of practice], [only] those who have conquered their senses, who possess devotion and faith, and who are learned [should be admitted].

Only those who have ascended to the stages of devotion (*bhakti-bhūmikā*) already described here possess the qualification (*adhikāra*); for others, [such practice] leads only to downfall. Enough of this elaboration. The truth is that for those other than the qualified persons mentioned, the worship of Viṣṇu and others is according to the purely Vedic path alone.
The distinction between the Right-hand (dakṣiṇa) and Left-hand (vāma) practices is as follows:

having entered the Kula path, those who have not conquered their senses should perform worship using only water and such items; this is the Right-hand path. Those who have conquered their senses should perform the ritual service with the substances prescribed [in the scriptures]; this is the Left-hand practice.
Someone [objects]: "That is trivial, because he has not even understood the meaning of the term *vāmācāra*. And so it is said in the *Trikūṭārahasya*:
"O Dear One, I shall explain *vāmācāra*, the practice for the realization of Śrīvidyā."
By performing which, a practitioner of mantras will quickly become a possessor of supernatural powers in the Kali age.
A garland made from human teeth, a skull-cup as a vessel,
a seat such as a lion skin, and a bracelet fashioned from a woman's hair.
Beginning with these words, [the matter] has been described in detail. Among those [descriptions], even the name of the primary substance does not appear.

However, that detailed account was elaborated at length by our supreme preceptors during the occasion of explaining the name *Lalitā*—specifically, in the context of [the goddesses] situated on the paths of the left (*savya*) and right (*apasavya*). Those who desire to know the particulars [should consult that].
Therefore, it should be understood [from this]. Likewise, it is also stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, I do not expand upon it here.
One who has not conquered their senses has no authority in the Kaula path;

as for what is stated in the *Paramānandatantra-ṭippaṇī* regarding the worship of those with unconquered senses using scented water, that is incorrect, for a secondary alternative is permitted only when the primary method is unavailable, and never otherwise.

Because this contradicts the statement in the twentieth chapter of the *Paramānanda Tantra*— for it would be as impossible as a hare's horn for one who lacks authority over the primary [practice] to have authority over a substitute— therefore, for those who have not conquered their senses,
if there is a desire for worship at first sight, they should perform the worship of another deity by means of another path, and by that...
Having ascertained that one's inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is fully ripened and firm, one should thereafter take refuge in the Kaula path. As it is said in the *Kulasāra*:
"From the repeated service of other deities..."
"A person whose mind is fully matured and who has attained authoritative knowledge in the Kaula [tradition] should enter here after restraining the external senses; no one else. Thus it is said.
Also in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Only for one who has not uttered the names of other deities throughout ten million births does faith arise in the utterance of the name of the Illustrious Goddess."
"Just as one becomes a worshiper of the Śrīvidyā in one's final birth, so too should the recitation of the *Nāmasāhasra* be performed in one's final birth. (p. 133)
In the Yāmala as well:
"Having realized that the mind has been purified through the performance of rituals prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti over many births, one should become a worshipper of Śrīvidyā."
In the *Pheṭkāra-tantra* it is also said: "This vidyā must be kept secret in every way from those who have not conquered their senses;
therefore, this vidyā is powerful, but it would not be a vidyā if it were made public."
"The family flower, the family substance, the family worship, and the family recitation—these should not be disclosed to such persons if one desires one's own welfare. [Siddhi-śrī] Thus it is said.
Even the sacred teaching is forbidden for one who has not conquered the senses; what need is there to mention its acceptance?
Therefore, one who has not conquered the senses has no qualification for the Kaula path; enough of this excessive detail. || 31 ||
This is the purification of the arghya; may there be auspiciousness. || 31 ||
Thus ends the third section, named the Śrīkrama, in the Kalpasūtra.
This refers to the performance of the mandala and so forth, which is stated to be done with that water following the purification of the general *arghya*;

the ritual action beginning from that point up to the end of "one should offer oblations into the Kuṇḍalinī" constitutes the purification of the *arghya*, that is, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *arghya*. Although this was already established by the prescription of the entire collection of rites in the previously mentioned sūtra, [it is stated here again for clarity].

Although it can be understood that this refers to the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *arghya* offering, it appears more appropriate to read the word as *saṃskārān* (the plural), referring to several consecrations such as the removal of curses (*śāpavimocana*).
Furthermore, upon the repetition of the *sūtra*, that which is to be purified must be indicated.
"And the remaining space [should be filled] up to the first [line] from the temple. (Thus ends the third section—Śrī:
Some might mistakenly take other vessels; so that this may not happen, the supremely compassionate Paraśurāma composed this aphorism for the purpose of removing such confusion. This...
The meaning is that purification is exactly as described and nothing else. By the word "śivam," the conclusion of the section on the *arghya* offering is indicated.

In the *Nibandha*, regarding the purification of the special *arghya* during the mandala worship, the worship of the center with the *vidyā* was prescribed in the *sūtra*, yet that has been omitted here. Furthermore, the following have not been mentioned: the drawing of the fourth vowel, the mantra "hrīṃ mahālakṣmīśvarī," the worship of the goddess Sudhā, and so forth, ending with the offering of flowers by means of the *gālinī* mudrā.
It is included. Since there is no authoritative evidence for it here, that which is composed merely by one's own intellect is not to be accepted. || 31 ||
Thus ends the third section, named the Śrīkrama, in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.
The Fourth Section: The Lalitākrama.
Regarding the invocation of the Supreme Consciousness (paraciti) into the Śrīcakra:
he begins by demonstrating the method of invoking the deity who resides within the heart into the Śrīcakra.
Then, having caused that primordial consciousness— which resides in the heart-center, which is skilled in piercing the forest of lotuses within the *suṣumṇā*,

which has dispelled the darkness of delusion, and which is the radiance of the lamp of Śiva— to emerge through the nostril, he placed her, whose body was assumed at will, upon the crest of the *trikhaṇḍa-mudrā*.
The extraction of the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* is to be seen in the context of Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15/8–11; [having brought it] into the hand in the *Kusumāñjali*: || 1 ||

The word *atha* indicates a specific sequence, as in the expressions "then [from] the tongue" or "then [from] the chest. Alternatively, it indicates the conclusion of the preceding section. The heart-wheel (*hṛccakra*) is the Unstruck (*anāhata*); it is also conventionally referred to as the "small space" (*dahara*). It is situated there; in the scriptures, that very place is well known as the abode where the deity resides.
And so says the Śruti: "Therein is a small ether, free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon.

Also, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Situated within the lotus of the heart. Therefore, the heart-cakra is the dwelling place of the deity. For one residing there, worship with external offerings is not possible.

Therefore, this qualification should be understood as intended to indicate that it is a permanent location, for the purpose of bringing [the consciousness] out from that place; for the Suṣumṇā also [extends] from the Mūlādhāra to the lotuses situated within the Brahma-randhra.
There is a specific channel (nāḍī) in the form of a staff that serves as the support for the interconnection [of the channels]. As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"That which is celebrated everywhere by the supreme sages as Suṣumṇā is proclaimed to be the support of the wheels (cakras) of the body, beginning from the base."
Thus [it is said]. Regarding that [forest], those lotuses which are the "purities" (*viśuddhi*) and so forth constitute a forest—a difficult path.
The "piercing" (*nirbhedana*) of that [forest] is the preparation of a path conducive for coming and going; she is skilled (*kuśalām*) in that regard.
By this qualification, [it is implied that she is skilled] in the process of returning from the heart to the *Śrīcakra* and other such locations after the completion of worship.

The absence of effort is indicated. Regarding the word *nirastā*: that by which delusion (*moha*), which is ignorance (*ajñāna*), has been cast away—that is, dispelled—is like darkness; she is such [a one]. To strengthen the meaning of this epithet, he states another qualification: *śiva*. She is the radiance, the nature of light, of the lamp whose essence is Śiva. By this—

By the statement that [Śiva] has the nature of light, as expressed by the preceding qualification, it is implied that his destruction of the darkness of ignorance is easily established. Furthermore, just as there is an inseparable relationship between a lamp and its light, so too is there an inseparable relationship between Śiva and Śakti.
This very point has been clearly stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Śakti is triangular in form, and the supreme Śiva is the form of the Bindu;
therefore, there is a relationship of inseparable concomitance between the Bindu and the triangle."
In the Śrīdevībhāgavata as well:
"In whatever substratum a certain property exists as inseparable,"
"That subject (dharmin) shall be of the nature of Śiva, while the attribute (dharma) assumes the form of Śakti. Thus [it is said].

In the investigation of reality, it has already been explained previously [in the third section on "Non-concomitance," page 92, in the *Śrīkrama*, in the commentary on Sūtra 9] that the difference between these two entities is adventitious and not real;
this is the meaning. Carrying the first consciousness—the undivided consciousness—through whichever nostril, one...

The breath exits through the nostril without effort; having caused it to exit by that path, one should perform an activity conducive to its exit. In this context, such an activity is precisely the mental visualization of exiting from the seat of the heart by the aforementioned path. The subsequent activity—

"She assumes a form through sport" (līleti). This refers to her who has assumed—that is, accepted—a body by mere sport, that is, by her own will alone, as described in the verse of meditation (*dhyānaśloka*). By this, it is indicated that, unlike other bodies, she has assumed a beautiful form for the sake of favoring her devotees without the necessity of dwelling in a womb. And it is said in the *Gītā*: [text follows]
"Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata,
and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself. (Śrī Bhagavadgītā,
Chapter 4, Verse 7)

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as well: "Whenever there shall be an affliction arising from the Dānavas, at each such time I shall descend and effect the destruction of the enemies. (Śrī Saptaśatī, Chapter 12)
The final verse.

Having assumed that form, she is the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* (this *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* is to be seen in the context of *Dvi. Pa. Śi.* 15.8–11). She is called *trikhaṇḍā* because she shatters (*khaṇḍayati*) the three—namely birth, death, and old age—or else the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; the meaning is that she bestows absolute liberation alone. Or else:
The three sections (*khaṇḍas*) are the *kalās* consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). That whose nature consists of these is the Three-sectioned (*trikhaṇḍā*).
As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*:
"When that consciousness, Ambikā, consists of the three *kalās*, she is called Mudrā."
"Having assumed a three-part form, she is eternally present;
she is proclaimed to be the pervader of the entire king of wheels. Thus [it is said].
And the meaning of the term *mudrā* is as follows: it is called *mudrā* because it gladdens (*modana*) and dissolves (*drāvaṇa*) the universe. As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*:
"When there is the manifestation and reflective awareness of the universe upon the wall of the conscious self..."
She acts according to her own will, endowed with the full desire to create.
The power of action (kriyā-śakti), moreover, [is so called] because it gladdens and dissolves the universe.
"O Goddess, this is called Mudrā... || Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: when the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), by its own will, performs the acts of illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*amarśana*) after the act of vision (*īkṣaṇa*) upon the wall that is non-different from its own self— desiring full transformations— this...

The state (*bhāva*) of the world consists of the six transformations of being: "it exists," "it is born," "it grows," "it transforms," "it wanes," and "it perishes. Among these, the second transformation is *prakāśa* (illumination), because its characteristic is the manifestation of clarity; the third transformation is *āmarśana* (self-awareness), because its characteristic is the state of becoming heart-pleasing through the thought "this is that. And thus:

After Tripurasundarī has reflected upon the existence of the creation residing within her own heart, there arises in her a will directed toward the second and subsequent transformations of the universe; this is the desire to create (*vicikīrṣā*). Thereafter, she acts through the sequence of the production and growth of the universe. These two are precisely the aforementioned *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

Consciousness (*cit*) characterized by such will and form is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). This power of action is a *mudrā* because it rejoices in and dissolves the creation and growth performed by Tripurasundarī.
Rejoicing (*anumodana*) means being favorable toward an action performed by an agent distinct from oneself. Dissolving (*drāvaṇa*) refers to [the dissolution] of that which is dense.

Expansion (*prasara*) consists of bringing about a state of relaxation in the limbs of that which was contracted. This very power of action, through its coexistence with the state of being a seal (*mudrātva*) in its own function, becomes three-partite (*trikalāmayī*) and three-segmented (*trikhaṇḍā*) by merging with the gaze (*īkṣaṇa*) and other [faculties]; such is the meaning of the supreme secret. Therefore, this pervasive power (*vyāpikā*) is the most excellent of all.

The application (*viniyoga*) of this *mudrā* has been established for its invocation (*āvāhana*). Such a *mudrā* is described here in its invisible form (*adṛṣṭa-svarūpa*). Its visible form (*dṛṣṭa-svarūpa*), however, is seen to consist of various types of finger-interlacing according to different *tantras*. It is not seen in this [text]. Therefore—

Having unified the meaning of the Tantra as understood through the lineage of the Gurus, it is clarified hereafter. Having brought together and grasped in his hand that which is characterized by such an external form consisting of three parts—a joined palms (*añjali*) bound with a crest-lock (*śikhaṇḍita*), strung together, and adorned with flowers—[he offers it]. || 1 ||

Having uttered "Māyā-lakṣmī Parā" and the name of the Goddess, one should perform the ritual assignment with "I fashion [thee] as the embodiment of nectar and consciousness; obeisance. Thus having fashioned [her], || 2 ||

*Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *Śrīṃ*—this is the meaning of the word *Lakṣmī*; *Parā* is *Sauḥ*. The authorities regarding this matter have already been shown previously. Having thus uttered the three seed-syllables (*bīja*), the name of the Goddess—the sole sovereign of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*)—is *Lalitāyāḥ*, ending in the genitive case as is appropriate. Then...
One should recite [the mantra] ending with "namas" without modification. Thus, at the beginning, there is the threefold Tārā (tritārī) obtained through the common technical rules:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ*. Then follows: *śakticakraikanāyikāyāḥ amṛtacaitanyamūrtiṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*. This mantra consists of thirty-three syllables. By means of this—
Having fashioned and meditated upon the form of the Supreme Deity.

In this case, since it would be redundant to again conceive a form for that which already possesses a body assumed through divine play (*līlā*) as stated in the preceding sūtra, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside by the stronger order of meaning (*arthakrama*). Thus, the sequence is as follows:
first, the conception of the form of pure consciousness alone by means of this mantra; thereafter, [the conception] of the form...
The distinction is this: the imagined [deity] exits through the path of the nostrils and is then brought into the hollowed palms of the hands filled with flowers. || 2 ||
Having uttered the speech joined with *hasa* (the syllable *h*), the sweet-toned *kalārī*, and also the fourteenth and sixteenth [vowels] joined with *hasa*,
[one should pray]: "O Mother, who dwells within the forest of great lotuses (*mahāpadmavana*), whose form is the bliss of the Cause (*kāraṇānanda-vigraha*),
who acts for the welfare of all beings, O Supreme Goddess, come, come!"
Thus, having invoked the supreme consciousness (paraciti) into the Baindava-cakra.

137) By the maxim "the inclusion of the whole" (samudāyagrahaṇa), which was stated previously in the section on grammatical assignment (nyāsa-prakaraṇa), there is the inclusion of the mere consonants alone in cases such as *has* and so forth, according to traditional usage (*sampradāya*). [The word *hṛsva*] is joined with *ha*, *sa*, and *ra*.

The word *vācam* is *hsraiṃ*. This collection of the letters *ka*, *la*, *ra*, *i*, and the nasal bindu, joined with *ha* and *sa*, is *hsklrīṃ*. Likewise, *ha*, *sa*, *ra*, the fourteenth vowel *au*, *ṣa* (the sixteenth consonant), and the visarga—these are the fourteenth (*ra*), the sixteenth (*ṣa*), and the visarga (*ḥ*) combined with *ha*, *sa*, and *ra*.

Having uttered "hsrauḥ" and recited [the mantra] as heard up to the end of "parameśvarī," one should invoke the Supreme Consciousness (paraciti) within the Bindu-cakra. As for the nature of the mantra: first is the Tritārī, followed by "hasraiṃ hsklrīṃ hsrauḥ."
O Mother, who dwells within the Mahāpadma forest, whose form is the bliss of the cause,
who acts for the welfare of all beings, O Supreme Goddess, come, come!
Thus, the mantra consists of thirty-eight syllables. It resides in that inner region which is the interior of the Great Lotus Forest (*mahāpadmavana*).
The nature of the Great Lotus is described in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"O Sage, listen attentively as I describe the site of the Lotus Forest."
There, within an interval of six yojanas, upon that ground inlaid with excellent jewels,
there are indeed great-stalked land-lotuses all around.
Regarding Setubandha, it is said that Mahāpadmavana is a multitude of thousand-petaled lotuses.

She is she whose very form (*vigraha*) is *kāraṇānanda*, which is unlimited bliss (*aparicchinnānanda*). Alternatively, *kāraṇa* means "first" (*prathama*); that which is born therein is *kāraṇaja*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born there. Thus, it is *kāraṇa*, and that is *ānanda*. Therefore, [the compound] is *kāraṇānanda*.

The remainder is as before; the remainder is clear. Alternatively, the ritual act of invocation (*āvāhana*) consists of drawing forth the light of consciousness externally, fashioning a limited form by means of the mantra, bringing it into the hand, and then, by means of the mantra, performing everything up to its placement upon the pedestal.

Since there is no obstacle to many ritual actions— beginning with the *avadāna* (cutting of portions) and ending with the *pradāna* (offering)— constituting a single *padārtha* (unit of action), it follows that wherever there is simultaneous worship (*tantra*) of various deities in rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*),
the performance according to sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) is established for that entire collection, because that collection constitutes a single *padārtha*.
This mantra serves as the means for such a partial invocation and for settling upon the seat.

The author of the Nibandha, however, has presented the procedure for the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) as stated in the Jñānārṇava, along with the mudrās for invocation and so forth; that [view] is not to be respected, due to a lack of authoritative evidence.

Regarding the procedure for the sixty-four offerings: one should perform the sixty-four offerings. All offering mantras should be preceded by the *tritārī* and concluded with *kalpayāmi namaḥ*. || 4 ||

By the phrase "sixty-four," there is an exclusion of any other form of worship—such as the sixteen-fold worship and so forth mentioned in other tantras—for those who follow this tantra. Now, is this a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*), a mandatory injunction (*niyama-vidhi*), or an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*)? Not the first, because [it would exclude something] by no one...

Because it is not eternally unobtained through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the second [type of injunction] is not applicable even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*) due to the absence of prior attainment. If it is argued that it must then be the third [type], we grant that as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nevertheless, in every respect, this is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); rather, regarding the aspect of metaphorical application (*upacāra*), it is original, while regarding the sixty-four aspects, it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). This is because, in an injunction for metaphorical application, the metaphors themselves are infinite.

In that regard, since various numbers are obtained, the number sixty-four is also obtained as an alternative. Nor should it be argued that by thus accepting a restrictive apūrva (unseen potency) for a single [act], there would be a confusion of injunctions; for such a consequence is accepted.

In the sentence "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," since both Agni and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are optionally obtained, there is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) regarding that portion, while it is an unprecedented injunction (*apūrva*) regarding the sacrifice itself; this is because such is observed. Nor is this a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*) by means of the subsequent sūtra, "Having prescribed the sixty-four metaphorical applications" (the sentence mentioned in the fifth sūtra immediately following).
It should not be said that "by this [is meant] the procedure for the ritual service (*upacāra*)," because if that were the case, the sixty-four words in this sūtra would be redundant.
Nor should it be suspected that the subsequent statement "sixty-four" is useless when this is so;
for, having restated the sixty-four services, it prescribes a specific sequence. In no way [does it refer to] the ritual service itself.
That [text] is the prescriber of the number; "one should perform" (kuryāt) is a clear injunctive suffix, and this very [text] is the prescriber of the ritual application qualified by that number.

Alternatively, since the sequence is established by the mere order of the recitation (*pāṭha*), it is impossible for the subsequent phrase "having performed the sixty-four offerings" to prescribe that sequence; therefore, the phrase "of those already prescribed," namely "having performed the sixty-four offerings," is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) in the form of a conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). The fruit of this, however, is found in another tantra.

There are certain offerings not included among the sixty-four mentioned, others besides those already stated; [this rule is] so that worship may not be performed with them, but rather, having conceived of them as substitutes, one should offer them by using the very name of the substance heard in the mantra.
And thus, when possible, worship should be performed with more than the aforementioned offerings. For this very reason:
In the Tripurārṇava it is said:
"If possible, one should worship with more than the aforementioned services."

This statement contains the very logic already explained. The purpose of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), not the exclusion of connection with something else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Therefore, its intent is simply that not even one [of the sixty-four] among the metaphorical offerings (*upacāra*) should be absent; it does not intend to exclude any further items. Consequently, regarding those in excess of these...
To whatever extent the occurrence of palanquins, elephants, horses, dances, and so forth is possible, conceptualization to that same extent should be understood as not contradicting the Sūtras.
In this context, the meaning of the term "service" (upacāra) is a specific pleasure produced by an imagined substance; the phrase "one should perform" means one should generate that [pleasure].
Nor should it be asked: "What kind of pleasure could arise for a deity who is eternally satisfied by the substance offered?

It is true that no pleasure arises in one who is eternally satisfied; nevertheless, just as there is the conceptualization of a limited body [for the deity], so too, by the conceptualization of pleasure within that body, there is simply the production of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) within one's own self.

However, through the imagined [form], there arises bliss for the Supreme Deity. For this very reason it is said in the *Śivamahimnaḥ-stotra*—[one should perhaps read the reading "atra mahimani" here]—"for the one who delights in his own Self, the mirage of sense-objects does not cause delusion.
For this same reason, in the mantra of ritual application (*upacāra-mantra*), the verb "I fashion" (*kalyayāmi*) alone has been employed. The remainder is quite clear.
Having recited the *tritārī*, one should perform, in sequence: "I offer water for the feet, *namaḥ*"; the removal of ornaments; anointing with fragrant oil; entry into the hall of purification;
sitting upon the jeweled throne in the bathing pavilion; rubbing with divine bathing unguents; and bathing in warm water.
Having performed a complete ablution with all the sacred waters poured from golden jars, having wiped himself dry with a washed cloth, and having put on a reddish silk garment; p. 139)
She puts on a dawn-colored upper garment, enters the pavilion for anointing, and sits upon a jeweled throne within that pavilion;
she then applies divine fragrances— sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, storax, musk, camphor, musk-pouch, gorocanā, and so forth— to her entire body.

For the mass of hair, black aloe-wood incense; for the head, a garland of seasonal flowers— primarily mallikā, mālatī, jātī, campaka, aśoka, śatapatra, pūga buds, punnāga, and kalhāra— as well as ornaments and entry into the pavilion.
Seating upon a jeweled throne in the pavilion of ornaments; a crown of fresh jewels; a crescent moon;
vermilion at the parting of the hair; a forehead jewel; black collyrium;
a pair of braids; a pair of jeweled earrings; a nose ornament; lac-dye for the lips; and the first of all ornaments.

In one hand: the *kanakacintāka* pendant, the *padaka*, the *mahāpadaka*, the pearl necklace (*muktāvali*), the single-string necklace (*ekāvali*), the *channavīra*, the four pairs of armlets (*keyūra*), the series of bracelets (*valayāvali*), the series of signet rings (*ūrmikāvali*),

the girdle (*kāñcīdāma*), the waist-cord (*kaṭisūtra*), the auspicious ornament (*saubhāgyābharaṇa*), the anklet (*pādakaṭaka*), the jeweled anklet (*ratnanūpura*), and the toe-ring (*pādāṅgulīyaka*).
In one hand a noose, in another hand a goad, in another hand a bow of sugarcanes, and in [another] hand flower-arrows;

[she wears] glorious ruby slippers; together with attendant deities dressed in attire identical to her own, she mounts the great wheel and sits upon the couch in the lap of Kāmeśvara, holding a goblet of nectar-wine.

Having performed the sixty-four services (upacāras) with the words: "I offer water for sipping (ācamanīya), a betel-roll with camphor (karpūra-vīṭikā), a joyful smile of blissful playfulness, the auspicious waving of lights (ārārtika), an umbrella, a pair of chowries, a mirror, a palm-leaf fan, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings (naivedya); obeisance," [he should proceed]. || 5 ||

In this context, although the three *tārās* are established by the general rule (*sāmānyaparibhāṣā*) alone, their re-specification indicates that they are constituent parts [of the mantra], just as in the case of the *Dīpanātha-mantra*. The remainder is clear. As for the actual form of the mantra, it is: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ pādyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*. The inclusion of the name [Lalitā] is not with the words "of Lalitā" (*lalitāyāḥ*), but rather through the insertion of the name itself.
Because there is an absence of proof.

The author of the *Nibandhana*, however, being ignorant of logic and acting according to his own whims, introduced the name [of the recipient] by his own arbitrary will. Nor should it be argued that [the compound] would be non-expressive because the recipient (*sampradāna*) is required as a factor (*kāraka*), yet there is no word denoting it.

Since the expectancy [of the sentence] is satisfied through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and since scholars of logic do not accept an elliptical word as being a constituent part of a mantra— otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to recite "I cut thee for food" (*iṣe tvā chinadmi*) and "I wipe thee for strength" (*ūrje tvā unmārjmi*) at the time of performance— the mantra is only that which is actually heard in the text. This is so even if it possesses the nature of a name (*nāmadheya*).

If it is thought that there is an entry by name, then the characteristic of a name-mantra (*nāmamantra*) is that it ends in *namaḥ* or ends in the dative case. In this regard, [the mantra] ending in the accusative case is not possible because of the intervention between [the deity and the word] *kalpayāmi*. This is the essential point. Furthermore, in all cases, for the ritual mantras (*upacāramantra*), [the formula is] *kalpayāmi namaḥ*.
Since the matter is already established by this very [preceding statement], the sūtra "having uttered the *tritārī*" (p.
140), being otherwise redundant, serves to establish the actual nature of the mantra; that which has been stated is what should be recited in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the employment of graceful words" (*lalitāpadaprayogāt*), the reason for the introduction of such rootless, graceful words must be stated. Not knowing this, the author of the commentary—
who is merely a reciter of poetry— has revealed his own lack of scholarship by citing "because of the frequent employment of graceful words by the author of the Sūtras" as the reason.

By the word "krameṇa" (in sequence), it is indicated that in place of the nominal stem "pādyam" (water for the feet), other words such as "ābharaṇāvaropaṇa" (removal of ornaments) and so forth should be uttered. "Snānīyodvartanam" refers to a specific fragrant powder that serves as the means for removing the oil adhering to the body. Here, [the items] ending in the accusative case [are to be supplied].

All these [terms] refer to specific pleasures produced by their respective objects. "Kucottarīya" refers to a bodice. "Ālepa" is the contact of the body with fragrant substances; the "maṇḍapa" is a particular structure that produces that [pleasure]. "Kaṅkuma" is saffron from Kāśmīra. "Śaṅku" is a specific type of tree. As it is stated in the Viśvakośa: "Śaṅku [denotes] a peg and poison."

In the lexicon (*śastra*), because there is not much difference between the letters *sa* and *śa*—according to the maxim that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]"—it refers to a fragrant species of tree. *Mṛgamada* is a sub-variety of musk (*kastūrī*). Alternatively, *mṛgamada* is a part of a specific type of animal (*otu*).

In the Mahārāṣṭra language, it is well known as *javvāji*. *Kastūrī* is musk (*mṛganābhi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other world-renowned fragrant substances are included. *Sarvāṅgīṇa* means pertaining to all limbs (*sarvāṅgasambandhi*).
From the word *sarvāṅga*, by adding the suffix *kha* in the sense of connection, the form *sarvāṅgīṇa* is established.
Such is the unguent: *agaru* is well known; among those, there is especially high-quality black *agaru*.

There are flowers produced in all six seasons, such as *mallikā*, *mālatī*, and so forth. There is vermilion (*sindūra*) in the parting of the hair—the path through the midst of the mass of locks—and a jewel in the place of the forehead mark (*tilaka*). There is black collyrium (*kālāñjana*).

"Extremely black collyrium" refers to *sauvīrāñjana*. "Ear-ornament" (*pālī*)—known in the Mahārāṣṭra language as *bālī*—refers to its pair or couplet. On the lower lip (*adhara*), "lac-dye" (*yāvaka*) is the juice of lac used to produce redness; it is the primary ornament.
The *maṅgalasūtra* is a special ornament for the neck, resembling a golden lotus, worn by the women of Andhra;
it is well known in the Andhra language as *golakuṭṭikaṇṭhu*. A *padaka* is a neck ornament, well known in the Mahārāṣṭra language as *tanmaṇi*. A *mahāpadaka*...
A particular ornament for the neck; known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *peṭayā*.
A pearl necklace (*muktāvali*) is known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *kaṇṭhā*. A single-string necklace (*ekāvali*) consisting of twenty-seven pearls is known as the *nakṣatramālā* (star-garland).

According to Amara, "ekāvalī" is a single-stringed necklace, while that same [necklace] with many strings is called a "nakṣatramālā. According to established treatises, "channavīra" is an ornament consisting of a cross-strap worn over both shoulders.
A "pair" (*yugala*) refers to a couple; a "quartet" (*catuṣṭaya*) consists of two on each arm.

The bracelets are their *kaṅkaṇas*; the *āvali* is a row or series of them. The *ūrmi-kās* are finger-ornaments; the *āvali* refers to a row of them. Regarding the ornaments of the waist, he says "girdle" (*kāñcī*). It is established in the *Nibandha* that the *saubhāgyābharaṇa* is a specific type of ornament hanging from the lower part of the hips.

The mention of the foot-anklets, jeweled bracelets, and toe-rings as being "only one" (uttara-meka-vacana) is not intended to be significant, because that meaning is contradicted by the context. He describes the weapons with the word "eka" (one), etc. *Puṇḍrekṣu* means variegated-colored sugarcane. *Puṣpabāṇān* refers to arrows made of flowers. The sequence of the weapons is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"In the lower right hand are arrows, while in the lower left is a bow;
in the upper left is a reddish-noosed cord, and in the upper right is a supreme goad. Thus it is said.
The *mahācakra* is the *śrīcakra*. The couch (*paryaṅka*) is the very lap of Kāmeśvara; sitting upon it [is performed] there.
The *āsava* in the form of nectar is wine; the cup (*caṣaka*) is joined with that. The water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is clear.
The characteristics of the *karpūravīṭikā* (camphor roll) are stated in another Tantra:
"With cardamom, cloves, camphor, musk, saffron, and so forth; with nutmeg, jasmine petals, betel nuts, betel leaves, long pepper, and ginger."
"A betel-roll combined with camphor and powders of the heartwood of khadira. Thus it is said.
Lāṅgalī is *nārikela* (coconut). Ūṣaṇā is *pippalī* (long pepper). Nāgara is *śuṇṭhī* (dry ginger).

Khadirasāra is well known as *kāt* in the Mahārāṣṭrī language. His laughter is such that it possesses a playful manifestation (*vilāsa*) through the rising (*ullāsa*) or emergence (*udaya*) of bliss (*ānanda*). Even in the world, laughter is an indicator of the arising of bliss; therefore—
Such a qualification is appropriate. Regarding the characteristics of the *ārārtika* (the waving of lights) for auspiciousness, it is stated in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
"Thereafter, one should perform the *ārārtika*; listen, O Dear One, to its procedure.
In a vessel made of gold or other materials, distinct from iron, [one should prepare] with vermilion powder."
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp using various colors— [it should be] charming,
auspicious, and golden— or else having prepared a svastika, one should then fashion [figures] made of flour that resemble damarus in appearance.
Having placed in a vessel, in sequence, seven, five, three, or even two portions of food cooked in ghee, together with wicks and filled with ghee;
Having ignited [the fire] through illusion, one should subsequently consecrate it with the nine jewels;
then, having displayed the wheel-mudrā, one should worship with the nine jewels.
Rising up himself, he should lift that vessel up to his head, [saying]:
"O Goddess Navātmikā, together with all the wheels and the Mistress of the Wheels!"
Accept this divine *ārārtika* for my spiritual accomplishment.
Thus, ringing the bell, [he should worship] the Goddess from her feet to her head.
Having whirled the vessel three times with the right hand and set it down, one should perform a prostration;
thus one should perform the ārārtika... [end].

*Tālavṛnta* means a palm-leaf fan. The rest is clear. Regarding the rule for substitute substances when the items mentioned among the sixty-four *upacāras* are unavailable, it is stated in another Tantra:
"In the absence of the respective substances for the offerings, one should use flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*)."
Meditating with the mind, one should perform [the rite]; by that, one shall obtain the fruit of worship. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the specific rule for worship with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in the *Yoginītantra*: "The Supreme Goddess Tripurā should not be worshipped with white unbroken rice grains."
"A wise person should offer pure, unbroken grains of rice, colored with saffron from Kashmir, or with turmeric, or with the paste of red sandalwood. Thus it is said.
This conceptualization of a substitute also applies exclusively to cases other than those involving perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
As it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"But when the ritual services (*upacāra*) are not obtained, one should mentally recollect [them] with flowers and so forth."
Furthermore, O Maheśvarī, regarding perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings:
in the absence of the five beginning with perfume, worship is always (or in every way) indeed in vain. Thus it is said.
Having displayed the nine mudrās,
one should display the nine mudrās.

The nine mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Yoni, will be described [in this work; the extraction of all these mudrās mentioned on their respective pages may be seen in the commentary on verse 15 of the *Dvitiya Paṭala* of the *Śrīkrama*, or in the commentary on the fifteenth sūtra of the *Lalitākrama* in the fifth section]. By the word "and" (ca), the tenth, the *Trikhaṇḍā*, is also included.
Having shown [it]; the word "of the Goddess" (devyāḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 6 ||
The threefold satiation with the root mantra; having performed the threefold satiation. || 7 ||
The word "in the bindu" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Some, however, have stated that the *tarpaṇa* (libation) is prescribed as a form of consecration for the *viśeṣārghya* itself, consisting of taking a small portion from it and placing it into another vessel right there; but that is not correct,
because there is no section concerning the purification of the *viśeṣārghya* [that would support such a view].

Because this would entail abandoning the subject at hand and imagining something irrelevant, and because it contradicts the preceding sūtra which states, "This is the purification of the arghya. Nor should one suspect how it is known that [the mantra] is in the *bindu*, for such knowledge is possible through the hearing of the fourth *kūṭa* in the phrase "by the root" (mūlena). However, there is this much distinction:

Regarding the phrase "having worshipped those other than these," since it is heard here that one should "satisfy" (santarpya), the act of *tarpaṇa* (libation) applies here, while worship (*pūjana*) applies elsewhere.

As for the distinction in practice: here there is the casting of only a drop (*bindu*), whereas at the place of worship there is the casting of both a drop and flowers along with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Furthermore:

(143) By the word "with the root-mantra" (mūlena), expressed in the instrumental case, there is heard an independence from anything else; this refers to the eight-syllable mantra beginning with "Śrīpādukā," as found in the *Mūlasūtra* (the eighth chapter) of the *Śrīgaṇanāyakapaddhati* on page 82, section Khaṇḍa.

This eight-syllable mantra has been stated; since its application is prescribed specifically for worship (*pūjā*), one should utter "svāhā" during fire-offerings (*homa*) and "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*) during libations (*tarpaṇa*). According to the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, the application at the end of the root mantra is simply "I satiate" (*tarpayāmi*).
Is it not observed in other tantras that two words are used interchangeably for the same action,

such as "brāhmaṇais tarpyā" (the Brahmins are to be satiated) with "kṣīreṇa" (with milk), or "brāhmaṇaḥ śivāṃ pūjayet" (the Brahmin should worship Śivā) with "sāttvikenaiva dravyeṇa" (only with pure substances); and in some cases, even the root *yaj* is seen in this very sense, as follows:
"O Supreme Goddess, I shall worship you with a thousand jars of wine"—
if it is argued that *tarpaṇa*, *pūjana*, and *yajana* are synonyms (the reading *paryāyāḥ* is correct), this is not so;
for synonymy is not established merely by usage in a single sense, since they may also function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward a different meaning.

Because [the meaning] is possible through the primary application (*prayoga*). Otherwise, the same consequence would follow for the words "Gaṅgā" and "bank" as well. For this very reason, in the injunction "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," although the verbal root *ālabhati* has the sense of "touching," since the connection between the substance and the deity is untenable without a sacrifice, the root *ālabhati* is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote "sacrifice."

It is thus postulated. Likewise, because there is no logical inconsistency, the literal meaning of the verbal root in the Agnihotra injunction "one should touch the calf" (vatsam ālabheta) has been accepted exactly as it is heard. In the present case as well, since there is no sublation—just as in the case of the sentences concerning Vāyu and others—the principle is the same as in "one should touch the calf," namely that the word *santarpya* retains its literal sense.
It is indeed logical that its meaning is based on what has been heard.
If it is asked, "Since the substance has not been mentioned here either, by what means should the libation (*tarpaṇa*) or worship (*pūjana*) be performed?", it is said in reply:

the prescribed libation and so forth require a means (*sādhana*), and the consecrated special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*) requires a purpose (*kārya*). Thus, between these two which possess such mutual expectancy, they are joined according to the maxim of the lost horse and the burnt chariot (*naṣṭāśvadagdharathanyāya*).
The syntactic unity of the sentence is established as follows: "Having prepared the special *arghya* offering, one should worship the deity with it."

Nor should it be argued that this being the case, since the general *arghya* (water offering) would likewise be equal [to the specific one], it too would result in being a means for worship; for there is no such expectancy as "What is to be done with this? because of its Vedic application (*viniyoga*) in the triangular *viśeṣārghya* mandala and so forth, as indicated by the phrase "with that water" (*tajjalena*).

Nor should it be argued that this is the same in both cases because of the scriptural injunction for the use of the special *arghya* (viśeṣārghya) in the third person— namely, "and having thus worshipped the Guru’s sandals with those drops three times"—
since this is the purification of this very *arghya*, as stated in the final thirty-second sūtra of the third section of the *Anuttara*.

Since the subsequent sūtra describes only the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the special *arghya* up to that point, [the phrase] "with drops" (*bindubhiḥ*) and so forth is also included within that refinement; furthermore, regarding the worship of all the deities of the wheels (*cakradevatārcanāni*) as established in the Śyāmākrama [this is Sūtra 22 in the second section of the Śrīśyāmākrama].

Because of the statement that one should perform [the rite] by throwing handfuls of unbroken rice and flowers with the right hand, accompanied by the first drop fallen together with the *śrīpātra* held between the thumb and ring finger of the left hand, the acquisition of the ritual substances is free from obstacles.

Nor should it be argued that because this [mantra] occurs within the section on Śyāmā, its application must rest solely there; for it has already been established that Śyāmā is merely a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the worship of Lalitā. And a subsidiary element has no independent context (*prakaraṇa*) of its own.

This is the established conclusion of the Mīmāṃsakas: therefore, since the context (prakaraṇa), being more powerful, sets aside the proximity (sannidhi) and there is no obstacle to its application everywhere.

Nor should it be argued that, despite this, an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*)— formed by the "tongs" (*saṃdaṃśa*) of the two *śyāmā* verses— will override the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) according to the principle of the "advance-step" (*abhikramaṇa*) and the "fore-offerings" (*prayāja*),
because the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the word "all" (*sarva*) is the most powerful of all.
Because there is the possibility of sublation by the intermediate context.
Furthermore, since the five *makāras* that manifest those [deities] are established by the text of the Siddhānta which is recited without reference to a specific context,
and since the substance [of worship] is obtained by the phrase "worship with them," there is no scent of any logical inconsistency.

These very same arguments should be applied to the statement found throughout the section on Gaṇapati: "In all names of deities, one should append the eight-syllabled formula 'śrīpūrvaṃ pādukāṃ pūjayāmi'," [this statement is also seen in the *Gaṇanāyakapaddhati*, chapter 8, sūtra 8, on folio 2 of the second section].
"Three times" means three repetitions; here, the repetition of the mantra should be understood as being due to the distinction between the substances. || 7 ||

Regarding the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅgapūjana), he says: having worshipped the six limbs in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions of the Goddess. || 8 ||

In this context, what is called "worship" (pūjana) consists solely of the scattering of flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and drops [of liquid]— as seen in the *Śyāmā-krama* (6th Khaṇḍa, Sūtra 22)— and not in the form of offering the five articles of worship (pañcopacāra) and so forth,
in accordance with the *Kalpasūtra* taught in the *Śyāmā-krama* and the tradition of the learned.

This being the case, regarding the moderns' view that wherever this response "having worshipped" (*pūjayitvā*) occurs, the word "having gratified" (*santarpya*) from the preceding sūtra is to be supplied there as well, resulting in a dual injunction: in the case of the Root Deity (*mūladevī*), there is merely *tarpaṇa*—the offering of the *bindu* substance; whereas *pūjana* consists of the offering of flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).

Thus, some perform the practice as follows: "I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Head-Śakti following the Tritārī and the Śiromantra; I satiate the Śrīpādukā of the Head-Śakti. However, that performance is rooted in delusion, for in that case, it would fall under the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (ardhajaratīya). [The correct sequence] begins with the Tritārī and ends with the Śiromantra.
To begin with, it would be a source of great laughter to state that there are two repetitions starting from "the head and the powers" (*śiraśśakti*).

Furthermore, since worship is performed with the mantra "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the subsequent mantra, it follows that worship and libation must occur in that specific sequence. This being the case, regarding the offering of the *bindu*, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*):
This contradicts the sūtra which states that one should perform [the rite] with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) fallen together with the *bindu* at a single time.
Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of there being no connection with the left hand, since both [actions] could be performed with the right hand due to their sequential nature.

Nor should it be said that the necessity of the left hand arises from the rule "clenched by the thumb and ring finger of the left hand," according to the Sūtra [Sūtra 22 in the Śrīśyāmākrama, Section 6 of this work], for [the same applies to] the right hand.

Because it is impossible to enjoin the left hand when it has already been obtained through the necessity of its presence while one is occupied with the act of throwing flowers and unbroken rice (akṣata), [the mention of the left hand] is merely a restatement (anuvāda). For this very reason, at the time of proceeding toward the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra, the Sūtra of the Chandogas states: "with the left hands..."

Regarding the statement "they strew with their hands," the Bhāṣya explains that since the right hand is already occupied in the act of assisting the Adhvaryu and others—according to the injunction, "The Prastotṛ assists the Adhvaryu;

the Pratihartṛ assists the Prastotṛ; the Udgātṛ assists the Pratihartṛ"—the left hand, which is already established by the requirements of the situation (*arthaprāpta*), is merely restated (*anūdyate*).
However, some, following the word "santarpya" (having satiated), prescribe both the libation and the worship;

fearing the application of the "half-old woman" maxim (*ardhajaratīyanyāya*), they recite the mantra after the three *tārās* and at the end of the heart-mantra as follows: "I worship and satiate the Heart-Śakti Śrīpādukā; obeisance."
In that case, it is impure, because there is no means of valid cognition for its continued existence.
Furthermore, it is contradictory to claim that in an injunction, libation (*tarpaṇa*) comes first and worship (*pūjā*) afterwards, while the order is reversed in the mantra;

therefore, in the preceding statement, "libation" refers merely to the sprinkling of drops. Since there is no further expectancy for its continuation, only worship is enjoined. And as for the meaning of the term "worship":

The offering consists of scattering a collection of bindus, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Thus, the form of the mantra should be understood as follows: first the *tritārī*, then the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), and then "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Heart-Śakti.
In this very same way, it should be understood everywhere hereafter.

In the phrase "Agnīśa" (Agni and Īśa), the term "Agni" and so forth refers to the directions associated with those respective deities. By the word "in the directions," the four cardinal directions beginning with the East are intended. Regarding the young maidens of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayuvatī*), one should know that there are six locations: the four intermediate directions beginning with Agni, the center, and the four cardinal directions beginning with the East taken together as one.
Regarding this, some say:
"The direction in which one sees the sun is called 'east' for that person;
at sunrise, for the observer of the sun, Mount Meru is situated to the north."
Thus,
they say that just as the determination of directions is well-established in Vedic and Smārta rituals, the same determination of directions applies likewise to the practice of Śrīvidyā.

Others, however, maintain that since the conventional determination of directions has its application in Vedic rituals, one should designate the direction between the worshiper and the object of worship as the East, according to the Tantric injunction: "One should conceive of the East as being between the worshiper and the worshipped.
Thus, the portion in front of the Goddess is the East, the portion behind the Goddess is the West, and the Goddess's right side is the South.
They stated that the determination of the intermediate directions follows from the northern direction on the left side.
146) Both of these [methods] are to be disregarded because they are coarse measures. In reality, however, in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the context of the worship of the Śrīcakra—
O Goddess, when the mantra-practitioner extracts the wheel while facing the northern direction,
then that northern direction is called the eastern direction.
O Goddess of gods, when the practitioner facing the western direction raises the wheel, then the northeast is the southeast; of this there is no doubt.
Then the western direction should be known as the eastern direction, without a doubt;
likewise, the wind-corner (northwest) becomes the fire-corner (southeast), and the northeast becomes the rakshasa-corner (southwest).
"When the practitioner facing south raises up the wheel,
the eastern direction indeed becomes the north, and the southeast corner becomes the southwest."
In the phrase "the north-western direction," having referred to the direction that is conventionally known as the north, the function of the eastern and other directions is prescribed—

just as in the injunction, "The threshing-post becomes the sacrificial stake" (*khalevālī yūpo bhavati*). Thus, since the function of the directions is prescribed by referring merely to the directions themselves, it is established that one should not lift the wheel while facing an intermediate direction.
Because there is no further injunction following the restatement of the eastern direction, that [passage] has been omitted. Likewise, in the *Kulārṇava*:
"When the practitioner (mantrī), facing whichever direction, worships Tripurā, then the east is behind the Goddess, and the west is in front of Tripurā."
Thus, by means of these unambiguous statements, the determination of the directions regarding the Śrīvidyā is established according to the method described.
In tantric rites other than those of the Śrīvidyā, the direction between the worshipper and the object of worship is the East.
In all śrauta and smārta rites, there is the inclusion of such statements as "he who should look [at the sun]," and so forth. Enough with further elaboration.

By the statement "of the Goddess," it is established that one should worship the six-limbed maidens (ṣaḍaṅgayuvatīḥ) there, having arranged them in the directions starting from the southeast (āgneya) within the Binducakra itself, according to the aforementioned scripture. || 8 ||
The daily worship: From this point onward,
[the text] demonstrates the daily worship of the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) of Śrī Lalitāmbā and other matters, up until the end of the tenth sūtra at the conclusion of the fourth section.
Now, preceded by the extraction of the mantras of the fifteen Nityās, he describes the worship of the Nityās:

*vāksakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ*—this is Kāmeśvarī. In all instances, the phrase *nityāśrīpādukā* (the sandals of the venerable Nityā) should be appended. *vāgbhagabhuge bhagini bhagodari bhagamāle*.

O Blessed One! O Secret of the Yoni! O Source of the Yoni! O You who cause the yoni to descend! O You who bring all yonis under control! O You whose form is the yoni! O Ever-Moist! O You whose very nature is the yoni! Bring all yonis to me, O Giver of Boons!
O Excellent Semen! O Excellent Semen! O Moistened by the Yoni! O Flowing with Moisture! Make wet! Cause to flow! O Infallible One! O Yoni-Vicce! Agitate! Cause to tremble!
[For] all sentient beings,
O Mistress of the Yoni: aiṃ blūṃ jeṃ blūṃ bheṃ blūṃ moṃ blūṃ heṃ blūṃ heṃ.

*Klinne sarvāṇi bhagāni me vaśamānaya strīṃ hara bleṃ hrīṃ bhagamālinī*—this is *Bhagamālinī*. *Tāro māyā nityaklinne madadrave svāhā*—this is *Nityaklinnā*. *Praṇavaḥ kroṃ bhroṃ krauṃ jhrauṃ chrauṃ jrauṃ svāhā*—this is *Bheruṇḍā*. *Praṇavo māyā vahnivāsinyai* [svāhā].
