*Namaḥ* is Vahnivāsinī. *Māyā klinne vāk kroṃ nityamadadrave hrīṃ* is Mahāvajreśvarī. *Māyā śivadūtyai namaḥ* is Śivadūtī. *Praṇava māyā huṃ khe ca che kṣaḥ strīṃ huṃ kṣeṃ hrīṃ phaṭ* is Tvaritā. Kumārī is Kulasundarī.

*Hasakalaraḍa-vāgbhava-hasakalaraḍa-bindumālinī-hasakalaraḍa-caturdaśa-ṣoḍaśā*— thus is the Nityā. *Māyā*, *phreṃ*, *srūṃ*, *aṅkuśa-pāśa-smara-vāgbhava-blūṃ-pada-nityamada-drave*, *varma*, *phreṃ*, *māyā*.

Nīlapatākā; Vijayā is *bhamaraya-ūm*; Sarvamaṅgalā is *svaum*. [The mantra is: *Tāro namo bhagavati jvālāmālini devadevi sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike jātavedasi jvalanti jvala jvala prajvala prajvala trijātiyuktamāyārephasaptakajvālāmālini*.

With "varma phaṭ agnijāyai," one worships Jvālāmālinī; with "aṃ ckauṃ," one worships Citrā. Thus, the fifteen Nityās are to be worshipped within the fifteen vowels situated on the lines of the first triangle. Upon emission, one should worship the sixteenth [Nityā] with the root-vidyā.

*Vāk* is *aiṃ*. The remainder is as recited [in the root text]. At the end of every mantra, after the name of each respective *Nityā*, there is the application of the eight-syllable formula. For example: first the *Tritārī*, then *aiṃ sakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ kāmeśvarīnityāśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*. This should be understood to apply in the same way for what follows.

Although the eight-syllable yoga beginning with "śrīpādukā" is obtained through general statements, nevertheless, because it is not obtained as such when composed with the word "nityā," this undertaking is for that purpose in all mantras for the worship of the Nityās. He states the second [mantra] as "vāk"; he states the third as "tāra. "Tāra" is the Praṇava (Om).

The syllable *māyā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) is to be recited, and the remainder as heard [in the tradition]. The realized meaning is: first the *praṇava* (oṃ), then *māyā*, then as heard, ending with *svāhā*. He states the fourth [mantra] as beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*. He states the fifth as beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*. He states the sixth as beginning with *māyā* and ending with *hrīṃ*.
The seventh [mantra] is stated with the words ending in "māyāyai namaḥ. The eighth is stated with the words ending in "praṇava" and "phaṭ.

The ninth is stated as "kumārī"; the meaning is that *kumārī* is a young girl, who is herself the *Kulasundarī*. The tenth is stated with the words beginning with "hasa" and ending in "ṣoḍaśā. Here, according to the logic previously mentioned, [the sequence begins with] *hasake*, and so forth.

The reference is exclusively to the consonants (*vyañjana*). Otherwise, by the statement in another tantra that "the twelve-halved [syllables] would be eternal," and because the status of having three syllables is established in the mantra— given that the twelve-halved [syllables] reside in the three seeds when the mantra's phonemes are extended [by analogy]— here too the possession of three syllables, established by that extension, would be contradicted.
Following *hasakalaraḍa* is *vāgbhava*, *aiṃ*; again, following that is *mālinī* joined with the *bindu*, the letter *ī*.
This is because of the lexicon (*kośa*) which states: "Govinda and Trimūrti are [the letters] *mālinī* and *vāmalocana*. [These are] the fourteenth and the sixteenth.
As previously stated: thus, *hsklrḍaiṃ*, *hsklrḍīḥ*, *hsklrḍauḥ*, and *nityānityāśrī* constitute the nature of the mantra.
Furthermore, that which is written in the *Nibandha* as the letter *ha* together with the vowel *a* is motivated solely by ignorance.

If it were written according to another tantra, then since there is the sūtra stating, "Having uttered the *ka*-group and *kala hrīṃ* in the *Vaśinyādi-nyāsa*," one would have to seek a justification for the inclusion of the consonant alone (*hal-mātra*) apart from that other tantra. Therefore:
By the reasoning already stated, the Nityā-vidyā consists of exactly three syllables.
The eleventh [verse] begins with "māyā" and ends with "māyā. The first three seed-syllables (*bīja*) are clear.
Regarding the hook (*aṅkuśa*), it is *krom*; the noose (*pāśa*) is *ām*. According to the *Yoginītantra*, the "great noose" (*mahāpāśa*) is that which exists at the beginning and the end.
Its meaning is as follows: the letter *a* is the beginning; its "end" (*anta*) refers to the preceding position, and the letter *ā* is situated there. Thus...

"Kāma, Agni, Vyāpaka, and Aṅkuśa"—it is said in that very [text]. Kāma is the letter *ka*, Agni is *ra*, and Vyāpaka is the Praṇava (*oṃ*); when combined, they become *krom*. This is the meaning of "Aṅkuśa. Smara is *klīṃ*, Vāgbhava is *aiṃ*, and Varma is *huṃ*. Thus, [the mantra is]: *hrīṃ phreṃ srūṃ kroṃ āṃ klīṃ*.

The nature of the mantra is: *aiṃ blūṃ nityamadadrave huṃ phreṃ hrīṃ nīlapatākānityāśrī*. Regarding the twelfth [syllable], it says *bhamaraya-ūṃ*; here too, by the previously mentioned logic, only the consonant (*hal*) is to be taken. This one-syllabled lore (*vidyā*) is proclaimed as Vijayā.
Because of the statement in another tantra.
Therefore, in the *Nibandha*, the utterance of the five syllables and the utterance of the vowel *au* are due to negligence;

the actual form should be known as *rbhmyūm*. Although in another tantra it is stated that [the mantra] is "joined with the *aṅgada* and the *bindu*," the *aṅgada* is the vowel *au*; thus, the final vowel is *au*.

It appears so; nevertheless, because the sixth vowel is uttered in the Sūtra, that which is stated in other Tantras—being contrary to the Sūtra—must certainly not be respected by those who follow the Sūtra.
He states the thirteenth [syllable] as *svauṃ*. He states the fourteenth as *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) ending with *agnijāyā* (the word *svāhā*).
It is joined with the three *jātis*: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*, which are the *māyā*s; *vahnijāyā* is *svāhā*. The remainder is clear.
He states the fifteenth as *aṃ ckrauṃ*. He now states the rule regarding the location for the worship of the fifteen *Nityās*.

"First," and so forth. The meaning is that one should worship, in sequence, one *Nityā* for each of the fifteen vowels— beginning with *ā* and ending with the *anusvāra*— which reside upon the three lines of the first triangle, the triangle situated near the *bindu*.
In this context, since the fifteen vowels situated on the lines are indicated there as if already established (*siddhavat*),
the rule should be inferred that five vowels are to be meditated upon on each individual line.
Since no specific order is mentioned, they should be arranged starting from the western side, proceeding clockwise from the top of each line.

On the line between Īśāna [and Vāyu] are *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*. On the line from Īśāna to Āgneya are *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*. Starting from Āgneya and extending to the West are *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *am*; such is the discernment of the meditative visualization (*bhāvanāviveka*). That from which emanation has departed or issued forth is *visṛṣṭi*, namely the Bindu-cakra. This is the manner of its emanation.

This should be seen in the *Setubandha*, the commentary on the *Uttaracatuśśatī*. Having worshipped the *Ṣoḍaśī* in her form as the totality (*samaṣṭi*) with the fifteen-syllable root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), [one should know that] the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of these [deities] is a triangle distinct from the fashioned triangle; this is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
And having visualized the great triangle, [extending] from the southeast to the north in sequence. Thus [it is said].
In the *Tantrarāja*, however, worship is said to be performed in the *bindu* alone. Thus, it should be performed in each respective case by the followers of those various tantras. (9)

He describes the worship of the three currents (oghatripūjā): Having worshipped, according to tradition, the sandals (pādukās) belonging to the divine, perfected, and human currents— numbering [respectively] seven, four, and eight— within the center of the initial triangle in the middle [of the mandala], one should thereafter worship the Lord upon one's own head.

This is the worship of the limbs of the *layāṅga*; may there be auspiciousness. [In some versions, there is an additional reading: "Some worship the triad of creation, maintenance, and dissolution according to the Yoga Sūtras, as well as the five pentads, the five types of envy, and the deities of the *prapañca* and other installations (*nyāsa*).

Thus ends the fourth section, named the *Lalitākrama*, in the *Kalpasūtra*. Śrī: The first triangle is the eastern triangle; or rather, the "eastern triangle" refers to the previously mentioned triangle, and its "middle" is the inner region, and its "end" is the final constituent part.
The realized meaning is: "therein," referring to that inner region which is situated near the tip facing oneself.

The term *ogha* is qualified by the numbers seven, six, four, and eight—derived from the etymology "that in which these numbers reside"—referring to the sages (*muni*), Vedas, [faces], and serpents (*nāga*) respectively. The sandals (*pādukāḥ*) are [arranged] according to tradition through the distinctions of the *Kādi* and *Hādi* Vidyās.

Because the guru-maṇḍalas of the sandals (pādukās) are distinct, whichever sandals have been accepted by a particular person, they are called "sandals" according to tradition for the sake of attaining those respective [powers]. They are divine, perfected, and human; such are the perfected ones (siddhas) who belong to the currents (oghās). As previously stated...

Regarding the qualification of the *ogha* (floods): in both instances, the transposition of case endings is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage. The distinction is as follows: there are seven celestial (*divya*) beings, four perfected ones (*siddha*), and eight human (*mānava*) beings. Having sacrificed to and worshipped them—the sequence established by the use of the absolutive suffix (*ktvā*) and the order of the recitation—is restated here by the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*). This is what was said: namely— [nāma-]
[From the 9th Sūtra of this Western Section up to the 10th Sūtra above: Following this, that which is to be explained— beginning from the single Sūtra located in the upcoming fifth section—

is the worship of the nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa-pūjana*), the limb of dissolution (*layāṅga*), and the nature of dissolution (*layasvarūpa*) according to the sequence starting from the square (*caturasra*) and ending with the point (*bindu*).
Because its essential nature is dissolution (*laya*), the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) ought to be performed.

By this, the worship of the *bindu* and other elements mentioned in other Tantras is excluded. The intended meaning here is that in every worship of a Yantra, one must follow either the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), or withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
The term is understood according to its specific definition; that is to say, worship begins starting from the *bindu* (the point) by way of the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

However, in this particular sequence, it should not be taken in that way; rather, the commencement of worship in this sequence must be performed by way of the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), which is known as the "limb of balance" (*layāṅga*). But in the case of worshipping deities distinct from these [primary] deities, one begins from the *bindu*.
"Mārmikam" means "pertaining to the vital point. "Śivam" indicates the conclusion of the section. || 10 ||

Thus ends the fourth section, named the Lalitākrama, in the commentary on the Paraśurāmasūtra. It should be understood that the worship is not yet complete here, but rather that this is merely a section; furthermore, upon the repetition of the sūtra, that which is to be purified must be indicated.
"And the remaining portion shall be complete by the grace of the Primordial Goddess. Thus ends the fourth section.
[The Fifth Section: Worship of the Nine Enclosures of Lalitā;
Worship of the Individual Deities of the First Enclosure. From the next page until the completion of the Sūtra, once again...]
There is also the practical application for collective worship (*samaṣṭyarcanaprayoga*).

By this word [in the tenth sūtra], it should be understood that the word "this" (*etacchabda*) refers to the phrase "worship of the limbs of this dissolution" (*etallayāṅgapūjana*) found in the subsequent sūtra. Having elaborated upon the worship thus indicated—
He demonstrates this: now, in the first square,

[the powers] of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), lordship (īśitva), mastery (vaśitva), irresistible will (prākāmya), fulfillment of desires (bhuktīcchā), and attainment (prāpti)—
Ending with the accomplishment of all desires (*sarvakāmasiddhi*), [the goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Mahālakṣmī are placed in the middle square;
in the third square are Saṃkṣobhaṇā, Drāvaṇā, Ākarṣaṇā, Vaśyā, Unmādanā, Mahāṅkuśā, Khacarī, Bījā, and Yonī.
All those [deities] in the eastern sections, divided into three parts, are to be worshipped. || 1 ||

The word *atha* indicates the commencement of the section on the worship of the nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa-pūjā*). In the center of the three squares, within the first and outermost square, there is a series of dual compounds beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with *sarvakāma*.
All of these are to be performed as "accomplishments" (*siddhi*). The term *siddhi* is to be joined at the end of each word. Thus it is said:
Then [recite] "Tritārī, I worship the Śrī-pādukā of the siddhi of aṇimā. The same applies hereafter.

In this context, the three words beginning with *aṇimā* do not end in the suffix *-man*, but rather in the feminine suffix *-ā* (ḍāp), according to the reading of the sūtra on compound endings which states *aṇimā-laghimā-*. Thus, "aṇimāsiddhi" is devoid of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

The reading, although not strictly according to the technical treatises (*śāstra*), is as if it were the work of a sage (*ārṣa*) due to its adherence to traditional transmission (*sampradāya*). Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound; the meaning of the genitive case here is indeed non-difference (*abheda*), as in the expression "the head of Rāhu.
Regarding the first square (*caturasra*), since there would otherwise be the possibility of worshipping *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis] at will, this [text] establishes a fixed rule for them.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
[One should worship] Aṇimā at the western gate, Laghimā also at the northern,
Mahimā at the eastern gate, and that called Īśitva at the southern.

The perfection known as mastery (vaśitva) is in the northwest; the perfection of irresistible will (prākāmya) is in the northeast; likewise, the perfection of enjoyment (bhukti-siddhi) is in the southeast, and the perfection of the fulfillment of desires (icchā-siddhi) is in the southwest.
"Below, there is the accomplishment of attainment and all desires; likewise above. Thus it is said.

The tradition regarding the arrangement of the directions has been explained previously. Furthermore, "above" and "below" should not be understood according to worldly convention, but rather according to the Tantric system. As it is stated in the *Tattvavimarśinī*:
"The location above is proclaimed to be between the directions of Indra and Īśāna."
"The location below is proclaimed to be between the directions of Nirṛti and Ambupa (Varuṇa). Thus [it is said].
In the middle square are Brāhmyā and the others—those beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Mahālakṣmī.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers.
Thus, the eight Mothers—the seven well-known ones plus Mahālakṣmī—are to be worshipped in the central square.
Regarding the sequence for this, the Vāmakeśvara Tantra states:
"Brahmāṇī at the western gate, and Māheśī also in the north."
One should place Kaumārī at the eastern gate and Vaiṣṇavī at the southern gate.
Likewise, one should place Vārāhī in the northwest, Aindrī in the northeast, Cāmuṇḍā in the southeast, and Mahālakṣmī in the southwest. Thus it is said.

Now, regarding the worship of the ten mudrās in the third square, he says "in the third": the word *sarva* (all) which was previously used in the names [of the goddesses] is applied here; for example, after the three *tārās*, one says:
"I worship the venerable sandals of the power *Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*. Such are these powers of the mudrās.

The meaning of the six mudrās has already been stated [in this very work, *Lalitākrama*, in the fourth section, in the commentary on the 135th verse of the first chapter]. These [mudrās] are delimited by properties that are subsumed under the general category of "mudrā-hood. Furthermore, the meaning of the term *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* (the All-Agitating) is as follows: [she agitates] all things (*padārtha*), that is, all beings (*bhūta*).

"She agitates" means "she produces"; thus, *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* (the All-Agitating One) refers to that which is the causal power (*kāraṇatā*) defined by the effect-nature delimited by all effects—this is what is meant.
This very one is called the *vāmā* power. This has been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
Furthermore, due to the predominance of the womb-source (yoni), this [power] is the agitator of all;
it is this very one in which the power Vāmā is predominant. Thus [it is said].

The *yoni*s are the causal states; they are characterized by their abundance, that is, by their predominance. For this very reason, even in the external form consisting of the interlacing of fingers—specifically in the thumb—the plurality of *yoni*s arises from the conjunction of the tips of the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger with the [thumb].

It is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By this, it should be inferred that even that which is of invisible form is likewise so. The second [form] is *Sarvavidrāviṇī* (the All-Dissolver): she dissolves all unarisen things and causes them to grow through nourishment; thus she is *Sarvavidrāviṇī*.
Because she protects all things, she is of straight nature (*ṛjusvabhāvā*) and abounds in the *Jyeṣṭhā-śakti*.
As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*: "Jyeṣṭhā, who brings about the stability of the agitated universe, abides in abundance.

The meaning of "agitated" (*kṣubdha*) is "that which has arisen. Furthermore, there is a well-known worldly verse: "He who is a protector is straight (*ṛju*). For this very reason, even in the external form of this mudrā, by means of the thumb...

In the four fingers joined from the little finger to the ring finger, straightness is observed. Thus, within the three lines of the first triangle situated in the eastern direction, it is well-known in the scriptures that its locus is precisely upon that straight line. The third is the "all-attracting" (sarvākarṣiṇī), whose nature is to attract all things.
This Jyeṣṭhā consists of both the Left and the Right. As it is stated in the Yoginītantra (p.
"Jyeṣṭhā, by virtue of her equality with Vāmā, has established herself as the primary principle of emanation."
This is the mudrā called Ākarṣiṇī (the Attractress). Thus [it is said].

It should be understood that both of the delimiters (avacchedakas) of the denotability (śakyatā) of the two previously mentioned words [jyeṣṭhā and vāmā], which denote the two mudrās, also serve as the delimiters of the denotability of the word *sarvākarṣiṇī*, just as in the case of the word "flower" [denoting a specific type of flower]. Even there, the delimiter of denotability is the state of being Vāmā qualified by the state of being Jyeṣṭhā, and not the reverse; for if it were so, [the following would occur]:

The primacy of Jyeṣṭhā must be stated by virtue of her being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Given this primacy, because Jyeṣṭhā is exceedingly straight, the index finger and middle finger—which serve as qualifiers following the lead of the principal [Jyeṣṭhā]—must also be straight; thus, they do not possess curvature in their external form.

It may be so. However, since Vāmā is predominant, it is logical that she is crooked; and accordingly, Jyeṣṭhā—who is subordinate and follows the lead of the predominant one—is also crooked. For this very reason, in the external form of the finger-knotting (*aṅguligrathana*), there is crookedness in all the fingers. The fourth [mudrā] brings everything under control. All...

She is so called because she brings everything from the earth up to Śiva under her control, making it subject to her own will. In the world, space is of two kinds: the limited (*dahra*) and the elemental (*prākṛta*). Within the limited space as well, there exists another, extremely subtle space, which is famously known from the *Śruti* as "the subtle aperture at its end. She is firmly embraced within that [subtle space].
That form of Paraśiva which consists of the essence of bliss is designated by the term "the one who brings all under control" (*sarvavaśyakarī*). As it is said in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*:
"The Great Goddess is of the nature of the point (*bindu*) situated between the two voids."
"Because of this intimate union with the essence of Śiva and Śakti, she is remembered as the one who brings others under control. Thus [it is said].

Because it is described as being in the form of a *bindu*, its nature as the *kha* (the void) is likewise [implied]. For this very reason, even when the fingers are interlaced, her external form takes the shape of a *bindu*, and the firm joining of all the fingers is clearly manifest.
The fifth [finger] is a subtle line between the aforementioned *śiva*, *śakti*, and *bindu*, thin like the awn of a grain of *nīvāra*.

"In the center is the flame of fire" is well-known from the Śruti. That flame possesses a dual nature and the nature of Jyeṣṭhā. Just as in the world a single staff possesses both the power to produce a jar and the power to destroy it, so too is that staff.

Sometimes, becoming predominant in its power of production, it produces a jar; sometimes, predominant in its power of destruction, it destroys that same jar. This is observed in many instances in the world.
Likewise, the aforementioned line stands in the place of a staff; when that [line]—
At that time, she who is characterized by the agency of protecting the world and is dominated by the power of Jyeṣṭhā is denoted by the term *Sarvonmādinī*. As it is said in the *Uttara-catuḥśatī*:
"She consists of a subtle crest of form shimmering within the interior of the Bindu."
But Jyeṣṭhā, whose primary power is Śakti, causes universal intoxication. Thus [it is said].

For this very reason, at the time of binding the fingers, the thumb, the ring finger, and the index finger are seen to be straight, while the two middle fingers take on the form of two dots (*bindu*). Furthermore, at the time of binding that which occupies the position of the *śikhā* as defined by etymology, it should be understood that only the two ring fingers are involved.
At that time, since the non-dual *madhyamā* consists of the form of two *bindus*,

it is logical that the nameless non-duality situated between them possesses the nature of a "flame" (*śikhā*), as is well known to be the flame in the center of those two. As for the sixth [channel], this very aforementioned pair of flames is when *vāmā* is predominant.

Then, [she is] the Great Goad of All (Sarvamahāṅkuśā). The universe, residing within the womb of Paramaśiva in a subtle form, is [controlled] by the goad, just as an elephant staying inside [a stable] is [controlled] by a goad.
It is drawn outward; thus, because of drawing everything outward, it is called the "Great Hook of All" (*sarvamahāṅkuśā*).
Because it vomits forth the universe residing within the belly of Paraśiva, the *śikhā* (flame) dominated by that Vāmā is called the "Great Hook of All.
This too has been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
But in the second decade, she is preeminent as the power of Vāmā, consisting of the Great Hook (mahāṅkuśa), and likewise emitting the universe. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, in the previous mudrā, the straightness of the two ring fingers is seen to become curved. In the world, at the time of vomiting, a person becomes curved, taking the shape of a bow; this is well known. Herein lies the distinction: being solely on the left side is the ground for the application of the term *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*.
The state of being the left [power] (vāmātva) qualified by being the eldest (jyeṣṭhā) is the ground for the application of the term *sarvākarṣiṇī* (the all-attraction);
the state of being two points (*bindu*) functioning within the subtle ether is the ground for the application of the term *sarvavaśyakara* (the all-subjugation);
and the state of being a line functioning between the two points in which the power of the eldest (jyeṣṭhā-śakti) predominates [is the ground for the application of the term *sarvonmādinī*].

The delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the denotability of the term *sarvonmādinī* is the predominance of the power of Vāmā; likewise, the delimiting factor for the denotability of the term *sarvamahāṅkuśā* is [the predominance of Jyeṣṭhā]. In this manner, the distinction should be perceived by one of subtle intellect. The seventh is *sarvakhecarī* of living beings.

She possesses the power capable of destroying the suffering of diseases and other afflictions produced by one's own karma; for this very reason, she resides within the *sarvarogahara-cakra* (the wheel that removes all diseases). This is also stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"Aroused from the friction of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), she has the form of consciousness (*vitti*)."

"It is held that Khecarī destroys the defects consisting of the omission of actions arising from conceptual construction, and removes the diseases whose nature is conceptual construction. Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows: *dharma* is power (*śakti*), because it resides in Paraśiva. *Adharma* is that in which no *dharma* exists;

thus, *adharma* is the Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva. Alternatively, the negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) "that which is not the *dharma* of anything" is more appropriate, since *dharma* in the form of power does exist in Paraśiva; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with what was previously stated in the first alternative regarding those two.

*Saṃghaṭṭa* is union; by that [union] she has arisen. Whatever rites—whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—have arisen from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the sins resulting from the omission of those give rise to diseases. *Khecarī* is the destroyer of those. Therefore, in its external form, it is an illustration of such a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti.

The rotation of the two arms. The eighth is the Seed Mudrā (*bījamudrā*), which is the power presiding over that existence which is the first modification of being among the six modifications of the world, existing in a subtle form.
As it is said in the *Uttaracatuḥśatikā*:
Furthermore, within the expanse of space vibrating with the embrace of Śiva and Śakti,
she who always manifests the universe abiding in a subtle form is the Mahāmudrā in the form of the seed-syllable. Thus it is said.

The meaning is this: even in the extremely subtle banyan seed, there is some space because of its all-pervasiveness. Just as a great tree exists within it in a subtle form, so too do the thirty-six principles exist in a subtle form within the womb of Śiva and Śakti. That very existence persists in such expressions as "the pot exists" or "the cloth exists. It is that [existence].

This means "seed-mudrā. Because she occupies the position of the seed of all, she is "the one containing all seeds" (sarvabījā). Precisely because of her subtlety, at the time of interlacing the fingers, her state as having few origins (*alpayonitva*)—in comparison to [mudrās] such as Saṃkṣobhiṇī—is the indicator of her subtlety. She who...
The ninth is *yonimudrā*, which is its unique defining characteristic (*asādhāraṇadharma*): the state of being a *mudrā* while possessing the nature of a *kalā*.
The essential nature of being a *mudrā* has been explained previously. Now, the category of *kalā* is being discussed. [It exists] in that which is qualified by power (*śaktiviśiṣṭe*).
When, in the supreme Śiva whose nature is light, the Śakti is set aside and only the essential nature alone is extracted,

there arises the state of being denoted by the term *turyabindu* (the fourth point), just as water, when its fluidity inherent in it is set aside and only its essential nature is extracted, possesses the state of being denoted by the term "water. Here, "setting aside" (*apahāna*) means—

The very absence of entry into the category of the delimitor of possibility (*śakyatā'vacchedaka*) is not something to be excluded from that [category] separately, because such exclusion is impossible. When there is the intention to describe that pure Śiva as being related to Śakti, He possesses the status of being denotable by the term *kāma-bindu*. This is due to the non-difference (*abheda*) of that very relationship.

In Tantric usage, the emission (*visarga*) that enters into the category of the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of possibility is called *hakāra*, which is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Following such a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), when there is the intention to express the inclusion of internal bliss arising from the mixture of the red and white drops (*bindu*), it is called *kalā*. Such is the nature of *kalā*. [Ṭ.]

The distinction is that bliss (*ānanda*) is included as an additional factor within the defining limit (*avacchedaka-koṭi*) of the impossibility of [expressing] the state of the *kalāpada*. Thus it is "additional" (*adhika*).
[Note: *ba*]. This is the *yonimudrā*. As it is said in the *Nityāhṛdaya*:
"Furthermore, this is the ground for the attainment of the complete manifestation."
The Yonimudrā is the form of the Kalās... thus [it is said].

She who brings everything under control consists solely of two *bindus*. Since the bliss arising from the union of these two *bindus* within her body is also included within the defining characteristics (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) [of her nature], she should be understood as distinct from that [previous state]. The tenth [form], *Trikhaṇḍā*, has been described previously. Thus...
The true nature of the ten mudrās, which has become manifest through the extraordinary grace of the venerable Guru,
has been clarified according to my own understanding for the easy comprehension of people.
Thus, the infinite fruit of knowing their true nature, as elaborated at length in the Tantras, is not written here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, the ten mudrās are to be worshipped in the third square. Regarding this as well, there is a restrictive statement in the Tantra concerning their attainment according to one's desire:
"In the front, on the right, on the rear, on the left, and in the intermediate spaces."
And the ten mudrās above and below... [thus it is said].

The meaning of this is that the ten mudrās are to be worshipped in the east, south, west, and north, as well as in the four intermediate directions beginning with the southeast, and above and below. || 1 ||
The collective worship of the first enclosure:
Having described the individual worship of the first enclosure, he now describes the collective worship:
"These manifest yoginīs in the Trailokyamohana-cakra are together with their mudrās, siddhis, and weapons."
Having performed the collective worship of them alone with the thought, "May they, together with their powers, vehicles, and retinues, be fully honored with all ritual offerings," || 2 ||
These [Yoginīs] range from Aṇimā up to Trikhaṇḍā. "Prakaṭayoginīs" is their collective name (samaṣṭi-nāma), just as "man" is the collective name for individuals such as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth.
Furthermore, among the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva, the state of being "manifest" (prakaṭatva) in these aforementioned Yoginīs refers to that which is gross (sthūla).
The Earth is that [form], because it exists within the square *bhūpura* (earth-fortress). As it is said in the *Nityāhṛdaya* (p.
"There, in the wheel (*cakra*) called Trailokyamohana, are the manifest *yoginīs*."
The Yoginīs are to be known as manifest within the self that is the expansion of the gross universe.
Because it is established... thus.

"Trailokyamohana" (Deluder of the Three Worlds) is the name of the outermost wheel consisting of three squares, according to both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) usage. [The term refers to the three lines forming the square by way of the *yogarūḍhi* power—Ba. "Samudrāḥ" (Oceans) refers to those ten [lines] which were previously described in detail.

Among those, one mudrā for each is prescribed for each individual cakra; the tenth, the *trikhaṇḍā*, is all-pervasive. There is authoritative evidence for this point in the *Yoginītantra*. Furthermore, the venerable Lord Paraśurāma will also describe the display of one mudrā for each during the worship of the respective cakras.

[The meaning is: "in the worship of the lower enclosure. And thus, the meaning is: "accompanied by whichever mudrā belongs to whom. Regarding the phrase "together with their accomplishments" (*sasiddhayaḥ*): here, "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the fruit to be achieved through each respective power (*śakti*). Since that fruit exists in its own form as a subtle essence, the powers themselves are also said to be "together with their accomplishments. [Regarding the term] "with weapons" (*sāyudhāḥ*).

This is clear. Here, by the term "powers" (*śakti*), that property which delimits the capacity to produce various specific effects—residing in [the Lord] together with those powers—is to be understood. For in the world, causality is not known to be unconditioned; therefore, some kind of delimitor must be admitted for the causality residing in itself.
Furthermore, as for the nature that has been accepted, whether it is different from its substratum or not is another matter.
They are "accompanied by such powers" (*tādṛśaśaktyā sahitāḥ*). "With their vehicles" (*savāhanāḥ*) is clear. "Together with their retinues" means accompanied by their attendants.
The remainder of the meaning of the mantra is clear. Of those [goddesses], beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Trikhaṇḍā—

Having performed the collective worship (*samaṣṭhyarcana*) by means of a mantra composed of the names of the assembly, it is understood here that [the mantra] serves as a component of the prayer (*prārthanāṅga*) on account of its internal indicative mark (*liṅga*), because the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is heard; for there is the traditional rule of Pāṇini stating, "The optative (*liṅ*) and the imperative (*loṭ*) are used in the sense of praying. Nevertheless, regarding the mantra: *mama agne varco vihveṣv astu*... [etc.]

Just as the injunction "He places the *vihavyā*s" sets aside the indicative mark (*liṅga*) [of the mantra's inherent meaning] to establish that they are ancillaries to the act of placing (*upadhāna*), so too should their status as ancillaries to worship (*arcana*) be understood. Since the status of being an ancillary to worship is perceived through the phrase "having performed the collective worship with the words 'May they be fully honored'," the weak hearing of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) does not constitute a sublater [of that status]. || 2 ||

Having recited the Karaśuddhi mantra and touched the Mistress of the Tripura-cakra with the syllable *drāṃ*, one should display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā. The names of the Cakra-yoginīs and the Mistress of the cakra are different; the rest is the same. || 3 ||

Here, by the term "purification of the hands" (*karaśuddhi*), one should recite the mantra that constitutes the limb of the *karaśuddhi* ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as taught in the section on ritual placements (*nyāsaprakaraṇa*).

[This *karaśuddhi* placement mantra is found in the third subsequent section (*pāścātya-tṛtīya-khaṇḍa*), in the 15th *sūtra* of the *Śrīkrama*, and its commentary on page 102. Having recited that, [one addresses] "Tripurā," the presiding goddess (*nāyikā*) of the *Trailokyamohana-cakra*.

"Tripurā-cakreśvarī" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the Mistress of the Wheel who is Tripurā. In the word "Tripurā," the absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). Having thus perceived and fully worshipped such a Mistress of the Wheel—here too, because it is of the nature of worship, the remainder of the mantra "Śrīpādukā" exists; however, in the collective worship (*samaṣṭyarcana*), it is "Śrīpādukām."

Since there is no remainder of the mantra, the word "iti" in the phrase "having performed the collective worship (samaṣṭyarcanaṃ vidhāya)" serves to exclude any further [mantric] residue. Having recited "drāṃ," which is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā—(p.
156)—[one should proceed].

One should display the *savaṃsaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā, which consists of the interlacing of the fingers, according to the method to be described; [the word] "of the Goddess" (*devyāḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, when the fingers are interlaced in the manner to be described in front of the Goddess, it is shown to her. The same should be understood for the subsequent [mudrās]. This being the case here:
Having stated the mantra for the collective worship (*samaṣṭhyarcana*) and the mantra of the presiding goddess of the wheel (*cakreśī*),

[in the upcoming fifth sūtra,] he extends certain syllables— after excluding some others— from the subsequent collective worship mantra and from the mantra of the presiding goddess of the wheel, saying "the wheel" (*cakra*).
The names of the wheels (*cakra*), such as "Fulfiller of All Desires" (*sarvāśāparipūraka*) and so forth,

will be mentioned in the subsequent sūtras that reveal their respective obscurations. The names of the Yoginīs, such as "Secret" (*guptā*) and so forth, and the names of the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*), such as "Tripurā" and so forth, are non-different from the phonemes (*varṇa*) of those [names].
The clusters of syllables beginning with "samudrāḥ" [as stated on folio 154, page 2, in sūtra 2: "the oceans together with the accomplishments," etc.
are the same. The meaning is that, in place of the names of the wheels (*cakra*) and so forth mentioned in their respective sections, the names to be mentioned hereafter should be recited. || 3 ||
The worship of the second enclosure:
Now he describes the worship of the second enclosure— on the sixteen petals [are] Kāmākarṣiṇī, and those ending with Nityākalā, [namely] Buddhyākarṣiṇī.
The attractor of ego, the attractor of sound, the attractor of touch, the attractor of form, the attractor of taste,

the attractor of smell, the attractor of mind, the attractor of fortitude, the attractor of memory, the attractor of name, the attractor of seed-syllables, the attractor of the self, the attractor of nectar, and the attractor of the body— these are the secret Yoginīs.

Having recited the self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) as before—beginning with "In the wheel that fulfills all hopes, the mudrās..."—and having worshipped Tripureśī, one should display the All-Enthraller (*sarvavidrāviṇī*) with the syllable *drīṃ*. (The object to be perceived is the visible realm. || 4 ||

The term "nityākala" refers to a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) that occurs at the end of a name; by this etymological derivation, this qualification is to be applied by attaching it to all fifteen [mantras] beginning with *buddhyākarṣiṇī*. In all cases, there is no masculine gender substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*), in accordance with the recitation of the first mantra. The remainder [of the formula] begins with "śrīpādukā," and so forth.

As before. Regarding the sequence for the sixteen-petaled [lotus], the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* states: "One should worship the Great Goddess on the sixteen-spoked [wheel] in counter-clockwise order (*vāmāvarta*). Furthermore, when there is a desire to know the specific detail as to from which petal the commencement therein should be made, it is established in the *Setubandha* that one should begin from the corner in front of the Goddess.
He states the names of the Yoginīs and the Cakra for the purpose of entering the mantra that is the subject at hand: "These are the Guptayoginīs.
With respect to the outer square (*bhūpura*), the Yoginīs residing there are "hidden" (*guptāḥ*) because they are situated within the sixteen-petaled lotus.
The remainder is the same; thus he reiterates the meaning already established by the preceding sūtra: "They possess their respective mudrās."
By this [statement], the purpose of the restatement is so that other words having that same meaning may not be inserted into the mantra; as before, "previously."

The meaning is "exactly as it was uttered. [In this section, on the following page 154, from the second sūtra beginning with "samudrāḥ" up to "santu," this is the meaning. Self-protection (ātmarakṣā) [is the mantra ending with the word "rakṣa" as stated in the sixteenth sūtra of the Śrīkrama on page 102, section 3]. That is its mantra. The rest is clear. || 4 ||
The third enclosure worship:
he describes the third enclosure worship—
on the petals of the directions.

Having contemplated these most secret Yoginīs— Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, Madanāturā, Ārekhā, Veginī, Aṅkuśā, Mālinī, and Anaṅgā— who are accompanied by their respective Mudrās within the *Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra*, and so forth; having recited the *ātmasana* as in the previous chapter and worshipped Tripurasundarī with the syllable *klīm*.
One should display the mudrā that attracts all. [Note: For the purpose of extracting this "mudrā that attracts all," see Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15–8/7 Vi. dṛśyaḥ. || 5 ||

Here, the word *dik* (direction) indicates the number eight, because the number eight exists in the directions. Thus, by the etymological derivation "that in which there are petals possessing a number residing in the directions," it refers to the third wheel.
Furthermore, the number eight in the directions is obtained by including the intermediate directions (*avāntaradiś*), [making] four...

According to the Vedic scripture, "the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions," the status of being a direction (*dig-tva*) remains uncontradicted even for the intermediate directions, by the maxim: "even if something has entered further [into a category], there is no loss of its original nature. The term *anaṅgapūrvāḥ* refers to those deities whose names begin with "Anaṅga" (Cupid), such as the deities of flowers and so forth mentioned previously.

In this context, the referent of the compound is a substance (*dravya*), not a collection of colors such as those of flowers and so forth, because otherwise the connection with the word "touching" (*saṃmṛśya*) would be untenable. Furthermore, the sequence for the worship of these deities is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"One should worship Anaṅgakusumā in the east and Anaṅgamekhalā in the south."
In the west is Anaṅgamadanā, and in the north is Madanāturā.
"Anaṅgarekhā in the southeast, Anaṅgaveginī in the southwest, Anaṅgāṅkuśā in the northwest, and Anaṅgamālinī in the northeast. Thus it is said.
Because they are internal to the deities of the previous wheel, these [deities] possess a state of being more secret; the rest is almost self-evident. || 5 ||
The worship of the fourth enclosure:
he describes the worship of the fourth enclosure—
on the spokes of the world [of the lotus] are Saṃkṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Āhlādinī, Saṃmohinī, and Stambhinī.

Jṛmbhiṇī, Vaśaṅkarī, Rañjanī, Unmādinī, Arthasādhinī, Sampattipūraṇī, Mantrayī, and Dvandvakṣayaṅkarī— having contemplated all these goddesses, beginning with Sarvā and ending with Dvandvakṣayaṅkarī (these fourteen deities have long vowels ending in -ī).
"The Sampradāyayoginīs are with their mudrās in the Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka-cakra" (p.
such is the remainder of the mantra after reciting the *cakrāsana* [as found on folio 103, recto, line 3].

In the *Śrīkrama*, this is the mantra for the Cakrāsana found in the commentary on the 18th Sūtra: "Having worshipped Tripuravāsinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), one should manifest the seal that brings all under control with the syllable *blūṃ*. [See Dvipayasīmantinī, 15.8]. || 6 ||

*Bhuvanāre* means on the fourteen-spoked [cakra]. There, the worlds (*bhuvana*)—fourteen in number—are the spokes (*āra*). The rest is like the "direction-petals" (as explained in the preceding twenty-eighth sūtra).
The phrase *sarva ādiḥ* ("the whole is the beginning") regarding the components of the name has also been largely explained by the rule *anaṅgapūrvāḥ*.

When there is a requirement for a sequence, according to the Yoginītantra, it is by the counter-clockwise order—starting from the west itself toward the south; thus, the meaning is that one begins in the west and then the south is to be taken from there.
The resulting sense is: "beginning from the west, in a non-pradakṣiṇa (counter-clockwise) direction. || 6 ||
The worship of the fifth enclosure:
he describes the worship of the fifth enclosure— on the outer ten-spoked [wheel].

Having first worshipped all these Yoginīs who have transcended the *kula*, namely Siddhipradā, Sampatpradā, Priyaṅkarī, Maṅgalakāriṇī, Kāmapradā, Duḥkhavimocinī, Mṛtyupraśamanī, Vighnanivāriṇī, Aṅgasundarī, and Saubhāgyadāyinī, within the wheel that accomplishes all aims (*sarvārthasādhakacakre*)...

Having stated the remainder of the *Manu* [note: the remainder of the *Manu* should be understood as extending from "the oceans" (*samudrāḥ*) on folio 154, section 2, sūtra 2 of this volume, up to "may they be" (*santu*)], having uttered the mantra of the throne (*mantrāsana*), [note: the mantra of the *cakrāsana* is found in the *Śrīkrama*, section 3, folio 103, sūtra 18 of the *Anugata*], [one should worship] Tripurā, the Mistress of the Śrīcakra.
Reflecting thus, he should bestow the seal of Unmādinī. || 7 ||
Within the nine wheels there are two sets of ten spokes; the meaning is "therein," referring to that which is the outer ten-spoked wheel among them.

The remainder has been largely explained. Here too, when there is a requirement for a sequence, the order is exactly as in the previous wheel, because the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* applies the sequence of the previous wheel by the phrase "in that very same way. (7)

The worship of the sixth enclosure: he describes the worship of the sixth enclosure— within the inner ten-spoked [lotus], [to the goddess] Jñānaśakti, who bestows sovereignty, consists of wisdom, and destroys disease, [is the] support...

These Garbhayoginīs— whose names are preceded by all [the appropriate] prefixes, who remove the sins of one's own nature, who consist of bliss, whose nature is protection, and who bestow desired fruits— should be worshipped in the Sarvarakṣākara-cakra. The remainder [is found in this section, 154–159].

On folio 2, from the word *samudrāḥ* up to *santu*, the remainder of the mantra should be understood. Likewise, having uttered the *sādhyasiddhāsana*, [this *sādhyasiddhāsana* mantra exists on folio 103 of the *Anugama*, in the 18th *sūtra* as taught in the *Śrīkrama*]: "Tripuramālinī is to be honored; *krom*."
One should display the Sarvamahāṅkuśā [as seen in Dvi-pa-śi 15-7/6]. || 8 ||

All the suffixes are preceded by all [the bases]. She is to be honored and worshipped. As for the sequence, it is as before—meaning counter-clockwise—according to the procedure previously stated from the *Yoginītantra*. The remainder is to be understood according to the previously explained method. || 8 ||

The worship of the seventh enclosure: he describes the worship of the seventh enclosure—on the eight-spoked [wheel], the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī; at the place where "namaḥ" occurs, [one should recite]: "These are the eight goddesses beginning with Vaśinī. (3)

[These are found in the *Khaṇḍa* on the *Śrīkrama*, in the 20th Sūtra, on leaf 104. These secret Yoginīs, whose names are the mantras of worship, reside in the wheel that removes all diseases (*sarvarogaharacakra*). The remainder is clear. Having uttered the Mūrtividyā [this Mūrtividyā mantra is found in the 4th *Khaṇḍa*, leaf 136, in the 2nd Sūtra], [Tripurāsiddhā].
Having propitiated Māra, the Khecarī [mudrā] should be bestowed with the mantra "śivabhṛgu-ṛddhiyukphreṃ. || 9 ||

In the section on the *yoginī-nyāsa*, regarding the eight mantras of Vaśinī and the others that have been extracted, one should perform the modification (*ūha*) by substituting the word "namaḥ" with the name of the worship mantra, specifically the mantra "Śrīpādukā.
This means that in place of the word "namaḥ" together with the dative case ending, the worship mantra should be employed; otherwise, [the rite would be ineffective].
Because there would be the contingency of hearing the fourth [case-ending], since that which was previously heard [as the first] would be heard [again] due to the absence of any sublater [of it].

Nor should it be argued that upon the removal of the word *namaḥ*, the dative case ending—which is conditioned by its connection [to that word]—is also removed, according to the maxim "when the cause ceases, the effect ceases. For the word *namaḥ* is not the cause for the existence of the dative case, but rather for its production. Thus, regarding that dative case which has been produced by taking the word *namaḥ* as its cause:
Because there is no sublation [of the cognition] while it remains until the point of its cessation.
Nor should it be argued that the word *namaḥ* must cease to exist even before the emergence of the dative case;
for if that were so, there would be no basis for the dative case itself due to the absence of its originator.

This is because, once it is established that the placement-mantra (*nyāsa-mantra*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the worship-mantra (*pūjā-mantra*), the dative case—along with the word *namaḥ*—is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the archetype.
The word *namaḥ* is sublated by the excellence of its appropriate arrangement; by what could the dative case-ending be sublated?

When the *nirvāpa* mantra, which includes the word *agni*, is obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*) in a Vedic rite, there is a sublation of the word *agni* alone by the word *sūrya* in a sacrifice to Sūrya due to a contradiction in meaning, but not of the dative case-ending. It is the same here as well. Therefore:
The worship mantra consists of the word "namaḥ" together with the fourth [case-ending], which supersedes [the others]; the rest is almost self-evident.
(160) The *mūrtividyā*, the mantra for the conceptualization of the form, has been stated in the section on invocation (*āvāhana*). Śiva is the letter *ha*;
Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*; and Ṛddhi is the letter *kha*. The authorities regarding this have been cited previously. [atra prākvāma-103-]

It should be understood that these have been shown in the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, section 18 of the third part of the *Śrīkrama*. The syllable *phreṃ* joined with those [syllables] becomes *hskhphreṃ*. The meaning is that having uttered this, one should reveal the *Khecarī*. || 9 ||
Regarding the worship of the weapons (*āyudhapūjā*), he says:
having uttered the seed-syllables of the arrows, [one should recite] "Homage to all expanding arrows, *dhaṃ thaṃ*."
"Āṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the bow for the sake of deluding all; Kroṃ, obeisance to the noose for the sake of subjugating all;
[obeisance] to the goad for the sake of paralyzing all"—thus is the worship of the weapons, beginning with the arrow, in the four directions outside the great triangle. || 10 ||
The "seeds of the arrows" are the seed-syllables of the five mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī, which are the arrows of Kāmeśvara.
As it is said in the *Kulasāra*:
"Indeed, those which are the five seed-syllables of the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī..."
O Goddess of the Gods, one should proclaim all of those at the beginning of the autumn month. Thus [it is said].
[The additional reading -ba. is: "the seed-syllables. This has been stated in the *Mālinītantra*:
"Having written two 'tha's situated in fire (ra) in sequence, they are adorned with a face (a), a circle (u), an eye (i), and a drop (m)."
This pair of arrows is declared to be the "Deluder," situated upon the ground.
O fair-faced one, it is enriched with the fourth vowel and the bindu, having the form of sound (nāda);
it is joined with the letter 'pha' (the last of the labials) by means of the wheel (the circle), and adorned with the left ear (the letter 'u').
O Dear One, the Moon, possessing the letter of creation (s), is joined with the Bindu and the Nāda.
"Know these five arrows to be mine, O beloved of my life. Thus [he said].

The meaning of this is as follows: in the sequence of the Mātṛkā, the letter *da* comes immediately after the letter *tha*. Having written that [letter] twice, one places the first *da* between them, conjoined with "fire," which is the letter *ra*.
This is the vowel *ā*, because in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, that is its designated position. And there is also the *bindu* (the nasal dot) added to those two.

Combined: *drāṃ* is thus formed. In the second letter *da* as well, there is the state of being situated in fire (*ra*), joined with that, followed by the "eye"—the left eye, the vowel *ī*—because of its position in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, and conjoined with the *bindu*; thus *drīṃ* is formed. In this way, the two seed-syllables are completed.

There are two *bāṇas*. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists of the first two *bāṇas*. Thus, *mādana* is the letter *ka*, and *bhūmi* is the letter *la*; it is situated therein with *la* below and *ka* above—this is the intended meaning.
It is enriched by the fourth vowel, *ī*, and the well-known *bindu*; thus, it is *klīm*.
It is complete. The letter *ba* is the phoneme *pha* with its vowel;
its etymology is like that of the letter *tha*. It is joined with the letter *la*, which is the wheel, and the left ear, which is the vowel *ū*; by means of that *bindu*.

And "vlūm" is properly formed by the combination [of *vi* and *lūm*]. *Sarga* (emission) and *visarga* (expulsion)—the moon possessing these is the letter *sa*; thus, it is *saḥ*. In this way, the meaning is: "Know these five to be my arrows: *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vlūṃ*, and *saḥ*. The seed-syllables of the arrows of Kāmeśvarī are given in the *Yoginītantra*:
"O Goddess of the Suras, skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these, joined with the second vowel [Ī], are his arrows. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: *tvak* (skin) is the letter *ya*, according to the lexicon which states, "the pervasive wind is *tvagvālī*"; *asṛk* (blood) is the letter *ra*, according to the lexicon which states, "*ro* is blood" and "*repha* is Krodhinī"; *māṃsa* (flesh) is the letter *la*, according to the lexicon which states, "Pinākī is designated as flesh"; *medas* (fat) is the letter *va*, according to the lexicon which states, "*vo* is fat" and "Varuṇa is subtle. [This continues] up to bone and marrow.

The letter *sa* has the color of semen (*śukra*) located in the final part [of the body], for according to the lexicon: "Bhṛgu, who has ten feet, is semen. Alternatively, as stated under the section on the letter *ṣa*: "The letters *sa* and *ṣa* are bone and marrow; the letter *śa* is declared by the wise to be known as the 'tusk-eared bone'"; and likewise: "Taurus is the Lord of the White, and marrow is yellow."

From the treasury: the meaning is that he resides at the end of those two. The aforementioned letters, when joined with the second vowel and conjoined with the letter *ā*, possess the union of the *bindu* as well, because they are of the nature of seed-syllables (*bīja*). Thus, *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *lāṃ*, *vāṃ*, and *sāṃ* are the arrow-seed-syllables (*bāṇabīja*) of the Goddess. Among the aforementioned letters—

In another Tantra, the *binduyoga* is described as follows: "All the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), the third sibilant (*uṣman*) accompanied by the *bindu*, *ananta*, and the [vowels] *ya-ra-la-va*. The semi-vowels are *ya-ra-la-va*; the third sibilant is *sa*; and *ananta* is the vowel *ā*. Here, by the term "seed-syllables of the arrows" (*bāṇabīja*), all of these are included:
*yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sāṃ*. (As stated in the *Setubandha*).

Having written the two mantras: "Obeisance to all the expanding Kāmeśvarī arrows: drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ" and "Obeisance to all the expanding Kāmeśvara arrows," and having further written before them, "And this has been stated in accordance with the Kalpasūtra," [one should know that] in reality, however, according to the Svatantra, it is at the beginning...

The meaning is that after pronouncing the ten seed-syllables of the arrows— namely, the two *dvitārīs* (the two preceding syllables), followed by the five beginning with *yāṃ* and the five beginning with *drāṃ*, making ten in total— one writes: "I worship the venerable sandals of the power of the arrow of universal expansion (*sarvajṛmbhaṇabāṇaśaktiśrīpādukām pūjayāmi*)."

In the *Nibandha*, however, having written down only the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kāmeśvara, the form of the mantra is written as "Obeisance to all the expanding arrows" (*sarvajṛmbhaṇebhyo bāṇebhyo namaḥ*). Since the status of being a "seed-syllable of an arrow" (*bāṇabījatva*) is common to both,
by the phrase "having uttered the seed-syllables of the arrows," it is understood that only the arrows of Śiva are to be uttered, and not those of the Goddess.

Since there was not even a scent of authoritative evidence to bring out the intention of the Blessed Rāma, and on the contrary, when considered by a gross standard of measurement, the worship of his arrows had already been commenced, it was appropriate to worship those very arrows. Setting aside [the Lord’s] arrows, he drew only the arrows of Śiva; that act of his was truly audacious.
And it should not be argued that, such being the case, the use of the singular number in the subsequent mantras—*dhanuṣe*, *pāśāya*, *aṅkuśāya*—would be untenable;
for its validity is possible by way of the principle established in the *Pāśādhikaraṇa*. Alternatively, having uttered the ten seed-syllables (*bīja*), [one should proceed].
"Salutation to all the *jṛmbhaṇa* arrows"—thus, the worship of the two [arrows] is performed by means of a single formula (*tantra*).

And their status as deities (*devatātva*) is intertwined like that of Agni and Soma. It is exactly the same in the case of the *pāśa* (noose) and the other [weapons]. And thus, just as in the expression "seeking the sacrificial food for the lord of the sacrifice," there is a single deityhood residing in the pair of bows.
Because [the deity] is present [in all], and because that which is delimited by the nature of being a deity is one (p.
162), the use of the singular number is justified with reference to that; and the plural number following the word *bāṇa* [is likewise justified].
Since it conforms to being presided over by the deities, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, just as in the expression "medha for the two lords of the sacrifice" (*medhapatibhyām medham*).

Let it be that the author of the *Nibandha* did not err while enumerating the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Śiva and Bāṇa; however, because this occurs within the section on Lalitā, only the seed-syllables of Śakti and Bāṇa are to be understood here.
This is because, although the *Kalpasūtra* mentions "having uttered the Bāṇa-seed-syllables" without qualification, the context (*prakaraṇa*) determines the specific meaning.
It should be stated that this is because [the practice] is observed in such cases as "one worships the Āgnīdhra fire-shed from the southeast" (*saṅkocasya āgneyyā'gnīdhramupatiṣṭhate*).
O Maheśānī, one should worship the arrows of Kāma, his bow, and likewise his noose,
in sequence within the four corners in the middle of the wheel.

Thus, by the statement of the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, the worship of those very weapons of Śiva is prescribed within the section on Lalitā; however, in the present *Kalpasūtra*, where it is heard without qualification that "one should utter the seed-syllables of Bāṇa," when a restriction must be made by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), this is superseded by another statement which is even more powerful than that context.

Because the application is restricted solely to that which is explicitly heard [in the text], there is a disparity: in the case of "He worships the Āgnīdhra altar with an Āgneyī verse," there is no other statement that overrides the context (prakaraṇa).

Nor does this constitute a loss of the thesis— that one does not rely on other tantras— because there is no inconsistency in the thesis if one follows other statements for the sake of determining the meaning of the Sūtra.

Furthermore, in many manuscripts, the reading in the *Kalpasūtra* is: "Dhaṃ thaṃ, obeisance to the bow for the purpose of deluding all; Āṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the noose for the purpose of subjugating all. This too is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the grasping of the two arrows; otherwise, [the mantra] would apply to both the bow and the arrow as connected entities.
Why should one recite the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) that indicate the grasping? Furthermore, this very reading is observed in many manuscripts.

Therefore, the worship of both is mandatory. Even if it is considered that the establishment of the [opponent's] view is certain because the reading of the two seed-syllables is not seen in some manuscripts, even then—
In all manuscripts, without dispute, the seed-syllable of Śiva’s bow (*śivadhanurbīja*) is *dhaṃ* in the bow-mantra;

it is the fourth [letter] from the "Aruṇa-group" (the dental class), and also the second from the same, O Pārvatī—thus [it is stated] in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*: "The pair of male and female bows. The meaning of this is: the "Aruṇa-group" is the dental class (*tavarga*); therein, the fourth is the letter *dha*.

The second *thakāra* signifies, in sequence, the male and female bows; by this, *dhaṃ* is established as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śiva’s bow. Likewise, *hrīṃ* for the noose (*pāśa*) exists without dispute in all manuscripts.
And that is the seed-syllable of the Śakti-noose, because of the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "Māyā is called the female noose. Thus...

In some places there is a description of the male weapon-seeds, and in others a description of the female weapon-seeds; this form of composition, involving the grasping of both types of weapons, is a characteristic common to all manuscripts. Furthermore, the statement from another tantra has already been written down clearly. Thus, the application of the singular number has been demonstrated.
Since there is no contradiction, it appears to me without doubt that both weapons are to be worshipped here;
let the virtuous and wise examine this further, as the nature of Dharma transcends the senses.
And thus, in whichever manuscript there is only "dhaṃ" in the mantra for the bow, that is "thaṃ."
This also indicates the syllable *hrīṃ* in the third mantra, and it indicates *ām* as well,
because that [syllable] has the nature of Śiva’s fetter (*pāśa*), according to the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*: "The great fetter of the Puruṣa is proclaimed to reside at the beginning and the end."

This meaning was also previously explained during the extraction of the *nīlapatākā* mantra. As for the *aṅkuśa* seed-syllable, however, it is common to both [mantras] because the *Yoginītantra* reads without distinction: "Kāma, Agni, the pervasive, and the *aṅkuśa*."
In this system, there is a single recitation by means of the *tantra* (conjunction). Thus, the nature of the mantra is as follows:
*yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sāṃ drāṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ sarvajṛmbhaṇebhyo bāṇebhyo namaḥ bāṇaśrīpādukāṃ [bāṇaśaktiśrī-śrī. pūjayāmi | thaṃ dhaṃ*.

"Salutation to the bow for the purpose of deluding all; I worship the auspicious sandals of the bow. Hrīṃ Āṃ, salutation to the noose for the purpose of subjugating all; [I worship] the auspicious sandals of the noose. Kroṃ, salutation to the goad for the purpose of paralyzing all; [I worship] the auspicious sandals of the goad. Thus, when the seed-syllables of power (śakti-bījas) come first.
Its predominance is the indicator.

However, some followers of Tantra, having uttered the ten seed-syllables, recite: "Oṃ Kāmeśvara-kāmeśvarī-bāṇebhyo namaḥ. That is extremely incorrect; because the term "kāmeśvarī" (feminine) and "kāmeśvara" (masculine) form a *dvandva* compound, the rule "pumān striyā" (when a male and a female are mentioned together, the masculine remains as a single remainder) would apply, resulting in a singular form, not a *dvandva*.

A great triangle is the first triangle; outside of it, within an eight-pointed [figure], there are triangles in the cardinal directions starting from the west and proceeding clockwise. As it is stated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
"The western, northern, eastern, and southern directions in sequence."

In this commentary, regarding the weapon-mantras (*āyudhamantra*), if there is no application of the word "śrīpādukām" as a supplement, one must consult that very source for the original authority (*mūla*).
Furthermore, the statement "the eight-syllable mantra is to be preceded by 'Śrī' and followed by 'pādukā' and so forth in all names of deities"—

by the phrase "in the names of deities," it is indicated that the eight-syllable mantra is applied only where the name of a deity is taken; there, having first grasped the name of that respective deity, one says "Śrī-pādukām."

"I worship"—this very eight-syllable mantra has been stated previously as well, and not elsewhere. It should not be argued that it is not so because, in the present prescriptive statement (*vidhāyaka-vākya*), there is no mention of names such as Bāṇa and others; for the commentator (*nibandhakāra*) must necessarily [interpret] the phrase "in the names of the deities" (*devatānāmasu*) as meaning "in mantras composed of the names of the deities."

This must be stated: otherwise, their connection within the three currents would be contradicted in reality. In that regard, there is no mention of deities in the injunctive statement; rather, there are only the three currents. Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence. || 10 ||
The worship of the eighth enclosure:
he describes the worship of the eighth enclosure—
[the deities] preceded by all [of the previous ones], beginning with Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti, in the triangle.
The great goddesses Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī; the fourth is in the bindu. 11.
That supreme power (*parā śakti*), which is of the nature of light belonging to the lamp that is the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*), becomes threefold when oriented toward emanation (*sṛṣṭi*):

namely, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. These are, respectively, predominated by *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*. The term used in the Tantric scriptures to denote their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) is "Ambikā. These very [powers] are, in order:

These are called the powers of will, knowledge, and action. In order to make known that these constitute the individualized form (*vyaṣṭi*) of Tripurasundarī, [the author] later applied the qualification "most secret" (*atirahasya*) to the Yoginīs. In this regard:

By the term *vāgbhava*, the first *kūṭa* is to be understood; by the term *kāma*, the second *kūṭa*; and by the term *śakti*, the third *kūṭa*. However, these are not the individual letters of the *Bālā*, for in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, it is specifically the *kūṭas* that are intended.

Because it has been so accepted. Although in other tantras a conjunction of both the *vāgbhava* and the first *kūṭa* is seen, nevertheless, since only the [seeds] such as *vāk* and so forth are mentioned here, one should take only the *kūṭas* in accordance with the *Yoginītantra*.
This refers to the entire triad of *kūṭas*. These are those of which [it was said] previously...
The meaning is that those four [deities] are to be worshipped by name in the triangle—that is, in the three corners of the triangle and at the point (bindu).

The author of the commentary (*nibandhakāra*) wrote "Lalitāśrī" as the internal common root for the mantra of the fourth deity. That is trivial; for while the names of the four deities appear in sequence in the *sūtra* as Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Mahādevī, [the commentator] has disregarded what is well-established in the scriptures.

He introduced the name "Lalitā," which was fabricated by his own imagination, into the mantra; in this matter, scripture is not an authority. Even regarding mantras of inconceivable power, those who habitually act according to their own whims—great men even place their trust in their words. The root cause here is simply the laziness born of the illusory power (māyā) of the Blessed Lord.

It is not otherwise. Nor should it be argued that the word *lalitā* is merely a synonym for *mahādevī*, and therefore there is no obstacle to its usage; for if one were to use the phrase *vahnim īle* (I praise the fire) in place of the mantra *agnim īle*, it would result in something unprecedented. Enough of this improper obsession.
The sequence is stated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
"Kāmeśvarī in the front corner, then Vajreśī in the south, likewise Bhagamālinī in the north, and Tripurasundarī in the center. (11)
Regarding the non-difference of Kāmeśvarī and the others from the Root Goddess:
indeed, it has been enjoined that one should worship with the mantras of the fifteen Nityās and with the Root-Vidyā;
likewise, in the present context, worship with the Root-Mantra for the Fourth Deity is mentioned, and he will also state this for the Bindu-cakra.

The worship with the root mantra is likewise performed for the Mistress of the Final Wheel as well. Thus, since the three sacrifices are performed by means of a single mantra, there may arise the doubt whether they constitute a single deity worshipped in the form of repetition, or whether they involve distinct deities; [the author] establishes the identity of the deity as follows:
Immediately following these three, there is the worship of the Root Goddess (Mūladevī) for the sake of non-differentiation.

The fourth [Goddess], Kāmeśvarī, and the others among the sixteen Nityās, as well as the ninth, who resides in the Bindu-cakra—these are all one and the same. One should not conceive of any distinction between the mantra and the deity therein; she is that Great Goddess.
Thus, the special worship is repeated at four locations. || 12 ||
p.

165) Immediately following these three, Kāmeśvarī and the others, there is the worship of the Root Goddess (mūladevī) in order to demonstrate that they are non-different from her. This is likewise the case in other contexts as well.

The worship at the end of Tripurasundarī indicates the non-difference between each [deity] and their respective preceding deity-cluster (kūṭa). He clarifies this very point with the words "Kāmeśvarī" and so forth: in the present wheel, [the mantra] following Kāmeśvarī and the others is the fourteenth [nityā], while that following the fifteen nityās is the sixteenth.

Beyond the eight wheels, in the ninth *bindu*, she who is indicated by the letter *ca* is again to be worshipped as the sole Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*) within that very *bindu*, following the worship of the Mistress of the eight wheels. In these instances, there is no difference in the deity nor any difference in the mantra. Thus, all the eternal goddesses of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) are one.

The intention is that it is stated at the end of each [section] in order to make known that [the deities] are non-different from Tripurasundarī. Now, one might object: "If there is identity of deity, identity of substance, and identity of mantra, then worship performed only once would be appropriate; why then are there three worships? To this he replies: "Special worship is repeated in four locations. This means: in the four locations already indicated.

And thus, even though the sacrifice is one, the sense is that the repetition of it is necessary because it serves as the means for producing the *apūrva*. Nor should it be argued that if there is repetition, the mantra should not be repeated— just as the *prokṣaṇa* mantra is not repeated—
because in cases such as the *agnihotra*, the mantra is indeed repeated despite the repetition [of the action] when there is an intervention by another act.

Because it has been observed [in other cases]. Likewise, here too, even though the action consists of repetition, the repetition of the mantra is justified by the intervention of another action of a different genus. || 12 ||
Having spoken incidentally, he states the subject at hand:
"These are the most secret Yoginīs in the wheel that bestows all accomplishments; the remainder is to be observed.
Having uttered the *āvāhanī* (invocation), [this is the *āvāhanī* mantra found on folio 4, section kha, chapter 3, in the Sūtra and its commentary]: [Mantra follows] This is the *āvāhanī* mantra.
Then, having honored Tripurāmbā—[the object of perception] or rather [the subject]—one should assume the form of the seed-syllable and mudrā, *hsaum*. 13.

The word "remaining" (pariśiṣṭam) implies that what follows is as before; this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Āvāhanī" is the vidyā extracted from that specific context. "Having honored" means having worshipped. "Kṛtiḥ" means it should be performed. || 13 ||
Regarding the worship of the ninth enclosure, he says:
having worshipped the Goddess with the root mantra in the *bindu*-cakra, she is this Parāpararahasyayoginī within the All-Blessed (*sarvānandamaya*).
"May Cakreśvarī, together with the ocean, along with her siddhis, weapons, powers, vehicles, and retinue, be fully worshipped with all offerings"—

having thus recited the root mantra once more and worshipped the Great Mistress of the Wheel (Mahācakreśvarī), one should display the Yoni-mudrā by means of the Vāgbhava-mantra. [These two mudrās are for the two objects of perception.]

166) Here too, the author of the commentary (nibandhakāra) appended the phrase "I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Lalitā" at the end of the root [mantra]. That is incorrect; for in the preceding sūtra, it was stated that no distinction between the mantra and the deity should be made there.

In the statement "that [is] for the Great Goddess alone in four places," it is explicitly stated by direct utterance that the worship of the Great Goddess is to be performed in all four locations. To abandon a word heard in the scripture and imagine a word not heard therein is unscriptural;
otherwise, one would have to interpret the injunction, "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," [in an unintended way].
Thus, in this sacrifice, by inserting a synonym for Sūrya, the formula would be "I offer what is pleasing to Divākara.

Nor should it be argued that there is a discrepancy because the word "Sūrya" was heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) there, whereas here the preceding sūtra is not an originative injunction but rather prescribes a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the form of a repetition.
This is not an absolute rule that the hearing of the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) itself must be required.

For instance, regarding the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) of the Nakṣatreṣṭi, the originative injunction is merely this much: "He offers here. No word denoting a deity is heard there. Nevertheless, in the mantra, [it says]: "Svāhā to Agni, to the Kṛttikās."

Regarding the word "svāhā," when the term for Agni or another deity is heard therein, they employ the expression "agnim ājyena" (Agni with clarified butter) during the initial anvādhāna rite, and not "vahnim ājyena" (Vahni with clarified butter).
If the rule were restricted solely to the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), then one could act here according to one's own preference; however, such is not the case for this sequence.

The intention of the *nibandha* (commentary) can be described as follows: since the word "Lalitā" is explicitly heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)—"one should begin the sequence of Lalitā, the sole mistress of the wheel of powers"—her inclusion [in the subsequent rule] is justified.
If that were the case, then instead of omitting her, one would have had to state in the preceding sūtra: "of Lalitā alone in four places."

Even Brahmā is unable to describe the fruit of saying "of the Great Goddess" alone. In my view, however, although the two words *Lalitā* and *Mahādevī* have the same meaning, where no distinction is heard [in the text], the word *Lalitā* is used; whereas where it is heard, the utterance of the word as it was heard produces something unprecedented (*apūrva*).

Having understood that there must be a renunciation of the word "Lalitā," one should state the result as "for the pleasure of Śrī Lalitā" at the beginning of the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth. In the present context, however, it is appropriate to employ the term "Mahādevī," which leaves no room for other interpretations. Therefore, by this same principle, when the term "Mahādevī" is obtained within the mantra of the ninth Cakreśvarī:
Specifically, because it is heard there [in the scripture] that "having worshipped Cakreśī," the term *mahādevī* is set aside, according to the maxim:

"Between that which has scope and that which has no scope, the one with no scope is stronger. Nor does this imply that while the non-difference of the mantras was demonstrated in four [verses], now—in three [cases]—the mantra containing *mahādevī* occurs in only one.

As for the objection that "the mantra-break [reading] *mahācakreśvarīghaṭita* has fallen [into error); how can this be?"—it should be stated that this fault is common to both [versions] and thus is not a valid objection, since the author of the *Nibandha* also wrote *lalitāmahācakreśvarīśrī*. On the contrary, it is the mantra of the *Nibandha* author...

Due to its composition with *lalitāpada*, there is an absolute difference [between this and the previous]. In my view, by merely substituting *cakreśvarī* in place of *devī*, the resolution will be achieved by relying on the grammatical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]"; enough of this excessive detail.
The etymological derivation of the term *Mahādevī* is given in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Since her body is vast and immeasurable in its dimensions,
and because the verbal root *maha* signifies 'to worship,' she is therefore remembered as *Mahādevī*."

By means of the *vāgbhava* syllable, namely *aiṃ*, that is, by the first *kūṭa*; for since a single phoneme is observed among the seeds of the eight previous mudrās, it is necessary that this [syllable] situated in that same row be of the same nature.
Therefore, it is appropriate to take *aiṃ* alone. || 14 ||
167) Having thus performed the worship of the nine enclosures (navāvaraṇapūjā), including the offering of incense and so forth, he states the remainder of the ritual actions to be performed next:
Having offered incense, lamps, mudrās, libations, food offerings, and so forth, as before [as seen in the second chapter, section fifteen of the Viśeṣa-dṛśya].
