Regarding the phrase "for the sake of attaining the previously mentioned qualities" at the end of the offerings of incense and so forth, the term "previously mentioned qualities" should be understood here as referring to the qualities taught in the sequence of Sūtras 4, 6, and 7. Thus, it is "as before" in relation to the incense and other offerings.

The meaning is that those previously mentioned attributes (*dharmas*)—namely incense and so forth—should be performed as possessing those attributes. Those attributes are to be understood as follows: for incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*), they are the previously mentioned mantras; for the ritual gestures (*mudrās*), they are the same as before; and for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), they consist of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) repeated three times. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
Substances such as betel leaves, camphor, and the waving of lamps (nīrājana), as well as the kindling of fire and so forth, are to be accepted.
The author of the Nibandha, being a worshiper of the Ṣoḍaśī, stated that one should also display the Trikhaṇḍā;
however, he was mistaken, as such a rule is not mentioned in the Sūkta.
The essential nature of the mudrās beginning with Trikhaṇḍā is presented here for the purpose of demonstrating the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī.
[This is the extraction of all mudrās, from Saṃkṣobhiṇī up to Yonimudrā; Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15].

[It is visible in the object. Since the knowledge of its specific nature is necessary, the method for displaying that mudrā is briefly stated here along with its authoritative basis. In this regard, the *trikhaṇḍā* is first mentioned as being employed during the invocation (*āvāhana*). The definition of the *trikhaṇḍā* has been stated [as follows]:
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
Having crossed the hands and touched them together, one should make the two thumbs equal;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers.
"O Maheśvarī, one should employ the little finger in its own place;
this is declared to be the 'Three-Sectioned' [mudrā] for the rite of summoning Tripurā. Thus it is said.

*Parivartana* (the turning) consists of the joining of the fingers of both hands. This form of authority accompanies [the rite] everywhere. One should make the two thumbs straight and touching each other, and likewise do so for the little fingers and the middle fingers. Having extended the right ring finger obliquely over the left ring finger, from the region below those two—

Having brought the two index fingers together in a curved shape, one should hold the tips of the two ring fingers with those two index fingers. The meaning obtained from the analysis of the compound *anāmike antargate* is as follows: when this [mudrā] is formed according to the stated method, three sections are visible. At the top is the joining of the two straightened thumbs; in the middle...

The union with the Middle [Finger] (Madhyamā) is of that same nature; and likewise, the union with the Little Finger (Kaniṣṭhā) below is of that same nature. This being so, the three digits (kalās)—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—previously mentioned, are clearly manifest within this [Mudrā].
Therefore, although the analysis of the compound *trikhaṇḍā* here is "that in which there are three segments (khaṇḍas), namely the digits (kalās)," [it refers to this state].
The method for constructing the two sections has been explained; however, the method for arranging the middle section has not been stated.

Nevertheless, in order to fulfill the etymological meaning of "three-sectioned" (*trikhaṇḍā*), one should complete the three sections by taking recourse to another tantra. The three sections are described in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Maheśānī, by means of the yoga of rotating the two hands,
O Dear One, one should join them and hold the ring fingers with the two index fingers.

One should join the two middle fingers together at their centers, then place the two little fingers below them; likewise, having joined the two thumbs, one should arrange them in three pairs according to this sequence.
"This three-part mudrā of mine is for the purpose of summoning Tripurā. Thus [it is said].
The nature of Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī is described in that very same [text]:
Having placed [the hands] in the middle with the middle fingers meeting, the little fingers and thumbs pressed together,
the index fingers made like staves, and the ring fingers above the middle fingers.
But this first mudrā is the agitator of all. Thus it is said.
In the *Tantrarāja*, however, it is said:
"Having joined the nails of the little finger, the ring finger,
and the middle finger together, one should place the two thumbs upon the positions of the little fingers and straighten the index fingers."
The seal that agitates all is the agitator of the three worlds. Thus it is said.
The *sarvavidrāviṇī* mudrā is described in that same [text]: "O Maheśānī, if the middle fingers of this very mudrā are made straight, then it becomes the *sarvavidrāviṇī*."
The phrase "in each middle [finger]" means for the sake of non-curve. By this, the straightness of both the index and middle fingers is to be understood.
The third mudrā is also described in that same place: "O fair-eyed one, one should bend the pair of middle and index fingers."
"This very mudrā is that which effects their attraction. Thus [it is said].
In that very context, the fourth mudrā, which brings all under control, is described:
having formed the hands in the shape of a hollowed cup, with the two index fingers shaped like hooks,
one should turn them in sequence so that the middle fingers lie beneath them.
Gradually, O Goddess, having joined the little finger and the ring finger in that same manner, all [the fingers] should be made firm at the tips of the thumbs.
"O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is known as the one that brings all under control. Thus it is said.
The meaning of this is as follows: having formed the two hands into the shape of a hollowed vessel (*puṭa*), with their backs joined to each other and the fingers pointing upward;

then, having inserted the fingers—excluding the thumbs—into the joints of one another's fingers, one should make the fingers, from the index finger to the little finger, take the form of a hook (*aṅkuśa*). Having done so:
Then one should place both thumbs facing downward upon the index fingers; this is the "All-Subjugating" (Sarvavaśaṅkarī) mudrā—such is the intended meaning.
The fifth [mudrā] is also in that same [context]:
having brought the two hands face-to-face, with the little finger placed between the middle fingers.
The two index fingers are straightened out on the outside of that ring finger.
Then, the two thumbs are shaped like staffs and placed at the tips of the nails of the middle fingers;
this mudrā is named Unmādinī, which causes all women to become moist with passion. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: one should extend the right little finger over the left little finger along the path above the two ring fingers up to the middle fingers; then, one should firmly grasp the tips of those two little fingers with the two middle fingers. Over the nails of the grasped middle fingers, the two thumbs should be placed in the form of a staff.

One should place [the ring fingers] thus; likewise, one should make the two ring fingers straight and facing each other. One should also make the two index fingers straight on both sides of the two ring fingers. This is the Sarvonmādinī mudrā, which brings women under one's control.
The sixth mudrā, Sarvamahāṅkuśā, is also revealed in that very same place:
"Having placed the pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a hook, one should likewise apply the two index fingers in that same sequence."
This is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes and goals. Thus it is said.

Of this [mudrā] of the All-Intoxicating One: by that very sequence, namely the sequence of the ring fingers; the ring fingers are in the shape of a hook (aṅkuśa). In the same way, both index fingers should also be formed. The remainder is like the previous mudrā—this is the intended meaning.

Therein he explained the seventh, the Khecarīmudrā: "O Maheśānī, having placed the left hand upon the right and the right hand upon the left, and having crossed the two arms, one should rotate the hands."
O Goddess, having joined the little finger and the ring finger in that same sequence,
both middle fingers are likewise pressed down from above by the two index fingers.
O Maheśānī, one should also make the two thumbs straight;
this, O beloved, is the mudrā named Khecarī, the most excellent of all.

The meaning of this is as follows: first making the two arms straight, one should place the left arm upon the right; then, having passed the left hand along the underside of the right hand toward the left side, one should interlace the fingers of both hands in the manner to be described. That is as follows:
Having led [the fingers] from the left ring finger and little finger down through the right middle finger to the right index finger,
and likewise having led them from the right ring finger and little finger down through the left middle finger to the left index finger,
one should firmly hold the ring and little fingers of both hands as they come near with the two index fingers.
One should grasp them. In the middle [position], one should place both [fingers] entirely upright, straight, and joined together at their tips.
Having made the two thumbs straight, one should bring about a resemblance to a vulva (*yonisādṛśya*).
This is the Khecarīmudrā. Although all the aforementioned meanings are not present in the previously cited statement, nevertheless—
Having placed the left arm upon the right arm and the right [arm] upon the region of the left, one should subsequently join them by turning them in due order.
One should restrain [the breath] with the two index fingers upon the pair of the little and ring fingers;
then, having made the two middle fingers straight, they should likewise be straight like a *yoni*.
The two thumbs joined in the khecarī mudrā are placed at the earthly station (pārthivasthāna).
Thus, the meaning should be understood as having been elicited by bringing it into syntactic agreement with the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*.
The eighth mudrā is also revealed in that very same place: "O Dear One, having turned the two hands over and touched them so as to form the shape of a half-moon,
one should then simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs."
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down upon the little fingers below;
likewise, the two ring fingers should be joined at the very bottom in a curved position.
"This is the seed-seal (bījamudrā), which swiftly brings about all accomplishments. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should position the two ring fingers (anāmikā) crossed over the path of the two middle fingers (madhyamā), such that the middle fingers rest upon the lower part of the ring fingers. Then, one should arrange it so that the pair of middle fingers is supported by the pair of ring fingers, with both ring fingers situated at the very bottom.
One should join them until they become curved; one should join the pair of the thumb and index finger so that it takes the shape of a half-moon. This is the *bījamudrā*.
He specifies the ninth, the *yonimudrā*, in that very context: "The two middle fingers are positioned curved over the index fingers;
likewise, the two little fingers are placed between the ring fingers."
Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs—this is the first mudrā, which is known as the yoni-mudrā. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should place the two ring fingers (anāmikā) crossed over the middle phalanges of the two middle fingers (madhyamā) along the downward path, with the tips of the index fingers (tarjanī) curved above them. One should join the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā), which are crossed and touching the backs of the ring fingers.
One should join the two tips of the thumbs (aṅguṣṭha) to the two middle phalanges of the middle fingers. This is the Yoni-mudrā.
It occurs. Even if this specific meaning is not obtained from that statement, nevertheless:
"On the back of the ring finger, at the middle joint of the middle finger, by the joining of the little finger and the thumb, the Mahāyoni is formed as the Trikhāṇḍikā."
Thus, in another place [it is said]: "The meaning of this is that which is *trikhaṇḍā* is the *mahāyoni*. From that, however, there is this distinction:

the joining of the thumbs at the middle joints; the joining of the little fingers by means of the back part of the ring fingers. The rest is the same as in the *trikhaṇḍā*—this is the meaning. Together with this...
When the unity of meaning of the preceding statement is established, the meaning written previously is accomplished.
p.

171) Thus, the ten mudrās, which are supremely profound, have been explained in detail along with their arguments and authorities according to my understanding as a digression. Let us now return to the subject at hand. || 15 ||
Now, he begins to explain the meditation on the *kāmakalā*:
"Having formed the face with one *bindu*, the two breasts with two *bindus*, and the vulva with the latter half [of the *kalā*], one meditates upon the *kāmakalā*."
Having meditated. || 16 ||

Meditation on the *kāmakalā* is of two kinds: subtle (*sūkṣma*) and gross (*sthūla*). Among these, the meditation on the subtle *kāmakalā* has been explained in detail by our supreme preceptors in the *Setubandha*, a commentary on the *Uttaracatuśśatī*, and in the *Varivasyārahasya*.

Since this has already been explained, for such a practitioner—the foremost of devotees who performs such meditation—that writing [of this treatise] would now be like the horns of a hare; it would merely serve to display one's own pedantry, like the study of the Vedānta scriptures in the present day. Therefore, having first set that aside...
We shall describe only the gross [form], for the benefit of those of duller faculties.

For example, having conceived three parts within the fourth vowel or the letter *ha*, and having conceived there the form of a woman: one should conceive the face in the upper part, the pair of breasts in the middle part, and [the lower body] in the lowest part.
And having performed the visualization of the *yoni*, one should meditate. As it is said in the *Kuṇḍalinīvimarśa*:

"One who is adept in internal contemplation within the portions imagined in the center of the Power (*śakti*) should contemplate [the faces] as being above, in the middle, and below, respectively—the face, the breasts, and the downward-facing [vagina]."
In this verse, many hold that the meaning of the word *śakti* is the vowel *ī*; some, however, say it is the letter *ha*.

Its meaning is the downward-facing *yoni*. The rest is clear. One who meditates upon you, O Queen of Hara—having made the *bindu* the face, the pair of breasts below it, and below that the half-moon of Hara—is [the embodiment of] the art of Love.
Thus it has also been stated by the venerable Bhāgavatapāda. In the *Setubandha*, however, the gross meditation (*sthūladhyāna*) on the syllable *ī* alone is taught in the following verse:

"When one contemplates the syllable *ī*—which consists of the bindu and visarga, and which is the nature of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti—as one's own self, there arises the experience of supreme bliss. This is like the perception of Viṣṇu in a *sālagrāma* stone.

This is the rule for the meditative concentration (*dhyāna-adhiṣṭhāna*) upon the Blessed Lady. Thus, one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been conquered by gross meditation (*sthūla-dhyāna*), and who is like the crest-jewel of such a worshipper, should—having learned from the mouth of the Guru the subtle art (*sūkṣma-kalā*) as written in the *Setubandha* and other texts—worship according to his desire; others may not.

Those of the present day are suited for that [coarse meditation]. And such meditation is obtainable solely through the grace of the Supreme Deity and the venerable Guru. This point has been very clearly stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"If one is incapable of subtle meditation, one should meditate on the gross according to what has been taught. And thus:

Having placed the face, the two breasts, and the vulva upon any one of the previously mentioned syllables within the three parts, and having mentally fashioned the *kāmakalā* according to the method to be described [meaning: in accordance with the statements found in both the commentary on the seventeenth sūtra located below], one should meditate [in whatever space is available]. || 16 ||
Following the previously mentioned conceptualization of the limbs for each specific color, he describes the particular mode of meditation regarding the distinguished [form]:
"Having touched the heart of auspiciousness" (17).

(172) The "heart" of good fortune— that is to say, the locus and the material cause of all human goals such as dharma and the rest— having contemplated and meditated upon it in the form previously described.
The word "iti" from the preceding sūtra is also carried over here. This very meaning has been clearly stated in the Yoginītantra:
"In this way, that syllable which has arisen in the form of Kāmakalā..."
"O Supreme Goddess, it is the abode of the liberation from the poisons of desire and the rest. Thus [it is said].

Regarding this, the statement in the *Nibandha* that the fire-oblation (*homa*) is optional is baseless; for there is no authority elsewhere to extend the application of the sūtra "if the performance of the fire-rite is accomplished," which occurs within the section on Gaṇapati. || 17 ||
Now, regarding the offering of oblations (balidāna), he describes the types of offerings:
having drawn a triangle, a circle, and a square on the left side and worshipped them with perfumes and unbroken rice grains, one should utter the Vāgbhava syllable.
Having placed the primary, secondary, and intermediate vessels there with water filled half-way with rice grains, [reciting] "Obeisance to the Pervasive Mandala. || 18 ||
Here, by the phrase "on the left side," one's own left side is to be understood because it is the first to come to mind.

Regarding the "constructed" (vihite), meaning fashioned as a triangle, a circle, and a square: according to the method of emergence (*nirgamarīti*), the triangle should be taken as facing oneself, in accordance with the tradition of the learned.

However, some maintain that the deity who receives the offering in the triangle faces toward the corner formed by the junction of the two horizontal lines, because there is a fixed rule that the deities residing within the triangle face in that manner. And thus it is said in another Tantra:
Having meditated upon [the goddess] facing Mūladevī, one should place the vessel for the bali offering before her.

Because of this statement, there is a rule that the goddess must be oriented toward the Root Goddess (Mūladevī); thus they say that even the triangle must face the Goddess alone and not toward oneself. That is not so, for in the triangles situated within the Śrīcakra of Anaṅgakusumā and the others, [the goddesses] are turned away from the corners.
Since many deities facing Mūladevī are actually perceived, such a restrictive rule is unestablished; therefore, this [objection] amounts to nothing.
By the phrase "perfumes, unbroken rice," etc., the exclusion of other [substances] is indicated. He states the mantra for the worship:

"the Vāgbhava," and so forth. The Vāgbhava is *aiṃ*. The remainder is clear. "Filled with half" means accompanied by food (*bhakta*) and water; this is an adjective qualifying the vessel. In a single bowl.

One should fill half the vessel with food and half with water. Having placed one such vessel and three vessels of milk and other substances there upon the mandala, one should place the offering vessel (balipātra) made of copper;
the offering vessel must be made of copper and never anything else.

Thus, according to the statement from the *Tripurārṇava*: "One should not mix [the substance] with spices and the like, because in this Tantra, the requirement for a substance is satisfied by the very material prescribed here."
173) Here, the author of the commentary has recorded the offering of a sacrifice with a seal of the *bāṇa* [mudrā], the striking of the left heel, and so forth.
He should be asked: "What is the authority for this? If he should reply that it is found in the sūtra of the *Śyāmāprakaraṇa*:

If it is argued that "because they have been mentioned [elsewhere], those same factors (*dharmas*) are included here as well," then is that inclusion due to a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) or without a requirement? In the first case, regarding the offering to Bali (*balidāna*), the requirement for the substance, deity, and mantra was raised, but it has already been satisfied by the very words of the original context (*prakṛta-vākya*). Therefore, the inclusion of the *bāṇamudrā* and the striking with the left heel is [not justified].

Furthermore, we do not know what kind of desire could have arisen for him while he was performing that very act. Moreover, what harm has been done by the ritual elements such as the striking with the heel found in the section on the Śyāmā?
Offerings (*bali*) to Kṣetrapāla, Vāgīśvarī, and others are also present there; indeed, there are other mantras as well besides those already mentioned.

[They] exist. What offense has been committed by the author of the treatise? For, although the status of being situated within the *Śyāmā-prakaraṇa* is equal [in all cases], we do not know the root reason why he favored some and, being angry with others, abandoned them.
Furthermore, since the properties of the mandalas such as the triangle (*trikoṇa*) and so forth are obtained from that very source, their re-mention here [is redundant].

If it is asked why, the answer is simply that there is a restriction on speech and nothing else. Therefore, a path for the promotion of dharma based on one's own whim is not to be trusted; only that which has been explicitly stated should be performed. 18.
Regarding the mantra for the offering of the *bali*, he says:
having recited three times "Oṃ hrīṃ, to all beings who create obstacles, huṃ svāhā," one should give the *bali* offering. || 19 ||

By the word "thrice" (triḥ), the repetition of the mantra is prescribed; therefore, the offering of the bali-oblation occurs at the end of the three recitations. And the deity is to be known from the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra. || 19 ||
Having gratified [them] with circumambulations and so forth, with prostrations, recitations, and hymns of praise. || 20 ||
One circumambulation should be performed for Aja, Īśa, Śakti, Gaṇapa, and Bhāskara; through such circumambulation,
there are four, two, three, and seven attainments of all goals respectively.

This is because it is stated thus in the *Śaktisaṅgamatantra*: "Aja" refers to Viṣṇu; "Vedas" refers to four; "half" means two (being half of four); "candra" means one; "vahni" means three; and "adri" means seven. The meaning is that these numbers are to be understood in order during the clockwise circumambulation starting from Aja. This has also been stated by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.
"I perform circumambulation around you" is stated only in the singular;
this verse exists in the *Śrībālāmānasapūjāstotra* and in my own *Bālātantracandrikā*.

In the case of the salutation (*namaskāra*), however, the desire itself is the regulating factor until the scripture is fully acquired. Regarding this specific feature of the salutation, it is stated in the *Paramānandatantra* (p.
One should prostrate like a staff upon the ground outside the hall of worship before the Goddess;
however, within the mandala, one should not perform a full prostration with eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga) nor a prostration like a staff (daṇḍavat).
"With both knees, both feet, the head, and the pair of hands—this prostration with four limbs is prescribed for the auspicious mandala. Thus it is said.
Regarding the characteristics of the mandala in the Yoginītantra:
"O Śaṅkarī, that place where the Goddess is worshipped is proclaimed as a mandala measuring one hundred dhanus in each of its four directions. Thus it is said.
The measurement of a bow is four cubits; however, in the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvara*, it is said:
"One should know that the mandala extends as far as the deity can be seen."
In the Rahasyārṇava, however, it is said:
"Wherever the worship of the door is performed, they know that to be the inner maṇḍala."
And this has been described as delimitation by space. As for delimitation by time, it is stated in the *Śaktisaṅgamatantra*:
"Know that maṇḍala to extend from the commencement of the worship of the doors until the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*). Thus it is said.
Also in the Tripurārṇava:
"O Goddess, having begun the worship of this maṇḍala, [it continues] until the offering to the orb of the Sun. Thus it is said.
This very maṇḍala is to be understood according to the rules for the maṇḍalas that will be described hereafter.
Having gone then to the house of worship, one should worship the King of the Wheel (cakrarāja).
One should recite the vidyā a thousand times, or three hundred, or even just one hundred.

Thus, the number of recitations (*japa*) mentioned in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* is to be understood. This recitation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual action, because it is "sandwiched" (*sandaṃśa*) by the ancillaries on both sides. Or else: "The repetition [of the mantra], O Guru, as well as the daily worship (*nityārcā*), belongs to both the *samaya* and the *āmnāya*."
The threefold worship and the recitation of mantras are considered the primary elements in ritual worship.

Thus, because the *Svatantra-tantra* states in its thirteenth chapter that recitation (*japa*) is primary, and because a statement made through direct [scriptural] testimony overrides all other [contradictory evidence].

The hymns mentioned in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra, such as those dedicated to Gaṇeśa, the planets, and the lunar mansions; the recitation of the Thousand Names (Sahasranāma); the hymn of confession for transgressions (Aparādhastuti); and, when there is opportunity, the recitation of the Saptashatī—these should be performed. Furthermore, it is prescribed in that very same text: "Then, having joined one's palms in reverence, one should praise [the deity] with these exploits.
Having thus gratified [the deity] by means of these and other such acts... || 20 ||
(175) The Worship of Śakti. Now he explains the worship of Śakti:
Having worshipped that single Śakti, who possesses that form, with the offerings appropriate for a young girl, and having gratified her with the fivefold offering (pañcaka), || 21 ||

She is described as "tadrūpiṇīm," meaning she has the form of Tripurasundarī; by the singular word "ekām" (the one), it is meant that she is without a second in terms of beauty. By this, the characteristics of Śakti mentioned in other Tantras are indicated.
She is to be gratified with the Bālā mantra and with offerings as they may be available, through the fivefold expansion (pañcakam).
It should be understood that this occurs when that desire exists; this is the point indicated by the word "having satisfied" (*santarpya*).

Satisfying (*tarpaṇa*) means bringing about contentment; it is an activity that brings to an end those various desires directed toward specific objects based on one's power (*śakti*). For if that desire does not exist, the activity that brings it to an end is likewise impossible.

Thus, it is established that the meaning is "only when there is desire. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "one should worship with the five offerings (pañcaka) and the secondary offerings (upacāra).

Therefore, this meaning is proven. The characteristics of Śakti are described in the Kulārṇava—[these verses beginning with "surūpā" are found on page 64 of the printed edition of the seventh chapter (ullāsa) of the Kulārṇava Tantra].
She is young, peaceful, well-disposed, joyful, and pure;
free from doubt, endowed with devotion, and dedicated to the Guru and the scriptures.
"Priyākṣarā (or Priyekṣaṇā-Śrī), discerning of distinctions, eager for the worship of the deity, captivating, of virtuous conduct—such is Śakti, endowed with auspicious marks. Thus it is said.
In the Yoginītantra it is also said:

"Whether she be of the same caste or of a lower caste, whether she be a woman established in her family or an unchaste woman, even a courtesan— if she is engaged in the worship of the mantra, she should be honored."
Even faults are to be condemned in the ocean of noble lineage; she who is harsh, shameless,
and a defiler of the family is likewise to be rejected.
She is of bad conduct, difficult to propitiate, fearful, angry, fickle, and lazy.
One addicted to sleep, extremely wicked, deficient in limbs,
afflicted by disease, foul-smelling, miserable, deluded, aged, insane, or a betrayer of secrets.

And at the time of worship, one should avoid such [a practice] joined with mantras. [In this manuscript of the *Mudritakulārṇava*, there is a reading: "one should avoid it during the union with the Śakti. Thus [it is said].
And as it is said in the Yoginītantra:
"Whether she be qualified or disqualified, or even if she is beset with many faults,
one should by all means worship with devotion a married woman who has arrived at the proper time."

176) This [statement] intends to grant permission for that which was prohibited by the preceding statements in the absence of a primary [alternative], just as one might tell a lie during a marriage ceremony. Or rather, it refers to that prohibition which was established by the preceding statements.

"Devoted to the worship of the Śakti," or "the qualified woman"—by this [phrase], he establishes that at that time there may be worship even of a mere married woman (suvāsinī) beyond those [specific categories]. And this very position is the appropriate one. || 21 ||
The disposal of the remnants of the oblation:
regarding the disposal of the remnants of the oblation, he says—having offered the remnants of the oblation into the fire of consciousness (cidagni) together with the learned ones. || 22 ||
In this regard, the state of being a refined person (*śiṣṭatva*) is shown in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Alas! That liquor which, when consumed, could delude even the gods—that *maireya* drink, having drunk it, the man who does not undergo a transformation [of mind] is a refined one."
"Having become devoted to Śiva in Japan, he was liberated, as was that Kaulika. Thus it is said.

Such refinement is rooted in the observance of the rules (samaya). By this qualification, it is made known that those moderns who consider themselves Kaulikas but are merely fickle-tongued should not be admitted into the mandala.

"Together with those who observe the rules" (sāmayikaiḥ saha) means "concomitance" (sahatvam), which is the state of being performers of the same type of action, as in the expression "he goes together with his son."

Because it has been observed as such in passages beginning with "ityādi," even in the present context, since there exists the agency of performing a single type of action in the form of an oblation (*homa*), their simultaneity (*sahatva*) is justified. Regarding the phrase "having offered the remnant of the oblation" (*hutvā haviḥśeṣam*) into the fire characterized by consciousness (*cidagni*), the remainder— which has been consecrated and offered with reference to the deity— the injunction by the word "having offered" (*hutvā*) is intended solely to prescribe the mental conception of that [act] as a mere oblation.

It is indicated that desire for the gratification of the senses should never be acted upon; the implication is that one would fall into the very pit of desire for sensory gratification upon entering the mandala. Furthermore, this refinement of the utilized substance is like the rule "he divides the āgneya offering into four parts," referring to the remnant of the oblation (haviḥ-śeṣa).
Because of the non-hearing of a second [instance].
By this [rule], contemporary practitioners place a single vessel filled with unconsecrated substance,

drop a few drops of special *arghya* into it, and offer that substance to the initiates (*sāmayikas*). To accommodate their preferences, the author of the manual [mentions] the milk-vessel and so forth for the Goddess.

He wrote two sentences stating, "Having placed [it] at the rear" and "one should pour a little milk from the special *arghya* vessel into the jar. Having taken this as the root text, such improper practice that has arisen—which is a cause for downfall—is refuted by its contradiction with the written Sūtra; for in that case, there is an absence of the status of being a remnant of the oblation (*haviḥ-śeṣa*). And if...

If the status of being a remnant of the oblation were established merely by the dropping of a drop, then there would be great disorder, as there would be no fault in accepting goods from a marketplace after merely dropping a drop upon them.
And as it is stated in the Tripurārṇava:
"Whatever is first offered for the purpose of worship shall indeed be sacrificial and pure; by seeing or touching it, one becomes pure."
In that very manner, everything obtained within the maṇḍala becomes nectar (*amṛta*). Whether brought by a Brahmin or by another, one should offer it to the deity.
"O daughter of the mountain, that which is joined with the first [syllable] and the others, when consecrated, should be accepted by all without distinction and free from doubt. Thus it is said.
If it is argued that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) becomes conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) by being joined with a conditioned substance (*saṃskṛtadravya*),
even so, the conjunction with a conditioned substance is twofold:
one occurs when a conditioned substance is poured into an unconditioned vessel, and [the other] occurs in a specially consecrated vessel (*viśeṣārghyapātra*) which is itself conditioned.

Another [view] is by means of the addition of an unconditioned substance (*asaṃskṛtadravya*). In this regard, the latter position is superior to the former, because it is observed in Vedic rituals such as the *soma* sacrifice in the *droṇakalaśa*, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in the *dhruva* vessel, and so forth. Furthermore, if the external worldly [substance] were to be consecrated by means of a consecrated substance, [it would be illogical].

In that case, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has already been demonstrated [as follows]: "Even in the case of goods in a marketplace... and so forth, up to the passage ending with "...there would be a great calamity.
Furthermore, even this aforementioned over-extension does not apply to the position that external objects are cast into the vessel.

This is effective. Therefore, the second position alone is superior. Even in that case, this method applies only to a place brought by a devotee for the purpose of worship, and not elsewhere, as it would be unscriptural; nowadays, people procure substances according to their own whims through their intellect and employ them as mentally purified.
"It will be sufficient for its very downfall."
In reality, however, this [practice] belongs to the followers of other tantras, but not to the followers of the Sūtra. For in the Sūtra,

by the statement "having offered the remnants of the oblation" (*haviśśeṣaṃ hutvā*), it is impossible— even for Bṛhaspati— to establish that the substance contained in the jar is a "remnant of the oblation" unless it has been consecrated according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

Since only that which remains after being offered to the deity constitutes the remnant of the oblation (*haviśśeṣa*), the conclusion (*rāddhānta*) of those who follow the Sūtra is that the purificatory act of disposal (*pratipatti-saṃskāra*) by means of the oblation must be performed solely with the remnant of the sacrifice, and not with any other substance.

If it is argued that when the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the worship of the retinue (*āvaraṇapūjana*) have been performed, and they are employed for that very purpose, then this [subsequent] ritual act would be redundant—[we reply:

no. Just as, according to the two injunctions, "he makes the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) the size of a horse's hoof" and "he cuts off [the portion] the size of a thumb-joint," a remnant of the oblation (*haviśśeṣa*) necessarily remains once those have been performed; so too [is the case here].
In another tantra: "The general vase should contain water less than five palas;
the causal jar (hetukumbha) should not exceed ten palas, nor be less than half of that."
And half of that is the special arghya offering...

Thus, in following the *Māna* [tradition], for those who follow the *Sūtra*, when the *hetukumbha* is accepted as the measure for the *viśeṣārghya* (which occupies the position of the *hetukumbha*), the substance for the *viśeṣārghya* amounts to one hundred and sixteen *guñjās*. And if, because it shares the same name, the measure of the *viśeṣārghya* itself is accepted [as the standard], then likewise—

There is no dispute that [the quantity] is measured at eight hundred *guñjās*. In the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) and other rites, the application of one drop for each individual deity is observed. This being the case, there certainly remains sufficient material for the fire-oblation (*homa*) for both the initiates (*sāmayika*) and oneself. In this scripture, the specific state produced by the acceptance of the material is called *ullāsa*.
That too must occur when the substance is of the highest excellence; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
p.
178) Here,

since the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the rules for the entry of the learned ones (*śiṣṭa*) into the mandala have not been stated, how can one [proceed] together with the learned ones?

When there is an expectation as to how one should perform the *homa*, another tantra must be taken as a refuge for that matter. That being the case, the properties of the mandala are first stated. These have been taught in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
"One whose limbs are wounded, one whose limbs are feverish, and one whose garments and hair are soiled..."
Likewise, one who is in a state of ritual impurity, one wearing a turban, one wearing a bodice, or one who has already eaten.

One whose limbs are putrid, one whose mouth is impure from food remnants, one who has experienced the birth-death impurity, one afflicted by epilepsy, one beset by distress, and one suffering from vomiting and dysentery.
One who has not performed expiation and has not bathed should never enter the maṇḍala;
even if he enters it once through delusion, he shall incur the curse of the deities.
"But if they possess intense devotion toward the vision [of the deity] and so forth, one should perform the worship outside the vicinity of the door of the shrine. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific rule for one who has consumed [the substance] in the ocean of Tripura:
"When that which was consumed unexpectedly during the day arrives at night, then one should partake of it after bathing by the command of the Guru and others, and not otherwise. Thus it is said.

This service, too, takes place entirely outside the maṇḍala. For there is no scriptural authority prohibiting entry into the maṇḍala that would override [the rule] stating: "O Supreme Goddess, having eaten, one should by no means enter the maṇḍala."
And as it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"O Kuleśvarī, he who partakes of the *kuladravya* without having bathed, or after eating, or without devotion— or even after anointing himself— shall fall into poverty."
Thus, let the scripture prohibiting the consumption of the *kuladravya* (family substance) by one who has already eaten be set aside as it pleases;

however, entry [into the maṇḍala] must not be performed because there is no authority that overrides the prohibition against entry. Nor can it be argued that entry is implied by the rule for "making one's own" (*svātmīkāra*), since there is no such rule for making one's own outside of the maṇḍala.

This must be stated: since it has already been established that the consumption [of the substance] is prohibited by the very prohibition of entry—namely, "Having consumed [it], one should not go to the mandala"—then [the following applies]:
"If one consumes the Kula-substance through delusion or even through negligence..."
O Goddess, he who would serve [them] shall indeed incur the curse of the deities.

By this [statement], the prohibition against the external consumption of the *kuladravya* (family substance) would be rendered meaningless; therefore, by this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the consumption of the substance even externally is established.
Having thus described those unfit for entry, [the text] also states the qualities of the one who enters in the *Paramānandatantra*:
"Bathed, pure, wearing washed garments, marked with *puṇḍra*, and possessing auspicious intentions..."
Having washed his feet and hands, and having bowed with devotion while meditating upon the Goddess.
Then, in accordance with the teacher’s command, one should enter within the mandala;
meditating upon the form of the deity, the wise person should prostrate to the mandala.
Thereafter, one should perform the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali); its procedure is now described:
having devoutly washed both hands with the water from the general pitcher (sāmānyakumbha).
Having perfumed [the area] with incense and other fragrances, and having taken up flowers with devotion,
one should then stand up, O Goddess, and remain facing the deity.
I bow to the triad of gurus beginning with Śrīnātha, Gaṇapati, the three seats (pīṭhas), Bhairava, the lineage of Siddhas,
the triad of Baṭukas, the pair of feet, the sequence of Dūtīs, the maṇḍala, the thirty-two Vīras, the nine [Vīras], the fivefold lineages of Vīras, and the rest.
I pay homage to the circle of Gurus, accompanied by the glorious Mālinī, the king of mantras.
O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, the practitioner who has attained the fifteenth day and so forth should also recite the collective Vidyā of the Yoginīs there.
O Śaṅkarī, having meditated upon the deity with the form described for meditation and worshipped them,
O Parameśvarī, one should then meditate upon the preceptor and the others and worship them.
Having realized that everything has Śiva as its essence, one should prostrate according to the prescribed rule;
he should then receive the second vessel from the most excellent of teachers.
O Śaṅkarī, the vessel should be held in the right hand by one who is initiated;
however, O Śaṅkarī, it may also be taken up by another with the left hand.
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, it should be grasped with the left hand by all;
having covered it with the other hand, one should take it or even cause it to be given.
A vessel that is not covered becomes a portion for the Asuras;
however, when it is used for purposes such as libations (tarpaṇa), one should omit the covering.
O Goddess, listen with a restrained mind to the sequence of seating,
whether in the form of a circle or else as a square.
Having placed the teacher in the center, one should enter according to seniority;
however, while seniors are present, one should not enter into the immediate vicinity of the teacher.
(180) One should not stand on equal footing with the Guru, nor likewise in the midst of women;
one should not stand before the Guru, O Goddess, nor indeed transgress the command of the Guru.
Having thus understood the tradition, one should sit within the auspicious maṇḍala;
the preceptor likewise, having risen and prostrated before the elders, [should do so].
Having received their command, the practitioner should then sit upon his own seat;
rising up, he should indeed offer a vessel to that eldest one.
O Goddess, even the youngest, rising and bowing, should receive the elders;
O Maheśvarī, having honored them all, the vessels should be given.
O Ambikā, if one should bestow the vessel even upon a disciple without first honoring him,
that Goddess becomes angry with him, for everything is indeed identical with her.
Having washed the vessel and carefully covered it with flowers and other offerings,
one should likewise present it to the preceptor and pay homage with devotion.
Having accepted that grace, one should indeed recite the mantra and then read the hymns and so forth. Thus it is said.
In the Tripurārṇava it is said:
"O Ambikā, one should offer a vessel joined with gold and other materials;
or even by giving whatever is placed within the vessel, one obtains infinite fruit."
Regarding the specific procedure for *suvāsinīs* in the *Yoginītantra*:

"Having thus satisfied [the deities] and performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), the *suvāsinīs* should give the third or fourth vessel containing the remnants to the presiding authority of the sacred seat (*pīṭha-adhikārin*). Thus it is said.
In the Tripurārṇava, there is a specific distinction:
"O Daughter of the Mountain, the remainder and the chewing [of the offering] should be received from a hero, an elder, or likewise from a teacher;
in their absence, it should be received from another elder."
In the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra*:
"In the absence of the Guru and others, one should offer the remainder of the chewing [of the sacramental substance] to the eldest [brother].
In his absence, having meditated upon the Guru at the crown of the head, one should take that remnant and place it [there]. (Śrī.)
O Daughter of the Mountain, either at the beginning or at the very end,
one should drink from the vessel once, leaving no residue and making no sound.
"But that vessel which still contains a remnant [of liquor] is equal to the drinking of wine. Thus it is said.
Even regarding the non-touching of the rim of the vessel, a prohibition is stated in that same [text]:
"But drinking from a distance without touching the rim is like the drinking of cattle."
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"O Dear One, having taken the vessel in one's hand, one should not remain for long;
O Mother, one should not stand anywhere with the vessel in hand while speaking."
One should not touch the bowl with one's foot, nor let a drop fall to the ground;
one should not strike one bowl against another, nor let a bowl fall down.
One should not lift the vessel without its base, nor should one set it down without support;
one should not leave the vessel empty, nor should one wave it about, O Dear One.
"A wise person should not leap over a vessel, nor should he strike a vessel, O beloved;
having washed it, one should store the vessel—this is the command of the Supreme Lord. Thus [it is said].
In the *Paramānanda-tantra*, there is a specific instruction:
from the placement of the *arghya* water until the dismissal of the vessels, one should perceive everything as consisting of Śiva; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
All castes there are twice-born; one should never conceive of any distinction therein.
After the dismissal [of the deity], a wise man should never establish identity [between them].
O Goddess, the process of making [the deity] one's own is threefold, according to the sequence of the divine, the hero, and the animal:
that which ends with the dismissal [of the deity] is the divine; after that, it is called the heroic.
"The unconditioned animal is said to be the very first for Brahmins;
it is not an animal for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, while for Śūdras there may be all three. Thus [it is said].
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"The divine [Śrī] bestows both enjoyment and liberation; the heroic (vīra) bestows enjoyment.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Rahasyārṇava*:
"Having thus performed worship according to the ritual procedure up until the dismissal (*udvāsana*), the Brāhmaṇa,
the Kṣatriya, and likewise the Vaiśya should drink that substance at the end."
But a Śūdra, according to his own desire, may do so either by means of the prescribed rite or otherwise.
Having offered that to the deity and having satisfied [the deity], one should afterwards drink it. Thus [it is said].
182) Thus many essential dharmas have been described. Those exceeding these are to be understood by consulting numerous tantras; they are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

In this regard, the rules for the mandala prescribed for the Sāmayikas who follow the Kalpasūtra and for others are the same. As for the fire-oblation mantra, for those following the Sūtras, it is precisely the mantra "ārdraṃ jvalati" (the moist [fire] blazes), because when there is a requirement for a mantra, this one is more proximate than the mantras of other tantras. For others...
This is the path taught in one’s own [tantric] tradition. Here, the following systematic arrangement is considered:

for the sake of attaining the fruit of the worship performed by oneself, since the ritual consecration (*pratipatti-saṃskāra*) must necessarily be performed by the presiding authority of the sacred seat (*pīṭha-adhikārin*), he—whether capable or incapable of meditating upon the mandala—may at will accept the ritual substances.
However, regarding the occasional [sāmayika] rite, only one who is capable of the meditation prescribed by the scriptures may offer the substance after the material oblation (dravyahoma);
no other may do so. For it is said:
"In the fire of consciousness, which blazes incessantly within without fuel, acting as the adversary to the darkness of delusion..."
In that certain [reality] where the wondrous rays of light are blossoming, I offer the universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.

With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses as oblations into the fire of the Self, which is kindled by the fuel of dharma and adharma, via the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
Thus, the method of meditation prescribed by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra is essential. It is also stated in the *Devīyāmala*:
"Having conquered the consciousness through fire-oblation (*homa*), one should meditate upon the Self by means of the self."
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"That man who, having drunk that auspicious maireya wine, is not transformed,
but remains intent on Śiva while reciting [mantras], he is liberated and he is a Kaulika."
Also in the *Paramānandatantra*:
"Having accepted that grace, one should indeed meditate with unwavering focus upon Ambikā."
In the Gaṇeśvarasaṃhitā of the Vīracūḍāmaṇi: Having tasted the substance according to the prescribed rule, one should bring the mind to a state of immobility;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the supreme light, the eternal light of the Self.
There are many such scriptural injunctions prescribing meditation preceded by the restraint of the mind, up to the following:
"O Goddess, one should offer oblations only so long as the state of deep sleep has not occurred and there is indeed a state of changelessness; otherwise, it would be fruitless."
But when a transformation has arisen, O Goddess, he is excluded from the yoga of meditation;
he is a beast for the Yoginīs and is cast out from the maṇḍala.

Thus, even in the *tantra*, there is the undesirable consequence of the failure of meditative visualization (*dhyāna*) during a fire-offering (*homa*) using an extra vessel; by this as well, the necessity of visualization is established. There are many such instances. For fear of excessive length, I have not written more here—this much will suffice.
And thus, the first fruit of the practice of the substance (*dravya*) is one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), because without that,
meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is impossible. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Paramānandatantra*:
O Goddess, one should offer oblations for only so long as one is immersed in bliss,
until the mind attains immobility and the consciousness also reaches a state of clarity.
"But when a transformation has arisen due to being devoid of the yoga of meditation, O Goddess, he is a beast for the Yoginīs and is excluded from the maṇḍala.
Thus, it shows the undesirable fruit resulting from an unqualified person's acceptance of the substances. Also, in the Yoginītantra:
Relying upon the family substance, one should bring the mind to a state of immobility. Thus it is said.
In the Tripurārṇava it is also said:
"O Maheśvarī, this Kaula path is the supreme dharma among all;
it is equal to the vow of walking on the edge of a sword, for its cause is the immobility of the mind."
In that regard, the state of having a restrained mind is indeed exceedingly difficult to achieve in every respect for one who is devoid of devotion and faith.

Thus, millions of such statements from the Tantras are found, stating that the consumption of substances must be performed for the sake of meditation by means of restraining the mind, and that otherwise it causes obstruction.
While summarizing the meaning of such Tantric statements, Śrī Paraśurāma [says]:

He said, "Together with the learned. One capable of such meditation, even on days of vows and the like, should—without hesitation and regardless of whether he is respected or not—enter the mandala, request the vessel, perform the oblation, and accomplish the meditation.
As it is stated in the Tripurārṇava:
Thus, one who is bound by convention, free from pride and hypocrisy, and motivated by devotion,
should go to the supreme maṇḍala— whether uninvited or invited.
Or even one observing a vow may offer oblations; no fault exists therein.
However, he who, out of apprehension regarding his vows and the like, does not go [to the temple] even though he is capable of doing so, [commits a fault].
"His vow would be frustrated and he would meet with misfortune;
therefore, even if summoned as the youngest, one must indeed enter the mandala. Thus it is said.
In this context, the seniority and juniority of the Brahmins should be understood according to the priority or posteriority of their initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Even a child who was initiated first is considered senior in the Kula tradition."

"Even if a twice-born man is initiated later, while a person of the lowest caste was initiated earlier, that twice-born man is the junior and the other is the senior; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures."

184) Because it is stated in that very [text], even one who is initiated later among Kṣatriyas and others is indeed a twice-born (dvija) and is senior. In certain instances, regarding the acceptance of leavings (ucchiṣṭa), it establishes seniority even on the basis of birth (yonisambandha). Thus it has been said:
In the Tripurārṇava it is said:
"Whether through a connection of Vidyā or likewise through a connection of birth,
one should consume the leavings even of those who are senior and have been initiated."

"Even if he is his own father, one who has been initiated should not consume the leavings of one who is devoid of initiation, even once; by eating them, he incurs a fall from his status. Thus it is said.

Now, as an incidental discussion, it is analyzed by whom and how many vessels (dravya) should be consumed. In that regard, for one engaged in the worship of the Child-form (Bālopāsti), there are three vessels; for one who has received the instruction in the Pañcadaśī mantra, there are four vessels; and for one who has received initiation (dīkṣā) such as the Ṣoḍaśī and others, there are five vessels. This is stated in the Paramānanda Tantra:
O Śivā, for a worshipper of Saubhāgyatā, there shall be the four principles;
however, for worshippers of Bālā and the others, their worship is according to the prescribed injunctions.
But for them, there is a triad of principles; everything else is the same. Thus it is said.
"For those who have received initiation, O Śiva, the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) shall be the fifth;
having offered the three, four, or five vessels in sequence into the fire of Śiva. Thus it is said.
Indeed, by drinking again and again, and drinking until one falls to the ground,
and rising to drink once more, there is no further rebirth.
The Goddess is satisfied by bliss, Bhairava himself by fainting, and all the gods by vomiting; therefore, one should practice this triad.

If it is asked, "Since unrestricted drinking has been taught in the *Kulārṇava* and other tantras beginning with those words, how can there be a restriction regarding the vessel?"—listen to the intention of the scripture, provided you are an ignorant person desiring to know the reality. Regarding the written statement, "Having drunk again and again," and the *Kulārṇava* passage beginning with, "One should drink the substance until the throat; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt."
This is not according to one's own whim or suitable for everyone, but rather for those who have fully ascended (*pūrṇārūḍha*).

For this very reason, in the *Kulārṇava*, immediately preceding the statement "up to the throat," there is a formal declaration: "O Goddess, drinking is prescribed for those endowed with the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*"), followed by such statements as "one should drink the substance up to the throat."
The characteristics of the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* (the full initiation) are also described in that very same *Kulārṇava*:
"He who remains equal in all circumstances when blame or praise, cold or heat, pleasure or pain, and so forth arise— the lord of yogis, free from joy and resentment," and so on.
One who knows the reality of the three principles, the meaning of the root mantra, and the feet of the Śrī [Guru],
who is devoted to the deity and the guru, and is endowed with the Śāmbhavī mudrā.
"And he should be one who has received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) as a Kaulika, but not [merely] by initiation. Thus it is said.
p.
185) He who is thus fully consecrated (*pūrṇābhiṣikta*) is indeed one who has ascended to the fullness (*pūrṇārūḍha*); for him alone is the rule "up to the throat" (*āgalāntam*).
Therefore, in the *Amṛtārahasya*:
If a knower of Brahman, having drunk wine while repeatedly practicing the family tradition (kulācāra),
falls upon the ground such that dust particles adhere to his body,
he rejoices in the world of Brahmā for as long a time as there are those grains of dust.
In this statement, by the collective term "knower of Brahman" (*brahmajñānī*), he expresses the specific meaning as declared in the *Kulārṇava*.

Nowadays, those ignorant of the meaning of the Tantras, blinded by passion, and failing to consider their own qualification, display Tantric injunctions such as "having drunk, having drunk" to the world, while themselves acting according to their own whims.

They even eclipsed the intellects of others; they shall experience the torments of hell for as long as the moon and sun exist. [In this context, "upalabheran" would be the form according to grammatical rules.
On this point, the authority is found in the Paramānanda Tantra:
As long as the gaze does not waver and as long as the mind does not waver, for that long one should consume food; beyond this, it is like drinking the blood of a sacrificial animal.
"As long as there is no impairment of the senses and no distortion of the face, for that long one should drink the substance; otherwise, a downfall occurs. Thus it is said.

Just as a practitioner should accept substances according to his own capacity, so too the teacher should bestow the vessel only after observing the disciple's fitness. As it is said in the Kumārītantra: "In the Kaulika tradition, one bestows the supreme vessel without hesitation."
Thus, he sinks into that very office along with it.
In that very same [text]:
"O Śivā, when the drinking of the substance occurs with a single effort, at the commencement of that, the vessel should be neither less nor more. Thus it is said.

Regarding the measure of the drinking vessel, it is stated in the *Nīlātantra*: "A vessel is that which contains the substance used for drinking, accomplished by a single effort"—this is its meaning. Furthermore, in another tantra:
"O Ambikā, having failed to understand the distinctions between the various states of bliss (*ullāsa*), one falls into delusion."
"Indeed, those who drink it out of a longing for the tongue or for the gratification of the senses are cast by the Mothers into the Tāmisra hell. Thus [it is said].

And thus, for those of the present day— even for those who have fully conquered their senses [or, according to the Āraśrī, for those who have not]— it is appropriate to pursue [the practice] right up to the point of the exhilaration of the commencement (*ārambha-ullāsa*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the Tantra:
The undertaking [of this work] is proclaimed as being for the sake of those who are incapable, ignorant, and childish.

The definition of *ārambha* (the commencement) and its *ullāsa* (manifestation) is given in that very same [text]: "To whatever extent a vessel is declared for someone, to that extent is his *ārambha*."

Enough with this excessive proliferation resulting from one topic leading to another. The remainder of this matter will be discussed later in the *Ullāsavilāsa*, in its final section (*caramakhaṇḍa*).
(By the term "final section," it should be understood that this refers to the commentary on Sūtra 68 of the tenth section;
furthermore, the recurrence of the word "sūtra" indicates that the text requires correction.)
"And the remaining portion shall be complete through the grace of the Primordial Goddess. Thus ends the fifth section—Śrī.
We shall now speak [further]. 22.
The dismissal of the Goddess:
having bound the *khecarī* mudrā and said "Forgive me," one should dismiss her and merge her into oneself. Thus all is auspicious. || 23 ||
Thus ends the fifth section, titled "The Worship of the Ninefold Enclosures of Lalitā," in the Kalpasūtra.
Having bound Khecarī Mudrā, immediately after that binding—
whether performed knowingly or unknowingly, O Śivā, knowing that whatever has been done is your own work, forgive me, O Supreme Goddess.
Having thus asked for forgiveness, one should perform the dismissal (*visarga*). Dismissal means leading back to her own place the goddess who was invited for the sake of worship.
One should join [her] within oneself, that is, establish her in the heart-lotus. The word "Śiva" indicates the conclusion of the section.
Thus ends the fifth section, titled "The Worship of the Ninefold Enclosures of Śrī Lalitā," in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.
The Sixth Section: The Śyāmā-krama.

O Śyāmā, Mother of Music, who resides in the abode of Paraśiva; you who are expert in bearing the primary burden of ministering to the marriage [of the soul]; whose own heart is filled with compassion for my state of wretchedness!

Obeisance to you, Śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśī; in this secluded place, you have girded yourself with the intent to protect those fallen into the forest-fire of worldly existence by raining down nectar—please speak!
The procedure for the worship of Śyāmā:
the venerable Lord Paraśurāma, desiring to expound the Śyāmākrama,

[first describes] that which pertains to one who has already undertaken the worship of Śrīvidyā, in order to generate in those practitioners the knowledge of the object of worship (upāsya) within that [Śyāmā].

By the scriptural statement, "He who sacrifices to another deity indeed sacrifices beyond his own deity; he falls away from his own deity and does not reach the higher one; he becomes worse off," it is established that the worship of a deity other than the one deity one has accepted for oneself produces undesirable results. By this [statement],...
And for the sake of removing the turbidity from those whose minds are turbid, he first describes the nature of her qualities:
"This very Siṃhāsaneśvarī is the Great Vidyā, the Sovereign Empress; Śyāmā occupies the position of her chief minister, and the constant contemplation of her sequence must be performed. (1)

The nature and indifference (*udāsyatva*) of Parāśakti are what will be described hereafter. The word "this" (*iyam*) refers to what follows; the word "which" (*yā*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. She who is "great" (*mahatī*), possessing limitless greatness, [occupies] the throne (*siṃhāsana*), which is Paraśiva because he is her own substratum (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
The Sovereign (Īśvarī) is the agent who carries out the intentions regarding the creation, maintenance, and concealment that are centered upon Him.
As it was stated by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda—[this verse is the first of the *Saundaryalaharī*; this is its first half].
"If he were endowed with power, he would be capable of exercising authority; if it were not so, the god would indeed not be able even to move. Thus [it is said].
Also, in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*, in the praise of Vidyāvatī:
"Salutations to that Goddess whose eyes are like beautiful fish, the embodiment of auspiciousness— to whom even Śiva is indeed rendered purposeless when separated."
This [consciousness] is distinct from illusion; it is of the nature of consciousness, not of the nature of insentient matter. As it is said in the Sūtasaṃhitā:
"It has the form of existence, is supreme bliss, and brings about the destruction of saṃsāra."
"She is Śivā, the supreme goddess, non-different from Śiva and the bestower of auspiciousness;
for even Śiva is indeed purposeless when devoid of her who is non-different from him. Thus it is said.

(188) Objection: If the primary agency regarding creation and so forth belongs to Śiva, while that of Śakti consists merely in being its executor, then the primary status of being the creator and controller of the universe resides in Śiva; and this [Śakti] is merely an auxiliary. Likewise...

If it is argued that Śiva alone is to be worshipped because of his primacy and not Śakti, listen: for it is precisely through logical necessity—that the entire collection of effects such as earth and so forth is untenable without a cause—that either Śiva or Śakti is postulated. Indeed, we do not perceive Śakti or Śiva with the physical eye. When one begins to postulate in this manner, here...

The Vedāntins maintain that the attribute of the supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is *māyā*; this very *māyā* is *avidyā*, which is insentient by nature. She alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, whereas the supreme Brahman is the cause of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-upādāna*). Consequently, because it has an insentient material cause, the world is also insentient by nature; and because its material cause is *māyā*, it is false (*mithyātva*).

The Tantrikas do not accept that position. For instance, as for that which is called *māyā* or *avidyā*, is it a property (*dharma*) of consciousness (*cit*) or a property of something else? In the first case, since even the Vedāntins admit the non-difference between a property and its substratum (*dharmadharmiṇoḥ*), it would be impossible for a property of consciousness to be insentient (*jaḍatva*). If, on the other hand, it were a property of the non-conscious (*acit*), [the following would apply...]

Furthermore, there would be a loss of non-duality (advaita), and there would be a contradiction with such authoritative scripture as: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. Therefore, since there is no other way out, one must necessarily admit that this Māyā is an attribute of Consciousness (ciddharma). This being the case, its insentience (jaḍatva) is discarded from afar. Nor is it the case that there is no power (śakti) distinct from Consciousness.
This is what must be said; we too express that very same point.

However, even though there is an absence of fragrance apart from the earth, a slight distinction is indeed postulated in accordance with the conventional usage of "attribute" (*dharma*) and "substratum" (*dharmin*); likewise, although both are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), a slight distinction is [postulated] for the sake of conventional usage.
It must be so conceived. And thus, the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world is not possible for either [of the two], because the world is insentient by nature.
Indeed, darkness cannot arise from light. Therefore, the world always exists within consciousness in a subtle form, just as a banyan tree exists within its seed.
In consciousness (*citi*), there is only the agency of expansion and contraction preceded by the loosening of its own parts, but not the status of being their material cause (*upādānatva*).

Just as a merchant spreads out goods for sale in the morning and contracts them at night, such is the agency of consciousness. The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is its auxiliary (*sahakāriṇī*).

[Objection: Why is a power (*śakti*) admitted that is distinct from consciousness (*cit*), possesses a slight degree of difference [from it], and serves to effect its agency? Let the agency reside in consciousness itself. Otherwise, by the same logic, a single power would have to be established as the substratum of the potter’s agency in making a jar. [Reply: No, because of the Śruti, Smṛti, and worldly usage.
Because of its existence. There is a Vedic revelation stating, "His power is heard to be indeed manifold. Also in the Devībhāgavata:
"Śakti creates the cosmic egg; she indeed protects everything;
by her will, she destroys this entire world of moving and non-moving beings."
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka, nor Sūrya,
nor Varuṇa are capable in any way whatsoever of accomplishing their respective tasks.
For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;
she alone is the cause in all actions, as is perceived through direct observation.
(189) The entire web of objects, being devoid of power, is unable to accomplish anything;
yet it becomes capable, O Supreme Goddess, when it is joined with power.

Thus, in great detail: from the cowherd girls up to the learned scholar (*paṇḍita*), they engage in the practice of saying, "I have the power to perform this task," or "I do not have the power," without dispute. Therefore, power is established by many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is that which must be brought to fulfillment.
The entire world also always exists within the womb of Śiva in a subtle form.

Alternatively, the world is of the nature of a transformation of that power which belongs to Consciousness (cit). As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "O friend, this phenomenal world is a play of Consciousness; how can it cause you suffering? [Śrī: Thus.
By this, because a slight distinction between consciousness (*cit*) and power (*śakti*) is admitted, the scriptural texts teaching the changelessness of consciousness are not contradicted;

and because absolute difference is not admitted, the scriptural texts establishing non-duality (*advaita*) are also not sublated. Such a power is experienced in every entity only after the production of an effect, and not prior to it.
The venerable Śrī Vidyāraṇyasvāmin also stated this very point in the *Pañcabhūtaviveka*:
"His power, Māyā, which is beyond the [five] principles (nistattva) and is to be known through its effects, is like the power of fire;
for no one perceives a power anywhere prior to its effect."

Thus, when that which is established as being identical with Śiva, consisting of His attributes, and effectuating the agency inherent in Him—that is, the state of devotion to Śiva—is accomplished, that alone is to be worshipped. Śiva in His form as pure consciousness (cidrūpa) is not to be worshipped, because He is not an object of worship [the meaning is:
because He is Brahman unconditioned by power].

Worship (*upāsanā*) consists in the chanting of the names and qualities inherent in the object of worship. Since there is an absence of qualities in the Absolute (*kevala*), which is devoid of power (*śakti*) and free from attributes (*nirguṇa*), how could meditation, praise, chanting, and so forth, be possible for it? This has been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"In Śiva, who is subtle, there exists neither name nor abode without Śakti. Thus [it is said].
And there is the Śruti: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, failing to reach it.

Furthermore, because He is to be known only as the remainder after the negation of everything by "not this, not this," knowledge whose sole object is Śiva is opposed to ritual acts such as meditation (*upāsanā*).
Since such a final state is to be accomplished through worship, Śiva alone is not to be worshipped. As it is said in the Devībhāgavata:
"Even Śiva becomes a corpse when he is devoid of Kuṇḍalinī."
Also in the Yoginītantra:
"O Great Goddess, even when that knowledge is attained, there is neither bliss nor protection whatsoever."

Furthermore, even if the mind were somehow impelled into a circular form for the purpose of grasping formless objects, it would not be able to remain so for even a moment, because it is devoid of both virtuous and non-virtuous dharmas.
As it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"Their affliction is greater, for their minds are attached to the Unmanifest. (p. 190)

Therefore, for the sake of stabilizing that very mind, some form must be conceptualized. And that form which is conceptualized within the Supreme Brahman, accompanied by name and abode, is precisely what is denoted by the term "Śakti.
This too has been stated in the Bhāgavata:
Thus, that all-pervading power is discerned as Brahman;
it is described by the wise in two ways: with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā).
That which possesses attributes is to be cultivated by those possessed of passion, while that which is without attributes is to be cultivated by those free from passion.
She is the untroubled mistress of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
"When worshipped according to the prescribed rite, she grants all desired objects. Thus it is said.
Thus, by means of the collection of proofs and reasonings stated above, the Supreme Śakti is to be worshipped, as is Paraśiva who is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).

Since the mental state (vṛtti) directed toward Him consists of the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha), it is established that the state of being the Empress, the Mistress of the Lion-Throne, is to be accomplished through the worship of Ambā.

Śiva is indeed devoid of attributes (nirguṇa); yet, when He is endowed with the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and, thinking "May I become many, may I procreate," becomes intent on creation, He alone is designated by the term "Śakti. Thus, the essential truth to be understood is that Śiva Himself is to be worshipped in the form of Śakti.

She who is such as this is the "position of the chief minister" (*pradhānasacivapada*); here, the term *sacivapada* refers to the attribute of being a minister, and her "position" (*pada*) means her locus, which is Śyāmā. One should always perform the "contemplation" (*vimṛṣṭi*), that is, the following of her sequence. Here, by the word "always" (*sadā*), it is meant for as long as one lives.

Just as there is a restriction of the lifelong injunction for the Agnihotra by another statement, "He offers in the evening; he offers in the morning," so too, in the context of this very Śyāmā, there is a restriction by the sentence occurring earlier: "Performing this daily worship in this manner, having performed a hundred thousand recitations... (This occurs here in the sixth section).
37. Regarding the *Mūlasūtra*: there is a restriction that worship should be performed only once up until the completion of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*), but not thereafter. || 1 ||

Regarding the justification for the worship of Śyāmā: one might raise the objection, "Since she is the sovereign queen, the controller of all, and independent, why abandon her to worship Śyāmā, who merely follows her? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] intends to establish the validity of worshipping her.
First, he confirms this by means of a worldly analogy: "For it is proper to seek to please a king through the mediation of a prime minister. (2)

In the world, those eager for an audience with a king first attend upon his chief minister and obtain the audience with the king through him; it is observed in the world that by this means the result is achieved quickly and without effort. Likewise, here too, one should first practice the worship of Śyāmā, who is the primary [deity].
The sense is that this is logical. By the word "at the door" (*dvāre*), it is indicated that [this practice] is a prerequisite for the primary meditation;

by the phrase "it is logical" (*nyāyyam*), even its absolute lack of necessity is indicated. However, anyone who is capable may, disregarding ministers and others, personally secure the king's favor and thereby obtain the fruit.

The position that "he accomplishes [the goal] directly" also exists in some cases in the world; nevertheless, the meaning is that it is more appropriate and preferable to propitiate the king through the mediation of his principal minister. This is the underlying idea: one who is unable to directly obtain the grace of the principal deity...

Having first completed his initiation (*dīkṣā*) and performed the worship of Śrī Gaṇapati, he then performed the worship of Śyāmā, the worship of Vārāhī, and the worship of Parā, and [attained] their grace.

Having completed [the preliminary rites], one should thereafter commence the worship of Śrī Lalitā. However, one who is capable may, after initiation and following the worship of Gaṇapati, begin the sequence of Śrī Lalitā. The truth is that this is an option, just as it is said: "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice; one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice."

One who desires superior results should perform the worship of Lalitā according to the stated sequence; one who desires lesser results should perform the worship of Lalitā after the worship of Gaṇapati—this is the settled rule. || 2 ||

Having thus demonstrated the morning duties ending with the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) for the qualified practitioner of worship, he begins the section on the practice of worship itself: "Rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, while still remaining upon the bed, one should bow to the venerable *pādukā*."

Having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) and contemplated the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvid*) blazing from the root-center (*mūlādhāra*) up to the end of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), one should mentally recite the root mantra three times; then, having gone outside,
[perform] the release of impurities, urine, cleansing with tooth-sticks, rubbing the tongue, spitting phlegm, and purifying the nose.
Having performed twenty mouthfuls of rinsing. || 3 ||

The *śrīpādukā* is the *gurupādukā*—[the intended meaning of *gurupādukā* here is the *pādukā* of the three Gurus]. Regarding "the vital breaths," the definition of *prāṇāyāma* is stated in the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*:
"One should perform three *prāṇāyāmas* with either the root mantra or the *praṇava*."
Alternatively, the wise one [should do so] with the seed-syllable of the mantra according to the prescribed procedure.
One should fill the breath with sixteen [counts] and retain it (kumbhaka) with four times that; one should exhale with half of the retention, or if unable, with a quarter of that.
