"In the event of inability to do that, it should be performed with the fourth [vowels]; thus is the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama).
Without prāṇāyāma, there is no fitness for worship and other rites. Thus it is said.
In the *Samayāṅgamātṛkā*: "One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* once with the root-mantra;
then one should retain it (*kumbhaya*) in the central channel four times, O fair-faced one."
One should exhale through the path of Piṅgalā according to the sequence of the number of eyes (two), again and again in that same order, so that it occurs three times. Thus [it is said].

The recitation of the tooth-cleansing twig (*dantadhāvana*) and other items, which are already established by *smṛti*, is for the purpose of obtaining the stated sequence; therefore, they should be performed according to the order of recitation. Although the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) will also be explained later in the Sūtra (in the ninth aphorism of this section, on page 194), nevertheless...

The detailed demonstration of those capable of performing breath-retention (vāyudhāraṇa) is for the sake of showing them; it should be understood that this applies to those who are incapable as well, as established by the Sūtra. The remainder of the passage ending with "twenty mouthfuls" (viṃśatigaṇḍūṣān) is clear in meaning. || 3 ||
Having performed the desired [rites] of bathing with mantras, ashes, and water, and having put on a garment. (4)
The mantra-bath is described in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"Having first performed the wiping of the limbs with a wet cloth while reciting the root mantra seven times from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head..."
"O Goddess, one should touch [the body] with both palms; this is proclaimed as the mantra-bath.
This bath is prescribed for one who is incapable [of the full ritual], for the sake of purification. Thus it is said.
The ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) is described in the Śivarahasya: "Having taken pure ash in one's hand, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
by anointing all the limbs with it, it is declared to be the ash-bath."

The ritual bath with water (*jalasnāna*) is described in the *Śrīlalitāprakaraṇa* [this is stated in the *Mūlasūtra* and its commentary in the third section of the *Śrīkrama*, on page 88, line 4]. Here, the primary form of the water-bath is intended; however, when the time for ritual action has arrived and water or other materials are unavailable, or if one is unable to perform it due to being occupied with urgent matters for the sake of the Guru, one should perform the "mantra-bath" (*mantrasnāna*) and so forth.
The ritual action [is as follows]. This has been stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*, beginning with "Now listen to the auspicious mantra," and continuing:
"But in the absence of water at the proper time, for one who is perishing on a difficult path..."
For the sake of swift success in one's journey and remaining untiring in weighty duties, one should perform the mantra-bath... [thus it is said].
For this reason as well, there is a brief bath described in the *Vīratantra*:
"One should cleanse the two hands below the wrists, the feet, the ankles, and likewise the face; this shall be the five-limbed bath (*pañcāṅga-snāna*), which bestows purity. Thus it is said.
These baths are to be understood as being established according to the gradation of one's capacity and the gradation of impurity.

Other [baths], such as the mental bath of meditation [meaning the bath of knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth], have not been written here for fear of excessive length; they should be sought from other Tantras. || 4 ||
He prescribes the twilight ritual (sandhyā):

having performed the twilight worship, having meditated upon the Goddess together with her retinue within the orb of the sun, having offered the arghya three times with the root mantra, and having satiated [her] according to one's capacity. || 5 ||

"This is the originative statement for the *sandhyā* ritual. Regarding the inquiry as to how it is to be performed, [the text] says, beginning with 'in the solar disc' and ending with 'having offered libations.
The libation is also performed with the mantra: 'Having uttered the root-mantra, I offer libations to Śrī Śyāmā, svāhā,' according to the *Mālinītantra*."

For it is stated in the extraction of the *tarpaṇa* mantra at the end of the root [text] (*mūla*), on page 193 of the present work: "Having uttered the *Mālinī*, one says, 'I satisfy the beloved of Agni' (*tarpayāmy agnivallabhām*)."

Since no mantra has been explicitly stated, when there is a requirement for a mantra, one should employ a mantra found in another tantra. By the phrase "according to one's capacity," it is indicated that the number [of repetitions] is not an essential factor in the act of satiation (*tarpaṇa*).

Regarding this, the author of the commentary (*nibandhakāra*) has declared that this section concludes the daily observance (*āhnika*) for independent worship and for the period of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), but not when performed as an ancillary part of the *Śrīkrama* practice. That is not correct;
according to the worldly maxim cited previously, the worship of Śyāmā is established as preceding the worship of Lalitā.

The limit for its performance is established by the subsequent statement— [it should be understood that "subsequent statement" means the statement found in Sūtra 37 of this section]— as being up to one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*). And thus, having worshipped Śaṅgītamātṛkā, one should worship Saṃvitsāmrājñī (and so forth), ending with Kola-mukhī.

Thus, by means of the *ktvā* suffix in the subsequent sūtra— [it should be understood that "subsequent sūtra" refers to the word *iṣṭvā* occurring at the end of the sentence within the first sūtra of the *Saṅgītamātṛkā* belonging to the seventh section of the present cycle of Vārāhī]. By means of the *ktvā* suffix.

The fact that the worship of Vārāhī precedes [the main rite] is clear. This being so, all that constitutes the worship of Śyāmā and the recitation of mantras (japa) connected with the time prior to the worship of Kolamukhī is an auxiliary limb for the commencement of the Śrī Lalitā-krama; it is not anything other than that which belongs to the Lalitā-krama.
Even the scent of the Śyāmā-krama, when being practiced, is perceived in the Sūtra.
This being the case, on what authority did [the author] write that the daily ritual (āhnika) is not to be performed elsewhere at the time of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) and so forth?
Only he himself knows his intention. In reality, the Śyāmā-krama is not an auxiliary limb of the practice of Lalitā.

It is not established in the Sūtra. Since the recitation of the daily lesson (āhnika) is directed toward the sequence that constitutes a constituent part [of the system], the entire daily lesson proceeds without hesitation even with respect to that sequence which is a constituent part. || 5 ||
Having described the rites beginning with entering the sacrificial hall and ending with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he begins to describe the worship after the twilight prayers:
"Having entered the sacrificial hall and sat upon a seat, [one should say] 'Obeisance to the Lotus Throne of the Support-Power' (*ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*). (6)
Now he describes the method of breath control (prāṇāyāma):

having placed his joined palms to his head, saying "Obeisance to the Śrī-pādukās of the entire assembly of manifest and secret Siddha-yoginīs" (note: the word *cakra* is not present in some versions), he performs the worship of his own Guru’s sandals (and the worship of Gaṇapati).
Having performed [the rite] || 7 ||

Having performed the worship of one's own guru’s sandals—the sandals of the Śyāmā-guru which will be described [in this section, Sūtra 32, on page 203]—one should scatter flowers and consecrated rice (akṣata) upon one's own head. 7.

Having performed the placement [of the mantra] as a pervasive covering over the palms, from the thumbs to the little fingers, over the elbows, and upon the body, with the weapon-mantra: *Aiṃ Hraḥ Astrāya Phaṭ*. || 8 ||

The definition characterized by pervasiveness was stated previously [it should be understood as being in the *Gaṇanāyakapaddhati*, in the second section on names, within the commentary on Sūtra 4, on page 75]. By means of the distinctions of the fingers and so forth...
The repetition of the mantra applies to each principal act, according to the maxim "repetition pertains to each principal."

Having drawn in the air with "Yaṃ" through the Piṅgalā [nāḍī] and dried the body; having drawn in the air with "Raṃ" and burned the body; having drawn in the air with "Vaṃ" and sprinkled the ashes of the burnt body with nectar; having drawn in the air with "Laṃ" and made it firm; and having drawn in the air with "Haṃsa" and generated the consciousness of Śiva.

The word *yam* is connected with the word *viśoṣya* (having dried up), because as the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*), it possesses the capacity for drying. Drying (*śoṣaṇa*) means the extraction of the watery element; however, the drawing in of air occurs quite silently.
The *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* [nāḍīs] are described in the *Nāradīya*:
The right nostril is known as Piṅgalā, and the other is remembered as Iḍā. Thus it is said.

With the seed-syllable of fire, *raṃ*, there is the burning of the body. With the nectar-seed-syllable, *vaṃ*, there is the sprinkling of the burnt ashes with nectar for the purpose of generating the body once again. With the earthly seed-syllable, *laṃ*, solidity is produced within the sprinkled ashes. Then, upon that [body], by means of the mantra *haṃsaḥ*—
The accomplishment of the consciousness of Śiva.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) up to this point, one should also perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) as taught in the Śrīkrama. || 9 ||
Having uttered the root mantra once, one should draw in the breath; having uttered it three times, one should retain it (kumbhaka); and having uttered it once, one should exhale.
Having thus performed exhalation, inhalation, and retention three, seven, ten, or sixteen times, one becomes a body composed of light.

"Each one" means once. Likewise, in what follows as well, the attainment of simultaneity is achieved through the compound *recaka-pūraka-kumbhakam*, which is a dvandva compound. Here, although there is an inversion of order—since *pūraka* (inhalation) falls in the middle, while *recaka* (exhalation) is first and *kumbhaka* (retention) is last—nevertheless, there is no intention regarding this sequence; rather, [the point is as follows:]

In this literary work, the sequence follows the order of the previous recitation. From the verse beginning with "tridhā" (in three ways), it is shown that as the number [of repetitions] increases, the fruit becomes greater. By the phrase "tejomayatanuḥ" (one whose body consists of light), the purifying power of the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is indicated. || 10 ||
Now he describes the fivefold placement beginning with the six limbs, as well as the network of placements:
[one should place] the six limbs, the Mātṛkā together with the Bālā [mantra], and [the deities] Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava at the root, the heart, and the mouth.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa). || 11 ||

The word "having placed" (*vinyasya*) is to be supplied and applied everywhere. Thus, the meaning is "having placed the six limbs. This is the nature of this mantra; for this purpose, it is explained in the preceding sūtras 15–20 of this section and in their commentary.

[Regarding the visible: We shall clarify this further above. This is one placement (*nyāsa*). "Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā* together with the vowels" is the second placement. [The term] *mātṛkā* refers to the external *mātṛkā*.
The locations for the placements are to be understood from other tantras.

The *tritārī-kumārī* and *kevala-kumārī* mantras, which will be explained below, [this *tritārī-kumārī* mantra is manifest; it is clear right here in this section (20) in the commentary on the Sūtra. By the word "kumārī," the three-syllable *bālā* mantra is to be understood. That too is clear right here below, and there as well. optionally.
In the case of its attainment, the qualification "together with Kevalabālā" serves as its sublater;
therefore, in the *mātṛkānyāsa* mantra, there is always the application of Bālā, whereas elsewhere the application of Bālā is optional.
Due to the great renown of the various locations of Vyāsa, they are not recorded here. And the nature of the mantra is: *aiṃ klīṃ*.

*Sauḥ aṃ namaḥ*. The same applies hereafter. The *mūla* is the location of the *mūlādhāra*. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the triad beginning with Rati upon the three locations starting from that. This is the third placement (*nyāsa*). || 11 ||
Having divided the root into seventeen parts: six in the aperture of Brahma, three in the forehead, four between the eyebrows, six in the right and left eyes, eight and seven in the mouth,
one each in the right ear, left ear, and throat, eight in the right and left shoulders, ten in the heart, and ten [in the navel].
Having thus performed the placement (vinyāsa), one places eight [syllables] on the right and left breasts, nine on the navel, two on the svādhiṣṭhāna, and six on the ādhāra.

Having broken and divided [the mantra], he describes the manner of division and the places for deposition (*nyāsa*) to be performed with the divided segments by means of the words beginning with "six" (*ṣaḍ*). The words expressing numbers such as "six" refer to the syllables situated in the root [mantra]. Having uttered the first six syllables ending with *namaḥ*, [one performs the deposition].

One should place [the mantras] in the *brahmarandhra*. The same applies hereafter. Regarding the statement "six and eight on the right and left eyes," six syllables are to be applied to the right eye as they follow in sequence, and eight to the left eye according to their respective numbers.
This same principle is to be understood for the right and left shoulders, and so forth. In all instances, there is the conjunction with the *tritārī* and the *kumārī*.
It should be performed. The *svādhiṣṭhāna* is a six-petaled lotus located in the secret place (*guhyasthāna*). The *ādhāra* is the *mūlādhāra*.

[For the knowledge of the true nature of this *ādhāra*, see the commentary on the third *sūtra* in the *Śrī Gaṇeśakrama* on page 88, and likewise the commentary on the twenty-eighth *sūtra* in the *Śrīkrama* on page 111.]
This has been explained previously. This is the fourth nyāsa. || 12 ||
He states the fifth [step]:
furthermore, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of seventeen sections from the support (*ādhāra*) up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*) in the locations not previously mentioned.

The difference from the previous [text] consists merely in the inversion of the locations, such as the *mūlādhāra* and so forth, and not in the sequence of sections (*khaṇḍa-krama*), because— as noted in the marginalia (*ba*)— there is no evidence to indicate an inversion of the sections; furthermore, there is no evidence for an inversion of the seventeen sections.
The author of the commentary has written the sections in reverse order; his authority for this is his own will alone and nothing else.
This is the fifth Nyāsa. 13.
196) Having thus described the network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla), he speaks of the worship of the temple (mandirārcana):

Having visualized a pavilion situated on a jewel-island in the midst of the ocean of nectar, adorned with pearl garlands and the like, and provided with four gates— at its four gates starting from the east, one should worship: *sāṃ* to Sarasvatī, *lāṃ* to Lakṣmī,
*śaṃ* to Śaṅkhanidhi, *paṃ* to Padmanidhi, and *lāṃ* to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand.

Salutation to Surādhipati (the Lord of the Gods), who has Airāvata as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Rāṃ Agni (Fire), who holds a spear in his hand, the lord of splendor, who has the goat as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Ṭāṃ Yama, who holds a staff in his hand, the lord of the departed spirits, who has the buffalo as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Kṣāṃ Nirṛti...
Obeisance to Khaḍgahasta, the lord of the Rākṣasas, whose vehicle is a man, together with his retinue;
vāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand, the lord of the waters, whose vehicle is a makara, together with his retinue;
yāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, the lord of the vital breaths, whose vehicle is a ruru deer, together with his retinue.
Salutation to Soma, who holds a conch in his hand, the lord of the constellations, whose vehicle is a horse, together with his retinue;
salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, the lord of knowledge, whose vehicle is a bull, together with his retinue;
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, the lord of Satyaloka.

"Obeisance to the one whose vehicle is a swan, together with his retinue; Śrīṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand, the lord of serpents, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, together with his retinue; Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site. Thus, one should worship eleven deities in the eleven directions. || 14 ||
The eleven directions—the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, below, and the totality—are to be known. The remainder is to be inferred by oneself. || 14 ||
Regarding the application of specific seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the mantras of the Śyāmā cycle,
[the text] states the application of specific seed-syllables for all mantras in the Śyāmā cycle:
"At the beginning of the mantras of the Śyāmā cycle, there is the application of the *tritārī* and the *kumārī*, or the *kumārī* and the *tritārī*."
The maiden previously mentioned is a young girl; the rest is as explained above. || 15 ||
The meaning is clear. || 15 ||
The injunction regarding the specific qualities of the performer states that he should have his limbs smeared with fragrant substances, his mouth perfumed with betel, and his mind made serene. (16)
p.
197) The Method for Drawing the Śyāmācakra:
Now, he explains the method for drawing the Śyāmācakra.

Having drawn the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja) upon circles of gold, silver, copper, sandalwood, or gems—consisting of a dot, a triangle, a pentagon, an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-petaled lotus, an eight-petaled lotus, a four-petaled lotus, and a square. || 17 ||

On the mandalas and on the wooden boards, the five-cornered [shape] has the form of a five-pointed sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Its emanation should be understood as proceeding from the central point (bindu) outward according to the method of emergence. || 17 ||
The Procedure for the General Arghya: Now, he describes the procedure for the general arghya—
by means of pure water over which the root mantra has been recited three times, [one should draw] a square, a circle, a hexagon, a triangle, and a bindu.

Having performed the entry with the *matsyamudrā*, one should establish the support (*ādhāra*) with the mantra: "Aṃ, to the *ātmatattva* and the *ādhāraśakti*, vauṣaṭ. Then, having worshipped the fire-potencies (*agnikalā*), namely Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā, [one recites] "Uṃ."

Having established the vessel with "Vauṣaṭ! To the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), to the lotus-faced one," and having worshipped the solar digits (sūryakalā) within the vessel—namely Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā—one should offer [the oblation] with "Maṃ! Salutation to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), to the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala)."

Having thus filled [the vessel] with pure water, and having worshipped the lunar digits (candrakalā)— namely Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā— and having assigned the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) to the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions;

Having protected it with the Astra-mantra, enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, displayed the Dhenu-yoni-mudrā, and consecrated it seven times with the root mantra (mūla-mantra), one should sprinkle the sacrificial hall and the articles of worship with droplets of that water.
By means of this entry, the water is consecrated specifically for the purpose of drawing the mandala, and not for filling it.

Since there is no authoritative evidence [for filling the vessel], it should be understood that the filling is to be done with pure water alone, not consecrated by mantras—this is the additional point [in manuscript *ba*].
This is according to the method of entry. And that [mudrā] is described in the Tantra as the Matsya-mudrā (Fish-seal):
"The left hand is turned face down, and the right hand is likewise positioned."
"This is proclaimed by the Tantrikas as the Matsya-mudrā (the Fish Seal). Thus [it is said].
O Goddess, one should place the palm of the right hand upon the back of the left;
the two thumbs should be properly aligned, straight, and facing downwards.
This is declared to be the Matsyamudrā for the construction of mandalas and the like.
Thus it is also stated in the *Paramānandatantra*. Regarding the definition of their supports (*ādhāra*), in that same work (p.
"The supports for these [elements] are either circular or triangular."
And it may be in the shape of a womb, or a hexagon, or even an octagon.
It may have no feet, or three, five, six, seven, or eight;
it should have an opening in the middle like the back of a bowl, and it must not touch the ground.
"O Ambikā, it should be performed in such a way that [the mind] remains submerged within. Thus [it is said].
One should perform the worship of the fire-energies (*vahnikalā*) upon the support (*ādhāra*) using these names in the dative case ending with *namaḥ*.

That they end in *namaḥ* and that they end in the dative case should also be understood to apply to the energies of the sun and the moon. "Having established the vessel" implies, as the ellipsis suggests, that it has been placed upon the aforementioned support. This is the worship of the names of the energies beginning with Fire.

[Proceeding] by way of circumambulation starting from the west and so forth. The measurement has been stated previously [here, the meaning of the word "previously" may be seen on page 107 in the commentary on the twenty-third sūtra of the Śrīkrama]. The remainder is clear. The method regarding Agni and Īśa has already been shown previously [by the phrase "already previously," this refers to the fourth section on pages 144–145].

This is to be understood from the *Lalitākrama*, the *Mūlasūtra* in eight [chapters], and its commentary, as well as from the subsequent *Mūlasūtra*: "with the *astra*" means with the *astra* mantra; "with the *kavaca*" means with the *kavaca* mantra.
However, some maintain that by the word "having enveloped" (*avakuṇṭhya*), one should understand the inclusion of both the *avakuṇṭhana* mudrā and the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*).
The nature of the *avakuṇṭhana* mudrā is stated in the Tantra:
"The two hands are in the form of fists, with the two index fingers straight."
One should rotate them simultaneously; this is the *avakuṇṭhinī* mudrā.
Thus they sang.

The *dhenu* is the *dhenumudrā*. This is well-known in the world; nevertheless, its authoritative description is written here: "The four fingers beginning with the index finger of both hands are interlaced; the right index and ring fingers are placed upon the left middle and little fingers."
The left index and ring fingers [are placed] upon the right middle and little fingers;
with the tips pointing downward, this is the Dhenu-mudrā.

Thus it is stated in the *Paramānandatantra*. As for the *yoni* (the *yonimudrā*), it was previously mentioned seven times; [it is to be seen at the end of the commentary on the fifteenth *sūtra* of the *Śrīlalitākrama*, folio 5, section khaṇḍa 170, or else in the context of *ddi.pa.* 15.8/2]. With the droplets of that water...
With droplets from the general arghya offering. || 18 ||
Regarding the procedure for the special *arghya*:
having prepared a mandala marked with the syllable *ī* consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square [or a six-cornered circle],
having scattered flowers upon it, and having established the support as before, one should worship the fire-energies (*agnikalā*).
Having established the vessel, [one recites] in that vessel: *hrīṃ aiṃ mahālakṣmīśvari paramasvāmini ūrdhvaśūnyapravāhini*.

"O you who consume Soma, Sūrya, and Agni; O you who shine in the supreme ether! Come, come! Enter, enter! Accept, accept the vessel! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Having thus scattered a handful of flowers and worshipped the digits of the Sun (Sūryakalā), [one should proceed].
Bring forth the nectar of immortality to fill this great vessel, produced from the fragments of the cosmic egg and filled with the entirety of all essences.

Having thus filled the first [square] and placed the second, one should write the letters *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* in the three corners marked by the three lines beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*, and the syllable *haṃsa* in the center; then, having consecrated it ten times with the root mantra and worshipped the digits of the moon (*candrakalāḥ*),
one should assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions, and protect it with the weapon mantra (*astra*).
Having enveloped [it] with the Kavaca mantra, one should display the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās. || 19 ||

With those waters connected to the common *arghya* offering; "marked with the letter *ī*" is an epithet of the triangle. The sense is that one should write the letter *ī* (or *īṃ*) in the middle of the triangle. This is not intended for creation by way of entry as before, but rather by way of exit.

Because the recitation begins with the triangle and concludes with the square, it is generally observed that the triangle is within everything and the square is outside of everything. "As before" means as stated previously in this same section on page 197,
in sūtra 18, beginning with "Oṃ, for the principle of the self" (ātmatattvāya), and so forth.

The meaning is: "like the vessel for the general *arghya*. Regarding the phrase "having worshipped the fire-calors (*agnikalā*) beginning with Dhūmrārcis and having established the vessel," the term "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is understood here as well due to its appropriateness. Therefore, in the establishment of the vessel:

The attainment of the previous mantra [here, the "previous mantra" refers to that which exists in this very section, on page 197, in the eighteenth root-sūtra above, beginning with *uṃ vidyā-tattvāya*]. The first and second [mantras] have been declared here in this sūtra;
therefore, the third, fourth, and fifth are not present here because they have not been mentioned. [For it is not] merely the sequence of Gaṇapati.

If it were the middle [line], there would be the particle *ca* as in the word *cetivat*, or there would be an indicator (*liṅga*) such as "having accepted the group of five" (*pañcakamurarīkṛtya*) by which that [meaning] could be obtained. Therefore, it is only as stated: those lines which have 'a', 'ka', and 'ya' at their beginning are the three lines. Starting from the letter 'a' and ending with the visarga is one line consisting of letters; then, starting from 'ka' and ending with 'ta' [is the second].

Therefore, the sense is that it ends with *thādisānta*. Since no specific [direction] is mentioned, one should write the three syllables *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* in the three [corners], proceeding clockwise from one's own [starting] point; then, having written *haṃsaḥ* in the center, situated toward the north.
This entire process of writing, which serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*), is performed upon the substance contained in the vessel. And thus:

The meaning of this is that one should contemplate the refinement of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) by means of such a script. This occurs ten times; subsequently, it is a qualifier for the phrase "having rotated the root mantra. One should display the *dhenu* and *yoni* [mudrās]; thus, the *dhenumudrā* [the extraction of this *dhenumudrā* is on page 198, following here in the commentary on the eighteenth sūtra, or in the second volume].

Having displayed the *yonimudrā* (the extraction of the *yonimudrā* is found on page 5 of section 170 of the *Śrīlalitākrama-sūtrabhāṣya*, verse 15; or see *Dvi-pa.* 15-8/2), one should prostrate. In some manuscripts, the reading is "this is the purification of the *arghya*. || 19 ||
(p. 200) Having thus described the placement of the vessels for the worship of the Wheel Goddesses (cakradevī), he states the mantra for the visualization of the form of the Śrī-devatā:

Having uttered "Śrīmātā" in the center of the wheel and consecrated the form with the mantra "Obeisance to the Form of Gīśvarī," and having again uttered "Śrīmātā" and invoked her with the mantra "I invoke the immortal consciousness of Gīśvarī," one should worship her with the sixteen offerings, [placing them] in the directions of Agni, the Three-eyed One, the Rakṣas, and Vāyu, as well as upon the head of the Goddess.

And surrounding [the central deity] are the worshipful Aṅgadevis; their mantras are those beginning with Sarvajana, consisting of eight, seven, eleven, ten, and again ten, twenty-eight sections, along with the Tritārī, Kumārī, Vāk, and others of similar kind, joined with the general Manu-mantra. || 2 ||

"In the center of the wheel" is connected with the word "having invoked. From "Śrī... up to "...ityantaḥ," excluding the word "having spoken," is the mantra for the visualization of the form (*mūrtikalpanamantra*). From the second "Śrī... up to "...āvāhayāmi," excluding the word "having spoken," is the invocation mantra (*āvāhanamantra*). The sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) along with their authoritative sources are in the second section.
[It should be understood that these are shown in the second section, on page 82 of the Sūtra-bhāṣya. They have been shown:
Āśuśukṣaṇi (Agni), Tryakṣa (Īśāna), Rakṣas (Nirṛti), and Prabhañjana (Vāyu).

The sense is that these are located in the cardinal directions according to the stated order, and in the intermediate directions (*vidik*) respectively. "In the head of the Goddess" means in the center.

The goddesses of the limbs (*aṅgadevyaḥ*), who are the goddesses of the six limbs, are to be worshipped in the directions beginning with the east. He begins to state their mantras with the words "tanmantrā" (their mantras). It should be understood that the mantras of the six goddesses of the limbs consist of six sections (*khaṇḍas*) starting from the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) with the words "sarvajanetyādi. In that regard, how many syllables does each single peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) contain?

In response to the inquiry, he says "eight," etc.; the meaning is that the six sections beginning with "sarvajana" have respectively eight and so forth as their number. That is, the first section has eight syllables, the second seven syllables, the third eleven syllables, and the fourth and fifth ten syllables each, while the sixth [has nine].

The result is that there are twenty-eight syllables. He states that the nature of the mantra is not only the syllables of the aforementioned number contained within the root mantra, but other syllables are also to be joined;
namely, at the beginning of these sections, the *tritārī*, the *kumārī*, the speech (*vāk*), and the *jāti* for the heart.

Beginning with "śirase," those [mantras] together with their respective suffixes—such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and so forth—are joined with them in due order. Thus, the nature of the mantra is as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ aiṃ sarvajanamanohāri hṛdayāya namaḥ*. The aforementioned seed-syllables (*bīja*) are *aiṃ* and so forth.

The following seven [mantras], beginning with these, are to be applied everywhere at the outset: 7. *sarvamukharañjini* śirase svāhā. 7. *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvarājavaśaṅkari* śikhāyai vaṣaṭ. 7. *sarvastrīpuruṣavaśaṅkari* kavacāya huṃ. 7. *sarvaduṣṭamṛgavaśaṅkari* netratrayāya vauṣaṭ. 7. [The seventh mantra follows].

The nature of the mantra is: *sarvasattvavaśaṅkari sarvalokavaśaṅkari amukaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā | sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ astrāya phaṭ*. Although thirty-three syllables are seen in this mantra, they appear to contradict the number twenty-eight stated in the Sūtra.

Nevertheless, the twenty-seven syllables ending with *svāhā*, when combined with the six preceding seed-syllables (*bījas*), become a single syllable for each of the three *kūṭas* within the fifteen-syllable *kūṭas* that constitute the venerable sixteen-syllable mantra— just as each individual *kūṭa* consists of a single syllable. And thus:
It is endowed with the number twenty-eight.

The author of the commentary (nibandhakāraḥ) made the section end with "svāhā"; likewise, in the case of the twenty-seven-syllable [mantra], there is an absence of the aforementioned application. || 20 ||
Regarding the worship of the enclosures:
subsequently, one should perform the worship of the enclosures. || 21 ||
Although this subsequent Sūtra appears to be redundant, it should not be regarded as such.

For this is the statement for the origin (*utpatti*) of the *āvaraṇa-pūjā*, while the subsequent statements constitute its detailed procedure (*itikartavyatā*), just as in the case of "One should sacrifice with Soma" and "He takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu."

By this, since it is prescribed by a single injunction and thus constitutes a single ritual act, it is established that even if there is an omission of a deity belonging to a single part of the covering in the middle, the entire performance must be repeated. || 21 ||
Now he states a certain general rule (paribhāṣā) that is useful for all [rites]:

one should perform the worship of all the wheels (cakras) and deities by scattering unbroken rice grains and flowers from the right hand, accompanied by the first drops falling from the *śrīpātra* held with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand pressed together.

All the deities of the cakras, beginning with Gaṇapati and ending with Parā, who are to be worshipped according to the general procedure, as well as others; the *śrīpātra* is the vessel for the special *arghya*. By the phrase "together with the falling [of the drops]," it is indicated that the falling of the *bindu*, the flower, and the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) occurs at one and the same time. || 22 ||
He describes the deities of the first enclosure and their location:
"In the triangle [are] Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava. (23)

"In the triangle" means in the corners of the triangle. Since no specific sequence is mentioned here, the order follows a clockwise direction starting from one's own front. Alternatively, [one may place them] in the southeast corner, then in the western corner, and then in the northeast;
by this, the conclusion is reached in the north. Thus ends the first enclosure.
He shows the location for the worship of the second enclosure and so forth: at the base of the five spokes, in the order beginning with the east, [one places] *drāṃ* for the arrow of liquefying,
*drīṃ* for the arrow of drying, *klīṃ* for the arrow of binding, *blūṃ* for the arrow of deluding, and *saḥ*.

"Salutation to Unmādana-bāṇa"—thus, before that [deity], one should worship Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makarake-tana, and Manobhava, which are attended by the mantras *māyā*, *kāma*, *vāgbhūḥ*, *blūṃ*, and *strīṃ*. || 24 ||

The word *namaḥ* is appended to all mantras. *Puraḥ* means in the east. *Mūle* means at the base of the five-spoked corner. *Tadagre* means at the tips of the five-spoked corners; this is the meaning. The sense is that Kāma and the others, joined respectively with the five beginning with Māyā (*hrīṃ*), are to be worshipped. As for the actual form of the mantra: *hrīṃ kāmaśrīpādukāṃ*.

I worship. The same applies hereafter. As before, it should be understood that [the name] is devoid of the dative case-ending and the word *namaḥ*. Thus ends the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa). || 24 ||
202) He states the location for the worship of the third enclosure and so forth:
at the base of the eight petals are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Māhendrī.

Cāmuṇḍā and Caṇḍikā, along with those beginning with the final letter [kṣa] joined with the vowel pairs and the moon (the letter i), are to be worshipped. In front of them are Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi. || 26 ||
The eight letters— āṃ, īṃ, ūṃ, ṛṃ, ḹṃ, aiṃ, auṃ, and aḥ—

which are the final ones among the eight pairs of vowels (aṃ, āṃ, iṃ, īṃ, uṃ, ūṃ, ṛṃ, ṝṃ, ḷṃ, ḹṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, aṃ, aḥ) accompanied by the moon (the nasal *anusvāra*), should be joined with these [eight] in sequence at the beginning; thus Brāhmī and the other goddesses are to be worshipped.

The nature of the mantra is: *āṃ brāhmīśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. The same applies hereafter. "In front of that" means at the tips of the eight petals. The singular number is used for the sake of the class (*jātāvekavacanam*). The word "are to be worshipped" (*pūjyāḥ*) is to be supplied [to each]. Thus ends the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇam*). || 25 ||
He states the places for the worship of the fourth enclosure:
on the sixteen petals are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śānti, Śraddhā, Sarasvatī, Kriyāśakti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi,
Mohinī, Pramathinī, Āśvāsinī, Vīcī, Vidyunmālinī, and Surānandā.
The Nāgabuddhikas. || 25 ||

Here, the deities of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) are Vidyunmālinī and Surānandā—one deity for each [petal]. The remaining deities are clear. Since the sequence has not been explicitly stated, [the worship] proceeds clockwise starting from the petal in front of the Goddess.
Thus ends the fourth enclosure (caturthāvaraṇa). || 26 ||
He states the locations and so forth of the fifth enclosure:

"On the eight petals, Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhana, Unmatta, Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these Bhairavas, joined with Daṇḍin, Svara, the pairs, and so forth, and ending with [the letter] Bha, are to be meditated upon. (27)
Regarding the term *sadaṇḍī*: according to the *Medinīkośa*, "daṇḍī" refers to the *anusvāra* (dot), as in "daṇḍī is the fifteenth [vowel], the void (*śūnya*).

The meaning is that they are to be worshipped with those mantras ending in Bhairava which are joined at the beginning with the aforementioned pairs of vowels and so forth, together with the *anusvāra*, such as *aṃ*, *iṃ*, *uṃ*, and so on. For example: *aṃ*.
I worship the venerable sandals of Asitāṅga Bhairava. In this same manner, the seven subsequent mantras are to be inferred.
Thus ends the fifth enclosure. || 27 ||
He states the mantras and so forth of the deities of the sixth enclosure:
"The four-petaled [lotus] consists of Māyuktataṅgī and Siddhalakṣmī, as well as Mahāmāyuktataṅgī and Mahāsiddhalakṣmī. (28)

It should be understood that [the name] is appropriate in both cases; thus, *Mātaṅgī* and *Mahāmātaṅgī* are established. The remainder is clear. The distinction is that the four—*Mātaṅgī*, *Siddhalakṣmī*, *Mahāmātaṅgī*, and *Mahāsiddhalakṣmī*—are to be worshipped. Thus ends the sixth enclosure (ṣaṣṭhāvaraṇa). || 28 ||
203) He describes the worship of the seventh enclosure:
Gaṃ Gaṇapati, Duṃ Durgā, Baṃ Baṭuka, Kṣaṃ Kṣetrapāla—these are to be worshipped in the square.
The sequence, however, begins from the southeast corner and proceeds to the corners ending with the northeast. Thus ends the seventh enclosure.
Regarding the worship of deities situated outside the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*),

the *Śrīkrama* states— in accordance with the tradition of other tantras— that one should worship the deities situated outside the enclosure just as one does the primordial deities (*āmnāyādidevatā*).
Having worshipped there once more, beginning with "Salutation to Sarasvatī" and ending with "Salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site. || 30 ||

"In that very place" means as previously stated [in the fourteenth sūtra of the Anugana on folio 196]. Wherever they have been worshipped following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), there one worships the *śrīpādukā* with those same mantras joined together. For example: "Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Sarasvatī."
Likewise, even further on, the conjunction of the word "śrīpādukām" at the end of each "namaḥ" is indicated in the Sūtra by the imitation of the form ending in "namaḥ."

The statement in the *Nibandha* that these [deities] should be worshipped in a square enclosure is weak, because it follows the natural implication that they should be worshipped again in the very same place where they were previously worshipped once. Even in common worldly experience, when it is said, "Place Caitra outside the house" and "Feed Maitra in the house," how could one understand from the statement alone that "Feed Caitra in that very same place"? [It would be impossible.]
Therefore, let the noble ones investigate with subtle intelligence that it is the hearer. 30.
Regarding the worship of the preceptor of the Śyāmā-vidyā— the worship of the preceptor who initiated the Śrī Śyāmā-vidyā (as the *kośas* state: "the preceptor who initiated the initiation")—
he describes their location as follows:

Having worshipped the gurus of the tradition who possess the form of the swan (haṃsa), who are full of supreme light, and whose activity is eternal, on the first line of the square [mandala]. || 31 ||

The meaning is that one should worship those lineage-gurus—who are Haṃsamūrti, Paraprakāśa, Pūrṇa, Nitya, and Karuṇa—on the eastern line of the square altar, ending in the north. And the nature of the mantra is: "The venerable sandals of the lineage-guru Haṃsamūrti."

I worship. In this way, the phrase "the lineage guru" (sampradāya-guru) should also be applied to the subsequent mantras, according to the maxim that "that which is heard at the end of a compound is connected with each [member] everywhere. || 31 ||
Having thus completed the worship of the *cakra*, he describes the worship of the Guru’s sandals (*gurupādukā*):
"One should worship the general and specific sandals upon one's own head. (32)

The mantra of the general *gurupādukā* is set forth in the *Dīkṣākhaṇḍa* [in the sūtra and its commentary on folio 66]; the mantra of the specific *gurupādukā* is in the final section (*caramakhaṇḍa*).
The mantra "Śyāmāgurupādukā" has been extracted; with these two mantras, one should worship the pair of sandals upon one's own head. || 32 ||

Having thus described the worship of the Goddess, including the worship of the *gurupādukā* and the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*), he now explains the offering of the oblation (*balipradāna*) following the worship of the principal deity:
Having again worshipped the Goddess and performed the sixteen services with the Bālā mantra. || 33 ||

The word "with" (*mūlena*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is indicated that the worship of the principal goddess occurs prior to the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*). The term "with *bālā*" (*bālayā*) is clear. || 33 ||
Regarding the offering of the *bali*,
he shows the method for the *bali* offering:
having fashioned a triangle, a circle, and a square with pure water, [one should place] water filled with half-rice within that.

Having scattered flowers and placed a vessel containing fragrant flowers—whether with or without a base, or intermediate—that is shared [with the deity], he should offer the half-portion of glory. || 34 ||
With pure water contained in a jar; that [jar] which contains water mixed with half-portioned cooked rice;

accompanied by these—namely, the first (initial), the second (subsequent), and the third (middle)—wherein fragrant flowers are present; having thus placed and established the offering vessel together with its base.
He shows the mantras for the offering of the *bali* and their ritual procedure: "Having uttered 'Śrīmātā', [say] 'O Gīśvarī, accept this *bali*, accept it, huṃ phaṭ svāhā!';
having uttered 'Śrīmātā', [say] 'O Gīśvarī, protect me who has come for refuge, protect me, huṃ phaṭ svāhā!'"

Having offered the *bali* with the three mantras: "O Lord Kṣetrapāla, accept this *bali*, accept it, phaṭ svāhā!", together with the gestures (*mudrās*) of striking the left heel, clapping the hands, and opening the mouth upward. || 35 ||

The three mantras ending with *śrīmātaṃ iti huṃ phaṭ svāhā* [are as follows]. Regarding the *nārāca-mudrā*, it is stated in the *Paramānanda-tantra*: "The clenched fist, with the thumb and index finger raised, and the tip of the index finger touching the top of the thumb."
And thus, the mudrā held with both hands is known by the name Nārāca. So it is said.

The meaning is this: first, having formed fists with both hands, one should release them; then, between those two thumbs and index fingers that have emerged from the fists, one should place the thumb with its tip pointing upward and the index finger straight with its tip pointing forward. This is the meaning of the *nārāca-mudrā*. || 35 ||
205) Having thus explained the sequence for offering the *bali*, he now instructs on the worship of the *suvāsinī* and so forth:
Having summoned the dark-hued Śakti and worshipped her with the *bālā* mantra, having placed the beginning and end [of the offering] into her hand,
having purified the *tattva*, and having accepted the remainder of that, one should partake of the remnants of the oblation together with those who are worthy. || 36 ||

Since no specific [deity] is mentioned after "having worshipped," [the worship is to be performed] according to one's means. By the phrase "having purified the principle" (*tattvaṃ śodhayitvā*), the mantras for the purification of the principles (*tattvaśodhana-mantra*) are also implied; these mantras are well known to be four.
These three *tattva*-mantras are found in the commentary on Sūtra 62 of the *Dīkṣā-prakaraṇa* (on page 39), and the fourth is as follows: [text of the fourth mantra].
The mantra is to be known as *sarvatattvāya svāhā*. Thus, the fourfold set of reality-mantras (*tattvamantra*) is to be known.

Having caused [the disciple] to take the four vessels, and having caused him to take the fourth vessel with its remainder, he himself should accept that remainder. Regarding the disposal of the sacrificial remains (*haviśśeṣa*), he says "by those who are fit" (*yogyaiḥ*). The meaning of the word "fit" (*yogya*) is as follows:

It has been explained by the term *śiṣṭa* (the "remnant") as stated in the *Śrīkrama* [on leaf 176, in the fifth section of the latter part, sūtra 22 and its commentary—the meaning of the term *śiṣṭa* is thus revealed]. And in this way, its purpose (*prayojana*) and its procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—all of that must be understood according to the method taught in the *Śrīkrama*. || 36 ||
Regarding the limit for the Śyāmāpūjā:
since there is a desire to know the limit as to how long the Saṅgītamātṛkāpūjā should be performed, he states that limit:

Performing daily worship in this manner, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the feeding of Brahmins according to the rule of one-tenth of that number. || 37 ||

In this manner, by the phrase "performing the constant worship" (*nityasaparyām*), he indicates that worship is a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of the recitation (*japa*). For if worship were the primary element and recitation the subordinate limb, then the statement that worship lasts as long as the hundred-thousand-fold recitation is completed would be contradicted. Indeed, it is not so.

In both worldly and Vedic usage, it is observed that the primary action follows the subordinate one; for instance, one does not say, "As long as the soldier runs, so long does the king run," but rather there is the common expression, "As long as the king runs, so long does the soldier run. Therefore, the recitation (*japa*) is the primary action, because worship is described as having that [recitation] as its limit. For this very reason:

Upon the completion of the recitation (*japa*), the worship (*pūjā*) is concluded. By the phrase "having performed a hundred-thousand recitations" (*lakṣajapaṃ japtvā*), the recitation characterized by a count of one hundred thousand is prescribed here. According to the sequence of its tenth part: the fire-oblation (*homa*) is one-tenth of the recitation; the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is one-tenth of that;
and the feeding of Brahmins is one-tenth of that—this is the meaning. (37)
The duties for one who has taken the *śyāmā* vow:
Now he states these duties for one who has taken the *manuja* vow—
one who has taken the *manuja* vow should not cut a *kadamba* tree, nor should he say with his voice, "Kālī."
One should not turn away from gatherings involving lutes, flutes, dancing, singing, or recitation of verses, nor should one revile a singer. || 38 ||

(206) "One who mutters this" means one who mutters the Śyāmā; these rules do not apply only during the time of the recitation, but rather from the commencement of the recitation for as long as one lives. Therefore, it is like the rule: "One who has maintained the sacred fires should not run when it rains. || 38 ||
Having thus explained the duties of the Śyāma lay-devotees, he also describes the duties of the Lalita lay-devotees, both because of the topical connection and their importance:
"The duties of the Lalita lay-devotees..."
A devoted practitioner of Lalitā should not eat pieces of sugarcane; he should not think of Vārtālī during the day;

he should not feel disgust toward the substances of accomplishment (*siddhadravya*); he should not act with cruelty toward women; he should not approach the wife of a *vīra*; he should not kill such a person, nor should he seize his property, nor take anything by his own will.
One should observe the fivefold code of conduct: one should not sit with those who have fallen from their lineage, nor should one engage in excessive idle chatter;
when a woman is conversing, one should not walk by without returning her greeting; and one should protect the sacred books of the lineage.
May there be auspiciousness. 39.
Thus ends the sixth section, named the Śyāmā-krama, in the Kalpasūtra.

By the phrase "a piece of sugarcane," it is indicated that there is no fault in its derivatives, such as molasses, sugar, and so forth. *Vārtālī* means the female pig. One should not feel disgust toward the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) even in one's own mind, nor should one condemn them. *Niṣṭhurā* refers to cruelty, such as the cutting off of the nose and other such acts.

The compound *vīrastriyam* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*, not a *karmadhāraya*. If it were a *karmadhāraya*, then in the subsequent phrase "one should not kill him" (*na taṃ hanyāt*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the masculine gender being unconnected [to the referent]. Therefore, because of the presence of this subverting factor (*bādhaka*), even the simpler *karmadhāraya* is abandoned. Furthermore, in the term *vīrastrī*, the meaning of the word *vīra* is one whose state of duality has been utterly uprooted and destroyed.
As it is said in the Tantra: "He who effects the dissolution of the 'this' which is the counter-correlative of the 'I',
and whose intellect is immersed in the bliss of his own Self— he should be known as a Vīra."

That hero; that substance is *vīradravya*. One should accept—that is, take possession of—it by one's own will for the sake of satisfying one's own senses. Those who have fallen from the *kula* are those who, having first embraced the path of the *kula*, later abandon the path they accepted because they have become distrustful due to the sins committed in previous births.

Thus it is said in the Devībhāgavata: "One who has resorted to the path of the Kula but abandons that path due to sins committed in previous births should neither stay nor converse with such a person."

Then the sacrificial animal is to be known as excellent; having seen it, one should enter the waters. [From the *Śrīsūtra* regarding non-return: "That which is to be purified must be indicated, as well as the remaining portion; by the grace of the Primordial Goddess, [this work] is complete. Thus ends the sixth section. Śrī.
One should touch it well. Thus.

"One should not engage in idle chatter with many" means that one should not speak with them [in large groups]. By the word "many," it is indicated that for the sake of protecting one's own path and avoiding the misfortunes arising therefrom, one should speak only as much as is necessary. "Without conversing" means without giving a reply. "Family books" refers to the books of the family's scriptures.
The explanation of the word "śivam" is as before.
Thus ends the sixth section, named the Śyāmākrama, in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.
Oṃ,
salutations to the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
The Śrī Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra.

May the descendant of Bhṛgu, whose lotus-hand holds a blazing axe, who is adorned with a circle of matted locks, and whose soul is gracious, grant long life. [This concludes] the commentary composed by Rāmeśvara.
First Section: The Ritual of Initiation (Dīkṣā-vidhi).
Commentary and Background Note: [In this context, by the word "vṛtti," one should understand the commentary titled *Saubhāgyodaya* upon this root text.]
For the knowledge of the time and other details regarding the composition of this commentary on the *Attikāra-abhidhāna*, see Section 1 of the Second Appendix below.
Herein is the benediction.
I salute the elephant-faced Lord, whose chest is reddened by the unguent smeared from the breasts of Śrī Vallabhā, and whose radiance is like that of ten million rising suns.
I contemplate this supreme Mother, who is the radiance within the Supreme Śiva, closely united with the state of full I-consciousness,
yet who subsequently assumes the state of duality.

Those powers, who exist as the five *pretas* and are the guardians of the abode of Supreme Śiva— namely desire, intellect, action, and the rest— who are my own rays and have become the protectors of the world's manifestation and its end;
she who, in the form of *paśyantī* and the others, manifests the entire web of words for all people.
May this Goddess of Speech, who destroys the impurity of the mind, sport within my mouth.

I bow to the Lord of Nāthas, who shines with the illustrious Yaśovantī on his left side, who is the thunderbolt for the mountain of ignorance, and whose abode is fashioned within the lotus of my heart by the Creator.
I bow to that lord of heroes, the sixth glorious incarnation of Viṣṇu, who, having been born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, slew the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times over.
I bow to Subrahmaṇya as my father and to the venerable mother as my mother; for the attainment of the fruit [of my efforts], those two alone are my refuge.
Having investigated various tantras and the extensive treatises on Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya,
and having thoroughly refined them using manuscripts collected from various regions;
In accordance with his understanding, he expands upon the hidden meaning of the *Kalpasūtra* composed by Jāmadagnya for the sake of attaining perfection in the worship of Śrīvidyā.
Rāmeśvara, born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, was impelled by the illustrious Lalitā.
The Section on Initiation (Dīkṣā-adhikāra): Here, indeed, the venerable Lord Śrī Paraśurāma, out of compassion for those of dull intellect in this modern age,
[has compiled] the innumerable [teachings] fashioned by Śrī Śiva— [from which it is understood that this work contains the essence of all tantric scriptures].

"The Lord Śiva is the agent"— this is to be seen here in the second supplement (pariśiṣṭa), section 3. Having thoroughly examined all the tantras and having condensed them, he makes this declaration, demonstrating the short path that accomplishes the fourth human goal (puruṣārtha):

Now, therefore, [the Blessed One, Śrī Jāmadagnya Rāma, begins this section from here—the method of meditation upon Him, and the account of the previous birth of His father, the great sage Śrī Jamadagni; this is to be seen in the second supplementary section (Dvi0 Pariśiṣṭa), chapter 2, on the subject]. [From here onwards, up to the preceding verse 33, regarding initiation (dīkṣā):]...

Everything that needs to be known regarding the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) up to the end of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya should be understood; however, it should be known that the commencement of the practical application (*prayoga*) of initiation begins from the thirty-fourth sūtra. We shall now explain [it]. || 1 ||
Now, the word *atha* indicates auspiciousness:
"In ancient times, these two—the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—emerged from Brahman after piercing his throat; therefore, both are auspicious."

This is because of such traditional authority (*smaraṇa*). Furthermore, the word *ataḥ* indicates immediate succession (*ānantarya*). When there is a requirement for a limit to this succession, either the performance of an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) or the purification of various systems (*nānātantrapariśodhana*), being proximate, connects as the limit. Alternatively, *athātaḥ* taken together indicates the commencement [of a work], as in "Now, therefore, [the exposition of] the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*atha ato darśapūrṇamāsau*).

"We shall explain"—thus [it is said] in the commentary on the Āpastamba Sūtra. Now, this word *atha* (now/then) is generally employed by the elders at the commencement of a section (*prakaraṇa*). In some cases, it is also used to indicate immediate succession (*ānantarya*), as for example in:
"These Bhṛgus have been explained; now, therefore, [the section] on the Aṅgirases," and so forth. Likewise, not...

Furthermore, here the meaning of *ānantarya* (immediacy) is because no other preceding [factor] is perceived; this is according to the text. The author of the Sūtras will analyze the category of *dīkṣā* (initiation) further on. And the category of *vyākhyā* (exegesis) is the detailed explanation of a word whose intended meaning is hidden. In the present context, regarding those things of hidden meaning—
The definition is thus fulfilled: a *kalpasūtra* is that which provides an analytical exposition by way of synthesizing the various *tantras*.
"I am the one who employs words conducive to the knowledge concerning initiation" (p.

The meaning is established. We shall explain [it]—the use of the plural number is intended to include other teachers who promote the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*), just as in common worldly usage, when one says "we shall perform a heavy task," others are also included. By this...

It has been indicated that the explanation of the *dīkṣā* is extremely difficult; or rather, its meaning is this: when one intends to express either the singularity or the duality of "we" (*asmad*), the plural form of *asmad* shall be used. And thus, since the word *asmad*, which denotes the agent, ends in the plural, it is for the sake of establishing grammatical agreement (*sāmānavacanatva*) with that [the verb] that [the plural is employed].
"We shall explain" is the plural form.
Refutation of the Doubt Regarding the Invalidity of the Tantras:

Now, it may be argued that it is improper for those who follow the Vedas to provide an exposition of the *Kalpasūtras*, because they are included among the *Tantras*, and since the *Tantras* have as their sole basis greed, they lack authority. As it has been stated in the *Vārttika*:
The Bhaṭṭapādas state:
"And here, many other causes such as greed are perceived;
when these are present and observed, there is no inference of another underlying cause."
And the Śākyas and others, while teaching the Dharma everywhere,
never do so without being liberated from the net of causes.
Nor do they state that [the Smṛtis] have the Veda as their source, unlike Gautama and others;
rather, reasons are put forward which stand far removed from Dharma.
And these are precisely those who do not offer even verbal worship;
for they are indeed heretics, mere ritualists, and rationalists.
Thus, those other [works] which have not been accepted by the knowers of the three Vedas (trayīvid),
which have fallen under the shadow of some mixture of [heterodox] doctrines, and which are intent upon the purposes of winning over the world, gain, honor, and fame— [are likewise to be rejected].

These are composed on the basis of views contrary to the three Vedas, disconnected [from them], and rooted in greed and other such factors, as well as in direct perception, inference, analogy, presumptive testimony, and reasoning; they are the foundations for dharma and adharma as accepted in the texts of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and Śākya schools.
[These practices], which are capable of neutralizing poison, subjugating others, causing expulsion, or inducing madness,

and which possess the power of displaying occasional supernatural attainments, are merely scented with the fragrance of a few meanings consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti— such as non-violence, truthful speech, self-restraint, charity, and compassion.
Those [texts] which teach various matters primarily for the sake of livelihood,
and which are based on practices such as the conduct of barbarians and mixed dietary habits—
it is precisely these that are established here as being unworthy of reliance, both because they contradict the Vedas and because their underlying motives are evident.
And so it is stated in the second chapter of the *Brahmagītā* within the *Śrīsūtasamhitā*: "One who abandons this Vedic path and resorts to another path is like one who,
having rejected the milk-rice held in his own hand, licks his own elbow."
If living beings could attain liberation through a path other than the Veda,
then they would also perceive jars and such objects even in total darkness without the aid of light.
"Therefore, the matter proclaimed by the Veda is indeed true, truly declared by me;
for a matter known through any other [means] is not true from the perspective of ultimate reality."
"In each of those cases, they propound arguments according to their own strength;
it is my conviction that all such disputations are contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti."
In the forty-first chapter of the Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa:
"What is the use of saying more here? Without that which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti, one who performs even the slightest [act] becomes a sinner; of this there is no doubt."
Thus, the censure of those following paths other than the Vedic is heard. Also, in the *Agni Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between the mass of Vedas and the denizens of hell:
"Those who have received initiation into the Tantras with minds corrupted by greed..."
"Having abandoned the Vedic path, we are being consumed by that [fire]," so it is said.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the *Puṣkara-māhātmya*:
"And those in the world who are heretics, tantrikas, and atheists—
for them this sacred ford is difficult to attain..."

Thus, by means of this censure of Tantric practitioners, the untrustworthiness of the Tantra is made clear. Likewise, because such censures of Tantra are frequently encountered in many other Purāṇas as well,
it is perfectly evident that the scripture which prescribes the worship of the *pañcaka* (the five) is rooted solely in greed.

It has been established that the scripture concerning the acquisition and retention of the residence of the Visarjanīya has greed as its sole root. What need is there to mention that for one who serves the group of five (pañcaka), its being rooted in greed is beyond dispute? Therefore, if it is argued that this scripture should not be explained by theists—do not say so; [for this is the meaning of the scripture which accepts the authority of the Tantric treatises].
Do the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda accept the Purāṇas, such as the Padma and others, as authoritative sources, or not?
If they are accepted as authoritative, then in them the authority of the Tantras is frequently heard regarding specific qualified practitioners (*adhikāri*). For instance, in the Sūtasamhitā:
In the second chapter of the *Brahmagītā*:
"Nevertheless, an object seen even in a dream by one dwelling in heaven certainly becomes an indicator for the attainment of true objects in the waking state."
In the same way, even those who have strayed from the path will undoubtedly attain the realization of the meaning proclaimed by the Vedas.

Therefore, in the final analysis, paths other than the Veda are certainly not to be abandoned. [By this much it is established that resorting to paths of dharma other than the Veda is not unscriptural, just as resorting to the Veda itself is not.]
In the Sūtasaṃhitā, in the Śivamāhātmyakhaṇḍa, the fifth chapter states:
"The worship of the Supreme Śakti is proclaimed to be of two kinds."
Through the division of external and internal, the external is considered to be of two kinds.
O best of the twice-born, it is both Vedic and Tantric;
however, that which is Tantric belongs only to the practitioner of Tantra and not to anyone else, while the Vedic belongs indeed to the follower of the Vedas.
"Thus, O Brahmins, the worship of all the gods is established. So it is said.
Thus, in the *Muktikhaṇḍa* of the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"Of the *Tantras* such as the *Pāñcarātra*... [By this, the Vedic foundation of Tantric works such as the *Nāradapāñcarātra* and others is established, and from them, for the Vaidikas...]
Thus, it is established that both the statement regarding the acceptance of portions not contradicted by the Vedas and the teaching of Paraśiva are proven.
For those who hold the Vedas as their foundation are orthodox;
indeed, they are not independent, and therefore, upon examination, they are found not to be rooted in delusion.
"Nevertheless, O Goddess, that portion of the paths which is not contradicted by the Veda is said to be authoritative for certain qualified aspirants. Thus,
O Goddess, I am attainable by the Tantrikas through an intermediary."
"And: 'I am attainable without mediation by those who are solely devoted to the Vedas. Thus it is said.
Thus, in that very same Yajñavaibhavakhaṇḍa, in the nineteenth chapter:
"The Dharma proclaimed in the Śaiva Āgamas was previously declared to be twofold:
one arising from the downward stream (adhaḥsrotas), and the other arising from the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas)."
O twice-born ones, the arising of the upward-streaming dharma is superior to the arising of the downward-streaming dharma;
it is divided into many parts according to the classifications of the Kāmika and other tantras.
"In that same work, in the twenty-second chapter, it is said: 'The Dharma arising from the downward flow is thus divided into many types;
yet the Smārta Dharmas are greater than the Dharma arising from the upward flow.'"

Therefore, O best of Veda-knowers, other paths possess authority only regarding liberation and not in this [context] alone; here, their status as a means of knowledge exists only through a sequential process.
Therefore, Mahādeva, abiding on the path of Vedānta, bestows liberation without delay; however, he does not do so for one situated elsewhere, even though he may grant it gradually.
"It bestows supreme liberation; such is the eternal Vedic revelation. Thus it is said.
In that very same [text] (p. 6):
"Therefore, a mortal established in the Veda should not resort to any other path."
Therefore, there is no doubt that the paths are authoritative according to the distinction of the qualified practitioners.
In that very same [chapter], when one [section] has been completed, the verses therein are as follows:
Regarding the essential nature of the Lord, likewise regarding the cause of bondage,
as well as the cause of the world, liberation, and likewise knowledge and so forth.
Even those wise ones who discern the portions of the various paths that are contradictory to the Vedānta [do so] for the sake of those of dull intellect whose minds are shrouded by great delusion.

They have proceeded according to mere desire and not according to reality—just as a man, having pointed out a blade of grass, caught hold of a cow that was running away. [Note: Here it should be observed how much the Tantric scriptures rely upon the established tenets of the Vedas.]
Having first displayed such trivial and desirable things, Maheśvara subsequently bestows supreme knowledge in accordance with [the disciple's] spiritual maturity.
"Therefore, since these paths and this measure as well as non-measure have been declared by Śiva according to the path already described, how could Śiva be a speaker of falsehood?"
Likewise, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The scriptures declare that this knowledge must be guarded as one would protect the lover of one's own mother."

Thus is the presentation of the scriptures as authoritative sources. Likewise, it should be understood that here the instruction for performing rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) according to the Tantric method, as well as the attainment of the resulting fruits through that method, have been described.
In the *Brahmottarakhaṇḍa*, within the section on the greatness of *pradoṣa*, the worship of *pradoṣa* is set forth according to the Tantric tradition.

The instruction given to the Brahmin and the prince, and the attainment of the fruit by him—thus the historical account (itihāsa) is clearly understood. In the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, in the hymn of Gajendra, [the Lord is addressed as] "to the great ocean of the tradition of the Śarva-āgamas.
Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that "āgamas" refers to the *tantras* such as the *Pāñcarātra*. Likewise...
"In the hymn of praise to Brahmā, this form is likewise to be worshipped by those seeking the highest good, whether through the Vedic or Tantric path, O bull among men. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the eleventh skandha, in the instruction on the feeding of the camel, in the procedure for the worship of the door, and in the worship of Kali,
there are these words: "O King, those who desire to know the Supreme worship by means of both the Vedas and the Tantras."
"Listen likewise to how it is even in the Kali age through the prescriptions of various tantras. Thus [it is said].
"By means of the procedures of various tantras"—this indicates that in the Kali age, the path of Tantra is predominant;
such is the explanation of Śrīdharasvāmī. Likewise, in the Eleventh Book (*Ekādaśa-skandha*), within the *Uddhava-upadeśa* (p.
"The Vedic, the Tantric, and the mixed—thus my sacrifice is threefold" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.7).

Thus, worship of two kinds—distinguished as Vedic and Tantric—was taught by the Blessed Lord. By this much it is established that the Tantric worship of the Blessed One is also approved; this is perceived by everyone.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata*, in the *Arjunastuti*:
"Salutations to You, who are known through the Vedas and Āgamas, and whose intellect is pure."
Thousands of such statements establishing the authority of the Tantras are found;
they are not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length. Likewise, there are statements in the venerable Mahābhārata that establish the authority of the path of Yoga.

These [teachings] are heard repeatedly in the *Bhagavadgītā*, in the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*, and so forth; likewise, they are found at every step in the *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*, the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, and all other Purāṇas. This being the case, how could the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda declare the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Tantric systems to be invalid? Or rather, he would not.
It cannot be said that the Purāṇas lack authority,
for "the Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."

Thus, because of the enumeration of the sciences (*vidyā*), and because even in the Veda— where it says "the *Atharvāṅgirasas*, the Brāhmaṇas, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas"— the Purāṇa is included among the authoritative sources; by this, [it is established that] the Tantric scriptures,
the Brāhmaṇas, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras are rooted in the Veda.
[The authority] is indeed perceived. Thus, by these collections of statements and other such [arguments],
once the authority of the Tantras is established, it cannot be rendered invalid even by Brahmā himself.
The Refutation of the Doubt that All Tantras are Outside the Veda:

Now, it may be argued that while the Tantras possess authority for specific qualified persons—such as men who have fallen away from the Veda, women, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes—they do not possess authority for those who follow the Vedic path; nor does the Tantra have authority beyond the Vedic sphere.

It cannot be said that there is an absence of authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) restricting the scope of eligibility (adhikāra), because previously it was recorded in the Sūtasamhitā that [the practice] belongs only to the Tantrika and not to the other [Vaidika], specifically stating, "for the Vedic [belongs] to the Vaidika. Likewise, in the Muktikhaṇḍa of the very same Sūtasamhitā:
"But for those living beings who have completely fallen away from the Vedic path, the paths such as the Pāñcarātra are beneficial only through the power of time. Thus it is said.
In that very Sūtagītā it is said:
"For those human beings who have strayed from the path of the Vedas,
Śambhu— the omniscient Lord of all and the Guru of gurus— has proclaimed the Tantra."
For those devoted to the path of the Vedas, there is nothing at all beneficial there; everything spoken here is complete and true.

Thus, because of the statement regarding other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it is argued that therefore even the *pramāṇas* are *tantras* only for one who has strayed from the Vedic path and not for a follower of the Veda—[we reply:

No; as for the statement from the *Sūtagītā*, "and that which has fallen from the path of the Vedas," the word *tantra* therein refers to a specific *tantra*. That *tantra* is well known in the South as the *Śaivāgama*, and it is practiced by those popularly called *jaṅgamas*. If it is asked how this very [text] serves as proof:

There is an indicative proof in the very vicinity of the previously mentioned statement: "The sign (liṅga), which destroys all suffering, is declared in all tantras to be worn by those who have fallen from the path of the Vedas."
"That [knowledge] should never be retained by those who are devoted solely to the path of scriptural study. Thus [it is said].

In this regard, it is established by the Śaiva Āgamas that the wearing of the *liṅga* is a means for attaining manifold fruits. Furthermore, the practice is observed among those who follow that tradition, wherein they wear the *liṅga* on the right arm or around the neck. And as in this statement, [it applies] to those who have fallen from the path of the Vedas regarding all the Tantras.

The phrase "thus the answer has been set forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied. And thus, the fact that the wearing of the *liṅga* is taught in a particular Tantra serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the principle that such a Tantra is intended for those who have fallen away from the Vedic revelation (*śrutibhraṣṭa*). Just as the word "animal" (*paśu*) is restricted by the indicative power of the mantra "of the goat's omentum and fat," so it is here. Furthermore:
In the glorious *Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa*, the inquiry of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa:

"O King of kings, [please describe] that easy means of liberation accessible to women and Śūdras, which grants liberation to the castes such as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, as well as to those in the various stages of life (*āśramas*)."
"Speak that which benefits the world to my brother, who is your devotee. Thus [he said].
Following that, beginning with "Śrī Rāma said," one should indeed perform the worship of the ten enclosures (daśāvaraṇapūjā) as declared in the Āgamas;
the expert in Tantra should diligently perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed rite.
"By means of the path taught in the Āgamas—and in some places it is said 'taught by Agastya'—the best of those who know the Āgamas [should act] with the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Thus [it is said].

Thus, when the question is asked regarding the means to liberation for the castes such as Brahmins and the stages of life such as studentship, the answer— that worship as prescribed in the Āgamas must be performed— is a conclusion that leaves no other recourse; this, which establishes Tantric practice even within the Vedic fold, should be accepted by one who seeks the truth and is free from envy.

It is impossible to abandon [this interpretation]. For when asked, "Is Caitra skilled?", no authoritative person would say, "Maitra is skilled. Therefore, the reference to Śrī Rāma comes after [the discussion of] the Brāhmaṇas and others; for in the world, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who is not Vedic is not well-known. Nor is there a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya...

Or, one who has fallen due to a great sin such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and has strayed from the path of the Vedas— since in that case both Brahminhood and the state of having slipped from the Vedic path exist, it must be said that he alone is qualified for what is taught in the Tantras— in the inquiry concerning the auspicious [status] of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, and in the prescription of worship which constitutes the answer thereto:
Having attained the status of the twice-born according to the procedure prescribed by one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*,
a human being should first perform the morning bath for the purification of the body.
By means of the mantras proclaimed in the Vedic tantras, according to the procedure for smearing with clay.

Thus, by means of this copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*), it is prescribed that for a single person alone, both Vedic mantras and Tantric mantras serve as the instruments for bathing. And so, by accepting that this is a rule for the general practice of Tantra directed toward those outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*), the authoritative validity of the words of Śrī Rāma is maintained.
This is indeed impossible even for the teachers of the gods. Thus, in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, in the Eleventh Canto, in the instruction to Uddhava:
"For me, however, it is through both the Veda and the Tantras for the sake of accomplishing both."
In the conclusion of that very [work], it is said:
"Thus, by means of the paths of ritual action belonging to both the Vedic and Tantric traditions,
a person worshipping me on both sides attains from me their desired perfection."

Therefore, the statement "those who have fallen from the path of the Śruti" refers specifically to those who wear the *jaṅgama* and other sectarian marks (*liṅga*). Likewise, in the previously cited statement from the *Muktikhaṇḍa*, "the paths such as the Pāñcarātra," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) does not include the Śaiva Āgamas that are accepted by the *jaṅgamas*.
