Because it has been established that works such as the *Jñānārṇava* and the *Kalpasūtra* concern those who have fallen away from the Vedas, they form a single coherent whole with that [text]. Furthermore, in the *Śivamāhātmyakhaṇḍa*, beginning with the words "But the worship of the Supreme Śakti... and so forth...
O best of the twice-born, there are two [paths], the Vedic and the Tantric;
however, that which is Tantric belongs only to the Tantrika and not to anyone else, while the Vedic belongs indeed to the Vaidika.
The meaning of this statement is as follows: the Vedic [initiate] is one consecrated by the sacraments such as the initiation (*upanayana*) prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*;

the Tantric [initiate] is one consecrated by initiation (*dīkṣā*) preceded by the construction of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), pavilions (*maṇḍapa*), and so forth, as set forth in the Tantras. One is not called "Tantric" merely because he has strayed from the path of the Vedas, since such a person has already been rejected [earlier]. And thus, by this statement—

Occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as Vedic bathing and worship are prescribed on the occasion of the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*) and the like. On the occasion of Tantric initiation (*tantra-dīkṣā*), occasional rites such as Tantric bathing and worship are enjoined. Where there is only one occasion, there is only one [rite]:
purely Vedic for those such as Śūdras, and purely Tantric for others; where both [occasions] apply, there is the performance of both.
There is no contradiction whatsoever; by this much alone, the instruction for the three castes regarding both Vedic and Tantric rites is established (see *Dvaya-pariśiṣṭa*, 2, Viśeṣa-dṛśya, 2).
The meaning of this very point has been clarified in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"For those of the three twice-born castes, all Tantric rites are performed at the conclusion of the Vedic rites. Thus it is said.

The illustrious Rāma has also stated this very same point in brief: "by means of mantras proclaimed in the Vedas and Tantras. Therefore, the conclusion that the practice of all *tantras* is essentially outside the Veda (*vedabāhya*) is merely a manifestation of delusion arising from not consulting other scriptural statements. As for the *Pāñcarātra* and other such systems...
The engagement [with this practice] occurs precisely by aiming at that which has flowed onto the path of hearing, because it is performed by directly invoking its name.
It is exactly the same with the Kāpāla [system] as well—(p.
O lords of sages, there is no qualification for those who follow the Vedas in the Pāñcarātra, nor in the Kāpāla, nor even in the Kālamukha; it simply does not exist.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*, the intention of Bhaṭṭapāda is indeed established regarding this very point. For this reason alone, among the tantras, the name of the *Pāñcarātra* specifically is mentioned separately; however, there is no inclusion of all tantras therein, as that [section] pertains only to those that contradict the Vedas.

Furthermore, because practices contrary to the Smṛtis are frequently observed [in other systems], whereas not even the slightest practice contrary to the Vedas is found in the Śākta and other Tantras— as is the case with the Śākyas and others—
those statements such as "having abandoned this path of the Veda" and so forth refer to the Vaidika [practitioner].

For it is heard [in scripture] that one who completely abandons the Vedic path and resorts solely to the Tantric path must do so "except for" (vinā) those [texts] intent upon its censure; or else, having previously censured the Vedic path, [it is said]: "Therefore, the matter taught by the Veda is indeed true, truly true."

Regarding the doubt: since all [passages] consisting of specific arthavādas in the form of censure and praise, when taken together, establish a single injunction that "one must practice the path of the Veda," there is parsimony (lāghava). In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is a combination of the Tantric rite with the censure; therefore, by the praise "therefore [it is] declared in the Veda," there is an injunction for the Vedic rite.

If one were to assume [it is required], there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). The previously cited statement from the *Agni Purāṇa* and the *Padma Purāṇa* refer to specific Tantric systems, according to the reasoning stated above. For this very reason, even the venerable Vidyāraṇya Svāmī has stated in that same work that statements in the Tantras such as "one initiated in the Tantras" and so forth, which appear to be condemnatory, are actually intended to praise the Vedic path.

This has been explained. In this very same manner, the wise should infer other objects of the Yoga system, even though its authority has been rejected by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda; it is not written here because it is irrelevant to the present topic and for fear of excessive prolixity.
Compared to the statements of Bhaṭṭapāda, the authority of the Purāṇas and the Tantras is superior.

Therefore, it is indeed proper that a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) should be restricted in accordance with a stronger one; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between these two—namely, the Smṛti stating, "A Brāhmaṇa should observe celibacy for forty-eight years," and the Śruti stating, "One who has fathered a son and whose hair is still black should establish the sacred fires. In this manner:

For it is not well known that a man who has fathered a son and possesses black hair forty-eight years after marriage is eligible for the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*). Therefore, when there is a conflict between the two,
the term "Brāhmaṇa" found in the Smṛti must, in accordance with the more authoritative Śruti, be understood as referring to those who are blind and so forth.
Otherwise, their own treatise— which establishes that there is no contradiction with the Śruti because such individuals lack the qualification for the primary Vedic rites—
would be contradicted. Therefore, those who follow the Vedas do possess the qualification for performing the rituals taught in the Tantras of the Śāktas, Gāṇeśas, and others.

It has been established by the preceding arguments that this is indeed the intention of the Bhaṭṭapādas. By this, those who stubbornly deny that Vaidikas have no authority regarding Tantric rites are cast far away. By this same reasoning, the refutation of the authority of the Tantras written by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita should also be understood as overturned by the wise.

The systematic application (*vyavasthā*) of the statements in the *Purāṇas* has already been explained. As for the claim that the scripture prescribing the acceptance of the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) has only visible purposes and was composed on the basis of greed—that too applies equally to such Vedic passages as "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma" and "Wine-cups are taken. For indeed, [it is not the case that these lack a transcendental purpose].
Even Brahmā would be unable to establish the status of validity by casting aside the conviction that "this is a means of valid cognition.

Therefore, for the Vaidikas, the very first factor that establishes validity is precisely a specific conviction—that the Veda is a means of valid cognition—produced by the force of prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*). And from that, [it follows that...]

Only those [texts] that are not in contradiction with it possess authority because they are rooted in it; however, that which contradicts it is simply non-authoritative, even if it is Vedic. Furthermore—just as the Śrīsundarī Tantras...
The six sūtras of Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, and others, which constitute the supplements to the Taittirīya Śākhā, are authoritative; likewise, by this much,
the Bodhāyana-sūtra, the Āpastamba-sūtra, the Sundarītāpinī, the Pañcatāpinī, the Bhāvanopaniṣad, and the Kaulopaniṣad [are established].
The phrase "only the means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇānyeva*) is what is being suggested here.

The *Sundarītāpinī*, the *Pañcakabhāvanā*, the *Kaulopaniṣad*, and their remaining supplements are of the nature of commentaries on that [text], and are not fabricated by one's own imagination. Therefore, because they are of the nature of commentaries on the Vedas, they may be accepted without hesitation by those who follow the Vedic path.
These are to be adopted. We shall explain later how the practice of the five M’s and so forth is not in contradiction with the Vedas.
The qualification for the Sundarī-vidyā belongs exclusively to those of pure mind;

even though it is acceptable to the Vaidikas, not all Vaidikas possess the qualification for this. Just as, although the nature of Brahman is propounded in the Veda in the form of the Upaniṣadic portions, [not everyone is qualified] for the inquiry into it.

While there is eligibility for all, eligibility belongs only to those who follow the Vedic path and are endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*); thus, in this case, eligibility belongs only to certain individuals. To explain: for a Brāhmaṇa, beginning from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the first stage is the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*).
Immediately thereafter, having heard the censure of one ignorant of the meaning— "This Sthāṇu was indeed a mere bearer of burdens"—
and the fruit of knowing the meaning— "He who knows the meaning enjoys all prosperity," he studied poetry,
grammar, etymology, and logic in order to achieve proficiency in understanding the meaning.

Having studied the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā and understood the meaning of the Veda, one should not consider one's purpose fulfilled through knowledge alone; for, having heard the censure in the Smṛti against one who knows the meaning but does not perform the ritual acts, he ascends to the stage of performance and undertakes the ritual acts prescribed by all the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

When, having practiced those actions throughout many births, one's mind becomes thoroughly purified, and one is neither excessively attached nor excessively detached to *saṃsāra*, then one becomes fit for ascending to the stage of devotion (*bhakti*). As it is said in the *Bhāgavata*:
Neither through detachment nor through attachment does the yoga of devotion grant its perfection; rather, it is this [devotion] alone that bestows success upon him. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that when one is neither despondent nor attached, then the yoga of devotion bestows perfection.
Without ascending to such a stage of devotion, the attainment of the supreme human goal is never possible.
As it is said in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam:
"Devotion to the Blessed One that is signless is superior to spiritual accomplishment;
it quickly consumes the sheath, just as fire digests what has been swallowed. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the nature of devotion (*bhakti*),

the Naiyāyikas maintain that devotion is a specific, non-artificial, and innate form of knowledge characterized by the mode of "being worthy of worship. Others hold that devotion is the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) into the form of the Lord, directed toward Him.

The mental modification consists of transformation. Regarding this, the proof is as follows: "May that joy which belongs to the undiscriminating toward sense objects—[the joy] of me who remembers you—not depart from my heart."
Thus, in response to Prahlāda’s request for love directed toward the Blessed One, the Śrī Bhagavān spoke these words:
"You already possess devotion toward Me; it shall become even greater than this."
(As stated on p. 12:

"May there be the attainment of devotion," [and] by means of the granting of a boon, [he prayed: "May I have memory [of this]. [From here onwards, regarding the study of the meaningful Veda—both in terms of devotion and reverence—there exists a collection of authoritative proofs. Thus, it is simply a prayer for devotion.
It is understood that giving a cloth to one who asks for a pot is not appropriate. Therefore,
the ancient authorities (paurāṇikas) maintain that devotion (bhakti) is the continuous remembrance of the Blessed Lord, and it is also designated as unconditioned love (nirupādhikī prīti).

"May there be unswerving devotion to me through the yoga of undivided concentration"—this statement of the Blessed Lord also refers to the uninterrupted remembrance of the Blessed Lord. And this is appropriate, because this very same meaning has been stated in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. For instance:
"That which is the natural activity of the single-minded state within the *sattva* of those gods who possess the marks of virtue and whose actions are based on revealed scripture—
that indeed is devotion to the Lord (*bhāgavatī bhakti*). Thus [it is said].

The meaning is as follows: those by which the *guṇas* (the objects) are characterized—that is, known—are the senses; the presiding deities of these senses have a disposition toward Śiva alone, who is the embodiment of *sattva*.

That disposition which is without cause, free from desire, natural, and accomplished without effort is called *bhakti*. *Ānuśravika* action refers to the ritual action proclaimed in the *anuśrava*, which is the Veda.
The phrase "of whom" (*yeṣām*) is an epithet of the gods. By this, it is indicated that the means for devotion (*bhakti*) is the karma revealed in the sacred scriptures (*ānuśravika*).

Therefore, it is established that devotion is simply a mental state (*manovṛtti*) having the form of the Blessed Lord. Thus: "Now, therefore, the desire to know devotion; it is supreme attachment to the Lord"—this is the *Śāṇḍilya-sūtra*.

Regarding the fact that worship (*upāsana*) is a means to devotion: one who desires to ascend to such a stage of devotion should perform the worship of the Lord, which serves as its means. Worship, it should be noted, is the selfless renunciation of all things for the sake of the Lord.
Listening to the discourse of the Blessed One, chanting the mantras of the Blessed One,
and proclaiming the hymns of praise to the names of the Blessed One— any one of these serves as a cause for devotion. Regarding its nature as a cause for devotion,
it is stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam:
Furthermore, I shall describe the supreme cause of devotion to Me:
constant faith in My nectar-like stories, perpetual chanting of My names, steadfastness in My worship, and the praising of Me with hymns of praise.
Respect in service, salutation with all one's limbs,
the renunciation of wealth and of enjoyments and pleasures for my sake;
whatever sacrifice, gift, oblation, recitation, or vow has been performed for my sake.
"O Uddhava, for those humans who thus offer themselves through these means, devotion to me arises; what other goal remains for them? Thus [it is said].
Precisely because devotion (*bhakti*) is the means for worship (*upāsti*), Śrī Bhāskararāya states in the *Setubandha*: "Devotion is of two kinds:

secondary (*gauṇī*) and primary (*mukhyā*). Among these, the former consists of meditation, worship, recitation, chanting of names, and so forth, pertaining to the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahman*), and it admits of being combined [with other practices]. But supreme devotion (*parabhakti*)..."

13) It has been stated that [these] consist of a specific form of attachment (*anurāga*) produced by this [devotion]. Such devotion is possible only toward the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahman*). This Brahman with attributes, in accordance with the attachment of its own worshipper, [acts accordingly].

He assumes various forms such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others; it is precisely the means for devotion to those respective forms that are expounded in the Tantras and Purāṇas. The Vedic texts that serve as their source, known as Upaniṣads, are also found in the form of the Nṛsiṃhatāpinī, Rāmatāpinī, and so forth.
Regarding Sundarī, there are the Tripuropaniṣad, the Bhāvanopaniṣad, and others.
When verbal certainty regarding the Supreme Brahman taught therein is attained, at that time there arises neither excessive attachment to saṃsāra nor excessive detachment from it. And he—

One who possesses such qualification is eligible for the practice of devotion (bhakti-sādhana-upāsti). The attainment of such qualification and the desire to ascend to the stages of devotion are not obtainable through meager merit, but are gained through the virtuous deeds accumulated over many tens of millions of births; even so, the devotion to Sundarī is far more difficult to attain than that.
As it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"For one who has not uttered the names of other deities for ten million births,
only then does faith arise in the utterance of the name of the Śrī Devī."
"So that in his final birth he may become a worshipper of Śrīvidyā. Thus [it is said].
In another place as well:
"Only by one whose final birth has occurred, or who is Śaṅkara himself,
is this glorious fifteen-syllable Vidyā obtained."

"Śrīvidyā alone is the singular cause of liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. (In this regard, the Vedic scripture—"By means of knowledge one attains immortality"—is also to be cited. Thus it is said.
The Śruti also says:

"Those who have not heard [the Vedas] and those who have heard them; those who have performed sacrifices and those who have not—going to heaven, they do not look back, for they know Indra and Agni. Like grains of sand, they come together, impelled by the rays."
From this world and from that world, the seers with their variegated [sacrificial] gifts have bestowed [it].
Thus it is stated in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.
The qualification for the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*) is to be known solely by one’s own internal organ;
this qualification for the stage of such devotion is to be known solely by one’s own internal organ, and not by others.

It is not perceptible, nor can it be inferred through a particular state or a particular age, because their deviation is observed; for we see that even in childhood, individuals such as Prahlāda and Dhruva attained such a stage. In some cases, there is an inference based on a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); even that [inference] may be valid knowledge (*pramā*).
It may possibly be so; as for instance, in the *Āgastya-saṃhitā*, the words of a Brahmin in response to Virūpākṣa’s inquiry regarding his daughter:
"O daughter, O treasure-house of merit, by virtue of the accumulation of merits from former lives..."
"O lady of excellent vows, though you have only been established for three years on this most difficult stage of devotion,
receive from me the seed-syllable of Gaurī, which is the seed of the universe."
14) Thus, because the knowledge of the location of the maiden arises through inference alone; there is also an injunction in the Manthānabhairavatantra that inference must be performed:
"Having considered the suitability [of the disciple] for one, two, three, four, or five years,
as well as their devotion and qualities, according to the sequence of the castes and the mixed castes,
one who is single-minded should then impart the knowledge according to the order previously stated. Thus it is said.

Nevertheless, since it is possible for an inference to sometimes lead to unsuccessful activity, one who engages in the undertaking of initiation should act only after having properly investigated their own qualification (*adhikāra*). Otherwise,
if one who lacks qualification were to engage [in it], then it would result in the same consequence as when a Śūdra undertakes the study of the Vedas.

That same [result] would apply to this case as well, since the fact of being performed by one lacking qualification (*anadhikārin*) is equal. Therefore, having reflected within one's own mind upon qualification, only he who is fit to ascend to the aforementioned stage is truly a *brāhmaṇa*. [In this regard: "Indeed, women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—even they attain the supreme goal; how much more so the meritorious Brāhmaṇas?"

"Likewise, royal sages who are devoted"—thus the meaning of the Gītā also follows [from verses 9.31–32]. Whether a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, one of mixed birth, a woman, or whoever else it may be, anyone in this world who is not despondent, who is not attached, and whose senses are conquered—that person alone is qualified; it is established that one who has fallen outside the path of the Vedas is not qualified.
Therefore, the *Kalpasūtra* must be explained by those who follow the Veda;
for this very reason,
[this tantric work was revealed] to the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda by the Supreme Goddess in a dream.
It has been taught that these must necessarily be examined by those versed in the Tantras;

furthermore, the composition of the treatise named *Sāra* is also highly appropriate. Just as the Śiva [Lord Śiva] out of compassion composed the Tantras for those who had strayed from the path of the Vedas, so too did the venerable Bhagavatpāda [Śaṅkarācārya] out of compassion [compose this work] for those very same people.

It cannot be said that this is a fabrication, nor should it be stated that this is not an authentic work. The venerable Bhagavatpāda’s partiality lies solely with the Vedic tradition and not with anything else; were it otherwise, he might have composed a treatise following the teachings of the Buddha and others as well. Furthermore, in his own composition, the *Mānasapūjā*:
O Mother, reciting those mantras from the three Vedas with joy and great reverence, I perform this ritual bath for you; please accept it out of affection.

Thus, by the mention of the combination (*samuccaya*) of the Tantric and Vedic [traditions] in this verse, it is very clear that what is intended is that being Tantric and being Vedic are not contradictory. Therefore, this Kalpasūtra should be explained by the followers of the Vedas (*vaidika*).
Dispelling the Doubt Regarding the Prohibition of Tantric Practice in the Kali Age:

Now, it may be argued that while Brahmins may indeed possess the qualification for Tantra, they do not have it in the Kali age. This was stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, during the enumeration of things to be avoided in the Kali age:
The initiation into mantras and so forth for all [castes], the carrying of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
the departure on the Great Journey (mahāprasthāna), and the immolation of cows in the Gosava sacrifice.

Since these [practices] are heard of as being to be avoided in the Kali Yuga, all the preceding statements must be reconciled as referring to the Kṛta and other ages; for a prohibition does not function except by presupposing a prior possibility of occurrence.

It should not be argued that, since [the *ye yajāmahe*] is obtained through previous statements and its prohibition occurs by this [present rule], there might be an option (*vikalpa*) due to their equal force—similar to the principle of the final quarter of the tenth book stating "one does not perform those two for the animal sacrifice.
For an option would exist only if it were a prohibition; however, this is not a prohibition. Rather, [it is a restriction]: "In sacrifices, [one uses] 'ye yajāmahe'..."

If you argue that, just as in the case of the rule "one does not [perform] at the *anuyāja* offerings," the statement "the wise man should perform initiation" and the statement "in the Kali age, mantra-initiation should not be performed" form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), and thus—by means of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) implying that it must be performed in ages other than Kali—the possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) is precluded; we say: do not say so.
The statement "and the initiation into the mantra for all [is found] in the Brāhma [Purāṇa] and in many manuscripts" is not found there.
Therefore, such a reading as is found in small manuscripts is indeed unauthoritative. Even if one insists that it is authoritative, [it is stated] thus in the *Laiṅga*:

"The worship of Śambhu in the Kali age is performed by means of this very extent of ritual network; it is taught and remembered that even for Brahmins and others, the tantric rites are prescribed even in the Kali age, and only through the Āgama, and not otherwise. Thus it is said.
The statement that in the Kali Yuga worship must be performed according to the *tantra* system alone has already been cited previously:
"In the Kali Yuga, O Great Goddess, [the goddess] is well-worshipped by Brāhmaṇas and others [according to the tantra]."

Thus, since it is found in many tantras such as the *Rudrayāmala* that [this practice] is to be performed in the Kali age— as evidenced by the very words of the *Rahasyārṇava*— the statement in the *Brāhma Purāṇa*, following the force of the plural number,
establishes that it is to be performed in the Kali age with extreme vigilance after having conquered the senses and so forth. For this very reason:

At the conclusion of the words of Brahmā, it was not stated that "these should not be performed in the Kali age"; rather, it was said that these were withdrawn at the beginning of the Kali age by great-souled beings for the sake of protecting the world. Thus, the fruit of their withdrawal is stated to be the benefit of the world. The benefit is as follows: whoever has conquered the senses [should know] that these are the duties...

If one were to engage in action by casting the burden onto the scripture, thinking "these must necessarily be performed," then another person, blinded by passion, might likewise engage in action placing passion at the forefront and surely fall; therefore, renunciation is intended solely for the sake of favoring such a person.
It is not prohibitive in nature, like the rule "one must not eat on the eleventh day. Śrī Śiva [expresses] this very point:
It has been revealed in the tantras; in the Paramānanda-tantra it is said:
"Equal to the vow of walking on the edge of a sword, it is the cause for the restraint of the mind;
for one of steady mind, it is easily attained, fruitful, and bestows swift accomplishment."
O Supreme Goddess, for anyone else, it would be fruitless and a cause of suffering. Thus [it is said].
In the Tripurārṇava it is also said: "Here is wine, here is meat, and likewise various kinds of food;
there are young women, richly adorned with beautiful attire, their eyes reddened with intoxication."

"In that regard, O Goddess, the state of having a restrained mind is indeed exceedingly difficult to achieve in every respect; how could this be possible for one devoid of devotion and faith? Thus it is said.

Therefore, even in the Kali age, there is no obstacle whatsoever to initiation for those whose senses are restrained. [By this much, it is implied that only one of steady mind is entitled to perform the rites taught in the Tantras.]
16) Regarding the fact that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the first step:
is it not improper [to say] "we shall explain initiation," when its explanation has already been promised?

If it is argued that this would contradict the context because many other practices—such as the worship of Gaṇeśa and Śrīvidyā—which are distinct from initiation (dīkṣā), must be discussed immediately following that [initiation], we reply:
here, the meaning is simply the ritual action that serves as a means for devotion to Śrī Lalitā, understood through the function of *ajahatsvārthalakṣaṇā* (retaining its own primary sense). Here...

The utterance of the word *dīkṣā* is for the purpose of making known that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the beginning of everything. By this it is intended that no worship should be performed by one who is uninitiated. For this very reason, the *Paramānanda Tantra* states:
"Initiation shall be the first step of the mansion of liberation."

For this very reason, in the commentary on the Hiraṇyakeśi-sūtra— specifically regarding the statement "We shall explain the sacrifice" (yajñaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ)— the author of the Vaijayantī accepted a non-abandonment of the primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā vṛtti*) for the word *yajña* precisely because of such an inconsistency; [this serves as] proof that the ultimate doctrine of Tripura has Paramaśiva as its author.

In that context, regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is the instruction that one should proclaim the *Traipurasiddhānta* as an ancillary part of it. Here, in response to the inquiry, "What indeed is the *Traipurasiddhānta*, and from what source does its authority (*prāmāṇya*) derive?", the author first establishes the preliminary framework (*bhūmikā*) to state that the authority of such a Siddhānta arises from its being proclaimed by Śiva.

The Blessed Lord, the venerable Paramaśiva, having assumed various states through his divine play, [manifested] the eighteen branches of knowledge beginning with the Vedas and all philosophical systems (as indicated by the brief exposition of the eighteen sciences, all the philosophical systems, and the five traditions found in the commentary below this sūtra).

Having been questioned by the Goddess Bhairavī—who consists of pure consciousness and is non-different from his own self—with five questions through her five faces [the meaning of which is seen in the two supplements, such as: "From where did these traditions (āmnāyas) arise? What is their purpose?"], he expounded the five traditions (pañcāmnāyas), which are the very essence of the ultimate reality.
He paid homage to those who have become the essence. || 2 ||
In order that even the slightest suspicion of invalidity may not touch the sciences expounded here,
[the author] says "the Blessed One" (bhagavān):
"Of complete sovereignty, virtue, fame, and prosperity..."
And because of knowledge and dispassion, as well as these six, he is remembered as Bhagavat.

Thus, the Blessed One is endowed with such sixfold sovereign powers (*ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya*). Now, one might object: "The Supreme Śiva transcends all categories (*tattvātīta*); therefore, since he is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), his status as the author of *vidyā* is not possible. To this, he says: "The Bhaṭṭāraka. This means "the King," according to the lexicon which states: "A king is a Bhaṭṭāraka, a God. He is thus the possessor of the attribute of being the Lord of the Universe.
The meaning of that is "having illusion as its limiting adjunct" (māyopādhika). Alternatively, the Lord (bhaṭṭāraka) is the one who delights in the drama of the form of the world;

for the word *bhaṭṭāraka* is used in the *Prasannarāghava* play as an address to one who delights in drama, namely "O Lord," and because the term "the King is the Lord" belongs to the category of dramatic terminology. Just as his...

Likewise, both the status of being the creator of the world and the status of being the author of knowledge are indeed possible. Alternatively—since the Lord Paramaśiva is perfect, there is an absence of any object to be accomplished; how [then can he be a creator]?

What is meant by "the authorship of the sciences"? To this he says: "The Bhaṭṭāraka. This means "the King. Just as a king is seen to act for the benefit of others even when it does not serve his own interests, so it is here. Regarding the phrase "the eighteen sciences beginning with Śruti": this is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (qualifier-inclusive) *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning those sciences of which Śruti is the first. And thus, the Śrutis [are as follows]:...

The four auxiliary sciences (*tadaṅga*) are phonology, grammar, ritual, prosody, astronomy, and etymology; these, together with Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra, constitute the fourteen branches of knowledge (*caturdaśavidyā*).
To these are added the four sciences of medicine, archery, music, and the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*).

Thus, there are eighteen sciences (*vidyās*). "All philosophical systems" refers to the Śākta system and so forth. A "philosophical system" (*darśana*) is that by which something is seen; it means a treatise (*śāstra*) that is a means for attaining knowledge—specifically, the Śākta philosophical treatise. The same applies to what follows: the Śaiva system, the Vaiṣṇava system, and the Brāhma system.

There are six systems of philosophy: Saura-darśana and Bauddha-darśana, etc. Having effortlessly and without exertion assumed various states—including the state of Īśvara—and having taken on the forms of Pāṇini, Vyāsa, and others, He composed and created the grammatical treatises, Purāṇas, and so forth.
Regarding the proof of the Veda’s being of human origin:
Now, since the Veda is eternal and thus not of human origin, how can it be said to have been created by God? Nor is that [the case].
If it is argued that the very permanence [of the Veda] is unestablished because of the Śruti text, "By speech, eternal and multiform," we say: no.
For the Vedas were indeed created by the Lord, according to the Śruti text, "From Him the meters were born.
Furthermore, regarding these eighteen branches of knowledge with their diverse paths...
The original author is Śiva himself, the wielder of the trident, Maheśvara, who is the poet.

This is because of the traditional authority (*smṛti*) [of Manu]. Furthermore, the inference that "the Veda is of human origin because it is a collection of sentences, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works" is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, in the Śruti passage, "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings," lordship (*īśānatva*) consists precisely in the nature of being an author (*kartṛtva*). Nor does its being of human origin entail the defects of a person...

It should not be argued that [the Veda] would be subject to doubt regarding its lack of authority because of the possibility of error, negligence, a desire to deceive, or incapacity of the instrument; for in the case of the Lord (Īśvara), since ignorance and other such factors—which serve as the means of establishing defects—are absent, defects are impossible. By this, [the following is also refuted:]...

The eternality of the Tantras has also been refuted. Regarding the phrase "by speech, eternal and multiform," the eternality must be understood as figurative—consisting in the fact that they were not composed by a fallible person—in accordance with the collection of proofs already stated. Nor should it be argued: "What is the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) against the opposite view?"
Because it is more reasonable to grant further favor [to the Vedas], therefore all forms of knowledge are indeed composed by persons.
Regarding the specific purpose for the composition of this Tantra:
one might object that since the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) already exist, the further composition of this scripture is redundant;
therefore, he says, "consisting of consciousness" (*saṃvinmayī*). The intended meaning is as follows: the goal of human life is happiness, and that [happiness] is innate.

And [it is said to be] "artificial" (*kṛtrima*). The natural (*naisargika*) is that which has liberation (*mokṣa*) as its form. The artificial is what is called desire (*kāma*), the third human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Dharma is the means for both of these. Wealth (*artha*) is also a means for that [dharma]. Thus, there are four objects of human aspiration, either directly or through a succession of means. Among them:

Only the means for attaining artificial human goals have been explicitly set forth through the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*). As for the non-artificial human goal, its means is likewise non-artificial.

It was not clearly set forth. Furthermore, since artificial instruction is of no benefit to the world, [the Sage], desiring to uplift the world submerged in the mire of suffering, composed this traditional science (*āmnāyavidyā*). Alternatively, it is the means to liberation for those who are ignorant of the meaning of the entire Veda and who lack the qualification (*adhikāra*) for it.

He composed the *Āmnāyavidyā*, the essence of all the Vedas [see this for the meaning in Dvi-pariśiṣṭa-vivaraṇa 4]. In that context, "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) means undivided sentience, which is to say, light; "consisting of that" (*tanmayyā*) means non-different from that. By this, the sense is established that she asks her own self through the aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
This has been stated by Appayadīkṣita in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*:

"The single Brahman-consciousness— which is eternal, free from even a trace of defect, and unsurpassed bliss— appears as two distinct divisions, namely 'attribute' (*dharma*) and 'substratum' (*dharmī*), through the power of *māyā*."

"In that [state], dharma consists of experience pertaining to all objects and the power conducive to all effects; while the group of qualities such as desire and the like exists, the substratum remains one and the same. Thus [it is said].

Now, one might object: "Since even living beings such as ourselves possess the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayatva*), what is the distinction between them and the Śrī Bhairava? To this, the Lord has provided the qualifying epithet [Bhagavān].
The meaning of the word *bhagavat* has already been explained previously. And thus:

The word "Bhagavat" indicates that she does not fail to ask because her knowledge is obscured by the *āṇava* and other impurities as is the case with ordinary living beings; rather, although she is omniscient, she asks with some hidden intention.
For instance, Śiva, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*), himself becomes the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and introduces the question. In this regard:

The purpose here is this: to make it known that even a learned person, though capable and possessing knowledge acquired through reading books and the like, cannot achieve his goal (kṛtārtha) except by the path taught by the Guru; therefore, the question is posed while assuming another form. As it is said in the Svacchandatantra:
"Abiding in the roles of both teacher and disciple, Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through dialogues consisting of questions and answers. Thus [it is said].
The word "only" (*eva*) in the Śruti passage, "For the sake of knowing that, one should approach a guru alone," also expresses this very meaning.

To illuminate this same point, the two qualifiers "by the Blessed One" and "non-different from her own Self" are used. As for the meaning of the word *Bhairavī*: she is so called because of the supporting (*bharaṇa*) and delighting (*ramana*) of the universe.

She should be known as Bhairavī because, at the time of creation, she emits [the universe] from her womb after having remained within the belly of Paramaśiva during the dissolution; [in this regard, there are many proofs such as the verse in the *Śrī Lalitāsahasranāma* (verse 126) stating "the witness of the great dissolution," and other passages found in various Tantras]. By her...

"Questioned" means having been brought forward for inquiry. This is an epithet of the aforementioned Lord Paramaśiva himself. By means of his five faces—known as Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna—he [reveals] the five traditions (pañcāmnāyas): the Eastern tradition (pūrvāmnāya), the Southern tradition (dakṣiṇāmnāya), and so forth.
Regarding those named the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), and the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya)—
[see Appendix 4 for the knowledge useful for understanding the meaning of these five traditions]—
although the word *āmnāya* is primarily used in the sense of the Veda, as the lexicon states: "The feminine word *śruti*, 'Veda', is *āmnāya*."

Nevertheless, because they set forth the essence of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), it follows that—by implication—the Tantras reveal the core secrets of Vedic subjects and thus establish themselves as exponents of the sacred tradition and bestowers of liberation.
Here too, the word *āmnāya* is used figuratively. By this...

19) The view that the Tantras are independent authorities like the Vedas has been refuted for some. The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the uncreated fourth human goal (*turīya-puruṣārtha*); it is toward that which these [Tantras] are dedicated as their essence (*sāra*).

By this, it is indicated that the person [Śiva] is uniquely desirable and exceedingly secret. Out of compassion for those unable to grasp the entire meaning of the Vedas, Śiva extracted their essential meaning and composed the five Āmnāyas. || 2 ||

Being supremely compassionate toward those who are unable to grasp even that [previous teaching] due to their duller faculties, Śrī Paraśurāma undertakes to speak by summarizing the essential points contained therein, for the purpose of establishing the Traipura Siddhānta:
In this regard, the established conclusion is as follows: || 3 ||

In that regard, among the five traditional systems (āmnāyas), this "siddhānta" to be described here refers to an object that is the subject of a conclusion produced by the process of critical inquiry.

By this section of the text ending here, the suspicion regarding the lack of authority— arising from the possibility that the meaning of the doctrine to be expounded [is merely] fabricated by one's own imagination— is dispelled.

The meaning is this: that time at which this universe exists in a subtle form within the belly of Paraśiva is indeed dissolution (*pralaya*). Such a dissolution is known solely through the scriptures. In the same way, so too is creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
In that context, dissolution refers to the Supreme Brahman abiding in its own absolute nature, while [the state] of the individual soul (*jīva*)...

It is as if in deep sleep. At that time, the multitude of individual souls (*jīva-rāśi*), their unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and all five elements remain in a subtle form within Him, just as a banyan tree exists within a banyan seed. As it is stated in the *Śaktisūtrabhāṣya*: "Even while swallowing the universe, Paramaśiva does not do so in its entirety, but rather establishes it partially in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)."

Thus, that very *saṃskāra* (latent impression) serves as the auxiliary cause for the creative will (*sisṛkṣā*) of Īśvara; otherwise, the occurrence of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) would be unavoidable. This being the case in the world, when the couple are in a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), a portion of the white drop (*śuklabindu*) situated at the opening of the *vidhi* enters the womb and unites with the red drop (*raktabindu*).

When that occurs, Brahman alone shines forth, devoid of the manifestation of internal and external existence; its capacity to produce the embryo is observed. Likewise, at the time prior to creation, the union of Śiva and Śakti also takes place by virtue of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings. || 3 ||
There are thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). [The meaning of each of these, as well as the *sphoṭa*, shall be seen below, up until the end of this commentary on the aphorisms.
To elaborate upon that very point, he begins to set forth the web of principles:
The universe consists of thirty-six principles.

Thus, when He who abides in His own absolute nature forms a union with those powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action— thinking "May I be many; may I procreate"— the creations of objects and words arise respectively and simultaneously, like a sprout and its shadow.
(20) If it is objected that the powers of will, knowledge, and action would consequently be impermanent due to having a beginning, we reply: this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
For there exists a subtle form of that very [power] which is the cause of that triad and is named *Śāntā*.

Because [Śakti] is eternal as the very form of Paraśiva, it is Paramaśiva himself, qualified by such an adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the desire to emit (sisṛkṣā), who is denoted by the term "Kevalaśiva. He alone is the first among the principles (tattvas).
That aforementioned desire to emit, which consists of the latent impression (vāsanā) of the phenomenal world (prapañca), is Śakti; she is the second principle.

As it has been stated in the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*: "In that regard, the subject (*dharmin*) exercises agency over the fivefold creative acts of the worlds, while the attribute (*dharma*), having assumed the form of the Person (*puruṣa*), is the primordial cause. [Note: Here, the first written character appears as "vi".]
She maintains the state of being the material cause of the entire universe;
having assumed a female form, she becomes the divine queen of her own refuge, the Primal Creator.
Furthermore, the two divisions of Dharma proclaimed by the Knower of the Vedas are said to be like the two Brahmans (the two Brahmās) for their respective lords. Thus it is said.

The perception of the aforementioned world as "I" (ahantayā), which possesses such a clear cognitive state (*vṛtti*), is denoted by the term Sadāśiva; this is the third *tattva*. That which possesses a cognitive state directed solely toward difference, namely "this is the world," is denoted by the term Īśvara.
The fourth principle is the *tattva*.
That mental state (*vṛtti*) belonging to Sadāśiva, which takes the form "I am the universe," is denoted by the term *vidyā* and is the fifth principle.
The mental modification (*vṛtti*) residing in Īśvara, which takes the form "this is the world" and has difference as its object, is denoted by the term *māyā* and is the sixth *tattva*.
Possessing the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) of the previously mentioned *vidyā*, the cognition that is opposed to it is denoted by the term *avidyā* and is the seventh [tattva].

The principle (*tattva*): that very agency residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), which is contracted by some degree of limited agency, is designated by the term *kalā*; it is the eighth principle.

According to the manner previously stated, that very eternal satisfaction (nityatṛpti) residing in the individual soul (jīva), when contracted by a lack of satisfaction regarding certain objects, is designated by the term "attachment" (rāga); this is the ninth principle (tattva).
When the eternal nature (nityatā) residing in the soul is veiled, that same eternal nature [manifests as] "it exists," "it is born," and "it grows."
Because it undergoes transformation, diminishes, and perishes—due to its association with these six states—it is contracted and designated by the term "time"; this is the tenth principle (*tattva*).

Since there is non-difference between Paraśiva and the individual soul (*jīva*), just as there is absolute sovereignty (*sarvasvātantrya*) in Paraśiva, so too does He possess it in the individual soul.

The concealment of all sovereignty (*sarvasvātantrya*), which was previously effected by the aforementioned *vidyā*, depends upon another cause; that which it depends upon is designated by the term "Niyati" (Restriction), the eleventh [category]. (Note: The parenthetical portion *vi[atra-ādyā-ityādyanekapadāni pāṭhāntare pṛthaksantyanyatra*] indicates that various words such as *vi*, *atra*, *ādyā*, and so forth exist separately in other variant readings.)

The *tattva* [is as follows]: the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the substratum of such [principles] as necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), attachment (*rāga*), limited agency (*kalā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), is the twelfth *tattva*. Nature (*prakṛti*), which is the state of equilibrium of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, and is synonymous with the mind (*citta*), is the thirteenth.
The principle [of mind]: when sattva and tamas are overcome and rajas predominates, that which is denoted by the term "manas" and serves as the cause of volition is the fourteenth principle.
Having overcome *rajas* and *tamas*, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) dominated by *sattva*— designated by the term "intellect" (*buddhi*)—
is the fifteenth principle (*tattva*), which serves as the cause of determination.
When the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), dominated by *tamas* and having overwhelmed *rajas* and *sattva*,

is designated by the term "I-maker" (*ahaṃkāra*), it is the sixteenth principle (*tattva*), the cause of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The sense organ that perceives sound, the ear (*śrotra*), is the seventeenth principle.
The sense-organ that grasps touch is the skin, the eighteenth principle;
the sense-organ that grasps form is the eye, the nineteenth principle;
the sense-organ that grasps taste is the tongue, the twentieth principle.

The olfactory sense-organ, which perceives odors, is the nose; it is the twenty-first principle (*tattva*). The vocal organ, which is conducive to the utterance of articulate speech, is the twenty-second principle. The hand, which is conducive to grasping and relinquishing, is the twenty-third principle.
The organ conducive to movement is the foot, the twenty-fourth principle (*tattva*).
The organ that produces the discharge of waste is the anus, the twenty-fifth principle.
The organ that produces sexual union is the generative organ (*upastha*), the twenty-sixth principle.
Sound, in the form of subtle space, is the twenty-seventh principle;
touch, in the form of subtle air, is the twenty-eighth principle;
and form, in the form of subtle fire, is the twenty-ninth principle.
Taste, in the form of subtle water, is the thirtieth principle (tattva).
Smell, in the form of subtle earth, is the thirty-first principle. Space, characterized by vacuity and being gross, is the thirty-second principle.
Air, characterized by the quality of constant motion, is the thirty-third principle;
fire, characterized by heat, is the thirty-fourth principle;
and water, characterized by fluidity, is the thirty-fifth principle.

Earth, possessing the quality of solidity, is the thirty-sixth and final principle (*tattva*). [In this text, both in the root verses and the commentary—36—the thirty-six principles along with their meanings are specified.
This aggregate of such principles is non-different from the conventional object of discourse known as the universe (*viśva-jagat*). Regarding the stated meaning:
The authority for this is found in the *Paramānandatantra*: "That which is solidity is earth; that which is fluidity is indeed called water;
heat is fire; movement is air; and space is the void."
The subtle form of these, however, is that in which the divisions have not yet emerged:
smell, touch, form, taste, and sound are indeed the *tanmātras*.
The five sense organs of these [beings]— namely the nose, the tongue,
the eye, the skin, and the ear— are indeed engaged in the apprehension of the five [objects].
The pentad of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure has the nature of being presided over by the *karmas*; therefore, it is not treated separately.
That instrument consists of what are called speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ;
it is said to be present throughout the entire body, though its manifestation is clearly evident [in specific locations].
O Śivā, the mind is the instrument of volition, while the intellect effects determination;
it is like a mirror, the ground for the reflections of conceptual constructions.
Egoism (ahaṃkāra) is declared to consist of this much conceit;
it is composed of the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, known as suffering, pleasure, and delusion.
That which is called the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) arises from the predominance of those respective [qualities];
however, the equilibrium of the causal qualities (guṇas) is called primordial nature (prakṛti).
The Puruṣa is said to be distinct from that [Prakṛti], being full yet possessing contracted powers;
likewise, he consists of consciousness (cit), bliss (ānanda), will (icchā), knowledge (jñāna), and action (kriyā).
The powers, though complete, become the *kalā*s and so forth through contraction;
indeed, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), whose nature is universal agency, became the *kalā*.
Knowledge exists in the form of limited agency, while omniscience is likewise [the capacity for] cognition;
the intellect is the awakener of the very objects that are reflected within it.
Due to contraction, that which is called *vidyā* (knowledge) is itself proclaimed as *avidyā* (ignorance);
and that same [power] is called *icchā* (will), characterized by eternal satisfaction, when it possesses contraction.
Passion (rāga) is in one case called "non-contentment" and in another it takes the form of "coloring";
the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is called "eternal existence," and time (kāla) arises from the connection with the six states of being.
The power of bliss is declared to be omnipresent sovereignty;
however, due to contraction caused by dependence on another, it is known as necessity (niyati).
O Goddess, you who possess this unbroken aesthetic flavor and are skilled in manifesting differentiation, you are the independent form, Māyā, the beloved of Bhairava.
By concealing her own nature through differentiation, she possesses the form of the *tattvas*;
yet, having abandoned the differentiation of her own nature, she is intent upon the realization of unity.
That which consists of the manifestation of the ultimate reality is designated as *śuddhavidyā* (pure knowledge);
it causes entities whose distinctions are clearly manifest to appear as non-different from itself.

O Goddess, Īśvara is said to be those [levels] which are manifest; however, this [level] whose nature is awakening is called Sadāśiva. (Note: In this context, the word division should be made as *tān aspaṣṭān*.)
She perceives only "I am," which consists of non-difference from her own essential nature.
The power that consists of the latent impressions of conceptual proliferation is so designated.
"Free from conceptual proliferation, consisting of the single essence of consciousness—this is declared to be the principle of Śiva. Thus it is said.

A detailed exposition of the essential nature of these principles, from Śiva down to the earth, exists at length in the *Mṛgendrasaṃhitā*; however, for fear of prolixity, it has not been written here, but only as much as is necessary has been recorded.
The Determination of the Number of Principles:

Now, if it is asked—"Since the Sāṅkhyas have established the doctrine that there are twenty-four principles, how can there be thirty-six principles?"—it is replied: there are twelve principles in addition to the twenty-four, beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Śiva. These are not...
Is your statement that [the thirty-six principles] do not exist because there is a lack of authoritative evidence, or that they are included within the twenty-four principles?
It is not the first, because the very words of the venerable Lord Paraśurāma serve as authoritative proof;
for it is heard in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Obeisance, obeisance to the Lord of the temple consisting of the thirty-six principles."

Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Paramānanda-tantra*: "This wheel of principles (*tattvacakra*) is indeed proclaimed to be of thirty-six kinds. Nor is the second [position] tenable, because it is impossible for [the categories] from Puruṣa up to Śiva—which possess mutually contradictory attributes as previously described—to be included [within those thirty-six]. Nor...

One should not argue that this contradicts the statement in the *Mahābhārata*, "The principles are twenty-four, but the Puruṣa is beyond them," because the subsequent twelve principles are extremely difficult to comprehend;

therefore, for the sake of those of dull intellect, only those principles that are most easily understood up to the limit of *prakṛti* are to be taught, and [the discourse] rests right there. And thus...

Since both statements are authoritative due to the distinction between their respective intended audiences (*adhikārī*), by this [argument] one who asserts that there are only five principles (*tattva*)—
relying on the *Vāsiṣṭha* statement that "in all cases there are five elements, and no sixth exists"— is refuted, for that [statement] is intended solely for those of extremely dull intellect.

If it is argued: "But if the possession of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmavattva*) is the determinant for the classification of principles (*tattva*), then a pot and a cloth—which possess the contradictory attributes of 'pot-ness' (*ghaṭatva*) and 'cloth-ness' (*paṭatva*)—would also result in being distinct principles," we reply:
No. Do you intend to establish that they are principles beyond the thirty-six? Or rather...

Is it being argued that, in relation to the reality of the form of a jar (*ghaṭarūpatattva*), the reality of a cloth (*paṭatattva*) would be something distinct? Not the first [alternative], because since there is no contradiction between the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) and the nature of being a cloth (*paṭatva*) with respect to hardness (*kāṭhinya*), which is the unique property of earth, their distinctness is not established. As for the second [alternative], it is simply an admission of what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is precisely the point.
It is stated in the Sūtasaṃhitā, following the description of the definition of reality (tattva):
"That which remains until the dissolution [of the universe] and bestows experience upon all beings is declared to be 'reality' (tattva); therefore, the body, a jar, and so forth, are not reality."
By this, this suspicion is utterly refuted.
p. 24) Although in other tantras there are initially only three principles— namely, the principle of the self (ātmatattva), the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva),
and the principle of Śiva (śivatattva)— therein, the principle of the self is twenty-fourfold, beginning with earth and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti).

Its specific characteristic is absolute insentience (*jaḍatva*). The *vidyā-tattva* extends from the *puruṣa* down to *māyā* and is sevenfold. Its definition consists in possessing both insentience and the capacity for illumination.
For instance, just as in a mass of iron that has attained identity with fire, there is a capacity for illumination despite its being insentient.
The insentience of an iron ball is evident during the state when it has not attained identity with fire;

likewise, in fire, both insentience and luminosity are evident during the state when it has attained identity with the iron ball. Similarly, in the case of the Person (puruṣa), who is of the nature of light, [these qualities appear] in the insentient factors such as Niyati and the rest when they have attained identity with him.

Luminosity resides in the *puruṣa*, while insentience resides in *niyati* and the other [evolutes]. Insentience in *niyati* and the rest, and luminosity in the *puruṣa*, are thus clearly established. In this manner, the *vidyā-tattva* possesses a mixed nature.
From *śuddhavidyā* up to Śiva, the *śiva-tattva* is fivefold; its unique characteristic is as follows:
The intermediate division of "being the illuminator of the absolute alone" has been made; nevertheless, even there, at the time of the conclusion, it is said:
"O Maheśvarī, such indeed is the wheel of principles (tattvacakra), consisting of thirty-six kinds."
Thus, since the very same doctrine that was stated there has been stated here as well, there is no contradiction with it.

In reality, however, in the twenty-second chapter of the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, it is asked: "O Lord of the Universe, O Master, how many principles (tattvas) have been enumerated by the sages?
Some say there are twenty-six, while others say twenty-five."

Beginning with "Some say seven, some nine, and some six," and so forth, after establishing twenty-eight principles according to His own view in response to Uddhava’s question, the Blessed Lord provides the justification for the views of those who maintain contradictory numbers such as seven and others.
Thus, various enumerations of the principles have been made by the sages;

all are logical because they possess sound reasoning. What is unseemly for the wise? [By this much, those who claim that the words of sages are not authoritative—asserting that there is no single sage whose word is a valid means of knowledge—are merely creators of a false interpretation.]
"Carried far away"—this is a piercing truth; even today, some such people remain utterly deluded regarding the true meaning of the word *guhā*.
Thus he spoke. This alone should be seen as the solution in this matter. || 4 ||
Having thus explained the division of the principles (*tattva*), he begins to describe the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*):
Śiva, when enveloped by the body as a sheath, is the *jīva*; when free from the sheath, he is Śiva.
a. Paraśiva.
Thus, even among the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), there is again a twofold nature in their general form:

some possess exclusively the state of being the object of vision (*dṛśyatva*), while others possess exclusively the state of being the seer (*draṣṭṛtva*). The former belongs to the insentient (*jaḍa*) principles, and the latter belongs exclusively to the sentient.
(25) [Objection:
But since the individual soul (*jīva*) is included within the categories of reality (*tattva*), whereas Paraśiva is not, a distinction between the two follows.
This being the case, how can the non-dualist (*advaita*) doctrine of the Tantrikas be established? To this, he says: "The body," etc. This...

The state [of bondage] is as follows: Paraśiva, who is entirely independent, by means of his inscrutable *māyā*, conceals that perfect sovereignty (*svātantrya*) which resides within himself and consists in being independent of anything else. That sovereignty, thus concealed, becomes limited sovereignty; this is called the *āṇava-mala*. Indeed, it is the *āṇava-mala* itself.
It is also called ignorance (avidyā).
If it is objected that "one's own perfect sovereignty conceals its own discourse," it is replied:

just as the sun becomes obscured by clouds created by its own rays, so too there is no impediment to its self-concealment through its own ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the difference is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).
It is real; thus, the sense is that there is no loss of non-duality.

If it is asked, "How can Paraśiva, whose essential nature is undivided consciousness, be concealed by the limited impurity (āṇavamala)?"—it is as follows: The power of Māyā is indefinable. Therefore, regarding this production of the impossible, there is no room for doubt as to how it occurs. For this very reason it has been said:
"What is impossible in Māyā, which brings about even the most difficult of things? Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Subhagodaya*:
"The intellect, divided by Māyā, eternally obstructs her own unimpeded power within all beings who are but its own parts, just as the shore obstructs the ocean."

Thus, covered by the impurity of *āṇava* (atomicity), the individual self (*aṇu*), being itself limited by the body, perceives other infinite selves—likewise limited by bodies—as distinct from itself. That is the impurity consisting of *māyā*. Thus, defiled by this impurity of *māyā*, which takes the form of the manifestation of duality, they perform auspicious and inauspicious actions.

They possess the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [experience]. This is the impurity of action (*kārma-mala*). These three kinds of impurities are designated by the term "body" (*śarīra*). Śiva himself, when veiled by that which is of such a nature—a sheath (*kañcuka*) or covering—is the individual soul (*jīva*). As it is said in the *Paramārthasāra*:
"That which is the supreme sovereignty of Maheśa, the accomplishment of the impossible—that is the Goddess Māyā-śakti, the self-concealment of Śiva. Thus [it is said].
In the *Subhagodaya* it is also said:
"This person, his form limited by her and all his powers withdrawn,
is like the sun at twilight— reddened yet with its rays retracted, incapable even of self-illumination."

Alternatively—the body is threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme. The first is that set forth in the verse on meditation; the second is of the nature of mantra; and the third consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The meaning is that Śiva, enveloped by these bodies, is himself the primordial principle (ādyatattva) and is indeed the individual soul (jīva). The implication is that since the state of being a soul exists in him alone, what need is there to mention others? By this, it is suggested that even the attainment of the nature of Śiva is not the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha).

Such living beings are of three kinds: pure (*śuddha*), impure (*aśuddha*), and mixed (*miśra*). The first are those beginning with Śiva and ending with Sadāśiva, because they lack ignorance (*ajñāna*). The impure are humans and others.
The mixed are Vasiṣṭha and others. He who is devoid of such coverings (*kañcuka*) is Paraśiva, who transcends the categories (*tattvātīta*).
This is the meaning. || 5 ||

Having thus described the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) as being the very essence of the goal of human life (puruṣārtha), he points out what that goal is: "Self-reflection is the goal of human life. (6)
The *vimarśa*—the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—of one's own nature as that of Paraśiva, in the form "I am He" (*so'ham*), is like this:

just as someone who has forgotten gold worn around their neck runs from place to place in search of it, but upon having their latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by someone else, sees it right there on their neck; even so [is this recognition].

The meaning is that the re-acquisition of the knowledge of one's own true nature—which has been forgotten—is the unconditioned human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, the attainment of such a human goal will not occur without the grace of the Lord. As it was said by the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (Gītā 7.14).
Furthermore, devotion to the Blessed One arises only through the worship of the Blessed One; therefore, the worship of the Blessed One is the means to liberation through a traditional succession. (6)

Regarding the description of the qualities of mantra: surely [it may be attained] even through yoga and so forth— by the word "and so forth," one should understand Vedānta, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā, Vaiśeṣika, and others.

Numerous scriptures are found stating that "the attainment of such a human goal occurs" [meaning: there are many authoritative rites prescribed in various scriptures that establish liberation as a human goal]. If it is asked, "Why is the necessity of *upāsanā* (meditative worship) being described?"—
There is a necessity for spiritual practice (*upāsanā*). However, the liberation obtained through yoga and other means is not free from rebirth.
As it is stated in the *Svacchanda-saṃgraha*:
"Even though he is liberated from bondage, the Lord binds him again."
"Bound, he transmigrates further as long as he does not find the Divine. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in another place:
"At the dawn of that day, Śrīkaṇṭha creates again those who have attained perfection through Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth;
therefore, such liberation is not equal [to the ultimate one]. Thus it is said.
p.

27) Therefore, since it is established that meditation alone is the primary means, and since recitation (*japa*) is also present within meditation, the mantra is the principal instrument therein. [From here, the Lord Rāma [explains] by means of the seventh, eighth, and ninth aphorisms.]
It should be noted that [this passage] introduces the gravity of the necessity for the mantras of the respective deities to become the very heart of one's worship.
Thus, in that context, he describes the qualities of those [mantras] in order to generate faith in the practitioner:
"Words consist of phonemes and are eternal" (7).
Mantras—sounds consisting of phonemes and having the nature of a collection of phonemes—are eternal;

this means they possess the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). It does not mean, however, that they are uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, because upon the cessation of ignorance, both the deity—who is distinct from one's own true nature—and the mantras that denote that deity cease to exist.

Nor should it be argued that since the Vedas and other scriptures— distinguished by their specific sequential order— are described as eternal and as enduring for a single kalpa, and since this [work] is likewise so, how can it possess an eternity consisting of lasting longer than even those?
For the mantras are of the nature of the subtle bodies of the deities, and [the duration] of the deities' bodies...
Because it exists simultaneously with ignorance. || 7 ||
Alternatively, as the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "The seven crores of great mantras issued from the mouth of Śiva.
Thus, since mantras also have a beginning, they cannot be coeval with ignorance (*avidyā*), because ignorance is beginningless.

For this very reason, since praise as "manifold" on account of possessing qualities common to others would be possible, [the author], out of dissatisfaction with that, states another unique quality of the mantras: "The inconceivable power of the mantras. (8)

The genitive case in the word *mantrāṇām* is used in the sense of the locative; that is to say, "in the mantras. *Acintya-śaktayaḥ* means those mantras whose power (*śakti*) is inconceivable (*acintya*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "their state of being such [is] existence" (*tattā asti*).

Furthermore, the inconceivability of their power consists in its being beyond the scope of logic (*tarka*). By this, it is shown that the previously mentioned *māyā* is inconceivable and difficult to restrain.

Nevertheless, it has been established that within the mantras there exists, by way of divine play (*līlā*), a power capable of removing even that [ignorance], a power exceeding it, which serves to dispel the ignorance that veils knowledge. || 8 ||

Regarding the auxiliary causes for the accomplishment of mantras—namely, the auxiliary causes required when a desired effect is to be produced by means of a mantra—he says: "Through tradition and faith, all success [is attained]. (9)

"Tradition" (*saṃpradāya*) refers to following the conduct of the lineage of gurus. "Faith" (*viśvāsa*) is the certainty regarding mantras as being the means for attaining results. The remainder [of the meaning] is that by means of a mantra accompanied by these two, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) come to pass. Although in the world, by means of a single staff and a single action, only a jar is produced and not...

A cloth [is produced]; thus, by means of a shuttle, a loom, and so forth, it is a cloth alone and not a jar. In this way, it is observed in the world that every cause produces one specific effect. Nevertheless, the word "all" (*sarva*) is used to indicate that among mantras it is not so; rather, a single mantra alone produces whatever is desired. By this—
Furthermore, for the sake of motivating the listener, the excellence of the mantra's path is also set forth. || 9 ||
(28) [Objection: But how can this statement, which conveys a meaning contrary to worldly consensus, be authoritative? To this, he says:
Validity consists primarily in trustworthiness. || 10 ||

Validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being the producer of a cognition that possesses a specific property (*tadvati*) and a specific mode (*tatprakāraka*), which in turn generates a successful practical activity (*saṃvādipravṛttijanakatva*).

"Established for all" (*sarvasiddhi*) means abounding in conviction regarding the previously mentioned statement. Here, the meaning of the term "conviction" (*viśvāsa*) is the ascertainment of the reliability (*āptatva*) of the speaker of the statement. From the word *bahu*, the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*) is understood.

The suffix *iṣṭhan* [is added]. In this regard, the Pāṇinian sūtra *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* means that these two suffixes, *tamap* and *iṣṭhan*, occur in their own sense (*svārthe*) when [the base] denotes a meaning characterized by excellence (*atiśaya*). Thus, once *iṣṭhan* has been produced in its own sense, by the rule *iṣṭhasya ca*, there would be the elision (*lopa*) of the *iṣṭhan* following a word ending in *bahu*. [This is governed by] the rule *bahor lope bhū ca bahoḥ*.

The meaning of that [sūtra] is: "there is the addition of *iṭ* and the substitution of *bhū*. Thus, when there is the substitution of *bhū* and the addition of *iṭ*, the word *bhūyiṣṭha* denotes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) characterized by extreme abundance.
Furthermore, the state of being abundant in trust toward the Person (*puruṣa*) is established through the relationship of being produced subsequently to Him and having Him as its object.

The state of not being a locus for doubt qualified by trust is [the meaning], because its coreferential connection with non-difference from the person who is the substratum of that [trust] is sublated. The word *bhūyiṣṭha* has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "an object of knowledge residing in a majority [of people]. Its coreferential connection with non-difference occurs when that [object] is authoritative (*prāmāṇya*).
The meaning is that the authority of this scripture is to be known only by a person who possesses absolute trust [in it].
The implication is that the authority of the scripture is entirely inaccessible to those characterized by fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*). As it has been said by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda:
"For those matters that are accessible through the scriptures alone, one should not refute them by means of logic."
Some, however, say that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a great abundance (*bhūyiṣṭham*) or plurality (*bāhulyam*) of faith. This is to be considered;

for, according to Pāṇini’s rule, the word *bhūyiṣṭha* refers to a person (*puruṣa*), and thus it cannot refer to the attribute of "abundance. And if one were to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) regarding the attribute, then...

The position that [prāmāṇya] has its locus in that which is dependent on me alone is indeed superior; not the other. For if it were otherwise, even though there is a plurality [of instances], since it is impossible for the dharma [prāmāṇya] to have an abhedānvaya (identity-relation) with prāmāṇya when the latter is merely figurative (lakṣaṇā), one would have to assume a figurative sense in the bahuvrīhi compound *anyapadārtha* as "the prāmāṇya related to the plurality of the denotable objects."

Furthermore, the relation must be stated as nothing other than "being cognizable by a cognition residing in its own locus"; and in that case, it is identical to my own position. Regarding this point, [your view] involves an excessive definition of *dharma* and the recourse to a cumbersome *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound. Therefore, this alone is the correct interpretation.
Better.
Śrī Skanda spoke very clearly regarding such an abundance of faith:
"O Agastya, what is the use of much speaking? Listen to my certain word; no doubt should be entertained here, for from that which is doubted, no fruit indeed arises."

"However many tantras and numerous networks of mantras exist among mortals"— he states another auxiliary factor: [the unification] of the guru, the mantra, the deity, the self, the mind, and the vital breath.
From the perfect realization of oneness, there arises the knowledge of the inner self. || 11 ||

The "guru" and so forth are clear [in meaning]. The "winds" are the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*). The "churning of their unity" is the production of oneness through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); by that, there is the realization (*vitti*) of the inner self, the *pratyagātman*.
The phrase "feeling arises" is the ellipsis; the identity of the self and the deity is clear upon the removal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The identity of the deity and the mantra exists by virtue of their relationship as the signified and the signifier. The same applies to the guru.
The identity of the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is shown in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Air is not essentially different from the mind; therefore, by its restraint, the mind attains stillness. Thus it is said.
Although such a certainty cannot actually exist at the time of meditation, nevertheless, this must be performed as a momentary, artificially induced factor as an auxiliary to meditation.

The fruit of worship in the form of *japa*—or rather, he states the fruit of worship performed with the mantra as the instrument, accompanied by faith in the tradition—is "the guru-mantra. The "grinding out of unity" (*aikya-niṣphālana*) is the determination of unity; through that, it is the knowledge of the inner self (*pratyagātma-jñāna*).
The word "bhavati" (it becomes) has a specific meaning.

Umānandanātha, however, maintains that regarding the phrase "the guru-mantra": in the *Ārambhollāsa*, there is the contemplation of the identity (*aikya*) of the guru, the mantra, the deity, and one's own self; this is one means (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the knowledge that the mind and the vital breath (*pavana*) are to be restrained by a single effort is another; through these two, the accomplishment of the goal (*kāryasiddhi*) occurs.

They have explained it thus; but that is to be reconsidered. From the act of "shaking off" (*niṣphālana*), only a single meaning—either in the form of a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) or in the form of the cognition that [the state] is to be restrained by a single effort—would be understood, not multiple ones, according to the maxim that "a word uttered once conveys only one meaning at a time. Otherwise, from the word *hari*...
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous cognition of all fourteen meanings.

Furthermore, if the members of a *dvandva* compound were to connect with distinct actions, then it would result in nothing more than a mere *anvācaya* (cumulative conjunction), because *anvācaya* occurs precisely when there is a difference in action—as in the example: "Go for alms and bring the cow."

Because of the definition of a *dvandva* compound: for the definition of a *dvandva* is indeed the simultaneous co-referentiality (*anvaya*) with a single action, and its fulfillment is impossible in every respect according to that [opponent's] view. Nor should it be argued that such usage as "Cut and look at the *dhava* and *khadira* trees" would not be possible; for such usage is simply unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*).
Because it has been established by all [the masters]. || 11 ||
Regarding the procedure for worship in the form of adoration (*arcana-rūpopāsti-vidhi*):

up to this point, by means of the praise of the mantra and the statement of its auxiliary causes, the ritual action having the mantra as its instrument and its corresponding injunction can be inferred. And thus, it is precisely of the nature of silent recitation (*japa*). In this way—
Having described the worship in the form of recitation (*japa*), he now prescribes the worship in the form of ritual adoration (*pūjā*):
"Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is established within the body; its manifestors are the five *makāras*. Worship with them should be done in secret; from public display comes hell. (12)

Just as Brahman is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), so too is it of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*).
