Just as [the Self] does not know its conscious nature when it is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*), so too it does not know its essential nature of bliss when it is veiled by suffering (*duḥkha*). This occurs whenever suffering in the form of a heavy burden or the like is removed.
Even now, one perceives the limited form of Brahman itself through the limitation of the body;
such bliss is limited and established within the body through the limitation of the body. Of that—

The "manifestors" (*abhivyañjakāḥ*) are those which produce direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding that [object], namely the five *makāras*. Up to this point, there has been a praise of the substances being enjoined for the sake of motivating the practitioner; the implication is: "Since these five *makāras* are thus excellent, one should therefore perform worship with them in secret, i.e., without public display."
By this [verse], the ritual act consisting of worship characterized by secrecy, the object, and both [the agent and the recipient] is prescribed.

If it is argued that, in the injunction of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭa-karma-vidhi*), praise must pertain to the action alone—since there is a rule that only that which is enjoined can be praised—we reply: no. Because in an injunction of a qualified object, the injunction of the qualifier is necessarily implied, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can serve as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that [injunction of the qualifier], just as in the case of the text: "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu."

Even in the injunction regarding a ritual distinguished by a deity, there is praise of the deity through the statement "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," and similarly, there is concealment in the ritual. This concealment consists in being devoid of both knowledge of the nature of the animal's behavior and general knowledge [of its state]. Because this is of the nature of a qualified injunction, the concealment serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). From the disclosure of that very [animal], however, hell (*niraya*) results.

Praise in the form of censure: for example, "If one were to collect [the materials] with the skin of domestic animals, he would afflict domestic animals with suffering"—this being in the form of censure, it serves as a supplement to the praise, "He collects them with a black antelope skin. Likewise, if by chance [the skin] becomes manifest before [the ritual], there is no expiation (prāyaścitta) arising from the omission of a constituent part of the sacrifice.
There is another expiation for the purpose of avoiding hell.
"From manifestation," meaning from the opposite of concealment; the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*); "niraya" means "niraka" (a place of exit).

The venerable Bhāsurānandanātha, however, has stated: "For those who possess other forms of initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is merely a deficiency in the ritual (*kratuviguṇya*) when their own duty (*svadharma*) is made manifest; but here, if there is such a deficiency, there is indeed hell. To that effect, the Lord Paraśurāma said: "From manifestation comes hell. According to that view, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

I, being of little intelligence, do not know the means for avoiding the faults such as the abandonment of the subject at hand and the postulation of a human purpose for what is not the subject at hand. || 12 ||
The Duties of a Lay Devotee (Upāsaka-dharma): Having thus described worship as the firmness of cultivation, he speaks of the duties of a lay devotee:
"From the firmness of cultivation comes the accomplishment of the Command" (13).

In such mental states as "I know this," the discernment that "this" (the object) appears as "I-ness" (ahantā) in relation to the objective referent (*padārtha*) is superior; this alone is the essential meaning of *bhāvanā* across all mental states.
Its firmness is its lack of laxity. Through this, the perfection of the Command (*ājñāsiddhi*)—the capacity for both restraint and grace—is attained.

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By way of praising the firmness of cultivation (*bhāvanādārḍhya*), the injunction for such cultivation at all times is to be inferred.
[Non-censure of all philosophical systems (darśanas). From this, the reverence for the Blessed One’s Tantric teaching is even more to be contemplated. Censure.
He states another rule for the lay follower: 14.
Not censuring any philosophical system.

The meaning is that one must not engage in the censure of those philosophical systems (*darśana*) and scriptures that enjoin the worship of other deities. By censuring them, doubt arises among their adherents, leading to a lack of confidence in the very systems they themselves have adopted. Since such a person lacks qualification for this [present] scripture, they fall away from both.
It would perish like a scattered cloud. Śrī Kṛṣṇa also spoke of this very same meaning:
"One should not cause a disturbance of the intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action."
"One should not revile the worlds," so also says the Śruti.

Is it not established that the absence of the transgression arising from the mental confusion of others is the fruit of this [meditation], and that this is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? If it is asked, "How is this included among the duties of the meditator (*upāsaka*), which produce excellence for the sacrifice (*kratu*)?", it is replied: This too is useful for the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*) produced by meditation.

If you ask how this is so, it is as follows: if one remains indifferent toward the destruction of others—as if they were scattered clouds—and only then proceeds to censure them, then by being indifferent toward the destruction of others, the vision of all beings as oneself has not been attained; thus, on account of the non-establishment of the identity of all selves (*sarvātmatā*).
There is no failure in establishing the fruit arising from worship. In the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, there is subservience to the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*).

This very [subservience] constitutes the capacity to bring about the *apūrva* (unseen potency) to be accomplished by the sacrifice. Since, in the present context, subservience to the sacrifice is established by the aforementioned reasoning, there is no defect whatsoever. || 14 ||
He states the third dharma, which is non-counting: "Non-counting of anything whatsoever. (15)

If even the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati) should speak in contradiction to one's own scripture, then he must not be counted as a Guru. For this very reason, the Śruti also says: "One should not count anyone [as a Guru]. || 15 ||
He states the fourth [topic], the disclosure of the secret to a worthy disciple:
"The disclosure of the secret to a worthy disciple. (16)

The word "should be done" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*). It is an exception to the prohibition "one should not speak of the secret of the Self," and not an exception to the rule "worship [the deity] in secrecy"; for if it were the latter, it would follow that there could be no public manifestation of worship among fellow-initiates (*sāmayika*) other than one's own disciple. Therefore, this secret of the Self—

One should not explain the form of one's own established doctrine to those among the initiates who are not [true] disciples; the meaning is that one should explain it to a good disciple. The quality of being a disciple has been set forth in the *Tantrarāja* (p.
Handsome, fair-faced, pure, endowed with faith, and of very steady resolve; free from greed, firm-limbed, acting after due consideration, and having conquered his senses.
"One who is faithful, possessing firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity—such a person should be a disciple; any other causes suffering for the guru. Thus [it is said].
In the *Ātmapurāṇa* as well, it is said:
"The knowledge of Brahman, having been thoroughly exhausted [by others], went to a Brāhmaṇa most devoted to Brahman, saying:
'Always protect me, like a woman of noble birth.'"
Beginning with these words:
"Always avoid me from those [teachers] in whom such faults as these exist;
for by acting thus constantly, I shall be like a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) to you."
The characteristics of unworthy disciples (asattvalakṣaṇa) are to be known in detail from the Kulārṇava [see Appendix II, 6 for the knowledge of the characteristics of unworthy disciples]. || 16 ||
He states the fifth duty, the constant pursuit of knowledge: "The constant pursuit of knowledge. (17)
"Always" means at all times, specifically during periods other than those occupied by the performance of the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) such as worship; "always" is the intended meaning.

The ellipsis to be supplied is that one must perform the "continuous application" (*anusaṃhati*) of the *vidyā*—that is, the mantra denoting one's own deity to be worshipped—and the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the meaning expounded therein.

Alternatively, the meaning is that one should always perform recitation (*japa*) with the mind in continuous connection. Nor should it be suspected that recitation is improper for one who is devoid of rules regarding posture and so forth, because there is no rule whatsoever in the case of mental recitation. As it is said in the *Paramānandatantra*:
In the mental [recitation], the merit is multiplied infinitely; there is no restriction at all therein.
Whether walking, lying down, sitting, or eating, wherever one may be—even if unclean or lacking ritual purity—no fault exists in that practice.
Also in the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra*: "He who, whether restrained or unrestrained, and even while performing his daily obligatory rites, recites the Vidyā mentally alone at all times,"
Nevertheless, that pure one becomes instantly serene. Thus it is said.

(33) If there were no restriction on the term "one who is always in distress," then it would follow that even the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) could be abandoned. Therefore, as in the case of the statement "all desire wealth," a restriction is necessary. || 17 ||
The sixth duty is stated as: "Constant immersion in Śiva-nature. (18)

The meaning of "constantly" (*satatam*) here is the same as that of the word *sadā* found in the previous sūtra; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the immersion (*samāveśa*), that is, the manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), of Śiva-nature must be brought about. The intended sense is that one should contemplate "I am Śiva" at times other than those occupied with the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).

In reality, however, this is conceived as an alternative to the previous method; otherwise, it would be impossible to accomplish both meditations simultaneously. The implication is that at times other than those for worship and so forth, one should perform either one [of the two]. [Thus, by implication, one should bring the Self within for the sake of worship.]

The intended meaning is that after having conceived [the deity] externally in the form of an image and so forth, and having worshipped it, there may arise for the devotees a manifestation of contemplation—consistent with the established tenets of Vedānta—in the form: "I am that very same God" or "He is my own Self."
Or rather: the former teaching is for those of dull faculties, while this is for those of primary faculties. || 18 ||
He states the seventh [requirement], the avoidance of desire and so forth:
the avoidance of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, unrighteous violence, theft, and what is loathed by the world.
[Contrary to worldly norms and hated by women] || 19 ||

Desire (*kāma*) is indeed an object-oriented longing, taking the form "may this be mine. Anger (*krodha*) is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) produced by the predominance of *tamas*. Greed (*lobha*) is a particular kind of extreme attachment that acts as an obstacle to the relinquishing of ownership over objects such as wealth. Delusion (*moha*)...

Intoxication (*mada*) is the failure to discern what ought and ought not to be done; it is pride. Envy (*mātsarya*) is the attribution of faults to those possessing virtues, born of hatred. Unprescribed violence (*avihitahiṃsā*) is the slaughter of animals and the like for the sake of consumption out of passion. Theft (*steya*) is the taking of another's property without their consent. That which is loathed by the world is [to be avoided] even in private, even with the thought that it is one's mother.
Conversation with the wives of others and so forth. The ellipsis "the abandonment" (tyāga) must be supplied, meaning that the avoidance of these [actions] should be practiced. || 19 ||
The eighth dharma, single-minded devotion to one’s guru, is stated as follows:
"Single-minded devotion to one’s guru is free from doubt" [extending until the conclusion of this sūtra and its commentary].
There is an instruction regarding the practice of honoring [the teacher] as the sole guru, and so forth. || 20 ||
In the analysis of the compound *asaṃśayaḥ* as "that in which no doubt exists," it serves as an adjective qualifying the singular worship of the Guru;
the difference in gender is a Vedic archaism (*ārṣa*).
The meaning is this: if, while serving many gurus, one should speak something contrary to what was previously stated by a guru, then doubt would certainly arise;
however, when serving a single guru, no such doubt would arise. Therefore, the point is that one should serve a single guru.

Since the service of the guru and the confidence in the tradition are already established by the preceding sūtra alone, this re-enactment is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) whose purpose is to exclude reliance on another guru, signifying that one should not resort to a different guru after having taken refuge in one.
An Investigation into the Meaning of the Method for Worshipping the Sole Guru:
Now, it may be argued that resorting to *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) is not appropriate, because it entails three defects.
(Regarding this *parisaṃkhyā* mentioned here, it is stated in the *Arthasaṃgraha* composed by Laugākṣibhāskara, page 15).

In the analysis of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification), it is characterized by three defects: the abandonment of the meaning as heard, the postulation of a meaning not heard, and the sublation of what has been established. Here, the meaning of this verse is also easily understood; however—

Having referred to the teacher who is to be worshipped, only oneness is enjoined; the exclusion of others, however, follows from the fear of omitting a subordinate element (*aṅga*), because if one were to worship another teacher, that [oneness] would be omitted as it is a subordinate element of oneness. Nor can it be argued that even when resorting to two or more teachers, oneness exists in each individual teacher.

It must be asked: how can there be an elision of the suffix *aṅ*? For it is not "oneness" (*ekatva*) in the form of a numerical category that is enjoined, because as a property common to all things whatsoever, it would lack the power of exclusion (*avyāvartakatvāt*). Rather, what is intended is the state of being devoid of a second member of the same class; however, if one were to resort to another [technical] term for "heavy" (*guru*), the elision of that suffix would be unavoidable. Therefore, one should not resort to another term for "heavy."

If it is argued that the injunction of oneness alone is supreme—let the injunction of oneness be; Śrī Śiva has revealed this very same meaning in the Tantras by way of a different formulation. In the Rudrayāmala:
"It should not be given to the disciples of others; it should be given only to one's own disciples. Thus [it is said].
In the Kulārṇava it is said:
"Having properly obtained a Kula-guru, one should not resort to another guru."
Also in the Yoginītantra: "It should not be given to the disciples of others, nor to an atheist, O Mistress of the Kula."
Even in the *Upaniṣad* it is said: "The Guru is one. In some places, regarding the duty of the disciple, it states this very same point;

in other places, regarding the duty of the Guru, it says by way of a different formulation that one should not speak to another disciple. In both cases, the conclusion is the same: the fruit consists in the worship of a single Guru. This is the intended meaning of these [texts].

The meaning of these words appears as follows: it must be supplied [to the text] that "while a Guru exists who cuts through one's own doubts" regarding the previously mentioned *Rudrayāmala*, *Kulārṇava*, and *Yoginītantras*. Otherwise— (p.
"Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, goes from one teacher to another. Thus it is said.

In another tantra, the *Śaktirahasya*, it is stated: "The gurus in the Kaula tradition are infinite. Otherwise, such statements would be rendered devoid of meaning. By this [it is implied that] the previous guru was either not omniscient and thus incapable of cutting through one's own doubts, or, though capable, failed to cut through his own doubts.
A deceased disciple of such a kind, according to the saying "one greedy for honey [should seek another]," should resort to another guru.
Even if that other guru possesses little knowledge, as long as he is alive, one may accept what is taught by him with his permission. This too has been stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
And one should report to the Lord any mantras, āgamas, or other teachings heard elsewhere.
One should accept that by the guru's command and avoid what is undesirable to him. Thus it is said.

If one is personally unable to determine the relative degree of seniority among gurus, one should not abandon the path of whichever guru one has accepted. However, if one is capable of making such a determination, one should privately inform that guru of the matter with its supporting reasons and, with his permission, act according to the scriptures.

One should accept it. Even if the guru is alive but does not grant permission due to malice or other such motives, one may disregard him and follow the authoritative path prescribed by the scriptures. This has been clearly stated in the *Tripurārahasya*:
"The wise person, having reflected with his intellect upon what the guru has said and what is purified by the scriptures..."
"One should perform the Upāsana correctly; otherwise, it is lost. Thus [it is said].

All these points have been made known by the statement "like one greedy for honey. The intended meaning of this aphorism, "serving a single guru," should be described according to the force of the aforementioned arguments.

As for those who describe the intention behind the writing of Śrī Bhāskararāya in his *Kaulopaniṣad-bhāṣya*—namely, that "whatever is illogical is logical" and that "the oral tradition of the Guru must be accepted even if it is incorrect"—they do not understand the true nature of his intention. If one asks, "What is this intention? it is said in reply:
If, in the midst of the Kaulika practice, one's own guru or another Kaulika should act in contradiction to their own established doctrine,
and another compassionate person should seek to enlighten them, then, having informed the guru, one may accept [the correction] while the guru is still alive. Or,
if another who is a mere talkative pedant should set out to defile the Kaula path, [one should act] oneself...

Even if one is not proficient due to a deficiency in that regard, one should not abandon the conviction regarding its authority. For this very reason, it is written: "One should not criticize the Kaulika practice. Thus, there is no doubt in one's own mind regarding the Guru’s limited knowledge;
rather, through long residence, his mastery of many tantras is certain, yet he does not live.

If a statement found in some Tantra is contrary to that practice, then, because custom is weaker [in authority], its lack of authority— consisting in non-performance— is maintained until the source of authority upon which it is based is discovered, while one performs the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.

This is according to the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*. However, in the Kaula system, the distinction is that even what is contrary to the scriptures must be performed during the aforementioned state of certainty; this does not apply, however, when there is certainty regarding the dull-wittedness of the guru. Likewise, such an intention—namely, that [the teaching] is obtainable only through the tradition of a true guru—is directed toward the guru in that very context.

36) This is made known by the qualification "a particular being" (*sattvaviśeṣaṇa*). The reality here is this: the reason consisting in "possessing conduct contrary to many scriptures," which leads to the inference that [the teacher] is not omniscient, and the reason consisting in [possessing conduct] in every respect, which leads to the inference that he is omniscient, both reside in the teacher.
It is the state of being contradicted by that [scripture] in some instances, while being authorized by scripture.

Now, since the *Kādimata* states the characteristics of a Guru as being "handsome, fair-faced, pure, auspicious, and a knower of many tantras" (some manuscripts read "easily accessible"), how could a disciple appoint as a Guru one who frequently practices in contradiction to the tantras? For it is not possible for a learned man who has resided with one for a year for the sake of service to remain ignorant.
It is possible. If one asks how such an example can be both possible and logically consistent:

it is because for one who was previously initiated during a state of ignorance solely through the intensity of faith and had accepted such a guru, but later attained knowledge through study and other means, [the former state] occurs due to the aforementioned cause.

Because inference is possible, such a prior practice must certainly be abandoned. If one has by chance entered upon a wrong path, then even the tradition of a true guru must be abandoned once that entry onto the wrong path has occurred, because it is determined to be non-scriptural. Enough of this prolixity.
Amṛtānandanātha, however, states in his commentary on the *Yoginītantra*: "It should not be given to the disciples of others" (*na deyaṃ paraśiṣyebhyaḥ*).

This means that those who have attained all secrets and the entirety of the supreme truth through the lineage succession (*pāraṃparyakrama*) in other sciences (*vidyā*), and who have received the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), are the "disciples of others"; [the teaching] should not be given to them.

And this statement from the Kulārṇava is supreme; for it says: "This should be given to those outside [this tradition], just as a bee, greedy for honey, [flies] to others. Regarding such an arrangement, they say that the *pādukā* belongs only to that Guru who performs the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*.

That is not so; this statement is merely an indicator of the status of being a *guru* in one who performs the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*. If that were the case, the phrase "the sandals of him alone" would be redundant. If the status of being a *guru* and his name were enjoined within the *gurupādukā* mantra, then the rule "he who performs initiation is the *guru*" would mean that his name alone [would be placed] in the *pādukā*.
"Should be joined"—this is another sentence. And thus, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "that" (*saḥ*) [is required].

Moreover, if the injunction were merely for the weight (*gurutva*), since that is already established by the other statement—"should be joined to the mantra of the Guru’s name and sandals"—the futility of the remainder [of the text] would be unavoidable. Therefore, [the meaning follows] from the statement "greedy for honey" (*madhulubdhaḥ*).

When various gurus have attained perfection, this [rule] serves as the regulator when all names are applicable within the *pādukā-mantra*. If that were the case, the desired goal of others would not be accomplished; on the contrary, by this statement, only the attainment of various gurus is indicated. Therefore, the path we have described is indeed the superior one.
Moreover, the authority of practices contrary to the scriptures is observed even among experts of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, such as the marriage of a maternal cousin among the Āndhras,
as well as the absence of wearing bodices among Dravidian women.
Having seen a woman wearing a bodice who is not properly dressed,
or having seen a widow with her hair loose, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Thus, this contradicts the statement of Aṅgiras; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

37) If one were to trust only in the guru, then if he were to perform the voiding of urine and excrement while standing, it would follow that one must do so as well. And if there is some statement regarding one who is learned in many tantras...

Upon seeing something contrary to that [Vedic injunction], one apprehends its lack of authority regarding that practice; does this apprehension of non-authority apply only to that specific part, or to the whole? Not the first, because in the world, when there is a practice by someone like Caitra whose lack of authority has not been previously apprehended, if a lack of authority is ever apprehended, it would have to apply everywhere.

It is observed in the world that people do not place their trust due to the suspicion of invalidity; likewise here too, if there is a single instance of deviation, the consequence would be the non-performance of all [actions] due to such suspicion. And that suspicion does not depart anywhere without the observation of a fundamental basis. If one were to strive for the sake of purifying the basis in every case, then—

The rule for following the tradition would be rendered meaningless. Nor should it be argued that where there is an alternative consisting of two positions, the rule for practicing the tradition of one's own guru is meaningful;
for if these two positions were established according to a distinction between types of practitioners, then [it would follow] in the Tantric scriptures...

The state of being an object of conceptual construction would not exist in any way whatsoever. Just as, for example, regarding the base of the special arghya vessel, there were options such as three feet, four feet, or no feet at all, and the Guru practiced using exactly three feet, and the disciple likewise practiced accordingly; sometimes [the disciple] reached three feet, yet obtained four feet because of that.
The performance would [otherwise] not occur because it has not been performed by the Guru; in this way, there would be no emergence of an alternative (vikalpa).
For an alternative indeed consists in the coexistence of two positions within a ritual action performed by a single person through a difference in application.

Furthermore—the rule of placing trust in the words of the guru would be futile. For one who is intent on investigating the source in order to eliminate doubt, how could there be such extreme trust in the guru’s words? Therefore, having inferred the guru’s competence, [one should investigate] what kind of guru is intended here, for the sake of knowing that.
And one should have faith in the words of the true guru.

Umānandanātha, having concluded the statement "serving a single guru," applied the phrase "there is no doubt anywhere" to it; he explained that there is no doubt regarding the words of the guru, at the beginning of the scriptures, and everywhere else. That is not so;
for all accomplishment comes through both the tradition and faith, and authority consists primarily in faith.
Because this very meaning has already been established by these two [preceding passages], its repetition would result in tautology. || 20 ||
He states the ninth quality, non-possessiveness in all respects: "Non-possessiveness in all respects. (21)

In all instances, such as in the *Mañcapañcaka* and other texts, *niṣparigrahatā* means "the state of being without possession. One who has departed from *parigraha*—that is, from desire (*icchā*)—is *niṣparigraha*. Its abstract state is *tattā*. According to Amara, possessions (*parigraha*) consist of wife, retinue, acquisitions (*ādāna*), and curses; here, according to such a lexicon, desire itself is the root of acquisition and possession.

The word *parigraha* signifies desire; the meaning is that one should not accept anything out of the desire, "May this manifold world be mine. This very point is clearly established in the *Bhāgavata*:
That the consumption of *surā* was ordained for the one who subsists on odors, and likewise that the immolation of an animal is not violence;
that sexual union is for the sake of progeny and not for pleasure—those who know this thus recognize this pure *svadharma*.
But those men who, not knowing this, are arrogant, full of egoism,
and recklessly harm animals— they devour them after death.

Thus, "eating by smelling" is what is taught in the scripture; "eating" refers to the act of slaughtering animals and the like for the sake of a deity with the intention of relinquishing them, which is termed "touching."
Alternatively, in every case regarding all things whatsoever, one must cultivate the state of non-possessiveness by abandoning the notion of "mine";
that is to say, the sense of ownership everywhere must be relinquished.

Furthermore, the statement in the *Nityotsava-nibandha* that wealth should not be acquired with the intention of personal enjoyment is contrary to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Jaimini, who, in the fourth chapter, refuted the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and concluded that the acquisition of wealth is solely for the sake of the person (*kevalapuruṣārtha*).
He states the tenth duty, which is action preceded by the renunciation of fruits:
"The performance of action after having abandoned the fruit. (22)
The previously mentioned fruit is artificial, as are its means—namely, dharma, artha, and kāma.

The meaning of the word "fruit" (phala) is the desire directed toward that fruit. Having abandoned that [desire], one performs the prescribed action; this is the remainder [of the sense]. The meaning is that karma performed for the sake of desire (kāmya-karma) should not be done. This refers to kāmya-karma.

Since it is stated that "it should be performed" after having abandoned the fruit— rather than saying "it should not be performed"— it is understood that even those actions performed with desire (kāmya-karmans) must be carried out with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord.
But is it not said in the Bhagavad Gītā:
"O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship me:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom"?

If it is argued that this worship with desire (*sakāmopāsanā*) taught by the Blessed One is contradictory [to the injunction that action for desire should not be performed]—we say no. By the verse "Four kinds of people worship Me," the natural disposition of the world (*lokasvabhāva*) has been shown. He declared that "action for desire (*kāmya-karma*) should not be performed.
For this very reason:
And he who renounces the fruits of action—he is called a renouncer.
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is constantly disciplined, and who is devoted to the One alone, is distinguished as superior.
Thus ends the praise of action free from desire. || 22 ||
(On page 39) He states the eleventh duty: the non-neglect of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).
There is no omission of obligatory duties. || 23 ||

That which is both eternal (*nitya*) and an action (*karman*) is "eternal action" (*nityakarman*), such as bathing, the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*), worship, and so forth. The omission (*lopa*) of that—its non-performance—is "the omission of eternal action. An upāsaka in whom no omission of eternal action exists is one for whom there is no omission of eternal action (*anityakarmalopa*). The word "should be" (*bhavet*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. The meaning is that eternal action must necessarily be performed.

While it should have been stated that "the obligatory rite must be performed," this statement by way of negation indicates that in its omission, there is not only a deficiency in the sacrifice, but also sin and rebirth in hell. || 23 ||

Now, in response to the doubt as to how the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) should be performed when the five-fold time (*pañcakāla*)—which serves as its means—is not obtained, he says: "Even in the absence of the five-fold time, there is the recollection of the obligatory sequence. (24)

In the absence of the five [grains], there is no primary [material] available; however, this does not constitute a lapse in the ritual (*karmalopa*). Rather, even by means of a substitute (*pratinidhi*), the sequence of the obligatory rite (*nityakrama*), the obligatory worship (*nityapūjā*), its review (*pratyavamṛṣṭi*), and its performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) must be carried out—this is the remainder [of the sense].
Now, one might object: "In the sixth chapter, it was stated that in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, in the absence of rice (*vrīhi*), there is a lapse in the ritual."

Having formulated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached as follows: since the visible fruit of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) can be accomplished even by means of wild rice (*nīvāra*), there is no fault in the omission of the rule regarding *vrīhi* rice in the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), because obligatory rites are capable of tolerating the omission of certain auxiliary elements; thus, both obligatory and occasional rites (*naimittika*) may be performed even with a substitute (*pratinidhi*).

If it is argued that, because it is rooted in such reasoning, the practice of substitutes is observed even in Śrauta and Smārta rites, and that therefore a scriptural injunction (vacana) is redundant since the substitute is established here too by that very same logic—[we reply]:

No. For while [the substitute] might apply to occasional (naimittika) rites by the same logic as it applies to obligatory (nitya) ones, [the injunction is necessary] regarding the substitute in that context.

Let there be no accomplishment of the sequence of occasional rites (*naimittika*), because this is for that specific purpose. Nor does it follow from this that, in the absence [of the primary], that which is distinct from the obligatory (*nitya*) need not be performed; for if that were the case, it would take the form of an exclusionary injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) based on the Vedic text (see the verse in the commentary on Sūtra 20 of this same section, as found in the marginal notes).

It should not be argued that there is the occurrence of three defects— namely, the abandonment of one's own purpose (*svārthatyāga*), the assumption of another’s purpose (*parārthakalpanā*), and the sublation of what has been obtained (*prāptabādha*)—

because Pārthasārathi, in the *Abhyudayeṣṭyadhikaraṇa* of the *Tantraratna*, [establishes] the principle that "the sentence is completed with each individual subject" (*pratyuddeśaṃ vākyaparisamāpti*) out of fear that the statement "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts" (*tredhā taṇḍulān vibhajet*) would otherwise be rendered meaningless.

A split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) has been accepted; how much more so, then, in accepting three defects out of such fear? For this very reason, our supreme gurus, the venerable and worshipful P. Bhāskararāya, stated in the *Setubandha* on the *Uttaracatuśśatī*: "[Having understood this much, the venerable and worshipful P. Bhāskararāya, our supreme gurus, [are the authors of this commentary]. Thus it is said in the *Setubandha* on the *Uttaracatuśśatī*.

In the second verse, two hundred [units] further, within the section on occasional rites (*naimittika-prakaraṇa*), regarding the statement "one should especially perform the wheel-worship (*cakrapūjā*) for the Yoginīs," the word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*) found in the root text is first explained as meaning "in comparison to the daily worship (*nityapūjā*)," by way of the superiority of the Yoginīs and heroes, and the abundance of foods such as edibles and drinks.

The meaning is: "either because of dissatisfaction therein" (p. 40) or "by means of a special substance. Therefore, even when a special substance is unavailable for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), [the rite should still be performed].

Having explained that the statement "accomplishment by means of a substitute is indicated" grants permission only for the daily worship (nityapūjā) and not for other occasions, this very sentence is shown as the proof for this point. || 24 ||
He states the twelfth quality, fearlessness everywhere:
"Fearlessness everywhere [in all respects]. || 25 ||
In all cases, when adopting the fivefold manifestation (*pañcakasvīkāra*) and following the Kaula path, one must achieve the state of being "fearless" (*nirbhayatā*);
that is, he from whom fear has departed—fear arising from all those scriptures which teach of hell and other such states. This is the remainder of the sense. All of those [scriptures]...
The meaning is that while the scriptures may indeed terrify one who is possessed by passion, I am not passionate;
rather, being impelled by the scripture, I have no fear. Thus, through such firm determination, fearlessness is to be achieved. || 25 ||
The Dharma that constitutes the essence of all is the oblation (homa) into the supreme Śiva of one's own self;
he states the Dharma that constitutes the essence of all established doctrines (siddhānta):
"All that is knowable is the oblation-material (havya), the senses are the offering-spoons (sruk), and the powers (śaktis) are the flames."

One's own self is Śiva, the purifier; one is oneself the officiating priest. [The dignity of the venerable Brahmabhāvanā, as seen in the tantric texts beginning with this sūtra, is evident here. || 26 ||

The phrase "one should meditate thus" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the expression "by means of the modifications of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttibhiḥ*), the meaning of the words *vedya* and so forth in this sūtra is clearly explained in the commentary below.
The word *vedyam* (the object of knowledge) is to be supplied at the beginning; everything that is known through the modifications of the internal organ is [to be offered] as an oblation (*havis*).
One should contemplate [them as such]. Just as an oblation cast into the fire assumes the form of that [fire], so too,

when all objects of cognition (*vṛtti-vedya*) are offered as oblations into the fire that is Śiva, it is appropriate to contemplate them as oblations, because they attain the state of having the form of Śiva.
Only the *juhū* ladle, which serves as the receptacle for such an oblation and functions as the instrument of the *homa*, is understood by the term *sruk*;

although the *dhruvā* and other vessels are denoted by the word *sruk*, they are unsuitable within the context of the *homa-bhāvanā* because, despite being denoted by the term *sruk*, they lack the status of being instruments of the *homa*. [From here onwards—]

By the passage of the Bhāṣya ending with "by an irrelevant inquiry," it is shown that there is very little scriptural significance in the singular and plural numbers residing in the single word that serves as a qualifier.
Nor should it be argued that the plural number is untenable because of the oneness of the *sruk* ladles, [for the same would apply] due to the multiplicity of the sense organs (*indriya*).

The plural number is used so that the qualifier may be in grammatical agreement (samānavacana) with its [the qualified's] referent. Nor is there a rule requiring non-agreement in number in cases where something is superimposed upon another; for this very reason, it is said in the *Naiṣadha* (p.

By the use of the restrictive particle *eva* here, it is indicated that when one is unable to perform a ritual action oneself, people employ their son, wife, or others as a substitute agent (*kartṛ-pratinidhi*), and it is established by scripture that the fruit arising from that action accrues to them.
In this sacrifice, however, it is suggested that if the rite is performed by a substitute, the fruit born of the action does not belong to oneself.
The fruit of cultivation is the attainment of one's true self.
Thus, he states the fruit of cultivation performed in this manner:
"The fruit is the discernment of consciousness free from objects. (27)
The fruit is the discernment of consciousness (*citi*) which is objectless and non-conceptual in form;
this refers to the aforementioned meditation (the meaning being that it results from the "true meditation" described in the sūtras from the thirteenth on page thirty to the twenty-seventh). || 27 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the point of attaining such a fruit? To this he says:
"There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self. (28)

"Superior to the attainment of the self"—that is, superior to the attainment of one's own nature—the phrase "the supreme fruit" from the preceding sūtra is supplied here. It does not exist; that is, it is non-existent. The Śruti [supports] this meaning: "There is nothing whatsoever higher than the Puruṣa; that is the pinnacle, that is the highest goal," and "Knowing him thus, one becomes immortal here."

He explains: No one disputes that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). Therefore, the sense is that by such contemplation (*bhāvanā*), the attainment of the supreme human goal occurs. Previously—in the first section, on page 26, line 6 of the sūtra—it was stated that the investigation of the dog (*śvavimarśa*) is a human goal.
By this, the nature of the human goal (puruṣārtha) has been established; since this is a eulogy, there is no tautology.

Up to this point, having examined the two works concerning the names, meanings, and greatness of these five traditions (pañcāmnāya) as spoken by Śrī Paraśurāma— the established doctrine of the five traditions—
they have been renowned. A certain Keśavaśarman, being incapable of understanding their intended meaning, seeks to refute them.

Thus, with mere envy, he has uttered these senseless ravings; by the very sight of them, the wise will come to know their lack of logical foundation. For the sake of removing the doubts of those of dull intellect, I myself have demonstrated in my *Siddhānta-śiromaṇi* that his arguments are nothing but mere prattle.
It is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity; those who desire to know it should learn it from that very source. 28.
The conclusion of the established doctrine:
beginning with "In this regard, this is the established doctrine," he concludes the matter under discussion—this is the method of the treatise. || 29 ||

This very style of the scripture previously mentioned is the "śāstra"—that which teaches—and its "śailī" is its method; it is this [style] that constitutes the fivefold tradition (pañcāmnāya), such is the completion of the sense. || 29 ||
42) This knowledge is extremely secret; [the author] praises such a scripture in order to incite the listener to engage with it:
Like a courtesan, the sciences such as the Vedas are manifest;
this science, however, is hidden within all philosophical systems.
The sciences such as the Vedas are as easily accessible as courtesans; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the Smṛtis and other texts are included.

Just as the enjoyment of a courtesan is easily obtained through the expenditure of wealth and the like, so too the acquisition of the knowledge of the Vedas and other sciences is easily obtained through the giving of wealth and other gifts. That study is rooted in greed is established by the scripture itself.
Among the six types of action, it has been established that three constitute one's livelihood;

however, this knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation, cannot be obtained even by the expenditure of millions of gold pieces, but is obtainable solely through the grace of the Guru.

If it is asked, "Why would a guru not show compassion even when there is an expenditure of abundant wealth?"—the answer is: he certainly would not. For one who has attained the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), ten million pieces of gold are more insignificant than a blade of grass; how, then, could greed for such things arise?

[Objection: Let it be that one engages [in worldly activity] out of greed; nevertheless, since there is no loss to oneself when engaging in the giving of knowledge at the request of another, let one engage [in it]. Moreover, while the former types of knowledge were obtainable only by those possessing wealth, this [knowledge] can be obtained even by the poor; thus, its superiority is manifest. [Reply: No, for a learned man does not [act] merely at the request of another.
One who acts proceeds only after seeing the accomplishment of the purpose regarding the object he has set forth; he does not act fruitlessly.

In the present case, this knowledge of Brahman, when imparted to those with defiled internal organs, is not only fruitless, but moreover destroys the knowledge of the teacher himself. Regarding this matter, Yāska cites a Vedic scripture:
"Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is lacking in self-restraint; thus shall I be powerful.
The meaning of this is very clear."
The knowledge of Brahman, having been thoroughly refined, went to a Brāhmaṇa most devoted to Brahman, saying:
"Always protect me, as you would a woman born of a noble family;
I am your inexhaustible treasure, both in this world and in the next."
Beginning with these words—
“Always avoid me from those in whom such faults as these exist”—
for one who acts thus constantly, I am like a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) to you.
Otherwise, I shall become barren, like a creeper deprived of fruit.
By such statements as these, it is heard that the destruction of one's own knowledge occurs when a guru imparts knowledge to an unworthy recipient.
How, then, could he teach knowledge to an unworthy person merely out of a desire for others? A fit recipient for such instruction is difficult to find.
Therefore, the locative case in "among all philosophical systems" (*sarvadarśaneṣu*) is used in the sense of selection; the meaning is that this science, being hidden, is difficult to obtain.

But contemporary teachers are sellers of the knowledge of Brahman like merchants; in that case, there is neither true teacherhood nor the removal of the disciple's distress. On the contrary, he too, being engaged in a passion for the pursuit of wealth, surely falls. Thus, both of them perform only the means for falling, not the means for liberation.
Thus it is said in the *Kulārṇava* [Prabodhacandrodaya, Ba-Ba 1]:
"There are many gurus who plunder the wealth of their disciples;
but this guru, O Goddess—who removes the suffering of his disciples—is rare and difficult to find in the world."
Thus, enough with further elaboration. || 30 ||
The procedure for initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*):
having thus far restated the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—
meaning the established doctrine concerning the worship, mantras, and so forth of various deities— the practitioner must first...
He states the action to be performed:
"In that regard, the wise person should by all means undergo initiation. (31)

The seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) has the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*); the meaning of the base (*prakṛty-artha*) is the worship of Śrīvidyā; the sense of the sixth case is the relation (*saṃbandha*), which is the state of occurring immediately prior to that [worship]. This [relation] connects by way of being the substratum (*āśrayatā*) with the referent of the term "initiation" (*dīkṣā*). That [initiation], in turn, connects with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) by way of the relation of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*). And thus:

The specific understanding is that one should contemplate the desired object through initiation (dīkṣā) which immediately precedes the worship of Śrīvidyā; for this very reason, it is an originative injunction (utpattividhi). In every way, the wise person must necessarily have ascended—or, as some read, desire to ascend—to the aforementioned stage. This follows precisely from the inherent force of the word "this" (etat).

This is also a rule concerning qualification (*adhikāravidhi*). It is established that the qualification belongs only to one who desires to ascend to such a stage—or indeed to one who has already ascended—and not to anyone else.

If it is asked, "How can both the status of being an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) and the status of being an injunctive rule for qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) reside in one and the same injunction?"—the answer is: no, because such a thing is observed in cases like "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā" (*citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ*). Furthermore, it was established previously that in the case of meditation (*upāsanā*), there is qualification for one who has ascended to such a stage [and not for one merely desiring to ascend].
For initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed meditation (*upāsanā*); how then could there be a requirement for such a qualification even here?

And as for the statement that initiation is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to meditation—the wise man [is one who] has performed what is merely a restatement of a matter established by the maxim: "He who is qualified for the principal [rite] is [automatically] qualified for its subsidiary"—this is simply a reiteration of that point.

That [proposed] resolution is not satisfying, because the reiteration would result in futility due to the absence of a fruit, and because initiation possesses its own independent fruit and is therefore not a subordinate member (*anaṅga*). By this very [reasoning], p.

The eligibility for initiation (dīkṣā) is prescribed for one who has ascended to such a stage [of a seeker of liberation, according to the commentary]. As will be stated later, only one who has been initiated is eligible for spiritual practice (upāsanā). This being the case, the state of having ascended to the aforementioned stages is implied within spiritual practice [i.e., the state of being a seeker of liberation].
An Exposition of the Nature of Initiation (*dīkṣā*) and its Fruit:

Now, what is the nature of initiation? It cannot be defined as "an action that generates fitness for meditation," because there is no evidence for the existence of such a generative capacity. Certainly, perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not apply here, as [initiation] is a transcendental (*alaukika*) matter.

Nor can it be established through inference, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*). Nor is there a scriptural statement (*śruti*) such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," from which its status as a cause could be determined.
Furthermore, just as the twice-born lack eligibility for all ritual acts without initiation (*upanayana*), so too here [there is no eligibility] without that.

"O descendant of Bhṛgu, [one should perform] initiation"—thus, because the *Tripurārahasya* establishes that the causal relationship is rooted in negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), just as "in the absence of a staff, there is the absence of a jar," one might argue that the causal relationship is thereby proven.

However, this must be stated [as a refutation]: because the passage "the initiated person should practice meditation" is merely a praise (*stāvaka*) of the qualification for the practice of meditation (*upāsanādhikārin*).

If it is asked, "What then is the fruit of initiation (dīkṣā)?"—it is said: it is the destruction of that impurity in the form of sin accumulated over infinite millions of births. As it has been stated in the *Tantrāloka*—specifically in its commentary on the *Niśāṭana*, which is the [commentary] on the *Tantrāloka*—[the following is found]: (Note: The bracketed portion clarifies that the *Niśāṭana* is the name of the commentary on the *Tantrāloka*.)
Even when the internal knowledge consisting of the human principle has dissolved through initiation,
conceptual construction may still arise, because that which resides in the intellect has not yet ceased.
Liberation occurs only at the end of the body through the destruction of human ignorance;
however, upon the cessation of intellectual ignorance, it is certain due to the uprooting of conceptual construction.
"At that very moment liberation occurs," thus it was stated by the Creator in the venerable *Niśāṭana*.

The meaning of this is as follows: knowledge is twofold, namely, the spiritual (pauruṣa) and the intellectual (bauddha). Among these, spiritual knowledge consists of one's own essential nature (svasvarūpa). Intellectual knowledge is that which arises from the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), takes the form of the final mental modification (caramavṛtti), and is called the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). This [intellectual knowledge] also [removes] ignorance, which is of the nature of an obscuration.

It is of two kinds. Among these, the *pauruṣa* (personal) is the sin residing in the person; the *bauddha* (intellectual) is the notion of duality. In that regard, although the personal impurity is destroyed by initiation (*dīkṣā*), because the intellectual impurity is to be destroyed only by the knowledge of the scriptures, liberation occurs at that very moment upon the attainment of the knowledge of the established tenets (*siddhānta*) of the Āgama immediately following initiation—provided that [this occurs].

It is said that for him, knowledge of the scriptures was not acquired and only initiation occurred; yet at the end of his body, there is liberation. Nor should it be doubted how liberation occurs at the end of the body in the absence of the impurity of the intellect (*bauddhamala*), for the *Tripurārahasya* states:
"But those who possess initiation, having reached the world higher than the highest at the end of their bodies..."
They have been perfectly awakened by Sadāśiva, who is the very form of Śiva.
Thus, because such a doubt has been dispelled;

likewise, even in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the *agniṣṭoma* and other Vedic sacrifices, it is heard [in scripture]: "for the removal of evil" (*pāpmano 'pahatyai*).
Similarly, in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* as well, regarding the production of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) generated by the sacrifice through initiation, it is like the production of crops and so forth.
In the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*, it is established that [the practice] is like the plowing of a field, serving as a purifier of the self. (p. 45)

In the first chapter, there is also the sign that as soon as the five-syllable mantra entered the king's ear, infinite crows emerged from his body. Likewise, in the *Paramānandatantra*, in the etymological explanation of the term "initiation" (*dīkṣā*):
"Union with Śiva is bestowed (dīyate) and the bondage of the fetters is torn asunder (dīryate/kṣīyate);
therefore it is called initiation (dīkṣā).
Thus, in accordance with many such authorities, [the meaning of] the statement establishing negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is as follows:
Because it is of the nature of an explanatory passage (arthavāda), this definition would consequently be impossible.
If it is argued that, following the primary sense of the statement—"By this [work], in the *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*, the introduction to the twelfth chapter has been made;
now he asks for initiation (*dīkṣā*) which establishes her fitness for worship along with its ancillaries"—a justification is impossible, we say: no.
Because the very definition of being free from defects consists in having causal efficacy for the purpose of removing the impurities of human effort that serve as the means to liberation.

Nor should it be said that this investigation of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛtalakṣaṇa*) and the subsequent investigation into its purpose (*kaimarthyavicāra*), which depends upon the former, is like an examination of a crow’s teeth intended merely to display pedantry, because they are of no use for actual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
For there is indeed a distinction regarding performance: if [the injunction] generates the aforementioned capacity (*yogyatā*), then...

In the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for initiation, [the purpose is stated as] "for the sake of establishing fitness" according to one view, and "for the sake of the destruction of sin" according to the other view.

An investigation into the methods of the ritual resolve (*dīkṣā-saṃkalpa*). [From here follows the occasion for the disciple’s resolve to receive initiation and its investigation— furthermore, this is to be seen in the second chapter, section 10, verse 5, for the sake of knowledge concerning the object of all resolves.]
Furthermore, that which was written in the *Nityotsavanibandha*—
namely, "Desiring my own welfare, I shall receive initiation from such-and-such a guru for the purpose of acquiring such-and-such a vidyā"—
was written through extreme inattention. For instance, let alone the phrase "desiring welfare" (*śreyaskāma*).

For the destruction of sin is, in some sense, itself a form of spiritual welfare (*śreyaḥ*). As for the claim that [initiation] is "for the purpose of acquiring such-and-such a knowledge," that is utterly impure, because it has been established that initiation is the sole means for the destruction of sin.
Or, let us set aside the idea that it is for the purpose of acquiring knowledge—just like the son of a barren woman—nevertheless, one who desires spiritual welfare...

If that [result] were obtained by this very [means], then this word would be entirely redundant. Nor should it be argued that both the acquisition of knowledge and the attainment of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) are the results, and therefore both are mentioned; for although the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are the means to all results—as in the rule "the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* [is for] all [results]"—their distinct results arise only through a difference in performance (*prayoga*), not through a single performance.
The claim that there are two results is to be disregarded because it contradicts the logic established in the *Cāturthika* [section]. For this very reason, the *Tantraratna* states:
"In the world, it is observed that a single [cause] produces a single, fixed result of a specific kind through a single type of operation.

In that case, while the property of producing a single kind [of result] from all [causes] may be set aside by the scriptural statement, by what [authority] can its property of producing a single result be sublated?"

"Let it be refuted," said Pārthasārathi. Furthermore, the constituent element (padārtha) of initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists of the entry of power (*śakti*), the placement of steps (*caraṇavinyāsa*), and the instruction of mantras (*mantrōpadeśa*). Is it the performance of such an initiation that is the means to the fruit, or is it the undertaking of it? In the case of the first alternative (*saṃkalpa*):

In the first case, which means "I produce the action that serves as the means to the result," the phrase "I shall grasp the word denoting the action that serves as the means to the result" is redundant. In the second case, [the problem is] the status of grasping as the means.

[Otherwise, there would be] a rootless contradiction with previous statements. Furthermore, is the fruit of pronouncing "of such-and-such a guru" visible or invisible, like the pronunciation of the lunar day (tithi) and so forth? It cannot be the first [case], because apart from the manifestation of one's own will—namely, "May this person be my guru"—it is difficult to describe any other visible fruit; and that [visible fruit] occurs simply by the act of choosing him as written down.

What purpose could there be in pronouncing these? It cannot be the latter [that they produce a transcendental merit (*apūrva*)], because of the scriptural injunction stating that "having proclaimed the place and time," it is those [the names of the deities] that generate the *apūrva*. Indeed, there is no such statement as "having pronounced the names of the teachers" by which an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) might arise from them.

Furthermore, the desired result—consisting of the acquisition of the knowledge of the highest good—is inherent to oneself (*svaniṣṭha*). If that were the case, the use of the *parasmaipada* ending in "I shall grasp" (*grahīṣyāmi*) would contradict Pāṇini’s grammatical rule: "The *parasmaipada* is used when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent for roots marked with a svarita accent or the letter *ṇ*. Thus, because it is beset by many such defects, [the objection is invalid].
A mere intention (saṃkalpa) is to be disregarded; rather, for the sake of removing ignorance regarding human effort, the intention "I shall be initiated by means of the Śrīvidyā" alone is superior.

The enumeration of the eight limbs, which constitutes a part of the Tantric resolve (*saṃkalpa*), [this description of the eight limbs is not found in some source texts]. There is no enumeration of the eight limbs in the resolve for the disciple, because he lacks the qualification for Tantra due to his lack of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Hereafter...
In the teacher’s formal resolve (saṃkalpa), that mention is necessary; likewise, for the disciple as well, there must be a mention in the rite that occurs immediately after initiation.

If it is asked, "Since it is not mentioned in the *Aṣṭāṅga-sūtra*, why is it included here?"—this is true. Although there is no explicit mention [there], nevertheless, in all rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, a preliminary resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is observed as an invariable requirement. In the present case as well, such a resolve is likewise necessary. The necessity of the resolve is established in the root text.

The worship of Gaṇanāyaka is said to be even more extensive. What is called *saṃkalpa* is a formal resolve (*pratijñā*) concerning the performance of the rite at hand, preceded by the mention of the existing place and time, and accompanied by the mention of the fruit [to be attained]. As it is stated in the *Rahasyārṇava*:

"Uttering the name of the country where the practitioner resides, and marking that very place at that time, one should then form the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding the fruit of the rite, saying 'I [shall perform] this action' while extending the hand with water. Thus it is said.

In this context, because time— consisting of five components— is closely related [to the ritual] by way of the "maxim of accepting the horse" (*aśvapratigrahanyāya*) within the eightfold [formula], it is necessary for those who follow the Sūtras to mention the eightfold [formula]. Therefore,
the eightfold [formula] and the method of its accomplishment are now stated.

In that regard, the eight components are: 1) the yuga, 2) the parivṛtti, 3) the year, 4) the month, 5) the day, 6) the constant (nityā), 7) the weekday, and 8) the rising of the ghaṭikā. According to the Tantric scripture, there are 36 yugas in one [cycle], 36 parivṛttis in one yuga, 36 years in one parivṛtti, 16 months in one year, and 36 days in one month.
The constant [value] is 30, the days of the week are 9, and the rising of the ghaṭikās is 5. Thus, the means for the accomplishment of the eight limbs is described.
47) First, the method for calculating the Śaka era of Śālivāhana is stated:
28 (ibhākṣi), multiplied by 60 (ṣaṣṭi), equals 1680; this is then added to 38 (ibhāgny-aṅka).
Then, on the northern part of the Narmadā and its southern part, one should calculate [the distance] as forty-eight (48) units;
this is multiplied by sixty and divided by the "elephant-eyed" number (27).
One should further add the number of years elapsed since the Prabhava cycle;
this is declared to be the current Śālivāhana Śaka year.
The current enumeration of these qualities, beginning with power (prabhāva) and ending with the inexhaustible (akṣaya),
is recorded as being twenty-eightfold.

Having observed the number of the cycle from here and having understood it through its qualities, and knowing the Śaka year by means of sixty, this line of suspected syllables— “*na yatadīdṛśaśrīr me*”— indicates that the current Śālivāhana Śaka year is joined with 3179, the number of Nanda, mountain, eye, and fire (9271).

The elapsed Kali year count is as follows: in Śaka 1755, by adding this to 3179, the elapsed Kali year count is 4934. Having thus calculated the elapsed Kali year count, the method for determining the *ahargaṇa* (day-count) from it is performed.
Subtract 4897 from the number of elapsed Kali years;

whatever figure remains, ranging from one to ten, add that many sets of constant figures (dhruvaka) to the set of constants starting with viguṭī (vighaṭī) at the end of the day. In the case of a remainder of eleven:

One should add the pair of groups of ten and one from the first [cycle] to the *dhruvaka*. When twenty-one remains, one should add the first and the twentieth [groups] to the *dhruvaka*. In this manner, it should be understood for all numbers starting from thirty-one up to fifty-nine. The secret of that is as follows: when the number of elapsed Kali years is diminished by the product of seven, nine, four, and four, whatever remainder remains—
When that [number] is divided by sixty, if there are two remaining units at the time of writing,
then one should add a group of numbers equal in count to those [two] to the *dhruvaka*, and having divided [the result] by sixty,
one should add the quotient repeatedly above. That is the day-count (*ahargaṇa*) for the Aries transit (*meṣasaṃkrānti*) belonging to that year.

Thus, when the elapsed years of the Kali age, diminished by forty-nine, reach a point where there is no longer a remainder upon division by sixty— that is, when the elapsed Kali years are of such a number that sixty remains as the remainder when [the total] is less than ninety-three (729),
and the remainder after division by sixty is zero— then [there occurs] the "array of zero-figures" (śūnyāṅkajāla).
One should add it to the *dhruvaka*. That is the day-count (*ahargaṇa*) for the solar ingress (*saṃkrānti*) of Aries. They write down the numerical series to be added:
first, second, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, twentieth, thirtieth, fortieth, and fifty. [Fifty—]

This is not so; [it is said: "The net of fixed numbers is empty" refers to the nets of established doctrines (*siddhāntajālāni*). When the elapsed number of years of the *kalpa* is equal to the number represented by elephants (8), arrows (5), digits (9), and Vedas (4)—that is, 4958—then the number of years must be diminished by the number of mountains (7) and digits (9), i.e., 97. Then, whatever remains, when divided by sixty, the quotient obtained by that...

Having added that series of zeros multiplied [by the elapsed years] to the previous series of constant values (dhruvaka) and having corrected the constants, one should subsequently add the first series of digits as before and calculate the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated number of days). When the elapsed years of the Kali era are less than 844, there is no correction to the aforementioned constants.
Having thus calculated the group of days (ahargana), divide that total by nine; the remainder is the elapsed day, and the quotient obtained from it—(p. 48)—is [the number of completed cycles].

Divide that by four and set aside the quotient separately. Multiply the remainder by nine and add to it the number of elapsed cycles (*vāra*). This resulting number should be understood as the number of elapsed days.
Divide the previously set-aside quotient by sixteen; the remainder is the number of elapsed months. [The same applies to] the quotient obtained from that.

The remainder when divided by thirty-six is the number of elapsed years. That quotient increased by fifty and divided by thirty-six; the remainder is the number of elapsed revolutions, and the quotient is the number of elapsed yugas. Thus, when the day-count (ahargaṇa) corresponding to the time of the Aries transit has been calculated, thereafter, when [the mean position] is...

Sometimes, when there is a desire to calculate the *ahargaṇa* (the sum of days), the method for that is stated: therein, starting from Aries, on whichever day one desires the *ahargaṇa*, one should add to the *ahargaṇa* the number of that [day’s] transit (*saṃkrānti*)— which occurred immediately prior to that day— as will be described, and then starting from that transit...
One should add the number of days elapsed up to the desired day;

this becomes the *ahargaṇa* (day-count) for the desired day. Therein, from Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces, [one calculates] the subsequent [elements] ending with the *ghaṭikās* of the beginning of the Yuga.

The names are stated as follows: the names of the thirty-six years of the *yuga*-revolutions, corresponding sequentially to the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, should be understood as follows: first is the *yuga* consisting of the letter *a*, then *ayuga*, then *kayuga*;
likewise, this should be known for the subsequent *yuga*-revolutions among the years. [Then follow] the sixteen months.

The names [of the days] are, in sequence, the sixteen vowels. On the thirty-six days, the thirty-six letters from *a* to *kṣ*, together with the *anusvāra*, combined with the thirty-six tattvas beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, constitute the names in sequence. For example:

Regarding the phrase "the day of the Śiva-tattva": there are thirty phonemes, beginning with *a* and ending with the *anusvāra*, devoid of the final vowel (*au*), arranged in both direct and reverse order. There are fifteen Nityās, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā, which likewise total thirty when combined in both direct and reverse order. The names of these Nityās are as follows: *aṃ* Kāmeśvarī.

Regarding the phrase "in the eternal" (*nityāyām*): for the nine days (*vārāṇām*), there are nine syllables in sequence: *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, ṣa*. [These correspond to] Prakāśānandanātha, Vimarśānandanātha, Ānandānandanātha, Jñānānandanātha, Satyānandanātha, Pūrṇānandanātha, Svabhāvānandanātha, and so forth.

Pratibhānanda-nātha, Dattānanda-nātha, and Subhagānanda-nātha—these are the nine Nāthas. The nine vowels which are the [nine] days are the nine Nāthas joined with them, corresponding respectively to the nine days. For example: "Aṃ" is the day of Prakāśānanda-nātha.

The five syllables *a*, *e*, *ca*, *ta*, and *ya* should be known as the names of the five *udaya-ghaṭikās* in their respective order. Thus, the mention of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) is necessary at the beginning of Tantric rites and the like. Since the specific location is not mentioned in the Tantra, only that which is prescribed by Smṛti (traditional law) should be mentioned.
However, some tantrikas maintain that the eight-limbed [vow] is not *sahaja*, asserting instead a synthesis of the time well-known from the scriptures, stating:
"Having mentioned both place and time, one should likewise abide in the eight limbs. This is according to the *Paramānandatantra*.
That being so, in the phrase "place and time," what kind of time is intended? To fulfill this inquiry:
The eight-limbed path mentioned in the *Tantra* does not prescribe a synthesis [of all paths], due to the inherent force of the word "only" (*eva*).

Thus, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "I, belonging to such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), studying such-and-such recension (*śākhā*), and named such-and-such (beginning with *śarmā*), for the sake of attaining the fourfold aims of human life and for the sake of obtaining the grace of my desired deity, choose you— belonging to such-and-such lineage, studying such-and-such recension, and named such-and-such— as my preceptor (*guru*)."
What is the use of following the *Kalpasūtras*?
Whatever has been proclaimed— whether much or little— in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, when that much of the scriptural purpose has been performed, everything is considered performed.

Following this statement (p. 49), regarding whether this ritual application is performed by synthesizing all tantras or according to one's own preference without synthesizing other tantras: it cannot be the former, because the selection [of a specific tantra] is not mentioned in the Sūtra.

In the second [case], according to another tantra, it is improper to abandon the image, the selection of Brahmā and others, the preparation of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and its consumption. As for the third [position], it is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination and is simply untrustworthy. Furthermore, in another tantra—
"O Maheśvarī, for the sake of performing and causing the performance of the initiatory rite (*dīkṣākarma*),
I choose you as the Preceptor (*ācārya*)," [saying this] near her feet.

Thus, even when the act of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) is about to be performed, one should say simply, "I choose you as the preceptor" (*ācāryaṃ vṛṇe*); so he says. In all cases of choosing officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), whether in Śrauta or Smārta rites, the established practice is: "In this establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), I choose you as the Adhvaryu," or "In this rite called the Udyāpana, I choose you as my preceptor."

It is observed that here, however, having abandoned the term "karma" (action), it is written in the *varaṇavākya* that [the teacher acts] for the sake of accomplishing the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and for the sake of bestowing grace (*anugraha*). This is highly surprising. Therefore, those who follow the Sūtras should not perform the *varaṇa*. Nor, in the absence of *varaṇa*, by one who has not been chosen as a guru...

It must be stated how the ritual action (karman) is to be performed; for that [action] is possible even through a worldly invitation (varaṇa), such as saying, "Please bestow initiation upon me. Indeed, we do not reject the invitation in every respect; rather, we simply say that it is a constituent part of the ritual action.

In the same way, the *puṇyāhavācana* and the *nāndīśrāddha* are not to be performed [here], because they have not been mentioned. Nor can it be argued that there should be no inclusion of other ritual manuals (*tantrāntara*); nevertheless, the *puṇyāhavācana* and the *nāndīśrāddha*, being established by *smṛti*, are unavoidable. Otherwise, even the act of sipping water (*ācamana*), which is required by the rule "one should sip water after sneezing," would likewise not take place.
It should be stated that if the *puṇyāhavācana* and *nāndīśrāddha* prescribed in the Tantras are merely following those already established in the Smṛtis, then according to another Tantra:
"Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should pronounce the *puṇyāha* and worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors."

Thus, the injunction would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, this itself is the indicator that the ritual duties such as the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) prescribed in the *Smṛtis* do not enter as auxiliary elements of the rite. Furthermore, that which is for the sake of the person—such as "one should sip water after sneezing" and "one should not eat *kalañja*"—is already established and unavoidable.

Nor should it be said that, in this way, there would be no attainment even of the qualities characterized as disciple and teacher; for there is indeed an occasion for its attainment. In that regard, one should fulfill the expectancy by taking up even that which resides in another tantra, provided that without it the expectancy is not satisfied. Expectancy is a factor in verbal cognition.

There are two types: those that arise spontaneously (*utthita*) and those that must be elicited (*utthāpyā*). For example, when the first type occurs in the statement "He cooks," the questions "What does he cook?", "With what does he cook?", and "Who is cooking? arise spontaneously. In the second case, as in "He cooks a little," the question "How does he cook? must be elicited because of the fear that the word "a little" (*stoka*) would otherwise be redundant. In the first instance, [the expectation] arises by itself.

Since verbal expectancy (*śābdākāṅkṣā*) is not resolved without a word, it is necessary to supply a word either through *adhyāhāra* (mental insertion) or by taking one from another location in the text. In that case, rather than resorting to *adhyāhāra*, it is better to satisfy the expectancy with a word already present in another part of the same treatise. This being so, the wise person [who follows this—]

[Sūtra 31 on leaf 43: When it is stated that "one should initiate," since mere intelligence (*matimattva*) by itself does not serve as a differentiator, the inquiry necessarily arises: "What kind of intelligence [is required]?

Intelligence (*matimatva*) is defined as possessing the characteristics of a disciple as described in other tantras, which fulfills the expectation already raised. In this way, since the subsequent sūtra states, "the true guru (*sadguru*), having set in motion the sequence (*krama*)," [this definition] serves to fulfill the expectation of what constitutes "existence" (*sattva*). [Note: This [definition] also appears on page 53, line 34 of the following text.]

And the characteristics of the *guru* should also be applied. For this very reason, the teachers of the Baudhāyana school say: "One should not mix those together. Regarding this, Bhavasvāmin states that one belonging to a different *śākhā* should not mix those options mentioned in the *Śālikī-śākhā*; that is, one should not effect a combination within a single performance (*ekaprayoga*). [This applies] to the Brāhmaṇas.

Because of the multiplicity of Vedic branches, their infinity, and because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to summarize their entire meaning, the teachers composed the Kalpasūtras with the thought that people might attain all the fruits of ritual action by understanding and performing only that much which is easily comprehended.

The refutation of this [position] is found in that very same [work]: "Those stated without qualification and those stated with qualification are connected as supplementary elements (*śeṣatvena*). On this point, Bhavasvāmin says: "Those stated with qualification—namely, the specific qualities of what was stated in general—even if mentioned in other sūtras, are connected as supplementary elements (*śeṣatvena*), that is, as auxiliary members (*aṅgatvena*). Therefore, they are not mutually [contradictory].

An example of the term *saṃsādayet* (he should set down together) is as follows: according to Baudhāyana, there is the taking of the *vasatīvarī* waters alone for the purpose of pressing the Soma; however, in another Sūtra, there is a combination of both the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *ekadhānā* grains.
