Accordingly, when the *ekadhānā* grains are obtained by the followers of Baudhāyana, they should not [set them down] separately from one another.

"One should set them aside"—thus, according to Baudhāyana, only the mere cutting of the branch is mentioned. In another sūtra, both the cutting of the branch and its bringing forward are accompanied by mantras; yet even those he should not set aside.
Other examples may be cited along these lines. An example of an exception to this rule is as follows:

According to Baudhāyana, only a *palāśa* branch is prescribed for the *sānnāyya* offering; however, if such a branch cannot be obtained by those following his own *sūtra*, a *śamī* branch mentioned in another *sūtra* should be taken. In this regard, the root [of the argument] is that since there arises an expectancy as to what kind of branch should be taken when the aforementioned one is unavailable, another *sūtra* serves to fulfill that requirement.
[This is] the rule regarding the *śamī* branch. Thus, in the *Baudhāyana* [Śrautasūtra], it is prescribed without distinction: "He adds fuel to the fires.
When there arises a specific requirement as to how the adding of fuel (*anvādhāna*) is to be performed, [it is stated]:
"Having made a lap-space behind the *gārhapatya* fire," and "sitting with knees raised toward the *ānvāhāryapacana* fire."
[In this case, one might expect "the Adhvaryu" to be the subject. Thus, the ritual details mentioned in other Sūtras are fit to be connected as supplementary elements (*śeṣa*).
However, there is no such expectancy for the previously mentioned single *dhānā* (fried grain). Therefore, there is no combination (*samuccaya*).
By this, even those who follow this Sūtra [should not adopt] the three vessels or four vessels mentioned in other Tantras.

The statement that "the placing of the vessels is improper" is clearly incorrect. For if it were simply the case that one should place the vessels without any distinction, then a specific inquiry would arise as to how many vessels there are and how one should place them;
only then would there be the application of a scriptural rule intended as an exception to that general injunction. But such is not the case here.
By means of this, it would be so.

Therefore, in the *Nibandha*, for the sake of purifying the reality of both oneself and those present at the occasion, one should place a worldly water-pot (*kalaśa*) behind the Goddess and pour some consecrated substance into it.

Even that written record is baseless, because it describes the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) of only the remainder of the special *arghya* water—stating that "having offered the remnants of the oblation into the fire of consciousness together with the learned ones.

For this very reason, the teacher Baudhāyana, having stated that one should not cause a confusion of scriptures (*śāstra-saṅkara*), also spoke of the transgression incurred by causing such confusion: "He who, while abiding by his own scripture, acts according to another's scripture..."
"For him who disregards his own scripture, it is equal to the murder of a fetus. Thus [it is said].

Nor can it be argued that, although performance may not occur in the case of an indifferent act according to the manner previously stated, one must nevertheless perform every act for which there is much censure in another scripture upon its non-performance;
for in the section on curdling (*ātañcana*), having first censured the *kvala* fruit by stating, "That which is with *kvalas* is demonic" (*tadyatkvalaiḥ... rākṣasam*), [the text proceeds].

In another recensional branch (śākhā), it is prescribed: "He curdles [the milk] with curds" (*dadhnā'tanakti*). In yet another recensional branch, the curdling with *kvala* fruits is prescribed, as in: "The herbs, the *pūtika* plants, the *kvalas*. Similarly, there is much censure regarding the performance of the *patnīsaṃyāja* and the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings in the ancestral rite (*pitryā*).

It is heard in some places that the Baudhāyanas have not offered censure [against others]. Merely on that basis, disregarding the censure of others, the learned followers of Baudhāyana perform the *samiṣṭayajus* offering. Therefore, censure found in another treatise is ineffective.
And in the *Tripurārahasya* it is said:

"O Rāma, that action which is not mentioned in the Tantras, yet is indicated even in others, and is performed free from conceptual construction—that is [the true practice]. [Cited from the *Ḍāmarī*, A 1].
Therefore, it should be accepted from another source; this is the definitive conclusion of the treatise.

Thus, it must be stated that this [case] is one where there is an absence of conflict (*gativiraha*). When there is censure in another scripture for the non-performance of a rite, yet an option (*vikalpa*) is provided in one's own scripture, then the censure therein applies to that specific matter which is subject to censure in the other scripture; by that much alone, there is no loss of one's own scripture. For example, in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, there is a censure of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) within the context of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice.
In the Baudhāyana [tradition], no censure is expressed; rather, it is provided as an option alongside the *uttaravedi* by the general rule (*codakaśāstra*).

Since there is no deficiency even when one's own scripture prescribes the performance of the *uttaravedi*, the prohibition must also be respected—thus, either the *uttaravedi* alone should be performed, or the piling (*cayana*) [of the altar].

Likewise, here too, in such a situation, this statement is for the purpose of [prescribing] performance, not for the purpose of subverting the scripture that is heard as eternal. We shall explain another interpretation of this statement in detail in the section on Śrīvidyā.
Or let there be [the connection with the phrase "there is an abundance of fruit" found in the preceding commentary]:
O Maheśvarī, one should avoid whatever is prohibited in another Tantra,
because that is indeed a single scripture due to the unity of the mantra and the unity of the deity.
Therefore, one should avoid whatever is prohibited in one's own scripture;
however, one who is capable should incorporate other [practices] not mentioned in it that are [otherwise] independent.
However, as long as he performs other practices that are not contradictory to his own independent [tantra],
his prosperity will certainly increase even further;
moreover, he may indeed take whatever he desires from another [tradition].

According to the statements of other tantras, there is an abundance of merit when the recitation for a "meritorious day" (puṇyāhavācana) and other rites are combined; the secret is that there is no deficiency even if they are not performed. Furthermore, the addition of vessels, which contradicts one's own scripture, is indeed to be rejected, as will be seen from the words of the tantras written below.

[In the section on the preparation of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*) within the *Śrīkramīya*— the work consisting of thirty-one sections following the name *Agra-nāmāgāminī*— at the end of the commentary on the thirty-first sūtra: because there is a possibility of application according to the method to be described, and because there is not even a trace of inconsistency, that which has been indicated and required for the general ritual action (*karmasāmānya*) in a single performance [is here applied].
And the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that that which possesses an invariable relation must be apprehended from one thing and not from another;
we shall clarify this in detail later.
And thus, the person who, having synthesized all systems, has determined the full extent of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)—

One who is capable of performing [the rite] after having accomplished the single uniform procedure and composed the ritual manual (prayoga-vidhi) will certainly attain a greater degree of spiritual merit from such an action of the Omniscient One. However, one who is incapable of this may take only the essential elements, such as the desired results and so forth, from another tantra.

One will certainly achieve one's purpose through the practice of one's own scripture alone; however, it is not appropriate to apply the "half-old-woman" logic (*ardhajaratīya-nyāya*)—that is, to include certain elements from other systems while excluding others. The author of the commentary, failing to perceive even a scent of this logic, arbitrarily includes some [elements] while excluding others.
One who abandons [this] should be considered a "beloved of the gods" (devānāmpriya); enough, then, with excessive deliberation.

By the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*)—[it should be understood that this refers to the word *sarvathā* found in the thirty-first sūtra of this very section]—it is indicated that without initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is no absolute liberation. In this regard, the clear scriptural authority from the *Tripurārahasya* has already been cited previously. || 31 ||

Having thus prescribed the three initiations (*dīkṣā*), [the author] first divides them among those which possess internal subdivisions in order to establish their connection with a single time, and demonstrates the property that serves as the basis for that division. Among them...
It prescribes a quality consisting of a simultaneous connection with all three as well:
"There are three initiations—Śāktī, Śāmbhavī, and Māntrī.
Among these, the Śāktī [initiation] is from the entry of power (śakti), and the Śāmbhavī is from the placement of the feet.
The Mantra-practitioner should perform all [these rites] by means of the mantra as it has been taught. || 32 ||

By the end of the word "cetī" (and so forth), having made a distinction, there is the naming of those [powers]. Among them, he explains the meaning of the term "śāktī" as "from the entry of power" (*śaktipraveśanāt*); the word "born" (*jātā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Alternatively, in the phrase "from the entry of power," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
(53) The initiation (*dīkṣā*) beginning with the entry of the power (*śakti-praveśana*) means that it has the entry of the power as its cause. The same applies further on.

In the term "praveśanādi," the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in its own sense (denoting the action itself). As for what is called "the entry of the power" (*śakti-praveśana*), [it is explained] further on [at this very point].

This refers to the meaning of the two sūtras [35–36] in the *Dīkṣāvidhi*. The ritual action described beginning with "washed with that nectar" and ending with "having burnt the bonds" is called the "placement of the feet. This consists of the guru’s visualization of the red and white feet of Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara upon the head of the disciple.

The instruction of the mantra (*mantropadeśa*), however, is clearly defined as the utterance of sound by the Guru, intended solely for the hearing of the disciple. All [these acts] are those previously mentioned. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the three," their connection to a single time is indicated. The word "and" (*ca*)...

This term denotes simultaneity (*sāhitya*), and *sāhitya* consists in being connected at one and the same time. Thus, the resultant meaning is that one should perform all the initiations (*dīkṣās*) together. || 32 ||
He states the opinion of others: "Some say one by one. (33)

By the repetition [of the term], it is indicated that there is a conjunction of the three [periods] and merely a difference in time. By the word "or" (vā), it is suggested that a long interval of time should be observed in the middle, and not merely three days. || 33 ||
From here on,

he describes the procedure performed by the Guru: "The true Guru, having initiated the sequence with all its limbs and offered oblations while filled with youthful exuberance, calls the disciple and binds his face with a cloth."
Having sprinkled him with drops from the vessels of Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā, Vārtālī, Parā, and Pātra, and having caused him to hear the Siddhānta; || 34 ||
Having commenced and performed the ritual sequence together with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*)—that is, along with its constituent parts—the worship of the principal deity;

here, the ancillaries (*aṅgāni*) are Gaṇapati, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī, while the principal (*pradhāna*) is Lalitā. In this context, by the word "ancillary" (*aṅga*), the sequence of ancillaries (*aṅgakrama*) is indicated; the meaning is: the sequence of the principal [deity] together with the sequence of the ancillaries.
If it be asked, "How is this known?", listen: at the very beginning of this second section— in the first sūtra of the second section, which begins with "Thus, 'Being'..."—
it is stated that one who has received initiation from a true guru [should worship Gāṇanāyakī] for the removal of obstacles to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā.

Regarding the instruction "one should contemplate the manual," that which is performed for the removal of obstacles is seen in the world to be the primary [auxiliary] (*aṅga*). For example, when someone intent on an audience with a king is stopped midway by gatekeepers, the act of waiting upon them becomes an auxiliary to the audience with the king. And this is not so for every living being.

It should not be argued that this statement is redundant because the worship of Gaṇapati is already established even for every ritual action for the purpose of removing obstacles— based on the proclamation from the bell that "Gaṇapati is the destroyer of obstacles" due to the presence of the suspicion of impediments— since [the same result] could also be achieved by the recitation of the Vināyaka-stava.

In some places, because the destruction of obstacles is taught, when the worship [of Gaṇapati] is presented as an alternative, there arises a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that the removal of obstacles to the practice of the Śrīvidyā must be accomplished by this alone. Likewise, at the beginning of the third section, it says: "Having thus worshipped Gaṇapati, with all disturbances of obstacles dispelled..."

By the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) in the phrase "one should begin the sequence of Śrī Lalitā, the sole sovereign of the wheel of powers" (p. 54), it is understood just as in the expression: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī."

The status of Lalitā-worship as an ancillary (*aṅga*) is clear. Nor does it follow that, just as in the sentence "having piled the fire-altar" (*agniṃ citvā*), the preceding rite is primary and the subsequent rite is ancillary, so too here the subsequently performed Lalitā-worship would become an ancillary to the propitiation of Gaṇapati.

It should not be said that the priority of the preceding act of piling (cayana) is determined solely by the suffix -ktvā; rather, the primacy of the piling belongs to it because it possesses a fruit, as seen in the injunctions "one desiring offspring should pile" and "one desiring cattle should pile. In its proximity, the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice—which lacks a fruit—is subordinate, according to the principle that "that which lacks a fruit is subordinate when in proximity to that which possesses a fruit."

By the principle of "being a part of that" (*tadaṅgam*), it constitutes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Likewise, since the worship of Lalitā is heard in scripture to have liberation as its fruit, it is established that the very fruit which belongs to the worship of Śrī Lalitā through the medium of the worship of Vighna is itself the fruit of this [worship], and thus it possesses the status of an auxiliary. For this very reason, [it is said]: "Having performed the Vāravantīya Sāman upon the Revatī verses..."
In the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with this," the *vāravantīya* chant is not the primary element. Nor should it be argued:

"Why could this not simply be an injunction of mere temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*), like the rule 'Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma'? For in that case, by the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma," the Soma sacrifice [is established] in relation to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Since [the rites] have already been produced by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings, those sentences merely enjoin the sequence; however, in the present case, because there is no other sentence for the production of the Lalitā sequence, it enjoins an action qualified by that sequence. Furthermore, since in that [other case] both possess independent fruits, whereas here such is not the case, [the injunction does not apply].
It is merely a prescription for the sequence, nor is there any loss of the relationship between the primary and its subsidiaries.
By this, the objection that "having worshipped the Saṅgītamātṛkā in this manner, one should duly serve Kolamukhī"—
that both [the goddesses] would fall into a state of mutual relationship as limb and possessor of limbs— is also refuted.
Because it has the form of the fruit consisting in the sight of the king, there is no independent fruit [of its own].

And it should not be argued that this being the case, there would be the necessity of repeating [the rite] with every performance, as in the case of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice; for we do not say that it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the primary rites (*pradhāna*), but rather that it is an auxiliary to the commencement of the Lalitākrama, like the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice. For this very reason, it is heard in that scriptural statement: "One should commence the Lalitākrama."

The very resolve, "I shall bring about a sequence connected to a moment that is not the locus for the destruction of the act of worship performed by myself," is the meaning of the term *ārambha* (commencement). This occurs only once; therefore, there is no possibility of its repetition.

By this, even the doubt that the meditation on Gaṇeśa in the heart-lotus as an ancillary to the worship of Gaṇapati during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, and the meditation on Lalitā [during the same time], both occurring at one and the same time, would be contradictory, is also dispelled.
Thus, Śyāmā’s status as a limb [of the Goddess] is established in the *Śyāmopāstikhaṇḍa*;

her position as the chief minister is indicated by the term "Śyāmā"; and the status of Kolamukhī as the commander-in-chief and that of Parā as the sovereign queen are established in the section on their worship by the terms "mahārājñyāḥ" and "daṇḍanāyikāsthānīyā" respectively.
And by the phrase "the heart of the Lion-throne vidyā," this is made perfectly clear.
Therefore, these are the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*). The meaning that results is that one should arrange the sequence of the principal deity together with their sequence.
55) Although these may be designated by the term "limbs" (*aṅga*) as subordinate deities within the worship of the principal deity,
in the present worship all five— [here, by the word "five," Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā,]...

The pentad beginning with Vārtālī is to be understood as consisting of [these five]. They are equally primary. Elsewhere, having accepted their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) established in other contexts, and having indicated Gaṇapati and the others in that very form, the word "together" (*saha*) merely enjoins the performance of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for all of them simultaneously. When such a *tantra* exists, the sequence of deities follows the sequence of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) alone.

The entire collection of subsidiaries (*aṅgakalāpa*) that will be described hereafter is obtained through extension (*atideśa*). Among those subsidiaries, for those whose simultaneous performance (*tantra*) is possible, they are performed in that very manner; for those whose contradictory properties do not permit it, they are performed according to the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*). This...
The definitions of *padārthānusamaya* (performance by items) and *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performance by sections) are to be seen in the eighth topic of the *Pariśiṣṭa*.
For those cases where *padārthānusamaya* is not possible, one should proceed by *kāṇḍānusamaya*.
A wise person should apply these rules as appropriate; however, they are not written here for fear of excessive length in this book.
[The phrase "gradually" (*kramaṃ kramaṃ pravartya*), etc., is the word found on folio 53, following the *sūtra* located on folio 34.

By the very word "having set in motion" (*pravartya*), the performance of the *homa* is already obtained; however, the statement "having offered the oblation" (*hutvā*)—which is also to be seen below—is for the purpose of establishing that the time subsequent to the *homa* constitutes a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the summoning of the disciple.

Although, since the *homa* is optional at the time of the sequence ahead, it could have been stated as "having offered" (*hutvā*) even here—given that it is obtained optionally in this case as well—in order to indicate its necessity; nevertheless, because of the statement ahead: "having sprinkled him with the drops from the vessels of Gaṇapati, Lalitā, Śyāmā, Vārtālī, and Parā."

It is established that there is no completion of the sequence [of rites]. In that case, since there is an expectation regarding the time—namely, "When should the summoning of the disciple be performed?"—it is appropriate to prescribe that [time] alone, rather than prescribing both [the time and the act], because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Even in the alternative where the *homa* is not performed, [the time is defined by] being subsequent to the time indicated by it.
This is like the expression "the new moon day occurs with the calves.

By this, the statement in the *Nibandha*—"having summoned the disciple at the end of the dismissal of the special vessels"—is refuted; for since all [the offerings] have been removed from the special *arghya* vessels, there is no remainder of them.
Furthermore, it is contrary to the context of one's own manual to suggest that he should sprinkle him with drops of water from the general *arghya* vessel common to the five vessels.

In reality, however, the natural meaning of "having offered" (*hutvā*) is "having offered the remainder of the oblation into one's own self. For this very reason, the natural meaning of what will be stated later—"possessing the fresh radiance (*taruṇollāsa*) produced by such an offering"—is that "fresh radiance" (*taruṇollāsa*) is a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*). An explanation of this is provided in the commentary on the *Caraṇakhaṇḍa*.
This is clear [as indicated somewhat in Sūtra 82 of Chapter 10 and somewhat in Sūtra 18 of Chapter 18].

By the phrase "having summoned the disciple," it is indicated that until that point, the disciple has no entry into the interior. Having uttered the disciple's name in the vocative case, one should say, "Come. Just as the summoning of the cows in the Pravargya rite is an integral part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), so too is this an integral part of the ritual. Therefore, regarding the matter of his arrival, [one should not employ] any other means.
The meaning is that one should not reveal one's own intention.

By this, the statement in the *Nibandha*— that immediately after the selection (*varaṇa*), the teacher, together with his disciple, should at that very moment go to a secluded place for initiation— is refuted, because it is impossible to summon a disciple who is standing nearby, nor is [the selection] for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
It should be stated that it is an invocation, because when a perceptible cause is possible, it is improper to postulate an imperceptible one.
The remainder is clear.

Here, by the word "vessel" (*pātra*), the vessel for the special *arghya* offering is to be understood—specifically, the word "vessel" found in the phrase "by the drops from the vessel" (*pātrabindubhiḥ*) located in Sūtra 34, which follows [Sūtra] 53. If it is asked how this is so, it is as follows: if it were merely the general *arghya* vessel, then its...
Since the accomplishment of the tantra is like that of the *praṇītā* water, and because that [water] is one for all [participants], it would have been formulated as a concise rule:
"with drops from the general *arghya*. Nor is there a possibility of a concise rule such as "with drops from the vessels of special *arghya*" even in your own position.
It should not be argued that the effort [involved] in [the formula] "Gaṇapatilalita" and so forth is useless;

for if that were the case, since the plurality denoting the number to be enjoined would, by the principle of the *kapiñjala* section, terminate at three, there would be no obtaining of five vessels at all. Nor is this so even then.

It should not be said that the *laghusūtra* (short aphorism) "with five special *arghya* vessels" is possible; for we do not teach the addition or omission of syllables in a *sūtra* as a reason [for its validity]. Rather, in the case of the general *arghya*, because it is singular, the phrase "up to the end of *parā*" would be redundant. However, in the case of the special *arghya*...
The phrase "for the sake of obtaining five bowls" is meaningful; moreover, an excess of syllables cannot be restricted in the case of independent compositions.

In reality, however, there is no *tantra* (common procedure) for the general vessel (*sāmānyapātra*), because the consecration of the general *arghya* in [rites for] Gaṇapati, Lalitā, and others does not possess a single uniform form; and since a common procedure is impossible between two distinct sets of ritual characteristics (*dharma*). Nor can it be asked: "How can there be a *tantra* for principal rites that possess distinct characteristics?"
This is to be doubted. *Tantra* refers to the simultaneous performance of principal rites, not merely their single performance.

Here, however, a single performance is stated, which is indeed improper; for simultaneous performance certainly does occur. Therefore, this is not an indicator for the taking of the special *arghya* by means of the word "vessel" (*pātra*), but rather [it applies] after having offered.

Having stated "possessing youthful radiance," it is subsequently said "with the drops from the vessel" (*pātrabindubhiḥ*); therefore, by the word *pātra*, that substance which has become the means for the *homa* is indicated as being present in the mind, and not the ordinary *arghya* substance which is not so intended. Furthermore, for the Tantrikas, the word *bindu* refers primarily to the principal substance.

She is established by convention as "satisfied by the libation of the *bindu*," according to the usage in the *Lalitāsahasranāma*. For this very reason, the word *bindu* itself is also indicative [of her]. And thus, this is precisely the indicator for the taking of the special *arghya*.

Having sprinkled and consecrated that disciple, [the teacher performs this rite]; because it consists of the purification of the disciple, it is the duty of the guru. The remainder is easy to understand.
By this [statement], the line in the *Nibandha* which says, "reciting the root mantra,

he should sprinkle him with drops of water from the general *arghya* of the five vessels," is entirely baseless and imagined by the author's own fancy, because it prescribes reciting the root mantra where none was required.

Having caused [the disciple] to hear the *siddhānta*— that is, the collection of sentences that set forth the *siddhānta*, referred to by the term "previously mentioned" [which means the sentences concerning knowledge, training, and so forth, stated from the third *anugata*-sūtra up to the end of the thirty-first sūtra]— this causing to hear is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), just like the rule "he makes [the disciple] recite the *kḷpti* formulas."
It is not for the sake of understanding the meaning, because it is impossible to comprehend such an exceedingly profound subject within that much time.

Therefore, the previously mentioned statements— [by the term "previously mentioned," the meaning is the statements concerning the training in knowledge (*jñānaśikṣā*) and so forth, as taught from the third sūtra up to the thirty-first sūtra].
One should cause [the disciple] to hear [this] by way of its being the generator of the apūrva that acts as an auxiliary to the apūrva of initiation (dīkṣā). || 34 ||
(p. 57) Śāmbhavī Initiation.
Now he describes the Śāmbhavī initiation:
having meditated upon his head as having red and white feet, [one should contemplate it] as washed by that nectar.
One should adorn the entire body. || 35 ||

"Upon her head" means upon the head of the disciple. "Red and white feet": red, because Kāmeśvarī is of the nature of *rajas*. As it has been said: "One should meditate on the Supreme Mother as having red feet.
This is also stated in the *Śyāmārahasya*:
"The red foot of the Goddess is proclaimed to be the nature of *rajas*, while the white foot that supports it is of the nature of *sattva*. Thus [it is said].

By this, the white practice (*śuklacaraṇa*) is also explained. There is a singular compound because it consists of parts of living beings. Having meditated upon—that is, having contemplated—that nectar, he whose every sin has been washed away or destroyed by that nectar, which is the water associated with the feet; such a disciple he should make—this is the meaning.

Although the performance of the act by the student—the referent of the other word—is not possible, nevertheless, according to the maxim that "when a prescription or prohibition applies to something qualified, if it is obstructed in the qualified object, it transfers to the qualifier," the performance of the destruction of sin—which is the qualification of the student—is indeed possible; such is the sense. Of him, everything...
The Guru should adorn and decorate the body with perfumes, garments, ornaments, flowers, and so forth;
this is the Śākta initiation.
He now describes the Śākta initiation:
Having meditated upon that surging wave of light, blazing like a flaming fire, extending from its base up to the cavity of Brahmā, one burns away his bonds of sin with its rays. || 36 ||
The "root" (*mūla*) of that disciple refers to the location of the four-petalled lotus situated between the anus and the genitals, which serves as the support;
"up to the root" (*āmūlam*) means up to that limit. Having thus described the lower limit, he states the upper limit:
"up to the aperture of Brahma" (*ābrahmabilaṃ*), meaning up to that which has the aperture of Brahma—the thousand-petalled lotus serving as its support—as its boundary.

Having meditated upon consciousness—of which the remainder of the sentence is "consciousness"—as being blazing, and therefore possessing waves (laharī) of light, and thus resembling fire (anala) endowed with flames;
for it is precisely because of this resemblance to blazing fire that its capacity to burn the bonds of sin is logically established. [The burning of the bonds of sin...]
Thus there is no cultivation; for this very reason, it says "having burned."

Although it appears that, following the order of the text here, Śāmbhavī comes first and then Śāktī, nevertheless, because it was stated at the beginning, at the time of the division of initiations (*dīkṣā*), that they are "Śāktī, Śāmbhavī, and Māntrī," the conclusion must be interpreted otherwise in accordance with the beginning.

By the principle of the section beginning with "The Veda" (*vedopakramādhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, immediately after the burning of those bonds, [there is the removal] of that impurity in the form of their ashes.
Because it is logical that the water emerging from the feet serves the purpose of washing [the disciple], the sequence of purpose (*arthakrama*) is also established.
Thus, it is proven that one should first accomplish the *śāktī* initiation and afterwards perform the *śāmbhavī*.

Some maintain that the collection of subsidiary elements (aṅgakalāpa), beginning with "The Guru, having initiated the sequence" and ending with "having caused [the disciple] to hear the Siddhānta," belongs to these two [initiations] alone by virtue of both context (prakaraṇa) and proximity (sannidhi), just as the mantra for purification belongs to the Sānnāyya offering. That is not correct; for if that were the case, then in the third initiation—later on...

The injunction that "having caused [the sacrificer] to swallow the first sprinkled portions from the tips of the second segments" is untenable; for since the rule prescribes a specific sequence for the constituent parts (*aṅga*), and because there is no such sequence applicable there when they are not constituent parts, the categories of "first" and "second" do not exist. Furthermore, it is impossible to take what is unrefined and merely worldly (*laukika*).

Therefore, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the proximity (*sannidhi*) is set aside, and [the mantra] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for all three. And thus, when one follows the alternative that [one may recite] each one individually, then at the third initiation the previously mentioned auxiliaries are to be performed;
by this, through the flowing of nectar (*amṛta-kṣaraṇa*), one should remove both external and internal impurity (*mala*). Now...

The second occurrence of the statement "one should burn his bonds with its rays" (meaning: with the rays of that wave of light) has been written down and refuted, starting from the passage "from the *mūlādhāra* of the disciple," because since the external and internal impurities have already been removed by the previous initiation (*pūrvadīkṣā*), there is an absence of such impurity in this case.

Furthermore, because burning is impossible through the higher initiation (*uttaradīkṣā*). Nor should it be argued that the impurity (*mala*) removed by the previous initiation remains outside and is burned by the higher initiation; for fire manifested within the body can only destroy the impurity residing in the body, not that which has been cast outside. Therefore, our own tradition alone is correct.
"We perceive that it is right [to say], 'Excellent! || 36 ||
He begins to explain the application of the mantra-initiation (māntrī-dīkṣā):
[1] the three pungents (trikaṭu), [2] the three myrobalans (triphalā), [3] the four spices (caturjāta), [4] kakkola, [5] madayantī, [6] sahadevī, and dūrvā grass.

[7] Ashes, [8] clay, [9] sandalwood, [10] saffron, [11] gorocanā, [12] camphor, and [13] scented water— having filled a new pitcher with these, wrapped it in a pair of cloths (*navīnavāsas*), worshipped it with the *bālā-ṣaḍaṅga* mantra, and placed therein the maṇḍalas of Śrī Śyāmā and Vārtālī;

Having worshipped with the three enclosure mantras and protected with the weapon mantra, one should display the cow and the womb mudrās— [the second appendix, topic 15, concerning the knowledge of the extraction of many mudrās such as the cow, the womb, and so forth, is to be seen as an independent work]. || 37 ||

The three pungents (*trikaṭu*) are long pepper (*pippalī*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and black pepper (*marīca*). The three myrobalans (*triphalā*) are yellow myrobalan (*harītakī*), emblic myrobalan (*dhātrī*), and beleric myrobalan (*vibhītaka*).
As it is stated in the *Vaidyasāra*:
"Dry ginger, black pepper, and long pepper are declared to be designated as the three pungents."
"Triphalā is defined as the combination of pathyā, dhātrī, and vibhītaka. Thus it is said.
The "four-fold" consists of uśīra, elā, lavaṅga, and nāgakeśara. As it is stated in the *Madanamahārṇava* (p.
"Lavaṅga, elā, and uśīra are proclaimed as the 'three fragrances' (*trisugandha*)."
They declare that the "fourfold aromatic" (caturjāta) is combined with *nāgakeśara*. Thus it is said.

*Takkola*— well known in the Gurjara country by the name *Cinīkabālā* (and here the word *kaṅkola* should generally be understood)— is a specific substance resembling black pepper, to be consumed with betel leaf as a remedy for coldness.
Madayantī and sahadevī are well-known in medical science as wild plants; dūrvā, ashes, and earth are well-known [substances].

As for the inclusion of "seven clods of earth" (*saptamṛttikā*) under the term *mṛttikā* in the *Nibandha*, that is without foundation. If the term *mṛttikā* were everywhere intended to mean seven clods of earth, then the explicit mention of "seven" in the passage from the *Mūlanakṣatra-janana-śānti*—
namely, "joined with seven clods of earth and combined with five sprouts"— would be redundant.
Likewise, there would also be the same consequence in the case of the rule: "One should thus fetch earth for the purpose of bathing."

The phrase "yuktaṃ etaiḥ" (joined with these) is a *madhyamapadalopa* compound [meaning "joined with water"] because it is impossible for [the word] "vāsitaṃ" (scented/perfumed) to be construed with *dūrvā* and the other items. *Candana* is well known. *Kuṅkuma* is from Kashmir. *Rocanā* is *gorocana*. *Karpūra* is well known. By that water which has been perfumed with these— [End of sentence fragment]

A new, unused water-pot, wrapped in a pair of cloths, [should be consecrated] with the six-limbed ritual of Bālā [for the sake of knowing the extraction of the mantras of the deities, the application of the six limbs of the Śrī Bālā Tryakṣarī mantra, and its ṛṣis, meters, and subject matter; see Appendix 2, Section 9]. Aiṃ.
"Salutation to the heart"—thus, by repeating the three seed-syllables twice in sequence;

[regarding the procedure for performing the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) without the specific mention of the mantra for each limb, it is to be understood that this is found in the nineteenth Sūtra and its commentary in the *Śrīkrama* of the third section; however, the direct [textual evidence] is at Dvi-pa-śi. 9].

It exists in the [respective] locations. According to the method to be described, [one should place them] in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest corners, as well as in the directions starting from the east in the center, respectively. Here, by the name "six limbs" (ṣaḍaṅga), there is an extension of the aforementioned attributes. The meaning is that one should cast down—that is, install—the wheels of Śrī, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī.

When there is an expectation as to *where*, it must be in the water-jar (*kalaśa*) itself because of its proximity. Even there, by the force of the natural sense of the word, it is not to be placed upon a full vessel or similar object; rather, it is in the water [here, it should be understood that "in the water" means specifically in the water contained within the jar].

Although it could be argued that, since the specific location for the extraction has not been stated and by virtue of its inherent suitability, one might say "in the vicinity of the jar," nevertheless—

because worship on the ground is impossible without the installation of the *cakra*, and because such installation is thus obtained either through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) or by extension (*atideśa*)— it is already established and therefore [the specific location need not be stated].
Out of fear that the word "having thrown" would otherwise be redundant, the act of casting [the substance] into water is necessary.

Nor should it be said that its placement is not restricted to any particular location— since it would follow by implication (*arthāpatti*) and so forth— that it must be in the space near the jar; for there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating the jar itself as the locus rather than the space near the jar.

Furthermore, the worship of the wheel situated near the jar cannot be considered a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the jar, because it is not connected to it. Here, the consecration of the jar consists in first worshipping it with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*);
likewise, the sequence beginning with "protecting it with the *astra*" [is also part of that]. How can it be [considered such] when it is sandwiched between both?

That [offering] would be of a different nature, distinct from its consecration. Therefore, the casting of the wheels occurs in water alone; therein lies the worship, and the casting into the water takes place at the very moment the worship begins. Consequently, there is no room for the doubt as to how the wheels can be moved after the invocation (*āvāhana*).

Alternatively, the statement "having cast [the deity] into the vase" must be understood as an exception to the rule that one should not move [the deity] until the final dismissal (*visarjana*). This interpretation alone is logical; otherwise, the sequential ritual procedure along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) [would be disrupted].
Immediately after the word *nirvartya*, one should say "having cast it into the jar.
Regarding the three [deities], *Lalitā* and the others—these three goddesses, *Śrīlalitā*, *Śyāmā*, and *Vārtālī*, as mentioned in Sūtra 53 on page 34 of the *Anugata*:
thus they are to be understood. Of these, *Lalitā* and the others...
By the phrase "with the *āvaraṇa* mantras," there is an exclusion of the mere five-fold offering (*pañcopacāra-pūjā*). "Having worshipped" means having performed the ritual adoration.
This unprecedented worship is prescribed by this [text]. Following the worship, the extraction (*uddharaṇa*) follows as a matter of course.

However, the worship itself is performed with *kula*-substances alone—specifically those contained in the respective special *arghya* vessels—as well as with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), because only the performance of this unprecedented worship is enjoined. Having performed only that much, the extraction of the wheel (*cakroddharaṇa*) should be carried out.
The placement of scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) upon wheels that have been lifted out of water is established by logical necessity.
Having protected [the area] with the mantra "phaṭ"—[this being for the purpose of the weapon-mudrā (*astra-mudrā*) and the *dhenu-yoni-mudrā* situated before it; see Dvi-pa. Śi.
15.7/14, 15.8/1–2, 15.8/2]—and having rendered it unassailable by *rakṣas*, spirits, and *piśācas*, one should employ the well-known *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās.
Having displayed it, one should place it upon that. || 37 ||
Regarding the Mātṛkā Yantra, he says [the procedure for it immediately following that]:
"O Śrī, [it is] a golden pericarp joined with Śiva, with eight filaments provided with pairs of vowels."

In the Mātṛkāyantra, which consists of eight petals joined with the eight groups of letters beginning with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa* situated in the eight directions, and the syllables *ṭhaṃ* and *vaṃ* in the square,
[this Mātṛkā-cakra would become well-known by consulting the commentary below]. [The disciple...]
Having placed [the image] therein, one should bathe it with the water from that jar using the three vidyās. || 38 ||

Śiva is the letter *ha*; joined with that is the golden letter *sau*. That [letter] is in the pericarp, which is the central region of the lotus. Here, the *visarga* should also be added above the previously mentioned letters, because the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda stated: "The pericarp consists of the letters of space (*vyoma*), the moon (*indu*), water (*au*), and the tongue (*rasanā*). (Thus...)

It should be understood that [the seed-syllables] are produced as *ca*, *ha*, *sa*, and *auḥ*. All these are qualifiers of the lotus (*kamala*). The vowels are sixteen, beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga; their "pairing" (*dvandva*) means two by two.

By that [pairing], it is "endowed" (*juṣṭa*), meaning joined, with an "eightfold filament" (*kiñjalkāṣṭaka*), which refers to specific locations situated between pairs of petals—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

"Kaśca, caśca, ṭaśca, taśca, paśca, yaśca, śaśca, laśca"—this is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. According to the grammatical maxim that "a word heard at the end of a *dvandva* is connected with each member individually," the term "class" (*varga*) is connected with all [the preceding consonants]. Thus, beginning from the *ka*-class...
(61) There are five letters each up to the *pavarga*, four letters in the *yavarga*, and likewise the *śavarga*;
the *lavarga* consists of the letter *la*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has eight petals joined with these eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*) of letters."
The practical meaning is that one should write each group [of letters] on each individual petal.

When there is a requirement for a sequential order in the inscription of colors upon the filaments and petals, the sequence of the eastern direction must be maintained. Although the east cannot exist simultaneously for both the petals and the filaments, nevertheless, according to the method of drawing a lotus diagram (*padmakuṇḍala*), the east is determined relative to the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and [the others] follow accordingly.
The sequence for writing the phonemes upon the petals should be investigated.

In such a yantra known as the *mātṛkā*, which consists of a square (*caturaśra*) in which the syllables *va* and *ṭha* are situated within the eight directions beginning with the East and ending with the Northeast— [here, in the subsequent text, the word *asra* should be understood as ending in the dental *s*]— in such a yantra, one should [place] the disciple.
Having settled, that is, having established.

Thus, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus like a lotus pond, and having drawn a square devoid of doors outside of that— [here, in the forthcoming text, it should be understood that the word *asra* ends in the dental *s*]—
and having written "hsauḥ" in the pericarp, one should write "a, ā" in sequence upon the filaments starting from the east.
Having written two vowels on each filament and one vowel within the petals—

at the previously mentioned locations (which should be understood as being based on the divisions in the center of the petals situated in the directions starting from the East)— one should write the eight groups beginning with *ka* (*kādyaṣṭavargān*) one by one, placing each group inside [the respective petal], and outside of that, in a square (*caturaśre*).

[In this and the subsequent text, the word *asra* should be understood as ending in a dental *s*. The collective meaning is that one should write "vaṃ" and "ṭhaṃ" in the eight directions beginning with the east. This was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:
"The lotus whose pericarp consists of the syllables of space (*vyoma*), moon (*indu*), water (*au*), and earth (*rasanā*), and whose filaments shimmer with pairs of vowels..."
Within the petals, the three groups beginning with the five groups, the *ya* group, and the five vowels are placed in sequence;

it is surrounded by the city of the earth (*kṣoṇīpura*), which is joined with the letter *la*, the letter *la*, and the *lāṅgali* (the letter *ṅa*), situated in the directions and intermediate directions. [Note: In this upcoming text, the word *asra* should be understood as ending in a dental *s*.]
"The lotus of the letter [Haṃ] situated on the head destroys poison and disease; it is the conqueror of death. Thus [it is said].
*Vyoma* is the letter *ha*; *indu* is the letter *sa*; *au* is its own form; *rasanārṇa* is the *visarga*; *lānta* is the letter *va*;
*lāṅgali* is the letter *ṭha*; the remainder is clear.
One should bathe [the deity] with the three vidyās of Śrī, Śyāmā, and Vārtālī—[here, by the word "Vārtālī," Vārāhī is to be understood;

and by the word "vidyā," the root mantras of those three are to be understood]—in such a way that there is contact with water on all limbs. By the qualification "with that" (tena), it is implied that this applies even when other water is insufficient.
It is indicated that there is nothing to be grasped; this very state is called the "full consecration" (pūrṇābhiṣeka). || 38 ||
He concludes the initiation through mantras (māntrī-dīkṣā):

Having seated the disciple— who is dressed in fine silk, anointed with unguents, adorned with ornaments, wearing a garland, and is well-composed— beside him, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā upon his body, [the teacher places] three [mantras] into the hand of that disciple, whose face-cloth has been removed.

Having placed the second pieces—first sprinkled and then smeared with sandalwood—along with flower fragments, and having caused them to be consumed with the *tattva* mantras, one should instruct the girl in her right ear and subsequently recite the desired mantra.
The passage beginning with "sadukūlam" and ending with "pārśve niveśya" is clear in its meaning. Regarding the external *mātṛkā-nyāsa*:

this *nyāsa* must be taken from numerous tantric texts such as the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*, and not from modern books. Just as it is performed on one's own body as prescribed in other tantras, so too should it be performed on the body of the disciple.
Having placed it in the hand of one whose face was previously covered by a cloth, that is, one whose mouth-cloth had been bound and then released.

This refers to the three initiations according to the Tantric system; however, according to some opinions, in the case of sequential initiation, the emission (visarga) occurs at the conclusion of each respective initiation.
Alternatively, since the author of the Sūtra intends only initiation into the Tantra (tantradīkṣā), the "binding of the mouth" applies specifically to the Tantric perspective.
Just as in the case of the statement, "He first anoints the sacrificial post here with clarified butter [which was] first sprinkled," and likewise, "In this very manner,
they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the second tail-piece (*jāghanī*)."

In reality, however, because the sequence was prescribed previously and the consecrated materials remain as its residue, one does not discard the vessels for that duration— just as in the case of the rule "one prepares the *udayanīya* offering from the scrapings of the *prāyaṇīya*— for the sake of the consecration intended for future use.
Because it has been established, the gift consists only of the first and second portions that have been consecrated and sprinkled, but not of that which is unconsecrated.

Since the number three is obtained through the plural itself according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*, the further qualification "three" indicates that the placing is not done all at once for the three together, but rather one by one, just as in the expression "he lays on two enclosing-sticks."

With the three *tattva* mantras: "I purify the *ātmatattva*, namaḥ svāhā; I purify the *vidyātattva*, namaḥ svāhā; I purify the *śivatattva*, namaḥ svāhā. Because the causative form (*ṇijanta*) is heard in the word "having caused to swallow" (*grāsayitvā*), the consumption [of the substance] occurs immediately after receiving the permission of the preceptor (*ācārya*). [The mantra] for the *bālā* [goddess] consists of three syllables.

Having taught the final limb, one should state—that is, teach—the desired mantra in the form of either the *pañcadaśī* or the *ṣoḍaśī*; this is the meaning. [From here until the end of the commentary on Sūtra 39, the scriptural intent regarding the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the inclusion of both the *pañcadaśī* and the *ṣoḍaśī*.]

Now, one might object: "This is not the injunction for the sixteenth [syllable], because by the singular word 'manu' (the mantra), there is an injunction for the fifteenth alone. Nor should it be said, "What is the determining factor against the reverse? For, immediately after the instruction for the child, only the fifteenth is expected; thus, by the singular number, that very one is understood. [Not so.]

[The phrase] "lack of a determining factor" (vinigamanāviraha) is an addition in manuscript *ba* 2. Furthermore, if the instruction regarding the *ṣoḍaśī* were intended in this tantra, one would have extracted it;
since it is not extracted here, it must therefore not be intended—if this is argued, we say no. For it is not [the case that] by following a singular statement...

[The reading "tatsiddhiḥ" is an interpolation—ba 2. For indeed, there is a rule that in all cases, even when words expressing number are intended as qualifiers of the predicate (*vidheya*), their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is only with the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*);
this is because such a connection is observed even with that which delimits [the base]. And thus:

The singular number associated with the genus (*jāti*) is thus justified. If that were the case, how could the exclusion of the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice follow from it? Otherwise, in the injunction "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," there would be no prohibition against killing two Brāhmaṇas. Let it be granted, then, that the singular number is intended to be significant; even so, it does not [establish the desired conclusion].
The cessation of the sixteenth [day] is the most excellent according to the scriptural statement;
63) it occurs after the subsequent instruction of that single sixteenth day.

Since there is no obstacle to the instruction of the *pañcadaśī* at the time of the instruction of the *Śyāmā-raśmimālā-ādividyā*, the claim that it is not included [in the list] because it was not extracted is also untenable; for if the *pañcadaśī* were likewise not extracted, its instruction would also not have occurred.

Nor should it be said that she is extracted by the phrase "the power Mādana" in the midst of the five rays to be meditated upon in the *mūlādhāra*, for that fifteenth [vowel] is not extracted as common to all; rather, this group of five garlands of rays exists within the text from the twenty-eighth sūtra of the ninth section (of the *Khaṇḍa*).

She consists of the five rays as her constituent parts; for this very reason, she is called "Mahāvidyā" (the Great Knowledge) therein. Otherwise, even for Brahmā, it would be difficult to justify the meaningfulness of the word "tasyāḥ" (of her).
Therefore, the Vidyā is one, accompanied by the previously established limbs, sub-limbs, minor limbs, and the sandals.
How could knowledge, which is a constituent part of that [ignorance], become the primary entity?

Furthermore, when it is said that "what is not cited in an independent treatise (svatantra) is not to be accepted," is this intended meaning of the author of the Sūtra being extracted [by you], or is it being extracted by means of another statement to the effect that "what is not cited in an independent treatise is not to be accepted"?
It cannot be the first, because there is no indicative mark (liṅga) within the Sūtra itself that extracts such an intention. Moreover—

The three-syllable mantra of Bālā has not been extracted anywhere, yet [the author] himself says, "teach Bālā. By this, the intention of the author of the Sūtras is very clear: that even if it has not been extracted, it should be accepted. Nor [is this the case] in the *Raśmimālā* [meaning: in the sūtra on the common procedure for all [tantras], section 10, fragment 29].

It must be stated that since she is extracted as a limb (*aṅga*) of Śrī and as Bālā consisting of nine syllables, when it is said "having taught Bālā," she alone is to be understood. If the nine-syllable mantra is intended by the term "Bālā," then, in the subsequent extraction of the mantras of the fifteen Nityās, [in Sūtra 9 of the Lalitā section] it says: "Bālā, Kulasundarī, or... [and so on].

[It has been said: "Or it is called Kumārī. [If one were to argue that] because the *Kulasundarī* mantra prescribes the inclusion of the syllables of "Kumārī" within the *Kulasundarī* mantra, it would follow that this [mantra] also consists of nine syllables; and if we were to accept this consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), we shall state the refutation in the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the *Kulasundarī* mantra. Thus...

In the section on the Śrīvidyā-nyāsa, regarding the statement "having performed the six-limb (ṣaḍaṅga) assignment by repeating the Bālā [mantra] twice," the performance of the six-limb assignment by repeating the nine-syllable [mantra] twice is contrary to all traditions. Therefore, the Bālā used here is not the nine-syllable one, but rather the three-syllable one; for this very reason, it is stated in the Raśmimālā:
In the nine-syllable mantra, the limb of Śrī is stated as "bāle" and not "bālā.

We shall explain a collection of arguments even more extensive than this in the extraction of the Raśmimālā-mantra (beginning from the ninth sūtra of the tenth section, starting with "pañcemā—" and ending with the twenty-eighth sūtra). Alternatively—

The connection should be understood as: "We shall explain by means of a text consisting of fifty sūtras. Therefore, there may be a three-syllable [mantra]. However, the *bālā* has not been extracted anywhere; rather, it is treated as being taught by taking what is established in another tantra.
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtra: "having caused [the disciple] to swallow [the mantra] with the *tattva*-mantras," yet those mantras have not been extracted.

Thus, in the Vārāhī-prakaraṇa, the three qualities-mantras and so forth have not been extracted; therefore, it is established as the final conclusion that this was not the intention of the author of the Sūtra.
Not the second, because such a treatise is not found anywhere.

Furthermore, at the conclusion of this initiation, three qualifications of the disciple are heard: "the disciple, having contemplated fullness," "one who has known what is to be known," and "one who possesses authority over all mantras. Among these, "fullness" means being devoid of any remainder of that which is to be received from the Guru. If...
(64) If the fulfillment of all defects of initiation occurs through the fifteenth [lunar day] alone, then since the remaining performance of the sixteenth-day rite exists,
how can there be an injunction for the cultivation of fullness? In this very way, the state of having known what is to be known becomes untenable.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the author of the Sūtras, the purpose is fulfilled and perfection is attained by the fifteenth [day] alone, and thus there is no inconsistency in liberation being accomplished by that alone; for even so, what would be the point of the instruction on the fifteenth [day] regarding one who is qualified for all mantras?

Either the qualification for the sixteenth [day] is accepted, or the term "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*) is restricted to that which is distinct from the sixteenth. It cannot be the first, because it would follow that the sixteenth produces a lesser result than the fifteenth; for one who is qualified for a major task is also qualified for a minor task.

Just as one who is authorized to cross the Ganges is also authorized to cross a small canal, but the reverse is not observed in the world; nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because there is no evidence for such a restriction.
Therefore, when investigated thus without partiality, we see no obstacle whatsoever to the inclusion of both the fifteenth and sixteenth [tithis] by the term "desired mantra."

Or, let it be granted for the sake of others' satisfaction that the author of the Sūtras intended only the initiation of the Pañcadaśī; nevertheless, one who has received that initiation— or even a minor initiation— must not enter a maṇḍala of the Ṣoḍaśī belonging to a follower of another Tantra, just as a king does not enter the house of a servant.

Maheśvarānandanātha says: "That is not so. For instance, regarding the 'smallness' (alpatva) of initiation (dīkṣā), does it mean having a mantra of few syllables, or does it mean having a mantra that accomplishes small results? In the first case, it would follow that the initiation of Vārāhī is superior to that of Śrīvidyā, and the initiation of Śyāmā is even more superior than that."

In another tantra, it is heard that the very same fruit which belongs to the initiation of the *ṣoḍaśī* also belongs to this [initiation]; this is understood through such words as "one has accomplished all that was to be done," "one who has known everything that is to be known," and "one becomes liberated while living" [the meaning is: by the words found in the aphorisms at the conclusion of those respective sections]. And thus, because they are equal, there is no [difference].
The state of having received an incomplete initiation.

If it is objected: "In that case, what is the status of the scriptural statement found in another tantra that the initiation of the fifteen-fold [vidyā] (pañcadaśī-dīkṣā) is an inferior initiation?"—[the answer is: No, because in that tantra where there is a combination of both the sixteen-fold (ṣoḍaśī) and the fifteen-fold [vidyās], the initiation of the fifteen-fold is considered inferior since its fruit is incomplete, whereas the initiation of the sixteen-fold possesses the full fruit.

Regarding both those who follow the Tantras, one has been initiated into the *pañcadaśī* (the fifteen-fold system) and the other has been initiated into the *ṣoḍaśī* (the sixteen-fold system). Since the former has remaining duties to perform, he is considered incomplete; therefore, it is logical that one who has received initiation from a Guru should not enter his mandala. But here, since the equal fruit is established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*), how can there be a state of being a Guru?

Lightness. One should investigate this without dogmatic insistence. Nor should it be argued that there is indeed lightness or heaviness of the result corresponding to the lightness or heaviness of the cause; for if that were so, consider two people seeking only fire: one of them produces fire by means of iron and stone.

It is produced by the friction of a single fire-drill. In that case, compared to the former, for the production of the subsequent fire, there is an increase in time, an increase in persons, and an increase in effort; thus, due to the weight of many causes, that fire would possess the capacity to produce greater heat. Likewise...
Because the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) of Āpastamba is twice as long as the procedure for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) according to the *Baudhāyana-sūtra* (p.
[this applies] to the followers of the Āpastamba-sūtra.

There is the attainment of twice the heavenly rebirth; there is the attainment of a more weighty status for one following the Baudhāyana-sūtra compared to one following the Āpastamba-sūtra. Therefore, apart from the production of superior results, it is difficult to define any other "weightiness" (*gurutva*) in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Since that [qualification] is absent in the present case, how can there be the status of one who has undergone the "light initiation" (*laghudīkṣā*) for a follower of the Sūtra? Even though the practice of the Guru-sādhana yields an equal result, one engages in it because the scripture itself states that the fruit does not accrue to its qualified practitioner without the practice transmitted through the lineage of his own previous Gurus; it is not out of a desire for an increase in the fruit. As in the *Atirātra*...

In passages such as "He takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup" and "He does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*," the establishment of a gradation of results is appropriate because, in the absence of such a scriptural injunction, a systematic arrangement can be established according to the difference in the qualifications (*adhikārin*) of the practitioners. Therefore, in this case, there is no deficiency or excess regarding the number of initiations (*dīkṣā*).
The remainder should be inferred by the wise.

This position has been refuted while provisionally accepting it for the sake of pleasing others; in reality, however, it was stated previously that there is no obstacle to including the *ṣoḍaśī* by means of the term "desired mantra."

Nor should it be said that in the passage, "and at the time of death at dawn, having mentally repeated the root-vidyā ten times— whether beginning with *ka* or beginning with *ha*," the phrases "beginning with *ka*" or "beginning with *ha*" are qualifiers of the vidyā that serve as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of the *ṣoḍaśī* [vidyā] here; for by those two qualifiers...
Granted that the *ṣoḍaśī* might be excluded by those two [mantras] recited in proximity to the performance at the time of dawn as being subordinate to it,
nevertheless, what power do they have to exclude the *ṣoḍaśī* everywhere?
It is like the king’s command, "Bring a horse," given at the time of going to the garden.
Even when there is no obstruction to vehicles such as palanquins for traveling to a grove, a statement involving horses and foot-soldiers is never capable of precluding other means of transport.

Therefore, the instruction on the *ṣoḍaśī* is necessary even for those who follow the Sūtras. Beyond this, the wise should investigate further, setting aside all dogmatic insistence. In the discernment of the true nature of Dharma, partiality toward one's own view leads only to hell; so, enough of further elaboration. (39)

The designation of the disciple's name: the teacher describes the remaining ritual actions as follows— then, having placed his own foot upon the disciple’s head, [he recites] all the mantras either once or in sequence.
Having instructed according to the disciple's qualification and having caused the disciple to touch one of his own limbs,
he should assign him a name consisting of two, three, or four syllables— beginning with the *mātṛkā* letters of that specific limb and ending with the word *Ānandanātha*. || 40 ||

By the word "tataḥ" (then), it is indicated that the dharmas to be described hereafter constitute subsequent subsidiaries (*uttarāṅga*). According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"In the absence of a specific instruction, one should understand the right foot [of one's own guru]"—one should place only the right foot. Regarding the phrase "all mantras," since there is a contraction of the term "all" by virtue of the context—just as in the case of the statement "all desire the *hāriyojana* cup"—[the reference is restricted].
Just as in that [previous] case, [one should worship] the mantras that constitute the limbs (*aṅga*) of Śrīvidyā— namely Gaṇapati, Śyāmā, Vārtālī, Parā,
Pañcadaśī, Nityā, Raśmimālā, and so forth— [from this point onward...]
The meaning is "those which are about to be described. Regarding the phrase "all at once" (*sakṛdvā*), the word *vā* has the sense of *eva* (only/just);

thus, the meaning is "at that very time. Alternatively, it means "gradually," or "at the time of each respective meditation. By the expression "according to one's qualification" (*yathādhikāram*), an option based on specific circumstances (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) is indicated. For one who possesses an abundance of devotion and faith, [the result occurs] at that very time.

"Gradually for one who possesses slightly less than that. Regarding the phrase "upon one's own limbs," the word *aṅga* refers to the parts of the body. One should give the command, "Perform the touch. Then, whatever limb the disciple touches, [the mantra] is such that its initial syllable is the letter which corresponds to that part in the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.
This is a specific qualification of the name. For example, upon touching the head, the syllable *a* is the first letter of the Mātṛkā;
that [name] which begins with it is "Amṛtānandanātha. This same principle should be applied everywhere. The phrase "or two syllables," and so forth, is clear in meaning.
It is evident that the name ends with the word "Ānandanātha. One should assign such a name to that disciple.
One should establish [it]. || 40 ||

Regarding the bestowal of the mantra for the Guru’s sandals, which was previously forgotten, he speaks again: "Before instructing the disciple, one should give him one's own sandals together with the six *tāra*s. (41)

Immediately after the second morsel has been consumed and before the instruction [of the mantra] is given, one should teach him the mantra consisting of his own sandals (*pādukā*)— formed by appending the name given at the time of initiation to the end of the word "one's own guru"— joined with the six *tāra*s. Regarding these six *tāra*s, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Dear One, Vāgbhava, Parā, Śrī, Kālībīja, Bhuvaneśī, and Manmatha—these six are proclaimed as the Tārās. Thus it is said.
"I worship the venerable sandals of Amukānandanātha."
By this, the mantra for the sandals placed in the commentary, which was devised without consulting the Sūtras, is refuted.

Although, according to the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama), the instruction would logically apply right here, nevertheless, its sublation by the order of the Vedic text (śrautakrama) is appropriate, just as in the case of the statement "the Āśvina cup is drawn tenth. || 41 ||
Having instructed him in conduct, discipline, and so forth;

having contemplated the heart-consciousness; having wiped his limbs three times with the threefold knowledge (the Gāyatrī); having embraced him and smelled the crown of his head, one should make him one's own self. || 42 ||

Having instructed— that is, having taught— the conduct (*ācāra*) which will be described in the tenth section [the meaning being that it refers to what will be stated from sūtra 57, "There is no conflict with all beings," up to sūtra 80],
he [instructed] *taṃ*— the remainder of the sentence being "the disciple"— [namely] the consciousness related to the space of the heart (*hārda*).
The meaning is: having touched and meditated upon the disciple as non-different from the consciousness (caitanya) residing in one's own heart.

[One performs] the cleansing with the three Vidyās—namely, the Śrī-Śyāmā and Vārtālī Vidyās. Having recited the three Vidyās once, the first cleansing is performed; then, unlike the procedure where one sprinkles twice silently and then thrice, [here it is done differently].

[The phrase] "with three [times]" means three times. If that were the case, one would have said simply "with the three vidyās. By using the instrumental case in the form "by means of the triad of vidyās," a specific unity [of the three] would be implied. Therefore, it is not so.

"Rubbing" (parimārjana) means touching the entire body of the disciple with one's own hand. Having embraced him, having smelled his head, one should make him one's own self-form; just as one's own self is free from the impurities of human nature that obstruct liberation, so should one make him. || 42 ||
The disciple’s entitlement to all mantras—

from the words "the true guru" up to this point [meaning from the beginning of Sūtra 34 on the final leaf until the end of the commentary on this sūtra]— constitutes the ritual performed by the guru; hereafter, [the ritual is that of the disciple].
The action performed by the disciple takes place as follows:

the disciple, having meditated upon fullness and thus accomplished his purpose, honors that Guru with wealth according to his capacity; thereby, having known what is to be known, he becomes authorized in all mantras—may there be auspiciousness! || 43 ||

Thus ends the "Rite of Initiation" (Dīkṣāvidhi) in the Kalpasūtra composed by the illustrious Paraśurāma— the destroyer of the wicked Kṣatriya clans born from the womb of the venerable Reṇukā, the preeminent disciple of the great god Mahādeva, the venerable Bhārgava Upādhyāya Jāmadagnya, and the great Kaula Ācārya.
The first section:

Fullness (*pūrṇatā*) has already been explained. Therefore, he is one by whom the goal has been accomplished, that is, the means to liberation (*mokṣa-sādhana*). Regarding the word *tam*: it denotes time; the meaning is "at this very time. If it is taken as an adjective qualifying the Guru, [the meaning is] "him."

Because it would be redundant. Alternatively, since there is a scriptural injunction stating that "when the Guru's guru is present, one should worship the *praguru* (great-grand-guru) alone," the word "him" (*tam*) is used to indicate that this [worship of the immediate guru] should not be bypassed in case of any other possible application of the ritual.
This is according to the principle: "The lord of a hundred thousand should give a hundred thousand [coins], while a poor man should give a single cowrie, each according to his capacity."

*Upacarya* means having propitiated. *Viditaḥ* means known; he by whom that which is to be known (*veditavyam*)—that is, what is fit to be known—is known, is the meaning of "the All-Knowing One" (*sarvajñaḥ*). He becomes the one authorized over all mantras, that is, over the seventy million mantras beginning with those of the Saura and Vaiṣṇava traditions. By this, through this instruction, the instruction of all mantras is accomplished.

The meaning is that there is no prohibition against reading books and the like. As it is said in another Tantra: "Only by one who is in their final birth, or by one for whom Śaṅkara himself is pleased, is this venerable sixteen-syllabled Vidyā (or the fifteen-syllabled Vidyā) directly obtained through a true Guru."
"In this regard, O Maheśānī, all the great mantras abide within it like trees within their seeds; therefore, it is most excellent. Thus [it is said].

The word "Śiva" serves as an indicator that the section commenced— the so-called *Dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*, which begins from the first sūtra on the final leaf, namely "Now, therefore, we shall explain initiation (*dīkṣā*)," and extends up to the end of the sixty-seventh leaf— has been completed. || 43 ||

Thus ends the section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*), comprising the first part, in the commentary on the *Paraśurāmasūtra* titled *Saubhāgyodaya*, composed by Śrī Rāmeśvara. Furthermore, in the repetition of the sūtras, that which requires correction should be indicated.
"And the remaining portion shall be complete through the grace of the Primordial Goddess. Thus ends the first section.

[Even more extensive and clear applications of initiation (dīkṣā) are found in the *Śrī Mahānirvāṇa Tantra* and other tantras, as well as in the *Dīkṣollāsa*, the *Dīkṣāprakāśa*, and the *Tāntrikasvatantrapaddhati*; however—]
Furthermore, since this method of application has also been stated in the Sūtras emerging from the mouth of the Blessed Lord, it is indeed most excellent.
68] The Second Auspicious Section: The Manual for Gaṇanāyaka.
The Procedure for the Worship of Śrī Gaṇanāyaka:
Having completed the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the first section, and desiring to expound the section on the worship of Śrī Lalitā,
[the author] begins by explaining the worship of Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, which serves as a preliminary limb (*pūrvāṅga*) to that worship.
Thus, having received initiation from a true guru, one should contemplate the ritual manual of Gaṇanāyaka in order to remove obstacles to the propitiation of Mahāvidyā. || 1 ||

In this manner, by the previously described method, he is one by whom initiation (dīkṣā) has been received from a true guru—one who possesses the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures. By this, it is indicated that only one possessing such initiation is qualified for the worship of Śrīvidyā, and no other. Mahāvidyā refers to the Pañcadaśī.

Or it is the *ṣoḍaśī* [Vidyā]. Its propitiation is its recitation (*japa*). Alternatively, because the Great Vidyā is Śrī Lalitā—due to the non-difference between the signifier and the signified—the propitiation of her is worship until the attainment of the fruit; [this refers to] those obstacles which act as impediments to its arising.

"Vighnas"—according to Amarasimha, "vighna," "antarāya," and "pratyūha" are synonyms; for their "apohāya," meaning for their destruction, one should "āmṛśet"—contemplate—the "gāṇanāyakīṃ paddhatim," meaning the path or way related to Gaṇeśa.
According to Amarasimha, "saraṇiḥ," "paddhatiḥ," "padyā," "vartanī," and "ekapadī" are synonyms; thus, the meaning is the path of worship. One should contemplate this.

One should accept it. It has been stated previously [in the commentary on Sūtra 53 of the first section (nāma-khaṇḍa), page 34] how this constitutes an ancillary part of the worship of Śrī Lalitā; thus the meaning should be understood. || 1 ||

Having thus stated the necessity of the worship of Gaṇanāyaka— beginning with the morning rites from meditation (*dhyāna*) up to the libation (*tarpaṇa*), as prescribed by the aforementioned sūtras [such as "Gaṇapati is the limb-deity (*aṅgadevatā*) of Goddess Lalitā," and so forth]— [the author now describes] the method of that worship.
He elaborates:
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he is seated in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the *dvādaśānta*.

With his entire body bathed by the spreading flow of the nectar-essence trickling from the pair of the Guru’s feet, he— having restrained the movement of his breath and mind— meditates upon the Lord who dwells within the center of his heart-lotus, blazing like ten million rising suns, pale-red as the dawn, the expiation for all defects, and the devourer of the many serpents; then, his own body turned crimson by the mass of that radiance, he goes outside.

Having voided his excrement and urine, and having performed the cleansing of his teeth, bathing, putting on his clothes, and the offering of water (arghya) to the Sun, he should offer arghya with the mantra: "We know that Great Gaṇapati who dwells in the rising sun; we meditate upon the one with the curved trunk; may that Tusked One inspire us. Then, he should perform his daily duties (nityakṛtya).
Having performed this, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in four rounds [this knowledge regarding the fourfold libation is very clear in both commentaries on Sūtra 3 of this section].
Longevity, health, sovereignty, strength, nourishment, great fame,
poetic talent, enjoyment, and liberation result from the fourfold repetition of the libation. (2)

Having risen from his bed during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, that is, at the time of dawn—the remainder of the sentence being "from the bed"—[the phrase] "at the *dvādaśānta*" (which does not appear in the B version of the manuscript, beginning with this and ending with "or else") refers to the point above the forehead, reaching as far as the top of the skull;
that is designated by the term *dvādaśānta*. As it is said in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"The dvādaśānta is above the forehead, ending at the top of the forehead. Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, within the gross body at the *dvādaśānta*, there are thirty-two lotuses situated along the *suṣumṇā* channel; among them, two are thousand-petaled lotuses— one at the very bottom named *akula*, which faces upward, and one at the very top.

There is another [cakra] named Dvādaśānta, which is downward-facing. The authority for this should be seen in detail in the *Setubandha*, our supreme teacher’s commentary on the *Yoginītantra-uttaracatuḥśatī*. It is not written here for fear of excessive length. By the word "this" [in the original], [it refers to] the Dvādaśānta—
Thus, this word situated in the sūtra is to be understood as a qualifier of "lotus" (*kamala*) by means of the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*).
