Although the word "dvādaśānte," ending in the locative case, cannot be construed with the "lotus" which constitutes a member of the compound— due to the lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*) consisting in its dependence on another word within the compound— [it is nonetheless connected].

Because a compound cannot be formed due to the absence of the semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) that necessitates compounding; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of usage such as *ṛddhasya rājamātaṅgāḥ* (the king's wealthy elephants). Nevertheless, even the term *dvādaśānte* is a compound ending in the locative case, like *ṛddharājamātaṅgāḥ*; the absence of the elision of the locative case marker (*saptamī-lopa*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The lotus known as the *dvādaśānta* has the pair of feet of the Guru situated in the center of its pericarp; from that couple flows a nectar, and by the expansion—
that is, the spreading— of the essence of that [nectar], all one's limbs are drenched and saturated.

The phrase "of whom" (*yasya*) implies "having become thus. The word "having become" (*bhūtvā*) refers back to what was previously stated; and "one whose movement of breath and mind is restrained" (*niyamitapavanamanogatiḥ*) is an adjective qualifying the agent of meditation, serving to define the agent as a constituent part of the meditation, just as in the injunction "he offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāman juhoti*). By whom the movement of both breath and mind is restrained—that is, by whom the vital breaths and the mind are made immovable.
The meaning is "having performed. Without the restraint of the mind and breath (*manaḥ-pavana-nirodha*), one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*) is not possible;
and without one-pointedness, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is not possible. Therefore, the sense is that both of these are essential.
Within the center of the heart-lotus is the *anāhata* [the *anāhata* being the name of that which resides in the heart].

By the phrase "blazing," it is indicated that [the wheel] acts as the burner of the sins residing within one's own body. By the phrase "as crimson as the edge of the rising sun," through this hyperbolic comparison (*abhūtopamāna*), it is indicated that there is nothing else like it within the entire universe. [It is] the expiation for all defects... of all.

The expiation (*nirveṣa*) of one's own faults: those from whom the *veṣa*—that is, the form (*svarūpa*)—has departed are *nirveṣāḥ*, meaning they are devoid of their own nature or destroyed; this is a designation emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). Thus, by the etymology "that from which the state of being devoid of form (*nirveṣatva*), i.e., destruction, [results]," it means that which destroys all faults residing within one's own body.

The meaning of the result is as follows: *anekapa* means an elephant (*dvipa*, *gaja*). Having meditated upon one whose face is such [as that of an elephant], his body was made *pāṭala*—that is, rendered white-and-red—by the mass (*paṭala*) or collection of the radiance of that deity. The suffix *cvi* is used here in the sense of "becoming what one was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāve*). Indeed, *pāṭala* is white-and-red.
Thus says Amara. By this, the meaning is that one should meditate for as long as the state of rosy-pinkness remains possible within one's own body.

Up to this point— meaning up to the end of the action described as "his body reddened by the rays of that [light]" found in the subsequent root text— the procedure for the place of rest has been completed, since it was stated [later] that "having gone outside. This going outside is obtained through recollection (*smṛti*).

And by this, the voiding of feces and urine is restated. Here, since there is a general injunction stating "having performed the cleaning of the teeth," the reading *sati* (being) is more appropriate. When the expectation arises as to how the performance is to be done, [it is fulfilled] by looking to the Tantric rules in preference to the Smārta ones.

By the principle of the "acceptance of the horse" (*aśvapratigrahanyāya*), because of their proximity, only those ritual properties (*dharma*) mentioned in other systems (*tantra*) are to be adopted, and not those belonging to the *smṛti* tradition. Since the sequence beginning with the bath and ending with the water offering to the Sun is more proximate to the *Śrīkrama* than other systems, the requirement for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*) is to be fulfilled from that very source.

The authors of the *Nibandha*, however, in their *Gaṇapatipaddhati*, having stated that the conjunction of the three seed-syllables of Śrī, Māyā, and Kāma must be employed when joining the *tritārī* in mantras, cited the *Śrīvidyārṇavatantra* as their authority for this. That [position] is to be considered; for instance, in the *Śrīkrama*, it is everywhere [stated as follows]:...

In the *Śyāmākrama*, one recites "the three *tārās*" at the beginning of the mantras; in the *Vārāhīkrama*, one recites "the *kumārī-yoga*"; and in this manual (*paddhati*), one recites "vāc" and "glauṃ," for it is said that "all mantras are to be recited" in the *Parākrama*. Furthermore, according to the *sūtra*, all the *parākrama-mantras* are to be preceded by the word "sauvarṇa."

Since it is recited in the *Gaṇapratikrama*, it is very clearly understood that for the author of the Sūtra—who would not have recited it there—there is no application of seed-syllables (*bīja*) at all in these mantras. This being the case, how can there be a following of the *Vidyārnava Tantra*?
Alternatively, since the conjunction of *vāk*, *māyā*, and *kamalā* will be mentioned in the *Śrīkrama* regarding the *Śyenayāga*...
Because it exists as a limb of all [the limbs] like fresh butter, it too would be obtained as a limb of Śrīvidyā; therefore, to set that aside and follow another tantra is irrational.
For one who abides by his own scripture yet proceeds according to another scripture [is acting improperly].
For him who disregards his own scripture, it is equal to the murder of an embryo.
And because of this traditional teaching (smṛti).
Having offered [the water] with the words, "To Mahāgaṇapati, who abides like the rising sun," this [phrase] connects as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

By the phrase "to him who abides like the rising sun," one should perform meditation upon such a sun; [regarding the offering of *arghya*—as noted by Śrī—] subsequently, from the passage beginning with "Siddhalakṣmī" (found on page 72, line 4 of the sūtra), one should [meditate upon] Vighneśvara.

"Having meditated" means according to the method stated at the end of the Sūtra; it is indicated that this should be performed according to the method to be described in the section on worship (saparyā-prakaraṇa).

In the *Nibandha*, the offering of three *arghya*s is mentioned; however, its source must be sought. This is because the singular number is clearly evident from the predicate word "arghya" ending in the singular. Nor is it a case of repetition (*abhyāsa*), as there is no word indicating such repetition.
Nor is it an extension (*atideśa*) of what is stated in the *Śrīkrama*, since by the explicit statement, only that which concludes with the *sūryārghya* is extended.
Because there is no evidence for the extension of those subsequent properties.
Having performed the daily duties, such as the Agnihotra sacrifice and others;
by this, the misconception that the libation (tarpaṇa) to be described later—which consists of four repetitions—is a subsidiary part of the *arghya* offering due to its proximity, is dispelled.
It is indicated that, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is indeed a subsidiary part of the meditation (*upāsti*) alone.

This is the originative injunction for the fourfold libation (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇa*). In this context, "fourfold libation" is the name of the ritual act (*karmanāmadheya*) and not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), because the fourfold repetition will be explained later—in the third sūtra and its commentary that follows. And thus: "He performs the Agnihotra."
In this case, as here, by changing the case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāmena*),

its status as the meaning of the third case is [established] through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇayā*) as the instrument (*karaṇatvena*) within the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root.

The sequence [of the argument] is as follows: there are four repetitions (*āvṛttayaḥ*) or practices; whatever the nature of the constituent actions may be, that constitutes the "fourfold repetition of libation" (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇam*). Although in the first libation there are twelve repetitions rather than four, nevertheless, according to the principle of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāya*), by following the logic of abundance (*bhūmātva*), this applies even to the libation that does not consist of four repetitions.

The common designation is "the fourfold libation" (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇa*). Here, since there is no connection with the verb *kāmayate* (to desire), longevity, health, and so forth do not connect as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Rather, it serves only as an auxiliary to the worship of Śrī Gaṇapati. Otherwise, [one would have to interpret] the statement, "He offers the *śamī* fuel; he becomes established in this world," [in the same way].

Because, according to the Vedic text, it would follow that even the *prayāja* offerings have results such as "firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth; therefore, the passage beginning with "longevity and health" (*āyurārogyam*) is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Furthermore, rather than writing "for the attainment of long life, health, and so forth," the author of the manual (nibandhakāra) has rightly written the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as "for the pleasure of Gaṇapati. However, the authoritative source for the section beginning with "in a river or similar place" and ending with "having performed the five-fold offerings" (pañcopacārān ācarya) must be sought.
The direction [of this argument] is that what is fabricated by one's own intellect is simply not to be believed. || 2 ||
He clarifies that very point:
having first performed the libation twelve times with the root mantra,
one should perform it four times for each of the twenty-eight syllables of the mantra ending in *svāhā*, as well as for the root mantra.
Having offered libations four times,
[one should again offer to] Śrī-Śrīpati, Girijā-Girijāpati, Rati-Ratipati, Mahī-Mahīpati, Mahālakṣmī-Mahālakṣmīpati [here the absence of sandhi is an archaic Vedic usage].

Among the thirteen pairs [of deities], one deity from each pair— namely Ṛddhi, Āmodā, Samṛddhi, Pramodā, Kānti, Sumukhā, Madanāvatī, Durmukhā, Madadravā, Avighnadrāviṇī, Vighnakartṛ, Vasudhārā, Śaṅkhanidhi, Vasumatī, and Padmanidhi— is recited four times, as is the root mantra four times.
Thus, one should perform the libations; in this way, there are four hundred and forty-four libations. || 3 ||

The libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with the mantra "Having uttered the root [mantra], I offer libation" (mūlam uccārya tarpayāmi). In this same manner, the word "root" (mūla) should be applied everywhere hereafter.

Regarding the phrase "libation four times," it is not the repetition of the action that is prescribed, but rather the repetition of the mantra itself. Although the word "twelve times" (dvādaśavāram) ends in the accusative case, it functions like the expression "he cooks a little" (stokam pacati).
It might be argued that this is an adverbial qualification (*kriyāviśe�ṣaṇa*), and thus only the repetition of the action is established;

nevertheless, since forty-four hundred tarpaṇas occur hereafter, a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*) is established by the number mentioned in the sūtra, and therefore it cannot be a mere repetition of the action. Hence:

Immediately after "twelve times," it should be supplemented with "having repeated. For this very reason, later on, the repetition of the mantra itself is clearly heard in the root text through the statement: "the root [mantra] four times, and each [of the others] four times.
If it were a repetition of the ritual action (*kriyā*), then the recitation of the mantra would logically follow only once. And that...
This is refuted by the requirement of the subsequent number. Alternatively, even if the action is repeated due to the distinctness of the substances, there will still be a repetition of the mantra;

nevertheless, since the repetition of the mantra is explicit later on, here too—as its concomitant—there must be a repetition of the mantra. After the words "four times," the word "having uttered" (*uccārya*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. By the phrase "ending with *svāhā*,"...

It is indicated that the *svāhākāra* is an integral component of the mantra for each syllable. (p. 72) Since the whole—the specific mantra—has Gaṇapati as its deity, it is evident that its constituent parts likewise have him as their deity. Therefore:

At the end of *svāhā*, the word *tarpayāmi* should also be joined. Thus, for each single syllable of the root mantra, there is the addition of the nasal dot (*bindu*) according to the tradition of the learned; then follows the utterance of *svāhā*, and then *tarpayāmi* as previously stated. In this manner, [the process is repeated] four times with the root mantra, and likewise for all [syllables].
This is to be applied to the [other] castes (*varṇa*). First, by the phrase "having offered libations twelve times," one group is indicated.

Following that, by the phrase ending with "having offered libations four times," another group consisting of the final libations is indicated. In this sūtra, moreover, by the word "again" (*punaḥ*), yet another group consisting of the libations for the thirteen couples is indicated.

And the purpose of indicating the three groups is as follows: since each individual group generates its own unique transcendental result (*apūrva*), if one forgets even a single [verse] within that group, the performance must begin again from the start of that specific group, not from the very beginning of the entire cycle.
This is just as when a portion of a mantra is omitted, one must repeat that mantra starting from its beginning.

"Śrī-Śrīpati" is one [pair], and "Girijā-Girijāpati" is another; in this manner, it should be understood that there is one pair consisting of a feminine ending and one consisting of a masculine ending. Based on the etymology "one for whom there are no obstacles (vighnāḥ) following the flow of joy (mada)," the word *avighna* is masculine. The rest is clear. Thus...
In the thirteen pairs [of deities], one should pronounce each deity in the accusative case and join it with the phrase "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*).

Thus, according to the method described, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for each single deity is performed four times; thereafter, it should be performed four times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) as before. In this manner, by the stated procedure, the libations are offered in sequence according to the specified number.
Thus, there are 228 root libations (*mūlatarpaṇa*), 112 libations for the [deities of the] letters (*varṇatarpaṇa*), and 104 libations for the couples (*mithunatarpaṇa*);
in total, these amount to the previously mentioned number of 444 libations. This is the meaning. || 3 ||

Having thus described the sequence of libations (tarpaṇa), beginning from the entry into the sacrificial hall and ending with the meditation on Vighneśvara, he begins to state the ritual procedure for worship:
"Now, the ritual of sacrifice— having come to the house and having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) at the doorway..."

On both sides [of the door], [one should worship] Bhadrakālī and Bhairava; above the door, having entered within with the mantra "Obeisance to Lambodara," one should stand upon the seat with the seat-mantra, perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa),
perform the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka) with the root-mantra, and [visualize] the deity within oneself.
His flanks are embraced by Siddhalakṣmī; he has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, is of a reddish hue,

and possesses eleven hands adorned with a citron, a mace, a *puṇḍra* fruit, a sugarcane bow, a trident, the Sudarśana discus, a conch, a noose, a lotus, a cluster of grain, his own teeth, and a jeweled pitcher.
Having meditated upon Vighneśvara, whose temples are split open, who is filled with bliss, and who is the master of obstacles, the destroyer of all hindrances; || 4 ||

Now, this is a statement concerning another topic. By this, the section on libation (*tarpaṇa*) is concluded. Thus, by means of this section, the relationship of subordinate and principal between libation and worship (*upāsanā*) is indicated. Consequently, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of libation to the sequence of the limbs of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The word "it is said" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. By the phrase "having returned home,"...

It is indicated that the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed outside the house at a river or similar location. Having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila)—that is, the place of sacrifice—with cow dung; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The purification of the site (*sthalaśuddhi*) is restated here as it has already been established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By this, the sequence is not intended to be significant. Furthermore, if one were to argue that the text is placed here for the sake of establishing the sequence—out of fear of its pointlessness (*vaiyyarthyabhītyā*) due to the lack of a specific result in a mere restatement—[it would be so].
When this is said, then the smearing (upalepa) should be performed immediately prior to the worship of the door (dvārapūjā).

Regarding the phrase "on both sides," since no specific direction is given, the right side comes first and the left afterwards. As for the "right and left," those should be understood as they are at the time of exiting from the door; it is precisely there that it should be done accordingly.

This is according to conventional practice, but not at the time of entry. "Namaḥ" (salutation) is the response; "one should worship" is the ellipsis. The deity is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. By the phrase "having entered within," it is established that the worship of the door must be performed while remaining outside. By the phrase "with the seat-mantra" (*āsana-mantra*), this seat-mantra [is as follows:]—hereafter.

In the sixth section of the *Śyāmākramīya*, in the sixth sūtra, it should be understood that the mantra to be recited is "Obeisance to the Lotus-Throne of the Support-Power" (*ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*). This is because it is the mantra recited in the *Śyāmāprakaraṇa* due to its proximity; for this very reason, one should not adopt [the mantra] found in other tantras.
Regarding that demonstration of baseless doctrines stated in the *Nibandha*: as for what is written in the *Nibandha*— namely, "having lit lamps all around," the chewing of betel,
and the sprinkling of the seat with the third seed-syllable of the *Bāla* [the third seed-syllable being *sauḥ*]— that...

This question arises: what is the authority (*pramāṇa*) for this in another tantra, or is it stated in this very tantra? [The meaning is that it is stated later in the *Śrīkrama*, in the third section, chapter 11, sūtra 11: "having offered the measure of the lamp" (*dīpānamito datvā*). In the *Śrīkrama*, the sprinkling of the seat (*āsana-prokṣaṇa*) is performed with the third seed-syllable of Bālā.

It is stated in the *Parāpaddhati* [in the commentary on Sūtra 6 of Khaṇḍa 8 of the *Agraparakrama*]: "Is there for all of them an extended application (*atideśa*) scripture that brings them about? Not the first, because that has already been refuted. Regarding the second, the extended application is threefold: extended application by statement (*vacanātideśa*), extended application by name (*nāmātideśa*)," and so forth.

The extension [of ritual details] occurs through inference based on a desire [for similarity]. Among these, what kind of extension is it here? It is not a verbal statement—unlike such statements as "the rest is the same as the Śyena" or "the remainder is equal to the Śrīkrama. Therefore, the first [type of extension] is not applicable. Likewise, it is not by naming it—as in "one should perform the Agnihotra for a month"—saying "one should perform the Śrīkrama."

For there is no such conventional usage; therefore, the second [alternative] is not tenable. The third is extension (*atideśa*), as for example: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *saurya* oblation of cooked rice. When this is stated, because of the connection with the desire (*kāma*), there arises an expectancy regarding the action: "What should one do to achieve spiritual luster? This [statement] fulfills that expectancy. Then, when there is an expectancy as to "by what means should one do it?", the meaning of the verbal root [supplies the answer].

It connects as an instrument (*karaṇatvena*). Since the collection of subsidiary parts (*aṅgakalāpa*) has not been recited [in the injunction], how one should perform [the rite] remains a requirement for fulfillment. Therefore, a word is supplied—namely, "sauryaṃ carum" (a rice-offering to Sūrya)—because it satisfies that requirement through similarity, characterized by having medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) as its substance and possessing a manifest indicative mark (*vyaktaliṅga*), just like the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
The sentence is: "One should perform the offering like the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Consequently, the ritual details (dharmas) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa are extended [to this rite].
For there is no such expectancy here, since the primary rite together with its subsidiaries is recited in its entirety here.

Furthermore, if the acquisition of ritual properties (dharma) were to occur solely through extension (atideśa), then, since the mantra for the seat has already been established by the statement in the *Śrīkrama*, "seated upon the seat with the seat-mantra" (*pīṭhamanunā āsane samupaviṣṭaḥ*), its re-enactment would be redundant once it is obtained through extension; this is according to the logic of the *Gṛhamedhīya-ājyabhāga* rule.

74) It clarifies that "only what has been stated is to be performed, and nothing more than this. And in this way, how could there be the application of anything additional? Furthermore—the attainment of [other] attributes occurs through extension (*atideśa*) from the *Śrīkrama*.
In that case, does it apply to all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) or to some of the ritual elements (*dharma*)?

Regarding the first [alternative], by whom is the absence of consecration with the ninety-four mantras established? For it is not as if one chooses the *ṛṣi* or the *hotṛ* priest [by default]; likewise, in the Sūtra, there is no consecration with the ninety-four mantras.

There exists the notion that "it must be done," by which [the objection] is refuted. Furthermore, [in my view], since there is no relationship of original and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), as long as it is stated that "it must be done," there is an absence of such a statement here; therefore, it is logical that there should be no consecration (*anabhimantraṇa*) with the ninety-four mantras.
[The additional reading—*tava mate sandarbhaviruddham* (in your view, this contradicts the context)—is found in manuscript *ba*.]
The position that there is an extension of whatever dharma [is prescribed] would be pleasing only to those who are beloved of the gods,
not to the wise.

Therefore, we do not perceive even a mustard-seed’s worth of valid authority (*pramāṇa*) for attaining the previously mentioned dharma. Thus, certain [elements] here written in the *Śrīkrama* are rootless; likewise, those stated in the *Śyāmākrama* are without authority and have been interpolated into the *Śrīkrama* and elsewhere. For indeed, there is no dharma that is devoid of authority.

This must be so. Therefore, relying on a work that has been rendered confused at will by one who is ignorant of the scent of Mīmāṃsā but merely proficient in the Sanskrit language, even the wise perform [their rites]; herein, some do not even attempt a correction. In this regard—

We consider it logical that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is indeed the power of the Kali age and nothing else; therefore, those [rites] belonging to that [era] should not be performed. Only that which is explicitly stated should be done, and where something is indicated as being taken from elsewhere—as in the case of the *āsana-mantra*—that should be adopted. That which has been written down by anyone without deliberation is not an authority.

Due to the absence of authoritative evidence, no *apūrva* (transcendental result) would arise from its performance. If it were to arise, then there would likewise be an extension of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rules to the *agnihotra*, and an extension of the *jyotiṣṭoma* rules to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Therefore, this confusion [of rules] is based on mere whim and lacks authority.
The connection is not to be trusted; enough of this excessive detail.

Furthermore— indeed, in the treatise, a single modification (vikṛti) has never been seen or heard of before as having multiple original forms (prakṛti), nor has a single action (kriyā) been seen to have multiple original forms. This author [mentions] certain properties (dharma) located in other sections by the word "saurya," such as those consisting of the seat, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and so forth.

How could one who attempts to synthesize into a single place various rules found in different sections— such as those concerning the consumption of betel and so forth, which reside in the *Śrīvidyā-prakaraṇa* (and additionally, according to some manuscripts, in other tantras)— be considered a knower of the true nature of dharma?

And it is not the case that, just as those *dharmas* belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are extended (*atideśa*) to the Dvādaśāha, and from there— by means of that extension— the *dharmas* situated within that specific context are further extended to the Dvirātra and so forth; likewise, Śrīvidyā is the root archetype (*mūlaprakṛti*), and from her, by means of extension, [the practices] such as betel-chewing are obtained for Parā.

Let all those specific characteristics consisting of the preparation of the seat and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), which accompany that [deity], be extended by analogy to Gaṇapati, who occupies the position of the archetype (prakṛti) for the two-night sacrifice and others. This being so, it should not be argued that there would be a multiplicity of archetypes;
for if the supreme [deity] has Śrī as her archetype, then the wearing of ornaments follows by extension alone.

In that context of attainment (*prāpti*), the phrase "whose body is adorned" would be redundant. Likewise, many other elements such as the striking with the left heel and so forth would be superfluous. Therefore, a relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) between those two is not possible.

Consequently, for those [procedures] for which there is an explicit scriptural statement—as in this very case regarding the ritual ending with the water-offering (*arghya*) to the Sun—[that status is established].
Thus, in the section concerning others (*parāprakaraṇe*), one should accomplish [the rite] with the general and specific *arghya* offerings, just as in the case of Śyāmā;
this applies wherever there is an unfulfilled expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in every respect, precisely in such a context.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is not logical for there to be contact with other dharmas elsewhere [than where they are prescribed], provided that "one must do exactly what has been stated" applies; in this very manner, the abandonment of rootless and confused dharmas in other contexts is to be understood.
Prāṇāyāma is the restraint of the breath; having performed it in conjunction with kumbhaka, recaka, and so forth, the root mantra is employed within that prāṇāyāma.
The necessity of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): [To be seen in Dvi-Pariccheda, Śi-Adhikāra 10, Vi-Prakaraṇa].

Then, one should perform even the resolve, which is established by general scriptural authority, as follows: "I shall perform the ritual sequence of Mahāgaṇapati for the sake of achieving freedom from obstacles in the worship of Śrīvidyā. And it is not...

One should not suspect how the *saṅkalpa* (mental resolve) is to be included since it is not mentioned in the *sūtra*; for just as purity and the sacred thread (*upavīta*) are invariably connected with all ritual acts in general, so too is the *saṅkalpa*. There are also scriptural statements in accordance with this, such as:
Whatever is performed without having sipped water (ācamana) and whatever is done devoid of a formal resolve (saṅkalpa),
that action becomes Rākṣasa.
Thus says the Mahābhārata regarding the duty of giving:
"First the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) is prescribed, and afterwards its dedication;
if the practitioner does not perform [the dedication], he obtains an uncertain fruit of his action."
This is also because of the statement in the Rudrayāmala, and likewise because it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). Therefore, that [saṅkalpa] is necessary;
and since the worship of Gāṇanāyakī is also an ancillary (*aṅga*) of Śrīvidyā, the saṅkalpa is indeed necessary for that as well.
And the mention of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅgollekhana*) is as follows:
One must necessarily mention the Tantric time; otherwise, O Śivā, that ritual act becomes outward-turned, like an oblation poured into ashes.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Yāmala*, the delineation of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) is mandatory.

[This delineation of the eight limbs is found on page 45 of the commentary on the Sūtra of the first section (Anugata-1-khaṇḍīya), and it is also present in the context of Dvīpa-śi-10. In the same way, this should be understood for the *Śyāmā* and other [deities].

Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs—the six limbs of the root mantra—upon the locations beginning with the heart, one should place them upon all the limbs using both palms with the complete root mantra. This indeed is the method of pervasive application (*vyāpakakaraṇa*). As it is said in the *Paramānandatantra*:
The touching of the entire body with both palms constitutes the pervasive [mudrā].

In this regard, the portion of the Nibandha beginning with "to the Lord joined with the twelve red Śaktis" (with the variant "nāthāya" in manuscript Ba) and ending with "one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa," is not to be trusted.
p.
76) "In one's own self" means in one's own heart. The word *ātman* is well-known to denote the mind (*manas*); because the mind and the heart are identical, it has that [heart] as its referent.
The meaning of the first four adjectives is clear. *Mātuluṅga*...

*Phalaviśeṣaḥ*: a specific kind of fruit. *Gadā*: a specific weapon, a mace. *Puṇḍrekṣuḥ*: a sugarcane with various lines; that is to say, one of many colors and many forms. *Tadrūpakārmukaḥ*: a bow having that form. *Śūlaḥ*:
a specific weapon, a trident. *Sudarśanam*: the discus. *Śaṅkha-pāśau*: the conch and the noose, which are well-known. *Utpalam*: the blue lotus.
The lotus is [the tenth]; the remaining [terms] are well known. Thus, he is one whose eleven hands are adorned in this manner, beginning with the citron and ending with the jewel-vase.

Although ten arms for the form of Śrī Mahāgaṇapati are well-known, the mention here of eleven seems contradictory; nevertheless, by the word *pāṇi*, the trunk (*śuṇḍā-daṇḍa*) is also to be understood here,
because the terms *kara*, *hasta*, and *pāṇi* are used as synonyms, and it is universally known in the world that "karin" means an elephant (*hastin*).
And thus, with ten arms and the trunk as the eleventh, it was said by the Blessed One, the author of the Sūtra, that "the hands are eleven," according to that intention.

Regarding the rule for the placement of weapons (*āyudha-sthāna-niyama*): although the specific rule for the placement of weapons on the right, left, and so forth is not explicitly stated here, nevertheless, the positions for the weapons should be applied according to the general technical convention (*sāmānya-paribhāṣā*). As it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*:
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, listen as I describe the meditation upon your weapons:
the sword, the arrow, the goad, the mace, the discus, the trident, and the bhuśuṇḍika.
The spear, staff, thunderbolt, javelin, iron club, barbed dart, and tomara;
the garland, mace, axe, and so forth— these are held in the right hands [meaning, starting from the sword,
they are the symbols marked by the uppermost signs on the fingers].
In his left hands, he firmly holds a noose and a conch shell, a bow and a fruit, a shield and a khaṭvāṅga staff, a book, a bell, a hand-drum, and a severed head.
She displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holds a conch, a discus, and a flower-vessel, situated in pairs.
When not explicitly stated, [the weapons are assigned] everywhere according to logic by means of the sequences of left, right, clockwise, and the opposite.

[For the knowledge of how to bestow the weapons, see another method in the commentary on Sūtra 5 of the preceding section (Khaṇḍa 4). By men, [they are assigned] according to the sequence of left, right, downward, and clockwise.

when the specific place for the weapon is not mentioned, water should be poured [into the vessel] with the root mantra, starting from a sword and ending with an axe.

these are to be seen in the second part, verses 15.7–14, 15.8.1–2, and 15.8.2, for the purpose of extracting the mudrās of the weapons (astra) and so forth. Those beginning with the conch (śaṅkha) and ending with the vessel (pātra) are fixed on the left hand, or they may be placed on either side at will.

The five pairs beginning with the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa) are positioned facing forward. Whichever number of pairs is on the right hand, the other [number] is on the left hand. Starting from the upper left and proceeding to the upper right constitutes the clockwise order; conversely, the opposite is the counter-clockwise order. There is an option between these two.
This is the meaning. In the present context, the sequences of circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) and counter-circumambulation (apradakṣiṇa) are not possible regarding the weapons of Gaṇapati.

For instance, according to the aforementioned statements, the connection with the left hand is necessary for the citron (mātuluṅga), the bow, the conch, and the cluster of grain; whereas [the same applies] to the mace (gadā), the trident (śūla), the discus (cakra), the lotus (utpala), and the tusk (danta).

The connection with Dakṣa is likewise [to be understood]. Therefore, in accordance with the sequence of the Sūtra recitation and the statements of the Rudrayāmala, it is appropriate that the aforementioned pairs face one another directly. [These pairs are:
the citron and the mace, the bow and the trident, the conch and the discus, the noose and the lotus, and the cluster of grain.

Of these pairs of his own tusks, the first of each pair is placed in the upper left hand and the second in the upper right hand; in this sequence, they should be joined progressively downward. Thus, when the ten arms are occupied with the five pairs, the water-pot remains in the remaining trunk.

This is to be understood. Although the location of the teeth is not mentioned in the *Yāmala* statement, nevertheless, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is on the lower right. Since the ear of grain (*dhānyamañjarī*) is included among the fruits, there is thus a rule for the left side.
One whose temples (*gaṇḍa*)—the cheeks, intoxication, or rut-fluid (*dāna*)—are split open and flowing; as Amara states: "The word *gaṇḍa* means cheek, intoxication, or flow.

One who is full of bliss, meaning one who is full of supreme joy. The Lord of Obstacles (*Vighneśvara*), distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, who is the destroyer (*nighna*)—that is, the annihilator—of all the calamities (*dhvaṃsa*) consisting of clusters of undesirable things produced by obstacles.
One should meditate. || 4 ||

The meaning is "having consecrated [the water]. Having fashioned a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square with pure water worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, and having scattered flowers therein, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions, [beginning] with "To the fire-mandala... Having scattered—that is, having thrown—the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), namely the root six limbs, into the mandala consisting of the collection of the emanated triangle and so forth; the words "fire" (*vahni*) and so on denote the respective directions.

Although a short sūtra stating "in the intermediate directions" (*vidikṣu*) could have been used, the longer sūtra stating "fire, lord" (*vahnyīśa*) is employed for the sake of obtaining a specific sequence.

In this context, although it is understood from the entire statement— beginning with "Obeisance to the circle of fire" and ending with "filling it with pure water" [meaning: by the statement found in the root-sūtra]—
that everything is subsidiary to the act of filling, nevertheless, one offers the grass-bundle (prastara) with the *sūktavāka* mantra.

Just as in that [preceding] case, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), one must state that each of the three mantras ending with "namo 'dhārāya," "namaḥ pātrāya," and "namo 'mṛtāya" serves as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) respectively for the placement of the *ādhāra* vessel, the placement of the *pātra* vessel, and the filling of the vessel with water.

Because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). In reality, however, there is no contradiction even with respect to *vākya*, because the definition of a sentence as stated in Jaimini’s Sūtra—"That which has a single purpose is one sentence, provided that if divided, it would remain expectant"—is not met here. In some manuscripts, the phrase "namo 'rghyapātrāya" follows this.

The reading "ity ādhārapātre dhṛtvā" (having placed [it] in the support-vessel) is [the correct one]. In that case, there is no dispute. "Pure water" refers to what was mentioned previously. The ritual procedure for the worship of the eight [deities] beginning with Pīṭhaśakti and Dharma, along with Mahāgaṇapati, in five enclosures; he now describes the drawing of the yantra and so forth, preceded by the rules regarding the pīṭha (p.

Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmarūpiṇī, Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, and Vighnanāśinī with the syllable *ṛṃ*.

The section ending with "in front" and "on the pedestal" (purataḥ... pīṭhe) determines the support for the form (mūrtti). The sequence should be understood as follows: a square on the outside of everything, within that an eight-petalled lotus, within that a hexagon, and within that a triangle. Regarding the [powers] beginning with Tīvrā, they are the pedestal-powers (pīṭha-śakti).

Since no specific order is mentioned there, the nine powers (*śakti*) are to be worshipped in the eight directions starting from the east and in the center.
The fourfold group beginning with Dharma is in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest (*vāyavya*), and the fourfold group beginning with Adharma is likewise placed there.

One should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis) and the group of eight beginning with Dharma upon the seat itself, proceeding in a clockwise direction starting from the west; for it is heard in scripture that both [the powers and the qualities] occupy the same location. Regarding the directional rule for Dharma and the others, it begins from the northwest (vāyukoṇa).
As stated in the Paramānanda Tantra:
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty [are located] starting from the western [face];
and likewise the four beginning with adharma... thus [it is said].

Having worshipped by means of the fivefold service—that is, by offering in five ways consisting of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings—the mantras for this are as follows: *Laṃ*, I offer perfume to the self of earth; *Haṃ*, I offer flowers to the self of space; *Yaṃ*, I offer incense to the self of air; *Raṃ*...
I offer a lamp to the fire-self, *vaṃ*; I offer nectar-offerings to the nectar-self. Regarding this, the authority is found in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
"Scent and flowers... (Note: The specific details concerning these ritual offerings are to be seen in the second part of the *Śiṣyādhikāra*, verse 7).

"With the root mantra ten times" means ten repetitions. that is, in all cases of worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*) and the libation of the respective deities—

It recurs in the case of the distinctness of substances.
As for the writing of "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) as the remainder of the mantra in the *tarpaṇa* mantra within the *Nibandha*, that is incorrect.

Therefore, a difference in meaning is also necessary. Oṃ Hūṃ Indrāya vajrahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 2. Oṃ Hūṃ Agnaye śaktihastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 3. Oṃ Hūṃ Yamāya daṇḍahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 4. Oṃ Hūṃ Nairṛtaye khaḍgahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 5. Oṃ Hūṃ Varuṇāya pāśahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 6. Oṃ Hūṃ Vāyave dhvajahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 7. Oṃ Hūṃ Kuberāya gadāhastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 8. Oṃ Hūṃ Īśānāya triśūlahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 9. Oṃ Hūṃ Anantāya cakrahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. 10. Oṃ Hūṃ Brahmaṇe padmahastāya saparivārāya namaḥ. [End of section 6]
In the fourteenth thread of the *Śyāmākrama* section of the *Khaṇḍa*, the ten root mantras of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) are present; these are to be taken.

Alternatively, they may be used with the name-mantra joined with the eight-syllable mantra to be described hereafter. (In this context, the eight-syllable mantra is "I worship the venerable sandals" [*śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*], and the name-mantra is "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Indra" [*oṃ śrī indrāya namaḥ*].)
This is what is intended by the above. Thus ends the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*).

He states a certain general rule (*paribhāṣā*) useful for practice: "In all cases" (*sarvatra*). "In all cases" means in all general forms of worship (*pūjā*), regarding the names of the deities—that is, in the name-mantras (*nāmamantra*). The locative case signifies inclusion. [The name should be] preceded by *śrī*.
First, having uttered "Śrīpada," then "Pādukām," and then "Pūjayāmi"; thus, it amounts to "I worship the Śrīpādukā. || 8 ||
Furthermore, having performed the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth for Gaṇanātha,

and having thus worshipped the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*), one should again satisfy the deity Gaṇanātha ten times and honor him with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Then, at the end of the *praṇava* and *māyā* [mantras], [one offers] to all obstructing spirits and to all elemental beings (*sarvabhūta*).

Having recited "huṃ svāhā" three times and offered the *bali*, one should summon a single *baṭuka* with the thought that he is Gaṇapati, and a single *śakti* with the thought that she is Siddhalakṣmī;

having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice (*akṣata*), and having offered the *ādimā*, *upādimā*, and *madhyamā* [portions], [one prays]: "May there be no obstacles for me..."
Having caused the favor to be granted with the words "May there be success in the mantra," and having paid homage, one should recite it according to one's capacity. || 9 ||

Having worshipped—that is, having honored—the *pañcāvaraṇī*, which is the collective group (*samūha*) of the five deities of the obstructions (*āvaraṇadevatā*) in the manner thus described; [the term *pañcāvaraṇī* is derived from *pañca-āvaraṇa* with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule for *dvigu* compounds]. By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is indicated that just as in the previously mentioned worship of the five obstructions, one should likewise worship the *pañcāvaraṇī*.

This is likewise a restatement (anuvāda). Thus, the misconception that it is merely an injunction regarding the number (*kāma*) is dispelled. It is indicated that this falls within the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*). "Tenfold" means ten times.
The method of libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be understood as being at the end of the commentary on Sūtra 7 on pages 80–81 of this section.
This has already been explained previously. Furthermore, the sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) are enumerated in the *Paramānanda-tantra* as follows:
water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*). [Regarding these modes of service, see Dīpikā-pañjikā-śiromaṇi-vivaraṇa-dṛṣṭi.]
O Śivā, [one should offer] a bath, clothing, and ornaments;
fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and also a betel leaf;
as well as the waving of lights, the añjali gesture, circumambulation, and prostration.
"One should indeed count the offerings individually, O Goddess, sixteen for each. Thus [it is said].
Or, at the beginning, the sixteen services mentioned in the Sūtra [may be performed].
In this context, the fire sacrifice (homa) mentioned in the ritual manual as an ancillary part of the worship is without foundation.
The *praṇava* (oṃ) is well known; *māyā* is *hrīṃ*. At the end and beginning of these two, one should recite the remainder ending with *svāhā*.
This is the mantra for offering the oblation (*balidāna*). Having recited this mantra three times, one should then perform the offering of the oblation.

The desired materials for the *bali* offering should be taken as prescribed in the *Śrīkrama*. Regarding the location, it is stated in the *Śrīkrama* that it should be from one's own left side. The phrase "with the thought of Gaṇapati" is to be construed with the word "having worshipped.
This means having meditated upon [the deity] in the form of Gaṇapati. As for the order of recitation...

Setting aside the sequence of the ritual acts (*krama*), first comes the invocation (*āvāhana*), then the visualization (*bhāvana*), and then the worship (*arcana*); the same applies to what follows. Here, the invocation and other rites for both [deities] are performed according to the *padārthānusamaya* method (for the distinction between *kāṇḍānusamaya* and *padārthānusamaya*, see Dīpikā on the Śivopādhyāya-vivaraṇa, verse 8).

This is not like the application of collyrium and so forth, which follows the sequence of the sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*), because here there is no sublation and because it is possible for all [the items] to have an equal proximity to the primary element. Having applied the first clearly, the second at the end, and the third in the middle, this is the purificatory rite of realization (*pratipattisaṃskāra*) for those in the middle.
This is because of the mention of the "second" [offering]. Its meaning is that one should consecrate the substance with the gift.

Thus, after the worship of the covering (āvaraṇapūjā), there is simply the removal of any defects in the substance. The sense is that, having caused grace to be bestowed, one should personally bring about their satisfaction so that grace may accrue to both of them.
The passage beginning with "namas" and ending with "japet" is clear in its meaning.

Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Nibandha* regarding the worship of the *baṭuka* and the *suvāsinī* after the recitation has been clarified by this [work] as being contrary to the *sūtra*. || 9 ||
Regarding the dismissal of Gaṇapati:

if the fire-ritual (agnikārya) has been successfully completed, one should offer oblations into the fire previously consecrated according to rule with mantras beginning with Śrī and Śrīpati and ending with Vighnakartṛ, each concluding with "svāhā"; then, having returned, one should [worship] the Deity three times.

Having satisfied [the deities] with the appropriate offerings, having accepted the five elements (pañcaka), and having dissolved Mahāgaṇapati into one's own self, one whose resolve is perfected should dwell happily; may there be auspiciousness! || 10 ||

Thus ends the second section, the *Gaṇapatiprakaraṇa*, within the *Kalpasūtra* composed by the venerable Kulācārya, the great preceptor Śrī Bhārgava Paraśurāma— the foremost disciple of Mahādeva, born from the womb of Reṇukā, and the destroyer of the race of wicked Kṣatriyas.

By the word "yadi" (if), it is indicated that the oblation may be either performed or not performed. By the phrase "prior to Bali," the remaining sequence [of the location] is indicated. "According to rule" means: according to the manner of the procedure for the oblation explained previously in the ninth section; that is to say, by the method that will be described hereafter.
The nature of the mantra is "Śrī-Śrīpatibhyāṃ svāhā."

Regarding the division of the mantra written in the *Nibandha* as "svāhā to Śrī, svāhā to Śrīpati," the question is: is the couple one deity, or are there two deities? In the first case, the division into two mantras is inappropriate; in the second case, [it would apply] to the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the *Nibandha*, the inclusion of the collective mantra (*samaṣṭimantra*) in the form "I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī-Śrīpati" is improper;

therefore, it should be disregarded as being contrary to the context. Nor should it be argued that, according to your own view, the same application of the collective mantra would follow even during the fourfold libation (*caturāvṛttitarpaṇa*), for in that case, one worships each individual deity within the couples four times.
It does not proceed by saying "having satisfied the couples. In the section on worship, it simply says "one should worship the couples alone.
Therefore, the status of the couple as the deity is clear. The same applies to the place of the fire-oblation (homa).

By the expression "Śrī, Śrīpati, and so forth," it is made clear that the couple constitutes a single deity. Otherwise, he would have simply said "from Yādi up to Vighnakartṛ"; thus, the inclusion of Śrīpati would be redundant. Nor can it be argued that in the phrase "up to Vighnakartṛ" there is an inclusion of a single deity, for if each were a separate deity, why [would this be stated]?

It must be said that [the term] would not be informative (*jñāpaka*). If this were to be informative regarding the nature of the mantra, then since Śrī, Śrīpati, and so forth would already be obtained by the phrase "by those ending with the makers of obstacles" (*vighnakartṛntaiḥ*), the inclusion of "Śrī, Śrīpati, and so forth" (*śrīśrīpatyādi*) would be redundant; therefore, it is meaningful as being informative regarding the nature of the mantra. [The phrase is] "by those ending with the makers of obstacles."
Since it is meaningful as that which brings about the cessation of the subsequent couple, everything is consistent. Therefore,

for the sake of completing the count of four hundred and forty-four libations during the fourfold repetition of the *tarpaṇa*, according to the previously stated reasoning, [one should perform] each one—

Regarding the status of being a deity (*devatātva*): both in the context of worship (*pūjā*) and in the fire-oblation (*homa*), by virtue of the stated indicator (*jñāpaka*), the status of being a deity exists only as a collective function (*vyāsajyavṛtti*). Therefore, the nature of the mantra is exactly as we have described it.
By the phrase "up to those who cause obstacles," there is an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the fire and the couple.

Regarding the phrase "having offered" (*hutvā*), when there is an expectancy for a substance, it is clarified by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when no specific material is prescribed, clarified butter (*ājya*) is used," that the substance is indeed clarified butter. However, in the case of a specific desire, the specific substance may be sweetmeats (*modaka*) and so forth. By the expression "having returned," it is indicated that the place of the oblation (*homapradeśa*) is distinct from the place of worship (*pūjāpradeśa*). The remainder is as before. [This is] with those who are worthy.

Together with those who are conversant with the tradition, we shall clarify the intended meaning of this specific qualification in detail later on, at the end of the commentary on Sūtra 30 in the third section of the *Śrīkrama*—beginning with the words: "Nowadays, those whose senses are unsubdued... and so forth—after having fully accepted and adopted the fivefold set (*pañcaka*) in the *Śrīkrama*.

According to the procedure that will be explained hereafter, the word *saha* (together) does not necessarily imply that the accompanying element must be procured even in the absence of a suitable object; rather, in its absence, it does not impose an expiation for the omission of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) factor. Instead, when it exists, it indicates concomitance (*sāhitya*), and when it is absent, it signifies that one should [offer] the *prastara* bundle by itself alone, together with the branch.

It is like the expression "he strikes. Since the limits for the worship of Gaṇapati are not stated here—as is the case with Śyāmā and others—and since the number of recitations (japa) is also not mentioned, one must take refuge in another tantra. Regarding that, the statement from another tantra is found in the *Tantrasāra*:

"Being composed, one should meditate on the mantra and recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, together with four thousand and forty thousand [repetitions]. One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with eight substances, such as sweetmeats (modaka), ten thousand times [for each]. Thus it is said.

Having performed the dismissal with the *udvāsana-mudrā*, one whose resolve is accomplished and whose task is finished may wander happily. This indicates that for one who has performed the prescribed rites, there is not only the destruction of obstacles, but this further result as well. By this...

It is indicated by the phrase "having made a firm resolve" that whatever is desired is accomplished through the worship of Anaṅga-Svatantra-Gaṇanāyaka, even if it is not an auxiliary means for the practice of Śrīvidyā. (For the specific knowledge regarding the performance of this ritual manual for the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa— Śrī Prapañcasāra).
The *Gaṇeśapurāṇa*, *Śāradātilaka*, *Mantramahodadhi*, and other Tantric texts should be consulted.
"Śivam" is as before, indicating the conclusion of the section.
Thus ends the second section, titled "The Manual of Gaṇanāyaka," in the commentary on the Paraśurāma-sūtra named Saubhāgyodaya, composed by Śrī Rāmeśvara.
Upon the completion of the Sūtra, that which was to be purified must be indicated, and the remaining portion shall be fulfilled by the grace of the Primordial One. (Thus ends the second section. Śrī.
The Third Section: The Śrīkrama, the Chapter on Lalitā.
[I worship her] who is united with the three eternal currents (nityaughatraya), enveloped by the eight enclosures (aṣṭāvaraṇa) and the six limbs (aṅga).
For those who contemplate it, words issue effortlessly from the mouth through its grace.

Thus, having described the worship of Gaṇapati as an ancillary to the worship of Śrī Lalitā by means of the first section, he begins to explain the sequence for the worship of the Supreme Deity, Śrī Lalitā: "Having thus worshipped Gaṇapati, with all obstacles and impediments dispelled, [one should proceed] regarding the sole sovereign of the circle of energies (śakticakra)..."
One should begin the ritual procedure of Śrī Lalitā. || 1 ||
By the passage ending with "evam" and "vighnavyatikaraḥ," it is indicated that one should first perform the worship of Gaṇapati for some time, and only thereafter begin the worship of Śrī Lalitā.

Thus, having worshipped—that is, having practiced—in the manner previously described, all [obstacles] have been shaken off, meaning they have been dispelled. All [desires] are complete, meaning they are entirely fulfilled.
By whom the occurrences and aggregations of obstacles [are overcome].

This [phrase], "the worship of Gaṇanāyaka," constitutes the primary action (*pradhānakarman*) and is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). This is an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*); furthermore, due to the natural force of the preceding qualification, it is also an injunctive statement regarding entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*). Alternatively, this is not a qualification of the qualified person; for if that were the case...
Otherwise, the worship of Gaṇapati would result in being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the fire-worship (*agnīṣomapāsanā*). Nor is this a desirable consequence.

There are six means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that establish subordination, namely the third [book's] *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth. Among these, subordination established by the third means of proof, *vākya*, remains uncontradicted due to the absence of any *liṅga* or *śruti* that could invalidate it.

Since it is impossible to deny that the constituent parts are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this [text] rather enjoins the worship of Lalitā as qualified by the sequence consisting in its occurring subsequent to the worship of Gaṇapati. Alternatively, this commencement is qualified by a specific sequence which itself is qualified by the quality consisting in the prior worship.

By this, worship performed with grace at that time is enjoined. The phrase "with all obstacles and their complications dispelled" is a restatement of the previously mentioned result. Thus, what is called the "commencement" (ārambha) is a specific kind of resolve (saṅkalpa), such as "I shall commence the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. By the expression "one should commence the Lalitā-krama," [the practice is intended] for as long as one lives.
The resolve, "I shall perform [the worship]," is established. Its ancillary part is the propitiation of Gaṇapati.

Furthermore, this resolve, characterized by these qualities, is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) to the worship of Śrī Lalitā—just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—because it possesses the definition stated in Jaimini’s Sūtra: "That for which the substance is not intended to be processed. It is not [a proximate auxiliary].

Furthermore, it must be stated: what difference does it make in the performance [of the rite] whether [the worship of Gaṇapati] is a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) or takes the form of a specific injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) as just explained? If it were a qualification of the qualified person, then one who has not performed the worship of Gaṇapati due to negligence or the like—being thus unqualified—would be like a blind person or the like when beginning the worship of Lalitā.

Just as in the case of one who has performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, when there is a lack of fruit for the ritual performed up to that point and thus a state of vigilance arises, then— having abandoned the worship of Lalitā and having accomplished the worship of Gaṇapati—
one becomes endowed with the requisite qualification (*sādhikāra*) and may thereafter perform the worship of Śrīvidyā. This applies according to the view of the specific injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
Since the commencement [of the rite] is an ancillary part of the worship of Gaṇapati, and the commencement itself is an ancillary part of the worship of Lalitā,
86) when the commencement occurs through forgetfulness, something is prescribed for the purpose of removing the fault produced by the omission of an ancillary part.

Expiation does not follow the subsidiary parts (aṅga), but rather involves the repetition of the principal act (pradhāna). Nor should it be argued that, rather than omitting the subsidiary entirely, it is better to perform it—since the principal act does not depend upon the subsidiaries—and thus let there be no repetition, while the subsidiary alone is performed. This is not to be said.

To the extent that the primary subsidiaries (*pūrvāṅga*) possess the status of auxiliaries for the principal act (*pradhāna*) in producing the transcendental result (*apūrva*), they are required in rites performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*). However, because there is no auxiliary to produce the *apūrva* through the principal act in such cases, the principal act perishes immediately thereafter; thus, the performance of the subsidiaries alone would be futile. In obligatory rites (*nitya*), however, they must be performed as long as one lives.

When it is stated that "it must be performed free from the omission of any limb," a contraction of the term "all limbs" (sakalāṅga)— meaning "as many limbs as are possible" or "as many limbs as are known"— is appropriate, for fear that the scripture would otherwise incur invalidity due to being impossible to carry out in its entirety. And thus:

It was established in the sixth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that the production of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is postulated through the principal rite accompanied by as many auxiliaries as are known according to one's capacity. Thus, since the worship of Lalitā is obligatory, even if some unknown auxiliary is omitted, the *apūrva* is generated by the principal rite together with the other auxiliaries; therefore, the performance of that specific auxiliary would be redundant.

There is no re-performance of an ancillary rite (*aṅga*) in the form of the worship of Gaṇapati that was previously unknown. If something must be performed for the sake of dispelling obstacles, then either the recitation of the Vināyaka-stava or the muttering (*japa*) of its mantra should be performed. Such is the deliberation regarding these variations in the performance of rites.
This has been composed; let the wise investigate further than this.

The "wheels of power" (*śakticakra*) belong to the sole sovereign of the wheels of power; they consist of the five wheels beginning with the triangle, which are situated among the nine wheels that are the constituent parts of the *Śrīcakra*. As it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"By means of the four wheels of Śiva and the five wheels of Śakti..."
The Śrīcakra, perfected with nine wheels, is the body of Śiva and Śivā.
"The triangle, the octagon, the two decagons, and the fourteen-spoked [wheel]—these are the five wheels of Śakti. Thus it is said.

Of them, she is the one principal heroine; or alternatively, "śaktis" refers to married women, and the "cakra" is their assembly—among them, she is the one, the peerless heroine, the sovereign (nāthā), the most excellent. And it is not the case that [the compound is invalid], for the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) applies only when the particle *na* is used in the sense of exclusion (*nirdhāraṇa*). She is the controller of the world.

How is this meaning to be stated? Even though the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is prohibited [in this case], there is no obstacle to forming a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*), just as in the word *puruṣottama*. Alternatively, the powers (*śakti*) are those which bring about the respective effects residing in their respective objects;
the one, non-dual leader (*nāyikā*) who impels the collection of these powers is she. As it has been said:
In the Śrī Devībhāgavata:
"O best of sages, know that from Śiva down to the earth, all the powers who accomplish their tasks are impelled by me alone."

Alternatively, the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are Śyāmā, Vārtālī, and so forth; they themselves constitute the "wheel" (*cakra*), meaning the retinue, based on the usage of learned authorities such as: "The wheel is to be served; the king is to be served. The meaning of "the sole leader of those [powers]" (*tāsāmekanāyikā*) is that she is the peerless controller.
By this, the preeminence of Śrīvidyā is indicated. Thus: "the sole leader of the wheel of powers."

The quality belongs to Lalitā. Likewise, the deityhood of the qualified [entity] arises because, in the originative injunction (utpattivākya), the deity is that which is qualified by the qualities heard therein, as in "to Agni Pavamāna" or "to Agni... [etc.].
Just as in the case of "pāvakāya" and so forth, there is a rule that the deity heard in the original injunction (utpattivākya) must be mentioned in all instances;
thus, wherever the mention of the deity's name is mandatory, it must be mentioned precisely as qualified by its attributes— as, for example,
the mention of the sole sovereign of the Śakti-cakra in the twilight recitations (sandhyājapa), the twilight worship (sandhyāpūjā), and so on.

"I shall perform such-and-such a rite for the pleasure of Śrī Lalitā"—thus is the declaration. Otherwise, in the Pavamāneṣṭi, one would simply say, "I offer what is pleasing to Agni. Therefore, in this context, the mantras must be joined with the deity as qualified by the specific attribute. [This applies to] the sequence, the worship, and the spiritual practice.
Or one should begin.
The etymological derivation of the name Lalitā is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"She shines (lalate) transcending the worlds; therefore she is called Lalitā."

In this regard, our supreme preceptors have shown another etymological interpretation suggested by the word "ca" (and) in their *Sahasranāmabhāṣya*: "Lalita" refers to a specific action born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-bhāva*); she who possesses that is Lalitā.
By this, it is intimated that this form has the erotic sentiment as its primary essence. || 1 ||

Then, regarding the meditation and other practices to be performed during the *brāhmamuhūrta*, he teaches the meditations on the Guru and so forth through two verses— [the phrase "from here onwards, the daily rites to be performed by the worshipper of Lalitā" is found in the Ba manuscript].
At the hour of Brahmā, having abandoned sleep, a Brāhmaṇa should contemplate the Guru, who is the form of Paramaśiva, for the dissolution of his sins. || 2 ||
The Brāhma-muhūrta: having divided the day, which consists of sixty ghaṭikās, into thirty parts, the twenty-eighth muhūrta is the Brāhma. As it is stated in the Devībhāgavata:
"That which is the twenty-eighth muhūrta is named Brāhma."

Having risen at that time, the wise man should contemplate his own welfare. Furthermore, there is another definition of the *brāhmamuhūrta* well-known in the Purāṇas; therein, the prohibition against sleeping is also found in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, the *Ratnāvalī*, and other such texts, as follows:
The third watch of the final portion of the night should be known as the Brāhma-muhūrta; it is prescribed for awakening.

Five times five [twenty-five] units constitute the time of dawn (uṣaḥkāla); seven times five [thirty-five] units are the rising of the dawn-red (aruṇodaya); eight times five [forty] units constitute the morning (prātaḥ), after which the rising of the sun (sūryodaya) is traditionally recorded.
Regarding the fruit [of this], Dhanvantari says: "The acceptance [of gifts] by the virtuous for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and affection is supreme;
one who acts thus shall eternally attain residence in heaven."

And in the *Ratnāvalī*: "Sleep during the *brāhma-muhūrta* causes the destruction of merit; if a twice-born man sleeps then out of delusion, he is purified by a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance. Thus it is said.

In that context, the Brahmin, having abandoned sleep, wakes up; although the abandonment of sleep is generally established by memory at that time, it is enjoined here as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), since it was not otherwise established. Its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice is like the rule in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*): "One should not speak untruth."
Regarding the excellence of that state of being free from sleep, it is stated in the *Tripurārahasya*:
"When two muhūrtas remain until the rising of the sun,
that time is declared to be the dawn (uṣaḥkāla), which brings auspiciousness to practitioners."
O Rāma, at that time, whatever object a person contemplates with an unwavering mind, that very thing arises for him by the natural power of the timing and moment.
But he who, in this time that resembles a wish-fulfilling tree, does not awaken;
or having awakened, being of extremely dull intellect, does not contemplate his own welfare—[he is truly lost].
"Deprived of all his own interests, he sinks like a cow in the mud. Thus it is said.

Having arisen at such a time for the sake of destroying all sins— the dative case here is used in the sense of purpose (tādarthye)— Śiva [here, as in the commentary on the first sūtra on the previous seventh page,
where the author of the Vṛtti cites the verse beginning with "śrutipathagalitānām," even the venerable Sūta calls the Lord Śiva the "Guru of Gurus"; likewise, in this place as well, the Lord...].
Even the illustrious Rāma, son of Jamadagni, declared this Parameṣṭhin, the illustrious Śiva-Paramaśiva, to be his Guru.

This very quality of being most worthy of salutation and his status as my own deity belong to the Lord, the Guru of Gurus—[as stated by] the author of the *Dvitiyavrtti-diparisishtaka* on the *Paushkara-kalpa-sutra*.
He alone is the Guru, and none other than him.
Having thus touched [the object] and meditated upon it in the mind. || 2 ||

Having visualized the root-consciousness (*mūlasaṃvid*) blazing from its base up to the aperture of Brahmā (*vidhibila*), tawny like ten million flashes of lightning and as yellow as the rising sun; and having mentally repeated the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*)—beginning with *ka* or *ha*—ten times, the web of impurities (*kaśmalajāla*) is destroyed by its rays. || 3 ||

The root is the *ādhāra-cakra*; starting from that and extending up to the aperture of the crown (*vidhi-bila*), it is connected with the phrase "blazing" (*jvalantīm*). Like millions of flashes of lightning (*taṭit-koṭayaḥ*), it is tawny (*kaḍārām*) or brownish-red (*kapiśām*);
like the young sun (*taruṇa-divākaraḥ*), the sun situated in the middle of the sky, it is golden-yellow (*piñjarām*), and for that very reason, it is blazing.
Having meditated upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlasaṃvid*), which is the mind free from objects, and by means of its rays— the rays that are flames of the nature of consciousness—
one becomes such that the nets (*jāla*) or masses of impurities (*kaśmala*) have been struck down and removed;
then, with the mind, one should [recite] the fifteen-syllable *vidyā*, either the *Kādi* form worshipped by Kāma or the *Hādi* form worshipped by Lopāmudrā.
Having meditated upon the phonemes distinguished by their sequence.

In this commentary, the recitation of one's own guru’s sandals, the salutation with the five mudrās, and other verses composed according to one's own fancy have been written down; these are not intended by the Sūtra and are to be disregarded.
Likewise, [the same applies to] the mantras for cleaning the teeth and the rule regarding the twenty mouthfuls of water.
Those that are immeasurable should be abandoned. || 3 ||
Then, regarding the ritual of bathing and the twilight prayers (*snāna-sandhyā-karma*), he says:
when the time for the bathing rite has arrived, one should apply [the water] to the head three times with the root mantra.
Having drunk three handfuls of water consecrated with that [mantra] three times, having satiated the ancestors three times with water, having sprinkled oneself three times,
and having put on two garments [with the *mūla-mantra*—
this phrase is added in manuscript *ba2*], and having uttered "Hrāṃ," "Haṃsa" accompanied by the three long vowels [this phrase is added in manuscript *ta kośe*], and having uttered "Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Saḥ."
Having offered arghya three times with the mantra "Svāhā to Mārtāṇḍabhairava, accompanied by the power of light (prakāśaśakti), to Savitṛ," [he proceeds]. || 4 ||
p.

89) When the rite of bathing has arrived, that is, at the occasion for bathing; by this, its occurrence subsequent to the Vedic bath is indicated. This very meaning is clearly stated in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"After the Vedic rites have been performed by members of the three castes, all Tantric rites are then carried out. Thus it is said.

In this context, there is a repetition of the mantra for each individual añjali. Since the plural number in the word *añjalīn* establishes a plurality of substances, a repetition of the action is also required, because the repetition of the mantra when there is a plurality of substances has been established in the eleventh [book of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]. When the expectancy arises as to where [the offering] is to be given, it is understood to be "on one's own head," because that is appropriate due to its nature as a bath.

[The word] *pūraṇīyam* [is to be supplied]. "With the root" (*mūlena*) means while reciting the root mantra; that is its meaning. "Three times" (*triḥ*) refers to those [waters] consecrated by it, i.e., consecrated by the root mantra. The word "three times" connects with the word "consecrated" (*abhimantritāḥ*) because of their proximity, and not with the word "having drunk" (*pītvā*), because of the latter's distance. Therefore, [the sense is] of water consecrated by the root mantra three times, [which is to be taken] only once.

Regarding the consumption [of the nectar]: having satisfied [the deity] three times, one recites the root mantra and performs the recitation of the mantra once—namely, "I satisfy Śrī Lalitā, the sole leader of the wheel of powers"—because this is of the nature of a repeated action (*kriyā*). However, it has already been established previously that in the case of a fourfold libation, there is only a repetition of the mantra (*mantrāvṛtti*), not a repetition of the action. For indeed...
There exists a scriptural authority that establishes a distinction between substances; therefore, the mantra is used only once.

The same applies to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). The word "self" (*ātmānam*) refers to the body, because a refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by sprinkling cannot pertain to the primary meaning [of the self]. This is because no specific mantra is prescribed for the acts of satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
One should apply [the term] "with the root" (mūlena). As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"O Supreme Goddess, when no mantra is specified, one should employ the root mantra."

Because of the phrase "having offered with the root [mantra]," there is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*); yet, if that were the case, the word *tat* (that) in the phrase "those consecrated by that" would be redundant even when an ellipsis is supplied. Therefore, there must be an insertion (*adhyāhāra*). The donning of the garment, which is established by traditional law (*smṛti*), is restated here; its meaning is "reciting the root mantra while putting on the garment. [The portion in brackets is an addition found in manuscript *ba*.]

The fruit of that is to be understood as the knowledge that the rite of bathing has been completed. Having said this—and having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) "I shall perform the Tantric *sandhyā* following the Vedic *sandhyā*" (this additional phrase is found in the Ba manuscript)—one should omit everything up to this point; the mantra for offering the *arghya* water ends with *svāhā*. Even though [the purpose] is evident from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra itself...

If the deity has already been obtained, the mention of "Savitṛ" is redundant. Nevertheless, regarding the phrase "having offered the *arghya*," the meaning of the act of giving (*dāna*) consists of the renunciation of a substance intended for a deity, preceded by the destruction of one's own ownership. This takes the form: "This belongs to such-and-such a deity; it is not mine. In that context, according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, [the formula is]: "To Mārtaṇḍabhairava, this; not mine."

It is established. Just as in the case of "He worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," the dative form *savitre* is used to set aside that [previous rule]. Here too, since it is impossible to give again a substance already given once, it is established that there is a different substance for the subsequent half-portion (*aparārdhya*). And thus, due to the distinctness of the substances, there is a repetition of the mantra, just as in the following example:
The mantra for threshing various seeds. || 5 ||
Then, the meditation on the Śrīcakra and the offering of *arghya* to the Goddess within the solar disc (*savitṛmaṇḍala*) are prescribed:
having meditated upon the wheel of nine triangles (*navayonicakra*) in the center of that disc, [this is the Śrī Tripurā Gāyatrī, clearly stated as follows:
*Aiṃ tripurasundari vidmahe klīṃ pīṭhakāmini dhīmahi | tannaḥ klinnā*.

Having uttered "vācam uccārya," [one says] "tripurasundari vidmahe"; having uttered "kāmam uccārya," [one says] "pīṭhakāmini dhīmahi"; having uttered "śaktim uccārya," [one says] "tannaḥ klinnā pracodayāt. Having thus offered *arghya* three times to the Great Goddess, and having touched [the vessel] one hundred and eight times while reciting the mantra, one should observe silence. || 5 ||

In the center of that solar disc, which appears as a circular form, is the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*), a wheel in which there are nine *yoni*s: four facing outward and five facing toward oneself.
The meaning is "the Śrīcakra. This has been stated in the Kāmikāgama: "The nine-yoni is the Śrīcakra.
Also in the Sundarīhṛdaya: "The nine-yoni is declared to be the Śrīcakra, the cause of the origin of the universe.
The rest is clear. *Vācam* refers to the first *kūṭa*.

According to the authoritative source stating, "The lotus-face whose singular nature is the glorious *vāgbhava* peak," one should recite from the first peak up to the end of the word *vidmahe*. Then follows the middle peak, which is *kāma*;
as it has been stated in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*:
Between the Śakti and Vāgbhava [syllables], the Kāmarāja is renowned;
it is a mixture of red and white light... thus.

Having uttered that, one should recite: "O Pīṭhakāminī, meditate [on us]. Then, having uttered the third Śaktikūṭa, one should recite from the *Sahasranāma*: "She who bears the lower part of the waist which has attained oneness with the Śaktikūṭa. Thereafter, one should recite up to the end with "May it impel [us]. This...

It is also called the *Tripurā-gāyatrī*. The rest is as before. Having contemplated and recited [the mantra], the remainder is clear. Regarding this, that which was stated by the author of the *Nibandha* is as follows: beginning with the drawing of a one-cubit mandala in the water during the bath, up to the consecration seven times with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should [contemplate] oneself three times during the *sandhyā*.

The portion ending with "prokṣya" (having sprinkled) belongs to another tantra; it must not be touched by one who follows this tantra.
