If it were touched, then for what reason would the three daily junctions (sandhyās) and the sequence of the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) have been abandoned? If that [other tantra] is authoritative, let him state its source. || 5 ||
Regarding the entry into the sacrificial hall and so forth, he says:

"Having gone to the sacrificial hall, whether having performed the ritual preparation (*kḷptākalpa*) or being in a state of pure resolve (*saṅkalpākalpa*), [he should sit] on the seat with the seat-mantra."
He sat down together. || 6 ||

Having gone to the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), which is the place of worship; by this it is established that the twilight rites (*sandhyā*) are performed outside in water, such as in a river and so forth. "Adorned with arranged ornaments" (*kḷptākalpa*) refers to one by whom such decorations (*ākalpa*) or ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa*) have been worn. This wearing of ornaments is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the one performing the worship. Therefore, those things which are to be worn by the performer of worship in the world [are prescribed].

Those ornaments must necessarily be worn, and this is possible for the wealthy. This being the case, it would follow that a poor person—who is incapable of possessing ornaments as part of his physical being—would lack the qualification [for this practice], just like a blind person or others. Therefore, he says: "or one whose attire is fashioned by resolve" (*saṅkalpākalpa*). One who is such that his attire (*ākalpa*) is fashioned (*kalpita*) by resolve (*saṅkalpa*), that is, by a mental act.

Or rather, it means one who wears ornaments created by the mind; thus, the sense is that even a poor person has the entitlement [to this practice]. Furthermore, the inclusion of ornaments abounding in rubies (*padmarāga*) is intended, even though there are specific rules regarding particular ornaments found in other tantras.
As for the chewing of betel-leaf mentioned in the *Nibandha* during the worship of the door,
that is not intended by the author of the Sūtras. Alternatively, since the performance of the ritual takes place in the sacrificial hall, the act of entering is established by implication.

Furthermore, by stating the phrase "having gone again to the sacrificial temple" (*punaryāgamandiraṃ gatvā*), which is otherwise redundant because it would already be implied by the words "having entered within the sequence of Gaṇapati" (*gaṇapatikramastha*), the text indicates an extension of the properties (*dharmātideśa*) belonging to that [Gaṇapati] sequence.
For this very reason, this word does not appear in the Vārāhī-krama; therefore, it applies to the Śrī-krama and the Śyāmā-krama.
Let there be worship at the door; nevertheless, in the Śrīkrama, the consumption of betel-leaf is entirely without foundation.

The phrase "pīṭhamanu" has been explained previously. Regarding the word "samupaviṣṭa," the prefix *sam* indicates that one should remain seated on a single seat until the completion [of the rite]. Therefore, by means of whichever posture—such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or another—one does not experience fatigue while remaining until the conclusion, by that posture [one should sit].
The meaning is that one should remain [steadfast].

In the Nibandha, it is stated that there should be a consecration twelve times with the third seed-syllable of Bālā and a sprinkling with the root mantra; that should be understood as not approved by the Sūtra.
He states the *tritārī* (the triple-star mantra) which is useful for this worship:
"Having uttered the *tritārī*, one should cast a handful of flowers on the ground with the formula: *namaḥ raktadvādaśaśaktiyuktāya dīpanāthāya*. (7)

Having uttered the three *tārās* as will be described [meaning: in this very sūtra and its commentary, in the section below], one should recite up to the word "namaḥ. This is the mantra for the worship of Dīpanātha. With this, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the ground. A *puṣpāñjali* is a heap of flowers held in the hollowed palms.
As it is stated in the Agastyasaṃhitā, in the section on the ritual for Monday:
"A handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*) consists of a cluster of blossoms held between the two palms joined together. (7)
Regarding the procedure for the conjunction of the *tritārī* with all mantras, he states a certain general rule applicable to all mantras:
"The conjunction of the *tritārī* occurs at the beginning of all mantras. The *tritārī* consists of Vāc, Māyā, and Kamalā. (8)

In this context, by restricting the scope of the word "all" (*sarva*) through the force of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*), the meaning is that [the *tritārī*] applies to those [mantras] recited subsequently which constitute the ancillaries (*aṅga*) of the worship of Śrīvidyā.
By this, it is established that the conjunction with the *tritārī* does not exist in the mantras preceding these. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Setubandha*:

It is established that since the *tritārī* is recited in conjunction [with other mantras] in the *Kalpasūtra* after entering the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), it should be understood that this conjunction does not apply to the mantras prior to that point. By the word "at the beginning" (*ādau*), its exclusion from the end is indicated. While one could simply say "conjunction" (*yoga*), the prefix *sam-* was used so that the pronunciation of the *tritārī* would be made explicit. Therefore...

If, during the recitation of any part of the mantra, even a single syllable is omitted due to a defect such as lack of proficiency in pronunciation, then the mantra must be recited again; in that case as well, the application of the *tritārī* is indicated.
Alternatively, if after the recitation of the *tritārī*, the recitation of the mantra is interrupted by some obstacle—

In such a case, a momentary delay is indicated as being in the form of an unimpeded pronunciation of the *tritārī* once again. Even though, by this very [rule], the application of the *tritārī* is obtained in the mantra for the worship of Dīpanātha, therein—

The statement "having uttered the *tritārī*" is redundant; nevertheless, by saying "having uttered the *tritārī* there," it indicates that the *tritārī* is a constituent part of that mantra. Furthermore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) prescribes the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of mantras through their conjunction with the *tritārī*, and thus it is not useless.
As for that which is stated in the *Nibandha*— namely, the salutation to Gaṇapati following the worship of Dīpanātha, the salutation to the Guru,

the pervasive [assignment] from the thumb to the little finger, and the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (installation of the vital breath)— all of that belongs to other tantras or other contexts and should not be applied in the practice of Śrīvidyā.
In response to the inquiry as to what constitutes the "three-star" (*tritārī*), he says: "The three-star. *Vāk* is the twelfth vowel accompanied by the bindu.

*Māyā* is the fourth vowel accompanied by the bindu, following the second semivowel together with the fourth sibilant. *Kamalā* is the fourth vowel accompanied by the bindu, above the second semivowel together with the first sibilant. These are the meanings denoted by the term "three-star."
The word "become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. [Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—this is the combined three-syllable *tritārī* mantra.
We shall state later the authoritative evidence for the aforementioned meanings of speech (*vāk*) and the other [senses]. || 8 ||
Regarding the nature of the Śrīcakra and the materials for its accomplishment, he states the nature of the Śrīcakra and the materials for its accomplishment hereafter:
"In front, [it is] the form of the union of the five Śaktis and the four Śrīkaṇṭhas, consisting of three earth-seats, three folds, and the earth-king..."

Having set down the great king of wheels (*mahācakrarāja*), which consists of the lotus, the eight petals, the world-mountain, Brahmā, the sun, the directions, the intermediate directions, the triangle, the point, and the wheel— either written in vermilion and saffron or engraved in gold, silver, the five metals, jewels, crystal, and so forth. || 9 ||
The word *purataḥ* ("in front") is syntactically connected with the word *niveśya* ("having placed"). The five powers (*pañcaśaktayaḥ*) are the wheels of power (*śakticakrāṇi*);
the four Śrīkaṇṭhas are the four wheels of Śiva (*śivacakrāṇi*). Their nature of union is their non-differentiated essence (*abhinnasvarūpam*).
By this qualification, it is indicated that knowledge of such an essential nature is necessary at the beginning of worship and other rites.
The method of this union and the necessity of such knowledge at the time of worship are stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In the triangle, the bindu is joined; in the eight-spoked [wheel], the eight-petalled lotus."
Within the sixteen-spoked [cakra] of the two ten-spoked ones, there is the earth-dwelling within the world-petal.
He who knows the relationship of inseparable concomitance between the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the Cakras, is a knower of the Cakra.
Thus, he who worships the Śrīcakra even once without knowing its divisions does not obtain that fruit, and Mother Lalitā is not pleased. So it is said.

93) This very same meaning has been extensively set forth in the tantras; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, the relevant passages have not been written here. [One should draw] three squares surrounding the three seats of the earth, along with three lines of squares.
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the power of the square-shaped ground is stated in the words of another Tantra:
"Having drawn a circle outside of that, one should draw a square outside of that. This has also been written by our supreme preceptor in the *Setubandha* regarding the "ground-house" (*bhūgṛha*).
It is called "the square."
Regarding the justification for drawing three doorless squares within the Śrīcakra:

If it is asked, "In the statements of other tantras, by the use of the singular 'a square' (*caturasrakam*), only one square is understood; yet here it is said 'three squares. Since there is a contradiction between these two, how can this be?"—the answer is: no.

This is because various alternative arrangements are possible according to the differences among individuals who follow their respective tantras. Thus, for those who follow the Sūtra tradition, the *bhūpura* (enclosure of the earth) in the Śrīcakra is without gates, as it has not been explicitly mentioned [in that context].

But is it not the case that in the *Tripurārṇava* it is stated, "Then there is a triad of earth-purī (bhūpura) adorned with gates," and likewise in the *Nityātantra*, "Thus, the abode of the three earths is adorned with four gates," and in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, "The surrounding circle and the earth-purī are beautified by four gates"?
If it is argued that, following the precedent of other tantras, one should likewise postulate the significance of doors here as well—the answer is no.
For in the *Yāmala* scripture it is stated: "This Śrīcakra of the Supreme Deity is declared to consist of three enclosures (*vṛtta*) and three earth-fortresses (*dharaṇīsadana*).
Since other tantras likewise mention the earth-fortress (*bhūpura*) without reference to doors, such a conceptualization is difficult to justify.

Nor should it be said that this is untrustworthy because no author has ever written of a *bhūpura* (enclosed city) devoid of gates, for in the forty-third verse of the *Saundaryalaharī*, the gates are not mentioned.
This is because the venerable Bhagavatpāda himself accepts precisely the position we have stated;

likewise, in the *Prapañcasāra-ṭīkā*, Śrī Vidyāraṇyasvāmin has also written in accordance with our own view, using the passage: "In some instances, even a square is found within the Śrīcakra, though it lacks a gateway."

The same is the case in the *Aticirantana-Śiṅgabhūpāla-paddhati*. As we have proceeded to investigate this matter, other statements from various other treatises will also come to light; therefore, no further specialized effort has been made here, as this much suffices.
Thus, because the author of the *Nityotsava*, who possesses the conceit of being particularly faithful to the Sūtras,

has written at the occasion of describing the method for drawing the Śrīcakra that "one should manifest the four-gated *bhūpura*," it follows that he has not thoroughly scrutinized the Sūtra; he merely followed along with the crowd out of mere conformity.
It is clearly written thus.
Furthermore, the author of the commentary himself recorded in his own work that he was a disciple of Śrī Bhāskararāya.

In the *Setubandha* composed by Śrī Bhāskararāya, the third position is stated as follows: "It consists of three lines in each direction and lacks any general door. In this position, the *Kalpasūtra* [is authoritative].
It is written that it is favorable.

Furthermore, since the *Kalpasūtra* states that "the conjunction with the *tritārī* occurs at the beginning of all mantras" immediately after entering the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*), and since it is established in the *Setubandha* that this conjunction does not apply to those mantras preceding that point, this [rule] is deceptive regarding the *raśmimālā* mantras.

And in the *sandhyāvandana*, he incorporated the *tritārī*; likewise, he incorporated the fourfold gate. This being so, what kind of person is he who, not knowing even the system of the Guru, writes according to his own whim?
We do not know what kind of lay follower he is, nor what the relationship between teacher and disciple may be.

Furthermore, if one first inscribes the absence of the general door (*dvārasāmānyābhāva*) at the Setubandha, and subsequently deliberates upon its true nature, then in that very context— in works such as the *Yāmalakalpasūtra*— the position regarding the absence of the general door occurs without either a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) or an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the door.

Since it is written that what is being postulated merely by the non-mention of the door is nothing but audacity, how can it be said that [the author] is ignorant of the Guru’s doctrine? In that case, let us set aside the question regarding the door; however, there is ignorance of the Guru’s doctrine in the application of the *tritārī* to the *raśmimālā* mantras and the *sandhyā* mantras.

It has become like an adamantine cement. By this, we clearly perceive it as logical that even the tradition claiming this compilation was edited by the independent master of all systems, Śrī Bhāskararāya, is baseless.

"Three folds and three circles" (referring to this subject—see Dīpikā on Śārṅgadharapaddhati 11/11). Regarding this, many [authorities] hold that there are two circles for the pericarp of the sixteen-petaled and eight-petaled lotuses, and one circle outside of those;
thus, there are three circles, not three circles outside of two lotuses. As for the *Kalpasūtra* stating "three folds," [it refers to the following].

Regarding the statement in the *Yāmala*, "the three circles and the three abodes of the earth," and the statement in the *Yoginītantra*, "the square form is Jyeṣṭhā and the triple circle is Vāmā," they say that all of these refer exclusively to the aforementioned three circles.
Regarding the justification for drawing five circles within the Śrīcakra,
our supreme preceptors have stated here in the *Setubandha*, on the occasion of describing the drawing of the Śrīcakra by means of an alternative method that will be explained later:
Outside, one should draw two lotuses with eight and sixteen petals respectively; then one should draw a circle of qualities, and outside of that, a square.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, by the natural force of the words, there are three circles outside the two lotuses; in accordance with that, the remainder is the enclosure of the earth (*bhūpūra*). Here, the singular number is not intended to be restrictive.
In this way, there are five circles. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* (Chapter 10, verses 72–73):
These two verses are as follows:
"O Maheśānī, outside of this, there is a circle resembling the full moon;
O Mīnākṣī, make it joined with eight beautiful petals."
"Likewise, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should draw a sixteen-petaled [lotus];
outside of that, O Queen of the God of Gods, there should be three circles accompanied by the Mātṛkās.
Here, by the phrase "outside of that," it is very clearly stated that there are three circles in addition to the circle of the pericarp (karṇikā).

Other commentators of that [text], because the half-verse "tadbāhye" is written in their own manuscripts with insistence, and because the method of writing the syllables is not recorded in any tantra,
and because the mention of being accompanied by a *mātṛkā* would otherwise be incoherent, [conclude that it applies] to many...
Having restated the opinion of others— that [the passage] is an interpolation because it is not found in manuscripts—
he refutes it by stating: "If it were an interpolation, then since there would be no statement prescribing a third *vṛtta*, the consequence would be that there are only two *vṛttas*."
Since it is written in the *Saṃhitā* and in other tantras that there are clearly three external circles, [the authors of] the *Setubandha* established that there are five circles.
Regarding this, Maheśvarānandanātha states: "Having drawn a circle outside of that, one should draw a square outside of that."

In the *Paramānandatantra*, it is stated in the singular as "the circle" (*vṛttam*); in the *Tripurārṇava*, *Nityātantra*, *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, and *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, it is said: "Then the circles of the earth-forts" (*bhūpurāṇām*), "the circle consisting of three abodes of the earth," referring to the enclosure and the earth-fort (*bhūpura*) as a well-rounded form, O Supreme Goddess.
Having established that there are three circles (trivṛtta) based solely on the singular number [in the text] along with the two circles of the pericarp (karṇikā),

he then restates the view of the Setubandha and refutes it, stating that the Setubandha itself [is mistaken] because the citations from the Jñānārṇava of the Vāmakeśvaratantra are not found in many manuscripts.
Having cited the writing of Śrī Bhāskararāya as their authority, they refuted the Setubandha.

This method is unestablished (*asiddha*). It was not mentioned [in the *Setubandha*] because it is not found in many manuscripts at the point where the Siddhānta is presented; rather, it was introduced during the occasion of restating the opponent’s view (*vādimatānuvādavelāyām*).
And that is the opponent’s own writing. For that reason, how could the opinion of Śrī Bhāskararāya be refuted?

On the contrary, Rāya himself, by writing within my own book, has provided two refutations: first, that [the text] is indeed authoritative, and second, that it results in the occurrence of two metrical feet (vṛtta). Furthermore, no one wrote anything controversial regarding the statement from the Vāmakeśvaratantra. This being the case, such a groundless attribution of fault there is merely...

It is solely for the purpose of displaying one's own erudition. Therefore, without providing an interpretation for the statement from the Vāmakeśvaratantra which prescribes three meters, as well as for the Jñānārṇava, there can be no cessation of the five meters.

And if, solely on the strength of the etymological singular number, one were to accept that the term "three" (*traya*) in the phrase "the three circles" (*vṛttatraya*), which is heard after the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled [lotuses] have been mentioned separately by the dual form "the pair of lotuses" (*yāmalaka*),
is redundant in the sense of being a collective reference (*samudāyānuvādakatva*), then in this way, the form of Vāmā—

In the phrase "the three circles" (*bhramitrayam*), effort is made to conceive of the very rotation that constitutes the parts of the eight-petaled and sixteen-petaled [lotuses] as having the nature of Vāmā. If that is so, then the use of the singular number is equally applicable in the phrase "the square outside that" (*tadbāhye caturasrakam*). There are scriptural statements that support this:
In the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, it is stated in that very sixth chapter: "the halo and the city of the earth (*bhūpura*)," and in the *Pūrvatantre*:

"the form of Vāmā is four-cornered," and in the *Guṇavṛtta*: "one should then make a square outside of that. And in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "O Supreme Goddess, [one should make] a perfect circle, and then..."

There are scriptural statements such as "one should draw the image of the earth" (*bhu-bimbaṃ mālikhet*). Since such statements exist, for one who relies exclusively on the singular number, there is here in this *Paramānandatantra-ṭippaṇī* the writing of Maheśvarānandanātha: "A square, three squares" (with the addition "that triad of squares [is] by means of three finger-breadths" in manuscript *ba 2*).
It is indeed contrary to the context.

If it is argued that the singular number found in such Tantric statements as "and if there is a triad of earth-purāṇas adorned with doors" is not intended to be significant, then what offense has been committed by the use of the singular number in the word *vṛttam*?

In this way, the use of the singular for the plural is frequently encountered in both worldly and Vedic usage; for example, in common parlance, one says "the house" (*gṛhe*) [when referring to multiple rooms].
"In the case of such passages as 'There is grain; rice has been produced' (p.
96), where it says 'the cause for its arising,' the learned declare that the singular number is used to denote the genus (*jāti*). Brāhmaṇa...

The expression *mama daivatam* is an ancient usage. In the Śruti, regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice for one with many wives, there are numerous instances such as "having girded the wife, he sweeps the house," and so forth. Similarly, in the case of a paramour (*upapati*), there is by no means a total lack of recourse for the singular number.

Furthermore, in the aforementioned instances, one cannot justify the singular number by assuming that it indicates plurality through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the force of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). In the present case as well, if one were to adopt that same position, then in the passage from the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* stating "the quality-function (*guṇavṛtta*) from that," one would have to assume secondary indication for the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) itself.
The status of indicating the intended meaning (*tātparya*) must be stated; however, that is not possible.

Therefore, since the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, which contains the word "thence" (*tataḥ*), and the *Paramānandatantra*, which contains the singular form "therein" (*tatra*), possess equal authority—both being external to that [work]—it follows in accordance with the singular form from the latter... [that it occurred outside of it].

Why, then, is not the singular number itself intended, by resorting either to the view that this [word] is figurative (*lakṣaṇā*) or to the view that it is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*)? For there is no determining factor to show that, when one of two alternatives must be interpreted differently, the singular number is unintended based on the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the word *tataḥ*, rather than the opposite.

It must be stated: when it becomes necessary to interpret one of two meanings—namely, the meaning of the suffix and the meaning of the nominal stem—in a different way in accordance with the other, the nominal stem is more powerful;
therefore, it is the meaning of the number and the suffix that must be interpreted differently in accordance with it. As it has been said by the venerable Vidyāraṇyasvāmin:
The rule that a verse (*ṛc*) is to be recited three times is a property of its position;
it is not the primary [property of the word itself], because of its feminine gender and because of the predominance of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Thus, there are many arguments establishing the predominance of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For fear of excessive length, I have written only those composed from the sayings of learned authorities. Therefore, following the rule that the word *tataḥ* functions as a nominal stem, it must be interpreted as being in the singular number; otherwise, it would not be so. Thus, the wise should abandon their insistence.

When one who desires to know the absolute truth investigates all the Tantras, it is established that even though the mere words [of other systems] are disregarded, the five circles (pañcavṛtta) are intended in the Śrīyantra. Let us now return to the subject at hand.

Regarding the term *bhūpapatra*: "bhūpā" is a convention for the number sixteen; thus, it refers to that which has sixteen petals. *Dikpatra*: "dik" is a designation for the number eight; thus, it refers to that which has as many petals. *Bhuvanāra*: "bhuvana" is a designation for the number fourteen.

*Tāvadaram* means "that many spokes"; *tāvatkoṇam* means "that many angles. Regarding *druhiṇāram*, the term *druhiṇa* is a designation for the number ten, because in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* and other texts, the ten Prajāpatis such as Kardama and others—who are the causes of creation—are well known.
Thus, *tāvadaram* means "ten-spoked. By this, it is also [referred to as] "the Brahmā-angle" (*vidhikoṇam*).
This has been largely explained. The term *dik* (direction) has also been explained. The triangle (*trikoṇa*) and the point (*bindu*) are clear.

By the word *mayam*, the state of being a single unified totality (*samaṣṭi*) is indicated. Regarding *mahācakrarājaṃ*—the name of the Śrīcakra is *cakrarāja*; its greatness (*mahatva*) and its worthiness of worship (*pūjyatva*) are established by the grammatical rule that the root *maha* means "to worship."
And thus, the meaning is that it is worthy of worship by all, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others. *Sindūra* is well known;

*kuṅkuma* is saffron from Kāśmīra; [the word] is written with either of these two. Alternatively, since their association is understood through a *dvandva* compound, it means "written with saffron together with *sindūra*."
The moderns (navyās), however, state that when the array (prastāra) is written on the ground,
it should be filled with saffron powder if it is a Meru-array, and with vermilion powder if it is otherwise; the authority for this must be investigated.
Since the method of drawing [the yantra] has been explained in detail by our supreme preceptor in the *Setubandha*, it is not written here.
Up to this point, the procedure for constructing the daily yantra at the time of worship has been stated.
Now, he describes the method of worship even for a perfected yantra (*siddhayantra*), as well as the rules regarding the materials for constructing the yantra:

By the words beginning with *cāmīkara*: *cāmīkara* is gold (*suvarṇa*) and *kaladhauta* is silver (*raupya*). Although the word *kaladhauta* can also denote gold—according to the lexicon which states "silver and gold are both *kaladhauta*"—nevertheless, since gold has already been mentioned previously, it refers here specifically to silver. *Pañcaloha* (the five metals) [is as follows].
The characteristics of that [liṅga] are stated in the Tantrasāra and the Bṛhatpāñcarātra: "Silver is said to possess the qualities of a king;
there should be ten parts of gold, twelve parts of copper, and five parts of iron."
Six parts of brass (ārakūṭa) are proclaimed to be fivefold metal (pañcaloha). Thus [it is said].

*Ārakūṭa* is brass; the remainder is clear. "Jewels" refers to emeralds and the like, engraved upon them according to the previously mentioned scripture. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), copper, stone, and other materials mentioned in the *Paramānanda-tantra* are to be understood. This also serves as a qualification for the previously mentioned "King of Wheels" (*cakrarāja*).
Having placed such a Wheel-King (cakrarāja) before him.
In this context, worship is primary. In the absence of this, one should also accept a substitute as prescribed in other tantras. As it is said in the *Paramānandatantra*:
"The fruit is single-fold when [the deity is reflected] in a mirror, and double-fold when in a book."
There may be four types in an image, and sixteen in Śāligrāma stones.
O Goddess, they declare that the fruit of worship at Śivanābha is a hundredfold for the attainment of human goals,
while at the Narmadā it is a thousandfold.
"In the Kuṇḍalī, the vision of the deity becomes multiplied a hundred thousandfold;
however, the worship performed in the Cakrarāja bestows infinite fruit. Thus it is said.

However, according to the order of recitation, in the absence of each subsequent item, one should take each preceding one. It is precisely this intended meaning that is indicated by the scriptural mention of the gradation of results. *Kuṇḍalī* refers to the Śeṣa-kuṇḍalī (the coiled serpent). *Pustaka* refers to the book of the Kula scriptures. *Pratimā* refers to the form [of the deity] residing in the verses of meditation (*dhyānaśloka*).
The remainder is clear.

Since the consecration of a yantra is not mentioned in the Sūtras, it should not be performed by those who follow the Sūtras. Likewise, the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) should also not be performed by those who follow the Sūtras, because it is neither mentioned nor required therein. In reality, regarding the consecration of a yantra—
p.

98) Since it falls outside the scope of the ritual application for worship (*pūjāprayoga*), if one desires further prosperity, that which is taught in other tantras should be performed. [Regarding the matter of whether or not to perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of this yantra—ddi0]
Appendix 11-vi. Visible [rites]: For example, the recitation of the *Sahasranāma* and so forth. In performing these, there is prosperity (*abhyudaya*);

yet for followers of the Sūtras, there is no loss even by not performing them. Or, for instance, the *yajñopavīta* sacrament as recited in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*; because it is not recited in other Sūtras, it is governed by the rule "whether much or little" (*bahvalpaṃ vā*).

The people of the Draviḍa and Āndhra regions do not perform the consecration of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), holding that there is no loss [of merit] from its non-performance. However, the people of the Mahārāṣṭra region, considering it to bring about spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) when performed, do carry out the consecration.
In the same way, regarding the consecration of the *cakrarāja*, there is spiritual prosperity when it is performed; for those who follow the Sūtras, there is no loss from its non-performance. || 9 ||
Next, he describes the sequence of worship for the temple and so forth:
therein, in the Great Wheel (mahācakra), [one worships] the Ocean of Nectar (amṛtāmbhonidhi), the Jewel Island (ratnadvīpa), and the Great Garden of Various Trees (nānāvṛkṣamahodyāna).

To the grove of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣavāṭikā*), to the grove of *santāna* trees, to the grove of yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), to the grove of *mandārava* flowers, to the grove of *pārijāta* trees,
to the grove of *kadamba* trees, to the wall of *puṣyarāga* gems, and to the wall of *padmarāga* gems.
To the one with a perimeter wall of *gomedaka* gems, to the one with a perimeter wall of *vajra* gems,
to the one with a perimeter wall of *vaiḍūrya* gems, to the one with a perimeter wall of *indranīla* gems, to the one with a perimeter wall of *muktā* gems,
to the one with a perimeter wall of *marakata* gems, to the one with a perimeter wall of *vidruma* gems, and to the one with a pavilion of *māṇikya* gems.

To the pavilion with a thousand pillars; to the pool of nectar, the pool of bliss, and the pool of discernment; to the exhalation of the morning sun, the exhalation of moonlight, the great enclosure of erotic grace, the forest of great lotuses, and the sovereign palace of the wish-fulfilling gem.

To the eastern gate consisting of the Eastern Tradition; to the southern gate consisting of the Southern Tradition; to the western gate consisting of the Western Tradition; to the northern gate consisting of the Northern Tradition;
to the circle of jewel-lamps; to the great lion-throne made of gems.
To the one whose single bedpost is composed of Brahmā, whose single bedpost is composed of Viṣṇu,
whose single bedpost is composed of Rudra, whose single bedpost is composed of Īśvara,
whose single bed-plank is composed of Sadāśiva, and whose mattress is made of swan-down;
For a great pillow of swan’s down, for a saffron-colored bedspread, for a great canopy, and for a great curtain—[in this manuscript, the earlier reading "yavanikāyai" appears to be a scribal error;
thus, the word "yamanikā" or "javanikā" is appropriate here. Cf. Amarakośa, Book 2].
In the section on human beings—for example: "pratisīrā, javanikā, and tiraskāriṇī are synonyms for a curtain"—verse 120. Herein:

*pratisīrā*, *javanikā*, *tiraskāriṇī*—the term *tiraskāriṇī* is sufficient. With the forty-four mantras beginning with "namaḥ," all of that [is accomplished]; [with the forty-four mantras of the various chambers—variant reading 2].
Having meditated upon and having worshipped [them], || 10 ||

In that context, the words "standing in the sacrificial hall" (*yāgamandire sthite*) are to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Furthermore, this is an adjective for the term "great wheel" (*mahācakre*). Alternatively, "therein" (*tatra*) means "in what has been written," and is connected with the preceding sūtra's phrase "having placed in front" (*purato niveśya*); thus, it refers to the "great wheel."
"Having meditated upon and having worshipped"—this is connected with what follows. "The ocean of nectar" (*amṛtāmbhonidhi*) means the ocean of immortality.

"An island made of jewels" (*ratnamayo dvīpaḥ*) refers to a place fit for dwelling, that is, high ground; as Amara states: "A pleasure grove (*udyāna*) is a park for recreation. "A grove of trees" (*vṛkṣavāṭikā*) is a small garden (*upavana*).
"Vṛkṣavāṭikā" means a grove of trees in a domestic garden, according to Amara. "Kalpa" and so forth are names for celestial trees.
These five are the divine trees: Mandāra, Pārijātaka, Santāna, Kalpavṛkṣa, and Haricandana (which may be used in the masculine), according to Amara.
*Kadamba* is well known. The nine varieties of gems range from *puṣparāga* (topaz) to *vidruma* (coral);

their *prākāra* is a wall constructed all around the exterior of the house. *Māṇikya* is ruby (*padmarāga*), and its *maṇḍapa* is a pavilion. A *vāpī* is a long pond. *Udgāra* refers to a red-colored, delightful object.

As it is stated in the *Tryakṣarakośa*: "The word *udgāra* [is used] for the color red and for an object of great delight. Lamps made of jewels; their circle (*valaya*). *Haṃsatūla* refers to the fine feathers of a specific type of bird, resembling a fringe of down located beneath the wings, known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as...

*Parā* is well known [as a type of grass]. *Mahopadhāna* is well known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *loḍu*. A *kausumbhāstaraṇa* is a fine red-colored cloth spread over the bed to prevent staining by its impurities; it is called *palaṅgapūsa* in the Mahārāṣṭrī language.

This is well known. A *vitāna* is a cloth tied above from a higher position, serving to prevent the falling of earth and other materials. A *yavanikā* (curtain) is well known in the Marathi language as *ṣaḍudā* (see the two notes on pages 98, lines 4–5). The rest is self-evident.

In this manner, there is a conjunction with "namaḥ" for all [the mantras] ending in the dative case, as in the verse "yā te agne'yāśayā. Having first meditated upon the objects expressed by these forty-four mantras within the Śrīcakra, one should perform their worship:
first the meditation on one, then the worship, then the meditation on another.

Therefore, the sequence is "first [the meditation], then the worship," as obtained from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word *tattat* (each respective one). Otherwise, by logical principle (*nyāyataḥ*), meditation and worship would have been understood according to the method of performing each item separately (*padārthānusamaya*); thus, it should be understood that this [sequence] sets aside that [method] by means of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) in the word *tattat*. || 10 ||
He describes the offering of lamps, the worship of the wheel, and the placement of perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth:
"One should place the perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so on on the right side, and the lamps all around. (Regarding the matter of the lamps here—*ddi*).

In the supplement (13.29), it is stated: "Having offered [oblations] with the root mantra and worshipped the wheel, one should worship the first triangle with the three sections of the root mantra. (11)

In the phrase "akṣatādīn" (unbroken rice grains, etc.), the word "ādi" (etcetera) includes the first, second, and subsequent [offerings]. This [phrase] connects with the word "etasya" (of this). In that context, "giving" (*dāna*) does not mean a mere renunciation (*tyāga*) intended for some deity; rather, it means the gathering together of the materials for worship in one place, as in the expression "he collects the sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni sambharati*). Of this...

The fruit is the swift attainment of each respective [result] at the time of its specific offering. The giving and placing of lamps on both sides all around is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). By the word "having given" (*dattvā*), together with the particle *ca*...
The repetition [of the rule] has been indicated for the sake of completing the sentence with respect to each individual object of reference, because such repetition is necessary.

Therefore, the difference in meaning of the root *dā* does not constitute a fault. Nor should it be asked by what authority this is the meaning of the root *dā*; for we see such usage as "he gives the cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*) and "he gives his feet to the massager" (*saṃvāhakasya caraṇau dadāti*).

Just as in expressions such as "he gives fear to the enemy," there is a conceptualization of the meaning based on fitness (*yogyatā*), so too here there is a conceptualization of a fitting meaning. By the word *abhitaḥ* ("on both sides"), it is made known that however many lamps there are on one side, there are exactly as many on the other side. The result of this is the removal of darkness. By this [lamp-lighting], in the house of worship—
The meaning is that the absence of darkness in general is the effect. If a lamp is placed on one side, the darkness in the form of its shadow will fall behind it;
however, if lamps are lit equally on all sides, there will be no darkness anywhere. This is the restriction regarding both sides.
The meaning is evident. Having worshipped with the root mantra the wheel consisting of nine wheels—the collective wheel—with the fifteen-syllable mantra;

here, worship consists simply of the scattering of flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). With the three sections—the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—at the time of the initial construction of the first wheel...

Regarding the wheel, there are three spokes (*asra*); because they are doubled, they form a singular compound. It is not a *bahuvrīhi*. In that [latter] case, since the worship of a single part within a single wheel consisting of three triangles would not require three mantras, the fault of optionality (*vikalpa*) would arise—just as in the case of the mantra "May Bhaga divide you two. Nor is it like the rule "He takes up the spade with four [fingers]."

It should not be said that there must be a collective compound (*samuccaya*); nevertheless, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, the fault lies in the assumption of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the meaning of another word. In the case of a *dvigu* compound, however, three peaks are appropriate at the three corners. The word "having worshipped" (*abhyarcya*) is carried over from the preceding [verse]. Since no specific order is mentioned, [the worship proceeds] clockwise starting from one’s own front. || 11 ||
Regarding the causes for the purification of the self, such as drying and so forth,
he then states those causes for the purification of the self beginning with drying:
"Drying, burning, and bathing are performed by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) associated with the colors of air, fire, and water."
Having performed [the rite]. || 12 ||

The color of Vāyu is *yaṃ*, the color of Agni is *raṃ*, and the color of Salila (Water) is *vaṃ*. In Vāyu, the power of drying (*śoṣakatā-śakti*) is well-known in the world; therefore, that [power] exists even in its corresponding color. Consequently, by means of it, there is drying, which is the destruction of the water-element (*jalāṃśa*).
In the same way, by means of the color of Agni, there is burning, which is the reduction to ashes (*bhasmīkaraṇa*); likewise, [there is the removal] of those ashes.

Having performed the massing [of the body] by means of the water-form and the immersion; by the word "and" (ca), one should include the production of solidity by means of the earth-seed syllable *laṃ*—as taught in other tantras or located in the section on Śyāmā—as well as the arising of the body of Śambhu. Or alternatively:
Because it occurs in close proximity, only that which is situated within the section on Śyāmā should be accepted [as seen in the root text,

commentary, and subsequent sections, such as the ninth sūtra of the Śyāmākrama in the sixth division]. When there is an expectancy for an object (*karman*) regarding actions such as drying and so forth, the visible gross body or the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) serves as that object.

That which is well-known in other tantras should be accepted. By the statement "by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) conjoined with the syllables," while uttering the syllable *yaṃ*, one should restrain the vital breaths on all sides; thereafter, one should contemplate the drying up of the body.
Furthermore, regarding the wind in the section on Śyāmā [in the first section of the Śyāmākrama, sūtra 9, root text and commentary]:
And [the word] *dṛśyam* [is to be supplied]. Piṅgalā performed the practice of drawing [the breath] in;
this is made known by the phrase "by means of breath-restraints" (*prāṇāyāmaiḥ*). The same applies further on as well.

101) As for those mantras from the section on Vārāhī—beginning with "one should dry up the body of contraction" (*saṅkocaśarīraṃ śoṣayet*)—which have been written down in the *Nibandha*, they are rootless and should be rejected because they are not based on the *sūtras*. However, that which is situated in the section on Śyāmā...

The accomplishment of solidity and the arising of the body of Śambhu—established by the means of knowledge known as presumption (arthāpatti) indicated by the word "ca"—is to be performed [by the author of the Sūtras, Śrī...]. 12.
Regarding breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he then states the rule for breath control:
"Having performed breath control three times. (13)
Prāṇāyāma, however, should be understood in the manner that will be explained in the section on Śyāmā [meaning: in the manner stated in Sūtra 10 of Khaṇḍa 6 of the Śyāmākrama]. || 13 ||
Following the removal of obstructing spirits and the placement of the vajra-armour (*vajrakavaca*), the removal of those obstructing spirits must be performed; thus it is said:
"May those spirits depart who dwell upon the earth; may those spirits who create obstacles [depart]."

"May they perish by the command of Śiva! Having spoken thus, striking the ground with the heel of his left foot, clapping his hands, and turning his face upward, he should perform three *tālas* (rhythmic hand-claps) and, endowed with the sense of identity (*ahaṃbhāva*) with the Goddess, apply the network of the adamantine armor (*vajrakavaca-nyāsa*) upon his own body. || 14 ||

With the mantra "apasarpantu," there is a striking of the earth with the heel—that is, the back part of the foot—and a clapping or rubbing of the hands; the face is turned upward and then tilted sideways. The phrase "together with these" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Then, three *tāla* beats are made with the palms facing downward.

With the right thumb, middle finger, and index finger, one should strike the palm of the left hand three times with sound; having performed that and generated [the state], one should contemplate, "I am non-different from the goddess Upasaya. By the phrase "in one's own body," there is an exclusion of the deity’s body. One should apply the network of placements (*nyāsajāla*) in the form of an indestructible armor (*vajrakavaca*).
One should perform—that is, carry out—the collection of nyāsas that is about to be described. || 14 ||
Regarding the inquiry as to what this "net of nyāsas" is, and specifically the *karaśuddhinyāsa*, he first describes the purification of the hands:
"Having performed the purification of the hands from the middle fingers to the palms with Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, and the third [letter] joined with the Bindu."

Śrīkaṇṭha is Śiva, represented by the letter *a*; this is because in the *Yoginītantra*’s *Pañcadaśī*, there is a count of the letters beginning with the syllable *a* in the "ten [forms] of Śrīkaṇṭha. Ananta is the long vowel *ā*; according to the *Tantrasāra*, regarding the mantra *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ*, Ananta is conjoined with the *bindu* (nasal dot) and possesses *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), *brahmā* (*kroṃ*), *agni* (*ra*), and *tāra* (*oṃ*).

Thus, from the extraction [of the syllables]: "and those two, Śrīkaṇṭha and Ananta, are joined with the Bindu"—this is the compound. The third [syllable] is the third of the Bāla [mantra], namely *sauḥ*. And thus, with this mantra: *aṃ āṃ sauḥ*.

"By whom the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi) has been performed starting from the middle finger down to the palms"—the meaning is that one should place [the mantras] on the middle, ring, little, and thumb fingers, as well as on the palms and the backs of the hands.
This is the Karaśuddhi-nyāsa. || 15 ||
The Deposition for Self-Protection (*ātmarakṣānyāsa*). Regarding the deposition for self-protection, he says:
having uttered "Kumārī" (here, by the word *kumārī* and the subsequent word *bālā*, [the mantra] *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ* [is intended]).

Thus, the three-syllabled mantra of Bālā should be taken up; then, placing one's joined palms at the heart with the words "Mahātripurasundarī, protect me, protect me," [one should meditate on oneself as immortal consciousness]. || 16 ||

Having uttered "Kumārī" and "Bālā," and omitting the two syllables "pada," one should recite up to the end with "rakṣa rakṣa" while placing the joined palms at the heart. This is the ritual placement for self-protection (ātmarakṣānyāsa). || 16 ||
The Installation of the Four Seats:

Regarding the installation of the four seats, he says—having uttered *māyā*, *kāma*, and *śakti*, and having offered his own seat with the mantra "Salutation to the Seat of the Self of the Goddess"—[he proceeds]. (17)
The syllable *māyā* is clearly established as *hrīṃ* in many places; *kāma* is *klīm*. As it is stated in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"With the word *klīm*, the son of the sage called out to him from nearby."
But Sudarśana, having heard that, clearly grasped the primordial syllable.
Accompanied by the *anusvāra*, he uttered that seed-syllable known as Kāmarāja again and again, having then grasped it with his mind. Thus [it is said].

"Śakti is Sauri; Śakti is Parā and the third"—so it is stated in the *Kośa*. Although it might be possible to understand the term "Kāma-śakti" as referring to the second and third *kūṭas* of the fifteen-syllable mantra (just as *Tripurā-gāyatrī* refers to its specific components), since evidence for that meaning has also been shown, nevertheless—
Mādana (ka), conjoined with Śakti (i) and the fourth vowel (ī),
enriched above by the central moon-bindu— this is the extracted Kāmarāja.
It is joined with the end of Śānta (ha), conjoined with the *kādi* group (the consonants from ka to ma), and yoked with the end of the one whose final letter is Ai (the letter ṇa).

Thus, in the Yoginītantra, this is the very meaning of the extraction of this mantra: *mādana* is the letter *ka*; *śakti* (or *śakra*) is the letter *la*; the fourth vowel is *ī*; the end of *śānta* is *sa*; *kādi* is the *visarga*; and the end of that which ends in *aikāra* is *au*. Having uttered [these], one should then discard them.

The mantra ending in *namaḥ* is *manu*. Thus, having offered one's own seat with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ! Salutation to the Seat of the Self of the Goddess," one should scatter flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon that seat. || 17 ||
Then, with two verses, he extracts the mantras for the *cakrāsana* and so forth:

having uttered *Śiva-yuga-bālā*, [one says] *śrīcakrāsanāya namaḥ*; having uttered *Śiva-bhṛgu-yuga-bālā*, [one says] *sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ*; having uttered *bhuvana-amadanau bleṃ*, [one says] *sādhyasiddhāsanāya*.
Having performed the seat for the deity of the wheel-mantra within the wheel by means of the three mantras beginning with "namaḥ," [one should proceed]. || 18 ||

"Śiva is the letter *ha*; *ha* is Śiva, the sky, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)"—according to the *Kośa*, it is thus "Haṃsa. By that, Bālā is conjoined. Here, by the word "Bālā," the phoneme of Bālā is meant; thus, with reference to the phoneme of Bālā, the conjunction with the phoneme *ha* is prescribed. And so, it is established that the letter *ha* is a limb (*aṅga*) of the phoneme of Bālā. And thus:

According to the maxim that "the repetition of auxiliary elements occurs for each primary element," the conjunction with the letter *ha* applies to all three classes [of letters]. Furthermore, since a consonant is never seen at the end of a vowel, it must be joined at the very beginning. Thus, *haiṃ hklīṃ hsauḥ śrīcakrāsanāya namaḥ* is one mantra. [In this context], *śiva* is the letter *ha*, and *bhṛgu* is...

The letter *sa* is the seed of the universe (*jagadbīja*) within the section on the letter *sa*, known by the name Śakti; "I am that [Bhṛgu], Vegavatī," according to the Nandana-kosha. Bālā, conjoined with both of these, is: *hsraiṃ hsklīṃ hssauḥ sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ*; this is the second mantra. Bhuvanā is Bhuvaneśvarī; her mantra consists of the form of the Māyā-bīja.
Thus it is extracted from the *Devībhāgavata* according to the statement: "Śiva, Māyā, Agni, and Bindu. Here, Śiva is the letter *ha*;
Māyā is the letter *ī*; Agni is the letter *ra*; and Bindu is well known. Through the conjunction of these, the form *hrīṃ* arises.
Furthermore, she is Bhuvaneśī and Lajjā (the Embarrassment goddess), as stated in the lexicon: "Hṛllekhā is the family deity. In the present context as well, that very same [seed-syllable] is Madana.

This has been explained. And thus: *hrīṃ klīṃ bleṃ sādhyasiddhāsanāya namaḥ*—this is the third mantra. Having thus arranged the seats for the wheel, the mantra, and the deity within the wheel by means of these three mantras in sequence, this is called the "Installation of the Four Seats" (*caturāsananyāsa*). || 18 ||
The Six-Limbed Nyāsa of Bālā:
Next, he describes the six-limbed [nyāsa] of Bālā:
having performed the six limbs by repeating the Bālā mantra twice, with the placement of fingers numbered three, two, one, ten, three, and two respectively.

One who has performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) for the heart and other parts by means of the six syllables of the Bālā mantra, turning away from the child-mantra (*bālādvirāvṛttyā*), having sequentially fashioned and applied these six limbs with three or more fingers— such is he. This is the very meaning.
It is clearly stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā* (p.
"One should place [the mudrā] on the heart with the three fingers excluding the little finger and the thumb."
The knower of mantras should place [the syllables] from the middle and the navel up to the head.

Having placed the *śikhā* with the thumb, one should place the armor (*kavaca*) with the ten [fingers]. O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the placement of the eyes (*netra*) using the mantras prescribed for the heart.
"Then, O Dear One, one should place the weapon [mudrā] with the index and middle fingers. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the six-limbed placement (nyāsa) for the Child-form [of the deity]. || 19 ||
The Nyāsa of the Yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī:
Now, he describes the nyāsa of the yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī—
having uttered *sa-bindu na co blūm* [at the beginning of the names of the eight goddesses beginning with Śrī-Vaśinī who reside therein].
This is for the sake of knowing the extraction of the seed-syllables (bīja) beginning with *grāhyoccyārya blūm*.

[On the head: *vaśinīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ*. In all cases, there is the addition of the bindu (*m*) to the consonant groups (*varga*). Having uttered the *ka*-group and *klahrīṃ* [here it should be understood as *klhrīṃ*], one says: *kāmeśvarīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ*.
Having uttered *cuṃ* on the forehead; having said *nvlīṃ*, "Salutation to the goddess of speech Modinī," at the center of the eyebrows;
having pronounced *ṭuṃ*, "Salutation to the goddess of speech Vimalā," at the throat;
having spoken *tuṃ*, "Salutation to the goddess of speech Aruṇā," at the heart; and having uttered *puṃ* and *hslvyūṃ*.

"Salutation to Jayinī Vāgdevatā"—thus at the navel. Having uttered the four [vowels] beginning with *yā* and the syllable *jhryūṃ*, "Salutation to Sarveśvarī Vāgdevatā"—thus at the linga. Having pronounced the six [consonants] beginning with *śā* and the syllable *kṣmrīṃ*, "Salutation to Kaulinī Vāgdevatā"—thus at the base. || 20 ||

Having uttered those [vowels] beginning with *a* and ending with *visarga*, both with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and joined with the nasal dot (*anubindu*), the mantra of Vaśinī ends with "namaḥ. Thus: *aṃ āṃ aṃ aḥ blūṃ vaśinīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ*;

one should place this on the head. Now, since the application of the nasal dot has been mentioned for all [vowels] in this way, one might wonder if it does not apply elsewhere; therefore, he says: "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).

The meaning is clear. Regarding "the *ka*-group" (*kavarga*): the *ka*-group is well-known, [but here it is] with the bindu (*m*). In the case of *kalahrīṃ*, only the consonants are to be taken. This is according to the maxim: "Letters found in a composite whole are seen in its constituent parts. And this position was adopted by Śrī Bhāskararāya in the *Setubandha*.

Regarding the commentary on the phrase "the ethereal seed below," the line of explanation states that the ethereal element refers to the collection of *haṃsa* sounds, and from that, only the solitary letter *ha* is to be taken. The reason for taking it in this way here as well is found precisely in the *Setubandha*: "This mantra of Kāmeśvarī consists of twenty-three syllables."

Because when the letters *ka* and *la*, distinguished by the vowel *ra*, are included, the mantra "I worship the sandal of the two-tārās" results in the formulation "Hīṃ Śrīṃ Klhrīṃ, I worship the sandal of Kāmeśvarī-Vāgdevatā-Kāmeśvarī," which consists of twenty-five syllables; therefore—

There is the grasping of mere consonants alone. It has been stated in detail in the *Varivasyārahasya*, during the enumeration of the fifteen phonemes (*pañcadaśī-varṇa*), that consonants do not possess the status of being [independent] phonemes (*varṇatva*). And thus: *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ kalhrīṃ* for Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatā.
One should place "namaḥ" on the forehead. [The syllable] "cuṃ" represents the *cavarga* (the *ca*-group), because of the rule "cuṃ" being marked with an *u* (indicating it is an *it*), which,
by virtue of the grammatical rule "aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ," includes all homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*).

The inclusion of the *ca*-group (*cavarga*): having recited the mantra ending with "namas" for the *ca*-group, one should place it between the eyebrows. For the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*), it is as before. The remainder is clear. Regarding the letters *ha*, *sa*, *la*, and *va*, the inclusion of the consonants alone is as before. "That which is the beginning of the tetrad" means that which is the first of the group of four.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* (specifically a *guṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*) compound. And thus: [the syllables] yaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, vaṃ—[and so on].
In the expression "the six beginning with śa" (*śādi-ṣaṭka*), the compound is likewise as previously explained. || 20 ||
The Deposition of the Root Mantra:
Having thus described the deposition of the Yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī, he now speaks of the deposition of the root mantra and so forth:
"One should place the fifteen syllables of the root vidyā on the head, the base, the heart, and the three eyes."
Having performed the sixfold placement upon the two ears, the mouth, the pair of arms, the back, the pair of knees, and the navel, one should place [the mantra] in the wheel,
or else [place it] elsewhere.
The three eyes, together with the center of the eyebrows, should be known [as the first five locations]. The two ears refer to the pair of auditory organs.

The remaining locations are clear. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence upon the fifteen aforementioned locations using the fifteen root-syllables accompanied by the *bindu* and ending in *namaḥ*. "Sixfold" means of six types: Gaṇeśa, Graha...

The placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa) according to the divisions of constellations, yoginīs, zodiac signs, and sacred seats (pīṭha), as taught in other tantras, has been indicated by the expression "having placed [them] again and again," which suggests that this may be performed or omitted at will. || 21 ||

Having thus taught the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) for the purpose of achieving the state of being the Goddess, he now instructs on the procedure for establishing the vessels (*pātra*), which constitute a limb of the worship: *pātrāsādanam* [is as follows]: the preparation of the common *arghya* offering.
Thus, after teaching the ritual placements for the sake of accomplishing the nature of the Goddess, he then teaches the rule for the placement of the vessels that form part of the worship.
Having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square on the left side with pure water,
having worshipped it with flowers, and having established a conch vessel along with its base, having filled it with pure water and added the first drop;
Having worshipped with the six-limbed rite and having consecrated [the water] with the Vidyā, one should sprinkle oneself and the articles of worship with droplets of that water. || 22 ||

By the phrase "with pure water," it is indicated that the deity has been worshipped with perfumes, unbroken grains, and flowers, as stated in the *Gaṇapatipaddhati* (in the root text, Sūtra 5 on page 77 of Section 2). "Pure" means water filtered through a cloth. [On one's own left side...]

Having drawn [the mandala] from the triangle up to the square according to the method of exiting—because it consists of the rules and procedures for the observance (niyamavidhi) and because it possesses expectancy [of completion], in the manner of the fish-seal (matsyamudrā) as taught in the Śyāmākrama [meaning: according to the procedure stated in Sūtra 18 of Khaṇḍa 6]—and having worshipped it with flowers; [the phrase] "with its support" (sādhāram) refers to the words "therein" (tatra) and so forth.

Regarding the installation of the support-vessel (*ādhāra*) and the conch, and the filling of them with pure water, since there is no distinction in their proximity [to the ritual context], one may, according to one's preference, adopt either the mantra found in the section on Gaṇapati or that found in the section on Śyāmā. However, the worship of the *kalās* beginning with Pāvaka is not to be performed upon the support-vessel and the other vessels.
Because it has not been stated, because it has not been indicated, and because there is no expectancy for it here; yet, in reality,
in comparison with Śyāmā-Gaṇapati—

Since the mantras for the base of the special arghya vessel and so forth, which reside in the Śrīvidyā-prakaraṇa, are present here, those very ones should be employed. Even there, only as much as is required should be taken, and not what is unnecessary, just as in the rule: "He mixes the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk."

The conjunction with the initial *bindu* is the consecration of the conch-water. In the word "bindum" (the drop), the number inherent in the predicate (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant; therefore, by the offering of two drops, no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises. Nor should it be argued that because the accusative case-ending is heard in "bindum," that very [word] must be the subject (*uddeśya*).
Since there is no mention of an application (*viniyoga*) for the *bindu* when its application is required, it is not a consecration of the *bindu*;

rather, it is a consecration of the water, because the application of the water is heard [in the text] immediately following. Furthermore, since that which is to be consecrated must necessarily be the objective (*uddeśya*), the *bindu* is what is enjoined (*vidheya*). Consequently, the number associated with it is indeed intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*).
Having worshipped the deities of the six limbs in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu with the six-limbed mantras,
[the text says] "with the limb" (*aṅgena*); here the singular number is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*) indicating plurality,
because— according to the logic of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*— it is impossible for singularity to apply to the six mantras.

In reality, however, since the number of repetitions for the auxiliary mantras (*aṅgamantra*) is already indicated by the word "six" (*ṣaṭpada*) itself, the purpose of the singular suffix in *vacana* is indeed not intended to be significant. Thus, the use of the default singular number alone is appropriate. Nor should it be argued that this results in a loss of grammatical concord with the word "six," which expresses the qualifier; for [the concord] is maintained by the word "six."
Because there is no logical inconsistency in accepting [the term] as a compound, by this [word] also, it is simply a consecration of the water.

Alternatively, one should satisfy the deities of the six limbs within that very conch-water by repeating the three *kūṭas* twice, using the mantras for the six limbs in sequence, such as: "To the heart, *namaḥ*; I satisfy the *śrīpādukā* of the Heart-Śakti," and so forth. And what need is there to ask why the word "having worshipped" (*abhyarcya*) has the meaning of "satisfying" (*tarpaṇa*)?

It should be stated as "māna" (the measure). For it is said in the Vāmakeśvaratantra, "There one should gratify the Yoginīs," and in the Setubandha, the word "yoginī" is explained as referring to the deities of the six limbs of Tripurasundarī.

Having consecrated it with the fifteenfold Vidyā— that is, having refined that water through the act of consecration— one should sprinkle oneself, one's own body, and the ritual implements for worship, such as perfumes, flowers, and incense, with its droplets— those drops of the consecrated water. Herein:

By the logic of the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa* (the rule concerning the three partridges), it would follow that the means of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) consists of only three drops, as implied by the word "with droplets" (*vipruḍbhiḥ*). To set aside this logical conclusion, the prefix *sam-* is used. Thus, the meaning is:
one should sprinkle in such a way that the articles for worship are thoroughly drenched with water. || 22 ||
The Ritual for the Special Arghya (the Purification of the Arghya):

Having thus performed the production of the general arghya and having brought about satisfaction with it, he states the ritual for the special arghya and describes the satisfaction derived from that special arghya.
Having prepared a maṇḍala consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square with that water, one should worship the center with the Vidyā;

the triangle with the sections of the Vidyā; and the hexagon with the repetition of the seed-syllables (or, according to Ga., the double repetition of the seed-syllables). Then, uttering the speech [mantra], [one worships] "to the Fire-maṇḍala, whose self consists of ten kalās."
Having established [the vessel] with "Salutation to the support of the *arghya* vessel" and having worshipped the support, one worships the purifying digits (*kalā*). || 23 ||
"With that water" means with the water of the general *arghya* offering. "The rest is as before. "In the center" means in the middle of the triangle (*trikoṇa*).

"With the Vidyā" means having worshipped with the collective Vidyā; this [phrase] is to be supplied everywhere. "With the sections of the Vidyā" means with the three *kūṭas*. "The triangle" refers to the three corners of the triangle. The proof for this has been shown previously. "By the repetition of the seed-syllables" (refers to the following).
[This means: according to the method stated in the three sūtras numbered 19–22 on the preceding pages 103–105.

By the double repetition of the three *kūṭas*. The nature of a *kūṭa* as a seed-syllable (*bīja*) is established by authoritative evidence as being the form of each individual seed-syllable for the purpose of accounting for the sixteen syllables of the venerable *Ṣoḍaśākṣarī* (the Sixteen-Syllable Mantra).

This has been elaborated by our supreme preceptors in the *Varivasyārahasya*; it is not written here for fear of excessive length. Since the specific order is not mentioned, one may proceed either clockwise starting from the east or clockwise starting from one's own front.
This is because of the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "The mantra ends with *namaḥ*, or else it ends with *pādukā*."
"Vācam—Aiṃ. As it is stated in the *Devībhāgavata*: "The Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Māyā-bīja as the third—if these should reside in one's heart, no one at all is capable of harming him."

Having thus begun, and introducing a narrative to praise the first seed-syllable, Vāgbhava: "By one distressed by fear upon seeing a tiger or similar beast in the forest, even when uttered without the nasal drop (bindu) as 'ai ai', it is said that [the syllable] indeed granted his desire."

By praising the status of being the cause of the fruit through the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic for that which is devoid of the *bindu*, it is established that the *aikāra* with the *bindu* is the *vāgbhava*. Furthermore, from the extraction of the *bālā* mantra in the *Nityārahasya*: "O Goddess, the first is *vāgbhava*, the second is *kāmarāja*," and [from the statement]: "The solar vowel (*ravisvara*) joined with the *bindu* is declared to be the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable."

And from the seed-sheath (*bījakośa*). Since there is a desire to know what kind of support (*ādhāra*) it is, one should take up the "three steps" (*tripadādi*) and so forth as stated in another tantra for the sake of knowing the nature of the support here (see *pariśiṣṭa* 12; the subject matter is to be consulted). These are the names of the lunar digits (*kalā*) of Fire, Sun, and Moon.
The fire-related *kalās* are found right here before us, in the sixteenth root-sūtra of the sixth section of the *Śrīśyāmākrama*; they should be taken from there.

[Regarding the question of what vessel and of what form should be taken for that purpose, see Dviraṣṭaka-pañjikā-śiṣya-hitā-vivaraṇa 12. They [the *kalās*] are accompanied by the word "fire" (*vahni*) and end with the fourth case ending and the word "namas."

[The deity is] visible. One should worship [the deities] in the form of the eastern and other directions by means of their respective names, according to the statement in the *Paramānandatantra*: "One should worship the form of the eastern and other directions by means of the form of the eastern and other directions. However, Bhāskararāya, in the *Setubandha*, stated that this is done by proceeding clockwise from the west. || 23 ||

Above the *madana*, having arranged it with the mantra "Obeisance to the vessel for the *arghya* offering, which consists of twelve digits (*kalā*) for the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*)," and touching the vessel, one should contemplate the solar digits (*saurīḥ kalāḥ*). (The names of these digits of fire, sun, and moon are explicitly given hereafter.)
In the sixteenth root-sūtra of the sixth section of the *Śrīśyāmākramīya*, it is stated: "Then they should be taken up.

Having filled [the vessel] with the mantra: *sauḥ somamaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane arghyāmṛtāya namaḥ*, and having offered the first [syllable], one should worship the preceding and middle [syllables]. [Regarding the question: "Of what substance is the vessel for the Moon (*vidhu*) here?"
And of what form is that which is to be grasped? For that purpose, the sixteen digits (kalās) are to be seen. 24.

Madana has already been explained in the section on the ritual placement of the four seats (*caturāsananyāsa*). The rest is clear. Regarding the word "having touched" (*saṃspṛśya*), the phrase beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) precedes it; that is, having touched—that is, having worshipped—the solar digits (*saurīḥ kalāḥ*) such as *Tapinī* and the others, within that vessel (*pātre*).

Although the root *spṛś* does not have "worship" as its meaning, nevertheless, because it occurs within the sentence "having worshipped the lunar digits (*kalā*) of the Moon after worshipping the fiery digits," the vessel [the question arises]— for what substance and of what form should the vessel be taken here? (See Dīpikā, Paddhati, Śikhā, Vimarśinī 12).

And because of the statement in the *Yoginītantra*, "Having established [the deity] there, one should worship the digit of the Sun (*sūryakalā*)," it must be understood that the intent refers specifically to the act of worship. Having filled the first (*ādima*)—that is, the first—and the near-first (*upādima*)—the second—the middle (*madhyama*)—the third; this is also an elliptical indication for the fourth and fifth. [As stated] in the *Siddhāntagrantha*:

In the first section, it was stated that there are five *makāras* and that worship is performed with them in secrecy. In that very context, having given [the offerings] and established [them], [one offers] the sixteen digits (*kalās*) of the moon, beginning with Amṛtā and ending with Pūrṇāmṛtā. || 24 ||

There, having drawn a triangle with lines beginning from the southeast (or northeast), radiant with a swan situated within a pair of ploughs, its corners joined by Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti; having worshipped it with the *Haṃsa* mantra and constructed a circle outside followed by a hexagon;
having worshipped the hexagon with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) starting from the front side; and having consecrated it seven times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Having offered perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having sprinkled the articles of worship with their droplets, one should make everything consist of the Vidyā; then, touching it, one should mutter the ninety-four mantras.
There, having worshipped the first substance according to the previously stated sequence,
one should draw a single line from the west to the northeast using the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*.
Then, one should draw [the second line] from the northeast to the southeast using the sixteen consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*.

One should produce another line. Then, from the southeast to the west, one should produce the third line with the sixteen letters beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*. This being so, it consists of those letters whose initial [consonants] are *a*, *ka*, and *tha*—namely, the long forms of *ā*, *kh*, *p*, and so forth.

The triangle in which the lines are non-different from that [syllable] is "one whose lines consist of *akatha* and so forth. This is a qualifier of the triangle. It is "resplendent with the collection of syllables *haṃsa*," which is situated between *ha* and the pair of *lakṣas* (the two *la*s); having written "haṃ" on the right side of the substance.
To the north of that, one should write the two syllables *haṃ sa*, and to the north of those, one should write *lakṣe*. In this way, it takes the form described above.

Thus, these three syllables of Bālā represent Speech (*vāk*), Desire (*kāma*), and Power (*śakti*). Alternatively, they are the three root-peak-syllables (*mūlakūṭatraya*). This is the authoritative proof.

In both meanings, this has already been stated previously. Having drawn a triangle characterized by these three such qualifiers— that in which the corners are joined with those [lines]— and having worshipped it with the mantra "haṃsaḥ haṃsaḥ" using flowers and other offerings, one should draw a circle and a hexagon outside the triangle.

Having worshipped the six corners of the hexagon— starting from the front portion and proceeding clockwise from the tip facing oneself— with the root mantras of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and having offered [the substances] into that [hexagon] by reciting the root mantra seven times; these [substances] have been given and deposited therein.

With the intention that "by means of these [substances], one may become such a worshiper"—namely, perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, and lamps—the giving of these is to be performed as part of the specific ritual; thus, this is an implied injunction of qualification (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*). Having made it "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*)—that is, having meditated upon it as non-different from *vidyā*, which is supreme consciousness—one should recite those mantras, beginning with the first, numbering ninety-four.
