That is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which the cognition of its qualities [is predominant]. || 27 ||

[In this context, by the phrase "which are the Akhaṇḍa and others," it should be understood that the meaning is: "Which are the mantras beginning with the word 'Akhaṇḍa' mentioned in the word 'akhaṇḍādyaiḥ' in the aforementioned Sūtra 27? To the inquiry "Which are the Akhaṇḍa and others?", he says:
O Mistress of the Akula, place within this Self, which is the supreme nectar that produces unbroken, singular-flavored bliss, the spontaneous radiance [of consciousness].
O Supreme One, who abides in the non-clan (akula), whose form is nectar, and who produces pure gnosis—
bestow the state of immortality upon this substance which has a moist form!
Having made yourself one with that very form within my own essential nature, and having become the embodiment of supreme nectar, O Consciousness, manifest within me!
Thus, these three *anuṣṭubh* verses are the sciences (*vidyās*). || 28 ||

111) In the Vedabhāṣya, the learned author of the Sūtrabhāṣya analyzes the meanings of the five mantras beginning with "akhaṇḍa," whose meanings were previously stated to be difficult to comprehend; [this concerns] the meaning of the Vedic mantras.
Because they have been made explicit, setting aside those Vedic mantras whose meanings were thus revealed,

I shall reveal the meaning of certain easily understood Tantric mantras. Regarding the words "Akhaṇḍa" and so forth— the triad of mantras beginning with "Akhaṇḍa" is a constituent part of the prayer to the Goddess Sudhā, as indicated by its characteristic mark (liṅga).

It must be so. Furthermore, by the force of the subsequent accusative *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) regarding the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the consecration—[here, "by the force" is a qualification of the term "by the indicative mark (*liṅga*)"].

In accordance with this, in the *Paramānanda-tantra*, regarding the passage: "One should mutter these three, enriched by the three seed-syllables, there indeed four times," [the text specifies] while touching.
This must be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāryam*). And thus, its status as an ancillary element (*aṅga*) to the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is established.

Furthermore, the statement in the *Paramānanda-ṭippaṇī* that the passage beginning with "akhaṇḍa" is in the form of a prayer to the goddess Sudhā is erroneous. [The name is derived from the second Vedic recension; the word "āmananti" occurs in the twenty-seventh sūtra mentioned above.]
It should be understood here that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) indicates that the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) has become the object of the action (*karmakāraka*).
This is because no one accepts the sublation of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) by indicative mark (*liṅga*) in such a manner. Here, the meaning of the mantra is as follows:
"Akula" refers to the two thousand-petaled lotuses; it is the support of all lotuses and is single, with its face turned upward.
A lotus situated below the *mūlādhāra* is that one which is designated as *akula*.

Regarding the commentary on the verse from the *Yoginītantra* stating "in *akula* and in that which is known as *viṣu*," [it refers to] the eight-petaled lotus above the thousand-petaled lotus located at the very bottom, and above that, the six-petaled [lotus].

Regarding the cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra*: according to the *Setubandha*, the *kulapadma* has six petals and is situated below the *mūlādhāra*; below that are the eight-petaled and thousand-petaled lotuses, which are *akula*. Likewise, the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the *brahmarandhra* and facing downwards is also *akula*. Thus it is said:
In the Tripurārṇava:
Above the Suṣumṇā is the station of the Guru, facing downwards, adorned with a thousand petals, and possessing a splendor equal to the brilliance of ten million moons.
One should know that to be Akula... [as stated].
In the *Paramānanda-tantra* as well: "The practitioner, having risen in the morning, [should contemplate] his own Guru within the Brahma-aperture,
in the lotus at the end of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta) inside the previously mentioned Kula-lotus."

Thus, since it has been established that both thousand-petaled lotuses are denoted by the term *akula*, in the present context, only the one situated at the *brahmarandhra* is to be understood, because it alone is the source of the flowing nectar (*amṛta*). In this context, the "mistress of *akula*" is the presiding deity of that lotus located at the *brahmarandhra*; therefore, she is addressed as "O Mistress of *akula*. (In this root text...)

The term *akulanāyikā* and its meaning have been taken up; since the word *kula* alone appears in the root text and the commentary on verse 38 of the sixth chapter of the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*, I hope that the lack of contradiction between the words of both Śrī Śiva and Jamadagni may be properly reconciled. [That which is] unbroken, uninterrupted, of a single essence, and unmixed with suffering—*yaḥ*.

Ānanda is that which makes [the self] manifest; in such a state, there is the supreme, most excellent nectar (sudhā) situated in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which bestows immortality—[this is] within that Self, in its own essential nature, in this very substance.
Establish—that is, place and stabilize—the vibration, which is the power of manifestation (*prakāśa-śakti*), of that consciousness which is autonomous and independent.

In that context, "whose nature is like the nature of the nectar (amṛta) existing therein" refers to the deity presiding over the substance; this is an adjective for *parā*. Regarding the statement that "in the supreme mass of the bliss of good fortune" (*saubhāgyānandasandohe pare*) is a locative ending used as an adjective qualifying the object (*vastu*), that is incorrect because it would result in a remote syntactic connection (*dūrānvaya*). These are *anuṣṭubh* verses, meaning they possess the *anuṣṭubh* meter; for the scripture states, "The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables."

Thus, this is the fifth knowledge (*vidyā*). Having consecrated [the offering] with these five [mantras], one should prepare that *arghya* which consists of light and is free from defects. By this, it is indicated that the removal of curses and so forth mentioned in other tantras is accomplished by this very [mantra].
If it is asked, "How is this intention established by the expression 'consisting of light' (jyotirmaya)?"—it is said in reply:

"Light" (jyotis) is a synonym for illumination (prakāśa). The suffix -maya is used here in the sense of abundance (prācurya). Where there is admixture with impurity within an illumination, an abundance of that illumination is not possible, as is the case, for example, with the sun when it is eclipsed.

When impurity is removed, an abundance of light is experienced right there, just as it is in a mirror that reveals the face. Similarly, in this case as well, the nature of being composed of light cannot manifest in a substance afflicted by various stains such as the dust of sin; however, once all impurities have been dispelled through consecration with the aforementioned ninety-nine mantras, [it becomes manifest].
It becomes composed of light; for this very reason, it is said, "having made it composed of light.
By this, the claim of certain individuals—that there is also a combination with the rite for liberation from curses mentioned in other Tantras—is indeed unworthy of credence.

[From here until the end of the 30th leaf of the Sūtrabhāṣya, the author of the Vṛtti has adorned the placement of two vessels. Thus, the justification for the primacy [of this practice] is established;
and those such as Maheśvarānandanātha and others, in another Tantra, regarding the daily worship—

Regarding the statement "as before, however, there are three bowls," they argued that since there is no prohibition stating it should not be made from thread, those who follow the Sūtras should also make it from thread. To them, this question is posed: is the state of having three bowls established because there is no prohibition stating it should not be made from thread, or is it because it is mentioned in another Tantra?

Is this because there is no prohibition in its own scripture even though such a practice exists in another tantra, or is it because a prohibition against using two vessels is heard in another tantra? It cannot be the first, for if there were no prohibition such as "one should sacrifice with rice" implying "not with wheat," then the transcendental result (*apūrva*) would arise even through the use of wheat. Nor can it be the second; for if that were the case...

Since the worship of Saṅgītamātṛkā, Vārāhī, and others as taught in the *Paraśurāmasūtra* is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to Śrīvidyā—as seen in the *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*—the abandonment of such ancillaries by others would result in a lack of justification.
By this, the third position is also refuted. Nor is the fourth [position] tenable; for, as it is said: "Therefore... [and so forth].
"O Goddess, one should never, under any circumstances, use two vessels"—this is the prohibition. And as for the censure:
"O Śivā, by using two vessels out of laziness or otherwise, a man is deprived of the fruit of his worship and undergoes a transformation [of misfortune]."

Thus, the statement "three vessels" is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) supplementary to the injunction; otherwise, since the exclusion of two vessels would already follow from the injunction of three vessels, the prohibition would be rendered redundant due to the absence of a distinct result in the form of its own cessation. Furthermore, if it were argued that the injunction effects mere engagement while the prohibition effects the cessation of what is other than that, then [the case of] eleven...

In the case of the injunction "he performs the prayāja offerings," since there is no statement specifying "twelve" or "ten," the transcendental result (*apūrva*) would arise from ten or twelve prayājas. Therefore, since the prohibition is redundant once the two vessels have been excluded by the injunction itself, it is merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to that [injunction]. This is the function of the *arthavāda*.

The intent lies solely in the praise; there is no character of negation in that [praise]. How, then, can the establishment of the three-vessel system (*tripātratva*) in another tantra be based on the reason of negation?

Furthermore, when the question arises as to how many vessels (*pātra*) there are in this tantra, since no specific rule is heard in its own *sūtra*, the statement from another tantra— “as before, there are three vessels”— is indeed [the authority].

The opposing view holds that the possession of three bowls fulfills one's needs; however, since there is no possibility of obtaining even two bowls under such circumstances, the prohibition [of having more than one] is utterly irrelevant.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that in your view, since there is no prior attainment of two vessels (*dvipātra*), how can the authority of the sentence "one should not make two vessels" be considered;
for there is no rule that a prohibition contained within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must be preceded by a prior attainment, as it [the prohibition] possesses its own intrinsic validity.

Because there is no intention [to convey that meaning]. Therefore, even the prohibition of something not otherwise established is logically consistent, as in: "The fire-altar is not to be built in the intermediate space nor in the sky; if one were to build it in the intermediate space, he would afflict the intermediate space with pain.
Such a statement does not have its primary intention (*tātparya*) upon its literal sense, but rather upon mere praise (*prāśastya*). And that [praise] remains uncontradicted.

Furthermore, there is no authoritative basis for a relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti*) between the two tantras, such that one could prohibit what has been obtained [from the other]. Indeed, a prohibition of what has not been obtained is not heard of even in a dream.

Furthermore, even in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for the pleasure of others, let there be a negation of what has been superimposed; nevertheless, their desired conclusion is not established. For instance, the *Kalpasūtra* prescribes the use of two vessels, while the *Paramānandatantra* prohibits them; in that case, since the two tantras possess equal authority, [the matter remains in conflict].

It would result in a mere option (*vikalpa*) between acceptance and non-acceptance. If one were to accept the superiority of the prohibitive scripture solely by personal preference, the position of acceptance would be utterly sublated; thus, there would not even be an option. For those such as Maheśvarānandanātha and others who maintain that the practice of using two vessels is unscriptural, [the view] is an option.
For this is not desired, and it is difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, in the *Paraśurāmasūtra*, it is not stated explicitly in so many words that "two vessels must be made";

rather, the injunction must be inferred based on the textual reading regarding the employment of two vessels. Therefore, the statement "O Goddess, one should certainly not make two vessels" constitutes an explicit prohibition (*pratyakṣa-niṣedha*). And thus, by means of this explicit [prohibition], the inferred [injunction] is [sublated].

It is contradicted. One might argue that in cases where both apprehension and non-apprehension occur, it is logical to have an option (*vikalpa*) regarding both being perceptual; however, this is not the case here due to the disparity. [Response: In the *adhrigu-praiṣa* of the *agnīṣomīya-paśu* sacrifice, there is the mantra: "Sixty-four are his ribs. In that context, "ribs" (*vaṅkrayaḥ*) refers to the side-bones of this animal.

The meaning of that [text] is "twenty-six. This mantra is obtained by extension (*atideśa*) because it is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice within the Aśvamedha. Such being the case, there exists another mantra in the Aśvamedha: "Thirty-four ribs of the horse, the friend of the gods. By the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of that mantra, it is understood that the horse has thirty-four ribs.

Success! Regarding the mantra "In its accomplishment, there are twenty-six ribs for it," when there is a conflict with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "twenty-six," the modification (*ūha*) "there are thirty-four ribs for it" would logically follow in its place.
This being the case, it is further heard in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Aśvamedha sacrifice: "One should not say 'thirty-four'."
"One should say 'twenty-six' alone. Here, since the rule for modification (*ūha*) stating "thirty-four" is based on inference, it is set aside;
thus, the prohibition "not thirty-four" operates as a constant rule.
Having stated this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the reply follows: where there is an inferred injunction and a perceptual prohibition...
In that case, it must be admitted that both possess equal strength; for indeed, the state of being strong or weak is never inherent in an object.

Rather, [the preference for one over another] is caused by the speed or delay of their presentation when there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For example, in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), the spreading of the altar (*vedyāstaraṇa*) is obtained from the archetypal ritual (*prakṛti*). In that case, when there is an expectancy as to "by what means should the spreading of the altar be performed," if there were no word indicating the means, then...

Having recalled the means of spreading the grass-covers as they are known from the archetype (prakṛti), and having mentally superimposed the *kuśa* grasses upon that [means], one should subsequently perform the spreading with *kuśa* grasses according to the archetype; thus, the requirement [of the sentence] is to be fulfilled by the postulation of an inferred scriptural statement (*ānumānika-śabda-kalpanā*). Even more so than that, it is stated immediately: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds."

When the expectancy [of a sentence] is satisfied by the arrows presented through a direct statement (*pratyakṣavākya*), the scripture that serves as the indicator lacks expectancy regarding that portion and is therefore weak. In the present case, because the prohibition "one should not say 'thirty-four'" is dependent upon a prior application [of the rule], it follows only after the injunction has first been postulated by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "thirty-four for the *vājins*."

A prohibition, which arises subsequently to turn back a person who has already engaged in an action following a rule, is unable to completely sublate that upon which it depends; therefore, it sublates it only partially. Thus, in such a case—as in the example where the rule regarding *śara* grass arises prior to the rule regarding *kuśa* grass—the prohibition [sublates the former only optionally].

Prior to the postulation of an injunction, [the action] is capable of being undertaken. Therefore, in such a case, because the inferred injunction and the perceptual prohibition possess equal force, an option (*vikalpa*) alone prevails; this was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the fourth quarter of the ninth book in Jaimini’s system (*tantra*). In the present instance as well, since they possess equal force, there is an option.
It is difficult to avoid.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because the Sūtra mentions the placement [of the vessels] along with the procedure for two vessels, a rule for two vessels is not to be inferred in the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), and that the mention of two vessels follows another Tantra and should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaka*) of three as well— then, in all Tantras, there would be only the performance of three vessels.

Since the two vessels are accepted as being part of the Tantra, and since there is no one who initiates the practice of using two vessels, the injunction for two vessels is equivalent to a hare's horn; likewise, its prohibition is also equivalent to that. For this reason, how can your desired conclusion be established? This is a rope with snares on both ends. Therefore:
Those who follow the Kalpasūtras and the Yoginītantras should perform the practice of the two vessels without hesitation.

As for the objection raised in the nineteenth chapter of the *Paramānandatantra-ṭippaṇī*, titled *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*, during the commentary on the fifteenth verse: "But would not the two vessels mentioned in the *Paraśurāmasūtra*, the *Vāmakeśvara-tantra*, and other scriptures be contradicted?"

Listen: since the worship according to the secondary rule (*anukalpa-pūjā*) and its two vessels will be clearly explained in the next chapter, this *tantra*—the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* and so forth—is intended for that secondary rule of worship. For this very reason, it is easy to say that there is an absence of mantras for the removal of curses (*śāpamocana*) therein. Alternatively, it is intended for those practicing self-yoga (*ātmayoga*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tripurārṇava* that for those intent on the yoga of the Self, "there is no loss through the omission of limbs" (*nāṅgalopo na bādhitaḥ*). For this same reason, the venerable Bhāskararāya has established in his *Setubandha* that "the abbreviated worship involving a single vessel and so forth is intended for those who are habituated to practice. Now...
Or else, one may take the side of the supreme adversary. As it is said in the Tantra:
"Having indeed prepared a pair of vessels for direct perception, one shall incur a curse."
In some cases, it was taught by me myself for the time of the ultimate downfall.
Thus the venerable Maheśvarānandanātha stated three positions; that [last one] is to be reflected upon.

The method stated in the *Paraśurāmasūtra* does not apply as the primary rule. Thus, regarding the acceptance of substitutes, in the first case, there are the five *makāras* which manifest it; by means of these, the worship is performed in secret.

Similarly, regarding the phrase "having first purified," which means "having added the initial bindu" (the nasal *m*), and "having completed," which means "having satiated the initial [consonant] with the group of five (*mapañcaka*)," these and the subsequent sentences up to the limit of one hundred— standing as the aphorisms (*sūtra*)—
should indeed be inserted into the spiral (*kuṇḍala*). Furthermore, even in the event that the group of five (*mapañcaka*) is not obtained...

By the sūtra "the constant review of the sequence," the primacy of the *ma-pañcaka* (the five *m*s) in daily worship (*nityapūjā*) is made perfectly clear. This being so, the claim that the sūtra refers to a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) is merely a scribal error rooted in a failure to reconcile the preceding and following sūtras; it is therefore to be rejected.
