Or is the result that, through purification and so forth, a new body as a means for sacrifice (*yāga-sādhana-śarīra*) arises, which was previously unperceived, just as in the case of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*)? Not the first, because even by repeating a thousand times a mantra that releases one from a curse, no transformation of the prior form is observed. Nor the second.
In some tantras there is elaboration, and in some tantras there is condensation;
likewise, when one relies upon a single tantra, the ritual action is performed correctly.
O Rāma, everything has been accomplished by him through the path of the venerable Guru.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Tripurārahasya*:

"Whether it be much or little, whatever has been proclaimed for anyone in their own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, when that much of the meaning of the scripture has been performed by him, everything [all has been done— this is an alternative reading] is accomplished."
It would be accomplished.

Thus, by the authority of the *Bodhāyana-smṛti*, since the essential nature that generates the sacrifice is obtained in the primary substance through the very purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) as prescribed, the mantras for liberation from the curse (*śāpa-vimocana*) are not applicable there;
how, then, could this reason establish that the Sūtra refers to a substitute (*pratinidhi*)? Furthermore, in the absence of the primary [substance]...
In the acceptance of a substitute (*pratinidhi*), as many primary properties (*mukhyadharma*) as are applicable to the substitute proceed accordingly—

just as when there is an absence of *vrīhi* rice, the properties of *vrīhi* apply to *nīvāra* millet, or when there is an absence of *soma*, the properties of *soma* apply to *pūtīka* plants; and it has been established in the system of Jaimini (*Jaiminīyatantra*) that even modification (*ūha*) does not occur in such cases— and people indeed practice this.
The learned authorities are likewise [in agreement]. This being the case, who can prevent the absence of mantras for the release from curses in the case of a substitute?
Thus, by employing a reason that is utterly unestablished—like the claim that fire is not hot—they have most clearly revealed their own ignorance.

Nor is the second position tenable. To explain: regarding the ritual action (*karman*) expounded in all the *Sūtras* of Paraśurāma beginning from initiation (*dīkṣā*), does it refer primarily to the practice of yoga or merely to worship?
It cannot be the first, because the practice of yoga is not possible prior to initiation. [Furthermore, it is not taught] in the presence of those who have not been initiated.
Because of the prohibition, "One should not recite the *Śivapaddhati*," there is an absence of hearing the Tantric Siddhānta;
and since yoga is impossible without such hearing, it is impossible to say that this initiation is for those practicing yoga.
Regarding the second [alternative]: Is such a practitioner—one who performs the worship prescribed by this Tantra—already possessed of the initiation taught in this Tantra, or...?

Only one who has been initiated by means of another tantra and whose mind has reached maturity through the independent practice of time (kāla) possesses the qualification for the worship taught in this sūtra.
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because the meditation (dhyāna) favored by you is not accomplished in the moment immediately following initiation;

this is experienced by everyone. Thus, having performed initiation according to the Sūtra, one lacks the authority for the worship prescribed in this Tantra due to being a non-yogin; therefore, one must resort to another Tantra for the purpose of worship.
This must be done. For it is said:
"He who, while abiding by his own scripture, practices another scripture, incurs the sin of killing an embryo and treats his own scripture with contempt."
Thus ends the transgression of the prohibition. Furthermore, by the aphorism, "After initiation,

one should follow the procedure for Gaṇanāyaka in order to remove obstacles to the worship of Mahāvidyā," it is stated that the worship of Gaṇapati is the means for destroying the impediments to the adoration of Lalitā.

For the ripening of the mind, which is to be accomplished through the worship of Lalitā, occurs immediately after that; from that, the aforementioned yoga [arises]. Immediately thereafter, eligibility for the practice of the two vessels (dvipātra) must be stated. That [eligibility] is not possible in the worship of Gaṇapati, because since the worship of Gaṇapati is co-temporal with obstacles, at that time the aforementioned yoga is absent even in the worship of Gaṇapati.

Since two bowls are mentioned there, the application of two bowls must necessarily be accepted in that case. And thus, what prevents one from assuming elsewhere [the same rule] for one whose qualification has been seen to deviate there?
This follows the maxim: "What need is there for a woman who has once been seen to stray to wear a veil elsewhere?"

Nor should it be said: "The non-yogi, having abandoned the worship of Gaṇapati, should perform only the worship of Lalitā according to another tantra until the attainment of yoga-siddhi, but not the worship of Gaṇapati; or else, even in the worship of Gaṇapati, one may resort to another tantra. For if that were the case, then...
If one were to say that the Sūtra— "Having worshipped Gaṇapati, with all obstacles dispelled, one should begin the Krama of Śrī Lalitā, the sole leader of the circle of Śaktis"— is invalid,
then the mention of the worship of Gaṇapati in the Sūtra would be rendered purposeless; for there would be no performance of it prior to the worship of Lalitā.

Because he lacks the requisite qualification (*ayogitva*), he has no entitlement (*anadhikāra*) to it at that time; furthermore, even after the attainment of the fruit through the practice of *lalita-upāsti*, [the former practice] serves no purpose and thus need not be performed. Consequently, its futility (*vaiyyarthyam*) is unavoidable.
Nor should it be argued that because the prohibition of using two vessels occurs in the section concerning Lalitā, the lack of qualification for non-yogins applies only there;

whereas elsewhere, they certainly do have the qualification to employ two vessels, as there is no such prohibition. [This is not so], because at the time of performing the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga) of Śrī Lalitā, [the restriction is for the sake of ensuring] the accomplishment of freedom from obstacles.

This is because Maheśvarānandanātha— who, following the *Paraśurāmasūtra*, performed the worship of all Gaṇapatis and, at the time of arranging the vessels, abandoned the practice of using two vessels in favor of the practice of using three— did not approve of this position; nor [is it established] by another tantra.

The second position is that one who has been initiated and whose mind has reached maturity through independent practice possesses the qualification for the worship prescribed in the Sūtra; however, this is not so, because if that were the case, the mention of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Sūtra would be redundant. Thus, as a proof for this position, there is the statement from the Tripurārṇava regarding those intent on self-yoga (*ātmayoga*): [the text continues].

He wrote that one does not fall [from the practice] by the omission of a limb; however, that is extremely weak. Its meaning is that for those practicing yoga (*yogābhyāsinaḥ*), the omission of a limb is not a fault. His established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the rule concerning two vessels mentioned in the Sūtra is intended specifically for the particular qualified practitioner who is a yogi. And thus, in the practice of a yogi, there is no need for a third vessel.

Just as the fifteen-fold nature (*pāñcadaśya*) in the *sāmidhenī* verses connected with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice performed by a Vaiśya is not an essential constituent (*anaṅga*), so too there is no omission of an essential constituent (*aṅgalopa*) here; thus, since there is no fault in the omission of a non-essential constituent, this serves to establish one's own position.

118) The statement regarding the cause is like grasping the son of a barren woman as a means to accomplish his own purpose. And as for that which, in this regard, concerns the worship in brief using a single vessel and so forth for those who are habituated to practice—

The agreement regarding the *Setubandha* manuscript that was shown is also unproven; such a line does not exist anywhere in the *Setubandha*. On the contrary, it is established that there is indeed a performance for two actors (*dvipātraprayoga*). For instance, [the passage] belonging to the preceding *Catuśśatī*...
One should promptly place the *arghya* water in a vessel made of gold or other materials that has a stand, mixed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*),
camphor, saffron, and light musk.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon [the elements] as fire, sun, and moon;
and having recited the mantra ten times, one should thereby satisfy the Yoginīs.

In the course of commenting on these two verses, this statement from the *Pūrvatantra* refers to the general *arghya*, while the statement from the *Uttaratantra*— “one should establish the *arghya* in the center of both the Śrīcakra and oneself”—
refers to the special *arghya*; at the end of that [section], it says, “in the same way, the *arghya* especially.”

Having rejected the ancient commentary which states that "the best of practitioners should accomplish [this]" refers to either the vessel of the Guru or the vessel of oneself, and having also rejected another opinion which holds that the very statement found in the *Pūrvatanttra* refers specifically to the *viśeṣārghya* (special arghya), [it is established that] the procedure for the *sāmānyārghya* (general arghya) in the *Pūrvatanttra* [is supplemented] by that which resides in the *Uttaratanttra*.

By the statement "of the Śrīcakra and of the self," the rule regarding its very place and time is established; likewise, by the phrase "the arghya especially," the rule for the special arghya is established together with the extension of the previous dharmas. Having thus determined this, at the time of the conclusion, [it is stated]: "Therefore, according to this tantra, for both alone..."

Śrī Bhāskararāya merely established the arrangement of two vessels, stating that "the installation is desired. (And this [arrangement] is suitable for us but unsuitable for others. He did not say, "This practice is intended only for yogins."
As for that which is stated in the *Setubandha* regarding another section:

because the detailed exposition of the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*)—as found in the *Yoginītantra-uttaracatuḥśatī*—is absent in other tantras, and because even the *Tantrarāja* is dependent upon this [work], this tantra is "supremely excellent"; and as for this dependence upon it:

Because it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "One should meditate by means of the clear method proclaimed in the *Nityāhṛdaya*," this *Nityāhṛdaya* is the name of the *Uttaratantra*. For although the external sacrificial components are mentioned here only briefly, for those whose practice is characterized by firmness in the internal worship, fulfillment is possible through that much alone.

It is "to be conceived" because it has been written [in that manner]. According to the previously written version of this tantra, which follows the refutation of the two Maras, the intended meaning of the statement "the installation of only the two" refers to the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*.
However, since in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī* only those with purified internal organs (*śuddhāntaḥkaraṇa*) possess the qualification, its application is restricted to them alone.

"The established conclusion (siddhānta) intended is that there are two vessels; it is with this very intention that our commentary on the *Setubandha* also agrees. This too is not correct; for if that were the case, there would be no rule for the production of the water for the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) in the *Uttaratantra*.

For those who practice according to the *Kevalottara-catuśśatī-tantra* alone, the preparation of only the special *arghya* vessel would be required, not that of two vessels. Consequently, the statement in the concluding passage— that "according to this tantra, the installation of both [vessels] is desired"— would indeed be contradictory.
Therefore, by this word "tantra," the preceding and subsequent four hundred [verses] are unified; thus, the intended meaning is precisely that it applies to those who follow the entire tantra.

For this very reason, the commentary on the *Setubandha* is consistent in stating that the application (*viniyoga*) of the general *arghya*—which was produced in the first four hundred verses—will be explained in the eighth chapter. By this, it is clear that what is taught in the preceding and subsequent Tantras is one and the same. Such worship is accessible even to one whose mind is not yet mature; accordingly, there are two vessels.
It is difficult to ward off.

As for the statement in the *Setubandha* that even a brief description of the external sacrificial limbs (*bahir-yāgāṅga*) suffices for the fulfillment of those whose practice consists of the internal worship (*antaraṅga-upāsti*), that does not refer to one who follows this particular tantra; rather, it refers to one who,
having previously performed worship according to the *Tantrarāja*, [proceeds] over time...

Regarding the statement, "When the cultivation preceded by the purification of the mind has been perfected, one who acts thus constantly is liberated; there is no doubt in this," since the word "constantly" implies that even after the external sacrifice with its constituent parts (sāṅga-bahiryāga) is completed, the performance of the worship with all its limbs (sāṅgopāsti) must continue for as long as one lives, this [present rule] serves as a restriction (*bādhaka*) to that.

"One should meditate by means of the clear method taught in the *Nityāhṛdaya*. This means that one should perform that meditation which consists of the practice of the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*), as taught in the *Nityāhṛdaya*—the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*—by way of the clear method therein. For in the *Tantrarāja*, because of the great number of components of the external sacrifice, [one should instead] practice yoga.

For those who desire to practice yoga preceded by the performance of that [tantric discipline], there arises a doubt regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted due to a lack of time; thus, for one wishing to practice yoga, it is not necessary to perform the entire collection of ancillary rites (*aṅgakalāpa*) prescribed in the *Tantrarāja* for as long as one lives, but rather—

The followers of the *Tantrarāja* maintain that one should perform the external sacrifice using only the collection of minor limbs (*alpāṅgakalāpa*) taught in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī* and then engage in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for its fulfillment is considered to be achieved by that alone; thus, they intend to convey the principles of the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*. However, it is not on this basis that the entire *tantra* [is exhausted].

Even Brahmā is able to accomplish that which is intended for those devoted to the practice of yoga. This being so, since the statement in the *Tantrarāja*—by the phrase "the heart of the Nityās"—specifies that it is the *Uttara-catuḥśatī* (the latter four hundred verses) alone that is intended for the practice of yoga, the recitation of the *Pūrva-catuḥśatī* (the former four hundred verses) would otherwise be rendered useless. Therefore, by the authority of the *Tantrarāja*, [this teaching is] for those whose minds are fully ripened.

For those skilled in the practice of yoga, there is the worship of a single vessel in the form of a special *arghya* offering, as described in the latter *Catuḥśatikā*, using the collective mantra (*samaṣṭimantra*). For those whose minds are not yet matured,
who follow the *Yoginītantras*, there is the practice of two vessels, combining both the former and the latter *Catuḥśatikās*.
This is the essential truth regarding the intention behind the Setubandha; likewise for those who follow the Sūtras—enough of this prolixity.
Nor is the third position—that it belongs to another school—tenable; for there is a statement supporting that third position:
"By making a pair of vessels in the direct perception [rite], one would incur a curse."
In some places, it was taught by me myself as pertaining to the time of supreme attainment.

Regarding what has been written here: does the phrase "he who would violate that [rule] shall be tormented by a hundred [strokes]" indicate that violating the two vessels is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) in the form of a curse, while the second half of the verse is a supplementary explanatory statement (*arthavāda*); or rather, does the first half of the verse itself indicate that it is a means to an undesirable end?

By the second half [of the verse], two things are stated: the occurrence of an offense (*āpatti*) and its subsequent permission (*abhyanujñā*). Alternatively, the entire verse may be intended solely for the purpose of granting permission. It is not the first case, because the second half, being in the form of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), has as its primary intent mere glorification, rather than [prescribing] the time of the offense.

Because it is impossible for [the scripture] to be an authorizer [of what is already established], its own stated position remains unproven. Furthermore, one must state that by demonstrating that eating from two vessels is a means to an undesirable end, [the scripture] turns back a person who has set out toward eating from two vessels. In that case, the cause of engagement in the practice of eating from two vessels must be either passion (*rāga*) or another system (*tantrāntara*).
The first [position]— that "one must use three bowls"— is not tenable;
for as long as the injunction exists, a person of faith who fears the omission of a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) will never have an attachment to using two bowls.
The first alternative is possible. As for the second alternative, it is difficult to avoid, as has already been answered previously;

by this, the second position is refuted. Therefore, since there is no other way, in whichever tantra this statement is recited, the rule regarding the three vessels must certainly apply there. The first half of that verse is a commendatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to it, while the second half [establishes the rule].

For those who follow the *tantras* concerning the ritual of the three vessels (*tripātra*), it is permitted to adopt the practice of the two vessels (*dvipātra*) as taught in other *tantras* in the event of a supreme transgression.
A wise person should not speak untruth; untruth is the destroyer of Dharma.
When one has fallen into a life-threatening danger, speaking untruth does not incur any fault at all.
Thus, the third position alone is correct. This very point has been clarified by the teacher Bodhāyana:
"He who, while his own scripture exists, conducts himself according to another's scripture, thereby disregarding his own scripture, incurs a sin equal to that of killing an embryo."

"One should apply the injunctions of one's own ancestral scripture along with the qualities of other scriptures for the purpose of investigating ritual actions and in times of distress. Thus it is said.

An example of this has been shown by Bhavasvāmin: for instance, regarding the *saumya* ritual procedure (*tantra*) at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), it is stated in the Śāliki branch that it is "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*), whereas in another branch it is stated that "everything is like the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsavat*).

It should be performed by the followers of their respective branches according to what is stated [in their own texts]. However, in the event of an emergency (*āpatti*), even all [branches] must perform it silently. Thus...

Furthermore, how could one establish that the scriptural injunction permitting the use of three or more vessels during times of distress is intended only for those who have not yet fallen [into such distress]? Therefore, this argument is of no consequence. According to the *Paraśurāma-sūtra* and the *Yoginī-tantra*, one should unhesitatingly set out only two vessels.
It must be performed.
Now, having established that the statements in other tantras which criticize the practice of two vessels (*dvipātra*) are merely supplementary to the injunctions,

those who follow the *Sūtra* have made the proposition that one should employ only the two-vessel method and must not touch other tantras; thus, what was not stated in their own tantra but was indicated [there] has likewise been criticized in other [tantras].
If you ask, "What is the illustrative example of the injunction that [something] is to be taken from another tantra?"—listen: immediately prior to this very statement, it was said:
"In some tantras there is elaboration; in some tantras there is condensation."
O Rāma, by relying upon a single tantra and performing his duties correctly, he has accomplished everything through the path of the venerable Guru.

By this, having stated the cessation of those ritual components of worship that are not essential to worship, as well as all rituals not mentioned independently, [the author] indicates what is not stated in the Tantra and suggests [what is implied];
by this, certain ritual components of worship are included, while others are likewise excluded.

It is heard that there is great censure for the non-performance of certain elements that constitute the limbs of worship, such as the recitation of the Thousand Names (*Sahasranāma*). Regarding its non-performance—(p.
How can one be a devotee without reciting this hymn? How could one please Maheśvarī without chanting the Thousand Names?
A person of deluded intellect who desires spiritual accomplishment while excluding the Thousand Names of the Secret [Mantra] would be like one who, lacking eyes, attempts to see forms.

"Surely one desires the cessation of hunger without food"—from such statements, censure is heard even regarding the non-recitation [of mantras]. That which exists in another tantra must certainly be adopted.
This is precisely the intended meaning of the statement from the *Tripurārahasya*. However, whatever is not contradicted by one's own tantra [should also be accepted].

The intent of the statement from another tantra cited previously—"one should perform [it]"—is also precisely this: that one does not rely upon other tantras regarding the subsidiary components of a single ritual performance. Aside from what is indicated and required for the ritual subsidiaries, there is not even the slightest intrusion of anything situated in another tantra.
This is the supreme conclusion. For this very reason, it is stated even in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:

"Indeed, for whom is that dharma not desired for the sake of tranquility—a dharma ordained by one's own nature, which, though appearing distinct from the [four] stages of life (āśrama), is actually established by the will of the Supreme Person?"

Thus he states this very point. Regarding this verse, [the Lord] says that even for the sake of increasing one's own merit (*dharmabhūyastva*), the duty of another (*paradharma*) should not be performed after the performance of one's own duty, because it is useless; thus [he says]: "By one's own nature... This is the commentary of Śrīdhara Svāmī. By this, the verse is explained. || 30 ||
He states the ritual duty to be performed with the drops contained in that vessel:

"Having worshipped the sandals of the Guru three times on the head with those drops" [the knowledge of the mantra of the *Śrīgurupādukātantra* mentioned here is found in verses 6–10 of the second supplement].
[These subjects are to be seen on 6/11, 6/14, 6/16/1, 6/16/5, and from 6/18 to 6/20. The moist [element] blazes; I am the light. The light blazes; I am Brahman. That which I am, I am Brahman.
I am; I am Brahman. I alone am I; I offer myself with the mantra *svāhā*.
One should offer that drop as an oblation into the kuṇḍalinī of the self. || 31 ||
With those drops— namely, the drops of the special *arghya*— one should sprinkle three times, that is, thrice, upon the head at the "twelfth place" (*dvādaśāntasthāna*),
which means the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). This meaning has been clarified in the *Śrīgaṇapatikrama*, in the commentary on the sixth ninth-line verse of the second section.

Having worshipped the *gurupādukā* and having made an offering of substances (*dravya*) intended for the *gurupādukā*, one [should offer] that drop—the meaning being the drop remaining from the *gurupādukā-yāga*—with the mantra ending in *svāhā*: "The moist burns, *svāhā*.
This is because pronouns refer to what is proximate, and it is precisely the remainder given to the *pādukā* that is proximate; therefore, it belongs to that.

And from the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "Taking the remainder, one should perform the yoga while reciting. [One should place it] in the fire of consciousness within one's own *kuṇḍalinī*. The nature of *kuṇḍalinī* is described in another tantra (p.
Having meditated upon the white pericarp in the foundation, and then upon the red [pericarp],
one should visualize within the cavity of the pericarp-cluster a form consisting of three and a half circles.
Having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī energy, which is like a sleeping serpent and as slender as a lotus fiber... [thus it is said].
By the word "juhuyāt" (one should offer), it is indicated that in this rite a firm conception of *homa* (oblation) must be maintained, and not a conception of drinking.

By the word "bindum" (a drop), the extreme smallness of the oblation substance is indicated. By the accusative case in "bindum," the consecration of disposal (*pratipatti-saṃskāra*) is also indicated; [the meaning is] that the remainder offered to the sandals of the Guru is [to be disposed of] by means of the *homa*.
The meaning is that one should perform the consecration; therefore, in the absence of a remnant, there is no oblation.
Regarding the justification for the practice of accepting family property:

indeed, it should be understood that from this point until the end of the commentary on Sūtra 31, there is a refutation of the consumption of liquor; however, it must also be noted that in certain instances, its defense was also set forth.

In all the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, the drinking of liquor is included among the five great sins (mahāpātakas). As the venerable Yājñavalkya stated: "The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the four great sins; association with these is the fifth" (Prāyaścitta Adhyāya 3, Verse 21).

Manu also states: "Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife, and association with those who commit these acts—these they call the great sins" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.7.21).
Since [the consumption of substances] is enumerated among the five great sins (*mahāpātaka*), how can the use of substances for pleasure as taught in the Tantras be justified?
This must be so. Thus, in those very tantras where the consumption of substances is enjoined, prohibitions are frequently encountered within those same tantras. As it says in the Kulārṇava:
"Merely by the sight of liquor, one should perform the gazing at the sun."
Merely by smelling that [smoke], one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O Śivā, for touching liquor, the rule is that one should bathe if it reaches the knees, fast if it reaches the navel,
and observe a three-night fast if it is above the navel.
If one intentionally drinks liquor, one should cast that blazing [iron ball] into one's mouth;
having been completely burnt by it, one then attains purification.
Thus it is said: "This is declared to be the expiation for the fault arising from the consumption of intoxicants."
Also in the Tripurārṇava:
"If a twice-born man should drink liquor even once, whether out of desire or delusion,
he must be abandoned by those who know the Tantras, even if he is learned, without further deliberation."
In the Devīyāmala as well, it is said:
"A wise man should renounce both the smelling and the seeing of liquor."

The meaning of that is: "One should abandon even the vision [of the deity], how much more so the drinking [of wine]? There are likewise many other such statements from other tantras; they are not written here for fear of excessive length. Therefore...
If it is argued that the scripture concerning the appropriation of family property is not to be trusted, we say no;

for these statements merely prohibit the drinking of liquor which is prompted by passion. Otherwise, the engagement in [acts] for the sake of the sacrifice would be desired [by the scripture], just as [the injunction] "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa" implies the existence of the [contrary ritual rule] "one sacrifices a Brāhmaṇa to Brāhmaṇas."
Otherwise, it would result in the invalidation of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). This very point has been clearly stated in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*:

"That the consumption of liquor by smelling was ordained, as well as the immolation of an animal—which is not actually violence—and likewise sexual intercourse for the sake of progeny rather than mere pleasure; those who know this are indeed aware of their own pure duty (*svadharma*)."
But those men who, not knowing this, are arrogant, full of self-conceit,
and recklessly harm animals— they devour them after death.

Thus, according to the text: therefore, because the injunction for the acceptance of specific substances—which has no other scope—presupposes its being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), and because the prohibition is solely for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), there is no identity of purpose between them.
For this very reason, it is precisely to indicate this intention that [the texts] state "due to desire" (*kāmāt*) in the *Tripurārṇava* and "committed through desire" (*kāmakṛte*) in the *Kulārṇava*.
The verse has been recited. Likewise, in another Tantra:
"O lady of excellent hips, there is a fault elsewhere, but no fault is found in the sacrifice;
just as in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, there may be the killing of a horse."
Thus, by means of an illustration, he confirms the very point already stated.

In this *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*, having stated in the section on the purification of inner disposition (*bhāvaśodhana*) that even for a heroic Brāhmaṇa milk alone [is permitted], and for others not even that, Nṛsiṃhācārya has conducted an extensive deliberation in another place further on to reinforce this very thesis. To illustrate:
Substances that have been adorned with gazing, sprinkling, meditation, mantras,
and mudrās become fit for libation and cause delight to the deity.
In this context, *tarpaṇa* means drinking; however, this refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas, because for a Brāhmaṇa, the taking up of that [liquor] is prohibited.
Is it not so—
that it should always be drunk by Brāhmaṇas, by Kṣatriyas when battle approaches,
by Vaiśyas in the employment of wealth, but never by Śūdras?
Thus, in the Kulārṇava, regarding the Sautrāmaṇī ritual within the Kula tradition, it is said that a Brāhmaṇa should drink the surā liquor.
Thus, according to the *Samayācāra-tantra*,
in the Kṛta age the Goddess was worshipped in due order by the four castes with [offerings] made of milk, ghee, honey, and flour; in the Tretā age, She was worshipped with ghee by all classes.
In the Dvāpara age, she was worshipped with honey of all varieties;
in the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped by the gods with auspicious liquors.

If it is asked, "Since this is stated in the *Yāmala*, how can there be no qualification for a Brāhmaṇa?"—it is replied: "Brāhmaṇas [are purified] by earth, Kṣatriyas by milk, Vaiśyas by clarified butter, and others by honey and liquor"—thus, as stated in the *Laghustava*, there are indeed distinctions of substances according to the sequence of the castes; and in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said regarding the substance: "Indeed..."

"In that very same place it is stated: 'A Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with [liquor] produced from pure [grains] (sāttvika) alone. Likewise, after describing the various types of fermented liquor (āsava), it says:
'In this manner a Kṣatriya may also give [it], but he should never [give] that made from flour (paiṣṭī). "
Coconut water should not be kept in bronze, nor should cow's milk or honey be kept in copper.
A gift should never be given by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya to a Brāhmaṇa;

by such a mere act of giving, the Brāhmaṇa becomes diminished in lifespan (or, according to another reading, "the Brāhmaṇa becomes degraded"). [Note: In this case, due to the weight of the syllable *vrā* in the alternative reading, there is a fear of violating the meter.]
The reading "hīnāyūḥ" and so forth would be quite correct [as it causes one to return].
Thus, in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: Brahmins should be gratified with milk, those born of the royal lineage with ghee,
Vaiśyas of the third caste with honey, and those of the Śūdra caste with fermented liquors (āsava).
Thus, in the Bhairavītantra,
it is specifically ordained that the offering and consumption of wine must be performed;
a Brāhmaṇa, however, should prepare the honey-wine in a copper vessel.
Thus, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*,
it is said that by giving or drinking liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa;
and by giving the blood of his own body, he incurs the sin of self-slaughter.
Thus, in the *Haṃsamāheśvaratantra*, within the section on the Dharma of the Kali Age (*kalidharmaprakaraṇa*) in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*,

since the prohibition against Brāhmaṇas taking wine has been stated by Harinātha Upādhyāya as being intended for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the prohibition for a Brāhmaṇa is absolute; this is established by the elision of the vowel 'a' in the phrase "brāhmaṇais tu sadāpeyā" (by Brāhmaṇas, [it] is never to be drunk).
For a Kṣatriya, at the time of battle, because battle is impossible for one who is deficient; for a Vaiśya, at the time of investing wealth, otherwise.

Because if one of impaired intellect were to perform the gift of twenty, there would result the obligation to give a hundred or more. Therefore, the meaning is that she is never not to be drunk from by Śūdras; rather, she is always to be drunk from. And thus, in the verse, "In the Kali age, O Goddess, she is to be worshipped with liquors alone," it must be understood that the word *sarvavarṇa* (all castes), which is supplied as a complement, refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas.
Now, milk is produced from trees; clarified butter is produced from bark;
honey is produced from the juice of flowers; and fermented liquor is produced from rice.

If it is argued that because specific terms such as *kṣīra* (milk) and others are defined in the *Bhairavītantra* as particular types of fermented liquors (*āsava*), the Brahmin is understood to have an entitlement to them therein—this is what occurs here: the statement "How can milk and so forth be a *bhairavakalpa*? [is given], by which it follows that the *kṣīra* [referred to] is that which is produced from trees.

The meaning is that *vārkṣa* refers to *maireya*. The same applies to what follows. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of using terms such as *kṣīravṛkṣa* in reverse order, according to the maxim: "One should not state the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) without first stating the subject of reference (*anuvāda*).
As for *odana*, it arises from rice; therefore, even for a Śūdra, liquor (*āsava*) alone is to be used in place of *odana*.

The meaning is that separate rice (*odana*) and fermented liquor (*āsava*) should not be given by Brāhmaṇas and others. This is because of the written statement and because of such Smṛti texts as: "Raw food [given] by the hand of a Śūdra is called cooked food, and cooked food is called leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*)," and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that because the Śukra’s curse pertains specifically to Brāhmaṇas, the injunction for its removal in the case of liquor is untenable; for since it is established by scripture that Śūdras alone always possess the entitlement [to drink], the liberation from Śukra’s curse serves a transcendental (adṛṣṭa) purpose.

Furthermore, by the concluding passage: "In cases such as 'one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse,' the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than the indicative mark (*liṅga*); likewise, the directly stated prohibitive injunction, 'a Brāhmaṇa having given liquor' (*brāhmaṇo madirāṃ dattvā*), is stronger than the injunction for the offering of *maireya* liquor which is to be inferred from the [context of] liberation from a curse; this is because the reasoning is the same."
The Nṛsiṃha Paṇḍitas have strengthened their thesis that [the *jīvanmukti*] is for those other than Brahmins;

however, this is extremely weak. For instance, they have cited the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*, "by means of *sāttvika* substances," as a proof for their own position. This is based on a complete lack of critical investigation. As for *sāttvika* substance...

A name such as "vrīhi" and so forth is not something established by worldly convention alone. Therefore, when there arises the inquiry, "What is that substance which is *sāttvika*? the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *sāttvika* is to be understood solely through the scripture, just as the rules of grammar govern the relationship between base and suffix. That scripture is found in the *Tripurārṇava*:
Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī—these are declared to be the three types of intoxicating substances.
That which is produced from sugarcane juice or honey is Gauḍī; it is remembered as being of the nature of Sattva.
O Śivā, that which is produced from the flowers of the Madhūka, grapes, the Tāla tree, and so forth, is celebrated by the knowers as *mādhvī*; it is of the nature of *rajas*.
"That which is made from ground rice is known as *tāmasī* and nourishing (*pauṣṭikī*);
that which is for a Brāhmaṇa is declared *sāttvikī*, while that for a king (Kṣatriya) and a Vaiśya is *rājasī*. Thus [it is said].

This being the case, we certainly conclude that the claim in the scripture that [the rule] pertains to those other than Brāhmaṇas is rooted in ignorance. Likewise, one should know the statement found in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "One should not [drink] coconut water from a bronze vessel."
Having prescribed the rule regarding primary substances and substitutes in rituals performed by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas,
and having established an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the aforementioned substances for rituals performed by Brāhmaṇas, [the text] states—
as a supplement to that exclusion— that "by offering [the substance] in this manner alone, a Brāhmaṇa would become short-lived."
He praises by means of censure in the form of an explanatory statement (arthavāda): "How could this speech be effective for you?"

Nor should it be argued that the exclusion of Brahmins and others as agents occurs simply by virtue of being performed by Kṣatriyas and others— just as the exclusion of wheat occurs through the restriction to rice— and thus, how could such [an act] be obtained in a performance by a Brahmin, or how could there be an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) for the purpose of excluding it? For the example is dissimilar.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is untenable without a substance; thus, by way of this objection, when rice (*vrīhi*) is obtained as a possible option—just like other substances—it is restricted [by the rule] "only rice. By that much, since there is no further expectation for another substance in the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the exclusion of others follows as a matter of course (*ārthika*). This applies to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Although there is no requirement for a substance (*dravya*) in a performance carried out by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya due to the restrictive rule regarding substitutes (*pratinidhi*), such a requirement does exist when the performer is a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, since this [substance] would also apply in that case, its exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) is appropriate.
Thus, the thesis is established by this, just as the birth of a son is [effected] by means of a eunuch.

As for the statement from the Bhairavī Tantra, written as an authority, which says, "Brāhmaṇas are to be satiated with milk," that too is merely a deception of the ignorant; for in the Bhairavī Tantra itself, in proximity to this very statement, the substances such as milk are determined by the phrase "milk produced from trees. As for the milk...
Regarding the statement that "produced from a tree" means that its milk performs the function of being produced from a tree,
and thus the function of satisfying (tarpaṇa) known to belong to what is produced from a tree is enjoined with respect to milk— that is incorrect.
Does the triad of words beginning with "produced from a tree" have the meaning of substance in general, or the meaning of a specific substance?

In the first case, because there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the form of the word's primary meaning—the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), which consists in "being produced from a tree"—within the category of substance (*dravyatva*), there is secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) at the level of the general [category] for that which is primarily denotative of the specific meaning. This being so, there is an abandonment of the heard primary meaning; for by the very term "produced from a tree," [the application] to clarified butter (*ājya*) and other such things [is excluded].
If [the injunction] were possible, there would be the redundancy of words such as "tat-phala" (having that as its fruit) which have the same meaning.

In the second position—that the word "vṛkṣasamudbhava" (arising from a tree) refers to a specific substance—the effect of that specific substance is enjoined with respect to the milk. Is that [effect] something perceived, or is it a means for producing an unperceived [result]?

A scriptural purpose is enjoined. In the first case, the injunction would be purposeless, since [the meaning] can be understood from common worldly experience alone. In the second case, just as in the instance "the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," the function performed by the scriptural rule "one should tether the animal to the sacrificial post" is enjoined for the threshing-floor post; so too [is it here].

Is that which is already obtained through another scriptural injunction being enjoined here, or is that which is not obtained through another scriptural injunction being enjoined? In the first case, since the purpose of being produced from a tree—such as the satiation of Brahmins with milk—is already secured by the statement "milk is produced from a tree" alone, the scriptural injunction "Brahmins are to be satiated with milk" would be redundant; for indeed...

Having stated, "The threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," it is separately enjoined that "one should tether the animal to the threshing-floor post. This would be an injunction for an action not otherwise established; likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of even the son of a barren woman being enjoined as performing the duties of a husband and wife. In my view, however, [the injunction] is: "Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk."

The rule regarding the materials for the *tarpaṇa* rite serves as an indicator of a specific intended meaning, overriding the conventional meaning of the word "milk" (*kṣīra*) by means of the statement "milk produced from trees"; thus, there is no redundancy whatsoever, nor is there even a scent of inconsistency. Even though...

Since it lacks injunctive force (*vidhāyakatva*), its futility (*vaiyyarthya*) must be assumed. Nevertheless, [in the passage] "He offers the eight-potherd cake to Agni; [he offers] that which belongs to Soma..."

Having prescribed eight oblations beginning with *caru* in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice, the designation "Vaiśvadeva" was applied to the entire collection by stating, "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva. Consequently, in the injunction "In spring, one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," when the Viśvedeva sacrifice alone would otherwise be obtained for spring through the [general] term "sacrifice," that [specific application] is set aside by this new designation.

It is stated in the Jaimini-tantra that a statement is meaningful when it brings about the accomplishment of eight sacrifices; thus, it ought to be meaningful. Furthermore, one cannot, by employing the word *kṣīra* (milk) which is itself extremely well-established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), abandon its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*).
It should not be said that such an alternative explanation has never been seen anywhere; for it is stated in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"One whose death is imminent shall not see Arundhatī, Dhruva, nor likewise the constellation of the Seven Sages... [and so forth].

Having first stated this, Arundhatī herself explained it by means of the passage beginning with "the tip of the nose" and so forth. There are hundreds of such instances; however, due to a lack of necessity, no further examples have been written here.

In this statement, regarding the fourth quarter, the phrase "āsava derived from rice" (*taṇḍulodbhavam*) is indicative of that which is also derived from flour (*piṣṭodbhava*). As stated in the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra*:
"O Maheśvarī, [the substances are] milk, clarified butter, honey, and likewise āsava."
The wise should understand that [these substances] are produced respectively from tree bark, flowers, and flour.

In this regard, since the convention of "āsava" has been established even for that which is made from flour (*paiṣṭa*), by this [argument], the entire written objection— that in the opponent's view the reason consisting of the "throwing of the staff" would result in the erroneous application of terms such as "milk-tree" (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) in the opposite sense— is refuted, because [the opponent] has not stated the subject to be restated (*anuvādya*) as the means of proving that.

Because it is described as being a factor that apprehends the specific meaning and the intended purport (*tātparya*), there is not even a trace of the relationship between subject (*uddeśya*) and predicate (*vidheya*) here. For this very reason, in the section on Names (*nāmadheya-pāda*), it is held that in the case of "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the name itself lacks intrinsic authority regarding Dharma because it is not something to be enjoined; rather, [its authority is derived otherwise].
It is established in the authoritative treatises that [the Veda] is the means for the officiating priests, because it serves to remind them of the rules for performance.

Or, let it be granted for the sake of pleasing others that the designation "milk" is prescribed with reference to what is produced from a tree, even though it is not sanctioned by the scriptures; nevertheless, the penalty cast upon this view by the opponent is unbearable. For that imposition of a penalty is based on the established pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever is first mentioned [must be primary]," yet that [pervasion] is unproven.

Because there are hundreds of instances of deviation [in the Veda], such as "He offers with curd," "Those who are sacrificers are the officiating priests," and "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the statement by authoritative scholars that 'one cannot speak of a subject (anuvādya) without first mentioning it'?
[the answer is: in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka), that which is mentioned first generally becomes the subject (uddeśya).

His intention is as follows: in the present case, with respect to milk (*kṣīra*), the injunction that it "originates from a tree" (*vṛkṣasamudbhūtatva*) is indeed a contradiction due to its sheer pointlessness (*vaiyyarthya*). How was this not understood by the opponent? Likewise, regarding the statement "liquor originates from rice" (*āsavaṃ taṇḍulodbhavam*), [the opponent] asserts that the word *taṇḍulodbhava* means "boiled rice" (*odana*).

By writing that raw food belongs to a Śūdra because it serves as a means of accomplishing that [cooking], he became an object of ridicule even for children. By this [it is shown] on page 128 of the *Laghustavaratna*.

The argument regarding [the milk and other substances] being the means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*) has been set aside, because they are understood there as merely conventional terms (*saṅketika-śabda*). As for the claim that the direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), "A Brāhmaṇa, having given wine," possesses greater authority than the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the release from Śukra’s curse—that too is trivial; for it is not the case that a Brāhmaṇa...

In the statement, "By giving liquor, one is indeed fallen from Brahminhood," there is the hearing of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sense of prohibition, which takes the form of an injunctive suffix. However, the injunction is to be inferred through the censure of the act of giving liquor. Thus, we do not know what answer such a person—who asserts that this [injunction] is a directly heard scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)—could give in the assembly of the learned. And so it is.

Without providing a solution for the direct scriptural statement written by himself— which, along with the liberation from Śukra’s curse, prescribes that "in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and in the family tradition (kulācāra), a Brāhmaṇa should drink surā"— he merely asserts, out of his own mouth,
that it refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas, thereby [deceiving] all others.
One who generates delusion [regarding this] should be considered as excluded from the Tantras.

And thus, this systematic arrangement of the statements—namely, that [the offering] is with "sāttvika substance"—demonstrates the arrangement of the statement from the Mahākālasaṃhitā found in the *Laghustava*, which says, "The Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk. Likewise, there is the statement from the *Bhairavītantra*: "The Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk."

And as for that which is stated in the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra* in sequence— "by the Brāhmaṇas and others, with milk, clarified butter, honey, and fermented liquors [or honey and flour]"— and as for the statement in the *Laghustava*, because those are of a general nature, they are authoritative in light of the statement in the *Yāmala*.

The concluding summary here is: "Successively with the four substances made from milk, ghee, honey, and flour. And thus, since milk and the other substances are always obtained without distinction through the *Bhairavī* and other tantras, the statement in the *Yāmala* serves to establish a restriction, specifying particular substances such as milk for particular times and particular performers. As for that which...

"A Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with *sāttvika* substance while she resides in the ocean of knowledge"— since, according to the *Yāmala* statement, there is no possibility of restriction regarding the term "milk" (*kṣīra*) being applied to substances born of sugarcane juice and honey (which are *sāttvika*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) for the ritual performed by a Brāhmaṇa throughout the four ages.

It is attained. Thus, by the statement "the *rājasī* belongs to the king and the merchant," it is proclaimed by the experts that when the ritual is performed by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, it arises from the *madhūka* flower, grapes, the palmyra tree, and so forth; this is called *mādhvī*. O Śivā, that is the *rājasī*; thus ends the fourth [section].
It should be placed under the foot.

Thus, by this explanation, since the substances whose nature is the aforementioned [substances] are always obtained, the designation "milk" and so forth does not apply to the collection of these aforementioned things; rather, when a substance whose nature is bark— suitable for a Kṣatriya— is obtained in the Kṛta Yuga, even that which has grapes and the like as its nature [is included].

There is an option regarding the attainment [of the result]. Since the two statements concerning the Śūdra are of one form, there is no option once it has been performed. In the same way, this should be inferred for the Tretā and other ages as appropriate. In the Kali age, for a Brāhmaṇa, [the consumption of] that which has sugarcane juice or honey as its source is established by the statements of the Jñānārṇava and the Tripurārṇava.
"In the Kali age, she is to be worshipped by all castes with *āsava* alone. This being so:
"In the Kṛta age, O beloved, she is to be worshipped by Śūdras with manifest *āsava*;
in the Tretā age, by Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and in the Dvāpara age, by kings and others."
In the Kali age, O Great Goddess, she is worshipped by Brahmins and others.

If the statement from the *Rahasyārṇava*—“p. 129)” —is applicable, then, by means of statements other than those [already] established, a distinction regarding substances other than [ordinary] ones is obtained for all castes; furthermore, by the statement of the *Rahasyārṇava*, there is also an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) for anyone other than a Śūdra.

That being the case, when the three higher castes have performed [the rite], there is an option regarding the perceptible substance. Alternatively, even in the *Rahasyārṇava*, in a performance by a Śūdra associated with the Kṛta Yuga, an *āsava* (fermented liquor) having rice as its base is prescribed. Thus, through that other tantra, the attainment of *āsava* for the Śūdra is established.
The assumption that this is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*) out of fear of redundancy is not to be trusted;

for if that were the case, since a substance is required in a rite performed by Brāhmaṇas and others, milk and other materials would have to be taken from another ritual manual (*tantra*), rather than being subject to an option (*vikalpa*). In the same way, there is the statement from the *Rahasyārṇava* regarding the *tretā* fire.

It prescribes *āsava* for both Śūdras and Vaiśyas. This being the case, *āsava* is obtained for the Vaiśya by this [text], while clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is obtained for him by the statement of the *Yāmala*. Herein there is an option (*vikalpa*). Thus, in the Dvāpara age, there is an option between *āsava* and honey (*madhu*) for both Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas according to the two cited statements. However, in the Kali age, it is for both [classes].

Since there is no contradiction due to their being of a single nature, this alone is the case; indeed, this position is logical, not the position of exclusive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*). And thus, in the statement from the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, "where it is necessarily specified," the phrase "in the absence of the primary" (*mukhyālābhe*) must be supplied. [This applies] when the primary is unavailable.

The meaning of that is: "A Brahmin should add honey to it in a copper vessel. This being the case, such a practice contradicts the statement in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "In this manner [honey] may be in copper for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, but never for a twice-born [Brahmin]. Thus, because the two authorities possess equal force, an option (*vikalpa*) between them cannot be avoided.
Even according to the opponent's view.

As for the statement from the *Haṃsamāheśvaratantra* [Haṃsapārameśvara, ba 1], "A Brāhmaṇa who gives liquor falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa," if that were situated in that tantra near the rules regarding family substances (*kuladravya*) for Kṣatriyas and others, then it would be a supplementary explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), like the statement: "Others are indeed not cattle (*apaśavaḥ*)."

It is like the expression *aśvebhyaḥ* (from horses). If it were not in proximity to that [prohibition], then it would refer to Brahmins who have not conquered their senses, because the prohibition against giving wealth to such persons will be stated later. As for the statement from the *Kulārṇava*, "But by Brahmins it should always be drunk," one should apply elision (*praśleṣa*) to the vowel *a* there, making it *na pibet* (he should not drink). This is what is meant.

The opponent’s intention is that a prohibition has been established for Brahmins because they are intent upon the supreme human goals (puruṣārtha); this is because of the citation of reasons for such prohibitions, such as the impossibility of a Kṣatriya who is incapacitated engaging in battle at the time of combat. And that [prohibition] is indeed acceptable to us.

We also maintain that a Brāhmaṇa has no right to accept wealth beyond what is required for a sacrificial rite (*kratvartha*). Furthermore, as for the prohibition against taking liquor (*surāgraha*) in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice during the Kali age mentioned by Harinātha, that too is acceptable to us;
however, such a prohibition does not extend to the family tradition (*kulācāra*).
The status of being a *sautrāmaṇi* draught associated with the Kali Yuga is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the object of the prohibition of liquor;

since the family custom (*kulācāra*) is not pervaded by that [delimiting factor], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in applying the *kaimutika* logic. Therefore, as there is not even a trace of the objections raised by others regarding the case of Brāhmaṇas, [the practice remains valid].

Since [the practice] has been demonstrated for a thousand practitioners, for one who accepts the authority of the Tantra, the priority given to worship performed by Brāhmaṇas and others is established by scripture; moreover, even a Brāhmaṇa cannot abandon that [priority]. And thus—
O Dear One, one should neither recollect nor mutter [the mantra] without the perfuming of the substance;
O Great Goddess, for those who do so, there is suffering at every step.
There is no mantra without liquor, nor liquor without mantra.
Thus, in the *Kulārṇava*, it is said:
"And without wine (*ali*) and meat (*piśita*), worship shall be fruitless."

Thus, O Maheśvarī, in the conduct of the samaya, one who has tasted [the substance] without cause and is possessed by agitation shall perform neither worship nor recitation, neither meditation nor contemplation.
Thus, in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*,
he who performs my worship without wine (*ali*) and meat (*piśita*) shall become a creator of misery and a beast for the *yoginīs*.
Thus, in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Whoever performs your worship devoid of the primary substances shall be consumed by your wrath and reduced to ashes; it cannot be otherwise."
Thus it is established in the *Samayāṅgamātṛkā*: such statements as these are supported [by authority].

Furthermore, when examined with an unartificial mind, it appears that the portion ending with "and thus [the view] other than that of the Brāhmaṇas" is incorrect. Let scholars free from envy investigate further than this.
This very point is established likewise in the commentary on the seventh mantra of the *Tripuropaniṣad*, which states: "Having understood this, the wise rejoice."
As for that which was established in the *Saubhāgyānandasandoha*, where the author first asserted our own settled position and then—

on the grounds that the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) with Vedic mantras is prescribed and would thus have no scope if the rite were intended for the worship by Śūdras, leading to the fallacy of leaving the injunction without scope— proved that the qualification belongs to Brāhmaṇas; that [is as follows]:

However, that [interpretation] is extremely weak. In the case of the statement, "A chariot-maker (rathakāra) should perform the fire-consecration (ādhāna) during the rainy season," the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) sets aside the etymological derivation (*yoga*), thereby establishing the eligibility for the consecration for one born of a mixed caste (*saṅkara-jāti*).

Subsequently, the study of the Vedas required for that rite is also inferred; thus, by the logic of the sixth book (*ṣāṣṭha-nyāya*), the eligibility of the Śūdra is established through reasoning regarding the recitation of Vedic mantras.
As long as [the object] is being employed, because the authority [to do so] is unavoidable, for this reason one's desired goal is not accomplished.

Up to this point, the determination of eligibility (*adhikāra*) has been established for the Brāhmaṇa. Yet, even though this eligibility has been so determined, it does not apply to everyone; rather, does it apply only to one who has conquered the senses and is free from desire and the like? For this very reason, it is stated in the *Paramānandatantra*:
But this, O Great Goddess, is the supreme Kaula path,
which is rightly equal to the vow of walking on the edge of a sword, for it has the restraint of the mind as its cause.
"O Supreme Goddess, for one of steady mind, it is easily attained, fruitful, and bestows swift success; for another, however, it would be fruitless and a cause of suffering. Thus [it is said].
In the Tripurārṇava as well:
"This is the supreme dharma spoken by Śiva, which bestows the attainment of happiness."
It is easily attained by one who has conquered the senses, but not by another even in infinite births.

It is that which, merely by being remembered for a moment, is fully capable of producing delusion even in those who have renounced everything, whose vital energy is drawn upward, and who dwell in no fixed abode.
For this alone is declared here to be the cause for complete accomplishment:
from here wine, from there meat, and likewise various kinds of food.
There, among young women richly adorned with beautiful attire, their eyes rolling with intoxication,
it is indeed exceedingly difficult to maintain control over the mind in every respect.
"O Goddess, how could this belong to one who is devoid of devotion and faith? Thus [it is said].
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Because the tantras are extremely profound, their true nature is also strictly concealed.
[The practitioner should be] a Brahmin who knows the essential truth of the meaning of the Vedic scriptures, who is intelligent, and self-controlled."
"One who is capable of extracting the hidden meaning and essence of the Tantra through churning shall be an authority on the Kaula path; any other shall be a partaker of suffering. Thus it is said.
In the Kulārṇava it is said:
"That liquor which, when consumed by day, might even delude the gods—that *maireya* is auspicious;
the man who does not undergo transformation after drinking it [is liberated]."
"Having become devoted to Śiva in Japan, he was liberated, as was that Kaulika. Thus it is said.

Even by the Blessed Paraśurāma, in the Kaula practice (*kaulācāra*), it was stated as the primary duty: "The avoidance of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, unordained violence, theft, what is contrary to the world, and what is loathed by the world. [This is the Sūtra spoken by the Blessed One, found on page 33, line 19 of the final section.]

This has been established. Therefore, just as only those with sight have the qualification for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices according to the requirement of the auxiliary act of looking at the clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa) and so forth, and not the blind, likewise,
only one who has conquered the senses has the qualification according to the requirement of the auxiliaries such as the avoidance of desire, anger, and so forth, and no other.
This is the intention of the author of the Sūtra. In this same way, many other statements are found in other tantras as well;
however, they have not been written down here because they serve no further purpose and for fear of excessive prolixity.

Nowadays, those of the present time— who have no control over their senses, whose tongues are fickle, who are devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, who have assumed the status of Kaulas through blindness for women, and who are greedy for mere material wealth—
disregard written words and, without considering their own authority, act only to fulfill their own desires.

Disregarding such statements from the *Kulārṇava* as "having drunk, having drunk again, and having drunk yet again, one should drink the substance until the throat is full," these scoundrels— whether ignorant of its true intent or knowing it well—
engage in conduct according to their own whims.
They act [thus], yet they obtain no peace anywhere, neither here nor in the hereafter;
on the contrary, by the command of the illustrious Dharmarāja, they surely undergo the torments born of great transgressions. There is no doubt in this matter.
There is doubt. Such fallen persons should not be remembered in tantric assemblies;
for this very reason, even a detailed mockery of such Kaulikas has been made in the *Prabodhacandrodaya*.
Therefore, at the commencement [of practice], [one should rely on] those who have conquered their senses, who possess devotion and faith, and who are learned.

Only those who have ascended to the stages of devotion (bhakti-bhūmikā) as previously described possess the qualification for this; for others, it would lead only to a fall—enough of this elaboration. The truth is that for those other than the qualified individuals mentioned, the worship of Viṣṇu and others is solely according to the Vedic path.
The distinction between the Right-hand and Left-hand practices:

those who have not conquered their senses, having entered the Kula path, should perform worship with water and other such items alone; this is the Right-hand path. Those who have conquered their senses should perform the ritual service with the substances prescribed [in the scriptures]; this is the Left-hand practice.
Someone [objects]: "That is trivial, because he has not even understood the meaning of the term *vāmācāra*. And so it is said in the *Trikūṭārahasya*:
"O Dear One, I shall explain the *vāmācāra*, which is the means of accomplishing the *Śrīvidyā*."
By performing which, a practitioner of mantras will quickly become a possessor of spiritual accomplishments in the Kali age.
A garland made from human teeth, a skull-cup as a vessel,
a seat such as a lion skin, and a bracelet fashioned from a woman’s hair.
Beginning with these words, [the matter] has been described in detail. Among those [descriptions], even the name of the primary substance does not appear.

However, that detailed account was elaborated at length by our supreme preceptors during the occasion of explaining the name *Lalitā*—specifically, in the section concerning those who abide on the paths of the left (*savya*) and the right (*apasavya*). Those desiring further particulars [should consult that work].
From this it should be understood; likewise, it is also established by the Kālikā Purāṇa. For fear of excessive length, I do not elaborate upon it here.
One who has not conquered their senses has no authority in the Kaula path;

although it is stated in the *Paramānanda-tantra-ṭippaṇī* that those with unconquered senses may perform worship with scented water, that is incorrect, for a secondary alternative is permitted only when the primary one is unavailable, and never otherwise.

Because this contradicts the statement in the twentieth chapter of the *Paramānanda Tantra*— for it would be as impossible as a hare's horn for one who lacks qualification for the primary [practice] to have a qualification for a substitute— therefore, for those who have not conquered their senses,
if there is a desire for worship at first sight, they should perform the worship of another deity by means of another path, and through that...
Having ascertained that one's inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is fully ripened and firm, one should thereafter take recourse to the Kaula path. As it is said in the *Kulasāra*:
"From the repeated service of other deities..."

"A person whose mind is fully matured and who has attained authoritative realization in the Kaula [tradition] should enter here after restraining the external senses; no other [should do so]. Thus it is said.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa as well:
"For one who has not chanted the names of other deities for ten million births,
faith arises only in the chanting of the name of the Śrī Devī."
"Just as one becomes a worshiper of Śrīvidyā in one's final birth, so too should the recitation of the *Nāmasāhasra* be performed in one's final birth. (p. 133)
In the *Yāmala* as well:
"Having realized that the mind has been purified through the performance of rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* over many births, one should become a worshiper of the *Śrīvidyā*."
In the *Pheṭkāra-tantra* it is also said: "This vidyā must be kept secret in every way from those who have not conquered their senses;
therefore, the vidyā is powerful, but it would cease to be a vidyā through disclosure."

"The family flower, the family substance, the family worship, and the family recitation—these should not be disclosed to such persons if one desires one's own welfare. Thus [it is said in the *Siddhiśrī*].
Even the sacred teaching is forbidden for one who has not conquered the senses; what need is there to mention its formal acceptance?
Therefore, one who has not conquered the senses has no qualification for the Kaula path; enough of this excessive detail. || 31 ||
This is the purification of the arghya; may there be auspiciousness. || 31 ||
Thus ends the third section, named the Śrīkrama, in the Kalpasūtra.
This refers to the performance of the mandala and so forth, which was stated to be done with that water following the purification of the general *arghya*;

the ritual action beginning from that point up to "one should offer oblations into the Kuṇḍalinī" constitutes the purification of the *arghya*, that is, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *arghya*. Although [this] follows from the prescription of the entire set of rituals in the previously mentioned sūtra, [it is stated here for clarity].

Although it can be understood that this refers to the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *arghya* offering, nevertheless, since there are certain consecrations such as the removal of curses (*śāpavimocana*), the reading "consecrations" (*saṃskārān*) appears more appropriate.
Furthermore, upon the repetition of the Sūtra, that which is to be purified must be indicated.

"And the supplementary portion [of the temple] is complete from the primary sanctum. (Thus ends the third section—Śrī.)—Thinking that some might mistakenly take up other vessels, the supremely compassionate Paraśurāma composed this aphorism for the purpose of dispelling such confusion. This...
The meaning is that purification is exactly as stated and nothing else. By the word "Śiva," the conclusion of the section on the *arghya* offering is indicated.

In the *Nibandha* regarding the purification of the special *arghya*, it was stated in the *Sūtra* that the worship of the center [of the maṇḍala] should be performed with the *vidyā*; however, that has been omitted here. Furthermore, the following have not been mentioned: the drawing of the fourth vowel, the mantra "hrīṃ mahālakṣmīśvarī," the worship of Sudhādevī and so forth, ending with "having offered the flower with the *gālinī* [mudrā]."
It is included. Since there is no authoritative evidence for it here, that which is composed merely by one's own intellect is not to be accepted. || 31 ||
Thus ends the third section, named the Śrīkrama, in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.
The Fourth Section: The Lalitākrama.
Regarding the invocation of the Supreme Consciousness (paraciti) into the Śrīcakra:
he begins to demonstrate the method of invoking the deity residing in the heart into the Śrīcakra.

Then, having caused that primordial consciousness— which resides in the heart-center, which is skilled at piercing the forest of lotuses within the *suṣumṇā*, which has dispelled the darkness of delusion, and which is the radiant light of the lamp of Śiva— to emerge through the nostril, one should place her,
whose body is assumed through play, upon the crest of the *trikhaṇḍa-mudrā*. [This...]

The extraction of the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* is to be seen in the second part of the *Śiva-darśana*, verses 15.8–11, concerning the subject matter. Having brought [the flowers] into the hand in the *Kusumāñjali*: || 1 ||

The word *atha* indicates a specific sequence, as in the expressions "then [the tongue]," or "then [the chest]"; alternatively, it indicates the conclusion of the preceding section. The heart-cakra is the *anāhata*; it is also conventionally referred to as the *dahara*. Residing therein—this very place is well known in the scriptures as the abode of the deity.
And so says the Śruti: "Therein is a small ether free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon.

Also in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Situated within the lotus of the heart. Therefore, the heart-cakra is the dwelling place of the deity. For one residing there, external ritual worship with material offerings is not possible.

Therefore, this qualification should be understood as intended to indicate that the location is permanent, for the purpose of bringing [the deity] out from that place; for even Suṣumṇā extends through the lotuses situated from the Mūlādhāra up to the Brahma-randhra.
There is one particular channel (nāḍī) in the form of a staff that serves as the support for the interconnection [of the channels]. As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"This is proclaimed to be the support of the wheels of the body from the base upwards;
she who is everywhere sung of by the supreme sages as Suṣumṇā."
Thus [it is said]. Regarding that [forest], the "wilderness" (*aṭavī*) refers to the difficult path consisting of the lotuses such as Viśuddhi and the rest;
"penetration" (*nirbhedana*) means the preparation of a path suitable for coming and going. She is skilled (*kuśalām*) in that regard.
By this qualification, [it is indicated] that when returning from the heart to the Śrīcakra and other locations after worship, and again departing [from there], [she is skilled].

The absence of effort is indicated. "Nirastā" means that by which delusion—ignorance—is cast away, i.e., dispelled; it is like darkness (*timira*). To strengthen the meaning of this qualification, he states another qualification: "Śiva. [She is] the radiance, the manifestation in the form of light, of the lamp whose nature is Śiva. By this—

By the statement that [Śiva] is of the nature of light, it is implied through the preceding qualification that the destruction of the darkness of ignorance is easily established. Furthermore, just as there is an inseparable relationship between a lamp and its light, so too is there an inseparable relationship between Śiva and Śakti.
This very point has been clearly stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Śakti has the form of a triangle; the supreme Śiva has the form of a bindu.
Therefore, there is a relationship of inseparable concomitance between the bindu and the triangle. Thus it is said.
In the Śrīdevībhāgavata as well:
"In whatever substratum a certain property exists as invariably concomitant,"
"That substratum (dharmin) shall be of the nature of Śiva, while the attribute (dharma) maintains the essential form of Śakti. Thus [it is said].

The distinction between these two entities is adventitious (*aupādhika*) and not real; this has already been elaborated upon previously during the investigation of reality [*tattvanirūpaṇa*]—specifically in the third section on "Following Names" (page 92), in the *Śrīkrama*, and in the commentary on the ninth aphorism.

In this context, such an activity is precisely the mental visualization of exiting from the location of the heart by the aforementioned path. The subsequent activity—

"She assumes a form through sport" (līlā) means that she has assumed—that is, accepted—a body by mere will (*svecchāmātreṇa*), as described in the verse of meditation (*dhyānaśloka*). By this, it is indicated that, unlike other bodies, she has assumed a beautiful form for the sake of favoring her devotees without the experience of dwelling in a womb. Furthermore, the Lord is the cause of the world because He possesses the power of omniscience and omnipotence. For one who lacks these two powers cannot be the cause of the world; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, the Lord is the cause of the world because He is independent (*svatantra*). One who is dependent on another cannot be the cause of the world; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension. Furthermore, the Lord is the cause of the world because He is eternal (*nitya*). That which is non-eternal cannot be the cause of the world; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension. Having assumed that form, she is the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* (this *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā* is to be seen in the context of Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15/8–11). She is called *trikhaṇḍā* because she shatters (*khaṇḍayati*) the three—namely birth, death, and old age—or else the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; the meaning is that she bestows exclusive liberation. Or else:
The three segments (*khaṇḍa*) are the *kalās* consisting of will, knowledge, and action; that whose nature is these is the Three-segmented (*Trikhaṇḍā*).
As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*:
"When that consciousness, Ambikā, consists of the three *kalās*, she is called Mudrā."
"Having assumed the form of the three sections (trikhaṇḍā), she is always present;
she is proclaimed to be the pervader of the entire king of wheels. Thus [it is said].
The meaning of the term *mudrā* is as follows: it is called *mudrā* because it gladdens (*modana*) and dissolves (*drāvaṇa*) the universe. As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*:
"When there is the manifestation and reflective awareness of the universe upon the wall of the conscious self..."
She acts according to her own will, endowed with the full desire to create.
The power of action (kriyā-śakti), however, [is so called] because it gladdens and likewise dissolves the universe.
"O Goddess, [this] is called Mudrā... || Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: when the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), by its own will, after the act of vision (*īkṣaṇa*), performs manifestation and reflective awareness (*prakāśāmarśana*) while desiring full transformations upon the wall that is non-different from its own self— this...

The state (*bhāva*) of the world consists of the six transformations of being: "it exists," "it is born," "it grows," "it transforms," "it declines," and "it perishes. Among these, the second transformation is *prakāśa* (manifestation), because its defining characteristic is becoming clear or evident. The third transformation is *āmarśana* (reflection), because its defining characteristic is that it becomes heart-pleasing through the thought "this is it. And thus:

After Tripurasundarī has reflected upon the existence of the creation residing within her own heart, there arises in her a desire directed toward the second and subsequent transformations of the universe; this is *vicikīrṣā* (the will to create).
