Thereafter, she acts through the sequence of the emergence and expansion of the universe. These two are precisely the aforementioned *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

Consciousness (*cit*) characterized by such will (*icchā*) and form (*kṛti*) is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). This power of action is a *mudrā* because it rejoices in and dissolves the creation and growth performed by Tripurasundarī.
Rejoicing (*anumodana*) means favoring an action performed by an agent distinct from oneself. Dissolving (*drāvaṇa*) refers to [the dissolution] of that which is dense (*ghana*).

Expansion (*prasara*) consists of bringing about a state of relaxation in the limbs of that which was contracted. This very power of action, through its conjunction with the gaze (*īkṣaṇa*) and other factors in a state of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with its own seal (*mudrā*), becomes three-partite (*trikalāmayī*) and three-segmented (*trikhaṇḍā*).
This is the meaning of the supreme secret. Therefore, this pervasive power (*vyāpikā*) is the most excellent of all.

The application (*viniyoga*) of that [mudrā] was made for its invocation (*āvāhana*). The unseen nature (*adṛṣṭasvarūpa*) of such a mudrā has been explained. However, its seen nature (*dṛṣṭasvarūpa*), consisting of the interlacing of fingers, is observed to be of various kinds according to the differences between the tantras; it is not seen in this [text]. Therefore—

Having unified the meaning of the Tantra as understood through the lineage of the Gurus, it is clarified hereafter. Having brought together and grasped in his hand that which is such—a form consisting of three parts (trikhaṇḍātmaka) as its external appearance—with a crest-lock (śikhaṇḍita), knotted and joined with flowers, in that [hand]... || 1 ||

Having uttered "Māyā-lakṣmī Parā" and the name of the Goddess, one should perform the rite of visualization with the words, "I visualize [her] as the embodiment of nectar and consciousness; obeisance. Thus, having performed the visualization. || 2 ||

*Māyā* (hrīṃ), *Śrīṃ*, and *Parā* (sauḥ) constitute the meaning of the word “Lakṣmī. The authorities regarding this matter have already been shown. Having thus uttered these three seed-syllables (*bīja*), the name of the Goddess—“of Lalitā,” the sole sovereign of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*)—should follow in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) as is appropriate. Then...

One should recite [the mantra] ending with "namaḥ" and remaining unmodified. Thus, at the beginning, according to the general convention, the "Three Taras"—*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ*—are added; the mantra becomes thirty-three syllables: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ śakticakraikanāyikāyāḥ amṛtacaitanyamūrtiṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*. By means of this...
Having fashioned and meditated upon the form of the Supreme Deity.

In this case, since it would be redundant to again conceive of a form for that which already possesses a body assumed through divine play (*līlā*) as mentioned in the preceding sūtra, the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside by the stronger order of meaning (*arthakrama*). Thus, the sequence is as follows:
first, the conception of the form of pure consciousness (*cit*) alone by means of this mantra, and then [the conception] of the form.
The distinction is as follows: the imagined [deity] exits through the path of the nostrils and is then brought into the hollowed palms of the hands filled with flowers. || 2 ||

Having uttered the speech joined with *hasa* (the syllable *ha*), the sweet-toned *kalārī*, and also the fourteenth and sixteenth [vowels] joined with *hasa*, [one should pray]: "O Mother, who dwells within the great lotus forest, whose form is the bliss of the Cause,
who acts for the welfare of all beings, O Supreme Goddess, come, come!"
Thus, having invoked the supreme consciousness into the Baindava-cakra. || 3 ||

137) By the maxim "the inclusion of the whole" (samudāyagrahaṇa), which was stated previously in the section on grammatical assignment (*nyāsa*), there is the inclusion of the mere consonants alone in [the rules concerning] *has* and so forth, according to traditional usage (*sampradāya*). It is joined with *ha*, *sa*, and *ra*.

The word for speech is *hsraiṃ*. This is the aggregate of the letters *ka*, *la*, *ra*, *i*, and the bindu, joined with *ha* and *sa*, forming *hsklrīṃ*. Likewise, there are *ha*, *sa*, *ra*, the fourteenth vowel (*au*), *ṣa* (the sixteenth consonant), and *visarga*; these are the fourteenth, the sixteenth, and the fourteenth and sixteenth [vowels].

Having uttered "hsrauḥ" and recited [the mantra] as heard up to the end of "parameśvarī," one should invoke the Supreme Consciousness (paraciti) into the Bindu-cakra. As for the nature of the mantra: first is the Tritārī, then "hasraiṃ hsklrīṃ hsrauḥ."
O Mother, who dwells within the Great Lotus Grove, whose form is the bliss of the primal cause,
who acts for the welfare of all beings, O Supreme Goddess, come, come hither!
Thus, the mantra consists of thirty-eight syllables. [It refers to the one] residing in that inner region which is the interior of the Great Lotus Forest (*mahāpadmavana*).
The nature of the Great Lotus is described in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"O Sage, listen attentively as I describe the site of the Lotus Forest."
There, within an interval of six yojanas, upon that ground inlaid with excellent jewels,
there are indeed great-stalked land-lotuses situated all around.

Regarding Setubandha, it is said that the Mahāpadmavana is a collection of thousand-petaled lotuses. She is one whose very form (*vigraha*) is *kāraṇānanda*, which is unconditioned bliss (*aparicchinna-ānanda*). Alternatively, *kāraṇa* means "first" (*prathama*); that which is born therein is *kāraṇaja*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born there. Thus, she is both that and bliss (*ānanda*).

The remainder is as before; the remainder is clear. Alternatively, the ritual act of invocation (*āvāhana*) consists of drawing forth the light of consciousness (*caitanya-mahas*), fashioning a limited form (*mūrti*) by means of the mantra, bringing it into the hand, and then, by means of the mantra, performing everything up to its placement upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

Since there is no obstacle to many actions— beginning with the *avadāna* (cutting) and ending with the *pradāna* (offering)— constituting a single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*), it follows that wherever there is the simultaneous worship (*tantra*) of various deities in rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*),
the principle of *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performing all acts for one deity before moving to the next) is established for that entire collection, because that collection constitutes a single ritual act.
This mantra serves as the means for such a partial invocation and for settling upon the seat.

The author of the Nibandha, however, has presented the sequence of internal sacrifice (antaryāga) and the mudrās beginning with invocation as described in the Jñānārṇava; that [work] is not to be respected because it lacks authoritative proof.
Regarding the procedure for the sixty-four services: one should perform the sixty-four services. All service mantras should be preceded by the *tritārī* and should end with *kalpayāmi namaḥ*. || 4 ||

By the phrase "sixty-four," there is an exclusion of any other form of worship—such as the sixteen-fold worship mentioned in other tantras—for those who follow this tantra. Now, is this an exclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*), a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*), or an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*)? Not the first, because [it would imply] that by anyone...

Because it is not eternally obtained through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the second [alternative] is not possible, as there is no prior attainment even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*). If it is argued that the third [alternative] might then apply, we grant that as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nevertheless, in every respect, this is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); regarding the aspect of metaphorical application (*upacāra*), it is original, while regarding the sixty-four aspects, it is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*). This is because, in an injunction for metaphorical application, the metaphors are infinite.
In that regard, since various numbers are applicable, the number sixty-four is also applicable according to one view.
Nor should it be argued that if a restrictive apūrva (unseen potency) is accepted for a single [act] in this way, there would be a confusion of injunctions; for such a consequence is acceptable.

In the sentence "The cake on eight potsherds belongs to Agni" (*yad āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), since both Agni and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are optionally obtained, there is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) regarding that part [of the sacrifice], while regarding the act of sacrifice itself, it is a novel injunction (*apūrva*); this is because it is observed [in the scriptures]. Nor is this a restrictive injunction of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) by means of the subsequent sūtra, "Having prescribed the sixty-four modes of address" (*catuḥṣaṣṭhy upacārān vidhāya*), which is the sentence mentioned in the fifth sūtra following this one.
It should not be said that "by this [the rule for] the ritual of service (upacāra) is stated," because if that were so, the sixty-four words in this sūtra would be redundant.
Nor should it be suspected that, such being the case, the subsequent statement "sixty-four" is useless;
for, having restated the sixty-four services, it prescribes a specific order. In no way is there [redundancy] regarding the service itself.
That [text] is the prescriber of the number; "one should perform" (kuryāt) is a clear injunctive suffix, and this very [text] is the prescriber of the ritual procedure qualified by that number.

Alternatively, since the sequence is already established by the mere order of the recitation, and because it is impossible to prescribe a sequence by means of the subsequent phrase "having performed the sixty-four offerings," the phrase "of those [offerings] already prescribed" is a restatement (anuvāda) in the form of a conclusion regarding the performance of the sixty-four offerings. The fruit of this, however, is found in another tantra:
There may be certain offerings not included among the sixty-four mentioned, which are different from those already stated; however, worship should not be performed with them.
Rather, for this purpose, one should provide a substitute and offer [the substance] by means of the name of the material as heard in the mantra.
Thus, when possible, worship should be performed with more than the aforementioned offerings. For this very reason:
In the Tripurārṇava it is said:
"If possible, one should worship with offerings superior to those already mentioned."

This statement contains the very logic already explained. The intent of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), not the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Therefore, its intent is precisely that there should be no lack of even a single [type of] metaphorical application (*upacāra*) among the sixty-four; it does not intend to exclude anything additional. Consequently, regarding those exceeding this [number]...
To whatever extent the occurrence of palanquins, elephants, horses, dances, and so forth is possible, conceptualization to that same extent should be understood as not contradicting the Sūtras.

In this context, the meaning of the term "service" (upacāra) is a particular kind of pleasure produced by a substance being imagined; the phrase "one should perform" means that one should produce or generate that [pleasure].
Nor should it be asked: "What kind of pleasure could arise for a deity who is eternally satisfied by means of the substance offered?

It is true that pleasure does not arise in one who is eternally satisfied; nevertheless, just as there is the conceptualization of a limited body [for the deity], so too, by conceptualizing pleasure within that body, there is simply the production of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) within one's own self.
However, through the imagined [form], there arises bliss for the Supreme Deity. For this very reason it is said in the *Śivamahimnaḥ-stotra*:
"[In this greatness—this reading is likely intended here—] the mirage of sense objects does not delude one who delights in his own Self.
For this same reason, in the mantra of adoration (*upacāra-mantra*), the verb "I fashion" (*kalyayāmi*) alone has been employed. The rest is quite clear.
Having recited the *tritārī* (the three *tāra* mantras), one should perform, in sequence: "I offer water for the feet (*pādya*), obeisance," followed by the removal of ornaments,
anointing with fragrant oil, entry into the hall of purification, sitting upon the jeweled throne in the bathing pavilion, the application of divine bathing unguents, and bathing in warm water.
Having received the full ablution of all sacred waters poured from golden jars,
he was wiped with a washed cloth and dressed in a garment of reddish silk.
The donning of a dawn-colored upper garment; the entry into the pavilion for anointing; the sitting upon the jeweled throne in the pavilion for anointing;
and the smearing of all limbs with divine fragrances—such as fine silk, sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, storax, musk, camphor, musk-pouch, and yellow orpiment.
For his mass of hair, black agallochum incense; for him,
garlands of all-seasonal flowers— primarily mallikā, mālatī, jātī, campaka, aśoka, śatapatra, pūga buds, punnāga, and kalhāra— and the entry into the jeweled pavilion of ornaments.
Sitting upon the jeweled throne in the pavilion of ornaments; a crown of fresh jewels; a crescent moon;
vermilion at the parting of the hair; a forehead jewel; black collyrium; a pair of braids;
a pair of jeweled earrings; a nose ornament; lac-dye for the lips—the first of all adornments.

In one hand [he holds] a golden *cintāka* pendant, a large pendant, a pearl necklace, a single-string necklace, a *channavīra* ornament, four pairs of armlets, a series of bracelets, a series of finger-rings, a girdle, a waist-band,
an auspicious ornament, anklets, jeweled foot-ornaments, and toe-rings.
In one hand a noose, in another hand a goad, in another hand a bow made of sugarcane stalks, and in another hand flower-arrows;

wearing glorious ruby sandals together with attendant deities dressed in attire identical to her own, she ascends the great throne and sits upon the couch in the lap of Kāmeśvara, holding a goblet of nectarous wine.

Having performed the sixty-four services (upacāras) with the words, "I offer water for sipping, camphor betel-roll, a smile of playful joy and delight, the auspicious ārārtika lamp, an umbrella, a pair of chowries, a mirror, a palm-leaf fan, perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings; obeisance," [he proceeds]. || 5 ||

In this context, since the three-star mantra (*tritārī*) is already established by the general rule (*sāmānyaparibhāṣā*), its re-statement indicates that it is a constituent part [of the mantra], just like the mantra of Dīpanātha. The remainder is clear. As for the actual form of the mantra, it is: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ pādyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*. [The phrase] "not of Lalitā" indicates the non-inclusion of her name.
Because there is an absence of proof.

The author of the *Nibandha*, however, being ignorant of logic and acting according to his own whims, has introduced the name [of the deity] arbitrarily. Nor should it be argued that the expression lacks cognitive efficacy because the recipient (*sampradāna*) kāraka is required but there is no word denoting it.

Since the expectancy [of the sentence] is satisfied through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and since those learned in logic do not accept an elliptical word as a constituent part of a mantra— otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of reciting "iṣe tvā chinadmi" and "ūrje tvā unmārjmi" at the time of performance— the mantra is only that which is explicitly heard. This is so even if it possesses the status of a name-mantra (*nāmadheya*).

If it is thought that there is an entry by name, then the defining characteristic of a name-mantra (*nāmamantra*) is that it ends in *namaḥ* or ends in the dative case. In this context, [the mantra] ending in the accusative case is not possible because of the intervention between [the deity and the word] *kalpayāmi*. This is the essential point. Furthermore, in all cases, for the ritual mantras (*upacāramantra*), [the formula is] *kalpayāmi namaḥ*.
Since the matter is already established by this alone, the sūtra "having uttered the *tritārī*" (p.
140), being otherwise redundant, serves to establish the actual form of the mantra; that which has been stated is what should be recited according to the original injunction (*utpattivākya*).
Regarding the phrase "due to the employment of graceful words," the reason for the introduction of such fundamentally graceful words must be stated. Not knowing this,

the author of the commentary— who is merely a reciter of poetry— has revealed his own lack of scholarship by citing "because of the frequent employment of graceful words by the author of the Sūtras" as the reason.

By the word "krameṇa" (in sequence), it is indicated that in place of the nominal stem "pādyam" (water for the feet), other words such as "ābharaṇāvaropaṇa" (removal of ornaments) and so forth should be uttered. "Snānīyodvartana" is a specific fragrant powder that serves as the means for removing the oil adhering to the body. Here, [all items] ending in the accusative case [are to be understood].
All [these] are devoted to specific pleasures produced by their respective objects: the bodice (*kañcuka*) is the upper garment over the breasts;
"ointment" (*ālepa*) is the contact of the body with fragrant substances, and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is the particular place that produces it;
*kaṅkuma* is saffron from Kashmir; *saṅku* is a particular tree. As it is stated in the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *śaṅku* [is used for] a peg, poison..."

In the lexicon (*śastra*), because there is not much difference between the letters *sa* and *śa*—according to the maxim that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]"—it refers to a fragrant species of tree. *Mṛgamada* is a specific variety of musk (*kastūrī*). Alternatively, *mṛgamada* is a part of a specific animal (*otu*).

In the Mahārāṣṭra language, it is known as *javvāji*. *Kastūrī* means musk (*mṛganābhi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other world-renowned fragrant substances are included. *Sarvāṅgīṇa* means pertaining to all limbs.
From the word *sarvāṅga*, by adding the suffix *kha* in the sense of relation, the form *sarvāṅgīṇa* is established.
Such is the ointment: *agaru* is well known; among those, there is a preeminent *kālāgaru*.

*Mallikā*, *mālatī*, and so forth, refer to flowers produced in the six seasons. *Sīmanta* is the parting line in the midst of the mass of hair; therein is *sindūra*. At the place of the forehead mark (*tilaka*) is a gem. *Kālāñjana* is black collyrium.

Atikṛṣṇāñjana is black collyrium, or sauvīrāñjana. A pālī is an ear ornament, well known in the Mahārāṣṭra language as a *bālī*; its pair is a *yugma*. On the lower lip (*adhara*), *yāvaka*—the juice of lac—is used to produce redness; it is the primary ornament.

The *maṅgalasūtra* is a particular ornament for the neck held by the women of Andhra, known in the Andhra language as *golakuṭṭikaṇṭhu*. A *padaka* is a neck ornament known in the Mahārāṣṭra language as *tanmaṇi*. A *mahāpadaka*...
A particular ornament for the neck; known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *peṭayā*.
A pearl necklace (*muktāvali*) is known in the Mahārāṣṭrī language as *kaṇṭhā*. A single-string necklace (*ekāvali*) consisting of twenty-seven pearls is known as *nakṣatramālā*.

According to Amara, "ekāvalī" is a single-string necklace, and that same type is called a "nakṣatramālā. According to established treatises, "channavīra" is an ornament consisting of a cross-shoulder chain (*vaikakṣya-dāman*) worn on both sides. A pair of *keyūras*—that is, a pair of armlets—consists of two for each arm, making a total of four.

The bracelets (*balaya*) are their [the arms'] ornaments; *āvalim* means a row or series. *Ūrmikā* is an ornament for the fingers; *āvalim* refers to its series. Regarding the waist ornaments, he says "girdle" (*kāñcī*). It is established in the *Nibandha* that the "token of good fortune" (*saubhāgyābharaṇa*) is a specific type of ornament hanging from the lower part of the hips (*adhare jaghanālambī*).

The mention of the foot-anklets, jeweled bracelets, and toe-rings as being "only one" (uttara-meka-vacana) is not intended to be significant, because that meaning would be contradicted. He describes the weapons with the word "one" (*eka*) and so forth. *Puṇḍrekṣu* means a multi-colored sugarcane. *Puṣpabāṇān* refers to arrows made of flowers. The sequence of the weapons is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
In the lower right hand are arrows, while in the lower left is a bow;
in the upper left is a reddish noose, and in the upper right is a supreme goad. Thus it is said.
The *mahācakra* is the *śrīcakra*. The *paryaṅka* is the very lap of Kāmeśvara; [the term] refers to sitting there.
*Amṛtarūpāsava* is wine (*madya*); the cup (*caṣaka*) is joined with that. *Ācamanīya* is clear.
The characteristics of the *karpūravīṭikā* (camphor roll) are stated in another tantra:
"With cardamom, cloves, camphor, musk, saffron, and so forth; with nutmeg, jasmine petals, betel nuts, betel leaves, long pepper, and ginger."
"A betel-roll prepared with camphor and combined with the powders of the heartwood of khadira. Thus it is said.
Lāṅgalī is coconut. Ūṣaṇā is long pepper (pippalī). Nāgara is ginger (śuṇṭhī).

Khadirasāra is well known as *kāt* in the Mahārāṣṭrī language. His laughter is such that it possesses a playful manifestation (*vilāsa*) arising from the emergence (*ullāsa*) of bliss (*ānanda*). Even in the world, laughter is an indicator of the arising of bliss; therefore—
Such a qualification is appropriate. The definition of the *ārārtika* (the waving of lights) for the sake of auspiciousness is found in the *Paramānandatantra*:
"Thereafter, one should perform the *ārārtika*; hear its procedure, O Dear One:
in a vessel made of gold or other materials, distinct from iron, [one should fill it] with vermilion powder."

Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, beautiful and made of gold, using various colors— or alternatively, a svastika— then one should fashion [figures] made of flour that shine like hand-drums (ḍamaru).
Having placed in a vessel, in sequence, seven, five, or three food items cooked in ghee, along with a wick, and filled with ghee;
Having kindled [the fire] through illusion, one should subsequently consecrate it with the nine jewels;
then, having displayed the wheel-mudrā, one should worship with the nine jewels.
Having risen himself, he should lift that vessel up to his head, [saying]:
"O Goddess Navātmikā, together with all the wheels and the Mistress of the Wheels!"
Accept this divine *ārārtika* for the sake of my spiritual accomplishment.
Thus, ringing the bell, [he should worship] the Goddess from head to foot.
Having whirled the vessel three times with the right hand and placed it down, one should perform a prostration;
in this manner, one should perform the ārārtika... thus [it is said].

*Tālavṛnta* means a palm-leaf fan; the rest is clear. Regarding the rule for substitute materials when those mentioned among the sixty-four types of offerings (*upacāra*) cannot be obtained, it is stated in another Tantra:
"In the absence of the respective materials for the offerings, [one should perform them] with flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*)."
One should perform [the rite] while contemplating with the mind; by that, one shall obtain the fruit of worship. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific rule for worship with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in the *Yoginītantra*: "The Supreme Goddess Tripurā should not be worshipped with white unbroken rice grains."
"The wise man should offer pure, unbroken grains of śāli rice, colored with saffron from Kaśmīra, or with turmeric, or with the paste of red sandalwood. Thus it is said.
This conceptualization of a substitute also applies exclusively to cases other than those involving perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
As it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"But when the ritual services (upacāra) are not obtained, one should mentally recollect [them] with flowers and so forth."
"Furthermore, O Maheśvarī, there are perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
in the absence of these five, beginning with perfume, worship is always (or in every way) indeed fruitless. Thus it is said.
Having displayed the nine mudrās,
one should display the nine mudrās.

The nine mudrās, beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Yoni, will be described [in this work; the extraction of all these mudrās as stated on their respective pages can be seen in the commentary on verse 15 of the *Dvitiya Paṭala* of the *Śrīkrama*, or in the commentary on the fifteenth sūtra in the *Lalitākrama* section of the fifth book]. By the word "and" (ca), the tenth, the *Trikhaṇḍā*, is also included.
Having shown [it]; "of the Goddess" is the ellipsis. || 6 ||
The threefold satiation with the root mantra; having performed the threefold satiation. || 7 ||
The word "in the bindu" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Some, however, have said that the *tarpaṇa* (libation) is prescribed as taking a small portion from that very *viśeṣārghya*— which is of the nature of its consecration— and placing it in another vessel right there; but that is not correct,
because there is no section concerning the purification of the *viśeṣārghya*, and if it were so, [it would contradict the established procedure].

Because it would entail the abandonment of the subject at hand and the assumption of something irrelevant, and because it would contradict the preceding sūtra which states, "this is the purification of the arghya. Nor should one raise the doubt, "How is it known that [the mantra] is in the *bindu*? For, by hearing the fourth *kūṭa* in the phrase "by means of the root" (*mūlena*), such knowledge is possible (as noted in the third *ba* manuscript). However, there is this much distinction:

Regarding the phrase "having worshipped" (*pūjayitvā*) in the context of "beyond this," since the word "having gratified" (*santarpya*) is heard here, there is libation (*tarpaṇa*) here and worship (*pūjana*) elsewhere.

As for the distinction in practice: here there is the casting of only a drop (*bindu*), whereas at the place of worship there is the casting of both a drop, a flower, and consecrated rice (*akṣata*). Furthermore:

By the instrumental case in the word *mūlena* ("by the root-mantra"), there is heard an independence from other factors; thus, [the mantra] consists of the eight syllables beginning with *śrīpādukā*, as found in the *Mūlasūtra* (the eighth sūtra) within the *Śrīgaṇanāyakapaddhati* on page 82, section *khaṇḍa*.

This has been stated as the eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣarī-mantra*). Since its application is prescribed specifically for worship, one should utter "svāhā" during the fire-oblation (*homa*) and "tarpayāmi" (I satiate) during the libation (*tarpaṇa*); thus, according to the statement in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, the application at the end of the root mantra is simply "tarpayāmi."
But surely, in another tantra, the use of two words for the same action is seen in alternation,

such as "brāhmaṇas are to be satiated with milk" (kṣīreṇa brāhmaṇais tarpyāḥ) and "one should worship Śivā with pure substance" (dravyeṇa sāttvikenaiva brāhmaṇaḥ pūjayeccivām); and in some cases, even the root *yaj* is seen in this very sense, as follows:

"O Supreme Goddess, I shall worship you with a thousand jars of liquor"— if it is argued that "satisfaction," "worship," and "sacrifice" are synonyms (the reading *paryāyāḥ* is correct), this is not so;
for synonymy is not established merely by usage in a single sense, since they may also function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward a different meaning.

Because of the possibility of [direct] application (*prayoga*). Otherwise, the same would result for the words "Ganges" and "bank. For this very reason, in the passage "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," although the verbal root *ālabhati* has the meaning of "touching," since the connection between the substance and the deity is untenable without a sacrifice, the root *ālabhati* is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote "sacrifice."

It is thus postulated. Likewise, because there is no logical inconsistency, the literal meaning of the verbal root in the Agnihotra injunction, "one should touch the calf" (*vatsam ālabheta*), is accepted exactly as it is heard. In the present case as well, since there is no sublation—just as in the case of the *vāyavya* and other sentences—there is no reason to depart from the literal sense, just as in the case of "one should touch the calf."
It is indeed logical that it possesses the meaning of what has been heard.
If it is asked, "Since no substance has been mentioned here either, by what means should the libation (tarpaṇa) or worship (pūjana) be performed?", it is replied:

the prescribed libation and so forth require a means of accomplishment (sādhana), and the consecrated special water-offering (viśeṣārghya) requires a ritual purpose (kārya). Thus, between these two which are mutually expectant, they are joined according to the maxim of the lost horse and the burnt chariot (*naṣṭāśvadagdharathanyāya*).
The syntactic unity of the sentence is thus established: "Having prepared the special *arghya* offering, one should worship the deity with it."

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, since the general *arghya* water would also be equal [to the specific], it too would result in being a means for worship; for there is no such expectancy as "What is to be done with this? because of its Vedic application (*viniyoga*) in the triangular *arghya*-mandala and so forth, as indicated by the rule "with that water, [draw] the triangle."

Nor should it be said that this is the same for both cases because of the scriptural injunction regarding the specific *arghya* water with the third case ending in the phrase "having worshipped the Guru’s sandals three times with those drops";
for this is the purification of the *arghya*, as stated in the final thirty-second sūtra of the third section of the *Anugama*.

Since the subsequent sūtra specifies that the refinement of the special *arghya* (*viśeṣārghya-saṃskāra*) extends only up to that point, the [rites] beginning with "by means of drops" (*bindubhiḥ*) and so forth are also included within that refinement; furthermore, this concerns the worship of all the deities of the wheels (*sarvacakra-devatārcanāni*) as established in the Śyāmā-krama [Sūtra 22, located in the sixth section of this work, the Śrīśyāmākrama].

Because of the statement that one should perform [the rite] by scattering unhusked rice and flowers from the right hand, accompanied by the first drop fallen together with the second fragment held between the thumb and ring finger of the left hand, the acquisition of the ritual substances is free from obstacles.

Nor should it be argued that because this [mantra] occurs within the section on Śyāmā, its application must rest there alone; for it has already been established that Śyāmā is merely a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the worship of Lalitā. And a subsidiary element possesses no independent context (*prakaraṇa*) of its own.

This is the established conclusion of the Mīmāṃsakas: therefore, since the context (prakaraṇa), being more powerful, sets aside mere proximity (sannidhi) and there is no obstacle to its application everywhere.

Nor should it be argued that, despite this, an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*)— arising from the "pincers" (*saṃdaṃśa*) formed by the word *śyāmā* on both sides— will override the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) according to the logic of the *prayāja-abhikramaṇa* rule;
for the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the word "all" (*sarva*), being the strongest of all means of proof, [prevents such sublation].
Because there is the possibility of sublation by an intermediate context.

Furthermore, since the five *makāras* that manifest those [deities] are established by the text of the Siddhānta which is recited without reference to a specific subject, and since the substances are obtained by the phrase "worship with them," there is not even a scent of any logical inconsistency.

These very same arguments should be applied to the statement found throughout the section on Gaṇapati: "In all names of deities, one should append the eight-syllabled formula 'śrīpūrvaṃ pādukāṃ pūjayāmi'"; this statement is also to be seen in the *Gaṇanāyakapaddhati*, chapter 8, sūtra 8, on page 2, section khaṇḍa 1, verse 81.
"Three times" means three repetitions here; it should be understood that the repetition of the mantra occurs because of the difference in the substances. || 7 ||

Regarding the worship of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgapūjana), he says: having worshipped the six limbs in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the [other] directions of the Goddess. || 8 ||

In this context, "worship" (pūjana) consists solely of the scattering of flowers, unbroken rice grains, and drops [of liquid]— as seen in the *Kalpasūtra* of the Śyāmā-krama in its sixth section, verse 22— and not in the form of offering the five articles of worship (pañcopacāra) and so forth, in accordance with that sūtra and the tradition of the learned.

This being the case, regarding the moderns' [interpretation] that wherever this response "having worshipped" (*pūjayitvā*) occurs, one should carry over the term "having offered libations" (*santarpya*) from the preceding sūtra so that both rules apply: at the location of the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*), there is merely the offering of libations; the offering of drops of substance (*bindudravya*) is *tarpaṇa*, while the offering of flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) is *pūjana*.

And thus, they perform the practice as follows: "I worship the Śrīpādukā of the Power of the Head (śiraśśakti) following the Trītārī and the Śiro-mantra; I satiate the Śrīpādukā of the Power of the Head. Such a performance is rooted in error, for in that case, it would fall under the maxim of the "half-old woman" (ardhajaratīya). [The correct sequence] begins with the Trītārī and ends with the Śiro-mantra.
It would be a source of great laughter to say that there are two repetitions, starting from the phrase "the power of the head" (*śiraśśakti*).

Furthermore, since worship is performed with the mantra "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the subsequent mantra, it follows that worship and libation must occur in that sequence. This being the case, regarding the offering of the *bindu*, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*):
This contradicts the rule in the Sūtra which states that one should perform [the rite] with flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) fallen together with the *bindu* at a single time.

Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of there being no connection with the left hand, since both [actions] could be performed with the right hand alone due to their sequential nature.

Nor should it be said that the necessity of the left hand arises from the rule "clenched by the thumb and ring finger of the left hand" (this is Sūtra 22 in the Śrīśyāmākrama, Section 6 of this work), for [the same applies to] the right hand.

Because it is a restatement (*anuvādaka*), as it is impossible to enjoin the left hand—which has already been established by the necessity of its presence due to the person being occupied with the act of throwing flowers and unbroken rice grains—it follows that [the right hand] is prescribed. For this very reason, at the time of proceeding for the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, the Sūtra of the Chandogas states: "with the left hands..."

Regarding the statement "they strew with their hands," the Bhāṣya explains that since the right hand is already occupied in the act of assisting the Adhvaryu and others—according to the injunction, "The Prastotṛ assists the Adhvaryu; the Pratihartṛ assists the Prastotṛ; the Udgātṛ assists the Pratihartṛ"—the left hand, which is obtained by implication, is merely restated (anūdyate).
Some, however, following the word "santarpya" (having satiated), prescribe both the libation and the worship;

fearing the application of the "half-old woman" maxim (*ardhajaratīyanyāya*), they recite the mantra after the three *tārās* and at the end of the heart-mantra as follows: "I worship and satiate the Heart-Śakti Śrīpādukā; obeisance."
In that case, it is impure, because there is no evidence for its continued existence.
Furthermore, it is contradictory to claim that in the injunction, libation (*tarpaṇa*) comes first and worship (*pūjā*) afterwards, such that the sequence would be reversed in the mantra;

therefore, in the preceding statement, "libation" refers merely to the sprinkling of drops. Since there is no further expectancy for its continuation, worship alone is what is enjoined. And as for the meaning of the term "worship":

There is the casting of a collection of bindus, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Thus, the nature of the mantra should be understood as follows: first the *tritārī*, then the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), and then "I worship the venerable *śrīpādukā* of the Heart-Śakti.
In this very same way, it should be understood everywhere hereafter.

In the phrase "agnīśa" (Agni and Īśa), the term "Agni" and so forth refers to the directions associated with those respective deities. By the word "dikṣu" (in the directions), the four cardinal directions beginning with the East are meant. Regarding the six young maidens of the limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayuvatīnām*), one should know that there are six locations: the four intermediate directions beginning with Agni, the center, and the four cardinal directions beginning with the East taken together as one.
On this point, some say:
"The direction in which one sees the sun is called 'east' for that person;
for one who sees the rising sun, Mount Meru is situated to the north."
Thus, the determination of directions—
which is well-known in the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites— is likewise said to apply to the practice of the Śrīvidyā as well.

Others, however, maintain that since the conventional determination of directions has its application in Vedic rituals, one should designate the direction between the worshiper and the object of worship as "east" (prācī), according to the Tantric injunction: "One should conceive of the east as being between the worshiper and the worshiped. Thus, the area in front of the Goddess is the east, the area behind the Goddess is the west (pratīcī), and the Goddess's right side is the south (dakṣiṇā).
They said that the determination of the intermediate directions follows from the northern direction on the left side.
p.
146) Both of these [methods] are to be disregarded because they are gross measurements. In reality, however, in the *Jñānārṇava*, in the context of the worship of the Śrīcakra—
O Goddess, when the mantra-practitioner extracts the wheel while facing the northern direction,
then that northern direction is said to be the eastern direction.
O Goddess of gods, when the practitioner facing the western direction raises the wheel, then the northeast is the southeast; of this there is no doubt.
Then the western direction should be known as the eastern direction, without a doubt;
likewise, the northwest corner becomes the southeast, and the northeast becomes the southwest.
"When the practitioner, facing south, draws forth the wheel,
the eastern direction becomes the north, and the southeast corner becomes the southwest."
In the phrase "the north-western direction," having referred to the direction that is conventionally known as the North, the function of the [other] directions beginning with the East is enjoined—

just as in the injunction, "The threshing-block becomes the sacrificial post" (*khalevālī yūpo bhavati*). Thus, since the function of the directions is enjoined by way of a reference to the directions alone, it is established that one should not lift the wheel while facing an intermediate direction (*vidiṅmukha*).
Because there is no object to be enjoined (vidheya) following the restatement of the eastern direction, that [passage] has been omitted. Likewise, in the *Kulārṇava*:
"When the practitioner (mantrī), facing whichever direction, worships Tripurā, then the west is the east and the front of Tripurā is the west."
Thus, by these unambiguous statements, the determination of the directions regarding the Śrīvidyā is established according to the manner described.
In Tantric rites other than those of the Śrīvidyā, the direction between the worshipper and the object of worship is the East.
In all Śrauta and Smārta rites, there is the inclusion of such statements as "he who should look [toward the east]," and so forth; enough of this prolixity.

By the statement "of the Goddess," it is established that one should worship the six-limbed maidens (*ṣaḍaṅgayuvatī*) there, having first arranged [the directions] starting from the southeast within the *binducakra* itself according to the aforementioned scripture. || 8 ||

The daily worship [from here onwards shows the daily worship of the deities of the enclosure of Śrī Lalitāmbā and so forth, up until the end of the tenth sūtra at the conclusion of the fourth section].
Now, he describes the worship of the Nityās preceded by the extraction of the mantras of the fifteen Nityās:
*vāksakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ*—this is Kāmeśvarī. In all cases, the phrase *nityāśrīpādukā* should be appended. *vāgbhagabhuge bhagini bhagodari bhagamāle*.

O You who possess the vulva, O You whose secret parts are the vulva, O You who are the source of the vulva, O You who cause the vulva to fall [upon You], O You who bring all vulvas under Your control, O You whose form is the vulva, O You who are eternally moist, O You whose very nature is the vulva, bring all vulvas to me, O Giver of Boons!

O You of excellent seed, O You of excellent seed, O You who are moist with the vulva, O You whose fluid is moist, make [them] wet, make [them] flow! O Infallible One, O You who pierce the vulva, agitate, cause agitation!
[For] all sentient beings,
O Mistress of the Yoni (bhageśvarī): aiṃ blūṃ jeṃ blūṃ bheṃ blūṃ moṃ blūṃ heṃ blūṃ heṃ.
"O Bhagamālinī, make all my female organs moist and bring the woman under my control! Bleṃ Hrīṃ! This is the mantra of Nityaklinnā.

"Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīṃ), O Nityaklinne Madadrave Svāhā! This is the mantra of Nityaklinnā. "Praṇava (Om), Kroṃ, Bhrōṃ, Krauṃ, Jhrauṃ, Chrauṃ, Jrauṃ, Svāhā! This is the mantra of Bheruṇḍā. "Praṇava (Om) and Māyā (Hrīṃ) for Vahnivāsinyai..."

*Namaḥ* is Vahnivāsinī. *Māyā klinne vāk kroṃ nityamadadrave hrīṃ* is Mahāvajreśvarī. *Māyā śivadūtyai namaḥ* is Śivadūtī. *Praṇava māyā huṃ khe ca che kṣaḥ strīṃ huṃ kṣeṃ hrīṃ phaṭ* is Tvaritā. Kumārī is Kulasundarī.

*Hasakalaraḍa-vāgbhava-hasakalaraḍa-bindumālinī-hasakalaraḍa-caturdaśa-ṣoḍaśā*—thus is the *Nityā*. *Māyā* (hrīṃ), *phreṃ*, *srūṃ*, the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the noose (*pāśa*), the *smara-vāgbhava* (*aiṃ*), *blūṃ-pada-nitya-mada-drave*, the armor (*varma*: hūṃ), *phreṃ*, and *māyā* (hrīṃ).

Nīlapatākā; Vijayā is "Bhamaraya-ūm"; Sarvamaṅgalā is "Svaum. [The mantra is: Tāra (Oṃ), Namaḥ, Bhagavati, Jvālāmālini, Devadevi, Sarvabhūtasaṃhārakārike, Jātavedasi, Jvalanti, Jvala Jvala, Prajvala Prajvala, [followed by] the three seed-syllables (Tāra, Hrīḥ, Krom), Māyā (Hrīḥ), seven Rephas (Ra), and Jvālāmālini.

With "varma phaṭ agnijāya," one worships Jvālāmālinī; with "aṃ ckauṃ," one worships Citrā. Thus, the fifteen Nityās are to be worshipped within the fifteen vowels situated on the lines of the first triangle. At the time of dismissal, one should worship the sixteenth [Nityā] with the root-mantra.

The *vāk* is *aiṃ*. The remainder is as recited [in the root text]. At the end of every mantra, after the name of each respective *Nityā*, there is the application of the eight-syllable formula. For example: first the *tritārī*, then *aiṃ sakalahrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ kāmeśvarīnityāśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*. The same should be understood for what follows.

Although the eight-syllable yoga beginning with "śrīpādukā" is obtained through general statements, nevertheless, because it is not otherwise established due to its composition with the word "nityā," this undertaking is for that purpose in all mantras for the worship of the Nityās. He states the second [mantra] as "vāk"; he states the third as "tāra. "Tāra" refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).

The *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and the remainder should be recited as heard [in the tradition]. The realized meaning is: first the *praṇava* (oṃ), then the *māyā*, and then as heard, ending with *svāhā*. He states the fourth [mantra] as ending with *svāhā* after the *praṇava*. He states the fifth as ending with *namaḥ* after the *praṇava*. He states the sixth as ending with *hrīṃ* after the *māyā*.
The seventh [mantra] is stated with the words ending in "māyāyai namaḥ. The eighth is stated with the words ending in "praṇava" and "phaṭ.

The ninth is stated as "kumārī"; the meaning is that the young girl (kumārī) is herself the Kulasundarī. The tenth is stated with the words beginning with "hasa" and ending in "ṣoḍaśāḥ. Here, according to the previously mentioned reasoning, [the sequence begins with] "hasaka," and so forth.

The mention refers exclusively to the consonants (*vyañjana*). Otherwise, by the statement in another tantra— "the twelve-halved [syllables] would be eternal"— and because the status of the mantra as having three syllables is established through the extension (*atideśa*) of the mantra's phonemes, where it says "the twelve-halved [syllables] reside in the three seeds," the status of having three syllables established by that extension here would be contradicted.
Following *hasakalaraḍa* is *vāgbhava* (*aiṃ*); again, following that is *mālinī* joined with the *bindu*, which is the letter *ī*.
According to the *Kośa*: "Govinda and Trimūrti [are] *mālinī* and the pure eye. [These are] the fourteenth and the sixteenth.
As previously stated: thus, *hsklrḍaiṃ*, *hsklrḍīḥ*, *hsklrḍauḥ*, *nityānityāśrī*—this is the nature of the mantra.
Furthermore, that which is written in the *Nibandha* as the letter *ha* accompanied by the vowel *a* is certainly due to ignorance.

If it were written according to another tantra, then since there is the sūtra stating, "Having uttered the *ka*-group and *kala hrīṃ* in the *Vaśinyādi*-nyāsa," one would have to seek the justification for taking the consonant alone (*hal-mātra*) apart from that other tantra. Therefore:
By the reasoning already stated, the Nityā-vidyā consists of exactly three syllables.
The eleventh [verse] begins with "māyā" and ends with "māyā. The first three seed-syllables (*bīja*) are clear.
According to the *Yoginītantra*, the hook is *krom*, the noose is *ām*, and the great noose (*mahāpāśa*) is that which resides at the beginning and the end.
Its meaning is as follows: the "beginning" is the letter *a*; its "end" is the preceding position, and the letter *ā* is situated there. Thus...

"Kāma, Agni, Vyāpaka, and Aṅkuśa"—it is said in that very [text]. Kāma is the letter *ka*, Agni is *ra*, and Vyāpaka is the Praṇava (*oṃ*); when combined, they become *kroṃ*. This is the meaning of "Aṅkuśa. Smara is *klīṃ*, Vāgbhava is *aiṃ*, and Varma is *huṃ*. Thus, [the mantra is]: *hrīṃ phreṃ srūṃ kroṃ āṃ klīṃ*.

The nature of the mantra is: *aiṃ blūṃ nityamadadrave huṃ phreṃ hrīṃ nīlapatākānityāśrī*. Regarding the twelfth [syllable], it says *bhamaraya-ūṃ*. Here too, by the previously stated logic, only the consonant (*hal*) is to be taken; this one-syllabled *vidyā* is proclaimed as *Vijayā*.
Because of the statement in another tantra.
Therefore, in the *Nibandha*, the pronunciation of the five syllables and the pronunciation of the vowel *au* are due to negligence;

rather, the essential form should be known as *rbhmyūm*. Although in another tantra it is stated that "it is joined with the *aṅgada* and the *bindu*," the *aṅgada* is the vowel *au*; thus, the final vowel is *au*.

It appears so; nevertheless, because the sixth vowel is uttered in the Sūtra, that which is stated in other Tantras—which contradicts the Sūtra—must certainly not be respected by those who follow the Sūtra.
He states the thirteenth [syllable] as *svauṃ*. He states the fourteenth as *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) ending with *agnijāyā* (the word *svāhā*).

It is joined with the three *jātis* (*māyā*: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*), and the *vahnijāyā* is *svāhā*. The remainder is clear. He states the fifteenth as *aṃ ckrauṃ*. He now states the rule regarding the location for the worship of the fifteen *Nityās*.

"First," and so forth. The meaning is that one should worship each Nityā in sequence upon each individual vowel among the fifteen vowels— beginning with *ā* and ending with the *anusvāra*— which reside within the three lines of the first triangle, the triangle situated near the *bindu*.
In this context, since the fifteen vowels situated upon the lines are indicated there as if already established,
the rule should be inferred that five vowels are to be meditated upon on each individual line.
Since no specific order is mentioned, they should proceed clockwise starting from the top of their respective positions, beginning from the west.
On the line between Īśāna [and Vāyu], [the vowels] a, ā, i, ī, u; on the line from Īśāna to Āgneya, ū, ṛ, ̄ṛ, ḷ, ̄ḷ;

starting from Āgneya and extending to the West, e, ai, o, au, am—this is the discernment of contemplation (*bhāvanāviveka*). She from whom emanation has departed or gone forth is *Visṛṣṭi*, the Wheel of the Bindu (*binducakra*). This is the manner of its emanation.

This should be seen in the *Setubandha*, the commentary on the *Uttaracatuśśatī*. In that work, having worshipped the *Ṣoḍaśī*—which is the collective form—with the fifteen-syllable *Mūlavidyā*, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava* that the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of these [deities] is indeed another triangle, distinct from the fashioned triangle: [The text continues with the description of this triangle.]
And having visualized the great triangle, [extending] from the southeast to the north in due order. Thus it is said.
In the *Tantrarāja*, however, worship is said to be performed in the *bindu* alone; thus, it should be performed in each respective manner by the followers of those various tantras. (9)

He describes the worship of the three currents (oghatripūjā): In the center, having worshipped according to tradition the sandals (pādukās) of the numbers four, seven, and eight— belonging to the Divine, Siddha, and Human Currents— within the middle of the initial triangle, one should thereafter worship the Lord upon one’s own head.

This is the worship of the limbs of the *layāṅga*; may there be auspiciousness. [In some places, there is an additional reading: "Some worship the triad of creation, maintenance, and dissolution according to the Yoga Sūtras, as well as the five pentads, the five types of envy, and the deities of the *prapañca* and other installations (*nyāsa*).
Thus ends the fourth section, named the *Lalitākrama*, in the *Kalpasūtra*. Śrī:
The first triangle is the "eastern triangle. Alternatively, the "eastern triangle" refers to the previously mentioned triangle;
its "middle" is the inner region, and its "end" is the final constituent part.
The realized meaning is: "there," in that inner region which is situated near the tip facing oneself.

By the etymology "wherein the numbers seven (muni), six (veda), four (nāga), and eight (aṣṭau) reside," this qualifies the *ogha*. According to tradition, there are sandals (*pādukā*) distinguished by the various *vidyās* beginning with *ka* and *ha*.

Because the lineages of the sandals (*pādukā*) and the guru-mandalas are distinct, whichever sandals have been accepted by a particular person, they are called "sandals" according to tradition for the sake of attaining those specific [powers]. They are divine, perfected, and human; such are the perfected ones belonging to those lineages (*ogha*). As previously stated:

Regarding the qualification of the *ogha* (floods): in both cases, the transposition of case endings is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The distinction is as follows: there are seven divine (*divya*) beings, four perfected ones (*siddha*), and eight human (*mānava*) beings. Having worshipped—that is, having honored—them; by means of the suffix *-ktvā* and the order of recitation, the sequence obtained is restated by the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*). This is what was said, namely: [nāma-]...
From the ninth sūtra of this western section up to the tenth sūtra above;
following this, that which is to be explained— beginning from the single sūtra located in the fifth section to come—

is the worship of the nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa-pūjana*), the limb of dissolution (*layāṅga*), and the nature of dissolution (*layasvarūpa*) according to the sequence starting from the square (*caturasra*) and ending with the point (*bindu*).
Because its essential nature is dissolution (*laya*), the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) ought to take place.

By this, the worship of the *bindu* and so forth mentioned in other Tantras is excluded. The intended meaning here is that in every worship of a Yantra, one of the three sequences—creation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), or withdrawal (*saṃhāra*)—must be followed.
The term "explicitly stated" (*pratipadokta*) is understood here to mean that, by implication, worship begins with the *bindu* according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).

However, in this particular sequence, one should not adopt that; rather, the commencement of worship in this rite must be performed according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), which is called the "limb of equilibrium" (*layāṅga*). But in the case of worshipping deities distinct from these [specific] deities, one should indeed begin with the *bindu*.
"Mārmikam" means "pertaining to the vital points. "Śivam" indicates the conclusion of the section. || 10 ||

Thus ends the fourth section, titled "The Lalitākrama," in the commentary on the *Paraśurāmasūtra*. It should be understood that the worship (*pūjā*) is not yet concluded here, but rather that this is merely a section; furthermore, upon the repetition of the *sūtra*, that which is to be purified must be indicated.
"And the remaining portion shall indeed be complete through the grace of the Primordial Goddess. Thus ends the fourth section.
[The Fifth Section: Worship of the Nine Enclosures of Lalitā;
Worship of the Individual Deities of the First Enclosure. From the next page until the end of the Sūtra, once again...]
There is also a practice for collective worship (*samaṣṭyarcana*).

By this term [in the tenth sūtra of the Western tradition], one should understand that the word "this" refers to the phrase "worship of the limbs of this dissolution" (*etallayāṅgapūjana*) found in that location. Having expanded upon the worship thus indicated:
He demonstrates it: now, in the first square,

[the powers] are atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), lordship (īśitva), mastery (vaśitva), irresistible will (prākāmya), attainment of desires (bhuktīcchā), and reach (prāpti).
Ending with the accomplishment of all desires (*sarvakāmasiddhi*), [these are] in the middle square; from Brāhmī to Mahālakṣmī, they are in the third square;
[and] the *saṃkṣobhaṇa*, *drāvaṇa*, *ākarṣaṇa*, *vaśya*, *unmādana*, *mahāṅkuśa*, *khecarī*, *bīja*, and *yoni* [mudrās].
All those [deities] in the eastern sections, divided into three parts, are to be worshipped. || 1 ||

The word *atha* indicates the commencement of the section on the ninefold enclosure worship (*navāvaraṇa-pūjā*). In the center of the three squares, within the first and outermost square, there is a series of dual compounds beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with *sarvakāma*.
All of these are to be performed as "accomplishments" (*siddhi*). The term *siddhi* is to be joined to the end of every word [in the list]. And so it is said:
Then, [recite] "Tritārī, I worship the Śrīpādukā of the siddhi of aṇimā. The same applies hereafter.

Here, the three words beginning with *aṇimā* do not end in the suffix *-man*, but rather in the feminine suffix *-āp* (ḍāp), according to the reading of the rule on compound endings (*samāsāntasūtra*) which prescribes *aṇimā-laghimā*. Thus, "aṇimāsiddhi" is without the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution).

The reading, although not strictly according to the technical treatises (*śāstra*), is largely archaic (*ārṣa*) due to adherence to traditional transmission (*sampradāya*). Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound; the meaning of the genitive is indeed non-difference (*abheda*), as in the expression "the head of Rāhu.
Regarding the initial square (*caturasra*), since the worship of the powers such as *aṇimā* and others could be performed at will, this [text] establishes a fixed rule for them.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
[One should place] Aṇimā at the western gate, Laghimā also at the northern;
Mahimā at the eastern gate, and that called Īśitva at the southern.

The perfection known as mastery (vaśitva) is in the northwest; willpower (prākāmya) is in the northeast; the perfection of enjoyment (bhuktisiddhi) is likewise in the southeast, and the perfection of desire (icchāsiddhi) is in the southwest.
"Below, there is the attainment of success and the fulfillment of all desires; likewise, above. Thus it is said.

The tradition regarding the arrangement of the directions has already been stated. Furthermore, "above" and "below" should not be understood according to worldly convention, but rather according to the Tantric system. As it is said in the *Tattvavimarśinī*:
"The location above is proclaimed to be in the middle between the directions of Indra and Īśāna."
"The location situated below, between the directions of Nirṛti and Ambupa (Varuṇa), is proclaimed [as the place]. Thus [it is said].
In the middle square are Brāhmyā and the others—those whose first is Brāhmī—and likewise those whose last is Mahālakṣmī.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā are the seven Mothers.
Thus, the eight Mothers—the seven well-known Mahālakṣmīs plus [Mahā]lakṣmī—are to be worshipped in the central square.
Regarding the sequence for this, the Vāmakeśvara Tantra states:
"Brahmāṇī at the western gate, and Māheśī also at the northern [gate]."
One should place Kaumārī at the eastern gate and Vaiṣṇavī at the southern gate.
Likewise, one should place Vārāhī in the northwest, Aindrī in the northeast, Cāmuṇḍā in the southeast, and Mahālakṣmī in the southwest. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the worship of the ten mudrās in the third square, he says "in the third": the word *sarva* (all) is used as before in their names; for example, after the three *tārās*, one says:
"I worship the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*) of the power (*śakti*) Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī. Such are these mudrā-powers.

The meaning of the six mudrās has already been explained [in this very Lalitākrama, in the fourth section, in the commentary on the thirteenth verse on page 135]. These [mudrās] are delimited by properties that are subsumed under the nature of being such mudrās. And the meaning of the term *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* (the All-Agitating One) is as follows: [she agitates] all entities (*padārtha*), that is, all beings (*bhūta*).

"She agitates" means she produces; thus, *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* (the All-Agitating) refers to that which possesses the causality defined by the effect delimited as "all effects"—this is what is meant. This very [power] is called the *vāmā-śakti*. This has been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
Furthermore, due to the predominance of the *yoni*, this [power] is the agitator of all;
it is this very one in which the power of Vāmā is preeminent. Thus [it is said].
The *yoni* refers to the causal states due to their abundance— that is, their predominance. For this very reason,

even in the external form consisting of the interlacing of fingers, there is an abundance of *yoni*s when the tips of the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger are joined together on the thumb.

It is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By this, it should be inferred that even that which is of invisible form is likewise so. The second [form] is *sarvavidrāviṇī* (the dissolver of all): she dissolves (*drāvayati*) all things not yet arisen, causes them to grow, and nourishes them; thus she is *sarvavidrāviṇī*.
Because she is the protector of all entities, she is of a straight nature (*ṛjusvabhāvā*) and abounds in the *jyeṣṭhā-śakti* (the eldest power).
Thus it is said in the *Yoginītantra*: "Jyeṣṭhā, who brings about the stability of the agitated universe, abides in abundance.

The meaning of "agitated" (*kṣubdha*) is "that which has arisen. Furthermore, there is a well-known worldly verse: "He who is a protector is straightforward (*ṛju*). For this very reason, even in the external form of this mudrā, by means of the thumb—

In the union of the little finger and the ring finger, straightness is seen in the four fingers. Thus, in the first triangle, within the three lines, its locus is well-known in the scriptures as being precisely on the straight line situated in the eastern direction. The third [line] is the "all-attracting" (sarvākarṣiṇī), characterized by the nature of attracting all.
This Jyeṣṭhā consists of both the Left and the Right [currents]. As it is stated in the *Yoginītantra* (p.
"Jyeṣṭhā, by virtue of her equality with Vāmā, has established herself as the primary force of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*)."
This is the mudrā called Ākarṣiṇī (the Attractor). Thus [it is said].

It should be understood that both of the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for the two previously mentioned terms expressing the mudrās are also the delimiter of denotability for the term *sarvākarṣiṇī*, just as [the property of] being a flower is the delimiter of denotability for the word "lotus. Even in that case, the delimiter of denotability is the state of being Vāmā qualified by the state of being Jyeṣṭhā, and not the reverse; for if it were so, [the following would occur]:

The primacy of Jyeṣṭhā must be stated by virtue of her being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Since Jyeṣṭhā is preeminent due to her extreme straightness, and because the qualifier Vāmā follows the principal, she too conforms to the principal; thus, there is no curvature in the external form of the index finger and middle finger.

It may be so. However, since Vāmā is predominant, it is logical that Jyeṣṭhā—who is subordinate and follows the lead of the predominant one—should also possess crookedness (kuṭilatva) in accordance with her. For this very reason, in the external form of the finger-knotting (aṅguligrathana), there is crookedness in all the fingers. The fourth [mudrā] brings everything under control. All...

She is so called because she brings everything from the earth (kṣiti) up to Śiva under her control, making it subject to her own will. In the world, space (ākāśa) is of two kinds: the minute (dahra) and the elemental (prākṛta). Within the minute space as well, there exists another, most subtle space, which is famously known from the Śruti as "the subtle cavity within its interior. In the midst of that, she is firmly embraced.
That form of Paraśiva which consists of the embodiment of bliss is designated by the term "Sarvavaśyakarī" (the one who brings all under control). As it is stated in the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*:
"The Great Goddess, whose form is the Bindu situated between the two voids."
"Because it consists of the intimate union of Śiva and Śakti, this is remembered as the means for bringing others under one's control. Thus [it is said].

Because it is described as being in the form of a *bindu*, its nature as *kha* (space) is likewise [implied]. For this very reason, even when the fingers are interlaced, its external form takes the shape of a *bindu*, and the firm joining of all the fingers is clearly manifest.
The fifth is a subtle line between the aforementioned *śiva*, *śakti*, and *bindu*, thin like the awn of a *nīvāra* grain; of that—

"In the center is the flame of fire" is well-known from the Śruti. That flame possesses a dual nature and the nature of Jyeṣṭhā. Just as in the world a single staff possesses both the power to produce a jar and the power to destroy it, so too is that staff.

Sometimes, becoming predominant in its power of production, it produces a jar; sometimes, predominant in its power of destruction, it destroys that same jar. This is observed in many instances in the world.
Likewise, the aforementioned line stands in the place of a staff; when it—

At that time, she who is characterized by the agency of protecting the universe and is dominated by the supreme power (jyeṣṭhā-śakti) is denoted by the term *sarvonmādinī*. As it is said in the *Uttara-catuḥśatī*:
"She consists of a subtle crest of light shining within the interior of the Bindu."
"But Jyeṣṭhā, whose primary power is Śakti, causes universal intoxication. Thus [it is said].
For this very reason, at the time of interlacing the fingers, the thumb, the ring finger, and the index finger are seen to be straight,
while the two middle fingers take the form of two dots; even there,
at the time of interlacing that which occupies the position of the crest (śikhā) as described in the Nirukta, it should be understood that only the two ring fingers are intended.
At that time, since the non-dual Middle (*madhyamādvaya*) consists of the form of two *bindus*,

it is logical that the Nameless Non-dual (*anāmādvaya*) situated between them possesses the nature of a "flame" (*śikhā*), as is well known to be the flame within that [Middle]. As for the sixth [energy], it is precisely this aforementioned pair of flames when Vāmā is predominant.
Then, [she is] the Great Goad of All;
the universe, abiding within the womb of Paramaśiva in a subtle form, is like an elephant within [the body] controlled by a goad.
It is drawn outward; thus, because it draws everything outward, it is called the "Great Goad of All" (*sarvamahāṅkuśā*).
Because it vomits forth the world residing within the belly of Paraśiva, the crest-lock (*śikhā*) dominated by that [power] Vāmā is called the "Great Goad of All.
This too has been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"Furthermore, in the second decade, she is preeminent in the power of Vāmā and consists of the Great Hook (mahāṅkuśa);
likewise, she emits the entire universe."

For this very reason, in the previous mudrā, the straightness of the two ring fingers (anāmikās) is seen to be curved. In the world, at the time of vomiting, a person becomes curved in the shape of a bow; this is well known. Herein lies the distinction: being solely on the left side is the basis for the application of the term *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*.
The state of being the left [power] qualified by the state of being the eldest (*jyeṣṭhā*) is the ground for the application of the term "All-Attracting" (*sarvākarṣiṇī*);

the state of being two points (*bindu*) functioning within the subtle ether is the ground for the application of the term "All-Subjugating" (*sarvavaśyakara*); and the state of being a line functioning between those two points, in which the power of the Eldest (*jyeṣṭhāśakti*) predominates, is [the ground for the application of the term "All-Enchanting"].

The delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the denotability of the term *sarvonmādinī* is the predominance of the power of Vāmā; likewise, the delimiting condition for the denotability of the term *sarvamahāṅkuśā* is [the predominance of Jyeṣṭhā]. In this manner, the distinction [between these powers] should be perceived by one of subtle intellect. The seventh is *sarvakhecarī* of living beings.

She possesses the power capable of destroying the sufferings of diseases and other afflictions produced by one's own karma; for this very reason, she resides within the *sarvarogahara-cakra* (the wheel that removes all diseases). This has also been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"Aroused from the friction of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), she takes the form of consciousness (*vitti*)."

"It is considered Khecarī because it destroys the defects consisting of the omission of actions arising from conceptual construction, and because it removes the diseases whose nature is conceptual construction. Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows: *dharma* is power (*śakti*), because it resides in Paraśiva. *Adharma* is that in which no *dharma* exists;

thus, *adharma* is the Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva. Alternatively, the negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) "that which is not the *dharma* of anything" is more appropriate, since *dharma* in the form of power does exist in Paraśiva, which would otherwise contradict what was previously stated in the first alternative. Of these two...

*Saṃghaṭṭa* means union; [the state] arisen from that. Whatever actions—whether daily (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—have arisen through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the sins resulting from their omission give rise to diseases; *Khecarī* is the destroyer of those. Therefore, in its external form, it illuminates such a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti.

The rotation of the two arms. The eighth is the Seed Mudrā (*bījamudrā*), which is the power presiding over that existence which is the first of the six transformations of the world—a subtle state of being.
As it is said in the *Uttaracatuḥśatikā*:
Furthermore, within the interior of the sky vibrating with the embrace of Śiva and Śakti,
she, manifesting the universe which always exists in a subtle form,
is the Mahāmudrā in the form of the seed-syllable (bīja). Thus [it is said].

The meaning is this: even in the extremely subtle seed of a banyan tree, there exists a certain amount of space because of its all-pervasiveness; just as a great tree exists within that [space] in a subtle form, so too do the thirty-six principles exist in a subtle form within the womb of Śiva and Śakti. That very existence persists in such expressions as "the pot exists" and "the cloth exists. That...

This means "seed-mudrā. Because she occupies the position of the seed of all, she is "the one containing all seeds" (*sarvabījā*). Precisely because of her subtlety, at the time of the interlacing of the fingers, her state as having few origins (*alpayonitva*)—in comparison with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and the others—is an indicator of her subtlety. She who...
The ninth is *yonimudrā*, which is its specific, uncommon attribute (*asādhāraṇadharma*): being a *mudrā* while having the nature of a *kalā*.
The essential nature of being a *mudrā* has been explained previously. Now, the category of *kalā* is being discussed. [It exists] in that which is qualified by power (*śakti*).
When, in the Supreme Śiva whose nature is light, one sets aside His power (śakti) and extracts only His essential nature,

He becomes denotable by the term "the Fourth Bindu" (turīyabindu), just as water, when its fluidity inherent in it is set aside and only its essential nature is extracted, becomes denotable by the term "water. Here, "setting aside" (apahāna) means—

The very absence of entry into the category of the delimitors of capability (śakyatā’vacchedaka) is not something to be excluded from that [category] separately, because such exclusion is impossible. When there is the intention to describe that pure Śiva as being in relation to Śakti, He is denoted by the term *kāma-bindu*. This is because that very relationship is non-dual (abheda).

In Tantric usage, the emission (*visarga*) is the letter *ha*, which enters into the category of the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of possibility, while the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the letter *sa*. Following such a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), when there is the intention to express the inclusion of internal bliss arising from the mixture of the red and white drops (*bindu*), it is called *kalā*. Such is the nature of *kalā* [Ṭ].
The distinction is that within the category of the delimitors of possibility for the *kalāpada*, there is the inclusion of an additional element, *ānanda* (bliss).
[This is the "additional" portion—ba. This is the *yonimudrā*. As it is said in the *Nityāhṛdaya*:
"Furthermore, this is the ground for the attainment of the complete manifestation."
The Yonimudrā is the form of the Kalās... thus [it is said].

She who brings all under control consists solely of two *bindus*. Since the bliss arising from the union of these two *bindus* within her body is also included within the defining characteristics (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of her nature, she must be understood as distinct from that [other state]. The tenth, *Trikhaṇḍā*, has been described previously. Thus...
The true nature of the ten mudrās, which has become manifest through the particular grace of the venerable Guru,
has been clarified according to my own understanding for the easy comprehension of people.
Thus, the infinite fruit of knowing their true nature, as elaborated at length in the Tantras, is not written here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, the ten mudrās are to be worshipped in the third square. Regarding this as well, there is a restrictive statement in the Tantra concerning attainment according to one's desire:
"In the front, on the right, on the bamboo-lattice (vaṃśa), on the left, and in the intermediate space."
And the ten mudrās above and below... [thus it is said].
The meaning of that is: the ten mudrās are to be worshipped in the east, south, west, north, in the four intermediate directions beginning with the southeast, as well as above and below. || 1 ||
The collective worship of the first enclosure:
Having described the individual worship of the first enclosure, he now describes the collective worship:
"These manifest yoginīs in the Trailokyamohana-cakra are accompanied by their mudrās, siddhis, and weapons."

Having performed the collective worship of them alone with the thought, "May they, together with their powers (śaktis), vehicles (vāhanas), and retinues (parivāras), be fully honored with all ritual offerings (upacāras)," [he should proceed]. || 2 ||

These [Yoginīs], beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Trikhaṇḍā, are called the "Manifest Yoginīs" (*prakaṭayoginyaḥ*). This is their collective name (*samaṣṭināma*), just as "human" is the collective name for individuals who have specific names such as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth.
Furthermore, among the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) starting from Śiva, the "manifestness" (*prakaṭatva*) of these aforementioned Yoginīs consists in their being gross (*sthūla*).
The Earth is that [form], because it exists within the four-cornered *bhūpura* (earth-fortress). As it is stated in the *Nityāhṛdaya* (p.
"There, in the wheel that fascinates the three worlds (*trailokyamohana*), the *prakaṭayoginīs* reside."
The Yoginīs are to be known as manifest within the self that is the expansion of the gross universe.
Because it is established... thus.

"Trailokyamohana" (Deluder of the Three Worlds) is the name of the outermost wheel consisting of three squares; this is due to both *yoga* (etymological derivation) and *rūḍhi* (conventional usage). [The term refers to the three lines of the square-shape consisting of the abodes of the earth—Ba. As for "Samudrāḥ" (Oceans), these are the ten [lines] which were previously described in detail.

Among those [mudrās], one mudrā for each is present in each respective cakra; the tenth, Trikhaṇḍā, is all-pervasive. There is authoritative evidence for this point in the Yoginītantra. Furthermore, the venerable Lord Paraśurāma will also describe the display of one mudrā for each during the worship of the respective cakras.

[The meaning is: "in the worship of the lower enclosure. And thus, the meaning is: "accompanied by whichever mudrā belongs to whom. Regarding the term *sasiddhayaḥ* ("with their accomplishments"), here "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the fruit to be achieved through each respective power (*śakti*). Since that fruit exists indeed in its own form as a subtle essence, the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are also said to be "with their accomplishments. [Regarding the term] *sāyudhāḥ* ("with weapons"):

This is clear. Here, by the term "powers" (*śakti*), that property which delimits the capacity to produce various specific effects—residing in [powers] such as *aṇimā* and so forth—is to be understood. For in the world, causality is not known to be unconditioned (*niravacchinna*). Therefore, some kind of delimitor must be admitted for the causality residing in itself.
Furthermore, as for the nature that has been accepted, whether it is other than its substratum or not—that is another matter.
They are "accompanied by such powers" (*sāmarthyayuktāḥ*). "With their vehicles" (*savāhanāḥ*) is clear. "Together with their retinues" means accompanied by their attendants.
The remainder of the mantra's meaning is clear. Of those [goddesses], beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Trikhaṇḍā—

Having performed the collective worship (*samaṣṭhyarcana*) by means of a mantra composed of the names of the assembly, it is understood here—by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) contained within the mantra—that this serves as a limb of the prayer (*prārthanāṅgatva*), because the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is heard; for there is the traditional rule of Pāṇini stating, "The optative (*liṅ*) and the imperative (*loṭ*) are used in the sense of praying. Nevertheless, regarding the mantra: *mama agne varco vihveṣv astu* (O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations...).

Just as the direct statement (śruti) "He places the Vihavyā bricks" sets aside the indicative mark (liṅga) [of the word 'vihavyā'] to establish that they are auxiliary to the act of placing (upadhāna), so too should their being auxiliary to worship (arcana) be understood. Since the status of being auxiliary to worship is indicated by the phrase "having performed the collective worship with the thought, 'May they be fully honored,'" the weak hearing of the imperative suffix (loṭ) does not constitute a sublation. || 2 ||

Having recited the *karaśuddhi* (purity of hands) mantra and touched the Mistress of the Tripura-cakra while uttering "drāṃ," one should display the *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī-mudrā*. The names of the Cakras, Yoginīs, and Cakreśīs are different; the rest is the same. || 3 ||

Here, by the term "purification of the hands" (*karaśuddhi*), one should recite the mantra that constitutes the limb of the *karaśuddhi* ritual placement (*nyāsa*), as described in the section on ritual placements (*nyāsaprakaraṇa*).
