[This *karaśuddhi* placement mantra is found in the third subsequent section, in the fifteenth sūtra of the *Śrīkrama*, on page 102 of its commentary. Having recited that, [one says] "Tripurā," who is the presiding goddess (*nāyikā*) of the *Trailokyamohana-cakra*.

"Tripurā-cakreśvarī" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the Mistress of the Wheel who is Tripurā. In the term "Tripurā," the absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). Having thus perceived and fully worshipped such a Mistress of the Wheel, there is also the remainder of the mantra "Śrīpādukā" because this too consists of worship; however, in the collective worship (*samaṣṭyarcana*), it is "Śrīpādukām."

Because there is no remainder of the mantra, the word "iti" in the phrase "having performed the collective worship (samaṣṭyarcana)" serves to exclude any further [mantric] residue. Having recited "drāṃ," which is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā—(p.

One should display the *savaṃsaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā, which consists of the interlacing of the fingers, according to the method to be described; [this is] for the Goddess—so the ellipsis is to be supplied. Thus, when the fingers are interlaced in the manner to be described in front of the Goddess, it is shown to her. This is to be understood in the same way for the subsequent [mudrās]. Thus, in the present case:
Having stated the mantra for the collective worship (*samaṣṭhyarcana*) and the mantra of the presiding goddess of the wheel (*cakreśī*),

[in the next collective worship mantra mentioned in the upcoming fifth sūtra, and in the mantra of the *cakreśī*,] he extends certain syllables by way of analogy (*atideśa*), while excluding certain other syllables, as indicated by the word "wheel" (*cakra*).
The names of the wheels (*cakra*), such as "Fulfiller of All Hopes" (*sarvāśāparipūraka*) and so forth,

will be mentioned in the various sūtras below that reveal the respective coverings (*āvaraṇa*). The names of the Yoginīs, such as "Secret" (*guptā*) and so forth, and the names of the Mistress of the Wheels (*cakreśī*), such as "Tripurā" and so forth, are non-different from the phonemes of those [names].

The clusters of syllables beginning with "samudrāḥ" [as stated on folio 154, line 2, in Sūtra 1: "the oceans together with their accomplishments," etc. are the same. The meaning is that, by means of this, the names to be mentioned later should be recited in place of the names of the wheels (cakras) and so forth as they were stated in their respective contexts. || 3 ||
The worship of the second enclosure:
Now he describes the worship of the second enclosure— on the sixteen petals [are] Kāmākarṣiṇī and those ending with Nityākalā, [namely] Buddhyākarṣiṇī.
The attractor of ego, the attractor of sound, the attractor of touch, the attractor of form, the attractor of taste,

the attractor of smell, the attractor of mind, the attractor of fortitude, the attractor of memory, the attractor of name, the attractor of seed-syllables, the attractor of the self, the attractor of nectar, and the attractor of the body— these are the secret yoginīs.

Having recited the self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) as before, beginning with "The mudrās in the wheel that fulfills all hopes," and having worshipped Tripureśī, one should display the All-Enthraller (*sarvavidrāviṇī*) with the syllable *drīṃ*. (Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15-8/6; the object is the visible). || 4 ||

The term *nityākala* refers to a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) that occurs at the end of a name; by this etymological derivation, this qualification is to be applied by extension to all fifteen [mantras], beginning with *buddhyākarṣiṇī*. In all cases, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), in accordance with the recitation of the first mantra. The remainder [of the formula] begins with *śrīpādukā*, etc.

As before. Regarding the sequence for the sixteen-petaled [lotus], the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* states: "One should worship the Great Goddess on the sixteen-spoked [wheel] in counter-clockwise order (*vāmāvarta*). Furthermore, when there is a desire to know the specific detail as to from which petal that commencement should begin, it is established in the *Setubandha* that one should begin from the corner at the front of the Goddess.
He states the names of the Yoginī and the Cakra for the purpose of entering the mantra that is the subject at hand: "These are the Guptayoginīs.
With respect to the outer enclosure (bhūpura), because the sixteen-petaled lotus is situated within it, the Yoginīs residing there are "hidden" (guptāḥ).
The remainder is the same; thus he reiterates the meaning already established by the preceding sūtra: "They possess their respective mudrās."
By this [statement], the purpose of the restatement is so that other words having the same meaning may not be inserted into the mantra; as before, "pūrva" refers to what precedes.

The meaning is "exactly as it was uttered. [In this section, on page 154, from the second sūtra beginning with "samudrāḥ" up to "santu," this is the meaning. Self-protection [on page 102, in the third section, in the Śrīkrama, the mantra ending with the word "rakṣa" as stated in the sixteenth sūtra is that mantra]. The remainder is clear. || 4 ||
The worship of the third enclosure:
he speaks of the worship of the third enclosure—
on the petals of the directions.

Having meditated upon these most secret yoginīs— Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, Madanāturā, Ārekhā, Veginī, Aṅkuśā, Mālinī, and Anaṅgā— who are accompanied by their respective mudrās in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra,
and so forth; then, having recited the *ātmasana* as before and worshipped Tripurasundarī, [one should utter] *klīm*.
One should display the mudrā that attracts all. [Note: For the purpose of extracting this "mudrā that attracts all," see Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15–8/7 Vi. Dṛśya. || 5 ||

Here, the word *dik* (direction) indicates the number eight, because the number eight exists in the directions. Thus, by the etymological derivation "that in which there are petals possessing a number residing in the directions," it refers to the third wheel.
Furthermore, the number eight in the directions is obtained by including the intermediate directions (*avāntaradik*), [making] four...

According to the Vedic scripture, "the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions," the status of being a direction (*dik-tvam*) remains uncontradicted by the maxim: "even when [a thing] has entered further into the intermediate directions, there is no loss of its essential nature. The term *anaṅgapūrvāḥ* refers to those deities whose names begin with *Anaṅga*, such as the deities of flowers and so forth mentioned previously.

In this context, the referent of the compound is a substance (*dravya*), not a collection of colors such as those of flowers; for otherwise, the logical connection (*anvaya*) with the word "touching" (*saṃmṛśya*) would be impossible. Furthermore, the sequence for worshiping these deities is given in the *Yoginītantra*:
"One should worship Anaṅgakusumā in the east and Anaṅgamekhalā in the south."
In the west is Anaṅgamadanā, and in the north is Madanāturā.
"One should place Anaṅgarekhā in the southeast, Anaṅgaveginī in the southwest, Anaṅgāṅkuśā in the northwest, and Anaṅgamālinī in the northeast. Thus it is said.
Because these deities belong to the inner circle of the previous wheel, they are more secret; the rest is largely understood from what has already been explained. || 5 ||
The worship of the fourth enclosure:
he describes the worship of the fourth enclosure—
on the petals of the world [mandala] are Saṃkṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Āhlādinī, Saṃmohinī, and Stambhinī.
Jṛmbhiṇī, Vaśaṅkarī, Rañjanī, Unmādinī, Arthasādhinī, Sampattipūraṇī, Mantrayī,
and Dvandvakṣayaṅkarī— having contemplated all these goddesses ending in long *ī* (beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Dvandvakṣayaṅkarī, there are fourteen deities).
The remaining portion of the mantra begins with "the Sampradāyayoginīs are present with their mudrās in the Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka-cakra" (p.
after having recited the Cakrāsana [as found on folio 103, recto, line 3].

In the *Śrīkrama*, this is the mantra for the Cakrāsana found in the commentary on the eighteenth sūtra: "Having worshipped Tripuravāsinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī), one should manifest the mudrā that brings all under control with the syllable *blūṃ*. (See Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15–8/8; Vi. Dṛśya). || 6 ||

In the fourteen-spoked wheel (*bhuvanāra*), there are fourteen worlds (*bhuvana*); that is to say, it is where the spokes have the number of worlds (i.e., fourteen). The remainder is like the "direction-petals" (as explained in the preceding twenty-eighth sūtra).
The phrase "all [names] which are the initial parts of the components of names" is also largely explained by the expression "those preceded by *anaṅga*."
When there is a requirement for a sequence, according to the Yoginītantra, it is by means of the counter-clockwise order—from the western [direction] itself to the southern;
thus, the commencement is in the west, and from there one should take the southern [direction]. This is the meaning.
The resulting sense is: "beginning from the west, in a non-pradakṣiṇa (counter-clockwise) manner. || 6 ||
The worship of the fifth enclosure:
he describes the worship of the fifth enclosure— on the outer ten-spoked [wheel].

Having first worshipped all these *yoginīs* who have transcended the *kula*, namely Siddhipradā, Sampatpradā, Priyaṅkarī, Maṅgalakāriṇī, Kāmapradā, Duḥkhavimocinī, Mṛtyupraśamanī, Vighnanivāriṇī, Aṅgasundarī, and Saubhāgyadāyinī, within the wheel that accomplishes all aims (*sarvārthasādhakacakre*).
Having stated the remainder of the *Manu*— [it should be understood that the remainder of the *Manu*, from "the oceans" (*samudrāḥ*) on page 154, line 2, sūtra 2 of this section,
up to "may they be" (*santu*), is to be known]— and having uttered the *mantrāsana*,
[there is the *cakrāsana-mantra* in the *Śrīkrama*, sūtra 18, on page 103, line 3 of the *Anugata*]: [Tripurā, the Sovereign of the Śrīcakra].
Having reflected thus, he should bestow the seal of Unmādinī. || 7 ||
Within the nine wheels, there are two ten-spoked [wheels]. The meaning is: "therein" refers to that which is the outer ten-spoked wheel among those two.

The remainder is largely explained [elsewhere]. Here too, when there is a requirement for a sequence, the order is the same as in the previous wheel, because the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* applies the sequence of the previous wheel by means of the phrase "in the same way. (7)

The worship of the sixth enclosure: he describes the worship of the sixth enclosure— within the inner ten-spoked [lotus], [the goddesses] Jñānaśakti, Aiśvaryapradā, Jñānamayī, Vyādhivināśinī, and Ādhāra...

These Garbhayoginīs— [who are] the removers of the loss of one's own nature, consisting of bliss, whose nature is protection, the bestowers of desired fruits, and accompanied by all [epithets]— are to be worshipped in the Sarvarakṣākara-cakra. The remainder [is found] in this section [at 154–159].

On leaf 2, from the word *samudrāḥ* up to *santu*, the remainder of the mantra is to be understood. Likewise, having uttered the seat for the accomplishment of the goal (*sādhyasiddhāsana*), [on leaf 103 of the *Anugata*, in the 18th sūtra spoken in the *Śrīkrama*, this is the mantra for the seat for the accomplishment of the goal: *Tripuramālinī mānyā krom*.
One should display the Sarvamahāṅkuśā [as seen in the second chapter of the Śrīparamādya, verse 15-7/6]. || 8 ||

All the suffixes are preceded by all [the vowels]. "Worthy of honor" means worthy of worship. As for the sequence, it is as before—meaning counter-clockwise—according to the procedure previously stated from the *Yoginītantra*. The remainder is to be understood according to the method already explained. || 8 ||
The worship of the seventh enclosure:

he describes the worship of the seventh enclosure—[in the eight-spoked wheel, the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī; at the place where "namaḥ" occurs, these are the eight goddesses beginning with Vaśinī]. 3.

These secret yoginīs, whose names are the mantras for worship, reside in the wheel that removes all diseases (sarvarogaharacakra) in the *Śrīkrama* of the *Khaṇḍa*, on folio 104, in the 20th section. The remainder is clear. Having uttered the *mūrtividyā* [this *mūrtividyā* mantra is found in the *Khaṇḍa*, on folio 136, in the 2nd section], [Tripurāsiddhā].
Having propitiated Māra, Śiva, Bhṛgu, and Ṛddhi, the Khecarī [mantra] "Phreṃ" should be bestowed. || 9 ||

In the section on the *yoginī-nyāsa*, regarding those eight mantras of Vaśinī and the others that have been extracted, one must perform an adaptation (*ūha*) by substituting the word "namaḥ" with the name of the worship mantra, namely "Śrīpādukā.
The meaning is that the worship mantra should be used in place of the word "namaḥ" together with the dative case; otherwise [it would not be correct].
Because there would be the contingency of hearing the fourth [case-ending], for that which was previously heard as the fourth would be heard due to the absence of any sublater [of it]. (Note:
*a. śrī.* indicates a marginal gloss suggesting that the hearing of that [fourth case] would occur because there is no sublater.)

Nor should it be argued that when the word *namaḥ* ceases, the dative case ending (*caturthī*)—which is occasioned by its connection [to *namaḥ*]—also ceases, according to the maxim "when the cause disappears, the effect disappears. For the word *namaḥ* is not the cause for the existence of the dative case, but rather for its production. Thus, regarding that dative case which has been produced by taking the word *namaḥ* as its cause:
Because there is no sublation [of the cognition] during its persistence, up until the point of its cessation.

Nor should it be argued that the word *namaḥ* should cease to apply even before the emergence of the dative case; for if that were so, there would be no basis for the dative case itself due to the absence of its cause. This is because, once it is established that the placement-mantra (*nyāsa-mantra*) is the prototype (*prakṛti*) for the worship-mantra (*pūjā-mantra*), the dative case—along with the word *namaḥ*—is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from that prototype.

The word *namaḥ* is sublated by the excellence of its proper arrangement; by what could the dative case ending (*caturthī*) be sublated? When, according to the Vedic text (*śrauta*), the mantra for the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is obtained through its original form together with the word *agni*, then in the Sūrya sacrifice, because of the contradiction in meaning, there is a sublation of the word *agni* alone by the word *sūrya*, but not of the dative case ending. It is the same here as well. Therefore:
The mantra for worship consists of the word *namaḥ* together with the fourth case-ending; the rest is almost self-evident.
p.
160) The *mūrtividyā*, the mantra for the conceptualization of the form (*mūrtikalpana*), has been stated in the section on invocation (*āvāhana*). Śiva is the letter *ha*;
Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*; Ṛddhi is the letter *kha*. The authorities regarding this have been cited previously [at *Prākvāma* 103].

It should be understood that these have been shown in the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, the eighteenth [chapter] of the *Śrīkrama* in the third section of the manuscript. The syllable *phreṃ* joined with those [syllables] becomes *hskhphreṃ*. The meaning is that having uttered this, one should manifest the *Khecarī*. || 9 ||
Regarding the worship of the weapons (*āyudhapūjā*), he says:
having uttered the seed-syllables of the arrows, [one recites] "Obeisance to all the expanding arrows, *dhaṃ thaṃ*."
"Āṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the bow for the purpose of deluding all; Kroṃ, obeisance to the noose for the purpose of subjugating all;
[obeisance] to the goad for the purpose of paralyzing all"—thus is the worship of the weapons, beginning with the arrows, in the four directions outside the great triangle. || 10 ||
The "seeds of the arrows" are the seed-syllables of the five mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī, which are the arrows of Kāmeśvara.
As it is said in the *Kulasāra*:
"Those which are indeed the five seed-syllables of the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī..."
O Goddess of the Gods, one should recite all of those at the beginning of the month of Śara. Thus [it is said].
[The additional passage in manuscript *ba*: These are the seed-syllables (*bīja*). As it is stated in the *Mālinītantra*:
"Having written two *tha*-letters situated in fire (*ra*) in sequence, they are adorned with a face (*a*), a circle (*u*), an eye (*i*), and a dot (*bindu*)."
This pair of arrows is declared to be the "Mādana" (the Enchanter), situated upon the ground.
O fair-faced one, it is enriched by the fourth vowel and the bindu, having the form of sound (nāda);
it is joined with the letter *pha* [or *śra*] by means of a wheel, and adorned with the left ear.
O Dear One, the Moon, possessing the creative emission (sarga), is joined with the Bindu and the Nāda.
"Know these five arrows to be mine, O beloved of my life. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: in the sequence of the Mātṛkā, the letter *da* comes after the letter *tha*; having written two of those, one places the first *da* between them joined with *vahni*, which is the letter *ra*.
The letter *ā* is the "circular face" (*mukhavṛtta*), because that is its position in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. And there is a *bindu* [above] those two.
Combined: *drām*—this is the result. Regarding the second letter *da*, its position within the fire (*vahni*) remains attached;

immediately thereafter, it is joined with the "eye," which is the left eye, the letter *ī*, because that is its location in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, and also with the *bindu*. Thus, *drī* is the resulting form. In this way, the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) are produced.

There are two *bāṇas*. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists of the first two *bāṇas*. Thus, *mādana* is the letter *ka*, and *bhūmi* is the letter *la*; it is situated upon that, meaning the letter *la* below and the letter *ka* above.
It is enriched—that is, joined—with the fourth vowel, the letter *ī*, and the well-known *bindu*: thus [it becomes] *klīm*.
It is complete. The letter *ba* is the phoneme *pha* (with the *anusvāra*).
Its etymology is like that of the letter *tha*. It is joined with the letter *la* of the wheel; the left ear is the vowel *ū*, and by that [is added] the *bindu*.
And when joined with *vlūm*, it becomes *sampannam*. *Sarga* (creation) and *visarga* (emission)—the Moon possessing these is the letter *saḥ*.
Thus, the meaning is: "Know my five arrows to be *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vlūṃ*, and *saḥ*. The seed-syllables of the arrows of Kāmeśvarī are found in the *Yoginītantra*:
"O Goddess of the Gods, skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these, joined with the second vowel [Ī], are his arrows. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: *tvak* (skin) is the letter *ya*, according to the lexicon: "the pervasive wind is *tvagvālī*"; *asṛk* (blood) is the letter *ra*, according to the lexicon: "*ro* is blood, *repha* is Krodhinī"; *māṃsa* (flesh) is the letter *la*, according to the lexicon: "Pinākī is designated as *māṃsa*"; *medas* (fat) is the letter *va*, according to the lexicon: "*vo* is fat, Varuṇa is subtle"; [this continues] up to bone and marrow.

The letter *sa* has the color of semen (*śukra*) situated in the final region, for the lexicon states: "Bhṛgu is the ten-footed Śukra. Alternatively, according to the section on the letter *ṣa*: "The letters *sa* and *ṣa* represent bone and marrow; the letter *śa* is declared by the wise to signify the 'tusk-eared' [Śiva] and bone," and likewise under the section on *vṛṣa*: "The Lord of the White [Śiva] is Taurus, and marrow is yellow."

From the treasury: the meaning is that he resides at the end of those two. The aforementioned letters, when joined with the second vowel (i) and conjoined with the letter Ā, possess the union of the *bindu* because they are of the nature of seed-syllables (*bīja*). Thus, *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *lāṃ*, *vāṃ*, and *sāṃ* are the seed-syllables of the arrows of the Goddess. Among the aforementioned letters—

In another Tantra, the *binduyoga* consists of all the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), the third sibilant (*ūṣman*) accompanied by the *bindu*, the *ananta*, and the vowels *ya-ra-la-va*. Here, "semi-vowels" refers to *ya-ra-la-va*; the "third sibilant" is *sa*; and "ananta" is the vowel *ā*. In this context, by the term "seed-syllables of the arrows" (*bāṇabīja*), all of these are included: *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sāṃ*, according to the *Setubandha*.

Having written the two mantras: "Obeisance to all the expanding Kāmeśvarī arrows: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*, obeisance to all the expanding Kāmeśvara arrows," and having written before them, "And this has been stated in accordance with the Kalpasūtra," [one should know that] in reality, however, according to the Svatantra, it is at the beginning.

The meaning is that after pronouncing the ten seed-syllables of the arrows— namely, the two *dvitārīs* (the two preceding mantras), followed by the five beginning with *yāṃ*, and the five beginning with *drāṃ*— one should recite from the written text: "I worship the venerable sandals of the Śakti of the All-Pervading Arrow (*sarvajṛmbhaṇabāṇaśaktiśrīpādukām pūjayāmi*)."

In the *Nibandha*, however, having written down only the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kāmeśvara, the form of the mantra is written as "Salutation to all the expanding arrows" (*sarvajṛmbhaṇebhyo bāṇebhyo namaḥ*). Since the status of being a "seed-syllable of an arrow" (*bāṇabījatva*) is common to both [Śiva and the Goddess],
by the phrase "having uttered the seed-syllables of the arrows," it is understood that only Śiva’s arrows are to be uttered, and not those of the Goddess.

Since there was not even a scent of authoritative evidence for expelling the intention of the Blessed Lord Rāma, and on the contrary, when considered by a gross standard of measurement, the worship of his arrows had already been commenced, it was proper to worship those very arrows of his; thus, setting aside [the others], he drew only the arrows of Śiva. That act of his was truly a great audacity.
And it should not be argued that, such being the case, the singular forms "to the bow," "to the noose," and "to the goad" in the subsequent mantras would be untenable;
for their validity can be established through the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*. Alternatively, having uttered the ten seed-syllables...
"Salutation to all the yawning arrows"—thus, the worship of the two [arrows] is performed by means of a single formula (*tantra*).
And their status as deities is joined together like that of Agni and Soma. It is exactly the same in the case of the nooses and so forth.
And thus, just as in the phrase "seeking the sacrificial food for the lord of the sacrifice," there is a single deity-status residing in the pair of bows.

Because they are collectively engaged and because that which is delimited by the nature of being a deity is singular, the use of the singular number is justified with reference to that [deity]; furthermore, the plural number occurs after the word *bāṇa*.
Since it conforms to the substratum of the deityhood, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, just as in the case of the expression "medham medhapatibhyām."

Let it be granted that the author of the *Nibandha* did not err in mentioning the *bījas* of Śiva and Bāṇa; however, because this occurs within the section on Lalitā, only the *bījas* of Śakti and Bāṇa are to be understood here.
This is because, although the *Kalpasūtra* mentions "having uttered the *bāṇabījas*" without qualification, the context (*prakaraṇa*) determines the specific meaning.
It should be stated that this is because [such a procedure] is observed in cases such as "one worships the Āgnīdhra fire-shed with the *āgneyī* [verse] during the contraction.
O Maheśānī, one should worship the arrows of Kāma, his bow, and his noose,
in sequence, within the four corners in the center of the wheel.

Thus, by the statement of the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, the worship of those very weapons of Śiva is prescribed within the section on Lalitā; however, when a restriction must be made regarding the general injunction heard in the present *Kalpasūtra*— namely, "having uttered the seed-syllables of Bāṇa"— by means of the [specific] context (*prakaraṇa*), it is superseded by another statement that is even more powerful than that.

Because the meaning is established solely on the basis of what is explicitly heard [in the text]. In the case of "He worships the Āgnīdhra with an Āgneyī verse," there is no other statement that overrides the context; thus, there is a disparity between the two cases.

Nor does this constitute a loss of the initial thesis— that one does not resort to other tantras— because there is no inconsistency in the thesis if one follows other statements for the sake of determining the meaning of the sūtra.

Furthermore, in many manuscripts, the reading of the *Kalpasūtra* is: "Oṃ Thaṃ, salutation to the bow for the purpose of deluding all; Āṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the noose for the purpose of subjugating all. This too is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the grasping of the two arrows. Otherwise, [if this were not the case], both the bow and the arrows would be connected [to the same mantra].
Why should one recite the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) that indicate the grasping? Indeed, this very reading is observed in many manuscripts;

therefore, the worship of both is mandatory. Even if it is considered that the establishment of the other view is certain because the reading of the two seed-syllables is not seen in some manuscripts, even then—

In all manuscripts, without dispute, the syllable *dhaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the bow-mantra in the *Śivadhanuḥ*; it is the fourth [letter] from the red group (the retroflex class), and also the second from the same, O Pārvatī—thus, according to the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, it is the pair of male and female bows. The meaning of this is: the "red group" is the *tavarga* (the retroflex class); therein, the fourth is the letter *dha*.

The second *thakāra* signifies, in sequence, the male and female bows; by this, *dhaṃ* is established as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Śiva’s bow. Likewise, *hrīṃ* for the noose (*pāśa*) exists without dispute in all manuscripts.
And that is the seed-syllable of the Śakti-noose, because of the statement in the *Yoginītantra*: "Māyā is called the female noose. Thus...

In some places there is a description of the male weapon-seed-syllables (*pum-āyudha-bīja*), and in others a description of the female weapon-seed-syllables (*strī-āyudha-bīja*); this form of composition serves as a characteristic mark common to all manuscripts regarding the employment of both types of weapons. Furthermore, the statement from another Tantra has already been clearly recorded above. Thus, the application of the singular number has been demonstrated.
Since there is no contradiction, it appears to me without doubt that both weapons are to be worshipped here.

Because Dharma is beyond the reach of the senses, let the virtuous and wise examine this further than even this. And thus, in whichever manuscript there is only "dhaṃ" in the mantra for the bow, that is "thaṃ."

This also indicates the *hrīm* in the third mantra; and *ām* also indicates that [the letter *a*], because it is of the nature of Śiva’s bond (*pāśa*), as stated in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*: "The great bond pertaining to the person (*pauruṣeya*) is proclaimed to reside at the beginning and the end."

This meaning was also previously explained during the extraction of the *nīlapatākā* mantra. As for the *aṅkuśa* seed-syllable, however, it is common to both [mantras] because the *Yoginītantra* reads without distinction: "Kāma, Agni, Vyāpaka, and Aṅkuśa."
It is recited only once by way of its *tantra*. Thus, the nature of the mantra is as follows:
*yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ sāṃ drāṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ sarvajṛmbhaṇebhyo bāṇebhyo namaḥ bāṇaśrīpādukāṃ [bāṇaśaktiśrī-śrī. pūjayāmi | thaṃ dhaṃ* |

"Obeisance to the bow for the sake of deluding all; I worship the venerable sandals of the bow. Hrīṃ Āṃ, obeisance to the noose for the sake of subjugating all; [I worship] the venerable sandals of the noose. Kroṃ, obeisance to the goad for the sake of paralyzing all; [I worship] the venerable sandals of the goad. Thus, when the seed-syllables of power (śakti-bījas) come first.
Its predominance is the indicator.

However, some followers of Tantra recite the ten seed-syllables and then chant: *kāmeśvarakāmeśvarībāṇebhyo namaḥ*. This is extremely incorrect; because the rule *pumān striyā* (a masculine noun remains when joined with a feminine) would apply as a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) to override a copulative compound (*dvandva*), there should not be a *dvandva* here.

A great triangle is the first triangle; outside of that, within an eight-pointed star, there are triangles in the cardinal directions starting from the west and proceeding clockwise. As it is stated in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"The western, northern, eastern, and southern directions in sequence."
In this commentary, regarding the weapon-mantras (*āyudhamantra*), if there is no application of the word "śrīpādukām" as a supplement, one should consult that very source for the authority.

Furthermore, the eight-syllable formula is not to be applied to all names of deities by means of the phrase "the *pādukā* preceded by *Śrī*" and so forth; for by the expression "in those names of deities," it is indicated that the eight-syllable formula is to be used only where the name of a deity is specifically taken— that is, having first grasped the name of each respective deity, one should append "the *śrī-pādukā*."

"I worship"—this very eight-syllable mantra has been stated previously as well, and not elsewhere. It should not be argued that it is not so because the name "Bāṇa" and others is not mentioned in the specific injunction under discussion; for the author of the *Nibandha* (the commentary) must necessarily interpret the phrase "in the names of the deities" as meaning "in mantras composed of the names of the deities."

This must be stated: otherwise, its connection with the three currents would be contradicted in reality. In that regard, there is no non-inclusion of deities in the prescriptive statement; rather, the three currents themselves exist. Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence. || 10 ||
The worship of the eighth enclosure:
he describes the worship of the eighth enclosure—
[the goddesses] preceded by Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti, together with all [the others], in the triangle.
The great goddesses Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī; the fourth [is] in the Bindu. 11.
That supreme power (*parā śakti*), which is the nature of the light of the lamp that is Paraśiva, becomes threefold when oriented toward creation:

namely, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. These are, respectively, predominated by *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*. In the Tantric scriptures, the term "Ambikā" denotes their collective totality (*samaṣṭi*). These very powers, in their respective order—

These are called the powers of will, knowledge, and action. In order to make known that these constitute the individualized form (*vyaṣṭi*) of Tripurasundarī, [the author] later applied the qualification "most secret" (*atirahasya*) to the Yoginīs. In this regard:

By the word *vāgbhava*, the first *kūṭa* (syllabic unit) is to be understood; by the word *kāma*, the second *kūṭa*; and by the word *śakti*, the third *kūṭa*. However, the letters of the *Bālā* mantra are not intended here, for in the *Vāmakeśvara Tantra*, it is specifically the *kūṭas* that are meant. [Note: Regarding the bracketed remark, the text suggests that since the word "vāk" alone appears in the root text (*mūla*), one should consider that the phrase "by the word *vāk*" is what is intended.]

Because it has been so accepted. Although in other tantras a conjunction of both the Vāgbhava and the first *kūṭa* is seen, nevertheless, because only the [mantras] beginning with Speech (vāk) and so forth are mentioned here, one should take the *kūṭas* alone according to the *Yoginītantra*.
This refers to the entire triad of *kūṭas*. These are those of whom [it was said] previously...
The meaning is that those four, by name, are to be worshipped in the triangle—that is, in the three corners of the triangle and at the bindu.

The author of the *Nibandha* wrote "Lalitāśrī" as the internal root-mantra for the fourth deity; that is trivial. Since the names of the four deities are given in sequence in the Sūtra as Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Mahādevī, [the author] has abandoned what is well-known in the scriptures.

He introduced the name "Lalitā," which was fabricated by his own imagination, into the mantra; in this matter, scripture is not the authority. Even regarding mantras of inconceivable power, those who habitually act according to their own whims—whose words even great men trust—in this case, the root cause is simply the laziness born of the Śrī Bhagavān’s māyā.

It is not otherwise. Nor should it be argued that the word *lalitā* is merely a synonym for *mahādevī*, and thus there would be no obstacle to its usage; for if one were to use the phrase *vahnim īḷe* in place of *agnim īḷe* in the mantra, it would result in something unprecedented (*apūrva*). Enough of this improper obsession.
The sequence is stated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
"Kāmeśvarī in the front corner, Vajreśī to the south, Bhagamālinī likewise to the north, and Tripurasundarī in the center. (11)
Regarding the non-difference of Kāmeśvarī and the others from the Root Goddess:
indeed, it has been prescribed that one should worship with the mantras of the fifteen Nityās and with the Root Vidyā;
likewise, in the present context, the worship of the Fourth Deity with the Root [Vidyā] has been mentioned, and he will also state this regarding the Binducakra.

The worship with the root mantra is likewise performed for the Mistress of the Final Wheel as well. Thus, since the three sacrifices are performed by means of a single mantra, there may arise the doubt whether they constitute a single deity worshipped in the form of repetition, or whether they involve distinct deities; [the author] establishes the identity of the deity:

Immediately after these three, there is the worship of the Root Goddess (Mūladevī) for the sake of non-differentiation. The fourth [goddess] among Kāmeśvarī and the others is Nityā; she is the sixteenth among the goddesses of the wheels (*cakradevī*), and she who resides in the Bindu-wheel is the ninth—and thus she is one alone. One should not effect a distinction between the mantra and the deity therein; she is that Great Goddess.
Thus, at four locations, the special worship is repeated. || 12 ||
p.

165) Immediately following these three, Kāmeśvarī and the others, there is the worship of the Root Goddess (mūladevī) in order to demonstrate their non-difference from her. This is likewise the case in other locations as well.

The worship performed at the end of Tripurasundarī makes known the non-difference between each respective [deity] and its own preceding deity-cluster (*kūṭa*). He clearly demonstrates this very point with the words "Kāmeśvarī" and so forth: in the present wheel, after Kāmeśvarī and the others comes the fourth [deity], and after the fifteen Nityās comes the sixteenth.

Beyond the eighth wheel, in the ninth *bindu*, she who is indicated by the syllable *ca* is again to be worshipped as the sole Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*) within that very *bindu*, immediately following the worship of the Mistress of the eight wheels. In these instances, there is no difference in the deity nor any difference in the mantra. Thus, all the eternal goddesses and those of the surrounding enclosures [are one].
The intention is that it is stated at the end of each [section] in order to make known that [the deities] are non-different from Tripurasundarī. Now, one might object:

"If there is unity of deity, unity of substance, and unity of mantra, then worship performed only once would be appropriate; why then is there a triad of worships? To this he says: "The special worship is repeated in four places. This means: in the four places already shown.

And thus, even though the sacrifice is one, the sense is that the repetition of it is necessary because it serves as the means for producing the *apūrva*. Nor should it be argued that, since there is repetition, the mantra should not be repeated—just as the *prokṣaṇa* mantra is not repeated;
for in cases such as the *agnihotra*, the mantra is indeed repeated despite the repetition [of the action], provided there is no intervention by another action.

Because it has been observed [in other cases]. Likewise, here too, even though it consists of the repetition of an action, the repetition of the mantra is justified because of the intervention of another action of a different kind. || 12 ||
Having spoken of the incidental, he states the subject at hand:
"These are the most secret Yoginīs in the wheel that bestows all accomplishments; the remainder is to be observed.
Having uttered the *āvāhanī* [invocation], [this *āvāhanī* mantra is found on folio 4, section kha, chapter 3, in the Sūtra and its commentary].
Then, having honored Tripurāmbā—[the object of perception], or rather, that which is visible—one should assume the form of the seed-syllable and mudrā, *hsaum*. 13.

The word "remaining" (pariśiṣṭam) implies that [the procedure] is as before; this is the ellipsis. "Āvāhanī" refers to the vidyā extracted from that specific context. "Having honored" means having worshipped. "Kṛtiḥ" means it should be performed. || 13 ||
Regarding the worship of the ninth enclosure, he says:
having worshipped the Goddess with the root mantra in the *bindu*-cakra, she is this Yoginī of the supreme-non-supreme secret, who consists of all-bliss.
"May Cakreśvarī, together with her siddhis, weapons, powers, vehicles, and retinue, be fully worshipped with all offerings.
Having thus recited the root mantra once more and worshipped Mahācakreśvarī, he should display the *yoni-mudrā* with the *vāgbhava* syllable. (These two mudrās are for the two objects of perception.)

166) Here too, the author of the commentary (*nibandhakāra*) appended the phrase "I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Lalitā" at the end of the root text; that is incorrect. In the preceding sūtra, it was stated that no distinction between the mantra and the deity should be made there.

In the statement "that [is] for the Great Goddess alone in four places," it is explicitly stated by direct utterance that the worship of the Great Goddess occurs in all four locations. To abandon a word heard in the scripture and to imagine a word not heard therein is unscriptural (*aśāstrīya*). Otherwise, [one would have to interpret] "one desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya" [in a way inconsistent with the text].

Thus, in this sacrifice, by inserting a synonym for Sūrya, the formula would be: "I offer what is pleasing to Divākara. Nor should it be argued that there is a discrepancy because the word "Sūrya" was heard in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*) there, whereas here the preceding sūtra is not an original injunction but rather prescribes a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the form of a repetition.
This is not an absolute rule that hearing the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) itself is required.

In the case of the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) of the Nakṣatreṣṭi, the originative injunction is merely "he offers here" (*atra juhoti*); no word denoting a deity is heard there. Nevertheless, in the mantra [it says]: "Svāhā to Agni, to the Kṛttikās."

In the word "svāhā," taking the term "Agni" and other such words that are heard therein, they employ the expression "agnim ājyena" (with clarified butter for Agni) during the initial anvādhāna rite, and not "vahnim ājyena" (with clarified butter for Vahni).

If there were a restrictive rule that this must occur only in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), then here one might act according to one's own will. And [this is not the case] regarding this sequence.

The intention of the *Nibandha* can be described as follows: since the word "Lalitā" is explicitly heard in the originative statement (*utpattivākya*)—"one should begin the sequence of Lalitā, the sole mistress of the wheel of powers"—it is her [the goddess] who must be understood.

This being the case, although it would have been sufficient to say in the previous sūtra that [the sequence belongs] to Lalitā alone in the four places, [the author] has omitted her [from that specific mention].

Even Brahmā is unable to describe the fruit of speaking [of her] as "Mahādevī" alone. In my view, however, although the words "Lalitā" and "Mahādevī" have the same meaning, where no distinction is heard, the word "Lalitā" is used; whereas where it is heard, the utterance of the word as it was heard produces something unprecedented (*apūrva*).

"Having understood that there is an abandonment of the word 'Lalitā' [in this context], one should state the fruit as 'for the pleasure of Śrī Lalitā' at the beginning of the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth. In the present case, however, the use of the term 'Mahādevī', which has no other application, is appropriate. For this very reason, when the term 'Mahādevī' is obtained in the mantra of the ninth Cakreśvarī by this same method..."
Specifically, because it is heard there that "one should worship [her] as Cakreśī," the term *mahādevī* is set aside; this is according to the maxim:

"Between that which has an occasion [for application] and that which has no occasion, the one without an occasion is stronger. Nor does it follow that, such being the case, the non-difference of the mantras in four instances has been shown, while now in three instances a mantra containing *mahādevī* occurs in only one.

As for the objection that the mantra-division "mahācakreśvarīghaṭita" has fallen [into error]—how can this be? It should be stated that this defect is not to be raised, since it is common to both cases, given that the author of the *Nibandha* also wrote "lalitāmahācakreśvarīśrī0. On the contrary, [the error lies with] the mantra of the author of the *Nibandha*.

Due to its composition with *lalitāpada*, there is an absolute difference [between the two]. In my view, by merely substituting *cakreśvarī* for the word *devī*, the resolution will be achieved by relying on the grammatical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. Enough of this excessive detail.
The etymological explanation of the term *mahādevī* is found in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Since her body is vast and immeasurable in its dimensions,
and because the verbal root *maha* signifies 'to worship,' she is therefore remembered as *Mahādevī*."

By the term *vāgbhava*, namely *aiṃ*, which is the first *kūṭa*, [it is meant]; for since the identity of the phonemes is observed in the seeds of the eight previous mudrās, it is necessary that this one situated in that same row must also possess such a nature.
Therefore, the inclusion of *aiṃ* alone is appropriate. || 14 ||
167) Having thus performed the worship of the nine enclosures (navāvaraṇapūjā), including the offering of incense and so forth, he states the remainder of the ritual actions to be performed next:
Having offered incense, lamps, mudrās, libations, food offerings, and so forth, as before.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of attaining the previously mentioned qualities" at the end of the offerings of incense and so forth— by the expression "previously mentioned qualities," it should be understood that this refers to the qualities taught in the sequence of Sūtras 4, 6, and 7. This is as before, in the case of the incense and other offerings.

The meaning is that those previously mentioned attributes (*dharmas*) should be applied to the incense and other offerings (*dhūpādi*). Those attributes are to be understood as follows: for the incense, lamp, and food offering (*naivedya*), they are the previously mentioned mantras; for the mudrās, they are the same as before; and for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), they consist of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) repeated three times. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
Items such as betel leaves, camphor, and the waving of lamps (nīrājana), along with other substances that cause a blaze, are to be accepted.
The author of the Nibandha, being a worshipper of the Ṣoḍaśī, stated that one should display the *trikhaṇḍā* as well;
however, he was mistaken, because such an arrangement is not mentioned in the Sūkta.
The essential nature of the mudrās beginning with Trikhaṇḍā is presented here for the purpose of demonstrating the mudrās beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī;
[this is the extraction of all mudrās from Saṃkṣobhiṇī up to Yonimudrā, Dvi. Pa. Śi. 15].

[The object is visible. Since knowledge of its specific nature is necessary, the method for displaying that mudrā is here briefly stated along with its authoritative basis. Among these, the *trikhaṇḍā* is first employed in the rite of invocation (*āvāhana*). The definition of the *trikhaṇḍā* has been stated [as follows]:
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
Having crossed the hands and touched them together, one should make the two thumbs equal;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape with the ring fingers positioned inside.
"O Maheśvarī, one should employ the little finger in its own place;
this is declared to be the 'Three-Parted' [mudrā] for the rite of summoning Tripurā. Thus [it is said].

What is called *parivartana* is the joining of the fingers of both hands. This, being the form of authority (*adhikāra*) in all [mudrās], accompanies them always. One should make the two thumbs straight and touching each other, and likewise do so for the little and middle fingers. Having extended the right ring finger obliquely over the left ring finger, from the region below those two—

Having brought the two index fingers together in a curved shape, one should hold the tips of the two ring fingers with those two index fingers. The meaning derived from the analysis of the compound *anāme antargate* is as follows: when this [mudrā] is formed according to the stated method, three sections are visible. At the top is the joining of the two straightened thumbs; in the middle...

The union with the middle [finger] is of such a kind, and the union with the little finger below is likewise. This being so, the three aspects (*kalā*)—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—previously mentioned, are clearly manifest within her. Therefore, although this [goddess] is called "Three-Sectioned" (*trikhaṇḍā*) by way of the etymological analysis: "she in whom there are three sections (*khaṇḍa*), namely the *kalās*."
The method for constructing the two sections has been explained; however, the method for composing the middle section has not been stated.

Nevertheless, in order to fulfill the etymological meaning of "three-sectioned" (*trikhaṇḍā*), one should complete the three sections by resorting to another tantra. The three sections are described in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Maheśānī, having joined the two hands through the method of rotation,
one should hold the ring fingers with the two index fingers, O beloved.

One should join the two middle fingers at their centers, and then place the two ring fingers below them; likewise, having joined the two thumbs, they should be arranged in three pairs according to the sequence.
"This three-part mudrā of mine is for the rite of summoning Tripurā. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the nature of Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, it is stated in that very same [text]: "Having placed the middle fingers in the center, with the little fingers and thumbs held together,
one should make the two index fingers like staffs, with the ring fingers positioned above the middle fingers."
This, however, is the first mudrā, which causes the agitation of all. Thus it is said.
In the *Tantrarāja*, however, it is said:
"Having joined the nails of the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger with one another,
one should make the two thumbs rest upon the little fingers and straighten the index fingers."
The seal that agitates all is the agitator of the three worlds. Thus it is said.
The *sarvavidrāviṇī* mudrā is described in that very same [text]: "O Maheśānī, if the two middle fingers of this very mudrā are made straight, then it becomes the *sarvavidrāviṇī*."
The phrase "in each middle [finger]" means for the sake of non-attachment. By this, it should be understood that both the index finger and the middle finger are to be straightened.
The third mudrā is also described in that very same place: "O fair-eyed one, one should bend the pair of the middle fingers and the index fingers."
"This very mudrā is that which effects their attraction. Thus it is said.
In that very context, the fourth mudrā, which effects the subjugation of all, is described: having formed the hands in the shape of a hollowed bowl, with the two index fingers curved like hooks,
one should turn them in sequence so that the middle fingers are positioned below them.
Gradually, O Goddess, having likewise joined the little and ring fingers, all [the fingers] should be made firm at the tips of the thumbs.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is known as the one that brings all under control. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: having formed the two hands in the shape of a hollowed bowl (*puṭa*), with their backs joined to one another and the fingers pointing upward, one should then insert the fingers—excluding the thumbs—into the joints of the other fingers;
thus, the fingers from the index finger to the little finger should be made into the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*). Having done so:
Then one should place both thumbs facing downwards upon the index fingers; this is the "All-Subjugating" [mudrā], such is the meaning.
The fifth [mudrā] is also in that same context:
having placed the two hands face-to-face, with the little fingers positioned between the middle fingers.
The two index fingers are straight, positioned outside of those [other fingers].
Then, the two thumbs are shaped like staffs and placed at the region of the nails of the middle fingers;
this mudrā is named Unmādinī, which causes all women to become moist with passion. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: having extended the right little finger over the left little finger along a horizontal path above the two ring fingers up to the middle fingers, one should firmly grasp the tips of those two little fingers with the two middle fingers; then, the two thumbs, shaped like staffs, should be placed over the nails of the grasped middle fingers.

One should place them thus: one should make the two ring fingers straight, facing each other. On both sides of the two ring fingers, one should also make the two index fingers straight. This is the Sarvonmādinī mudrā, which brings women under control.
The sixth mudrā, Sarvamahāṅkuśā, is also revealed in that very same place:
"Having placed the pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a hook, one should likewise apply the two index fingers in that same sequence."
This is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes and goals. Thus it is said.

Of this [mudrā] of the All-Intoxicating One (*sarvonmādinī*): by that very sequence, namely the sequence of the ring fingers (*anāmikā*). The ring fingers are in the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*). In the same manner, both index fingers (*tarjanī*) should also be formed. The remainder is like the previous mudrā; such is the meaning.

Therein he explained the seventh, the Khecarīmudrā: "O Maheśānī, having placed the left hand upon the right hand and the right hand upon the left hand, and having rotated both hands [around the arms],"
O Goddess, having joined the little fingers and the ring fingers in that same sequence,
both middle fingers are likewise pressed down from above by the two index fingers.
O Maheśānī, one should also keep the two thumbs straight;
this, O beloved, is the mudrā named Khecarī, the most excellent of all.

The essential meaning of this is as follows: first, having straightened both arms and placed the left hand upon the right, one should then pass the left hand under the right hand and out toward the left side;
then, one should interlace the fingers of both hands in the manner that will be described. That is as follows:
Having led [the fingers] from the left ring finger and little finger along the downward path of the right middle finger to the right index finger,
and likewise having led them from the right ring finger and little finger along the downward path of the left middle finger to the left index finger,
one should firmly [hold] the ring and little fingers of both hands brought close together with the two index fingers.
One should grasp them. In the middle, one should place both [hands] entirely upright, straight, and joined together at the tips.
Having made the two thumbs straight, one should bring about a resemblance to a vulva (*yonisādṛśya*).
This is the Khecarīmudrā. Although all the aforementioned meanings are not present in the previously cited statement, nevertheless—
Having placed the left arm upon the right arm and the right [arm] in the region of the left, one should subsequently join them by turning them in due order.
One should restrain [the breath] with the two index fingers upon the pair of the little and ring fingers;
then, having made the middle fingers straight, they should likewise be straight like a *yoni*.
The two thumbs joined in the khecarī mudrā are applied to the earthly station.
Thus, the meaning should be understood as having been elicited by bringing it into syntactic agreement with the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*.
The eighth mudrā is also revealed in that very same place: "O Dear One, having turned the two hands over and touched them so as to form the shape of a half-moon,
one should then simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs."
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down from below by the little fingers;
likewise, the two ring fingers should be joined at the very bottom in a curved position.
"This is the seed-mudrā, which swiftly brings about all accomplishments. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should arrange it so that the two middle fingers are crossed over the path of the two ring fingers, with the middle fingers resting upon the lower part of the [crossed] little fingers. Then, one should arrange it so that the pair of middle fingers is supported by the pair of little fingers, while the two ring fingers remain at the very bottom.
One should join them until they become curved; one should arrange the pair of thumbs and index fingers so that they take the form of a half-moon. This is the *bījamudrā*.
He specifies the ninth, the *yonimudrā*, in that very context: "The two middle fingers are positioned in a curved shape above the two index fingers;
likewise, the two ring fingers are placed between the [middle fingers], and the same applies to the two little fingers."
Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs—this is the first mudrā, which stands as the Yoni-mudrā. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should place the two ring fingers (anāmikā) crossed over the middle phalanges of the two middle fingers (madhyamā) along the lower path, with the tips of the index fingers (tarjanī) bent above them. One should join the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā), which are crossed and touching the backs of the ring fingers.
One should join the two tips of the thumbs (aṅguṣṭha) to the two middle phalanges of the middle fingers. This is the Yoni-mudrā.
It occurs as follows: even if this much meaning is not obtained from that statement,
nevertheless— on the back of the ring finger, at the middle joint of the middle finger,
by the joining of the little finger and the thumb, there is the Mahāyoni, consisting of three segments.
Thus, in another place [it is said]. The meaning of this is: that which consists of three segments (*trikhaṇḍā*) is the Great Yoni (*mahāyoni*). Therein, the specific distinction is this:

the joining of the thumbs with the middle joints of the middle fingers; the joining of the little fingers with the back parts of the ring fingers. The remainder is the same as in the *trikhaṇḍā*—this is the meaning. Together with this...
When the single meaning of the preceding statement is established, the meaning written previously is accomplished.

Thus, these ten mudrās, which are supremely profound, have been elaborated according to my understanding, with detailed arguments and authoritative proofs, as a digression. Let us now return to the main subject. (15)
Now, he begins to explain the meditation on the *kāmakalā*:
"Having formed the face with one *bindu*, the two breasts with two *bindus*, and the vulva with the latter half [of the *kalā*], one performs the meditation on the *kāmakalā*."
Having meditated. || 16 ||

Meditation on the *kāmakalā* is of two kinds: subtle (*sūkṣma*) and gross (*sthūla*). Among these, the meditation on the subtle *kāmakalā* has been explained in detail by our supreme preceptors in the *Setubandha*, a commentary on the *Uttaracatuḥśatī*, and in the *Varivasyārahasya*.

Since this has already been explained, for such a practitioner—the foremost among worshippers who performs that kind of meditation—that writing [of this work] would now be like the description of a hare's horn; it would serve only to manifest one's own mere pedantry, like the study of the Vedānta scriptures in the present day. Therefore, having first abandoned [that approach],...

We shall describe only the gross form for the benefit of those of duller faculties. For example, having conceived three parts within the fourth vowel or the letter *ha*, one should conceive a female form therein: conceiving the face in the upper part, the pair of breasts in the middle part, and [the lower limbs] in the lowest part.

And having performed the visualization of the *yoni*, one should meditate. As it is said in the *Kuṇḍalinīvimarśa*: "One who is skillful in internal contemplation within the portions imagined in the center of Śakti should contemplate [the face, breasts, and vulva] respectively as being above, in the middle, and below, with the face downward."
In this verse, many hold that the meaning of the word *śakti* is the vowel *ī*; some, however, say it is the letter *ha*.

Its meaning is the downward-facing *yoni*. The rest is clear. He who meditates upon you, O Queen of Hara—the digit of Love—having made the *bindu* his face, the pair of breasts below it, and the half-moon of Hara (*harārdha*) beneath those; [he attains success].
Thus it has also been stated by the venerable Bhāgavatapāda. In the *Setubandha*, however, the gross meditation (*sthūladhyāna*) is said to be the letter *ī* alone;

for in the verse: "When one contemplates the letter *ī*—which consists of the *bindu* and *visarga* and is the nature of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti—as one's own self, there is the experience of supreme bliss," [it is taught that] just as one perceives Viṣṇu in a *sālagrāma* stone, so too [one perceives the Divine in this syllable].

This is the rule for the meditative empowerment (*dhyānādhiṣṭhāna*) of the Bhagavatī: one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been conquered by such gross meditation (*sthūladhyāna*), who is the crest-jewel of such a worshipper, should learn the subtle aspect (*sūkṣmakalā*) as written in the *Setubandha* and other texts from the mouth of the Guru and worship according to his desire; no others [should do so].

Those of the present day are suited for that [practice]. And such meditation is obtainable solely through the grace of the Supreme Deity and the venerable Guru. This meaning has been stated very clearly in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"If one is incapable of subtle meditation, one should meditate on the gross form according to the prescribed method. And thus:

Having placed the face, the two breasts, and the vulva upon one of the previously mentioned syllables across three parts, and having mentally fashioned the *kāmakalā* according to the method to be described later [meaning: in accordance with the statements found in both the commentary on the seventeenth sūtra located below], one should meditate upon it as space permits; this is the implied meaning. || 16 ||
Regarding the specific colors mentioned previously, after the description of the constituent parts, he states the method of meditation for the [deity] endowed with those qualities:
"Having touched the heart of Saubhāgya. (17)

The "heart" (*hṛdaya*) of good fortune— that is, the locus and, in other words, the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*)— of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*), beginning with *dharma*; having contemplated, that is, meditated upon, such a [reality] as previously described.
The word "iti" from the preceding sūtra is also carried over here. This very meaning has been clearly stated in the Yoginītantra:
"In this way, the syllable that has arisen in the form of Kāmakalā..."
"O Supreme Goddess, it is the abode of the liberation from the poisons of desire and the rest. Thus [it is said].

Regarding this, the statement in the *Nibandha* that the fire-oblation (*homa*) is optional is baseless; for there is no authority elsewhere to extend the application of the sūtra "if the performance of the fire-rite is accomplished," which occurs within the section on Gaṇapati. || 17 ||
Now, regarding the offering of the *bali* and its varieties,
he says: having drawn a triangle, a circle, and a square on the left side and honored them with perfumes and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should utter the *vāgbhava* mantra.
Having placed the primary, secondary, and intermediate vessels there with water filled half-full of parched grain (lāja), saying "Homage to the pervasive maṇḍala. || 18 ||
In this context, by the phrase "on the left side," one's own left side is to be understood because it is the first to present itself.
Regarding the construction of the triangle, circle, and square: according to the method of exit, the triangle should be drawn facing oneself, as is the established tradition of the learned.

However, some maintain that the deity who receives the offering in the triangle faces toward the corner formed by the junction of the two horizontal lines, because there is a fixed rule that the deities residing within the triangle must face in that manner. And thus it is stated in another Tantra:
Having meditated on [the goddess] facing Mūladevī, one should place the vessel for the bali offering before her.

Because of this statement, there is a rule that the deity must be oriented toward the Root Goddess (Mūladevī). They say that even the triangle must be oriented toward the Goddess and not toward oneself; however, that is not so, for in the triangles of the Śrīcakra located in [the mandalas of] Anaṅgakusumā and the others, [the deities] face away from the corners.
Since many deities facing Mūladevī are perceived, such a restrictive rule is unestablished; this [objection] is of no consequence.

By the phrase "perfumes, unbroken rice, etc.," the exclusion of other [substances] is indicated. He states the mantra for the worship: "The Vāgbhava," and so forth. "Vāgbhava" is *aiṃ*. The remainder is clear. It is accompanied by half [of the offering], namely cooked food (*bhakta*) and water filled with food; this is an adjective qualifying the vessel. That is, in a single bowl.

One should fill half the vessel with food and half with water. Having placed one such vessel and three vessels for milk and other offerings upon that mandala, the offering vessel (balipātra) here must be made of copper;
the offering vessel should be born of copper and never anything else.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Tripurārṇava*, one should not mix in vegetables and the like; for in this Tantra, the requirement for substances is satisfied by the very materials already specified.
173) Here, the author of the commentary has recorded the offering of a *bali* with a *bāṇa*-seal, as well as the striking of the left heel and so forth.
He should be asked: "What is the authority for this? If he should reply that it is found in the *sūtra* within the section on Śyāmā:

If it is argued that "because they have been mentioned, those same factors (dharmas) are to be understood here as well," then is that inclusion due to expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) or without expectancy? In the first case, regarding the offering to Bali, the expectancy for the substance, the deity, and the mantra was raised and satisfied by the very words of the archetype (*prakṛti*); [yet] there is an inclusion of the *bāṇamudrā* and the striking with the left heel.

Furthermore, we do not know what kind of desire could have arisen for him while he was performing that very act. Moreover, what harm has been done by the ritual elements such as the striking with the heel found in the section on Śyāmā?
Offerings (bali) to Kṣetrapāla, Vāgīśvarī, and others are also present there; furthermore, there are other mantras besides those already mentioned.

There are [objections]. What offense has been committed by the authors of these treatises? For, although the status of being situated within the *Śyāmā-prakaraṇa* is equal [for all], we do not know the root cause for why he accepted some while, being angry, he rejected others.
Furthermore, since the properties of the mandalas such as the triangle (*trikoṇa*) and so forth are already obtained from that very source, their re-enunciation here [is redundant].

If it is asked, "For what purpose? the answer is simply the restriction of speech and nothing else. Therefore, a path that promotes dharma according to one's own whim is not to be trusted; [dharma] consists only in what has been stated as the duty to be performed. || 18 ||
Regarding the mantra for the offering of the *bali*, he says: having recited three times "Oṃ Hrīṃ, to all beings who create obstacles, hūṃ svāhā," one should give the *bali* offering. || 19 ||

By the word "thrice," the repetition of the mantra is prescribed; therefore, the offering of the bali-oblation occurs at the end of the threefold recitation. And the deity is to be known from the indicative mark (liṅga) within the mantra. || 19 ||
Having gratified [him] with circumambulations and so forth, as well as with prostrations, recitations, and hymns of praise. || 20 ||
One circumambulation should be performed for Aja, Īśa, Śakti, Gaṇapa, and Bhāskara; by circumambulating them,
there are successes in all aims numbering four, one, three, seven, and eight respectively.

Because it is stated thus in the *Śaktisaṅgamatantra*: "Aja" is Viṣṇu; "Vedas" is four; "Half" is two (half of that); "Candra" is one; "Vahni" is three; "Adri" is seven. The meaning is that these numbers are to be understood in order during the clockwise circumambulation starting from Aja. This was also stated by the venerable Śrīmacchaṅkarabhagavatpāda.
"I perform circumambulation around you" is stated in the singular number alone;
this verse exists in the *Śrībālāmānasapūjāstotra* and in my own *Bālātantracandrikā*.

In the case of the *namaskāra*, however, it is desire alone that acts as the regulator until the scripture is fully acquired. Regarding this specific feature of the *namaskāra*, it is stated in the *Paramānandatantra* (p.
Outside the hall of worship, one should prostrate before the Goddess on the ground like a staff;
however, within the mandala, one should not perform a full prostration with eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga) nor a staff-like prostration.
"With both knees, both feet, the head, and the pair of hands—this prostration with four limbs is prescribed in the mandala for Śivā. Thus it is said.
Regarding the characteristics of the maṇḍala in the Yoginītantra:
"O Śaṅkarī, that place where the Goddess is worshipped is proclaimed as a maṇḍala measuring one hundred dhanus in each of its four directions. Thus it is said.
The measurement of a bow (dhanus) is four cubits (hasta). However, in the Bṛhad-vāmakeśvara it is said:
"One should know that the mandala extends as far as the deity is visible."
But in the Rahasyārṇava it is said:
"Wherever the worship of the door is performed, they know that to be the inner maṇḍala."
This has been stated as the delimitation by space. As for the delimitation by time, it is said in the *Śaktisaṅgama-tantra*:
"Know that maṇḍala to extend from the commencement of the worship of the doors until the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*). Thus it is said.
Also in the Tripurārṇava:
"O Goddess, beginning with the worship of this maṇḍala, [it continues] until the offering to the orb of the Sun. Thus it is said.
This very maṇḍala is to be understood according to the rules for the maṇḍalas that will be described hereafter.
Having gone then to the house of worship, one should worship the King of the Wheel (cakrarāja).
One should recite the vidyā-mantra a thousand times, or three hundred, or even just one hundred.

Thus, the number of recitations (japa) mentioned in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* is to be understood. This recitation is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, due to being "sandwiched" between the auxiliary elements on both sides. Alternatively:
"The repetition [of the mantra], the daily worship of the Guru, and likewise the observance of the rules (*samaya*) and the traditional teachings (*āmnāya*)," [are required].
The threefold worship and the recitation of mantras are considered the primary elements in ritual worship.

Thus, because the *Svatantratantra*, in its thirteenth chapter, declares the primacy of recitation (*japa*), and because a statement made through direct scriptural authority overrides all other [contradictory evidence].

The hymns mentioned in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra, such as those dedicated to Gaṇeśa, the planets, and the lunar mansions; the recitation of the Thousand Names (Sahasranāma); the hymn of apology for offenses (Aparādhastuti); and, when there is opportunity, the recitation of the Saptashatī—these should be performed. Furthermore, it is prescribed in that very same text: "Then, having joined one's palms in reverence, one should praise [the deity] with these exploits.
Having thus propitiated [the deity] by means of these and other such acts... || 20 ||
(175) The Worship of Śakti: Now he describes the worship of Śakti.
Having worshipped that single Śakti, who possesses that form, with the services appropriate for a young girl, and having gratified her with the fivefold offering (pañcaka), || 21 ||

She is described as "tadrūpiṇīm," meaning she has the form of Tripurasundarī; by the singular word "ekām" (the one), it is meant that she is without a second in terms of beauty. By this, the characteristics of Śakti mentioned in other Tantras are indicated.
She is to be propitiated with the Bālā mantra, with ritual offerings (upacāras) as they may be available, and with the fivefold expansion (pañcakam).
This is to be understood when that desire exists; this is the point made known by the word "having satisfied" (*santarpya*).

Satisfying (*tarpaṇa*) means bringing about contentment; it is an activity that brings to an end the specific desires directed toward various objects based on one's power (*śakti*). For if that desire does not exist, the activity that brings it to an end is likewise impossible.

Thus, it is established that [the worship] occurs "only through desire. Otherwise, one would have said simply, "one should worship with the five offerings (pañcaka) and the secondary offerings (upacāra).

Therefore, this meaning is proven. The characteristics of Śakti are stated in the Kulārṇava—[these verses beginning with "surūpā" are found on page 64 of the printed edition of the seventh chapter (ullāsa) of the Kulārṇava Tantra].
She is young, peaceful, well-disposed, joyful, and pure;
free from doubt, endowed with devotion, and dedicated to the Guru and the scriptures.
"Priyākṣarā (or Priyekṣaṇā-Śrī), who discerns distinctions, is eager for the worship of the deity, captivating, of virtuous conduct, and possessed of auspicious marks—such is Śakti. Thus it is said.
In the Yoginītantra it is also stated:

"Whether she be of the same caste or of a lower caste, whether she be a woman established in her family or an unchaste woman, even a courtesan— if she is engaged in the practice of mantras, she should be worshipped."
Even faults are to be condemned in the ocean of noble lineage; she who is harsh, shameless,
and a defiler of the family is likewise to be censured.
She is of bad conduct, difficult to propitiate, fearful, angry, fickle, and lazy.
One who is addicted to sleep, extremely wicked, deficient in limbs,
afflicted by disease, foul-smelling, miserable, deluded, aged, insane, or a betrayer of secrets.

And at the time of worship, one should avoid such [a woman] joined with a mantra. [In this case, the reading in the printed *Kulārṇava* manuscript is "one should avoid [her] during the union with Śakti. Thus it is said.
And as it is stated in the Yoginītantra:
"Whether she be qualified or disqualified, or even if she is beset by many defects,
one should always worship with devotion a married woman who has arrived at the [proper] time."

176) This [statement] is intended to grant permission for what was previously prohibited by earlier statements in the event that the primary [option] is unavailable, just like speaking untruth in marriage; or rather, it serves to establish the prohibition that was set forth by the earlier statements.

"Devoted to the worship of the Śakti," or "the qualified [woman]"—by this [phrase], he establishes that at that time, worship may be performed even for a mere *suvāsinī* (married woman) other than those [specific types]. And this alone is the appropriate position. || 21 ||
The disposal of the remnants of the oblation:
regarding the disposal of the remnants of the oblation, he says—having offered the remnants of the oblation into the fire of consciousness (cidagni) together with the learned (śiṣṭas). || 22 ||
In this regard, the state of being a refined person (*śiṣṭatva*) is shown in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Alas! That liquor which, when consumed, would delude even the gods—that *maireya* wine, having drunk it, the man who is not transformed [by intoxication] is refined."
"Having become devoted to Śiva in Japan, he was liberated, and so was that Kaulika. Thus it is said.

Such "culturedness" (*śiṣṭatva*) is rooted in the observance of the rules (*sāmāyika*). By this qualification, it is made known that those modern people who merely fancy themselves *kaulikas* but are nothing but talkative with their tongues are not to be admitted into the mandala.
The phrase "together with those who observe the rules" (*sāmayikaiḥ saha*) indicates companionship as the performance of a common action, such as in the expression, "he goes together with his son."

Because this is observed in such cases as the aforementioned [scriptural passages], here too, since there exists the agency of performing a single type of action in the form of a *homa* (oblation), their simultaneity (*sahatva*) is logically established. In the fire characterized by consciousness (*cidagni*), one offers the remnant of the oblation—the residue consecrated and offered with reference to the deity. By the word "having offered" (*hutvā*), it is intended that the cognition of a mere *homa* alone is to be enjoined therein.

It is indicated that desire for the gratification of the senses should never be acted upon; the implication is that upon entering the maṇḍala, one would surely fall into the pursuit of sensual gratification. Furthermore, this purification of the materials used is like the rule "he divides the portion for Agni into four parts," referring to the remnant of the oblation (haviśśeṣam).
Because it is not heard [stated] as being second.
By this [method], contemporary practitioners place a single vessel filled with unrefined substance,

add a few drops of special *arghya* water to it, and offer that substance to the initiates (*sāmayika*). Out of consideration for them, the author of the manual [mentions] the milk-vessel and so forth for the Goddess.

He wrote two sentences stating, "Having placed [it] at the rear," and "One should pour a little milk from the special *arghya* vessel into the jar. Having taken this as the root text, such improper practice that has arisen—which is a cause for downfall—has been refuted because it contradicts the written Sūtra; for in that [case], there is an absence of being a remnant of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*). And if...

If the status of being a remnant of the oblation (*haviśśeṣatva*) were to result merely by the addition of a drop, then there would be a great disorder, since no fault would arise from accepting goods from a marketplace after adding a drop of water to them.
And as it is stated in the Tripurārṇava:
"Whatever is first offered for the purpose of worship shall indeed be sacrificial and pure; by seeing or touching it, one becomes ritually clean."
In that very way, everything obtained within the maṇḍala becomes nectar;
whether brought by a Brahmin or by another, one should offer it to the deity.

"O daughter of the Mountain, that which is joined with the first [mantra] and the others, when consecrated by all of them without distinction, should be accepted by those free from doubt. Thus it is said.
If it is argued that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) becomes conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) by being joined with a conditioned substance,
even so, the conjunction with a conditioned substance is twofold:
one occurs when a conditioned substance is placed into an unconditioned vessel, and [the other] in the case of a specially consecrated *arghya* vessel which is itself conditioned.

There is another [view] which includes the addition of unconditioned substances (*asaṃskṛtadravya*). Among those, the latter position is superior to the former, because it is observed in Vedic rites such as the *soma* sacrifice in the *droṇakalaśa*, in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in the *dhruva* vessel and others. Furthermore, if by means of a conditioned substance (*saṃskṛtadravya*) the mundane, external [substance] were to be conditioned...

In that case, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has already been demonstrated previously— meaning by the passage beginning with "even in the case of goods in a marketplace" and ending with "there would be a great calamity.
Furthermore, even this aforementioned over-extension does not apply to the position that external objects are placed within the vessel.

This is effective. Therefore, the second position alone is superior. Even in that case, this method applies only to a place brought by a devotee for the purpose of worship, and not elsewhere, as it would be unscriptural. Modern people, however, procure substances according to their own whims through their intellect and employ them as "purified by the mind."
"It will be sufficient for its very downfall."
In reality, however, this [view] belongs to the followers of other tantras, but not to the followers of the Sūtra. For in the Sūtra,
