by the statement "having offered the remnant of the oblation" (*haviśśeṣaṃ hutvā*), it is impossible even for Bṛhaspati (the Teacher of the Gods) to establish that the substance residing in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) is a "remnant of the oblation" (*haviśśeṣa*), since it has been consecrated according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

Because only that which remains after being offered to the deity constitutes the remnant of the oblation (*haviśśeṣa*), the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) following the Sūtras is that for those who adhere to the Sūtras, the purificatory act of disposal (*pratipatti-saṃskāra*) by means of the oblation must be performed with the remnant of the sacrifice itself, and not with any other substance.

If it is argued that when the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the worship of the retinue (*āvaraṇapūjana*) have been performed, and the ritual application (*viniyoga*) occurs right there, then this [subsequent] rite would be redundant—this is not so. Just as, according to the two injunctions "he makes the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) the size of a horse's hoof" and "he cuts off a portion the size of a thumb-joint," a remnant of the oblation (*haviśśeṣa*) is necessarily established once those acts have been performed; so too here.
In another tantra: "The general vase should contain water less than five palas;
the causal vase (hetukumbha) should not exceed ten palas, nor be less than half of that."
And half of that is the special arghya-offering.

Thus, in following the *Māna* [tradition], for those who follow the *Sūtra*, when the *hetukumbha* (causal pitcher) is accepted as a constituent part of the measure of the *viśeṣārghya* (special offering water)—
which occupies the position of the causal pitcher— the substance for the *viśeṣārghya* becomes measured at sixteen hundred *guñjās*.
And if, on the other hand, the measure of the *viśeṣārghya* itself is accepted because it shares the same name, then likewise:

There is no dispute that [the quantity] is measured at eight hundred *guñjās*. In the *āvaraṇapūjā* (circumambulatory worship) and other rites, the application of one drop for each individual deity is observed. This being the case, there certainly remains sufficient substance for the sacrificial oblation (*homa*) for both the initiates (*sāmayika*) and oneself. In this scripture, the specific state produced by the acceptance of the substance is called *ullāsa*.
Since that too must exist when the substance is of the highest excellence, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
p.

178) Since the procedure for the fire-oblation (*hometikartavyatā*) and the rules for the entry of the learned ones (*śiṣṭa*) into the mandala have not been stated here, how can one [act] together with the learned ones?

When there arises the expectation, "One should perform the *homa*," another tantra must be sought for that matter. This being the case, the properties of the mandala are first stated. They are described in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
"One whose limbs are wounded, one whose limbs are feverish, and one with soiled garments and hair..."
Likewise, one who is in a state of ritual impurity, one wearing a turban, one wearing a bodice, or one who has already eaten [should not study].
One whose limbs are putrid, as well as one with an impure mouth, one under the birth-impurity of death,
one suffering from epilepsy, one beset by afflictions, and one afflicted by vomiting and dysentery;
One who has not performed expiation and has not bathed should never enter the maṇḍala;
even if he enters it once through delusion, he shall incur the curse of the deities.
"If, however, they possess intense devotion toward [the deity's] vision and so forth, one should perform the worship outside the vicinity of the door of the shrine. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific rule for one who has consumed [the substance] in the ocean of Tripura:

"When that which was consumed unexpectedly during the day arrives at night, then, having bathed by the command of the Guru and others, one should consume it; otherwise, one should not. Thus it is said.
This service as well takes place entirely outside the maṇḍala.
"Having eaten, one should not enter the maṇḍala under any circumstances, O Supreme Goddess"—
since there is no scriptural authority contradicting this, it constitutes a prohibition against entering the maṇḍala.
And as it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Kuleśvarī, he who partakes of the *kuladravya* without having bathed, or after eating, or without devotion— or even after anointing himself—
shall incur poverty."
Thus, let the scripture prohibiting the consumption of the *kuladravya* (family substance) by one who has already eaten be set aside at will;

however, since there is no such prohibition against entering, one must not enter. Nor can it be argued that entry is implied by the rule for "making one's own" (*svātmīkāra*), because outside the mandala there is no rule for "making one's own."

This must be stated: since, in that case, the prohibition of entry—expressed as "having consumed [it], one should not go to the mandala"—already establishes the prohibition of making it one's own, [the text continues]:
"Having consumed the kula-substance thus, even through delusion or negligence..."
O Goddess, whoever should serve [them] would indeed incur the curse of the deities.

By this [statement], the prohibition against the consumption of family substances (kuladravya) that has been inferred would be rendered meaningless; therefore, by this very indicative mark (jñāpaka), the consumption of the substance even externally is established.
179) Having thus described those unfit for entry, [the author] also states the qualities of the one who enters in the *Paramānandatantra*:
"One who has bathed, is pure, wears clean clothes, bears the *puṇḍra* marks, and possesses auspicious intentions..."
Having washed his feet and hands, and having bowed with devotion while meditating upon the Goddess.
Then, in accordance with the preceptor’s command, one should enter within the mandala;
meditating upon the form of the deity, the wise person should prostrate to the mandala.

Thereafter, one should perform the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali); its ritual procedure is now described: having devoutly washed both hands with the water from the general vessel (sāmānyakumbha).
Having perfumed [the area] with incense and other fragrances, and having taken up flowers with devotion,
one should then stand up, O Goddess, and remain facing the deity.
I bow to the triad of gurus beginning with Śrīnātha, Gaṇapati, the three seats (pīṭhas), Bhairava, the lineage of Siddhas (siddhaugha),
the triad of Baṭukas, the pair of feet, the sequence of Dūtīs, the Maṇḍala, the thirty-two Vīras, the nine [Vīras], the fivefold Vīrāvalī, and the rest.
I pay homage to the circle of gurus, accompanied by the glorious Mālinī, the king of mantras.
O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, the practitioner who has attained the fifteenth day and other such times should also recite the collective Vidyā of the Yoginīs there.
O Śaṅkarī, having meditated upon the deity with the form described for meditation and having worshipped her,
O Parameśvarī, one should then meditate upon the preceptor and the others and worship them.
Having realized that everything has Śiva as its essence, he should prostrate according to the prescribed rule;
he should then receive the second vessel from the most excellent of teachers.
O Śaṅkarī, the vessel should be held in the right hand by one who is initiated;
however, O Śaṅkarī, it may be taken up by another with the left hand.
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, it should be grasped with all the fingers of the left hand;
having covered it with the other hand, one should take it or even cause it to be given.
A vessel that is not covered becomes a portion for the Asuras;
however, when it is used for purposes such as libations (tarpaṇa), one should omit the covering.
O Goddess, listen with a restrained mind to the sequence of seating,
whether it be in the form of a circle or in the shape of a square.
Having placed the teacher in the center, one should enter according to seniority;
however, while seniors are present, one must not enter into the immediate vicinity of the teacher.
(180) One should not stand on an equal footing with the Guru, nor likewise in the midst of women;
O Goddess, one should not stand before the Guru, nor indeed should one transgress the command of the Guru.
Having thus understood the tradition, one should sit within the auspicious maṇḍala;
the preceptor likewise, having risen and prostrated before the elders, [should do so].
Having received their command, the practitioner should then sit upon his own seat;
rising up, he should indeed offer a vessel to that eldest one.
O Goddess, even the youngest, rising and bowing, should receive the elders;
O Maheśvarī, having honored them all, the vessels should be given.
O Ambikā, if one should bestow the vessel even upon a disciple without first honoring him,
that Goddess becomes angry with him, for everything is indeed identical with her.
Having washed the vessel and carefully covered it with flowers and other offerings,
one should likewise present it to the preceptor and pay homage with devotion.
Having accepted that grace, one should indeed recite the mantra and read the hymns and so forth. Thus it is said.
In the Tripurārṇava it is said:
"O Ambikā, one should offer a vessel joined with gold and other materials;
or by giving whatever is placed within the vessel, one obtains infinite fruit."
Regarding the specific procedure for *suvāsinīs* in the *Yoginītantra*:

"Having thus satisfied [the deities] and performed the fire-oblation (*homa*), the *suvāsinīs* should give the third or fourth vessel containing the remnants to the presiding authority of the sacred seat (*pīṭha-adhikārin*). Thus it is said.
In the Tripurārṇava, there is a specific distinction:
"O Daughter of the Mountain, the remainder and the chewing [of the offering] should be received from a hero, an elder, or likewise from a teacher;
in their absence, it should be received from another elder."
In the *Bṛhadvāmakeśvaratantra*:
"In the absence of the Guru and others, one should offer the remainder of the chewing [of the sacramental substance] to the eldest [disciple].
In his absence, having meditated upon the Guru on the crown of one's head, one should take that remnant and place it [there]. (Śrī.)
O Daughter of the Mountain, at the beginning or at the very end,
one should drink from the vessel without making a sound, doing so once and leaving nothing remaining.
"But that vessel which has a residue remaining is equal to the drinking of liquor. Thus it is said.
181) Regarding the prohibition even when not touching the rim of the vessel, it is stated in that same [text]:
"But drinking from a distance, without touching the rim, is like the drinking of cattle."
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"O Dear One, having taken the vessel in one's hand, one should not remain for long;
O Mother, one should not stand anywhere with the vessel in hand while speaking."
One should not touch the bowl with one's foot, nor let even a drop fall to the ground;
one should not strike one bowl against another, nor let a bowl fall down.
One should not lift the vessel without its base, nor should one set it down without support.
One should not leave the vessel empty, nor should one swing the vessel about, O beloved.
"A wise person should not step over a vessel, nor should he strike a vessel, O beloved;
having washed it, he should protect the vessel—this is the command of the Supreme Lord. Thus [it is said].
In the *Paramānandatantra*, there is a specific instruction:
from the placement of the *arghya* water until the dismissal of the vessels, one should perceive everything as consisting of Śiva; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
There, all castes are twice-born; one should never conceive of any distinction therein.
After the dismissal [of the deity], a wise man should never establish identity [between them].
O Goddess, the process of making [the deity] one's own is threefold, according to the sequence of the divine (divya), the hero (vīra), and the animal (paśu).
That which extends up to the dismissal (udvāsa) is the divine; after that, it is called the heroic.
"The unconditioned [animal] is declared to be the very first for Brahmins;
for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas there is no animal [offering], while for Śūdras there may be all three. Thus it is said.
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"The divine [Vīra] bestows both enjoyment and liberation; the heroic (vīra) bestows enjoyment.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Rahasyārṇava*:
"Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite up until the dismissal (*udvāsana*), the Brāhmaṇa,
the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya should drink that substance at the end."
But a Śūdra may do so according to his own desire, whether by means of a formal rite or otherwise.
"Having offered that to the deity and having satisfied [the deities], one should afterwards drink it. Thus [it is said].
182) Thus many essential dharmas have been described. Those beyond this are to be understood by consulting numerous tantras; they are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

In this regard, the rules for the mandala prescribed for the Sāmayikas who follow the Kalpasūtra and for others are the same. As for the fire-oblation mantra, for those following the Sūtras, it is the mantra "ārdraṃ jvalati" itself; for when there is a requirement for a mantra, this one is more proximate than the mantras from other tantras. For others...
This is the path taught in our own independent tradition. Here, the following rule is considered:

for the sake of attaining the fruit of worship performed by oneself, since the ritual consecration (*pratipatti-saṃskāra*) must necessarily be performed by the presiding officiant of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), he—whether capable or incapable of meditating upon the mandala—may at will accept the ritual substances.
However, regarding the occasional (sāmayika) rite, only one who is capable of the meditation prescribed in the scriptures may offer the substance after the material oblation (dravyahoma);
no other may do so. For it is said:
"In the fire of consciousness, which blazes incessantly within without fuel, acting as the adversary to the darkness of delusion..."
In that certain [reality] where the wondrous rays of light are blossoming, I offer the universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.
With the mind as the ladle, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses as oblations into the fire of the Self, which is kindled by the fuel of merit and demerit, along the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
Thus, the method of meditation prescribed by the indicative power of the mantra is essential. It is also stated in the Devīyāmala:
"Having conquered the mind through fire-offering (homa), one should meditate upon the Self by means of the self."
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"That man who, having drunk that auspicious maireya, is not transformed, and becoming devoted to Śiva while reciting [mantras], is liberated; he is a Kaulika. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
"Having accepted that grace, one should indeed meditate unwaveringly upon Ambikā."
In the Gaṇeśvarasaṃhitā within the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
"Having tasted the substance according to the prescribed rule, one should bring the mind to a state of immobility;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the supreme light, the eternal light of the Self."
There are many such scriptural injunctions prescribing meditation preceded by the restraint of the mind, up to the following:
"O Goddess, one should offer oblations only so long as the state of deep sleep has not occurred and there is indeed a lack of modification; otherwise, it shall be fruitless."
But when a transformation has arisen, O Goddess, he is excluded from the yoga of meditation;
he is a beast for the Yoginīs and is cast out from the maṇḍala.

Thus, even in the *tantra* regarding the fire-offering (*homa*) with an additional vessel, there is the undesirable consequence of the failure of meditative visualization (*dhyāna*). By this as well, the necessity of meditation is established. There are many such [instances]. For fear of excessive length, I have not written more here;
this much suffices.
And thus, the first fruit of the practice of the substance (*dravya*) is one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), because without that,
meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is impossible. For this very reason, it is said in the *Paramānandatantra*:
O Goddess, one should offer oblations for exactly as long as one is immersed in bliss,
until the mind attains steadiness and the consciousness also reaches a state of clarity.
"But when a transformation has arisen due to being devoid of the yoga of meditation, O Goddess, he is a beast for the Yoginīs and is excluded from the maṇḍala.
Thus, it shows the undesirable fruit resulting from an unqualified person's acceptance of the substances. Also, in the Yoginītantra:
"Relying upon the substance of the lineage (kuladravya), one should bring the mind to a state of immovability. Thus it is said.
In the Tripurārṇava it is also said:
"O Maheśvarī, this Kaula path is the supreme dharma among all;
it is like the vow of walking on the edge of a sword, for it is the cause of the mind's immovability."
In that regard, the state of having a restrained mind is indeed exceedingly difficult to achieve in every respect for one who is devoid of devotion and faith.

Thus, there are found by the millions such scriptural statements from the Tantras stating that the consumption of substances must be performed for the sake of meditation through the means of restraining the mind, as it causes obstruction when otherwise employed.
While summarizing the meaning of such scriptural statements from the Tantras, Śrī Paraśurāma [states]:

He said, "Together with the learned. One who is capable of such meditation, even on days of vows and the like, should—without hesitation and even if disregarded—enter the maṇḍala, request the vessel, perform the oblation, and accomplish the meditation.
As it is stated in the Tripurārṇava:
Thus, one who is bound by convention, acting with devotion and free from pride and hypocrisy,
should go to the supreme maṇḍala— whether uninvited or invited.
Or even one observing a vow may indeed offer oblations; no fault exists therein.
But he who, out of apprehension regarding his vows and the like, does not go even though he is capable, [commits an offense].
"His vow would be frustrated and he would meet with misfortune;
therefore, even if summoned by the youngest [brother], one must indeed enter the maṇḍala. Thus it is said.
In this context, the seniority and juniority of the brahmins are to be understood according to the sequence of their initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Even if he is a child, one who was initiated first is the elder in the Kula tradition."

"Even if a twice-born is initiated later, while one of the lowest caste was initiated earlier, that twice-born is the junior and the other is the senior; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures."
184) Because of the statement in that very [text], even one initiated later among Kṣatriyas and others is indeed a twice-born (dvija) and is senior.
In certain cases, regarding the acceptance of food remnants (ucchiṣṭa), it establishes seniority even based on the connection of birth (yonisambandha). As it has been said:
In the Tripurārṇava it is said:
"Whether through a connection of Vidyā or likewise through a connection of birth,
one should consume the remnants (ucchiṣṭa) even of those who are senior, provided they are initiated."
"Even if he is his own father, one who has been initiated should not consume the remnants of one who lacks initiation, even once; by eating it, he incurs a fall from his status. Thus [it is said].

Now, as an incidental discussion, it is examined by whom and how much substance (dravya) should be consumed. In that regard, for one engaged in the worship of the Child (bāla), there are three vessels; for one who has received the instruction in the *Pañcadaśī* mantra, there are four vessels; and for one who has received initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the *Ṣoḍaśī* and other mantras, there are five vessels. This is stated in the *Paramānanda-tantra*:
O Śivā, for a practitioner of the Saubhāgya-tantra, there are four principles;
however, for practitioners of Bālā and the others, their worship is according to the prescribed injunctions.
"But for them, there are three principles; everything else is the same. Thus [it is said].
"For those who have received initiation, O Śiva, the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) shall be the fifth;
having offered the three, four, or five vessels in sequence into the fire of Śiva. Thus it is said.
Indeed, by drinking again and again, and drinking until one falls to the ground,
and rising to drink once more, there is no further rebirth.
The Goddess is satisfied by bliss, Bhairava himself by fainting, and all the gods by vomiting; therefore, one should practice this triad.
If it is asked, "Since unrestricted drinking is taught in the *Kulārṇava* and other tantras beginning with those words, how can there be a restriction regarding the vessel?

listen to the intention of the scripture, provided one is ignorant and desirous of knowing the reality: "Having drunk again and again," and the statement written [therein], "One should drink the substance until the throat; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt"—such is the statement of the *Kulārṇava*.
This is not according to one's own whim, nor is it suitable for everyone, but rather for those who have fully ascended (*pūrṇārūḍha*).

For this very reason, in the *Kulārṇava*, immediately preceding the statement "up to the throat," the author first asserts: "O Goddess, drinking is prescribed for those endowed with the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*"), and then records such statements as: "One should drink the substance up to the throat."
The characteristics of the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* (the full initiation) are also described in that very *Kulārṇava*:
"He who is equal in all circumstances when there arises censure or praise, cold or heat, pleasure or pain, and so forth— the lord of yogis, free from joy and resentment," and so on.
One who knows the reality of the three principles, the meaning of the root mantra, and the feet of the Śrī [Guru],
who is devoted to the deity and the guru, and is endowed with the Śāmbhavī mudrā.
"And he should be one who has received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) as a Kaulika, but not merely by initiation. Thus [it is said].
p.
185) He who is thus fully consecrated (*pūrṇābhiṣikta*) is indeed one who has ascended to the fullness (*pūrṇārūḍha*); for him alone is the rule "up to the throat" (*āgalāntam*).
Therefore, in the *Amṛtārahasya*:
If a knower of Brahman, having drunk wine while repeatedly practicing the *kulācāra*,
should fall to the ground, he rejoices in the world of Brahmā for as long a time as there are particles of dust clinging to his body.

In this statement, by the collective term "knower of Brahman" (*brahmajñānī*), he expresses the specific meaning as declared in the *Kulārṇava*. Nowadays, those who do not understand the meaning of the Tantras and are blinded by passion, without considering their own qualification, show such Tantric injunctions as "having drunk, having drunk" to the people, while themselves acting according to their own whims.

They even eclipsed the intelligence of others; they would experience the torments of hell for as long as the moon and sun exist. [In this context, "upalabheran" would be the form according to grammatical rules.
Regarding this, the authority is found in the *Paramānandatantra*:
As long as the gaze does not waver and as long as the mind does not waver, for that long one should consume food; beyond this, it is like drinking the blood of a beast.
"As long as there is no impairment of the senses and no distortion of the face, for that long one should drink the substance; otherwise, a downfall occurs. Thus it is said.

Just as a practitioner should accept a substance according to his own capacity, so too the teacher should bestow the vessel only after observing the disciple's fitness. As it is said in the Kumārītantra: "In the Kaulika tradition, one bestows the supreme vessel without hesitation."
Thus, he sinks into that very office along with it.
In that very same [text] it is said:
"O Śivā, as long as the substance remains with a single effort of drinking, the vessel should be used at the commencement of that; it should be neither less nor more."

Regarding the measure of the drinking vessel, it is stated in the *Nīlātantra*: "A vessel is that which contains the substance used for drinking, prepared by a single effort"—this is its meaning. Furthermore, in another tantra:
"O Ambikā, having failed to understand the distinction between the various states of ecstatic joy (*ullāsa*), one falls into delusion."
"Indeed, those who drink it out of greed for the tongue or for the gratification of the senses are cast by the Mothers into the Tāmisra hell. Thus [it is said].

And thus, for those of the present day— even for those who have fully conquered their senses [or, for those who have not conquered their senses]— it is appropriate to pursue [the practice] up to the point of the arousal of the creative impulse (*ārambha*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the Tantra:
The undertaking [of this work] is proclaimed to be for the sake of those who are incapable, ignorant, and childish.

The definition of the *ārambha* (commencement) and *ullāsa* (exaltation) is given in that very same [text]: "To whatever extent a vessel is described for someone, the *ārambha* for that person is of that same extent."

Enough with this digression following upon another; the remainder shall be discussed later in the *Ullāsavilāsa*, in its final section (*caramakhaṇḍa*). (By the term "final section," it should be understood that this refers to the commentary on Sūtra 68 of the tenth section;
furthermore, the repetition of the word "sūtra" indicates that the text requires correction.)
"And the remaining portion shall indeed be complete through the grace of the Primordial Goddess. Thus ends the fifth section—Śrī.
We shall now speak [further]. 22.
The dismissal of the Goddess:
having bound the *khecarī* [mudrā] and said "Forgive me," one should dismiss her and merge her into oneself. Thus all is auspicious. || 23 ||
Thus ends the fifth section, titled "The Worship of the Ninefold Enclosures of Lalitā," in the Kalpasūtra.
Having bound the Khecarī-mudrā, immediately after that binding—
O Śivā, O Supreme Goddess, whether performed knowingly or unknowingly, whatever has been done, consider it your own duty and grant me forgiveness.

Having thus asked for forgiveness, one should perform the dismissal (*visarga*). Dismissal means leading back to her own place that [goddess] who was invoked for the sake of worship. One should join her to, or establish her within, oneself in the heart-lotus. The word "Śiva" indicates the conclusion of the section.
Thus ends the fifth section, titled "The Worship of the Ninefold Enclosures of Śrī Lalitā," in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.
The Sixth Section: The Śyāmā-krama.
O Śyāmā, Mother of Music, who bears the primary burden of office in the abode of Supreme Śiva;
O you who are skillful in the marriage [of the soul], whose own heart is filled with compassion for my state of wretchedness!
O Śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśī, you who have girded yourself in solitude to protect with showers of nectar those fallen into the forest-fire of worldly existence—salutations to you! Pray, speak.
The procedure for the worship of Śyāmā:
the venerable Lord Paraśurāma, desiring to expound the Śyāmākrama,
[first describes] that which belongs to one who has undertaken the worship of Śrīvidyā, in order to generate in the practitioners of that [Śyāmā] the knowledge of her status as the object of worship.

By the scriptural statement, "He who sacrifices to another deity indeed sacrifices beyond his own deity; he falls away from his own deity, does not reach the higher one, and becomes worse off," it is established that the worship of a deity other than the one deity accepted for worship produces undesirable results. By this [statement],...
And for the sake of removing the turbidity from those whose minds are turbid, he first describes the nature of her qualities:

"This very [Goddess] Siṃhāsaneśvarī is the Great Knowledge, the Sovereign Empress; Śyāmā occupies the position of her chief minister, and the constant contemplation of her sequence must be performed. (1)

The nature and indifference of Parāśakti are what will be described hereafter. The word "this" (iyam) refers to what follows; the word "yet" (yā) is understood as the remainder. She who is "Great" (mahatī), possessing limitless greatness, [occupies] the throne (siṃhāsana), which is Paraśiva because he is her own substratum (svādhiṣṭhāna).
The Sovereign (Īśvarī) is the agent who carries out the creative, preservative, and concealing volitions directed toward that [Śiva].

As it was stated by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda—[this verse is the first of the *Saundaryalaharī*; this is its first half]: *śivaḥ*... [the remainder of this verse follows in the original source].
"If he were endowed with power, he would be capable of exercising authority; otherwise, the god is truly not even able to move. Thus it is said.

Also, in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*, within the hymn to Vidyāvatī: "Salutations to that Goddess, whose eyes are like beautiful fish, who is the embodiment of auspiciousness— to whom even Śiva is indeed rendered purposeless when separated."
This [consciousness] is distinct from illusion; it is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and not of an insentient nature (*jaḍa-svabhāva*). Thus it is said in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"It has the form of existence (*sad-ākārā*), is supreme bliss (*parānanda*), and brings about the destruction of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)."
"She is Śivā, the supreme goddess, non-different from Śiva and the bestower of auspiciousness;
for even Śiva is indeed purposeless when devoid of her who is non-different from him. Thus it is said.

(188) But surely, the primary agency regarding creation and so forth resides in Śiva; if the power [of Śakti] consists merely in being the facilitator of that, then primary agency over the world, its governance, and so on, must reside in Śiva. And this [power] is merely an auxiliary. Likewise...

If it is argued that Śiva alone is to be worshipped because of his primacy and not Śakti, listen: for it is precisely through logical necessity (*anupapatti*)—that the entire collection of effects such as earth and so forth would be untenable without a cause—that either Śiva or Śakti is postulated. Indeed, we do not perceive either Śakti or Śiva with the physical eye. When one begins to postulate in this manner, here...
The Vedāntins maintain that the attribute of the supreme Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness, is *māyā*; this very *māyā* is ignorance (*avidyā*) and is insentient by nature.

She alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, whereas the supreme Brahman is the illusory cause (*vivartopādāna*). Consequently, because it has an insentient material cause, the world is also insentient by nature; and because its material cause is *māyā*, it is also false (*mithyātva*).

The Tantrikas do not accept that position. For instance, as for that which is called *māyā* or *avidyā*, is it a property (*dharma*) of consciousness (*cit*) or a property of something else? In the first case, since even the Vedāntins admit the non-difference between a property and its possessor (*dharmadharmiṇoḥ*), it would be impossible for a property of consciousness to be insentient (*jaḍatva*). If, on the other hand, it were a property of what is not consciousness...

Furthermore, there would be a loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*), and there would be a contradiction with the scriptural authority that states: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā (*māyin*). Therefore, since there is no other recourse, one must necessarily admit that this Māyā is an attribute of Consciousness (*ciddharma*). This being the case, its insentience (*jaḍatva*) is discarded from afar. Nor is there any power (*śakti*) apart from Consciousness.
This is what must be said; we too express that very same point.

However, even though there is an absence of fragrance apart from the earth, a slight distinction is indeed postulated in accordance with the conventional usage of "attribute" (*dharma*) and "substantive" (*dharmin*); likewise, although both are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), a slight distinction is [postulated] for the sake of conventional usage.
It must be so conceived. And thus, the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world is not possible for either [of these two], because the world is by nature insentient (*jaḍa*).
Indeed, darkness cannot arise from light. Therefore, the world always exists within consciousness in a subtle form, just as a banyan tree exists within its seed.
The agency of consciousness consists precisely in its performing expansion preceded by the loosening of its own parts, and not in being their material cause (*upādānatva*);

just as a merchant spreads out goods for sale in the morning and withdraws them at night, such is the agency of consciousness. The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is its auxiliary cause (*sahakāriṇī*).

Now, one might object: "Why is a power (*śakti*) admitted that is distinct from consciousness (*cit*), possesses a slight degree of difference from it, and serves to effect its agency? Let that agency reside in consciousness itself. Otherwise, by the same logic, a single power would have to be established as the substratum of the potter's agency in making a jar. To this we reply: No, because of [the authority of] scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and worldly usage (*lokavyavahāra*).
Because of its existence. The scripture states: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold. Also, in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Śakti creates the universe; she indeed protects it entirely;
by her will, she destroys this world of the moving and the unmoving."
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka, nor Sūrya,
nor Varuṇa are capable of accomplishing their respective tasks in any way whatsoever.
For joined with her, those gods perform their respective duties;
she alone is the cause in all actions, as is perceived through direct observation.
O Supreme Goddess,
the web of objects, when devoid of power, is unable to accomplish anything; however,
it becomes capable when it is joined with power.

Thus, in great detail: from the cowherd women up to the learned scholars (*paṇḍita*), they conduct their affairs without dispute, saying, "I have the power to perform this task," or "I do not have the power. Therefore, capacity is established by many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it is that which must be brought to fulfillment.
The entire world also always exists within the belly of Śiva in a subtle form.

Alternatively, the world is of the nature of a transformation of that power which belongs to consciousness. As it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "O friend, this phenomenal universe is but the play of consciousness; how then, O dear one, can it cause you suffering?"
By this admission of a slight difference between consciousness (*cit*) and power (*śakti*), the scriptural texts teaching that consciousness is changeless (*nirvikāra*) are not contradicted;

and by not admitting an absolute difference, the scriptural texts establishing non-duality (*advaita*) are likewise unimpaired. Such a power is perceived in any given entity only after the production of its effect, and not prior to it.
Regarding this very point, the venerable Śrī Vidyāraṇyasvāmin also said in the *Bhūta-pañcaka-viveka*:
"His power, Māyā, which is devoid of constituent principles (nistattvā) and is to be inferred from its effects, is like the power of fire;
for no one perceives a power anywhere prior to its effect."

Thus, when that which is established as being non-different from Śiva, consisting of His attributes, and effectuating the agency inherent in Him—that is, the state of devotion to Śiva (śivaniṣṭhā)—is accomplished, that alone is to be worshipped. Śiva in His pure conscious form is not to be worshipped, because He is not an object of worship [the meaning is: because He is Brahman unconditioned by Power].

Worship (*upāsanā*) consists in the chanting of the names and qualities inherent in the object of worship. Since there is an absence of qualities in that which is devoid of power and is absolute, how could there be meditation, praise, chanting, and so forth for the qualityless (*nirguṇa*)? This has been stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"In the subtle Śiva, without Śakti, neither name nor abode exists. Thus [it is said].
And there is the Śruti: "From whence words return, together with the mind, failing to reach it.

Furthermore, because He is to be known only as the remainder after the negation of everything as "not this, not this," knowledge whose sole object is Śiva is opposed to such acts as ritual worship (*upāsanā*).
Since such a final state is to be accomplished through spiritual practice (*upāsanā*), Śiva alone is not to be worshipped. As it is said in the *Devībhāgavata*:
"Even Śiva becomes a corpse when devoid of Kuṇḍalinī."
Also in the Yoginītantra:
"O Great Goddess, even when that knowledge is attained, there is neither happiness nor protection whatsoever."

Furthermore, even if the mind were somehow impelled into a circular form for the purpose of grasping the formless, it would not be able to remain there for even a moment, because it is devoid of both auspicious and inauspicious dharmas.
As it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater" (p. 190).

Therefore, for the sake of stabilizing that very mind, some form must be conceptualized. And that form which is conceptualized within the Supreme Brahman, accompanied by name and abode, is precisely what is denoted by the term "Śakti.
This too has been stated in the Bhāgavata:
Thus, that all-pervading power is discerned as Brahman;
it is described by the wise as being twofold: with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā).
That which possesses attributes is to be cultivated by those possessed of passion, while that which is without attributes is to be cultivated by those free from passion.
She is the untroubled mistress of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
"When worshipped according to the prescribed rite, she grants all desired objects. Thus it is said.
Thus, by the array of proofs and reasonings stated above, the Supreme Śakti is to be worshipped, as is Paraśiva who is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).

Since the mental state directed toward Him consists of the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha), it is established that the status of being the Empress Simhāsaneśvarī is to be accomplished through the worship of Ambā.

Śiva is indeed devoid of attributes (nirguṇa); yet, when He is endowed with the power of will (icchā-śakti) and, desiring "May I become many, may I procreate," is oriented toward creation, He alone is designated by the term Śakti. Thus, the essential truth to be understood is that Śiva Himself is to be worshipped in the form of Śakti.

She who is such as this [is Śyāmā]; here, the term *saciva-pada* refers to the quality (*dharma*) consisting of ministerial office (*sācivya*), and her *pada* is its locus or support. Whatever sequence belongs to her, its *vimṛṣṭi*—that is, its following or practice—that must always be performed. Here, by the word "always" (*sadā*), it is meant for as long as one lives.

Just as there is a restriction of the lifelong injunction for the *agnihotra* by another statement, "He offers in the evening; he offers in the morning," so too, in the very context of this Śyāmā, by the statement occurring immediately before, "Performing this daily worship and having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times," [this is found here in the sixth section— ]

37. Regarding the *Mūlasūtra*: there is a restriction that worship (*pūjā*) should be performed only once up until the completion of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*), but not thereafter. || 1 ||

Regarding the justification for the worship of Śyāmā: one might raise the objection, "Since there is a Sovereign Queen who is the controller of all and independent, why abandon her to worship Śyāmā, who merely follows her? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] intends to establish the validity of worshipping her.
First, he confirms this by means of a worldly analogy: "For it is proper to seek to please a king through the mediation of a chief minister. (2)

In the world, those eager for an audience with a king first attend upon his chief minister and obtain the audience with the king through him; it is observed in the world that by this means the result is achieved quickly and without effort. Likewise, here too, one should first perform the worship of Śyāmā, who is the primary figure therein.
The sense is that this is logical. By the word "at the door" (*dvāra*), it is indicated that [this practice] must precede the primary meditation;

by the phrase "it is logical" (*nyāyyam*), even its absolute non-necessity is indicated. However, anyone who is capable may, disregarding ministers and others, personally secure the King's favor and thereby obtain the fruit.

The position that "he accomplishes [the goal]" also exists in some cases in the world; nevertheless, the meaning is that it is more appropriate and preferable to propitiate the king through the mediation of a chief minister. The underlying point is this: whoever is unable to directly obtain the grace of the principal deity...

Having first completed his initiation (*dīkṣā*) and performed the worship of Śrī Gaṇapati, he then performed the worship of Śyāmā, the worship of Vārāhī, and the worship of Parā, and [attained] their grace.

Having completed [the preliminary rites], one should thereafter begin the worship of Śrī Lalitā. However, one who is capable should begin the sequence of Śrī Lalitā after initiation and following the worship of Gaṇapati. The essential point is that there is an option here, just as in the rule: "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice, or one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice."

One who desires superior results should perform the worship of Lalitā according to the stated sequence; one who desires inferior results should perform the worship of Lalitā after the worship of Gaṇapati—this is the settled rule. || 2 ||
Having thus demonstrated the morning duties ending with the twilight ritual (sandhyā) for one qualified for the practice of worship, he begins the section on that worship:
"Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, and while still remaining upon the bed, one should prostrate to the Śrī-pādukā."

Having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*) and visualized the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvid*) blazing from the base (*mūla*) up to the limit of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), one should mentally recite the root mantra three times; then, having gone outside,
[one should perform] the release of impurities, urine, teeth-cleaning, tongue-scraping, the expulsion of phlegm, and the purification of the nostrils.
Having performed twenty mouthfuls of rinsing. || 3 ||

The *śrīpādukā* is the *guru-pādukā* [the intended meaning of *guru-pādukā* here is the *pādukā* of the three gurus]. Regarding "the vital breaths," the definition of *prāṇāyāma* is stated in the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*:
"One should perform three *prāṇāyāmas* with the root mantra or with the *praṇava*."
Alternatively, the wise one [should do so] with the seed-mantra of the mantra according to the prescribed procedure.
One should fill the breath with sixteen [counts] and perform the retention (kumbhaka) with four times that; one should exhale with half of the retention, or if unable, with a quarter of it.
"If one is unable to do that, then it should be done with the fourth [vowels]; thus is the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama).
Without prāṇāyāma, there is no fitness for worship and other such rites. Thus [it is said].
In the *Samayāṅgamātṛkā*: "One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* once with the root-mantra;
one should then retain it (*kumbhaya*) in the central channel four times, O fair-faced one."
One should exhale through the path of Piṅgalā according to the sequence of the number of eyes (two), again and again in that same order, so that it occurs three times. Thus [it is said].

The recitation of the teeth-cleansing twig (*dantadhāvana*) and other items, which are already established by traditional law (*smṛti*), is for the purpose of obtaining the sequence as stated here. Therefore, they should be performed according to the order of recitation. Although the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) will also be explained later in the Sūtra (in the ninth section, on page 194), nevertheless...

The detailed demonstration of those capable of performing breath-retention (*vāyudhāraṇa*) is for the sake of showing them; it should be understood that for those incapable, the procedure remains as stated in the Sūtra. The phrase ending with "twenty mouthfuls" (*viṃśatigaṇḍūṣān*) is clear in its meaning. || 3 ||
Having performed the desired [rites] of bathing with mantras, ashes, and water, and having put on a garment. (4)
The mantra-bath is described in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"Having first wiped the limbs with a damp cloth while reciting the root mantra seven times from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head..."
"O Goddess, one should touch [the body] with both palms; this is proclaimed as the mantra-bath.
This bath is prescribed for one who is incapable [of the full ritual] for the sake of purification. Thus it is said.
The ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) is described in the Śivarahasya: "Having taken pure ash in one's hand, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
by smearing it over all the limbs, it is declared to be the ash-bath."

The ritual bath with water (*jalasnāna*) is described in the *Śrīlalitāprakaraṇa* [this is stated in the *Mūlasūtra* and its commentary in the third section of the *Śrīkrama*, on page 88, line 4]. Here, the primary form of the water-bath is intended; however, when the time for ritual action has arrived and water or other materials are unavailable, or if one is unable to perform it due to being occupied with urgent matters for the sake of the Guru, one may perform the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*) and so forth instead.
This is the task. As it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra*, beginning with "Now listen to the auspicious mantra," [it continues]:
"In the absence of water at the proper time, for one who is perishing on a difficult path..."
For the sake of swift success in one's journey and remaining untiring in weighty duties, one should perform the mantra-bath... [thus it is said].
For this reason as well, there is a brief bath described in the *Vīratantra*: "One should cleanse both hands below the wrists, the feet, the ankles, and likewise the face;
this shall be the five-limbed bath that bestows purity."
These ablutions are to be understood as being established according to the gradation of one's capacity and the gradation of impurity.

Other ablutions, such as the mental bath of meditation (the meaning of which is the bath of knowledge and so forth), have not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity; they should be sought from other tantras. || 4 ||
He prescribes the twilight ritual (sandhyā):

having performed the twilight worship, having meditated upon the Goddess together with her retinue within the solar disc, having offered three handfuls of arghya water with the root mantra, and having satiated her according to one's capacity. || 5 ||

This is the originative injunction for the *sandhyā*; here, in response to the expectation of "how" (the manner of performance), he says, beginning with "in the solar disc" and ending with "having offered libations. The libation also is performed with the mantra: "Having uttered the root [mantra], I offer libations to Śrī Śyāmā, svāhā," according to the *Mālinītantra*.

This is because of the statement at the end of the *Mūla* regarding the extraction of the *tarpaṇa* mantra: "Having uttered the *mālinī*, one says 'I satiate the beloved of Agni' (*tarpayāmy agnivallabhām*). (In the present context, p.

Since no mantra has been explicitly stated, when there is a requirement for a mantra, one should employ a mantra found in another tantra. By the phrase "according to one's capacity," it is indicated that the number [of repetitions] is not an essential factor in the act of libation (*tarpaṇa*).

Regarding this, the author of the *Nibandha* has stated that this section concludes the daily ritual (*āhnika*) for independent worship and for the period of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), but not for performance as an auxiliary part of the *Śrīkrama*. That is not correct;
according to the worldly maxim cited previously, the worship of Śyāmā is established as preceding the worship of Lalitā.

The limit for its performance is established by the subsequent statement— [it should be understood that "subsequent statement" means the statement found in Sūtra 37 of this section]— as being up to one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*). And thus, having worshipped Śaṅgītamātṛkā, one should worship Saṃvitsāmrājñī (and so forth), ending with Kōlamukhī.

Thus, by means of the *ktvā* suffix in the subsequent sūtra— [it should be understood that "subsequent sūtra" refers to the word *iṣṭvā* occurring at the end of the sentence within the first sūtra of the *Saṅgītamātṛkā* belonging to the seventh section of the present cycle of Vārāhī]. By means of the *ktvā* suffix.

The fact that the worship of Vārāhī precedes [the main rite] is clear. This being so, all that constitutes the worship of Śyāmā and the recitation of mantras (japa) pertaining to the time prior to the worship of Kolamukhī is an ancillary part of the commencement of the Śrī Lalitā-krama; it is not something other than the Lalitā-krama itself.
Even the scent of the Śyāmā-krama, when being practiced, is perceived in the Sūtra.
This being the case, on what authority did [the author] write that the daily ritual (āhnika) is not to be performed elsewhere at the time of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) and so forth?
He alone knows his own intention. In reality, however, the Śyāmā-krama is not an ancillary part of the practice of Lalitā.

It is not established in the Sūtra. Since the daily lesson (āhnika) is recited with reference to the sequence that constitutes its constituent parts, the entire daily lesson proceeds without hesitation even regarding that sequence which is itself a constituent part. || 5 ||

Having described the rites beginning with the entry into the sacrificial hall and ending with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he begins to explain the worship (*pūjā*) after the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*):
"Having entered the sacrificial hall and sat upon a seat, [one should say] *nama ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya* (salutation to the lotus-seat of the foundational power). (6)
Now he describes the method of *prāṇāyāma*:

having placed his joined palms to his head and said, "Obeisance to the *śrīpādukās* of the entire assembly of manifest and secret *siddhayoginīs*" (note: the word *cakra* does not appear here), he performs the worship of his own guru’s *pādukā* (and also the worship of Gaṇapati).
Having performed [the rite] || 7 ||

Having performed the worship of one's own guru’s sandals—the sandals of the Śyāmā-guru which will be described [in this section, Sūtra 32, page 203]—one should scatter flowers and consecrated rice (akṣata) upon one's own head. 7.

Having performed the placement [of the mantra] as a pervasive covering over the palms, the wrists, and the body with the weapon-mantra "Aiṃ Hraḥ Astrāya Phaṭ," starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger. || 8 ||

The definition characterized by pervasiveness was stated previously [it should be understood as being in the *Gaṇanāyakapaddhati* within the second section of the first part, on page 75 of the commentary on Sūtra 4]. [This is distinguished] by the differences of the fingers and so forth.
The repetition of the mantra applies to each principal element, according to the maxim "the repetition pertains to each principal object."

Having drawn in the air with the syllable *yaṃ* through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] and dried the body; having drawn in the air with *raṃ* and burned the body; having drawn in the air with *vaṃ* and sprinkled the ashes of the burnt body with nectar; having drawn in the air with *laṃ* and made it firm; and having drawn in the air with *haṃsa* and generated the consciousness of Śiva—

The word *yam* is connected with the word *viśoṣya* (having dried up), because as the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*), it possesses the capacity for drying. Drying (*śoṣaṇa*) means the extraction of the watery element; however, the drawing in of air occurs silently.
The *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels are described in the *Nāradīya*:
"Piṅgalā is the right nostril, and the other is known as Iḍā. Thus it is said.

With the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which is the seed of fire, there is the burning of the body. With the nectar, that is, the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, there is the sprinkling of the burnt ashes for the purpose of generating the body again. With the earth-seed-syllable *laṃ*, solidity is produced within the sprinkled ashes. Then, upon that [body], by means of the mantra *haṃsaḥ*...
The attainment of the consciousness of Śiva.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) up to this point, one should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) as taught in the *Śrīkrama*. || 9 ||
Having uttered the root mantra once, one should draw in the breath; having uttered it three times, one should retain it (kumbhaka); and having uttered it once, one should exhale.
Having thus performed exhalation, inhalation, and retention three, seven, ten, or sixteen times, one becomes a body composed of light.

"Each once" means one time. Similarly, in what follows as well, from the compound *recaka-pūraka-kumbhakam* (exhalation-inhalation-retention), the sense of simultaneity (*sāhitya*) is obtained. Here, although there is an inversion of order—since *pūraka* (inhalation) falls in the middle, while *recaka* (exhalation) is first and *kumbhaka* (retention) is last—nevertheless, the intention here is not regarding the sequence, but rather...

In this literary work, the sequence follows the order of the previous recitation. From the verse beginning with "tridhā" (in three ways), it is shown that as the number increases, the fruit becomes greater. By the phrase "tejomayatanuḥ" (having a body consisting of light), the purifying nature of the practice of *prāṇāyāma* is indicated. || 10 ||
Now he describes the fivefold placement beginning with the six limbs, as well as the entire network of placements:
[one should place] the six limbs, the Mātṛkā together with Bālā, and Ratī, Prīti, and Manobhava at the root, heart, and mouth.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa). || 11 ||
The phrase "having performed the ritual placement" (*vinyasya*) is to be applied and connected everywhere. Thus, the meaning is: "having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs" (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
This is the nature of this mantra; [this is for this purpose, as stated in the preceding sūtras 15–20 of this section and in their commentary].

[Regarding the visible: we shall clarify this above. This is one placement (*nyāsa*). "Having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā* together with the vowels" is the second placement. [The term] *mātṛkā* refers to the external *mātṛkā*.
The locations for the placements are to be understood from other tantras.
The *tritārī-kumārī* and the *kevala-kumārī*, which will be explained further on, are optional alternatives. (This *tritārī-kumārī* mantra is manifest;

it is clearly stated right here in this section, in Sūtra 20 and its commentary. By the word *kumārī*, the three-syllabled *bālā* mantra is to be understood. That too is clear right here below, and also in that [other] place. [End of note. It is an alternative.

Regarding the attainment [of the result], the qualification "together with Kevalabālā" serves as its sublater. Therefore, in the Mātṛkānyāsa mantra, there is always a connection with Bālā; elsewhere, however, the connection with Bālā is optional.
Due to the great renown of the various locations of Vyāsa, they are not recorded here. And the nature of the mantra is: Aiṃ Klīṃ.

*Sauḥ aṃ namaḥ*. The same applies to the subsequent [syllables] as well. The *mūla* (root mantra) is the location of the *mūlādhāra*. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the triad beginning with Rati upon the first three [locations]. This is the third placement (*nyāsa*). || 11 ||
Having divided the root [channel] into seventeen parts: six in the Brahma-aperture, three in the forehead, four between the eyebrows, six in the right and left eyes, eight and seven in the mouth,
one each in the right and left ears and the throat, eight in the right and left shoulders, ten in the heart, and ten [in the navel].
Having thus performed the placement (vinyāsa), one places eight [syllables] on the right and left breasts, nine on the navel, two on the svādhiṣṭhāna, and six on the ādhāra.

Having broken and divided [the mantra], he describes the method of division and the places for deposition (*nyāsa*) to be performed with the divided segments by means of the words beginning with "six" (*ṣaḍ*) and so forth. The words expressing numbers such as "six" refer to the syllables situated in the root [mantra]. Having uttered the first six syllables ending with *namaḥ*, [he proceeds].

One should place [the mantras] in the *brahmarandhra*. The same applies hereafter. Regarding the statement "six and eight on the right and left eyes," one should apply the six syllables to the right eye as they occur in sequence, and the eight to the left eye according to their respective numbers.
This should be understood in the same way for "the right and left shoulders" and so forth. In all instances, there is the conjunction with the *tritārī* and the *kumārī*.
It should be performed. The *svādhiṣṭhāna* is a six-petaled lotus located in the secret region. The *ādhāra* is the *mūlādhāra*.

(For the knowledge of the true nature of this *ādhāra*, please consult the commentary on Sūtra 3 in the *Śrī Gaṇeśakrama* on page 88, as well as the commentary on Sūtra 28 in the *Śrīkrama* on page 111.)
This has been explained previously. This is the fourth nyāsa. || 12 ||
He states the fifth [method]:
furthermore, having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of the seventeen sections, from the Support (ādhāra) up to the Brahma-aperture (brahmabila), in the locations not previously mentioned.

The distinction from the previous [text] consists merely in the reversal of the locations, such as the *mūlādhāra* and so forth; however, there is no reversal of the sequence of sections (*khaṇḍa*), because—as noted by [the commentator] Ba—there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) to indicate a reversal of the order of the seventeen sections.
Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence for a reversal of the seventeen sections themselves.
The author of the commentary has written the reversal of the sections; his authority for this is his own will alone and nothing else.
This is the fifth deposition (nyāsa). 13.
196) Having thus described the network of ritual depositions (nyāsa), he speaks of the worship of the temple: "The worship of the temple is as follows."

Having visualized a pavilion situated on a jewel-island in the midst of the ocean of nectar, adorned with pearl necklaces and provided with four gates— at its four gates starting from the east, one should offer salutations: *sāṃ* to Sarasvatī, *lāṃ* to Lakṣmī, *śaṃ* to Śaṅkhanidhi, *paṃ* to Padmanidhi, and *lāṃ* to Indra, who holds a thunderbolt in his hand.

Salutation to Surādhipati (the Lord of the Gods), who has Airāvata as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Rāṃ Agni (Fire), who holds a spear in his hand, the lord of brilliance, who has a goat as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Ṭāṃ Yama, who holds a staff in his hand, the lord of the departed spirits, who has a buffalo as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Kṣāṃ Nirṛti.
Obeisance to Khaḍgahasta, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who has a human being as his vehicle, together with his retinue;
Vāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand, the lord of the waters, who has a crocodile as his vehicle, together with his retinue;
Yāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, the lord of the vital breaths, who has a ruru deer as his vehicle, together with his retinue.
Salutation to Soma, who holds a conch in his hand, the lord of the lunar mansions, whose vehicle is a horse, together with his retinue;
salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, the lord of knowledge, whose vehicle is a bull, together with his retinue;
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, the lord of Satyaloka.

"Oṃ, salutation to the one whose vehicle is a swan, together with his retinue; śrīṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand, the lord of serpents, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, together with his retinue; Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the site. Thus, one should worship these eleven deities in the eleven directions. || 14 ||
The eleven directions—the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, below, and the totality—should be understood. The remainder is to be inferred by oneself. || 14 ||
Regarding the application of specific seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the mantras of the Śyāmā cycle,
he explains the application of specific seed-syllables in all the mantras of the Śyāmā cycle:
for the mantras of the Śyāmā cycle, there is the application of the *tritārī* and the *kumārī* at the beginning, or else the *kumārī* yoga or the *tritārī*.
The maiden previously mentioned is a young girl; the rest is self-evident.
The meaning is clear. || 15 ||
The injunction regarding specific qualities of the performer states certain qualities that constitute parts of the performer:
"Having smeared his limbs with fragrant substances, having his mouth perfumed with betel, and having become cheerful in mind. (16)
p.
197) The Method for Drawing the Śyāmācakra:
Now, he explains the method for drawing the Śyāmācakra—

Having drawn the king of wheels—consisting of a dot, a triangle, a pentagon, an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-petaled lotus, an eight-petaled lotus, a four-petaled lotus, and a square—upon mandalas of gold, silver, copper, sandalwood, or precious gems. || 17 ||

On the mandalas and on the wooden boards, the five-cornered [shape] has the form of a pentagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Its emanation should be understood as proceeding from the central point (bindu) outward according to the method of emergence. || 17 ||
The Procedure for the General Arghya (Sāmānyārghyavidhi). Now, he describes the procedure for the general arghya:
with pure water over which the root mantra has been recited three times, [one should draw] a square, a circle, a hexagon, a triangle, and a bindu.

Having performed the entry with the *matsyamudrā*, one should establish the support (*ādhāra*) with the mantra: "Oṃ, to the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), to the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), vauṣaṭ. Then, having worshipped the fire-potencies (*agnikalā*)—namely Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā—with the syllable "Um," [one should proceed].

Having established the vessel with the mantra "Vauṣaṭ to the Vidyā-tattva, whose face is a lotus," one should worship the solar digits (sūryakalā) within the vessel— namely Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā— and then [worship] with the mantra: "Maṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva, to the lunar disc."

Having thus filled [the vessel] with pure water, one should worship the lunar digits (candrakalā)— namely Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā— and then perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions.

Having protected it with the Astra-mantra, covered it with the Kavaca-mantra, and displayed the Dhenu-mudrā and Yoni-mudrā, one should consecrate it seven times with the root mantra (mūlamantra). Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial hall and the ritual implements with droplets of that water, [one enters].
[The consecrated water is for the purpose of preparing the mandala, not for filling it.]
Since there is no authoritative source [for a different method], the filling should be understood as being done with pure water consecrated at its root alone;
this is the additional [instruction]—[ba]. According to the method of entry, that [mudrā] is described in the Tantra by means of the *matsya-mudrā*:
"The left hand is turned downward, and the right hand is likewise positioned."
"This is proclaimed by the Tantrikas as the Matsya-mudrā (the Fish Seal). Thus [it is said].
O Goddess, one should place the palm of the right hand upon the back of the left;
the two thumbs should be properly aligned, straight, and facing downward.
This is declared to be the Matsyamudrā for the construction of mandalas and other such rites.
Thus it is also stated in the *Paramānandatantra*. Regarding the definition of their supports (*ādhāra*), in that same work (p.
"The supports for these [elements] are either circular or triangular."
And it may be in the shape of a yoni, or a hexagon, or even an octagon.
It may have no feet, or three, five, six, seven, or eight;
it should have an opening in the middle like the back of a vessel, and it must not touch the ground.
"O Ambikā, it should be performed in such a way that [the mind] remains submerged within itself. Thus [it is said].
One should perform the worship of the fire-energies (*vahnikalā*) upon the support (*ādhāra*) using these names ending in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*.
The fact that they end in *namaḥ* and the fact that they end in the dative case should also be understood to apply to the energies of the sun and the moon as well.

Regarding the phrase "having established the vessel," the ellipsis is "upon the support already established" according to the *Nirukta*. This is the worship of the names of the energies beginning with Fire.

In a clockwise direction starting from the west. The measurement has been stated previously [here, the meaning of the word "previously" may be seen on page 107 in the commentary on the twenty-third sūtra of the Śrīkrama]. The remainder is clear. The method regarding Agni and Īśa has already been shown [by the phrase "already shown," this refers to pages 144–145 in section 4].
This is to be understood from the *Lalitākrama*, the *Mūlasūtra* in eight [chapters], its commentary (*bhāṣya*), and also from the subsequent *Mūlasūtra*.
"With the weapon" means with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). "With the armor" means with the armor-mantra (*kavacamantra*).
However, some maintain that by the word "avakuṇṭhya," both the *avakuṇṭhana* mudrā and the *kavaca* mantra are to be understood.
The nature of the *avakuṇṭhana* mudrā is stated in the Tantra:
"The two hands are in the form of fists, with the two index fingers extended straight."
One should rotate them simultaneously; this is the *avakuṇṭhinī* mudrā.
Thus they proclaimed.

The *dhenu* is the *dhenumudrā*. This is well-known in the world; nevertheless, its authoritative description is written here: "The four fingers beginning with the index finger of both hands are interlaced; [the right hand's] index and ring fingers are placed upon the middle and little fingers of the left."
The left index and ring fingers [are placed] upon the right middle and little fingers;
with the palms facing downward, this is the Dhenu-mudrā.

Thus it is established in the *Paramānandatantra*. As for the *yoni*—[this *yonimudrā* is to be seen at the end of the commentary on the fifteenth *sūtra* of the *Śrīlalitākrama*, folio 5, section khaṇḍa 170; or alternatively, it is to be seen in the context of *ddi.
pa. 15-8/2*]—it was previously stated seven times, that is, sevenfold. With the droplets of that water...
With droplets from the general *arghya* offering. || 18 ||
The procedure for the special *arghya*:
Having prepared a mandala marked with the syllable *ī* consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square [or a six-cornered circle],
having scattered flowers upon it, and having established the support (*ādhāra*) as before, one should worship the fire-faculties (*agnikalā*).
Having established the vessel, [one should recite] in that vessel: *hrīṃ aiṃ mahālakṣmīśvari paramasvāmini ūrdhvaśūnyapravāhini*.

"O you who consume Soma, Sūrya, and Agni; O you who shine in the supreme ether! Come, come! Enter, enter! Accept, accept the vessel! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Having thus scattered the handful of flowers and worshipped the digits of the Sun (Sūryakalā).
Bring forth the nectar of immortality, filling this great vessel produced from the entire cosmic egg and filled with every essence.

Having thus filled the first [square] and placed the second, one should write the *halakṣas* (the consonants and the letter *kṣa*) within the three corners marked by the three lines beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*, and the syllable *haṃsa* in the center; then, having consecrated it ten times with the root mantra and worshipped the digits of the moon (*candrakalā*),
one should assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions, and protect it with the weapon mantra (*astra*).
Having enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should display the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās.

With those waters connected to the common *arghya* water; "marked with the letter *ī*" is an adjective qualifying the triangle. The sense is that one should write the letter *ī* (or *īṃ*) in the middle of the triangle. This is not intended as a creation according to the method of entry (*praveśa*), but rather according to the method of exit (*nirgama*).

Because the recitation begins with the triangle and concludes with the square, it is generally observed that the triangle is within everything and the square is outside of everything. "As before" means as stated previously in this same section,
on page 197, in sūtra 18, beginning with "Oṃ, to the principle of the self (ātmatattva)," and so forth.

The meaning is "like the general *arghya* vessel. Regarding the phrase "having worshipped the fire-calors (*agnikalā*) beginning with Dhūmrārcis and having established the vessel," the term "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is understood here as well due to its appropriateness; therefore, this applies to the establishment of the vessel.

The attainment of the previous mantra [here, the "previous mantra" refers to that which occurs on page 197 of this very section, in the eighteenth root-sūtra above, beginning with *uṃ vidyā-tattvāya*]. The first and second [mantras] are declared here in this sūtra;
therefore, the third, fourth, and fifth are not present here because they have not been mentioned. [Indeed,] it is not the case that [this applies to] the Gaṇapati-krama alone.

If it were the middle [case], there would be a *ca* (and) as in the expression "cetivat," or there would be an indicator (*liṅga*) such as "having accepted the group of five" (*pañcakamurarīkṛtya*) by which that [meaning] could be obtained. Therefore, it is only as stated [above]: those lines which have *a*, *ka*, and *ya* at their beginning are the three lines;
starting from the vowel *a* and ending with the *visarga*, there is one line consisting of vowels, and then [the line] starting from *ka* and ending with *ta*.

From that, the sense is "ending with *thādi-sānta*. Since no specific [order] has been stated, one should write the three letters *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* in the three [positions] by moving clockwise starting from one's own [right] corner; then, having written "haṃsa" in the center, situated toward the north.
This entire process of writing, which serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*), is performed upon the substance contained in the vessel. And thus:

The meaning of this is that one should contemplate the refinement of the substance (*dravyasaṃskāra*) by means of such a written form. Following this, the phrase "repeated ten times" is a qualifier for the root mantra. One should display the "cow and womb" (*dhenu-yoni*); this refers to the *dhenumudrā*. [Regarding the origin of this *dhenumudrā*, see page 198, following the commentary on the eighteenth sūtra of this very work; or alternatively, see Dvi. Pa.]

Having displayed the *yonimudrā* (as seen in the *Śrīlalitākrama*, Section 15, Sūtra-bhāṣya, Chapter 15, verse 8/2, folio 170, page 5), one should prostrate. In some manuscripts, the reading is "this is the purification of the *arghya*. (19)
(p. 200) Having thus described the preparation of the vessels for the worship of the Wheel Goddesses (cakradevīpūjā), he now states the mantra for the visualization of the form of the Śrī Devatā:

Having uttered "Śrīmātā" in the center of the wheel and projected the form with "Obeisance to the Form of Gīśvarī," and having again uttered "Śrīmātā" and invoked [the deity] with "I invoke the nectar-consciousness of Gīśvarī," and having worshipped her with the sixteen services, [one should place them] in the directions of Agni, the Three-eyed One, the Rakṣas, and Vāyu, as well as upon the head of the Goddess.

And surrounding [the central deity] are the worshipful Aṅgadevis; their mantras are those beginning with Sarvajana, consisting of eight, seven, eleven, ten, and again ten and twenty-eight sections, including the Tritārī, Kumārī, Vāk, and others, along with their respective classes and the general Manuyukta mantras. || 2 ||

"In the center of the wheel" is connected with the word "having invoked. From "Śrī... up to "...iti," excluding the word "having said," is the mantra for the visualization of the form (*mūrtikalpanamantra*). From the second "Śrī... up to "I invoke" (*āvāhayāmi*), excluding the word "having said," is the invocation mantra (*āvāhanamantra*). The sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) along with their authoritative sources are in the second section.
[It should be understood that these are shown in the second section (dvitīyakhaṇḍa), on page 82 of the Sūtra-bhāṣya. They have been shown:
Āśuśukṣaṇi (Fire), Agni, Tryakṣa (the Three-eyed One), Īśāna, Rakṣas, Nirṛti, Prabhañjana (Vāyu).
The sense is that they are situated in the cardinal directions according to the stated order, and in the intermediate directions (*vidikṣu*). "In the Goddess's crown" means in the center.

The goddesses of the limbs (*aṅgadevyaḥ*), who are the goddesses of the six limbs, are to be worshipped in the directions beginning with the east. He begins to state their mantras with the words "their mantras" (*tanmantrā*): the mantras of the six goddesses of the limbs are to be understood as the six sections (*ṣaṭ khaṇḍāni*) starting from the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) with the words "sarvajanetyādi. In that regard, how many syllables does each *kūṭa* consist of?

Regarding the inquiry, he says "eight," etc.; the meaning is that the six sections beginning with "sarvajana" have respectively eight and so forth as their number. That is, the first section has eight syllables, the second has seven syllables, the third has eleven syllables, the fourth and fifth have ten syllables each, and the sixth...

The result is that there are twenty-eight syllables. He states that the nature of the mantra consists not only of the aforementioned number of syllables forming the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), but other syllables are also to be joined; namely, at the beginning of these sections, the *tritārī*, the *kumārī*, the speech (*vāk*), and the *jāti* for the heart (*hṛdayāya*).

Beginning with *śirase* and so forth, these are the "homogeneous" (*sajāti*) [mantras] accompanied by them—namely, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and so on—which are joined with them in sequence. Thus, the nature of the mantra is as follows: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ aiṃ sarvajanamanohāri hṛdayāya namaḥ*. The aforementioned seed-syllables are *aiṃ* and so forth.

The seven [mantras] beginning with these are to be applied everywhere at the outset. 7 *sarvamukharañjini* śirase svāhā. 7 *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sarvarājavaśaṅkari* śikhāyai vaṣaṭ. 7 *sarvastrīpuruṣavaśaṅkari* kavacāya huṃ. 7 *sarvaduṣṭamṛgavaśaṅkari* netratrayāya vauṣaṭ. 7.

The nature of the mantra is: *sarvasattvavaśaṅkari sarvalokavaśaṅkari amukaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā | sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ astrāya phaṭ*. Although thirty-three syllables are seen in this mantra, they appear to contradict the number twenty-eight stated in the Sūtra.

Nevertheless, the twenty-seven syllables ending with *svāhā*, when combined with the six preceding seed-syllables (*bījas*), become a single syllable within each of the three clusters (*kūṭas*) that constitute the fifteen syllables of the venerable sixteen-syllable mantra— just as each cluster is treated as a single syllable. And thus:
It is endowed with the number twenty-eight.

The author of the commentary (nibandhakāraḥ) has made the section end with "svāhā"; likewise, in the case of that which consists of twenty-seven syllables, there is an absence of the aforementioned procedure. || 20 ||
Regarding the worship of the enclosures:
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the enclosures. || 21 ||
Although this subsequent sūtra appears to be redundant, it should not be regarded as such;

for this is the statement regarding the origin (*utpatti*) of the *āvaraṇapūjā*, while the subsequent statements constitute its detailed procedure (*itikartavyatā*), just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" and "one takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu."

By this, since it is prescribed by a single injunction and thus constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*), it is established that even if there is an omission of a deity belonging to a single part of the enclosure in the middle, the entire rite must be performed again. || 21 ||
Now, he states a certain general rule (paribhāṣā) useful for all [rites]:

one should perform the worship of all the deities of the wheels by scattering unbroken rice grains and flowers from the right hand, together with the first drops fallen from the *śrīpātra* held between the thumb and ring finger of the left hand.

All the deities of the cakras, beginning with Gaṇapati and ending with Parā, as well as others who are to be worshipped according to the general procedure; the *śrīpātra* is the vessel for the special *arghya*. By the phrase "together with the falling [of the drops]," it is indicated that the falling of the *bindu*, the flower, and the unhusked rice grains occurs simultaneously. || 22 ||
He states the deities of the first enclosure and their locations:
