"In the triangle [are] Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava. (23)

"In the triangle" means in the corners of the triangle. Since no specific order is mentioned here, the sequence follows the clockwise direction starting from one's own front (the southeast). Alternatively, [one may place them] in the southeast corner, then in the western corner, and then in the northeast;
by this, the completion toward the north is achieved. Thus ends the first enclosure.

He shows the location for the worship of the second enclosure and so forth: at the base of the five spokes, in the order beginning from the front, [one should place] *drāṃ* for the arrow of liquefaction,
*drīṃ* for the arrow of drying, *klīṃ* for the arrow of binding, *blūṃ* for the arrow of delusion, and *saḥ*.
"Salutation to Unmādana-bāṇa"—thus, before him [are] Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makarake-tana, and Manobhava, attended by Māyā, Kāmavāgbīja, Blūṃ, and Strī. || 24 ||

The word *namaḥ* is appended to all mantras. *Puraḥ* means in the east. *Mūle* means at the base of the five-spoked [lotus]. *Tadagre* means at the tips of the five spokes; this is the meaning. The deities beginning with Kāma, joined respectively with the five starting with Māyā, are to be worshipped. As for the form of the mantra, however, it is: *hrīṃ kāma-śrīpādukāṃ*.
I worship. The same applies hereafter. As before, it should be understood that [the name] is devoid of the dative case ending and the word *namaḥ*. Thus ends the second enclosure. || 24 ||
202) He states the location and other details for the worship of the third enclosure:
at the base of the eight petals are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Māhendrī.

Cāmuṇḍā and Caṇḍikā, along with the final letter of the alphabet joined with the vowel 'u' and the moon (the syllable *auṃ*), are to be worshipped. In front of them are Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi. || 26 ||
The eight syllables— āṃ, īṃ, ūṃ, ṛṃ,
ḹṃ, aiṃ, auṃ, and aḥ— which are the final ones among the pairs of vowels (aṃ, āṃ, iṃ, īṃ, uṃ, ūṃ, ṛṃ, ṝṃ, ḷṃ, ḹṃ, eṃ, aiṃ, oṃ, auṃ, aṃ,
aḥ) accompanied by the moon (the nasal *anusvāra*), should be joined with these in sequence at the beginning [of the names] to worship Brāhmī and the other goddesses.

The nature of the mantra is: *āṃ brāhmīśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. The same applies hereafter. "In front of that" means on the tips of the eight petals; the singular number is used for the sake of the class (*jātāvekavacanam*). The word "are to be worshipped" (*pūjyāḥ*) is to be supplied. Thus ends the third enclosure (*tṛtīyāvaraṇam*). || 25 ||
He states the places for the worship of the fourth enclosure:
on the sixteen petals are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śānti, Śraddhā, Sarasvatī, Kriyāśakti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi,
Mohinī, Pramathinī, Āśvāsinī, Vīcī, Vidyunmālinī, and Surānandā.
The Nāgabuddhikas. || 25 ||

Here, the deities of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) are Vidyunmālinī and Surānandā—one deity for each [petal]. The remaining deities are clear. Since no specific sequence has been stated, they are arranged starting from the petal in front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise.
Thus ends the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*). || 26 ||
He speaks of the fifth enclosure and its locations and so forth:

on the eight petals, Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhana, Unmatta, Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these Bhairavas, joined with Daṇḍin, Svara, and the pairs beginning with Ādi, and ending with Bhairava, are to be meditated upon. || 27 ||
Regarding the term *sadaṇḍī*: according to the *Medinīkośa*, *daṇḍī* refers to the *anusvāra*. Thus, *daṇḍī* is the fifteenth [letter], which is the void (*śūnya*).

The meaning is that one should worship with those mantras ending in Bhairava that are joined at the beginning with the aforementioned pairs of vowels and so forth, together with the *anusvāra*—namely, *aṃ*, *iṃ*, *uṃ*, *oṃ*, and so on. For example: *aṃ*.
I worship the venerable sandal of Asitāṅga-Bhairava. In this very same manner, the seven subsequent mantras are to be inferred.
Thus ends the fifth enclosure. || 27 ||
He states the mantras and so forth for the deities of the sixth enclosure:
"The four-petaled [lotus] has Māyuktataṅgī and Siddhalakṣmī, and Mahāmāyuktataṅgī and Mahāsiddhalakṣmī. (28)

It should be understood that [the suffix] *ī* is applied in both cases; thus, *Mātaṅgī* and *Mahāmātaṅgī* are established. The remainder is clear. The distinction is that the four—Mātaṅgī, Siddhalakṣmī, Mahāmātaṅgī, and Mahāsiddhalakṣmī—are to be worshipped. This concludes the sixth enclosure (ṣaṣṭhāvaraṇa). || 28 ||
203) He describes the worship of the seventh enclosure:
Gaṃ for Gaṇapati, Duṃ for Durgā, Baṃ for Baṭuka, and Kṣaṃ for the Kṣetrapālas; these are to be worshipped in the square.
The sequence, however, begins from the southeast corner and proceeds through the corners ending at the northeast. Thus ends the seventh enclosure. || 29 ||
Regarding the worship of deities situated outside the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*),

the *Śrīkrama* states— in accordance with the tradition of other tantras— that one should worship the deities situated outside the enclosure just as one does the primordial deities (*āmnāyādidevatā*).
Having worshipped once more in that very place, beginning with "Salutation to Sarasvatī" and ending with "Salutation to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site. (30)

"In that very place" means as previously stated [in the fourteenth sūtra of the Anugaṇa, on folio 196]. Where they have been worshipped following the ritual placement (nyāsa), there one worships the Śrīpādukā with those same mantras joined together. For example: "Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; I worship the Śrīpādukā of Sarasvatī."
Likewise, even in the subsequent instances, the application of the phrase "śrīpādukām" at the end of the word "namaḥ" is indicated in the Sūtra by the imitation of the form ending in "namaḥ."

The statement in the *Nibandha* that these [deities] should be worshipped in a square diagram is weak, because it follows the natural implication that they should be worshipped again in the very same place where they were previously worshipped once. Even in common worldly usage, when it is said, "Place Caitra outside the house," "Feed Maitra inside the house," and "Feed Caitra in that very [place]," what is the resulting experience? [It is understood that he was already there.]
Let the noble ones investigate this with their subtle intellect, [considering] "from hearing. || 30 ||
Regarding the worship of the preceptor of Śyāmāvidyā— the worship of the preceptor who initiated the practice of Śrī Śyāmāvidyā (as noted in lexicons: *pravartaka-pūjā-ācārya*)—
he describes their location as follows:

Having worshipped the Gurus of the tradition who possess the form of the swan (*haṃsa*), who are filled with supreme light, and whose activity is eternal, on the first line of the square [mandala]. || 31 ||

The meaning is that one should worship those lineage gurus—who are Haṃsamūrti, Paraprakāśa, Pūrṇa, Nitya, and Karuṇa—on the eastern line of the square, ending toward the north. And the nature of the mantra is: "The venerable sandals of the lineage guru Haṃsamūrti."

I worship. In this way, the phrase "the lineage guru" (sampradāya-guru) should also be applied to the subsequent mantras, according to the maxim that "a word heard at the end of a compound is connected with each [member] everywhere. || 31 ||
Having thus completed the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā), he describes the worship of the Guru’s sandals (gurupādukāpūjā):
"One should worship the general and specific sandals upon one's own head. (32)

The mantra of the general *gurupādukā* is set forth in the *Dīkṣākhaṇḍa* [in the sūtra and its commentary on folio 66]; the mantra of the specific *gurupādukā* is in the final section (*caramakhaṇḍa*).
The mantra "Śyāmāgurupādukā" has been extracted. With these two mantras, one should worship the pair of sandals upon one's own head. || 32 ||
Having thus described the worship of the Goddess, including the worship of the *gurupādukā* and the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*),
he now explains the offering of the oblation (*balipradāna*) following the worship of the principal deity.
Having again worshipped the Goddess and performed the sixteen services with the Bālā mantra, || 33 ||

The word "with" (*mūlena*) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), it is indicated that the worship of the principal goddess occurs prior to that of the deities of the six limbs. The term "with *bālā*" is clear. || 33 ||
Regarding the offering of the *bali*,
he shows the method for the *bali* offering:
having fashioned a triangle, a circle, and a square with pure water, one should place upon it water filled with half-cooked rice (*ardhānna*).
Having scattered flowers and placed a fragrant flower—whether with beginning, end, or middle—along with its base into the vessel, [he should perform the rite]. || 34 ||

Having placed and set down the offering vessel (balipātra) together with its base (ādhāra)— a vessel containing water mixed with half-portioned cooked rice, along with fragrant flowers, and accompanied by these three: the first (ādima), the second (upādima), and the middle (madhyama)— which is filled with pure water contained within a jar.
He shows the mantras for the offering of the *bali* and their ritual procedure:
"Having uttered *Śrīmātā*, [say] *Gīśvari*, accept this *bali*, accept it, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having uttered *Śrīmātā*, [say] *Gīśvari*, protect me who has come for refuge, protect me, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*."

Having offered the *bali* with the three mantras, "Kṣetrapālanātha imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa phaṭ svāhā," accompanied by the gestures (*mudrā*) of striking the left heel on the ground, clapping the hands, and turning the face upward. || 35 ||
The three mantras ending with "śrīmātaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā" are [to be recited]. Regarding the Nārāca mudrā, it is stated in the *Paramānanda Tantra*:
"The clenched fist with the thumb and index finger extended, and the tip of the index finger above the thumb."
And thus, the mudrā held with both hands is known as the Nārāca. So it is said.

The meaning is as follows: first, having formed fists with both hands, one should release them; then, between the thumb and the index finger that have emerged from those fists, one should place the thumb with its tip pointing upward and the index finger straight with its tip pointing forward. This is the meaning of the *nārāca-mudrā*. || 35 ||
205) Having thus explained the sequence for the offering of the *bali*, he now instructs on the worship of the *suvāsinī* and so forth:
Having summoned the dark goddess Śyāmalā and worshipped her with the Bālā mantra, having placed the beginning and end [of the mantra] upon her hand,
having purified the reality (tattva), and having accepted the remainder of that, one should partake of the remnants of the oblation together with those who are worthy. || 36 ||

Since no specific object is mentioned for "having worshipped," it is to be done according to one's means. By the phrase "having purified the *tattva*," the mantras for purifying the *tattvas* are also implied; these mantras are well known to be four [these three *tattva*-mantras are found on page 39 of the commentary on Sūtra 62 in the section on initiation, and the fourth is—].

The mantra for the *sarvatattva* [offering] should be known as "svāhā. Thus, the fourfold set of *tattva*-mantras should be known. Having caused [the disciples] to take the four vessels, and having caused them to take the fourth vessel with its remainder, one should personally accept that remainder. Regarding the disposal of the sacrificial remnants (*haviśśeṣa*), he says "by those who are fit" (*yogyaiḥ*). The meaning of the word "fit" (*yogya*) is as follows:

It has been explained by the word *śiṣṭa* (the "remnant") as stated in the *Śrīkrama* [on folio 176, in the fifth section of the latter part, sūtra 22 and its commentary—the meaning of the word *śiṣṭa* is thus revealed]. And in this way, its purpose and its entire procedure are all to be understood according to the method taught in the *Śrīkrama*. || 36 ||
Regarding the limit for the Śyāmāpūjā:
when there is a desire to know the limit of how long the Saṅgītamātṛkāpūjā should be performed, he states that limit as follows:

Performing daily worship in this manner, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the feeding of Brahmins according to the rule of one-tenth of that number. || 37 ||

In this manner, by the phrase "performing the constant worship" (*nityasaparyām*), he indicates that worship is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the recitation (*japa*). For if worship were the primary element and recitation the subsidiary, then the statement that worship continues for as long as the hundred-thousand-fold recitation lasts would be contradicted; indeed, it is not so.

In both worldly and Vedic usage, it is observed that the primary action follows the subordinate one; for instance, one does not say, "As long as the soldier runs, so long does the king run," but rather there is the common expression, "As long as the king runs, so long does the soldier run. Therefore, the recitation (*japa*) is the primary action, because worship is stated to have that [recitation] as its limit. For this very reason:

Upon the completion of the recitation (*japa*), the worship (*pūjā*) is concluded. By the phrase "having performed a hundred-thousand recitations" (*lakṣajapaṃ japtvā*), the recitation characterized by a count of one hundred thousand is prescribed here. According to the sequence of its tenth part: the fire sacrifice (*homa*) is one-tenth of the recitation; the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is one-tenth of that; and the feeding of Brahmins is one-tenth of that—this is the meaning. || 37 ||
The duties of a Śyāmā-manuṣyāpi:
Now he states these duties of a Manuṣyāpi—
one who is a Manuṣyāpi should not cut down a Kadamba tree, nor should one say "Kālī" with one's speech.
One should not turn away from gatherings involving lutes, flutes, dancing, singing, and poetry; nor should one revile a singer. || 38 ||

(206) "One who mutters this" means one who mutters the Śyāmā; these rules are not co-temporal with the recitation itself, but rather they begin from the start of the recitation and last as long as one lives. Therefore, it is like the rule: "One who has maintained the sacred fires should not run when it rains. || 38 ||
Having thus explained the duties of the Śyāma lay-devotees, he also speaks of the duties of the Lalita lay-devotees, both because of the topical connection and their importance:
"The duties of the Lalita lay-devotees are as follows..."
A devoted worshiper of Lalitā should not eat a piece of sugarcane; he should not think of Vārtālī during the day;

he should not feel disgust toward the substances of accomplishment (siddhadravya); he should not practice cruelty toward women; he should not approach the wife of a *vīra*; he should not kill such a person, nor seize his property, nor take anything by his own will.
One should observe the fivefold code of conduct, not sit with those who have fallen from their lineage, and not engage in excessive idle chatter.
When a woman is speaking, one should not walk by without acknowledging her. One should protect the sacred books of the lineage.
May there be auspiciousness! 39.
Thus ends the sixth section, named the Śyāmā-krama, in the Kalpasūtra.
By the phrase "a piece of sugarcane," it is indicated that there is no fault in its derivatives, such as molasses, sugar, and so forth.

*Vārtālī* means the female hog. One should not feel disgust toward, nor should one even mentally censure, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) which are perfected substances (*siddhadravya*). *Niṣṭhuratā* refers to cruelty, such as cutting off the nose and other such acts.

The compound *vīrastriyam* is a genitive tatpuruṣa (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*), not a karmadhāraya. Were it the latter, there would be the undesirable consequence that the masculine gender could not be construed with the subsequent phrase "one should not kill him" (*na taṃ hanyāt*). Therefore, because of this overriding factor (*bādhaka*), the karmadhāraya—though simpler—is abandoned. Furthermore, in the term *vīrastrī*, the referent of the word *vīra* is one whose state of duality has been utterly eradicated and destroyed.
As it is said in the Tantra: "He who effects the dissolution of the 'I' (aham) by means of its counterpart,
the 'this' (idam), and whose intellect is immersed in the bliss of his own Self— he should be known as a Vīra."
That hero; that substance is "hero-substance" (vīradravya). One should accept—that is, take possession of it—by one's own will for the sake of satisfying one's own senses.

Those who have fallen from the *kula* are those who, having first embraced the path of the *kula*, later abandon the path they accepted due to a lack of faith arising from the sins of previous births; these are the ones fallen from the *kula*.
Thus it is said in the Devībhāgavata: "One who, having resorted to the path of the Kula, later abandons that path due to sins committed in previous births,
should neither stay nor converse with such a person."

Then the sacrificial animal is to be known as excellent; having seen it, one should enter the waters. [From the *Śrīsūtra* on non-return: "That which is to be purified must be indicated, as well as the remaining portion; by the grace of the Primordial Goddess, all is complete. Thus ends the sixth section. Śrī.
One should touch it well. Thus.

"One should not chatter with many" means [not to speak] with them alone. By the word "many," it is indicated that one should speak only as much as is necessary for the purpose of protecting one's own path and avoiding the misfortunes arising therefrom. "Without conversing" means without giving a reply. "Family books" refers to the books of the family scriptures.
The explanation of the word "śivam" is as before.
Thus ends the sixth section, named the Śyāmā-krama, in the commentary on the Kalpasūtra.
1. Oṃ aiṃ, svāhā to the prāṇa. 2. Oṃ klīṃ, svāhā to the apāna. 3. Oṃ sauḥ, svāhā to the vyāna. 4. Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ, svāhā to the udāna. 5. Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, svāhā to the samāna.
In this regard, some display a mudrā for each individual oblation during the offering of the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*). It is as follows:
(1) *oṃ prāṇāya svāhā*—with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger;
(2) *oṃ apānāya svāhā*—with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger.
(3) *Oṃ vyānāya svāhā*—with the thumb, ring finger, and little finger; (4) *Oṃ udānāya svāhā*—with the thumb, index finger, and little finger; (5) *Oṃ samānāya svāhā*—with all [the fingers].
Thus, in the volume numbered 73 of the Ānandāśrama Saṃskṛta Granthāvali,
in the *Śrīgāyatrīpuraścaraṇapaddhati* composed by both Śrīmacchaṅkarācārya and [Bhaṭṭa] Ghāre, on page 45 as well as on page 52.

In other texts as well, such as the *Śāradātilaka* and others, there exist mudrās to be offered at the occasion of the *naivedya*; if these are required, they should be adopted from those sources. (This may also be seen in this very work, in the second chapter, section on the disciple, verse 15).
Furthermore, let it be considered that even when those [mudrās] are mentioned in many texts, their description is absent here.
For this very reason— though it appears that for some these [offerings] are not intended to be performed—
these five *prāṇāhuti*s should be offered only once;
for there is no clearer evidence found for the doubling of these five *prāṇāhuti*s.
It should be understood that these have been defined here only once.
The procedure for the satiation (tarpaṇa) of the chosen deity within the food offering (naivedya) is as follows:
As before, taking the special *arghya* water with sugar-candy and other ingredients:

(1) *Oṃ aiṃ*, may the deity Śrī Tripurasundarī (Amukī), who pervades the *ātmatattva*, be satisfied. (2) *Oṃ klīṃ*, may the deity Śrī Tripurasundarī (Amukī), who pervades the *vidyātattva*, be satisfied.
(3) Oṃ sauḥ, may the deity Śrī Tripurasundarī [Amukī], the essence of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), be satisfied.

(4) Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, may the deity Śrī Tripurasundarī [Amukī], the essence of all principles (sarvatattva), be satisfied. Having thus gratified the venerable Goddess and meditated upon her while she is eating, [one should proceed].
Having taken water well-scented with uśīra, sandalwood, and other fragrances, placed in a pure vessel, and set it beside the food offering (naivedya), one should recite:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O Sovereign of the Gods! You who bring supreme satisfaction to all."
Accept this excellent water, which is filled with unbroken bliss. || 1 ||
(Paraśurāma-kaśyapa-paddhati, p.
498) Oṃ Aiṃ, salutations to the venerable [Name] deity; having spoken thus, I offer water for drinking.

Having offered a small portion of the general *argha* water to the deity and visualizing that the Śrī Bhagavatī has consumed that water, one should hold the inner curtain (*antaḥpaṭa*) between oneself and the deity while [the offering] is shared with Śiva and the other deities; thus, the Śrī Jagadambikā Bhagavatī, whose form is bliss, partakes of it.
Her female messengers fan her; thus visualizing her,
one should meditate upon one's chosen deity as she causes all the gods to laugh and partakes of a great sacrificial offering served in golden vessels, and recite the following two verses:

1. Oṃ! She is being fanned on all sides by her friends, who are seated comfortably around her along with Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods, and who are waving a multitude of whisks with their tails rustling.
Devoted to jesting, play, and laughter, the Goddess of the Gods eats the six flavors from a golden vessel, laughing at those who eat in rows.
2. Oṃ! Well-cooked rice of the *śāli* variety, cooled with sugar, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes, and soup;
foods to be licked, drunk, and sucked; white, nectar-like fruits, *ghārikā* and other delicacies;
abundant ghee, excellent food, pleasing to the eyes, seasoned with mustard, cardamom, and black pepper.
Enjoy this retinue of deliciously cooked vegetables, which delights like the consumption of nectar. || 2 ||

13-30 | 8 || Having thus offered prayers, while eating, one should meditate upon the deity and recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times, or ten times in case there is no opportunity. This is the procedure for the recitation (*japa*), which extends up to the subsequent offerings of the fire-oblation (*homa*), the bali-offering, the full food offering (*naivedya*), betel, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and so forth.

"Raṃ—[He is] to be made compliant"—let it be noted that there is authoritative evidence for this in the commentary on the *Śāradātilaka*, chapter 4, page 305, verse 124; thus says the author of the second edition of the Pañjikā-Kaṇṭhasūtra.
Regarding this, the following is seen in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, chapter 13, verse 30: "The foremost [is] visible."

Then, having placed the garland upon one's own head and performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the root mantras of the respective deities, beginning with "Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the heart," [one recites]: "Oṃ,
you who are the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us."
May there be success for me, O Goddess! By your grace, O Maheśvarī!

Having spoken thus, and taking the water from the general *argha* vessel, one should say: "Oṃ, may the venerable goddess [Name] be pleased by this act of reciting the root mantra according to one's capacity," and having offered it to the Goddess, one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. (13-30; 8th section of the Viṣṇusaṃhitā)

30 | 9. This procedure for the offering of food (*naivedya*) up to this point is incomplete here and must be concluded. It should be understood that the subsequent incomplete procedure for the offering of food is found in this very work, in the second supplement (*dvi-pariśiṣṭa*), under section 30-25; it is to be completed from there. 499) 13–30 | In response to the doubt as to which among the offerings of food (naivedya), the bali-oblation, the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā), and the subsidiary fire-sacrifice (aṅgahoma) should be performed first, he provides a partial resolution.
In the *Mahānirvāṇatantra*, chapter 6, from verse 89 to verse 176,

the Blessed Lord Śiva states the following sequence: first the food offering (*naivedya*), then the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), then the fire sacrifice (*homa*), and thereafter the recitation (*japa*).

2. Also, in the *Śāradā-ṭīkā*, in the fourth chapter, on page 297, from verse 109 to verse 125, the sequence for the offering of food (naivedya), the bali, and the recitation (japa) is set forth in exactly this same order.
And in the *Śrīparaśurāmakalpasūtra*, by the venerable Blessed One, in the second section, tenth sūtra, on the root-text page eighty-three,
it is stated that the offering of the *bali* (oblation) occurs immediately after the *homa*, beginning with the words: "If there is completion of the fire-rite," and so forth.
By implication, the sequence is established as follows: first the food offering (naivedya), then the fire sacrifice (homa), and finally the bali offering with the remaining food and so forth.
Regarding the fire sacrifice that is an auxiliary to the worship, it may be performed or omitted at will.
On this very leaf, the author of the commentary (vṛttikāra) on the Pātañjala-kārikā-sūtra says:
"By the word 'yadi' (if), he indicates that the oblation is both performed and unperformed."
In the commentary on Sūtra 17 of the fifth section of the *Śrīlalitā-navāvaraṇapūjā*,
this very same author states in his subsequent *Nibandha* that the fire-oblation (*homa*) is optional; however, that claim is baseless,
as it contradicts the Sūtra "if there is completion of the fire-rite" (*yadyagnikāryasampattiḥ*), which occurs within the section on Gaṇapati and applies elsewhere as well.

It should be understood by the readers that, by means of the passage beginning with "due to the absence of a means of valid cognition establishing it" (*prāpakapramāṇābhāvāt*), the author has also refuted the view that the *homa* is merely optional (*pākṣikatva*). Thus [ends the section].
(30 | 10 vi0 saṃ0) Regarding the point marked as 10 above, what is intended by the word "limb" (*aṅga*) and what is its meaning?
Regarding the word *aṅga*: therein, only that which has been taught in the *tantra* is restated in part.

1. The Definition of an Auxiliary (Aṅga). As it is stated in a Mīmāṃsā treatise: "An auxiliary is that which, while not itself producing the primary fruit, produces the operation that brings about the primary fruit."
2. Regarding the *puraścaraṇa*, these are the ten ancillaries (*aṅga*);
among them, as stated in the *Pañcasaptatīkāyukta-saptaśatī*, on leaf [numbered] 1:
"Namely: 1. the *paṭala*, 2. the *paddhati*, 3. the *varma*, and likewise 4. the *nāmasahasraka*. (43)
And "the five hymns"—thus the five-limbed [practice] is prescribed for the worship of the deity. Thus it is said.
The integration of the five limbs as parts of the deity's body: the armor is the deity’s torso, and the cloth is the deity’s head. || 44 ||
The manual (paddhati) and the two hands of the deity are remembered as the mouth, consisting of a thousand [verses].
The hymns are the feet of the deity; thus the five-limbed [rite] is said to consist of these five. || 45 ||
Thus end the ancillaries concerning the subject matter of the five recensions. Thus.
There are also another five [methods] in that very same context, as follows:

1) recitation (japa), 2) fire-offering (homa), 3) libation (tarpaṇa), 4) sprinkling (mārjana), and 5) feeding of Brahmins (viprabhojana). These are proclaimed as the fivefold worship of the deities. (46)
This, when combined with the five limbs, is called the "ten-limbed" (daśāṅga) by the wise.
Thus, including those consisting of ritual action, there are five; in this way, ten ancillaries (*aṅga*) arise, and these are prescribed for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). So it is said.
And likewise, in the *Śāradā-ṭīkā*, chapter 16, page 660, the commentary also states:
"The worship of the ten limbs with devotion is called *puraścaraṇa*.
This is another authority for the ten-limbed *puraścaraṇa*; furthermore, these [are as follows]:
These are to be understood specifically with reference to the ritual practice of *puraścaraṇa*. Thus it is said.
4. Hereafter are the other five ancillaries, such as recitation (*japa*) and so forth, as stated in that very same *Śāradā*:

The root *bal* is used in the senses of giving (*dāna*) and killing (*vadha*), while *balak* is used in the sense of investigation (*nirūpaṇa*); thus it is stated in the *Kavikalpadruma*. O Blessed One!

With substances such as lac, resin (śilārasa), storax (śrīvāsa),

Always [illuminated] by lamps placed in golden vessels adorned with jewels, lit with cow’s ghee, capable of piercing the deepest darkness, possessing the brilliance of ten million rising suns,

O Mother, [I offer] to you curd, milk, milk-rice, great śāli rice, and santānaka flowers, along with soups, cakes, sugar, ghee, vaṭakas, honey, and plantain fruits.

There were cakes, soups, curd, milk, sugar, and ghee, preceded by most delicious foods and excellent meals.
O Mother of the World! Partake of these foods offered by me, seasoned with fresh ginger, black pepper, cumin, and coriander. (33)
This milk is most excellent; this ghee is abundant; this honey is radiant;

This exceedingly cool water, scented with *uśīra* root,

They were joined with copper-colored plantain fruits, and provided with grapes, akṣoṭa nuts, and other such fruits.

Combined with *kaliṅga* and *kośātaka*,

O Goddess! I offer these fruits to you. || 38 ||
With camphor, combined with cloves, mixed with the powder of *kaṅkola*, with delicious betel nuts along with *gaura* and *khadira*, with very glossy nutmegs,

O Mother! Accept this betel leaf for your lotus-like face. || 41 ||
Then, having scattered over you pearls interspersed with many gems— pearls as lovely as the three worlds— and having honored you with garments,

O Mother! I offer you a rain of gold as your sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 42 ||
O Mother, this golden pitcher— adorned with a golden handle, radiant as the orb of the full moon, beautified by various jewels, the delight of the three worlds,

O Mother of the World! With variegated chowries that possess jeweled handles of shining gold, white as the rays of the autumnal moon—

O Mother of the World! This jeweled crown, resembling the orb of the sun, which has been offered by me with devotion,

Indra and the other gods constantly perform the lustration ceremony with the lamps of their bowed crowns upon the footstool of your feet;

O Mother of the World! I perform the lustration ceremony with a thousand lamps. || 46 ||
With a gait pleasing to the heart, exceedingly tall, equipped with a jeweled saddle-cloth,

O Blessed One! This horse Vāyuvega, accompanied by a hundred steeds, has been selected by me for your transport. (47)
With its jar-like body covered by bees, with vermilion powder applied to it, with golden bells attached, its neck adorned with tinkling bells,

O Mother! May this intoxicated elephant be for your delight. || 48 ||
O Blessed One! I indeed offer this chariot, which shines with exceedingly swift horses, is equipped with four wheels made of jewels, and possesses a canopy of gold. 49.
This newly formed fourfold army shines with horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry, and in every direction it possesses the sound of kettledrums like the roar of clouds.
O Blessed One! With a weight of devotion, I offer this to you. || 50 ||
O Mother, this [world] of yours, with its seven oceans encircling it and endowed with abundant prosperity, has been offered by me.

With many hundred-thousand lotuses, naturally cool, endowed with exquisite fragrance, yellowed by pollen, and made resonant by bees;

With her mass of wavy, dangling locks disheveled by whirling,

O Mother! May it spread joy within your heart. || 53 ||
Her braid, restless with the playful movements of her face,
shone like a swarm of bees stirred by her radiant charms; she was a beautiful grace that brought joy to the hearts of young men.

Then, at the time of the dancing of the actresses with their lovely breasts, it appeared there every day in every house.

Her mass of hair is like a swarm of wandering bees, and from her lotus-face rises a flood of divine beauty accompanied by smiles.

O Mother of the Universe! With the sudden *jhāṅ* sounds of the *ḍamaru*, *ḍiṇḍima*, *jharjharī*, and *jhallarī* drums, and the resonant tones of the wet *ghaṭā* and *ardraghaṭā* vessels;
May their hearts, full of great compassion, bring you happiness. || 57 ||
At your gate, Gandharva maidens sing, playing the seven notes upon their lutes.
O Mother, listen for a moment with an attentive mind; you have been entreated by me. || 58 ||
Having instantly delighted your mind with the exceedingly beautiful dances of the female dancers in this manner, [he departed].
O Blessed One! I myself shall also delight your heart with various dances, instrumental music, and songs. (59)
O Goddess! Even the four-faced Brahmā and the others are not clever enough to describe your virtues;
therefore, among beings who possess but a single mouth, [who could do so]?
Who is capable of offering praise to you, O Lord?
At every step, she bestows upon those who worship her the immediate fruit of horse-sacrifices and other such rites.
I perform this circumambulation around you on all sides, which serves as the cause for the destruction of all evil.
With the palms of his hands glowing red like red lotuses and marked by upward-pointing lines and vajras;
Salutations to the two lotus-feet of Bhavānī, which are worshipped by the entire host of gods.
Having worshipped his pair of lotus-feet with lotuses,
and having placed a garland of golden lotuses around his neck;
O Goddess! May this handful of jewel-like flowers placed upon my head spread joy within the center of your lotus-heart. || 63 ||
Then, in this place, which was beautiful with couches made of jewels, radiant, adorned with a canopy of flowers,
and perfumed by spreading clouds of agaru incense;
O Blessed One! Your dwelling is indeed within the chamber of rest. || 64 ||
Having placed his feet— granting fearlessness and bestowing boons upon the three worlds— upon this jeweled golden pedestal covered with a vast and most soft cloth.
Sit upon this golden couch, O Mother! || 65 ||
O Goddess, upon your two feet marked with lotuses and surpassing rubies in hue, there are lac-dyes of even deeper red.
I compose this redness once again, though it has already been expressed.
Then, in a vessel made of refined gold, it was scented with mātaruśīra and colored with the juice of his own betel.
Let water be used for rinsing the mouth. || 67 ||
Then, O Mother of the World, for a moment may you joyfully rest by your own will upon this vast bed, resplendent with its exceedingly soft cotton down.
Make me sleep happily, remembering me in your heart.

White as a pearl, a *kunda* flower, or the moon; wearing a jeweled crown and adorned with gem-studded earrings; holding a rosary and flowers in her hands, while her other two hands grant the gestures of fearlessness and boons; moon-crested and three-eyed;
arrayed in various ornaments; and seated upon a golden throne that shines with the light from the crowns of the gods.
I meditate upon the Mother of the three worlds, who is full of bliss and perfectly serene, within my heart. 69.
O Goddess! Having accepted this worship performed by me for you with devotion,
please forgive all my transgressions immediately.
May whatever is deficient in this [work] immediately reach fulfillment through Your compassion; may Your joyful and eternal residence be within the lotus of my heart. (70)
The wise person who is unable to perform the actual worship should recite this hymn of praise;
he obtains the fruit of worship and attains his desired objects. (71)
Whoever, endowed with devotion, recites this worship of the Goddess every day,
shall become a poet within a year through the grace of Vāgvādinī.
Thus ends the Hymn of Mental Worship of the Goddess, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya.
May there be auspiciousness!

The Jewel of Praise, as follows:

O practitioner of mantras, having worshipped that Bhuvaneśvarī with these rites for the sake of accomplishment, one should always praise her—who shatters all afflictions—with this hymn for the sake of complete satisfaction. 48.

Be gracious, O Thou whose nature is the phenomenal world! O Pradhāna! O Thou whose essence is Prakṛti! O Thou who art known as the life-breath of all living beings! O Sovereign! With palms joined in reverence, I begin to bow before You, who by Your very nature are beyond the reach of thought.
When it proceeds to its full extent. || 49 ||
Praise is composed of sentences, and a sentence consists of words; a word, however, consists of syllables, and the syllable is You, O Great Goddess!
Surely it is You alone who will satisfy Yourself with these syllables that are identical to You, since the activity of speech is permeated by You.
It may be so. || 50 ||
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva do not fully comprehend Your supreme form, which consists of Māyā;
O Sovereign, these gods praise You as having a gross form, yet to say "O Mother, this is all there is" would be improper even for me.
Salutations to You, O Sovereign of all! You whose nature is the Bindu; salutations to You who are designated as the ultimate reality (Tattva).
Salutations to you, O Pradhāna who has attained greatness! Salutations to you, whose essential nature is the principle of Ahaṅkāra! || 52 ||
Salutations to you who are the form of sound! Salutations to you who are the form of space! Salutations to you who are the form of touch! Salutations to you who are the form of wind!
Salutations to you whose nature is form, fire, taste, water, and sound! Salutations be to you who are the essence of fragrance and the form of earth!
Salutations to you who are the form of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, mouth, speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ!
O you whose nature is mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness! O formless one! Salutations to you, O All-pervading One, O you of universal form! || 54 ||

Having become the sun, O Great Goddess, you sustain all creatures as their inner self; through the form of the moon, you nourish them further; and through the form of fire, you consume the oblations being offered—the threefold radiance proceeds from you alone.

O Goddess! You alone meditate upon Your supreme state—You who are endowed with four faces, who ride upon a radiant swan, who abide in the quality of *rajas*, who bear the name Brahmā, who perform the work of creating the world, and who have become the Mother of the universe. (56)

O Goddess! You alone are that very portion who, bearing a resplendent crown and the shining discus and conch, known in the worlds by the name Nārāyaṇa, assumes the quality of Sattva and effects the maintenance of the universe here.
With matted hair bound by the moon, the serpent, and the Gaṅgā; three-eyed, destroying the world at the end of the aeon;
resting in darkness and bearing the name Rudra—you shine forth, carrying the axe, the skull-topped staff, and the rosary.
With a thoughtful mind, holding a rosary and a jar of nectar, marked with lines, three-eyed, and adorned with the crescent moon upon your matted locks.
O Mistress! Even Sarasvatī, whose body is adorned with beautiful white garments and who is the sovereign of speech, is composed of you alone. 59.

O Goddess! Though You are devoid of creation and its origins, You alone are Durgā—bearing a sword, conch, and discus; formidable with a brandishing blade; borne by a roaring lion; with a blazing, lofty crown; causing the hosts of Daityas to flee; and praised by throngs of Siddhas.
Bhavānī, who shines as the daughter of the Lord of Mountains and occupies half the body of the Enemy of Tripura,
she who is worshipped by great yogis, the Great Goddess, the Excellent Protector, the Mother Ambikā— in truth, O Maheśa, she is none other than you.

O Great Goddess, I know you to be that Śrī, the beloved of the world and the sole sovereign of all realms, who dwells upon the dark-blue chest of the slayer of Kaiṭabha, which is illuminated by the shining Kaustubha gem.

O Great Goddess! Those seven Mothers, who bear the emblems of the goat, the bull, the house, the lotus, the eye, the plowshare, and the lordly elephant—even those of Mahābhairava—shine forth as Your own portions, manifesting in forms identical to Yours, O All-pervading One!
O You whose radiance is like that of a thousand rising suns, eternally filling every space of the entire universe;
O You with the crescent moon bound upon Your shining crown; O You whose hands hold the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the granting of boons—salutations to You!

O Sovereign! You alone are radiance, fame, beauty, day, night, the twilights, ritual action, sleep, darkness, hunger, intellect, wisdom, fortitude, speech, thought, humility, and prosperity; and whatever other distinct manifestations of power there may be.
O Hare! Salutations to You who are non-dual, yet manifested through the divisions of the Bindu, Nāda, Śakti, and Śānta;
O You whose essential nature is eternally the seven netherworlds, the worlds, the mountains, the oceans, the planets, the continents, the bodily constituents, and the musical notes! || 66 ||
Salutations to you, O All-encompassing One, whose very nature is the totality! O Great Goddess, whose power is woven through all things;
you who have taken refuge in both gross and subtle forms! O Goddess remembered as the embodiment of consciousness, yet whose own nature is beyond cognition!
May your entire mental activity be remembrance of you, and likewise may the activity of my speech be praise of you, O Great Goddess!
The activity of the body shall be the act of prostration; O Lord, be gracious and forgive me for this constantly! 68.
He who constantly practices with devotion this method of reciting the *hṛllekhā*, these specific modes of worship, and this hymn of praise,
shall indeed attain supreme prosperity and proceed to that pure state of the highest abode. (69)
Thus, this entire procedure prescribed for the Hṛllekhā has been stated in brief;
the practitioner who, with a disciplined mind, performs it in this way shall become both a yogi and an enjoyer of worldly pleasures. Thus [ends the section].

Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam, Skandha 1, Chapter 50:
Oṃ, the Vedas said:
Oṃ, salutations, O Goddess! O Mahāmāyā! O Creator of the universe!
O Śivā! O Attributeless One! O Sovereign of all beings! O Mother, the fulfiller of Śaṅkara’s desires! || 1 ||
You are the earth of all beings, as well as the vital breath of those possessed of life;
you are intelligence, prosperity, beauty, forgiveness, peace, faith, wisdom, fortitude, and memory.
You are the half-mora in the Udgītha; you are the Gāyatrī and likewise the Vyāhṛti;
you are Jayā, Vijayā, Dhātrī, Lajjā, Kīrti, Spṛhā, and Dayā.
O Mother of all people! We praise you, who are skilled in the creation of the three worlds, endowed with the essence of compassion,
auspicious knowledge, beneficial to all the world, most excellent, and proficient in the realization of the seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja).
The destroyer of the fifty [impurities]. || 4 ||
Brahmā, Hara, Śauri, the Thousand-eyed One (Indra), Vāyu, Agni, and Sūrya are the lords of the worlds;
yet they exist because of you, and thus are not supreme, since you are the mother of all things, both stationary and moving.
O Mother! When you, desiring to create this entire universe, bring forth the gods headed by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra;

and when you cause them to perform the maintenance, dissolution, and creation [of the world] while remaining yourself of one single form—truly, O Goddess, there is no way in which you are not yourself.
A mere trace of saṃsāra. || 6 ||
No one in the entire world is capable of knowing your form, nor is there any person here fit to recount the number of your names.
For how can a man who is unable to grasp even a small amount of water be clever enough to comprehend the vastness of the ocean?
He may be one whose mind is steadfast. || 7 ||
O Blessed One! Not even one among the gods understands your infinite majesty; O Mother, you alone are the sole sovereign of this world.
How is it that you alone create this entire universe as a mere illusion? You alone are the ultimate authority.
O Goddess! Regarding this very matter, a scriptural statement has been established.
(588) You are indeed devoid of effort, yet you are the cause of all the worlds; oh, how wondrous is your conduct, O Blessed One! It pains our minds.
How can you speak of one whose qualities and power are beyond the scope of all the Vedas, since even you yourself do not know his supreme nature?
O Mother! Do you not know of the falling at the feet of the Conqueror of Madhu? O Auspicious One! Or, having known it, do you wish to test the power of the Conqueror of Madhu?
Or perhaps, O Mother, this multitude of my sins is [insignificant] before your powerful lotus-feet, which are so skilled in receiving devotion?
Where is there any evil? || 10 ||

(Śrī Vedas pray to the supreme goddess Śrī Bhagavatī for the sake of the incarnation of Śrī Hayagrīva: Why this extreme indifference toward the host of gods? Is it your intention here that Hari’s head shall be destroyed?
It produces great wonder.
O Mother, you have caused us great suffering; you are skilled at severing our very birth. We do not know how there could have been any delay in the breaking of the crown of our heads.
O Goddess! Having perceived this fault produced by all the gods in their hearts, was some evil deed committed against you by the immortals cast upon Viṣṇu?
Or was it some excessive pride born of battle in Viṣṇu that led him to act thus? O Mother, your playful display could never be thwarted.
We know the state of affairs here. || 12 ||
Or is it, O Blessed One, that having crossed over the terrible [ocean] at a most beautiful sacred site after being victorious in battle against the Daityas, and having obtained boons from you,
they have now caused Viṣṇuśīrṣa to vanish, O Bhavānī? Or is it for the sake of seeing it?
Vinoda [consoled] Vāsudeva, whose head had disappeared. || 13 ||
O Primordial One, why are you angry with the daughter of the Ocean? Why do you look upon her who is bereft of a protector?
You must forgive this offense committed by one born of your own portion; raise him up and make me rejoice.
These gods, preeminent in their duties and renowned for their power, constantly bow down to you;
O Goddess, having raised up the God who is the sovereign lord of all, deliver the deities from the ocean of grief! 15.
"O Mother, we do not know where Hari has gone; indeed, there is no other means for our survival today.
Just as you are skilled in the work of providing the life-giving nectar, so too, O Goddess, are you the giver of life to the world. (Thus ends the fifth section.

In the third division, fourth chapter of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam— Oṃ, the Blessed Lord said:
"Salutations to the Goddess Prakṛti, and constant salutations to the Ordainer."
Salutations again and again to the auspicious one, the giver of desires, and to Vṛddhi and Siddhi. || 1 ||

Salutations to her whose form is truth, consciousness, and bliss; salutations again and again to you, Bhuvaneśī, the creator of the five cosmic functions and the forest-fire that consumes the cycle of worldly existence. || 2 ||
Salutations again and again to her whose form is the support of all, who is immutably established;
salutations again and again to Hṛllekhā, who has become the meaning of the half-measure.
O Mother, today I have realized that all this is situated within you; its origin and dissolution are from you alone.
And now I have truly understood that your power, whose majesty is far-reaching, consists of the totality of all worlds and is capable of creating them.
Having expanded everything without exception—the entire transformation of the existent and non-existent—you manifest it in its entirety to the Puruṣa at the proper time;
indeed, you illuminate us with the sixteen and seven principles like a magical illusion for our delight.
Nothing pertaining to the nature of reality shines forth without you; you abide pervading everything in its entirety.
O Mother! Even a man is said by wise people to be incapable of worldly activity without power (*śakti*).
You perpetually gladden the entire universe with your own sovereign powers and manifest everything through your splendor.
O Goddess! You shall surely devour [the world] by force at the time of the Kalpa's end; O Goddess, who indeed knows the extent of your majestic power? || 7 ||
O Mother! We have been saved by you from Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and indeed the worlds have been shown to us by you in their full extent;
O Bhavānī! that we have beheld your vision has led us to the abode of happiness and to the supreme pinnacle.
Of great power. || 8 ||
O Mother! I am neither Bhava nor Viriñca;
indeed, who else can know your inconceivable conduct?
For what worlds exist here within this collection of artistic compositions, O Bhavānī of great power? 9.
In this world, we have seen only Hari, Śiva, and the lotus-born Brahmā of celebrated power;
O Goddess! do they not exist in other worlds? What can we know, O Goddess, of your vast and supreme majesty?
Mother, prostrating before your lotus feet, I pray that this form of yours may forever dwell within my heart.
This belongs to you; even your name is always within the cavity of your mouth, and the vision of your lotus feet is forever yours alone.

"I am this servant who is always to be cherished by you; indeed, I contemplate you in my mind as my mistress. O Noble Lady! May this continuous relationship between us ever be like that between a mother and her son. (12)
You know the entire, complete manifold of the worlds, having reached the ultimate stage of the perfection of omniscience; O Mother of the World, what need is there for a common person to inform you?
O lady! Act as has been instructed; thus it shall be according to your intention.
"Brahmā creates, Viṣṇu protects, and Umāpati is the agent of destruction—this is the common renown among people.
Is this also true, O Goddess? Indeed, O Unborn One, we are capable of performing even this by Your will alone, for we are endowed with Your power. (14)
O Dhātrī, daughter of the mountain! It is not the world that sustains all; rather, it is your foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) alone that sustains everything.
O Giver of Boons, the sun shines because it is endowed with your radiance; you, the stainless one, shine as this entire universe.
"By your power, I am indeed Brahmā, the supreme Lord; yet we are all subject to birth, for we are not eternal."
Who else are the gods, headed by Indra? O Mother, you alone are the eternal and non-eternal, the ancient primordial nature (prakṛti). 16.
O Bhavānī! If you have compassion for the Ancient Puruṣa, then I know that today I am always in your presence;
otherwise, I would be the omnipresent, beginningless, effortless Lord, the soul of the universe and pure consciousness, forever free from the nature of darkness (tamas). || 17 ||
You alone are indeed the knowledge of wise men; you alone are truly the power of those who possess power, forever.
You are the form of fame, beauty, fortune, and stainless contentment; you are renunciation itself, the bestower of liberation in the world of men. 18.

You are Gāyatrī, the first digit of the Veda; you alone are the divine Svāhā and Svadhā, the subtle half-measure of supreme qualities. You are ordained as the sacred scripture and the Vedic revelation for the constant life-sustenance of the gods and the ancestors. 19
Indeed, for the sake of liberation alone you fashion this entire phenomenal world, since they have indeed attained the state of individual souls;
for they are surely portions of the beginningless and endless, sinless One, just as waves are spread forth from the full ocean.
When the individual soul has fully experienced your very work, it is well known that you withdraw all this;
like a drama composed by an actor, you cease once the internal task has been rendered futile, O You of celebrated power.
O Mother! You alone are my savior from this ocean of existence filled with delusion; I constantly come to you, O giver of relief to great suffering.
Protect me indeed during this false and ultimately fruitless time, fashioned by passion and other afflictions, which brings forth manifold miseries. (22)
Salutations, O Goddess! O Great Knowledge! I bow at your feet.
O Bestower of all goals, O Auspicious One, grant me the constant illumination of knowledge forever. Thus [ends the] Saṃhitā.

Oṃ, Śrī Śiva said:

O Goddess Śivā, if Hari is your source of manifestation, and if the lotus-born Brahmā is likewise your origin, then why am I not also endowed with your excellent qualities? For you, O Śivā, are skilled in the creation of all the worlds! || 1 ||
O Mother! You are the earth, the water, the wind, as well as the ether and the quality of fire;
you are those elements again, as well as the organs of sense and action, and furthermore, you are the intellect, the mind, and the ego.

Those who do not know and speak otherwise—that the entire world was created by Hari, Hara, or Brahmā—only when they have taken refuge in You do they ever fashion the world with its moving and unmoving beings. (3)

If the world were produced by earth, air, ether, fire, water, and so forth, along with their objects and qualities, then how, O Mother, could it clearly manifest today in the absence of Your nectar-like digit? 4.

through the playful curiosity of various costumes and diversions, you cease [this is an archaic usage lacking case endings and employing the middle voice], O Mother, and you take delight as you please. 5.

O Mother! If your mind were not always moist with compassion, how could I—who am composed of the quality of darkness (tamas)—have been created? O Ambikā! If your mind were not partial, how could this world have been fashioned in so many ways—filled with ministers, kings, and servants, and crowded with both the very wealthy and the destitute? (8)
Indeed, your three qualities alone are always capable of manifesting, protecting, and withdrawing [the world];
for Hari, Hara, and Dhruva were created by you in succession as the causes of the worlds.
These were indeed cultivated by me while I was a deer, as well as by Hari and the Lotus-born One when they were situated in celestial chariots.
Tell me, O Bhavānī! By whom have the worlds been made new, as if they were encountered on a journey? || 10 ||
O Mother of the World! You create and protect the universe by Your own power; how much more do You wish to destroy?
You always delight Your own Lord, the Puruṣa; yet we, O Śivā, truly do not know Your course. (This is an archaic usage. 11.
O Mother!

O Goddess! Even for us who have attained the state of young women, service to Your lotus feet always brings about manhood; yet, once separated from Your lotus feet, where could we clearly find happiness? || 12 ||

O Mother! O Auspicious One! having obtained a human body and even attained sovereignty over the three worlds, I have no desire at all to dwell anywhere else in the worlds, but only in Your lotus feet. (13)
O fair-toothed one! Having attained the state of a young woman in your presence, I do not possess even the slightest pleasure.
Wherein does masculinity lead to happiness, if your feet are not within the range of one's vision? 14.

O Mother! May this stainless fame of mine always prevail throughout the three worlds, having attained the state of a young woman and becoming intimately acquainted with your lotus feet, which destroy the cycle of worldly existence. (15)
Who on earth, having abandoned service at your feet, would desire a kingdom free of thorns? For this very moment surely passes as an entire age, if your lotus-feet are not near.

O Mother! Those stainless sages who are devoted to asceticism, having abandoned the worship of your lotus feet, have surely been deceived by fate; for humiliation has been ordained even amidst their prosperity. (17)

O Unborn One, neither by austerity, nor by self-restraint, nor by meditative concentration, nor even by sacrifices performed according to rule, does liberation from the ocean of worldly existence occur as it does from serving the pollen of Your lotus feet. (18)
O Goddess! If you have compassion for me, show mercy; tell me the pure and wonderful mantra.
Reciting it with equanimity, I indeed became happy, and [I attained] the most excellent, perfectly clear Navārṇava. || 19 ||
"In my first birth, I attained it, yet now the nine-syllable mantra does not shine forth for me. O Mother! Tell me the mantra today; O Savior! deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence. (20)
Brahmā said:
Thus addressed then by Śiva of wondrous splendor, O Goddess, Ambikā clearly uttered the nine-syllable mantra. (21)
Having taken it, Mahādeva attained supreme joy;
bowing at the feet of the Goddess, Śiva remained right there.
Reciting the nine-syllable mantra, which likewise bestows both desires and liberation.

For even half a moment, his conduct is pure; and Śivā, Ambikā, and Śakti are the names of the Lord.

"Are you not capable of creating the universe? Behold, everything has already been divided into four parts. (Śrīmad-Ādyā Prakṛti Bhavānī, who even gives birth to Brahmā, accepts him as her very own body.)

Was Hari, the protector, protected by you from Madhu or Kaiṭabha in the midst of the ocean?

Joined with you, I am capable of creating; joined with you, O Mother, Hari is able to protect;

In this most wonderful diversion of yours, which is a source of dispute for those of limited intellect, no one is deluded. (14)
The primordial God is indeed a non-doer, untouched by the qualities (guṇas), effortless, free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and eternally partless;

Of this mantra of the Śrī Lalitātriśatī Stotra, the Venerable Hayagrīva is the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh. The deity is the venerable Great Lady Lalitā. The seed-syllable is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa.

The application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of attaining the grace of Śrī Lalitā during recitation. Now, having performed the ritual assignment of the seers and other elements (ṛṣyādinyāsa):

"I revere the ever-victorious (Aparājitā), who holds an exceedingly sweet bow in her hand, whose arrows are joy and good fortune;
who is ruddy, possessed of supreme compassion, and is like a fresh *kula*-maiden."
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should recite [the mantra].
Oṃ, the illustrious Hayagrīva said:
She whose form is the letter *ka*, who is auspicious, endowed with auspicious qualities, dwelling on the auspicious mountain, lovely, and possessed of all arts. || 1 ||
She whose eyes are like lotuses, the destroyer of impurities, an ocean of the nectar of compassion, she who dwells in the Kadamba forest, and she who is fond of the Kadamba flower. || 2 ||
Her side-glances gave birth to the god of love,
and the fragrance of her camphor betel-roll caused the slopes of the sky to tremble.

She who removes the defects of the Kali age, whose eyes are like those of a doe, who is the embodiment of action, the witness over all actions, the instigator of deeds, and the bestower of the fruits of karma. || 4 ||
She whose form is the letter *E*, who is the single-syllabled [mantra] yet possesses the form of both one and many syllables;
she who is indefinable as "this" or "that," and whose form is the consciousness of singular bliss. || 5 ||

As it is said in the *Yoginītantra*:
"When the manifestation and reflective awareness of the universe [occur] upon the wall of the conscious self..."

This is the power of action (kriyā-śakti) of Tripurasundarī; it is called a *mudrā* because it both approves of and causes the melting (*drāvayati*) of the processes of origination and growth being performed. Approval (*anumodana*) means conformity with an action performed by an agent distinct from oneself. The expansion: this very power of action (kriyā-śakti), through its conjunction with [the powers of] seeing and so forth by way of co-inherence with the seal (mudrā) of its own function, becomes three-segmented and composed of the three times.

Sarvamahāṅkuśā:

Herein lies the distinction: being solely on the left side is the ground for the application of the term *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*.
The state of being the left [channel] qualified by seniority (*jyeṣṭhatva*) is the ground for the application of the term "all-attracting" (*sarvākarṣaṇī*);

The delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for the denotability of the term *sarvonmādinī* is the predominance of the power of Vāmā;
the delimiting factor for the denotability of the term *sarvamahāṅkuśā* is likewise [the predominance of Jyeṣṭhā].
In this manner, the distinction [between them] is to be perceived by one of subtle intellect. Thus [it is said].
